stories.Headline: Shenzhen prepares to host APEC leaders to discuss Asia-Pacific AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen prepares to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19, 2026, to discuss Asia-Pacific artificial intelligence cooperation. EngineAI Robotics Technology Co., Ltd. organized a robot fighting competition to test movement capabilities for future agricultural tasks in Malaysia. A Malaysian researcher suggested that humanoid robots could eventually guard orchards, harvest oil palm fruit, or pollinate durian trees. Yao Qiyuan, a co-founder of the firm, stated that expanding overseas involves developing new applications with local partners. The meeting follows the theme of building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together through deeper technological and industrial collaboration.

The city's core AI industry generated 220 billion yuan, or 33 billion U.S. dollars, in revenue during the year 2025. More than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size operate in Shenzhen, and trade with APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan. In the first half of 2026, 3D-printing equipment exports reached 8.27 billion yuan, which was a 127.5 percent year on year increase. The city released an AI action plan for 2026 to 2028 in September to strengthen cooperation with ASEAN and Belt and Road countries. A planned center in Qianhai, Shenzhen, will promote APEC cooperation on cross-border data flows as a platform for regulatory alignment.

Hu Zhenyu of the China Development Institute said Shenzhen is now exporting entire industrial chains rather than just individual AI products. Yao Qiyuan noted that his team could not have imagined the potential for Malaysian agricultural robots from their China offices. Bai Xue of the Shenzhen 3D Printing Association said integrated supply chains and AI innovation boosted the competitiveness of Chinese printers. Shi Xiaoliang of SmartMore Corporation hopes APEC will facilitate talent exchanges and the sharing of China's practical industrial AI experience. Yang Qian of X Square Robot stated that open-source technologies are lowering barriers to technology access for small and medium enterprises.

Eduardo Pedrosa, APEC Secretariat Executive Director, said Shenzhen is a global innovation center that can benefit the entire region and the world. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises are affected, as they account for over 97 percent of businesses across the APEC region. These smaller businesses provide most private-sector jobs and generate about half of the total output for the private sector. SmartMore Corporation has served more than 730 enterprises worldwide, including partners in Japan, the Republic of Korea, and various Southeast Asian nations. The Huaqiangbei electronics market now attracts technology enthusiasts interested in exploring AI glasses, robots, and various 3D printing machines.

APEC's 21 member economies were home to 3 billion people and held 61.6 percent of global real GDP in 2025. The APEC Artificial Intelligence Initiative for 2026 to 2030 was adopted in 2025 to promote secure and reliable AI ecosystems. On July 23, ministers in Chengdu adopted the 2026 APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Statement to transform manufacturing and agriculture. China announced in July that it would provide 5,000 AI training and seminar opportunities for developing countries over five years. These initiatives aim to foster resilient economic growth by advancing innovation across the various stages of the AI value chain.

The Chengdu Statement encourages member economies to provide affordable digital products and solutions to support micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. Future cooperation will focus on intelligent computing hardware, software ecosystems, AI solutions, and the creation of shared industry standards. The new center in Qianhai will provide services for businesses and conduct policy research to align different regional regulations. The articles leave open how specific agricultural applications in Malaysia will be implemented using the movement capabilities of fighting robots. It remains to be seen how the 5,000 training opportunities will be distributed among the various developing countries over five years.

stories.Headline: Bharat Semi raises $24 million to develop AI enabled image sensors
stories.Summary:
Delhi-based semiconductor startup Bharat Semi raised $24 million, or ₹215 crore, in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as reported on 16 November 2026. The all-equity round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures. Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels and individual investors also participated in the round. The company plans to use the capital to expand its engineering team and prepare its sensors for commercial production. Bharat Semi expects to begin initial commercial production in 2027.

The startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing and AI capabilities on one chip, eliminating separate processing components. Co-founder Vrinda Kapoor told TechCrunch the architecture could cut system costs by at least 70% versus conventional systems. The company says its sensors reduce data movement between components by up to 99% and lower system costs by up to 10X compared with conventional multi-chip modules. Bharat Semi was founded in 2021 by Vrinda Kapoor and Vinayak Dalmia. It currently employs around 75 people across India and the US, including engineering and business development teams in Santa Clara, California.

Bharat Semi has secured design wins with US defence technology company General Atomics and India's Kaynes Semicon, a subsidiary of US-based Kaynes Technology, though its image sensors remain under development. Kapoor said the company's separate semiconductor fabrication project, announced in India in 2024 with a technology partnership with the US Space Force, remains under development. She said the latest funding will not finance the proposed fabrication facility. The company plans to follow a fabless model for its image-sensor business, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. Bharat Semi plans to increase its US workforce to around 20 employees by mid-2027 and has started hiring engineers in Europe.

Bharat Semi's first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, and its second-generation sensors will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities. The company expects these prototypes to reach development milestones by mid-2027 and plans to get the newer sensors to customers by the end of 2027. The startup is initially targeting consumer electronics and surveillance markets, where cost, power consumption and latency are key considerations, and over the longer term plans to extend its technology to robotics, automotive, aerospace and defence applications. Its technology could help air conditioners detect room occupancy and adjust operations automatically, or allow drones to process visual information without additional computing hardware. The company is eyeing a share of the global image sensor market, expected to reach $49.8 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 7.7%.

The global AI sensor market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 48.8% to reach $139.4 billion by 2033, according to Grand View Research. Bharat Semi will take on established players such as Japan's Sony Semiconductor Solutions and US-based OmniVision, alongside emerging startups such as Oculi and France-based Prophesee. The funding comes amid India's efforts to establish a domestic semiconductor industry, following the launch of the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 earlier this year with a budget outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore. The startup plans to deploy the capital towards developing its next generation of products, expanding its engineering teams in India and the US, and accelerating go-to-market efforts with global customers. As AI moves from cloud-based systems to physical devices, it is creating demand for low-power, low-latency sensors that can process information and enable real-time decision-making.

Bharat Semi is yet to commercialise its technology, and the articles do not say when full commercial sales will begin beyond the 2027 production target. The company targets customers in the US and other global markets, but the articles do not name specific customers beyond the design wins with General Atomics and Kaynes Semicon. The articles do not give the size of the design wins or their value. They do not say how the $24 million will be split between product development and team expansion. The articles do not state whether further funding rounds are planned.

stories.Headline: FBI warns hackers use Artex AI tool to breach global networks in under three hours
stories.Summary:
The FBI warned that hackers are using an autonomous AI tool called Artex to launch cyberattacks globally and across the United States. These malicious actors have used the software to breach networks in under three hours, moving from initial targeting to privileged access. The agency issued a flash cybersecurity advisory on November 13, 2026, to alert businesses and various government organizations about this threat. Hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including defense, tech, government, law firms, phone companies, internet companies, and financial services. These campaigns included a widespread hack of customers of the American IT company ConnectWise and several financial institutions across South Korea.

The Artex framework is an open-source penetration testing platform that connects to frontier large language models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and non-U.S. models. It uses AI agents to automate scanning networks, identifying vulnerabilities, and testing security systems to find easy security flaws and stolen passwords. The tool was used to steal personal data from at least 68,000 people in South Korea due to a lack of multi-factor authentication. It also enabled access to Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 customers of the IT management giant known as ConnectWise. The FBI says the tool has been used in several cyberattacks since its first public debut in July or August 2026.

The FBI stated that AI makes sophisticated attacks faster and easier to automate, which makes them more difficult for organizations to detect. The agency noted that Artex intrusions are often noisy, generating reams of traffic and data that may trigger a company's defensive alerts. Federal investigators warned that the tool allows attackers with limited technical expertise to carry out operations that usually require considerable specialist knowledge. Microsoft identified a China-aligned threat actor called Storm-0940 as the group behind the Artex-assisted campaigns targeting hundreds of different organizations. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to requests for comment regarding the claims made by the FBI about the breach.

Barracuda disclosed it was breached by financially motivated criminals who used Artex to find an exposed credential from a third-party service vendor. Arve Kjoelen, the chief information security officer at Barracuda, said defenders relying on spotting malicious activity often arrive after the attack. Barracuda changed all customer credentials because its logs were not detailed enough to rule out access to stores of customer system data. The attacks on South Korean financial institutions were blamed on weak cybersecurity defenses and a lack of necessary protections for their networks. The FBI confirmed that the tool allows hackers to spread across networks to find mailboxes, databases, and other sensitive information.

Artex was originally developed for legitimate cybersecurity testing before being weaponized by state-aligned hacking groups and various cybercriminals to target global organizations. The tool's developer eventually made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks, but the open-source version continues to circulate widely. Researchers recently found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online without passwords, including the specific system used to target South Korea. Separately, a vulnerability in the Optimizely platform allowed malicious scripts to be placed on websites belonging to 178 different organizations worldwide. Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated that recent outages at Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and JPMorgan Chase were not caused by cyberattacks.

The FBI says the previous open-source version of Artex remains widely accessible for use in cyberattacks despite the developer's attempt to close it. The agency continues to monitor how AI-powered hacks escalate by finding simple security bugs and breaking into companies with relative ease. It remains unclear how many customers were affected by the breach at Barracuda, as the company did not provide a figure. The articles leave open whether all 2,250 ConnectWise customers suffered data theft or if the hackers only gained access to their environments. Future challenges include defending against AI-driven automation that can coordinate different stages of an intrusion faster than human defenders can respond.

stories.Headline: Nvidia appoints Colette Kress as interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigns
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia on November 12, 2026, following an affair with a Singaporean businesswoman. This leadership change occurred amid reports that Alice Huang is suspected by United States authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence. The resignation triggered a rough period for artificial intelligence stocks and increased scrutiny of the company's operations in China. Nvidia appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive to lead the company during this transition. The board has now begun the process of selecting a permanent successor to replace the former chief executive officer.

The transition may change financial commitments, including a 105 billion dollar backstop for a data center project intended for OpenAI. Nvidia previously took a 5 billion dollar stake in Intel last year and invested in the AI cloud provider CoreWeave. The company participated in a 2023 Series B round for CoreWeave and helped anchor the company's initial public offering in 2025. Michael Cembalest of JPMorgan estimated that the broader financial commitments of the chipmaker may have reached a total of 530 billion dollars. These arrangements are now under focus alongside the company's relationships with customers and its various AI infrastructure projects.

Jim Cramer of CNBC said that the leadership shake-up will not derail the broader artificial intelligence boom or the data center world. He believes that interim CEO Colette Kress will present a balanced and non-hyperbolic view when Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday night. Cramer expects Kress to take a more conservative approach to financial commitments, which he hopes will rein in some guarantees. He argued that while Jensen Huang was important, the idea that he represented the entire AI world is completely ludicrous. Cramer expressed confidence in the financial discipline of Kress and does not think the situation will cause a tsunami of selling.

KC Rajkumar of Lynx Equity Strategies adopted a more cautious position and warned that uncertainty could lead to revised industry earnings forecasts. He suggested that companies supplying processors, equipment, and infrastructure to the AI market may not have fully assessed the potential consequences. Rajkumar believes that a reduction in financing activity could prompt companies to reassess their revenue and earnings assumptions for the year 2027. Other chipmakers and equipment suppliers could be affected if projects lose funding or if Nvidia reduces its various financial arrangements. The analyst noted that some semiconductor stocks have attractive valuations, but earnings uncertainty makes investors hesitant to increase their holdings.

The resignation followed reports about Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, who is suspected of being an asset for Chinese intelligence. This scandal coincided with scrutiny of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick regarding the enforcement of US restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China. Axios reported on November 11 that Lutnick resisted efforts by other administration officials to strengthen the enforcement of these export controls. Reuters reported on November 12 that senior White House officials were discussing whether the Commerce Secretary should be removed from office. Lawmakers from both parties have called for greater scrutiny of the Commerce Department's practices regarding the diversion of restricted processors.

Nvidia is set to report its earnings on Tuesday night, and a successful Anthropic IPO later this week could restore investor confidence. Future investor conferences may provide more information about AI spending plans, project financing, and the current level of customer demand. The articles leave open whether the US government will introduce more restrictive export policies that extend beyond Nvidia's AI processors. It remains uncertain if a change in Commerce Department leadership will occur or if industry-wide project cancellations will actually happen. Analysts are waiting for more information to determine if existing earnings estimates for the semiconductor sector remain appropriate for 2027.

stories.Headline: Warsh says AI could speed growth but warns of job losses and market drops
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday that artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in an era of faster economic growth, in remarks that also acknowledged risks from the technology. Warsh said the adoption of AI could also lead to widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market if the healthy returns expected from the huge investments in AI infrastructure don’t materialize. Warsh’s remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the Fed’s San Francisco branch. The Fed chairman did not comment on what the Fed’s next steps would be on interest rates, nor did he say anything about recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month. That data led many of Warsh’s colleagues on the Fed’s rate-setting committee to signal their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed’s next meeting in December.

The Fed refers to AI as “super intelligence” following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Warsh said “What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation,” and that it appears to be changing the method and the speed of innovation. Warsh said that if idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average. Warsh said “As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free,” and that the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly. Warsh said that after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment.

Warsh said Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI’s impact may play out. The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy’s efficiency. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. Warsh has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy’s efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation. In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rates under that scenario.

Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. Jefferson said “If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms’ desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates.”

Warsh has long said, including before his nomination as Fed chair, that AI could significantly boost the economy’s efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation. Warsh on Monday did not address AI’s impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Warsh also spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI than he has in previous speeches. Warsh’s remarks underscored his generally optimistic outlook on the new technology, a view at odds with many of his colleagues. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke during a news conference at the Federal Reserve on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Washington.

The articles did not say what Warsh said about the recent government data showing inflation accelerated last month, because he said nothing about it. The articles did not say what the Fed staff’s different scenarios for AI’s impact are. The articles did not say what the five task forces Warsh appointed are. stories.Headline: Saskatchewan introduces bill letting courts order removal of deceptive AI content and award victims compensation
stories.Summary:
Saskatchewan introduced a bill on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, that would allow courts to order the removal of manipulative AI content and let victims seek compensation. The province said deceptive artificial media, often called deepfakes, exploit the public, undermine trust and create financial hardship. Justice Minister Tim McLeod told reporters after tabling the legislation that some individuals will use AI inappropriately. He said that if they attempt to deceive or target vulnerable individuals, the province wants a framework to hold them accountable. McLeod said Saskatchewan is the first Canadian jurisdiction to provide a legislative framework on deceptive AI.

The bill would let those who have fallen prey to deepfakes seek legal action against creators of deceptive content in audio or visual formats. If creators are found guilty, they would provide compensation to the victim at a cost determined by the court. The court could also force creators to destroy the content and remove it from platforms. The bill would require disclosures in certain cases, and if content could reasonably be believed as authentic, creators would need clear markings that it is AI. The bill does not limit AI use for parody or satire as long as it is not manipulative, and it would also apply to AI-generated intimate images.

McLeod said it would be up to policing agencies to enforce the law. He said if the bill passes, people would still be able to express themselves freely using the technology. He said that if it is all meant in good fun and does not rise to defamation or deception, those purposes will continue to be used safely. Asked if the province is working to find out who is responsible for deepfakes using Premier Scott Moe's likeness, McLeod said he cannot speak to any details. In a statement Tuesday, McLeod said that with new developments in the field emerging almost daily, Saskatchewan must be prepared to take advantage of AI's benefits and safeguard against its misuse.

Rod McKendrick of the Saskatchewan Seniors Mechanism told reporters there have been cases of grandparents receiving calls from scammers pretending to be their grandchildren and asking for money. McKendrick said the bill is another tool in that person's tool chest to use when something like that happens. He said this is happening but authorities are unable to do anything because there is no legislation. Premier Scott Moe previously raised concerns about online deepfakes using his likeness to promote cryptocurrency schemes. Alberta has passed legislation that prohibits the creation of fake AI content of politicians and targets the use of AI for spreading intimate images.

The Saskatchewan government said it is cracking down on artificial intelligence used to deceive the public. The province said deceptive artificial media manipulates the public, undermines trust and creates financial hardship. The bill said those who have fallen prey to deepfakes could seek legal action against the creators of the deceptive content. The court would also be able to force creators to destroy the content and remove it from platforms. The report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

The bill's passage would leave enforcement to policing agencies, McLeod said. The articles do not say when the bill might pass or what penalties the court could set beyond compensation determined by the court. The articles do not say whether the province is investigating the deepfakes using Moe's likeness, because McLeod said he cannot speak to any details. The articles do not say how the required AI markings would be applied or monitored. The articles do not say what specific cases of grandparent scam calls have been reported to authorities.

stories.Headline: DistroKid gives UMG and Sony data on AI music in Suno lawsuit
stories.Summary:
DistroKid provided data about AI-generated music on its platform to Universal Music Group and Sony Music after initially refusing, according to a Monday November 16 court filing obtained by Billboard. The data came in response to a third-party subpoena the labels served as part of their copyright infringement lawsuit against AI music service Suno. The subpoena sought numbers on how much of the music passing through the DIY distributor is thought to be made with Suno and other AI generators. DistroKid had refused at first, leading the labels to start a legal action last month to force compliance with the subpoena. The distributor then changed course and produced responsive documents, and Monday's filing withdrew the subpoena petition.

The subpoena sought figures on how much music moving through DistroKid is thought to be made with Suno and other AI generators. UMG and Sony say the data is key to proving Suno-generated music is eating into their market share and royalty distributions. Competition between AI songs and human music is a key part of the fair use inquiry, the test a judge will use to decide whether Suno infringed the majors' copyrights by training on millions of unlicensed tracks. DistroKid is not a party to the Suno suit. The subpoena dispute is now over, but UMG still has an ongoing lawsuit alleging DistroKid is to blame for a surge in AI music on streaming services like Spotify.

That case, filed in September, alleges the distributor engaged in deceptive business practices and violated copyright law by flooding streamers with what it called mass AI-generated, SEO-optimized, and copyright-infringing slop. In a statement when that lawsuit was filed, a DistroKid rep said the company takes copyright protection, fraud prevention and the integrity of the music ecosystem seriously. The rep said DistroKid works closely with digital streaming platforms, rightsholders and other industry partners on these efforts. The spokesperson said DistroKid strongly disagrees with UMG's allegations and is disappointed UMG chose litigation rather than established industry processes. The rep added that DistroKid is confident in its practices and intends to defend the company vigorously.

Reps for DistroKid and Sony declined to comment on the matter on Tuesday November 17. Reps for UMG did not return a request for comment. The articles do not name which other parties, beyond UMG and Sony, are affected by the subpoena data. The articles do not state how many recordings or how much data DistroKid produced under the subpoena. The articles do not give the date the subpoena was served or the date DistroKid first refused.

In a separate dispute, Universal and Sony are fighting Suno's attempt to put their second copyright lawsuit entirely on hold, in papers filed in Boston federal court last Friday November 13. The labels argued a full pause could keep the case frozen into 2028, and that under Suno's plan its 2025 and 2026 models and business conduct, including v6 launched in September, would be examined nowhere until at least 2028. The 17-page filing can be read in full online. Suno asked Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV on October 30 to pause the second case until he rules on summary judgment in the labels' first lawsuit, filed in June 2024. Suno's main defense in that case is fair use, arguing training its AI on copyrighted recordings is lawful without a license.

Suno also said that if Saylor rules in its favor on fair use, or on the labels' separate claim that it stream-ripped recordings from YouTube, the first case could foreclose the labels' theories in the second. The labels agree the fair use ruling will shape the second case and have offered to postpone the work of proving they own the more than 60,000 recordings at issue until Saylor rules. In the first case, fact discovery on the infringement claims has largely closed, while discovery on the stream-ripping claim runs until this Friday November 20. Summary judgment motions are due by June 22, 2027. The second lawsuit, filed on September 18, accuses Suno of copying 60,202 of the labels' recordings without a license to train its AI models.

US copyright law caps statutory damages for willful infringement at USD $150,000 per work, giving those recordings a theoretical maximum of just over USD $9 billion. The labels are also asking the court to order Suno to stop any further use of their recordings. If the labels get their way, Suno would have to hand over internal records on its later models, licensing efforts, fundraising and finances while the first case is still running. The dispute began in June 2024, when Universal, Sony and Warner Music Group sued Suno. Warner settled and struck a licensing deal with Suno in November 2025, and the case now covers 560 of Universal and Sony's recordings.

In May this year, Universal and Sony asked to add 61,026 more recordings to the original case after tracing them inside Suno's training data. The second suit asserts slightly fewer, 60,202. Saylor refused on August 18, saying adding them will have obvious consequences of complexity and delay, and steered the labels toward a separate lawsuit instead. In that ruling, Saylor wrote that evidence-gathering in any new case could proceed on a different schedule, or indeed be stayed pending resolution of the fair use issue. Suno says that means the court has already contemplated a stay. The labels counter that a stay was only one of several options Saylor listed, and point out he also said the new case could also be potentially consolidated, in whole or in part, with the first.

Suno launched its v6 models on September 9, nine days before the second suit was filed, saying they were built in partnership with Warner, BMG and Believe. In the first case, referred to in the filing as Suno I, the labels say Suno's document handover largely stops at February 2025, and no witness has been put forward to explain how v6 was trained. The labels say Suno has taken the position in Suno I that the full picture of its 2025 and 2026 models and licensing conduct are outside that case's scope. The labels argue that either the conduct is part of the fair use record in Suno I, in which case Suno should produce the discovery there, or it is not, in which case the discovery must proceed in the second case. The labels say the stay Suno seeks would ensure discovery on key issues proceeds nowhere and would lengthen the life of both cases on the court's docket.

The labels warn the danger to them is concrete, saying that by the time discovery into v6 could begin under Suno's proposal, the engineers who built the models may have moved on and their recollections will have faded. The labels add that the training pipelines those engineers used may have changed significantly or been superseded. Universal and Sony say delay would not merely postpone building the record, it would degrade it. The labels say this concern is already manifesting, as they recently learned the engineer responsible for Suno's data scraping and training data acquisition has left the company. In its motion, Suno said it was retaining relevant data in accordance with its legal preservation obligations, and that the record in the first case will preserve testimony from past years.

The labels reply that this covers documents, not what the engineers know, and that the first case's record preserves testimony about past models, not the one Suno is selling now. Instead of a full pause, the labels have proposed a partial stay with three parts. The first would put off proving ownership of the 60,000-plus recordings. The second would see evidence-gathering go ahead now on four subjects: Suno's later models including how v6 was trained, its efforts to license training data, its moves into new businesses and markets including funding rounds and investor pitches, and its recent finances. The third would let everything handed over in the first case count in the second, so neither Suno nor the labels have to do the same work twice.

In return, Universal and Sony would hand over evidence on the market for AI training-data licenses, including their own licensing of recordings to AI developers, and on how AI-generated music affects the value of their recordings. If Saylor opts for a broader pause, the labels want him to let the first case's record be used in the second immediately. They also want him to order Suno to preserve the training data, saved model versions, user-interaction and preference data, and engineering documents behind every model it has released or is developing. The labels want any pause to lift automatically once Saylor rules on summary judgment in the first case, rather than after any appeals are exhausted, with a joint status report due within 14 days. The labels say that in the two years since Suno I was filed, Suno has grown from a start-up into a company valued at approximately $5.4 billion with annual revenue in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

The labels say every month of stay is another month in which Suno entrenches a market position built on the recordings at issue in this case. Suno raised more than USD $400 million at a USD $5.4 billion valuation in June. In a footnote, the labels take aim at a Justice Department filing in the OpenAI copyright litigation that Suno cited in its motion. That filing criticized the market dilution theory the labels are pursuing, the argument that a flood of AI-generated music competing with their recordings weighs against fair use. The articles do not state what the labels say in response to that footnote beyond taking aim at it.

stories.Headline: Alecto raises $20m seed led by Insight Partners to expand its AI law firm beyond UK conveyancing
stories.Summary:
Alecto, a London-based AI law firm serving consumers, raised $20m in a Seed round led by Insight Partners, the company announced today. The firm was founded in September 2025 by Will Rice, who previously built fintech mortgage lender Gen H. Alecto said it reached $8m in annualised revenue within its first eight months of trading. The company said it has acted on more than $1.3bn in property transactions. Alecto began with UK conveyancing, the legal work needed to buy and sell property.

Firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group and law firm Mishcon de Reya also took part in the round. Angel investors include Simon Rogerson, founder and chief executive of Octopus Group, and John Reynolds, founder of SwiftKey. Alecto puts the UK conveyancing market at $3.3bn and the wider UK consumer legal services market at $23bn, with a global addressable market of several hundred billion dollars. The company said it aims to become the UK's leading provider of property legal services in 2027. Headquartered in Shoreditch, the business has grown from three people in January 2026 to 85, with what it says is more than 500 years of collective legal experience between them.

Will Rice, founder and chief executive of Alecto, said the legal industry has for too long expected customers to work on its terms, and that AI now presents the opportunity to put the consumer in control. Rice said people do not want to buy a lawyer's time but want results, and that Alecto exists to make the law accessible to everyone. He said the company is not building a law firm but replacing the traditional law firm. Rice said property is where Alecto proves the model, and that it is building the technology and operations to rapidly break into new countries and new areas of law. He said access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.

Alessandro Luciano, principal at Insight Partners, said consumer legal services represent a huge market opportunity as cost and complexity mean the necessary support is beyond the reach of so many people. Luciano said Alecto's approach redefines how those services are delivered, starting with one of the most important transactions in a person's life, buying a home. He said Rice brings deep knowledge of the property market to bear and the team's progress in such a short timeframe clearly demonstrates the pace of execution. Alecto argues that traditional legal services are constrained by the finite number of qualified lawyers and the hours they can work. The company said this leaves consumers facing high and often unpredictable costs, opaque processes, slow responses and unfamiliar industry language.

The raise follows other activity in legal AI this year. In March, legal AI firm Harvey signed Suits actor Gabriel Macht as a brand ambassador as competition in the market intensified. In May 2025, the Solicitors Regulation Authority authorised Garfield.Law, the first purely AI-based firm approved to provide regulated legal services in England and Wales. The regulator said named regulated solicitors remain ultimately accountable for that firm's professional standards. Rice spent six years building Gen H, a lender focused on helping more people get on the property ladder, and Alecto said the experience, industry knowledge and relationships he developed there underpin its initial focus on property.

The new funding will support expansion into additional areas of consumer law and new countries, with the first international launch planned for 2027, the company said. Alecto said it also sees an opportunity to serve people who currently go without legal support because of its cost or complexity. The company said it aims to build relationships with mortgage brokers and estate agents looking for better service for their customers and faster completion times. Alecto said its service is designed to move matters forward proactively and explain legal issues in plain language. The company said it combines AI with human expertise to deliver what it describes as a premium service at a mass-market price.

stories.Headline: Effingham County students pitch school projects for OpenAI funded grants
stories.Summary:
Three Effingham County residents sued OpenAI, local officials and others in November, alleging that plans for Project Camellia were kept secret until key decisions had been made, and the allegations have not been proven in court. OpenAI is the artificial intelligence company behind the ChatGPT platform. Project Camellia is OpenAI’s proposed $20 billion artificial intelligence data center campus at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents who raised concerns about transparency, electricity demand, water use, traffic and noise. County commissioners postponed a decision on the project’s preliminary site plan on Nov. 3 and were expected to revisit it Tuesday.

The District Innovation Challenge provides up to $15,000 for each of the Effingham County School District’s 17 schools, backed by $255,000 from OpenAI. Students and educators will work together on proposals that could address technology, STEM, artificial intelligence literacy, sustainability or other school and community needs. Following Tuesday’s districtwide kickoff, students and staff will develop project ideas, itemized budgets and presentations, and the district’s curriculum and technology departments will host presentations and question-and-answer sessions. In January, each school will review proposals and select a group of projects totaling up to $15,000 to represent it at the district level. Finalist student teams will present their ideas to a district panel in February.

Superintendent Yancy Ford said public education thrives when students are given real ownership over their learning and the resources to bring bold ideas to life. Ford said that through this partnership with OpenAI, students are not just learning about the future but are actively designing it for their classrooms, their schools and the Effingham County community. The panel will include Ford, school board representatives, district curriculum and technology leaders, and representatives from the data center and AI industries. Rather than serving as a high-stakes elimination contest, the panel will offer feedback and formally award funding to participating projects, the district said. OpenAI said it would continue working with county officials to address outstanding questions.

Supporters point to potential tax revenue and opportunities for local businesses from Project Camellia. OpenAI has pledged at least $80 million for community priorities tied to Project Camellia. The company also provided a $4.8 million grant to cover Effingham County students’ school breakfast and lunch costs for the 2026-27 school year. In October, OpenAI announced a $2 million grant for the first phase of Atlas Park, a planned recreation area at a former sand mine.

Students across Effingham County will have a chance to turn their ideas for improving their schools into reality through the new grant program. The Pike County Board of Commissioners will hold a special meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 18, to discuss and potentially approve a non-binding term sheet from SoftBank Energy and OpenAI for the PORTS-Pike data center project in Piketon. The special meeting will occur at 10:30 a.m. at the Pike County Administration Building, located at 230 Waverly Plaza in Waverly.

The county said the purpose is to consider, discuss and possibly act on the proposed non-binding term sheet, with possible actions including a resolution approving the term sheet and authorizing its execution and any related matters. The notice said the elected county board could also enter into a private executive session to discuss matters related to the data center deal. An agenda with more details has not yet been published for the special AI data center meeting. Japan’s SoftBank and OpenAI want to redevelop the U.S. Department of Energy Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant into a new data center.

The 3,700-acre U.S. government plant previously enriched uranium for nuclear weapons and later for nuclear energy plants, and it operated from 1957 to 2001. The plant property is owned by the U.S. Department of Energy, and adjacent privately owned properties have also been acquired as part of the planned AI data center development. At full buildout, there could be as many as 18 data center buildings at the southeastern Ohio site, and the AI development is projected to create 35,000 construction jobs and 2,500 permanent, operational jobs, according to the companies. AI chipmaker NVIDIA will provide the AI infrastructure at the data center, and the development also entails significant electricity infrastructure investments and upgrades.

stories.Headline: UH to predict invasive beetle spread with AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience are developing an artificial intelligence tool to predict where the invasive coconut rhinoceros beetle is most likely to spread. The project covers Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island and is dated November 17, 2026 in the university’s news release. Pascal Aigbedion-Atalor, an assistant professor in CTAHR’s Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences, leads the project. The $300,000 project aims to help field crews decide where to place traps and look for new infestations. The university announced the work through its news service and Big Island Video News and Hawaii News Now reported it the same day.

The team will use machine learning to analyze local conditions that help the beetle survive and map areas where it is most likely to spread. Researchers plan to test the predictions against field observations to improve the tool’s accuracy. The maps could help crews decide where to place pheromone-baited traps and focus their efforts to contain the beetle. Researchers could also adapt the approach to help protect Hawaiʻi crops from other invasive pests. Funding comes from the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research through its Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research program, with matching support from CTAHR.

Aigbedion-Atalor said knowing where the coconut rhinoceros beetle is likely to spread gives farmers and response teams a major advantage. He said the technology aims to help farmers and agriculture officials act early, target high-risk areas and protect valuable crops and landscapes. Kathy Munkvold, scientific program director at the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research, said stopping invasive pests before they spread is one of the best ways to protect American agriculture. She said the research gives farmers a head start against a devastating introduced pest, helping to protect crops, livelihoods and the future of Hawaiʻi’s agriculture. CTAHR Dean Parwinder Grewal said mitigating the CRB crisis cannot be accomplished by a single organization.

Grewal said it takes a combined effort, from state agricultural inspectors and federal biosecurity officials to private funders and everyday community members checking their backyards. UH researchers are working with state agencies, federal partners, private organizations and residents to help limit the beetle’s spread. The maps would support those efforts by showing crews where to focus their fieldwork. Last week, it was reported for the first time that a coconut rhinoceros beetle was discovered in the Puna district on Hawaiʻi island. The Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity said the live, male CRB was found in a trap in the Kurtistown area.

The university’s news release describes the project as a two-minute read and lists it under agriculture, AI, entomology and invasive species tags. The release names the College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience and the Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences as the units involved. Big Island Video News reported the story under a summary saying the tool will predict where the invasive CRB is most likely to spread in Hawaiʻi. Hawaii News Now reported that the project aims to help farmers and response teams identify high-risk areas on Kauai, Maui and Hawaii Island. Hawaii News Now also reported that UH officials said the technology could eventually be adapted to help protect Hawaii crops from other invasive pests.

Researchers plan to test their predictions against field observations, and the maps could help crews decide where to place traps and focus efforts to detect and contain new infestations. The articles do not say when the tool will be finished or when the maps will be available to field crews. The articles do not say how many traps would be placed or where on Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island the mapping would begin. The articles do not say whether the Kurtistown beetle find is connected to the new prediction project. The articles do not give the outcome of any testing of the predictions against field observations.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid investigations into alleged ties to a Chinese spy
stories.Summary:
Founder Jensen Huang was forced to resign as Nvidia CEO during a week of turmoil in November 2026. The board began probing allegations that Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing. U.S. intelligence officials and Congress are also investigating the matter. Nvidia will report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings after the market closes on November 17. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the report after serving as chief financial officer for over a decade.

The report will address second quarter revenue of 96.2 billion dollars, which was up 106 percent from last year. Data center revenue reached 89 billion dollars, while projected third quarter revenue is 108 billion dollars against 57.1 billion last year. Constellation Energy has a 690-megawatt deal with Amazon and an 890-megawatt deal with Alphabet for nuclear capacity. Bloom Energy reported third quarter revenue of 1.24 billion dollars and guided full-year revenue between 4.4 billion and 4.6 billion dollars. Energy Transfer recently announced agreements to transport natural gas to power plants currently under construction in Missouri.

Colette Kress and other executives will likely face questions about the investigation into Jensen Huang. They must address whether sales are accelerating and provide short-term and long-term guidance for the company. Management needs to clarify if demand for the next-generation Vera Rubin platform is progressing as expected. They must also provide a fourth quarter outlook to determine if demand is accelerating or moderating. The team must demonstrate that customers still have the appetite to build AI data centers at current paces.

Investors in AI power stocks are affected because these companies supply electricity and natural gas to data centers. Constellation Energy, Bloom Energy, and Energy Transfer could see very good weeks if Nvidia results are strong. Some AI stocks have pulled back in recent weeks despite the extraordinary growth numbers seen by Nvidia. The Motley Fool Stock Advisor team identified ten best stocks to buy, but Nvidia was not among them. This team noted that investing 1,000 dollars in Netflix in 2004 would now be worth 335,171 dollars.

Nvidia is central to the AI space because it makes the most popular AI accelerators on the market. Analysts believe the industry is ending the research phase, called Act 1, and entering the global rollout. Berkshire Hathaway ended September with 377.4 billion dollars in cash and Treasury bills under CEO Greg Abel. ASML is the only commercial manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines used by Intel, Samsung, and Taiwan Semiconductor. ASML reported third quarter revenue of 11.7 billion euros and net income of approximately 5 billion euros.

Markets will reopen on November 18, which could be a huge day for AI power stocks. ASML management guided for full-year revenue between 44 billion and 45 billion euros with a 56 percent gross margin. Some ASML customers are already expressing interest in equipment deliveries scheduled for the years 2029 and 2030. Anthropic will hold its initial public offering on November 19, providing investors with three key details. The articles leave open whether Berkshire Hathaway will use its cash to buy ASML or other AI stocks.

stories.Headline: Emory Law launches AI and the Law concentration as firms adopt generative AI
stories.Summary:
Emory University School of Law launched a formal AI and the Law concentration, offering fluency in generative artificial intelligence that is rapidly transforming legal work, Rosie Manins reported for The Atlanta Journal-Constitution on Nov. 17, 2026. The concentration began in the fall semester, and the ethical dilemmas posed by the technology are a big part of the specialized study, the article said. Ifeoma Ajunwa, one of three Emory Law professors leading the concentration, was named among the Top 50 Legal Innovators in Academia for 2026. The National Law Review and Wickard recently announced that national honor, which recognizes those shaping the future of legal education, according to the article. Emory Law is one of five law schools in Georgia, and the article said it is emerging as one of the top institutions in the country for making sure the next batches of attorneys know how to handle the technology.

The concentration includes formal courses in AI and the law, and Emory Law began the formal specialization in the fall, the article said. Other law schools offer AI-related courses but not a formal specialization, and Georgia State University College of Law is among the schools that have taught the topic, according to the article. stories.Headline: Telus ends partnership with Westbank to build two AI data centres in Vancouver
stories.Summary:
Telus Corp. ended its partnership with Westbank Corp. to build two artificial intelligence data centres in Vancouver over a recent weekend. The company decided to pull out of these specific projects but will still expand a data centre in Kamloops. This decision was reported on November 16, 2026, following a period of significant corporate and political changes. Telus has not provided a specific reason for exiting the partnership with the real estate firm. The company intends to share more about its artificial intelligence strategy in the coming months.

The plan involved a new 10-storey building at 150 West Georgia St. and redevelopment at 111 East 5th Ave. These two Vancouver sites and the Kamloops location were meant to form a sovereign AI factory cluster. Quebecor made an unsolicited cash and stock offer to buy Telus for 31 billion dollars on Monday morning. This bid represents a 60 per cent premium on recent shares and follows an initial offer from June. The projects aimed to create sustainable sovereign AI infrastructure and net-positive compute infrastructure for Canada.

Rob Goehring, executive-director of the AI Network of B.C., said a confluence of events likely made Telus skittish. He noted that the leadership team at Telus has been seeking cost-cutting measures and other strategic alternatives. Westbank confirmed that Telus is no longer a partner but they are proceeding with the projects as planned. Westbank stated they will announce a new partnership for the Vancouver initiatives in the coming months. Goehring mentioned that the interconnected parts of the AI ecosystem are all coming together now.

Mayor Pete Fry said the new city council are not fans of AI data centres in Vancouver. He agreed that the city might impose stricter requirements, such as fees and independent environmental reports. A motion proposes that developers commission third-party assessments on noise, heat, water use, and various other impacts. These requirements would apply to developers prior to permitting or rezoning for these types of facilities. Fry clarified that an AI data centre is not currently a defined land use under city bylaws.

Telus originally announced the agreement in May and planned to acquire 60,000 graphics processing units from Nvidia Corp. The company aimed to secure 150 megawatts of electricity for its B.C. data centres by the year 2032. The Mount Pleasant site was in rezoning but was paused in July before the October 17 elections. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down following a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy. Huang was previously seen as the person who drove the innovation and deals for the chip giant.

Westbank will now seek a new partner to complete the two data centre projects in the city. The city website announced an additional Q&A period for the Mount Pleasant project in early to mid-December. It remains open whether the new partnership will maintain the original sustainable standards for the infrastructure. The articles leave open how the Quebecor takeover bid will affect the future of Telus corporate strategy. It is unclear who will lead Nvidia Corp. following the high-profile scandal involving its former chief executive.

stories.Headline: Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda found AI Gigafactory Northern to build federated Nordic AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton Technologies, Telia and Verda founded AI Gigafactory Northern (AIGF Northern) on 16 November 2026, according to Data Centre Magazine and IT Pro. The consortium was set up to build federated AI infrastructure across the Nordic and Baltic region. The group intends to submit a bid to build and operate AIGF Northern under a call for tenders for AI Gigafactory consortia. That call was published by the European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). AIGF Northern will operate as a federated facility spread across multiple national sites, combining large-scale AI computing capacity with sovereign cloud services, high-capacity connectivity and decarbonised energy.

Five founding partners make up the consortium: Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda. Sites are planned in Oulu, Finland; Iru, Estonia; and Valmiera, Latvia, with a Swedish location still to be confirmed. The EU's InvestAI initiative aims to mobilise €30bn (US$33.1bn) for AI investment, split between €20bn (US$22bn) in private funding and €10bn (US$11bn) from EU and national public sources. VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and KTH Royal Institute of Technology provide research and skills backing for the consortium. Distributing computing capacity across these four countries will let the consortium draw on multiple sources of decarbonised energy and expand infrastructure wherever capacity becomes available, rather than depending on a single site or supplier.

Mikko Hautala, Chief Geopolitical & Government Relations Officer and Chairman of Nokia Defense, said Europe's AI ambitions depend on infrastructure it can trust, control and scale. He said AIGF Northern brings together the connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities needed to turn that ambition into reality. He said that by linking strengths across borders, the group can build a more resilient foundation for European innovation, competitiveness and technological sovereignty. Markus Päivinen, Managing Director of Nscale Finland, said scaling AI infrastructure in Europe requires the right foundation of partners and experience in deploying large-scale AI computing infrastructure for customers. He said Nscale's role is to ensure the AI solutions it delivers are enterprise-grade, flexible and ready to support organisations across Europe as demand accelerates.

Taavi Madiberk, CEO and co-founder of Skeleton Technologies, said Europe is stepping up its AI investment but building lasting AI capacity requires more than compute alone. He said it also requires the energy and power infrastructure to support that compute efficiently, reliably and at scale, using technologies developed and manufactured in Europe. Anders Olsson, Executive Vice President and Head of Telia Sweden, said customers and the continent have a rapidly increasing need for scalable and trusted AI services. Michael Champion, Chief Information Security Officer at Verda, said AI is becoming critical infrastructure and it is crucial that Europe has a strong foundation to support teams and organisations across research, industry and the public sector. He said the federated model being built with AIGF Northern is resilient, cross-border and anchored in the region.

Nokia supplies the secure, high-performance connectivity and network infrastructure needed to link sites and move data reliably between them. Nscale contributes cloud platform and AI infrastructure expertise to support environments for AI training and inference. Telia, together with its subsidiary Telia Cygate, provides connectivity, data transmission, infrastructure operations and cloud solutions to support the federated, multi-country model. Verda supplies AI-native infrastructure and cloud expertise for scalable training and inference. Skeleton contributes high-power systems designed to improve data centre efficiency and stability at scale, reduce strain on the electricity grid and support lower-carbon operations.

VTT, one of Europe's leading research organisations, brings capabilities in quantum computing, semiconductors, physical AI and photonics. KTH, Sweden's largest technical university, contributes expertise in AI research, education and skills development. The Nordic and Baltic region offers conditions suited to sustainable AI infrastructure, combining reliable decarbonised energy, advanced digital networks and a cool climate that cuts cooling demand. Partners are now engaging European and national stakeholders to refine the model and define next steps for growth, ahead of a planned bid under the EuroHPC JU call for tenders. The articles do not give the date of the bid or the outcome of the call.

stories.Headline: FIOR completes NCSC-assessed cyber resilience evaluation of its AI Gateway version 26.2
stories.Summary:
FIOR, a UK-based AI security company founded in 2025, completed an independent cyber resilience assessment of its AI Gateway, a product that identifies AI agents, controls their permissions and blocks unauthorized actions before they execute. NCC Group evaluated 72 security claims under the UK National Cyber Security Centre's Principles Based Assurance methodology, according to FIOR. The published report identifies no unmet claims and one area of doubt concerning accessibility. The assessment, announced Nov. 16, covers AI Gateway version 26.2. FIOR's CEO and CTO both said it is the first AI identity and enforcement platform to publicly complete an NCSC CRTF assessment.

The report, dated Nov. 9, records no unmet claims and no assumptions, and the single doubt concerns accessibility, with assessors recommending testing against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. The findings apply only to version 26.2, and later releases require reassessment. Version 26.2, released Nov. 12, adds expanded discovery, model and tool catalogs, threat intelligence and identity integrations. Each agent receives a unique X.509 certificate bound to hardware measurements through TPM 2.0 or Secure Enclave, and where enabled customers can use the post-quantum signature algorithm ML-DSA-65. The policy engine supports 45 or more constraints covering scope, rate, time and network, embedded directly in the agent's certificate.

Founder and CEO David Williams said the company had already made its first commercial deployments and sought the assessment to give government and enterprise customers an objective basis for evaluating the product, a process he said took under six months. Williams said many companies have told FIOR they cannot exploit the benefits of AI until they are confident the controls governing those agents are based on an identity that is secure. FIOR argued that inventories, written policies and after-the-fact monitoring cannot stop an unauthorized action in real time. FIOR positions the gateway as an independent enforcement layer between agents and the enterprise systems they access, checking identity and authorization before anything executes. FIOR said all processing happens inside the enterprise boundary, no information leaves the enterprise and no data is sent to an identity provider.

The assessment report, however, documents outbound HTTPS connections to a FIOR-hosted control plane and does not specify what data those connections transmit, leaving the company's claim that no information leaves the enterprise in need of clarification. The NCSC's Cyber Resilience Testing program helps buyers judge how well connected products protect themselves against common cyberattacks, and assessments are run by NCSC-assured Cyber Resilience Test Facilities, not by the NCSC itself, with NCC Group one of them. A CRTF assessment is not a certification, and products that complete one may carry the label "NCSC CRTF ,  Cyber Resilience Assessed." The process tests whether a product can protect itself, not whether every advertised security function works as intended or stops every form of malicious agent behavior. The assessment spanned secure development, the build environment, distribution and vulnerability management, support and maintenance, and usability, data protection and logging.

The assessment comes two weeks after the NCSC warned that UK critical national infrastructure should prepare for a ransomware attack using AI-powered malware by 2028. In its State of the Cyber Nation report, released Nov. 3, the agency said hostile actors' use of AI is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation within two years. NCSC CEO Richard Horne said the rise in incidents is not because AI has invented new attacks, but because weaknesses organizations have tolerated for years can now be found and exploited at scale. In August, the NCSC issued interim guidance on agentic AI after several incidents in which AI systems carried out unsanctioned or unintended actions. Joint guidance the NCSC issued in May with cybersecurity agencies from the U.S., Australia, Canada and New Zealand called for continuous runtime authentication with a central policy decision point for every agent action.

At a Nov. 11 World Bank webinar, ITU-T Study Group 17 Chair Arnaud Taddei said agents already act with no verifiable identity and no proof of authority. In July, SG17 launched the Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI, backed by 54 governments and 48 companies, and the group meets next in Paris November 30 to December 1. The group's work on enforcement points, runtime attestation and propagating revocation mirrors FIOR's gateway, hardware-bound identities and cross-gateway revocation. The overlap stops at delegated authority, because FG-TIDA is building a model to prove that a citizen or business has legally authorized an agent to act for it, something FIOR's identity and policy controls do not establish on their own. The government's Digital Standards Strategy 2026, 2030 aims to strengthen UK influence in global standards bodies while identity, biometric and AI frameworks are still being set.

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure stocks plunge as investors reduce exposure before Nvidia reports results
stories.Summary:
AI infrastructure stocks faced a wave of selling on Monday, extending losses beyond chipmakers to companies supplying computing capacity and networking equipment. CoreWeave, Oracle, and Nebius all plunged as investors reduced their exposure to AI businesses before Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday. CoreWeave and Nebius each lost 7 percent, while Oracle dropped 4 percent during the morning trading session on that Monday. Other affected companies included Iren and Applied Digital, which also traded lower as the broader AI sector experienced significant market weakness. This decline follows a period of turmoil for neoclouds fearing that debt fueled data center expansion could backfire if demand slows.

Nebius reported third quarter revenue of 980.8 million dollars, including 325.1 million dollars in non recurring strategic partnership payments that raised questions. The company disclosed a 40 billion dollar capital spending plan for 2027, which rattled investors sensitive to the pace of infrastructure buildout. Applied Digital maintains a 36.2 billion dollar lease book, with CoreWeave holding 11 billion dollars and a hyperscaler holding 20.2 billion dollars. Iren has a 3.4 billion dollar customer relationship with Nvidia, while CoreWeave bonds currently yield above 17 percent in the market. Marvell proposed an all stock purchase of Lumentum valued at approximately 115 billion dollars, though analysts question if the deal proceeds.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters that greater scrutiny could slow data center construction, but he does not expect significantly altered plans. He stated there will be no impact to planned capacity additions over the next year and the company will avoid unsecured debt. Dan Sheehan of Telos Wealth Advisors said CoreWeave earnings addressed the fear that had driven the previous selloff in AI stocks. Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei noted that CoreWeave delivered a great quarter and addressed funding concerns with strategic moves. Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress is scheduled to hold a meeting with employees on Wednesday following the departure of Jensen Huang.

Bank of America flagged that Nebius guidance implies a sequential revenue decline in the fourth quarter due to third party data center delays. SoftBank took a 3.7 billion dollar writedown on non refundable equipment payments, contributing to a second quarter net loss of 7 billion dollars. Republican Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called for Jensen Huang to step down as CEO amid a company crisis. Applied Digital CEO Wes Cummins stated the company must still finance approximately 800 MW of capacity over the coming 12 months. Investors in Nebius, Iren, Oracle, and Applied Digital previously cheered gains between 6 and 14 percent after CoreWeave reported strong growth.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following allegations of a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who was alleged to be a spy for Beijing. This controversy escalated with allegations that the relationship aided multi billion dollar Nvidia chip shipments to China, causing the AI industry to reel. Democratic midterm sweep candidates campaigned for tighter regulation and moratoriums on new data center construction, specifically in the crucial market of Texas. Most AI infrastructure stocks lost 32 to 48 percent this year, although Nebius surged 60 percent before the recent market decline. U.S. producer prices rose 6.5 percent annually in October, marking the largest yearly increase in four years for the United States.

Nvidia is expected to pull back on AI investments and credit guarantees following the exit of Jensen Huang as the company CEO. Nebius was due to report results before the opening bell on Thursday, while Applied Digital reports fiscal second quarter earnings in January. The market is pricing in risks for Applied Digital, which trades under 5x forward sales compared to an 11x average multiple. Analysts warn that CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the crunch in AI computing capacity eventually eases. The articles leave open whether the Marvell purchase of Lumentum will proceed and how the Nvidia leadership transition will impact investments.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO as the stock falls nearly 30% in a month
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has been in a tailspin over the past week after Jensen Huang resigned as president and CEO, and the uncertainty over who will run the business is weighing on its valuation. In just the past month, Nvidia has declined by nearly 30%, an unnerving situation with no guarantees things will get better in the weeks ahead. David Jagielski, CPA, of The Motley Fool wrote on November 17, 2026, that three tech stocks may be more attractive options for artificial intelligence investors right now. Those three stocks are Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO). Jagielski said he would go with these stocks today rather than Nvidia.

Alphabet has a market cap of $3.4 trillion, which remains lower than Nvidia's $3.7 trillion valuation. Alphabet holds a dominant position in online search through Google and video sharing through YouTube, plus opportunities in robotaxis through Waymo and AI chatbots through Gemini. Alphabet trades at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of a little under 20, in line with the average S&P 500 stock. Amazon has a market cap of $2.8 trillion, far lower than Alphabet's valuation. Amazon reported 12% revenue growth for the September quarter, and its cloud business, Amazon Web Services, grew at a rate of 39%.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said its chip-building business could be bringing in $50 billion in annual sales if it were a stand-alone operation. Jagielski said Amazon could likely scale that significantly higher, and its forward P/E multiple is just 24. Broadcom's most recent quarter ended on Aug. 2, when revenue rose 86% year over year to $29.6 billion. Broadcom's growth rate is expected to rise to 93% for the last quarter of its fiscal year. Broadcom's stock is down 2% this year and has fallen more than 30% from its 52-week high of $495, trading at a forward P/E of 18.

Jagielski said he had not always felt Broadcom was a good buy, as he felt its valuation was too inflated, but with the stock declining in recent months he believes there is much more value now. He called Broadcom a much safer investment with less downside risk, and said its custom chips have been in high demand amid the AI tech build-out. He said Alphabet is an underrated tech stock the market is not valuing fairly, and that it is worthy of a far higher premium. He said Amazon is another AI stock that should be worth more and may have far more room to rise. He said Broadcom's operations are not as diverse as Amazon's or Alphabet's, but given how well the business has been doing, it is hard not to like the stock.

SK Hynix, based in South Korea, is the world's second-largest producer of DRAM and NAND memory chips after Samsung, while Micron, based in the U.S., ranks third in both markets. Both companies generate most of their revenue from DRAM chips rather than NAND chips, and both rely on HBM, a specialized high-density DRAM chip that supports Nvidia's data center GPUs in AI clusters. SK Hynix became the first memory chipmaker to mass-produce HBM3 chips in 2022, started producing HBM3E chips in 2024, and began HBM4 chips in early 2026. Micron completely skipped the HBM3 generation, started mass-producing its first HBM3E chips in 2024, and made the leap to HBM4 chips in early 2026. SK Hynix still leads the global HBM market, while Samsung and Micron rank second and third, respectively.

In 2025, SK Hynix's revenue surged 47%, its gross margin expanded from 48.1% to 60.3%, and its net income soared 117%. For 2026, analysts expect SK Hynix's revenue to jump 275% and its net income to rise more than sixfold. In fiscal 2026, which ended in September, Micron's revenue more than tripled, its gross margin more than doubled to 80.7%, and its net income rose nearly tenfold. Analysts expect SK Hynix's revenue to rise 60% in 2027 and 17% in 2028, and Micron's revenue to soar 107% in fiscal 2027, followed by 16% growth in fiscal 2028 and nearly flat growth in fiscal 2029. SK Hynix trades at just three times this year's earnings, while Micron trades at four times this year's earnings.

As SK Hynix and Micron allocate more manufacturing capacity to HBM chips, they have less capacity to produce conventional DRAM and NAND chips, causing a shortage of other memory chip types. Inflation and elevated interest rates could curb AI spending and make it more difficult for smaller neocloud companies to expand. Construction of new data centers in the U.S. could be more tightly regulated in several Tier-1 data center states, including Texas, Ohio, and Georgia, after the Democrats swept the midterm elections in early November. Leo Sun of The Motley Fool said both stocks could experience significant volatility over the next 12 months. Sun said that if he had to pick one, he would stick with SK Hynix over Micron for three reasons: it is larger, it is growing faster, and it will remain the market leader in HBM chips.
