stories.Headline: Helient earns Microsoft Data and AI partner designation and launches AI advisory service for law firms
stories.Summary:
Helient, a technology solutions provider serving the legal and other security-conscious industries, announced on November 17, 2026, that it earned the Microsoft Solutions Partner designation for Data & AI (Azure). The Haddonfield, New Jersey company also introduced a new AI Advisory service designed to help law firms adopt Microsoft Copilot and related AI capabilities with greater security, confidence, and control. The designation reflects Helient's continued investment in helping organizations modernize data platforms, strengthen analytics, and prepare for AI adoption with Microsoft technologies. It builds on Helient's broader expertise across cloud infrastructure, security, data, and AI. The announcement was issued through PRNewswire from Haddonfield, New Jersey.

The AI Advisory service focuses on four key areas, starting with strategy, which means identifying where Microsoft AI can support meaningful business and workflow needs. Readiness covers reviewing data access, permissions, infrastructure, and the firm's Microsoft environment. Adoption means helping firms incorporate approved AI capabilities into everyday work. Security addresses information protection, policies, permissions, and risks associated with unmanaged AI use. The service is available to law firms considering Microsoft Copilot and related AI capabilities or looking to improve an existing deployment.

Brad Bono, Chairman and CEO, said earning the designation means a great deal because it recognizes the expertise and commitment of Helient's people. He said Helient has always believed deep technical knowledge matters most when applied in practical ways for clients, and that clients' way of working is changing quickly. He said Helient wants to make sure clients' technology evolves with them, giving them the foundation to use AI in ways that make sense for their business. Bono said there is a lot of noise right now and law firms are being asked to make decisions quickly. He said Helient's job is to slow down the right parts of that conversation, covering where AI is genuinely useful, what needs to be addressed before it is introduced, and how firms maintain control of their information.

Separately, Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake about a day apart in October 2026, both built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year, and Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members now report they have embedded AI in their legal departments and actively use it. Brown said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms, and he expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists.

Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, places the source of advantage inside the firm, in change management treated as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability rather than a one-time rollout. She adds that many firm leaders she has worked with know their firms need to change but have no team to lead it. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy and a former chief strategy officer, argues that rolling out a new tool can threaten someone's competence, confidence, autonomy, status or professional identity, and she learned it training legal secretaries to move from WordPerfect to Word. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute and author of Lean Six Sigma for Law Firms, compresses her method to three words in a fixed order: people, process, platform, and she sees many firms running it backward. Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers and former chief innovation officer at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, calls the gap between announcement and action "innovation by press release."

Gary concedes that some convergence is inevitable, because companies hear the same customers and face the same pressures, and simultaneous launches can signal a maturing market. He points to firms that stand apart through their history, noting that Thompson Hine's AI-enabled SmartPaTH Plus rests on more than a decade of investment in its SmartPaTH delivery model. The ACC has roughly 48,000 members, the in-house buyers whose expectations those surveys reflect. The gap between Goodwin's Regina OS launch and Davis Wright Tremaine's firmwide AI expansion was 4 days, and the gap between Harvey's and Legora's launches of products both named Intake was about 24 hours. Gary's third installment, promised on positioning, timing and strategic alignment, is the next marker in this conversation.

Helient is a Microsoft Solutions Partner helping organizations modernize, secure, and manage complex cloud and hybrid environments with practical expertise and a long-term perspective. With deep experience across Modern Desktop, Azure, infrastructure, security, and managed services, Helient helps organizations reduce complexity, improve operational stability, and move work forward with confidence. The articles leave open whether ACC members will begin reporting that law firm AI investments show up as lower or more predictable outside counsel spend. They also leave open which firms that staffed the change work would be named if that happened. The articles do not say what Gary's third installment will conclude.

stories.Headline: Port Washington mayor Ted Neitzke leads tours of a $15M AI data center site as residents raise concerns
stories.Summary:
A $15 million artificial intelligence data center is under construction in Port Washington, Wisconsin, developed by Vantage in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI, and it is drawing both community curiosity and criticism. The 672-acre site, with an additional 1,000 acres reserved for expansion, is larger than the entire Village of Whitefish Bay, and the construction site sees 3,500 workers daily. Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke has been leading van tours of the site to engage locals and address their concerns about the project. The first phase includes four data center buildings, each with a footprint of 800,000 square feet, large enough to hold two Lambeau Fields.

Vantage says the center will be operational by early 2028, providing internet and cloud services while storing, processing, and distributing data. The project is expected to bring significant tax benefits by transforming agriculturally zoned land assessed at a few million dollars into a site valued at $120 million, which is anticipated to support the majority of city services. Construction on the data center began in December 2022 and is scheduled to be completed by 2028. Neitzke said almost everything visible at the site is manufactured, made or fabricated in Wisconsin, so it is not just a Port Washington thing but a statewide one.

Neitzke said he was surprised and caught off guard by the unexpected backlash, saying he did not see that coming. He has emphasized transparency during the tours, addressing concerns about water usage, power supply and electricity rates, and he said the center does not use a lot of water and that power is protected and rates do not go up. He believes data centers are the newest of all the utilities, something everyone needs alongside clean water, clean sidewalks and electricity, and now information. He has also been advising elected officials across the country on how to navigate similar projects, saying local communities are in an amazing position to negotiate.

Clean Wisconsin and other groups have raised concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centers and the power plants required to support them. A Clean Wisconsin representative said Wisconsin is incredibly vulnerable right now to AI data centers, and that a project as large as the one in Port Washington will be vastly bigger in terms of energy needs than anything the state has ever seen. The representative said those are resources everyone relies on and that the conversation needed to happen well before now, when construction is going on and almost done. One contentious meeting resulted in the arrest of three women, and Al Poull, whose family has lived on a nearby farm for 126 years, acknowledged the changes, saying things change and it is just the way it is.

stories.Headline: New York City Council bans surveillance pricing under bill sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council approved legislation banning surveillance pricing across the city’s five boroughs, sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin, as reported on November 16, 2026. The bill prevents companies from using New Yorkers’ personal data and algorithms to sell goods and services at different prices to different consumers. The council described the measure as among the strongest surveillance pricing bans in the country. The op-ed, published November 17, 2026, was written by State Sen. Rachel May and Assembly Member Emerita Torres. May represents the 48th Senate District covering Syracuse and parts of Onondaga and Cayuga Counties, and Torres represents the 85th Assembly District covering southern and southeastern Bronx.

The One Fair Price Act passed both houses of the New York State Legislature with strong support and bans companies from using personal data to determine how much consumers pay. It preserves legitimate discounts including loyalty programs and senior discounts. New York is the second city and fifth jurisdiction in the United States to ban the practice, after Maryland, Connecticut, New Jersey and Seattle. The state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act this past June, and Gov. Kathy Hochul has until the end of the year to act on it. The articles cite data including geolocation, browsing history, ZIP code, gender and when a paycheck hits a bank account.

Menin said the City Council is putting consumers first by ending the deceptive and insidious practice of surveillance pricing. She said charging different people different prices for the same products is unethical and worsens the affordability crisis. She said the council takes consumer protection extremely seriously and will continue fighting to lower prices and stop predatory corporate tactics. May and Torres wrote that Governor Hochul has an opportunity to lead and urged her to sign the One Fair Price Act. They wrote that it is time to stop letting algorithms rig the economy against consumers.

UFCW International VP Ademola Oyefeso cautioned that New Yorkers not buying airline tickets or ordering groceries online, especially those with lower or fixed incomes, remain vulnerable as long as the council allows electronic shelf labels in grocery stores. He said AI-powered systems let retailers change prices throughout the day based on various factors even without a shopper’s personal data. He said consumers need a blanket protection against price manipulation, achievable by removing ESL capabilities from brick-and-mortar stores. The UFCW represents 1.2 million workers across North America, including grocery store associates. The NGA said ESLs are price tags enabling grocers to update prices and discounts quickly and accurately, not to change prices based on who is in the aisle.

The articles state that many consumers believe the economy is rigged, with wages largely stagnant and prices rising. They describe surveillance pricing as exploiting consumers and driving the affordability crisis by basing prices on willingness to pay rather than supply and demand. They give examples of parents charged higher prices for medicine and families shown higher airfares when attending a funeral. They state that when ZipRecruiter incorporated data about location, industry and employer benefits into its products, it dramatically increased prices, leading to an 84% increase in profits. Over 40 legislatures have introduced legislation to ban surveillance pricing, and several pieces of federal legislation have been introduced.

In June 2026 the state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act, and Governor Hochul has until the end of the year to act. The U.S. Senate Judiciary subcommittee Chair, Missouri Republican Josh Hawley, called surveillance pricing one of the biggest scams in American history. The Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act, led by Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., was introduced this past February with a House companion led by Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Rep. Val Hoyle, D-Ore. The UFCW introduced the Affordable Groceries and Good Jobs Campaign this year to ban surveillance pricing and ESLs in grocery stores. The articles leave open whether Governor Hochul will sign the One Fair Price Act.

stories.Summary:
The Karnataka Department of School Education and Literacy launched AI education for Class IX students in 1,800 government high schools for the 2026-27 academic year. The department announced the launch on its official social media platforms on Monday, November 16, 2026. The program was implemented under the National Skills Qualifications Framework and combined structured vocational and emerging technologies training into the secondary school curriculum. The Congress government in Karnataka announced the introduction of Artificial Intelligence, Python Programming, Data Analytics and other trending IT courses in schools across the state. The courses will be initially introduced in Class 9 across 1,800 government high schools from the 2026-27 academic year.

The prescribed Class IX syllabus introduces students to modern artificial intelligence concepts through hands-on modules and practical mathematical applications. The curriculum covers understanding how intelligent systems operate, with foundational exposure to modern generative AI tools, and learning core coding syntax in Python alongside data collection, organisation and pattern analysis. It also covers exploring how machines interpret visual inputs and process human language, and connecting classroom mathematics, specifically Statistics, Probability, Linear Algebra and Calculus, to real world AI model optimization and predictive outcomes. The courses include AI fundamentals, Python Programming, Data Analytics, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing and Generative AI. The program is designed to equip government school students with foundational digital literacy, computational thinking and industry relevant problem solving skills.

The Karnataka Department of School Education and Literacy rolled out the program and announced the launch via its official social media platforms. The department said in a post on X that expanding digital capabilities across state secondary institutions under the NSQF, it had launched AI education for Class 9 students across 1,800 government high schools for the 2026-27 academic year. The department further said that the state will hire guest faculties and subject experts for the purpose. It said that to deliver this specialized curriculum, the department has initiated the recruitment of qualified guest teachers responsible for instructing modules on AI fundamentals, Python Programming, Data Analytics, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing and Generative AI. It added that in addition to conducting hands-on pedagogical sessions, these guest faculty members will oversee student admissions, daily attendance and academic evaluations within the program framework.

The education department has initiated the recruitment of qualified guest teachers and subject experts to make sure there is seamless classroom delivery across all 1,800 selected institutions. Beyond conducting the structured theory and practical sessions, the appointed guest faculty will be responsible for maintaining student enrolment records, tracking daily classroom attendance and conducting periodic academic assessments under the NSQF framework. By introducing these advanced subjects like Python programming, NLP and Generative AI across 1,800 state-run high schools, Karnataka aims to give rural and semi-urban students early exposure to high-demand technology careers. Because the course is integrated under the NSQF vocational framework, students gain recognised skill-based competencies that complement their core secondary studies and prepare them for advanced STEM pathways in higher secondary classes. The program aims to prepare students for high-demand tech careers.

stories.Headline: South Korea bans smart devices at college entrance exams to prevent AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea decided on Tuesday to ban all smart devices inside testing sites for the national college entrance exam. This decision followed a confession from the top scorer of the national tax accountant exam regarding AI cheating. The suspect, identified as Han Won-seok, admitted to using generative artificial intelligence to cheat on several professional exams. He appeared before police as a suspect on Tuesday and apologized to other test-takers for his wrongdoing. The government announced these tighter checks on Tuesday, two days before the nationwide Suneung exam on Thursday.

The rules require all smartphones and smart devices to be powered off and surrendered before the testing begins. Proctors will inspect students' glasses, watches, collars, sleeves, and buttons for concealed micro-devices at 1,312 test centers. Student bags must be stored in hallways where proctors will regularly check for active electronic signals. The government will tighten wireless network monitoring and asked the Science Ministry to disable public Wi-Fi during exams. Education officials in Seoul trained staff to identify smart glasses by looking for thick frames and lens features.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called AI-assisted cheating a social evil and launched an emergency pan-government task force. She vowed to track suspected cases to the end and respond with test invalidation or criminal complaints. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin stated the ministry is considering radio-frequency and metal detectors for future national exams. President Lee Jae Myung ordered additional measures, including a proposed reward of 100 million won for tips. The government plans to use the Suneung reporting center to receive tips and work with the police.

A senior teachers' union official questioned if the measures would work since they rely heavily on teacher supervision. This official argued that the government is simply adding more duties to teachers instead of creating institutional safeguards. Students and parents experienced widespread anxiety ahead of the Thursday exam due to the recent high-tech cheating scandal. The Democratic Party of Korea is drafting a law to extend the Suneung ban from one to ten years. Party leader Kim Min-seok said this legislation could lead to the revocation of university admission or criminal penalties.

Han Won-seok used a hidden micro-camera to photograph questions and transmit them to an external laptop for AI solving. He then received the answers on a smartphone and used this method for two tax accountant exam rounds. He also cheated on the first round of the public accountant exam, achieving a near-perfect score in one subject. This score was highly suspicious because the average score for that specific subject hovered only in the 30s. Han first admitted to the scheme on a lawyer's YouTube channel before confessing to the Seoul police.

Police are now looking into potential accomplices and expanding their probe to other national exams across the country. The Kookje Shinmun newspaper called for a shift from rote memorization toward oral exams and interviews for evaluations. JoongAng Ilbo recommended adopting Chinese measures like security checkpoints, metal detectors, wireless signal jammers, and detection drones. The government continues to review ways to detect miniature cameras that can be concealed in clothing or belongings. The articles leave open whether the proposed ten-year ban will be fast-tracked in time for this week.

stories.Headline: Banned Nvidia AI chips appear at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang
stories.Summary:
Banned Nvidia AI chips were installed at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, according to reports from Bloomberg News on Friday. These restricted servers were placed in a facility connected to Megaspeed, a Singapore Nvidia cloud partner where Alice Huang previously worked. Documents filed with Chinese authorities show that a subsidiary of Shanghai Longteng pledged these servers as loan collateral in January 2025. The hardware included 22 Dell servers with H800 chips and 52 Super Micro systems with H100 and H200 chips. These specific Nvidia chip models require US export licenses for sale in China, but the US barred H800 exports since 2023.

The pledged hardware consisted of 193 servers totaling 485 million yuan, or 73 million dollars, including 119 Gigabyte Technology servers with unidentified chips. Alice Huang founded Shanghai Longteng in 2015 but sold her shares in 2017 to Huang Yu, the majority owner through January 2026. The data center president is Kang Wei, a business associate of Alice Huang and senior executive at the funding firm Shanghai Hexi. Some servers were first sold to Aperia Cloud Services, a Singapore Nvidia Cloud Partner, before they reached the Shanghai company. Dell halted all sales and support to Aperia International in February 2025 due to concerns about the smuggling of chips.

Megaspeed denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China, while Aperia denied wrongdoing and did not answer questions about Alice Huang or hardware. Jensen Huang stated in May 2025 that there was no evidence of chip diversion, but he resigned as chief executive on November 12. Interim CEO Colette Kress now leads the company after the board stated no company secrets or US national security were compromised. Nvidia declined to comment on whether a change in its Singapore revenue reporting related to the addition of Megaspeed to a block list. US authorities suspect Alice Huang of having intelligence ties to Beijing, and Singapore prosecutors charged five people in the Aperia case. Companies linked to Alice Huang invested in the Chinese AI developer DeepSeek, and her network was tied to a Huawei Cloud center. For the quarter ended October 26, 2025, Nvidia stopped breaking out Singapore revenue and reported by the location of customers' headquarters instead. This change occurred around the time Nvidia added Megaspeed to an internal block list in mid 2025, according to The Wall Street Journal. stories.Headline: Bill Gross launches AI platform to help 30 million Americans start one person companies
stories.Summary:
Serial entrepreneur Bill Gross launched an AI powered platform called Idealab.ai on November 17, 2026, to help people start new businesses. The founder of the technology incubator Idealab created this tool to provide free startup ideas and potential investment to users. Gross believes that artificial intelligence can lower the barriers to entrepreneurship and help offset job losses caused by automation. He hopes this new platform will eventually create 100 million jobs and 30 million one person companies in America. This initiative aims to spread wealth more broadly and reduce economic inequality by democratizing the process of starting a company.

The Pasadena, California based Idealab Studio offers a database of 1.2 million AI generated business ideas for free to the public. This platform analyzes thousands of news articles about consumer problems and unmet needs, such as potholes, to generate these concepts. Gross wants to mirror China, which he says has 30 million one person companies, to improve taxation and income equality. Census Bureau data shows more than 500,000 new businesses launched in October, following a peak of 550,000 monthly starts earlier. The platform recently attracted 130,000 visitors, with 28 percent from the U.S., followed by Saudi Arabia, India, and Russia.

Bill Gross, the Co-founder and Chairman of Idealab, spoke about his vision at the Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. He told Fortune that he dreamed of making a million companies to help people who do not know where to start. Gross stated that using AI as a leveling tool could distribute wealth to many more people than the biggest companies. He encourages multiple entrepreneurs to pursue the same concept in different markets, such as Egypt or Venezuela, and eventually collaborate. Gross believes this project is where he can have the most leverage and will likely do this for his life.

The platform attracts a specific demographic, as 80 percent of recent visitors were men and 8 to 15 percent were students. Between 50 and 60 percent of these visitors are currently employed by someone else, showing interest in independent work. Many Americans are affected by wealth inequality, as the top 1 percent of households own over 50 percent of stocks. Federal data shows the top 0.01 percent of households alone own over 16 trillion dollars of corporate assets and mutual funds. These figures highlight the macroeconomic headwinds and the growing national debt that Gross hopes his AI platform can help balance.

Bill Gross founded the original Idealab incubator in 1996, which has since been credited with 45 initial public offerings and acquisitions. He also founded the education software provider Knowledge Adventure and made his personal fortune by building various types of software. The articles note that more than six in 10 Americans express a desire to run their own private companies. Current U.S. business formation remains strong, but Gross sees additional opportunity for growth through the use of artificial intelligence. This background establishes his history as a serial entrepreneur before launching the new AI powered studio for the general public.

Gross intends to focus on this platform as his final company to make the most positive impact on the world. Users can continue to take the free ideas and only contact the company if they want funding or tools. The articles leave open whether the goal of 30 million one person companies in the United States is actually achievable. It remains unclear how many of the 1.2 million generated ideas will successfully turn into profitable, long term business ventures. The text does not specify the exact criteria Idealab uses to provide investment to the entrepreneurs who use the platform.

stories.Headline: OCC issues examiner framework for banks' generative and agentic AI use
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 4, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued its dedicated supervisory framework for examiners evaluating banks' use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence. The OCC issued Bulletin 2026-54, Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework, introducing a dedicated examiner framework for evaluating banks' use of "super intelligence." The framework covers generative and agentic artificial intelligence, collectively called AI for purposes of the article. The framework does not impose new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations. It provides insight into how OCC examiners may evaluate AI-related risks, including cybersecurity, customer data privacy, third-party risk management and operational resilience.

The framework addresses those technologies through 16 components organized around six pillars: purpose, risk, control, oversight, resilience and assurance. The OCC expressly states that the framework is intended for examiners and is not intended as a required self-assessment tool for banks. The framework is directed at OCC examiners supervising national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches and agencies of foreign banks. The federal banking agencies' April 2026 revised model risk management guidance expressly excluded generative and agentic AI from its scope. The framework's considerations may also be useful to other financial institutions, including state-chartered banks and credit unions.

The OCC states that the framework does not establish new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations. The OCC identifies cybersecurity threats specific to AI, including prompt injection, data and model poisoning, model extraction and sensitive information leakage. The OCC recognizes that AI introduces privacy risks beyond conventional data handling concerns. The OCC recognizes that conventional vendor due diligence and information security reviews may not fully address AI-related risks. The framework specifically addresses visibility into vendor-operated AI agents, notification of AI-related incidents, changes to AI functionality and contractual responsibility for model-related errors or customer harm.

The framework identifies AI-specific considerations involving incident detection, containment, suspension of AI functionality, preservation of relevant records, business continuity and customer remediation. AI tools may use sensitive customer information and then retain or reproduce it, infer information that was not expressly provided or use data in ways inconsistent with existing privacy policies. Agentic AI presents additional concerns because these systems may use credentials, access internal applications, modify records or execute transactions. Excessive permissions or insufficient human oversight could allow a compromised or manipulated AI agent to cause significant financial, security or operational harm. An AI agent could improperly disclose customer information, modify account records, generate inaccurate customer communications or execute unauthorized transactions without a traditional system compromise or outage.

The framework addresses increasingly autonomous AI technologies that can access sensitive customer information, interact with banking systems and execute transactions. These capabilities create significant opportunities for banks but also raise security and privacy concerns that traditional risk management programs may not fully address. Existing vendors may introduce new AI functionality, modify underlying models or deploy AI agents that interact with bank systems without corresponding changes to the institution's existing contractual protections. Some AI-related incidents may fall within the scope of existing data security incident response plans, but AI use can result in a wider array of incidents that may not be adequately covered by existing response plans. These events may require investigation, containment and customer remediation even when conventional cybersecurity monitoring does not identify an intrusion.

Banks and other financial institutions should consider reviewing their existing AI uses, governance, security controls and vendor arrangements. Banks should consider developing AI-specific contractual protections and incident response procedures where appropriate. Banks should consider whether existing vendor management practices sufficiently address these issues, and an AI-specific contractual addendum may provide additional protections. Banks should consider developing AI incident reporting and response procedures that supplement existing cybersecurity incident response plans. The central issue for banks is whether existing controls remain effective when AI systems can access customer information, interact with critical systems and act without direct human approval.

stories.Headline: Susanta Ghosh finds AI models need 90% less training data for accurate materials predictions
stories.Summary:
A collaborative team led by Michigan Technological University Associate Professor Susanta Ghosh found that artificial intelligence models need less data than previously thought to produce accurate predictions in the development of novel materials. The study was recently published in npj Computational Materials, and the work was conducted with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles. Developing new materials often starts with understanding their electronic structure, or how electrons are arranged and behave within them. Calculating these electronic structures typically requires expensive simulations in supercomputers, which led researchers to train artificial intelligence models on millions of simulated data points to make faster predictions. According to the recent study led by Ghosh in Michigan Tech's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, that much training data isn't necessary.

The research team found that AI models could discard 90% of their training data with virtually no loss in accuracy. Even after removing 99% of the training data, most predictions stayed highly accurate, while the models trained three or more times faster. The new findings apply to an expansive range of materials, including metals, water and complex alloys. Ghosh says the answer is by using a minimal dataset carefully selected by researchers that is sufficient to capture the diversity of the data. These findings challenge the necessity of extensive datasets for electronic structure predictions, and could make AI-driven materials development faster and less costly.

Ghosh is a faculty member of the Center for Artificial Intelligence in Michigan Tech's Institute of Computing and Cybersystems, and he believes this could have a large impact in the field of materials development and modeling. Ghosh said that much of the electronic structure data repeats the same information, and that a small, well-chosen sample captures nearly everything the AI needs to learn. He said that by identifying representative electronic-structure data and reducing training time by at least threefold, this work can accelerate AI-driven discovery of complex alloys across vast composition spaces. Ghosh's study was conducted in collaboration with a team led by Assistant Professor Amartya Banerjee from UCLA's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. The collaboration also included MTU alumnus Ponkrshnan Thiagarajan '23, who completed his Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering-Engineering Mechanics at Tech and is currently a postdoctoral fellow at the Hopkins Extreme Materials Institute.

Research was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, the National Science Foundation, and the University of California Office of the President. Michigan Technological University is an R1 public research university founded in 1885 in Houghton, and is home to nearly 7,500 students from more than 60 countries around the world. The university is consistently ranked among the best universities in the country for return on investment, and Michigan's flagship technological university offers more than 185 undergraduate and graduate degree programs. Those programs span science, technology, engineering, mathematics, computing, forestry, business, health professions, robotics, psychology, social sciences, humanities, and the arts. The rural campus is situated just miles from Lake Superior in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, offering year-round opportunities for outdoor adventure.

stories.Headline: HSF Kramer hires legal engineering team to strengthen its AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, known as HSF Kramer, tapped a legal engineering team to fuel its AI capabilities, according to Above the Law on November 16, 2026. The firm moved to build out legal engineering as a hot new job at the intersection of law and AI. The hire was reported by Above the Law in a piece published at 20:15 on that date. The move places HSF Kramer among law firms building internal teams for AI work. The article frames legal engineering as a role spanning law and artificial intelligence.

In October 2026, Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake, built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. The two announcements arrived roughly 24 hours apart, and Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Over 85% of surveyed Association of Corporate Counsel members say they have embedded AI in their own legal departments, and ACC has roughly 48,000 members.

Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members report they have embedded AI and actively use it. By his account, that share rose sharply over roughly two years. He said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms. He expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists. General counsel, he said, want the gains to show up as a visible drop in outside counsel spend, alongside more work done at a faster rate.

Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, put the advantage inside the firm, as change management treated as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability. She said many firm leaders she has worked with know their firms need to change but have no team to lead it. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy and a former chief strategy officer, said rolling out a new tool can threaten someone's competence, confidence, autonomy, status or professional identity. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute and author of Lean Six Sigma for Law Firms, compresses her method to three words in a fixed order: people, process, platform.

Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers and former chief innovation officer at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, said organizations do not change, people do. Gary is careful to say there is no reason to think any of these companies knew a rival's plans. He concedes that some convergence is inevitable, because companies hear the same customers and face the same pressures, and simultaneous launches can signal a maturing market. He points to Thompson Hine's AI-enabled SmartPaTH Plus, which rests on more than a decade of investment in its SmartPaTH delivery model.

Leung learned her point training legal secretaries to move from WordPerfect to Word, people colleagues called when a document broke. MacDonagh's idea for Legal Lean Sigma came from reviewing outside counsel bills as an in-house lawyer. Gary's third installment, promised on positioning, timing and strategic alignment, is the next marker in this conversation. The articles leave open whether ACC members will begin reporting that law firm AI investments show up as lower or more predictable outside counsel spend.

They leave open which firms would then be named. They leave open how HSF Kramer's legal engineering team will be staffed and measured. They leave open whether the gap Brown describes will push more work in-house. They leave open what Gary's third installment will say.

stories.Headline: Founders Law acquires AI platform Tilder and hires Chris Bridges as transformation chief
stories.Summary:
London-based Founders Law, a firm backed by Brent Hoberman, has acquired the AI legal platform Tilder and hired its founder, Chris Bridges, as chief transformation officer. Bridges will lead the firm's shift toward AI-powered legal services, according to an announcement dated November 17, 2026. The deal follows a period in which Founders Law grew revenue by more than 40% year on year, after 23% growth in 2025 and a launch in the UAE. Founders Law describes itself as the law firm for founder-led, high-growth companies and works as an embedded in-house legal team for venture-backed tech companies from seed to Series C.

Tilder reviews contracts against a client's own negotiating playbook, with AI doing around 80% of the work and a qualified lawyer supervising its output. The platform launched in February 2025 and is the technology behind one of the UK's first regulated AI-native legal services. Bridges began his career as an enterprise tech lawyer in BigLaw and, after seven years, co-founded the tech and media boutique Tacit Legal. He recently sold Tacit Legal but kept Tilder, which Founders Law is acquiring along with his work on Engine Legal, a planned AI-first managed services business for AI-native law firms.

Tom Bohills, founder of Founders Law, said the firm has grown quickly on the strength of its lawyers and continues to hire exceptional talent from top tier firms. He said the deal gives them a platform to keep scaling rapidly without compromising what keeps clients loyal, and called bringing Bridges in a huge statement. Bridges joins the senior leadership team and will build out a product, knowledge and engineering team, leading three phases of work over the next 18 months. The first phase is building Founders OS, a custom operating system designed around the firm's business model, and the second is embedding Tilder in lawyers' day-to-day work so every new instruction draws on a client's previous matters.

The third phase is packaging routine legal work into products at lower price points, the firm says. Bridges said that with the pace of progress seen in the past twelve months, he sees Tilder becoming increasingly autonomous. Hoberman, co-founder and executive chair of Founders Forum Group, which took a significant minority stake in Founders Law in 2022, said plenty of new firms promise AI-powered legal services but Founders Law is doing it with senior lawyers from top firms and a platform that is already proven. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the three phases and the 18-month timeline.

stories.Headline: Sarvam launches an inference platform to host eight AI models on Indian servers
stories.Summary:
Sarvam opened the Sarvam Token Factory to developers and enterprises on November 17, 2026. This new inference platform serves its own models and open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. The company first previewed the managed inference stack as Sarvam Inference at its Epoch event. It announced general availability for the Token Factory earlier in the same month. The platform allows developers to reach every model through one OpenAI-compatible API.

The service hosts eight models, including Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. Other available models are DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and Gemma 4 31B. It runs on NVIDIA B200 clusters in India, with on-premise deployment offered to enterprises. Pay-as-you-go models use shared endpoints, while others like Qwen 3.8 27B and Clef need Provisioned Throughput. Introductory pricing runs through the end of 2026 for certain models.

Sarvam reported that its platform matches or beats leading global providers on speed and cost for most models. The company stated that Sarvam 105B returns its first token in 0.2 seconds and generates 330 tokens per second. They claimed that none of their technical changes, including speculative decoding, reduced the accuracy of the models. Sarvam noted that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serves over 450 billion tokens daily. They reported that 95.7 percent of prompt tokens for that model are served from cache.

India-based teams are affected because they can now access low-latency tokens without sending traffic to overseas clouds. The platform competes with Together AI and Fireworks AI, which provide managed infrastructure for various models. Other competitors include Krutrim, which hosted DeepSeek models in January 2025, and OpenAI, which launched India-based inference on November 12. Anthropic also offers in-country inference for select Claude models through Amazon Bedrock. Together AI showed faster streaming and first token speeds on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

The system uses a control plane with a cache-aware router, admission control, and a planner. Its inference engine utilizes separate GPU pools for prefill and decode, with a shared G3 store. The stack builds on vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, Mooncake, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, and FlashInfer. An orchestrator agent proposes experiments, while an engineer must approve each deployment. Caching drives most gains, and MXFP8 weights helped Sarvam 105B fit on one B200 per replica.

The company will continue offering introductory pricing for Sarvam 105B and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 through 2026. Sarvam 105B costs 10 to 15 rupees for input and 25 to 60 rupees for output per million tokens. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 costs 14 rupees for input and 55 rupees for output per million tokens. The articles do not publish the specific rates for the provisioned model throughput. They also leave the future of the competition with other global inference providers open.

stories.Headline: TCL CSOT showcases AI-driven display innovations and IJP OLED developments at DTC2026
stories.Summary:
TCL CSOT held its Global Display Tech-Ecosystem Conference 2026 in Wuhan, China, starting on November 13, 2026. The event focused on the theme True Vision, AI in Motion to explore how AI reshapes display technology. Company executives, academics, and industry partners gathered to preview advances in AI-driven innovation, IJP OLED, and the APEX brand. Kevin Wang, Jun Zhao, and Xiaolin Yan attended alongside science writer and Wenjin Book Award winner Weigang Wan. These leaders presented new developments in display performance and the integration of artificial intelligence into manufacturing and research.

The APEX brand relies on four pillars: Amazing Display Experience, Protective of Eye Health, Eco-friendly to Build and Use, and Unlimited Imaginative Potential. Innovations include natural-light, full-spectrum, and low-glare technologies, plus energy-saving backlight technologies, zone-based control, and dynamic refresh rates. A 27-inch IJP OLED Oxide Internal Compensation QHD 500Hz Gaming Display features a response time of less than 1ms. Other products include a 115-inch 16K 2D/3D-Compatible Light Field TV and a 6.36-inch Blue Phosphorescent OLED Mobile Display. A 10.95-inch Full-Angle Lossless Privacy OLED Tablet and a 14-inch notebook display under 0.66mm thick were also shown.

Founder and Chairman Li Dongsheng stated that AI is a major force driving industrial transformation and changing how people live. CEO Kevin Wang explained that AI For Real means moving artificial intelligence from the lab into real-world applications. He noted that combining expertise with AI capabilities increases efficiency across operations, manufacturing, and research and development. Jun Zhao outlined the APEX philosophy, which aims to reproduce the visual world while caring for people and the planet. Xiaolin Yan emphasized that the next stage of research involves exploring the unknown rather than optimizing known data.

Partners like Merck presented PB-Lens, a planar optical lens made by coating reactive mesogen materials onto PET film. 3M showcased a full-color diffractive waveguide for AR glasses and Light Control Film for automotive OLED displays. Summer Sprout provided small-molecule red ink for IJP OLED, while Lenovo showed a Legion R9000P laptop with a 240Hz display. MSI presented the Claw 8 EX AI+ handheld device featuring an 8-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate. These collaborations affect the value chain from materials innovation and panel development to final end-device applications.

The company uses AI for Display to enhance operational efficiency and Display for AI to improve AI-powered device experiences. AI is currently reshaping business operations to make production more autonomous and decisions faster and more informed. stories.Headline: New York attorney general Letitia James creates ASSET unit to enforce AI safety laws
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on November 17, 2026, that a new unit focused on artificial intelligence safety and regulation is being created within the New York Attorney General’s Office. The unit is called the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit, or the ASSET Unit, and it will work to protect New Yorkers from potential harms of emerging technology. The office said the ASSET Unit will also oversee laws regulating AI, and the Attorney General’s Office is currently building the ASSET Unit team. The announcement was reported by WKTV in Albany, New York, and by The Defiant, which said the new team will lead the attorney general’s RAISE Act enforcement.

The ASSET Unit will enforce the Responsible AI Safety Education Act, known as the RAISE Act, which takes effect on January 1, 2027. Under that law, AI developers must publicly disclose their safety measures and must quickly report security and safety problems. The Defiant reported that developers will register and report safety incidents through a separate state office, while the new team leads the attorney general’s enforcement of the RAISE Act. The ASSET Unit’s work will include addressing issues like data privacy, digital scams, cybersecurity and online safety, according to WKTV.

James is the official responsible for creating the unit, and her office announced the ASSET Unit and described its mission to protect New Yorkers from the potential harms of emerging technology. Her office said the unit will oversee laws regulating AI and will enforce the RAISE Act once it takes effect. The Attorney General’s Office is currently building the ASSET Unit team, and the office is asking anyone with a news tip to send it to news@wktv.com. The articles do not include any further direct statements from James beyond the announcement of the unit and its purpose.

The context is that the RAISE Act takes effect on January 1, 2027, which is after the November 17, 2026, announcement, so the unit is being set up ahead of the law’s start date. The ASSET Unit’s enforcement work will cover the disclosure and reporting duties the law places on AI developers, while registration and incident reporting will run through a separate state office. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the office building the team and the law taking effect on that date. No further steps, deadlines or appointments are given in the articles.

stories.Headline: Demis Hassabis’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion to design medicines with AI
stories.Summary:
Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C round, the company said on Tuesday. The round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Big Tech giant acquired it in 2014. Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021. The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet, Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of new medicines using AI, and Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it says will help it deliver the next generation of medicines.

Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B. Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure, as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop new medicines using the technology, with Anthropic announcing it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnering with Novo Nordisk in April. Hassabis said that when they founded Isomorphic, their conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI. He said the round enables the company to accelerate its progress in building foundational biology models, deepening its systemic disease understanding, and driving its first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients. In a separate interview on the Masters of Scale podcast, Hassabis warned that the AI industry faces an accidental incident similar to an oil spill, saying poorly monitored AI systems could cause serious damage.

He said companies are rapidly building advanced AI systems, but safety measures are not keeping pace, and he suggested companies should increase investment in AI safety and ensure AI agents are properly monitored rather than operating without human oversight. Hassabis highlighted the risks of the next AI development phase, where systems improve themselves without human supervision, a process he called closed-loop recursive self-improvement. He cited DeepMind's AlphaZero as an example, which learned to play chess by self-training and quickly surpassed human ability, and he noted that such self-improvement works best in areas like mathematics, coding, and games where AI can verify its own answers. He said today's AI tools can boost human engineer productivity by three to five times, but human review and oversight are still involved, and the greater risk emerges when AI systems improve autonomously without human checks, accelerating development but making control harder. He also expressed concerns about AI agents and cybersecurity, suggesting better engineering could have prevented recent incidents.

stories.Headline: Hugging Face integrates OpenRouter to route language model requests through its Inference Providers service
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face announced on November 16, 2026, that its Inference Providers service now uses OpenRouter to route supported language model requests. This migration changes how the system handles chat, vision language, and agent requests by routing them through OpenRouter. Existing Hugging Face tokens and application code are intended to keep working for users during this backend transition. However, provider keys previously configured for server side routing no longer work through that specific route. Image, video, and audio generation tasks continue to use the existing Hugging Face provider infrastructure.

The new system routes requests from applications to the Hugging Face router, then OpenRouter, and finally to an eligible provider. OpenRouter serves over 600 models from 80 plus providers to more than 10 million users every month. The catalog includes 160 models from 38 labs, though one API check observed 164 entries. Users can choose routing policies like fastest, cheapest, or balanced, or pin a specific provider using a model suffix. This change does not affect dedicated Inference Endpoints or models that users run locally.

Hugging Face stated that the account and billing experience will remain on their side for the users. They explained that the router now picks the best provider based on live price, speed, and reliability. The company noted that failed requests are now retried on another provider instead of returning an error. They advised users to check their model availability, credit balances, and actual bills for Hugging Face managed billing. They also suggested that teams identify workloads relying on custom provider keys and decide where billing should live.

Users with custom provider keys are affected because their specific contracts, credits, or capacity may no longer be active. OpenRouter reported that open weight models grew 60 fold in weekly volume between October 2025 and September 2026. These models cost an average of 0.28 dollars per million input tokens, which is four times less than closed models. On the Intelligence Index, the open weight Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 46 compared to 65 for Claude Fable 5.2. This cost trade off is considered worth it for many different types of workloads.

OpenRouter previously conducted a routing experiment with 24 million requests and 103 billion input tokens over one week. That study showed a 6 percent increase in cost per request but improved throughput and time to first token. OpenRouter also found that its new routing method cut capacity errors by 46 percent and improved throughput by 16.3 percent. Open weight models represented 71.7 percent of tokens served by OpenRouter at the end of September 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 was the most used model this week with 59.2 trillion tokens.

Users should now verify model identifiers and eligible providers using the OpenAI compatible model catalog at the Hugging Face router. They must test their largest prompts, tool calls, and schema requirements to ensure the new routing works. The articles leave open the exact cutover hour, the specific rollout cohorts, and the available grace period. Future work mentioned by Hugging Face includes the implementation of account linking for the users. It remains unclear if a stream that has already emitted text can be restarted without duplicating output.

stories.Headline: Mullin says AI likely caused recent US outages and rules out cyberattack
stories.Summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Monday that artificial intelligence likely caused a recent spate of outages across the United States. He spoke to Fox News host Sean Hannity, who had explained how the string of outages had sown seeds of suspicion among people and even led some to panic. The outages included a rare nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday, November 13, 2026. Workday software, which offers HR and payroll solutions, also reportedly faced an outage on November 13, and a Microsoft outage impacted services like Outlook on November 12. United Airlines flights saw a system outage on November 16, and online banking services were impacted the same day by an issue at JPMorgan Chase & Co.

Mullin said the incidents were not linked and that US intelligence had no reason to believe a cyberattack was involved in any of these cases. He said the FAA ground stop appears to have been due to an old router, while the banking issue appears to have stemmed from a software glitch on JPMorgan Chase & Co's side. None of the companies which faced outages have pointed to a threat actor, he noted. Mullin said he could say with 98 percent certainty that the US was not seeing a cyberattack. He said no one was out there taking claims for it, and that officials were not seeing the traffic or the footprints going in and out.

Mullin said someone in the tech industry, whom he would not name but said was not Elon Musk, told him AI might be behind the outages. Referring to AI as super intelligence, keeping with President Donald Trump's orders, Mullin said the tech expert told him the programs are not designed to work as fast as super intelligence is. He said when a program is able to write code and goes in and self-fixes itself, it is like doing a change order on a house. He said the expert told him this caused a ripple effect that overruns systems not designed to run as fast as the technology is today. Mullin said that kind of makes sense to him.

Mullin said he is 98 percent certain the US is not the target of cyberattacks, noting that no group has claimed responsibility and that there is no digital footprint of outside activity. He said the incidents are all individually unrelated. Industry experts told the New York Post that companies are racing to update complex and often outdated systems with new AI tools ahead of the holidays, when spending surges and staff take time off. The experts warned that the problems could get worse before they get better. The outages hit United Airlines and several major banks on Monday, and all US flights were grounded for hours last week.

The FAA issued its rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, November 13, 2026. Workday software reportedly faced an outage the same day, and the Microsoft outage affecting services like Outlook came on November 12. United Airlines flights saw a system outage on November 16, the same day online banking services were impacted by an issue at JPMorgan Chase & Co. The FAA ground stop appears to have been due to an old router, while the banking issue appears to have stemmed from a software glitch on JPMorgan Chase & Co's side. None of the companies which faced outages have pointed to a threat actor.

Mullin said US intelligence had no reason to believe a cyberattack was involved in any of these cases. He said officials were not seeing any traffic that would make them think it was a cyberattack, citing intelligence officials he had reached out to over the string of outages. He said no one was out there taking claims for it, and that officials were not seeing the footprints going in and out. The experts warned that the problems could get worse before they get better.

stories.Headline: Ashish Mishra urges governance for AI agents that act without human oversight
stories.Summary:
Ashish Mishra, Lead Solutions Architect for Agentic AI Services at NTT DATA, published an article on 16 November 2026 about governing AI that acts rather than only answers. He described a voice bot his colleague had asked to suggest an itinerary for a trip to France, which instead supplied one for India. Mishra called it an obvious hallucination that could be verified easily. He wrote that the consequences can be far more serious when an autonomous AI agent makes the wrong decision and runs with it. He said organizations are moving away from “vanilla” AI, which simply answers questions, toward AI that can make decisions, act and carry out entire business processes.

Mishra wrote that existing governance will remain relevant, covering the quality and accuracy of AI, data protection, privacy, security and bias. He said agentic AI does not change any of that and simply gives organizations more to govern. Traditional AI produces an output and a person decides what to do with it, while agentic AI can use other tools and systems, communicate with people or initiate the next step in a process without any human intervention. He said this means questioning the output as well as the activity throughout the workflow. He wrote that every agent should have a clear business purpose and a named owner, its own identity and access only to the information and tools required for its job.

Mishra said the excitement around new technology is understandable but that letting it get ahead of the controls is a mistake he sees far too often. He wrote that by the time you discover a problem, the agent may already have acted on it. He said organizations without effective AI governance can face compliance failures and operational problems, and that when AI acts without guardrails those consequences are amplified. He said an action that is difficult or impossible to reverse needs a different level of control than a simple day-to-day task. He wrote that if something goes wrong, you should be able to see what information the agent was working with, which tools it used and what approvals it received.

Mishra wrote that AI risk is no longer confined to the information an agent produces and now extends to the running of the business. He said AI agents can take information from emails, documents and websites and interact with different tools, systems and even other agents. He said testing an agent before it starts working is essential but you cannot stop there, because the information it receives and the environment it operates in will continue to change. He said you need to know what an agent can retain, how long it keeps that information and whether anything sensitive could be exposed. He compared an agent carrying out one small, contained task to hiring a freelancer for a specific piece of work.

Mishra cited NTT DATA’s 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for AI Leaders, which found that 55.9% of AI leaders use a centralized governance model, compared with 37.6% of other organizations and 33.3% of AI laggards. He wrote that NTT DATA has learned many of these lessons by being its own client zero, experimenting with AI internally and encountering security and compliance issues before taking that experience to clients. He said one of the most important lessons is to start with the end in mind, being clear about what an agent should achieve, how its value will be measured and what it is prepared to let the agent do. He wrote that trying to add the right controls once an agent is already operating across your business is far more difficult. He said applying governance to AI agents does not limit their freedom but puts the right rules in place for them to operate as intended.

Mishra wrote that before you build, you should be clear on the agent’s purpose, who owns it, the data it will use and how much freedom it should have. He said that before an agent goes live you should check its permissions, testing and approvals and make sure you can reverse or stop an action if something goes wrong. He said that once it is working you should monitor how well it performs, the decisions and actions it takes, how much it costs to run and whether it delivers the results you expect. He wrote that if you cannot see every agent operating in your business, trace what happened or step in quickly, you should start with visibility. He directed readers to learn more about NTT DATA’s Agentic AI Studio and how it can help build, govern and manage AI agents across their lifecycle.

stories.Headline: BoomerangFX launches ChatGPT search ads and AI optimization for clinics
stories.Summary:
BoomerangFX launched its next-generation AI Search Marketing offering, bringing AI Search Advertising on OpenAI's ChatGPT and Search Optimization Intelligence for Claude and Gemini into its GROW SaaS product suite, the company announced on November 17, 2026. The offering is enhanced by AUVIA™, the AI Clinic Co-Pilot, connecting patient inquiries to conversion and end-to-end clinic practice management. BoomerangFX described the offering as the world's first specialty AI search marketing platform to connect ChatGPT ad campaigns, optimization for Claude and Gemini, and agentic patient engagement with integrated electronic medical records, scheduling and payments. The launch was announced from Miami, Toronto, London and Sydney. The offering is available through a GROW Platinum upgrade for existing and new clients.

The rollout begins in November 2026 in the USA, Canada and UK, with expansion planned across Ireland, Germany, Australia, India and Latin America. According to an August 2026 Pew Research Center report, 34% of U.S. adults now use AI chatbots for at least one health or medical reason. The GROW product suite's Smart Website Intelligence organizes treatment expertise, clinician credentials, practice locations and patient education into clear, accessible website content. Search Optimization Intelligence applies BoomerangFX's proprietary data science to help AI platforms discover, interpret and reference that information when prospective patients research care. The offering combines eligible paid AI Search Ads on OpenAI's ChatGPT with website and content optimization for organic discoverability through Claude and Gemini, and the company's multi-platform advertising model also leverages Google, Meta and Instagram for maximum reach.

Jerome Dwight, Co-Founder & CEO of BoomerangFX, said the next era of clinic growth will be shaped by how effectively practices turn AI discovery into lasting patient relationships. He said the company is bringing advertising, search visibility, patient conversations and clinical operations into one platform, helping clinics connect the demand they create with the experience they deliver. Dr. Stephen Mulholland, Co-Founder and Chief Clinical Architect of BoomerangFX, said aesthetic and wellness practices need technology that understands the language of their specialties and the expectations of their patients. He said connecting specialty-level marketing with responsive communication and a complete clinical record helps practices deliver a more consistent experience from the first question through continuing care. Clinical guidance is informed by BoomerangFX's medical advisory board, led by Dr. Mulholland, a globally recognized cosmetic surgeon, co-founder of InMode where he helped lead its 2019 NASDAQ IPO, co-creator of Morpheus8 and co-developer of BodyTite, FaceTite and AccuTite.

AUVIA™'s agentic workflows support immediate lead response and personalized follow-up to move inquiries into booked treatments with minimal manual intervention, and campaign and conversion signals feed ongoing optimization, linking marketing activity directly to patient engagement and booking outcomes. AUVIA™'s specialty knowledge framework spans in excess of 2,000 specialty treatment and clinical-indication entries, covering procedural nomenclature, treatment modalities and concerns such as cutaneous photodamage, dermal laxity and dyspigmentation, while clinical assessment and treatment selection remain with the practitioner. RUN provides the all-in-one practice management and EMR foundation, connecting scheduling, digital charting, consents, treatment records, e-prescribing, inventory and reporting with billing, payments and patient financing, while memberships, packages and rebooking sustain long-term patient relationships. GROW provides lead capture, pipeline management, Smart Website Intelligence and conversion workflows, and AUVIA™ engages prospective patients through personalized multilingual chat features, coordinates qualification and consultation booking, supports payment workflows and automates reminders and follow-up. ELEVATE generates demand through specialty positioning, intelligent website optimization, campaign development, paid media and ongoing optimization, and practice owners gain a coordinated operating model designed to improve conversion, reduce missed inquiries and increase the lifetime value of every patient.

The launch builds on the BoomerangFX team's experience delivering more than 10,000 Google, Meta and Instagram campaigns over the past decade, and its proprietary machine learning and data science models combine that marketing experience with specialty context and performance analysis. The company's product roadmap includes agentic workflows inside the system of record to drive clinic optimization and task management for busy clinics. ELEVATE has campaign experience in more than seven countries across medspas, cosmetic surgery, hair restoration, women's health, weight management, longevity and functional medicine, with international resources spanning strategy, branding, website design, paid advertising, SEO, social media, content, campaign optimization and performance reporting. BoomerangFX operates in the USA, Canada, the UK, Ireland, Germany, Australia, India and Latin America, with offices in Miami, Toronto, London and Sydney. The company unifies RUN practice management and EMR, GROW patient acquisition and conversion, AUVIA™ AI Clinic Co-Pilot, ELEVATE marketing, embedded payments and LEARN education for aesthetic, wellness and private healthcare practices.

Upgrade pathways are available for existing BoomerangFX RUN and GROW clients, and the launch extends the company's recurring subscription platform across patient acquisition, AI engagement, clinical software and payments. ChatGPT ad activation depends on market availability, practice specialty and advertiser approval. Search Optimization Intelligence supports organic discoverability on Claude and Gemini, while inclusion, rankings and recommendations remain determined by each platform, and paid placements are separate from AI-generated answers. OpenAI said on November 16, 2026 that it is sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. OpenAI said organizations deploying agents include Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need.

stories.Headline: Lucidity launches AI Action Engine to automate cloud cost fixes across its savings modules
stories.Summary:
Lucidity launched its AI Action Engine for cloud cost reduction, and the system is now available across the company's savings modules, according to IT Brief Australia on 18 November 2026. The launch adds an automation layer to Lucidity's existing cloud savings products, which the company says are used by more than 100 enterprises across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Lucidity launched the AI Action Engine at Microsoft Ignite, according to a GlobeNewswire release published by The Manila Times on 18 November 2026. The engine uses AI agents to move cloud savings from recommendation to the bill and sits behind every Lucidity savings module. The new engine is intended to move cloud cost reduction from identification to implementation, the company says.

The product works in three stages: it first analyses how cloud resources are used rather than relying only on billing data, then adds operational context to each potential saving, and finally applies approved changes while monitoring and logging the result. According to Lucidity, each opportunity includes information on whether a resource is in production, which sizing rules apply and whether a fix has already been made. Users can require approvals, set change windows and apply policies by account, environment or team, and Lucidity says disk changes can be made without downtime. Every change is reversible and logged, the system does not read application data, and the company is SOC 2 Type II certified. Lucidity says AI agents find about 2x more savings than generic FinOps tools, and customers can see up to 40% lower cloud costs.

Nitin Bhadauria, co-founder of Lucidity, said enterprises do not need another tool to report on cloud waste but need it gone, and that the AI Action Engine finds waste across the cloud and fixes it autonomously with hyper-customizable guardrails. Karunakar Bojjireddy, Head of SaaS Operations at Commvault, said disk operations used to take up the SRE team's time and that with Lucidity that involvement is removed from disk operations. Bojjireddy also said Lucidity has helped Commvault's storage utilization go from about 60% to nearly 90%. Lucidity argues that many FinOps products can identify underused resources, but engineering teams often lack the time to check whether recommended changes are suitable for production systems or whether the issue has already been addressed. The GlobeNewswire release states that FinOps tools surface savings but delivery waits on engineers, so most recommendations sit in the backlog.

Commvault, one of the main reference customers cited in the launch, uses Lucidity across an Azure estate covering more than 3PB, 3,500 virtual machines and 11,000 disks, according to the company. Lucidity says Commvault has reduced cloud storage costs by about 40% and recorded more than USD $2 million in Azure savings to date, with no downtime on backup servers. Lucidity says it has identified more than USD $500 million in savings, and it named World Market, Klöckner and Kemper among the companies using its products to improve storage utilisation and reduce spending. The company is positioning the product at enterprises that want to automate at least part of their cloud cost management work while keeping controls around production changes, and customers can choose which actions require approval and which can be automated. Ignite attendees can meet the Lucidity team at booth #5338 in San Francisco from November 17 to 19.

Founded in 2021, Lucidity began with cloud storage management and has since expanded across multiple cloud platforms, and it now works across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud for 100+ enterprises. The company says it has raised USD $32 million from investors including Alpha Wave Global, WestBridge Capital and Beenext. The Manila Times article was published by GlobeNewswire on November 18, 2026, and dates the launch announcement to San Francisco on Nov. 17, 2026. The IT Brief Australia article was written by Finance Editor Karen Joy Bacudo and published on Wednesday, 18th November 2026. The GlobeNewswire release lists Akhil Kintali, Product Marketing Lead at Lucidity, as its media contact.

The articles say customers can require approvals, set change windows and apply policies per account, environment or team, and that AI agents make changes with the customer's approval or on their own for actions the customer chooses. The articles state that every change is monitored, verified, logged and reversible, and that live disk changes run with zero downtime. The articles say Lucidity is SOC 2 Type II certified and never reads application data, and that only changes safe for the workload are surfaced. The articles leave open which specific actions customers can automate without approval and how the approval process is configured in practice. The articles do not say when the engine became generally available beyond its launch at Microsoft Ignite.
