stories.Summary:
Generative AI is causing a productivity revolution and ecosystem fears within the gaming industry. A report from GDC in 2026 shows 40 percent of practitioners use this technology. However, 55 percent of those surveyed believe AI brings negative impacts to the sector. Some developers fear their hard work will be easily copied by AI tools. Others worry that low quality AI games could trigger a new Atari Shock.

Tencent held its 28th anniversary LinkTime event on November 11 to discuss AI Native businesses. Ma Huateng proposed that core businesses should fully embrace AI during organizational restructuring. Rumors then spread that Tencent would lay off 8,000 people or 50 percent of staff. Zhang Jun clarified on November 12 that 50 percent referred to resource allocation. Tencent Culture released notes on November 16 urging employees to turn anxiety into excitement.

Tencent officials stated that AI resources are for business allocation rather than staff layoffs. Producer Penpen of Insomnia Games said AI knockoffs shorten the market window for original games. He noted that Game Jam platforms are now treated as idea banks by companies. Penpen believes there are no practical measures to protect original works from AI plagiarism. He stated that many developers around him have already given up on creation.

Independent developers are most affected, as seen with Needle in a Haystack Simulator. That game saw 14 Roblox knockoffs in 48 hours, 9 on Steam, and 40 on WeChat. The Drunken Goddess's Drunken Deception and ReVamp both restricted their public demos to avoid copying. Players are also affected by low quality AI works filling platform recommendation slots. Large companies report that AI tools help players unpack unreleased projects and expose assets.

The Steam Next Fest saw over 8,000 signups, which was double the June event total. Daily new pages on itch.io reached 6,000, though downloads and purchases did not grow. Historically, companies like Voodoo used references from games like Donut County to create hits. The game 2048 was replicated in one week from the prototype called Threes!. AI has not changed competitive logic but has made these existing patterns faster.

Steam stated in South Korea that it will not act as a tool gatekeeper. Itch.io removed terabytes of AI games and now requires developers to mark all assets. Anthropic modified Claude Code prompts to target game cloning, but these are easily bypassed. Insomnia Games is using profits from Bug Vivarium to fund expensive legal rights protection. The articles leave open whether developers can survive by creating more complex, stylized works.

stories.Headline: Connecticut lawmakers plan to let rejected job applicants review AI screening errors
stories.Summary:
Connecticut’s recent law requiring prospective employers to disclose their use of artificial intelligence in job screening is likely to be expanded so rejected applicants can see whether errors were made in their reviews, according to the two co-chairmen of the legislative General Law Committee. State Rep. Roland Lemar, D-New Haven, and state Sen. James Maroney, D-Milford, the current committee co-chairmen, also co-chair the state’s working group on AI. That working group heard suggestions from state and national experts on Monday as Connecticut plans further AI protections for consumers and in the workplace. The lawmakers and a working group of professionals are developing potential ideas for the next session of the General Assembly. The assessment was reported on Nov. 17, 2026, by govtech.com and CT Insider, the latter in a story by staff writer Ken Dixon.

One suggestion builds on a law passed this year requiring notification of job applicants whose applications are screened by AI models. During a two-hour meeting in the Legislative Office Building in preparation for the upcoming 22-week legislative session starting Jan. 6, the lawmakers said simply notifying applicants that they will be reviewed by AI is not enough. Job seekers should also be able to look at and possibly correct erroneous conclusions drawn by the nascent technology. Possible AI review errors include artificial intelligence’s failure to recognize an applicant’s education level, or misinterpreting an applicant’s previous resignation as a firing. This year, 23 states approved a variety of new laws governing artificial intelligence, said Tatiana Rice, senior legislative director for the Washington-based nonprofit Future of Privacy Foundation.

Lemar said corporations, or even a local small business, that use AI to determine whether someone is fired or hired or gets a raise should give access to the data used in that AI program. He said applicants should know what information they have that would make them ineligible for the job position. Lemar said people were just notified that AI is being used, and there should be a follow-up at some point when an adverse decision is made. He said a discouraged job applicant would check whether the system got the right college or the right credentials, or whether that was something just misfiled in the system. Maroney said he would like to get towards post-decision notice and then perhaps some form of the explanation, within a right-to-correct data, if it is third-party data.

In remote testimony, Rice said new key areas are automated decision making and employee monitoring. Rice noted that anti-discrimination laws in various states need to designate the responsibilities of job-screening AI developers and the companies that use the technology. Rice said resume screeners used in about 90% of Fortune 500 companies use AI in varying degrees to determine whether somebody is fit for a position, whether they get interviewed, whether they get hired, and for internal uses such as compensation and who may be eligible for promotions, stressing the need for humans to have the last word on reviewing applicants. Rice said states have a very productive role in protecting their own constituents and responding in a way that is both consumer-protective and implementable by a company, adding that states are the testing grounds for whatever may emerge for eventual AI legislation on a national basis. Crystal Weise, policy and programs director for the nonprofit AFL-CIO Tech Institute in Connecticut, stressed the need for meaningful human oversight that should not be inundated with AI-based decisions too numerous to give thoughtful oversight and review.

Weise said a potential pitfall is so-called confirmation bias that could get humans to go along with possibly flawed employment recommendations made by AI systems. Weise said some provisions require that the person doing the reviewing and oversight have training on how the system works and be aware of where it might go wrong. She said these systems are not perfect and the person needs expertise in that field. Maroney in recent years has become a nationally known legislative leader on artificial intelligence and online safety. The articles were distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC, and Hearst Connecticut Media, with the govtech.com piece credited to The Register Citizen, Torrington, Conn.

The articles state that Connecticut’s law requiring disclosure of AI use in job screening was passed this year. The articles state that the possible expansion is being developed as potential ideas for the next session of the General Assembly. The articles state that the working group heard suggestions from state and national experts on Monday. The articles state that the meeting was held in the Legislative Office Building in preparation for the 22-week legislative session starting Jan. 6. The articles state that 23 states approved a variety of new laws governing artificial intelligence this year.

The articles leave open what specific proposal, if any, will be introduced for the next session of the General Assembly. The articles leave open whether the expansion will be adopted. The articles leave open the details of any post-decision notice, explanation, or right-to-correct data for third-party data. The articles leave open how responsibilities would be designated between job-screening AI developers and the companies that use the technology. The articles leave open what training and expertise requirements reviewers would need.

stories.Headline: Genesis AI raises $500 million to develop general-purpose robots with human-level dexterity
stories.Summary:
Genesis AI raised 500 million dollars in a Series A funding round on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to develop general-purpose robots with human-level dexterity. This investment follows a seed round of 105 million dollars that the company received in July 2025 after emerging from stealth. On the same day, the Munich-based company Agile Robots closed a Series F funding round that also raised 500 million dollars. Agile Robots has now reached a total of 2 billion dollars in invested capital since its founding in 2018.

The funding for Genesis AI brings its post-money valuation to 3.5 billion dollars and will support the large-scale deployment of its artificial intelligence robot named Eno. The company intends to use these funds to hire more engineers and researchers while expanding data acquisition to solve complex manipulation tasks. Agile Robots reached a valuation of 8.5 billion dollars and plans to use its capital to accelerate global expansion and increase production capacity. This includes a new site in Fürstenfeldbruck, Germany, opened in early 2026, which can produce 10,000 wheeled and legged humanoid robots every year.

Genesis AI Co-Founder and CEO Zhou Xian stated that the company builds its own hardware and intelligence to improve the system in a closed loop. The funding round for Genesis AI was co-led by Eclipse, Khosla Ventures, and Premji Invest. Vinod Khosla of Khosla Ventures noted that a full-stack approach helps solve long-standing challenges in robotics, while Vedant Agrawal of Premji Invest praised the natural movement of the robots. Agile Robots CEO Dr. Zhaopeng Chen said that physical AI will fundamentally change how the world makes and moves things. Dennis Chang of SoftBank Investment Advisers, which led the Agile Robots round, believes the company can bring physical AI into everyday operations.

Genesis AI is currently focusing on industrial environments like laboratories, logistics, and manufacturing before expanding into healthcare, hospitality, and consumer applications. The company eventually hopes to have its robots build more robots after they become more affordable and capable. Agile Robots has already deployed 20,000 industrial solutions for the electronics, automotive, and logistics sectors. The company employs over 3,500 people and manages subsidiaries including Krause Automation, Franka Robotics, Idealworks, and BÄR Automation. Agile Robots also plans to strengthen its presence in the United States and develop new robotics applications.

stories.Headline: Democratic Party leader Kim Min-seok pushes for 10-year exam ban for AI cheating
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, the leader of the ruling Democratic Party announced a plan to target artificial intelligence cheating. Rep. Kim Min-seok said the party will push for legislation to bar cheaters from retaking national exams for ten years. This proposal includes the annual college entrance exam and follows a cheating scandal involving the national tax accountant exam. The top scorer of that exam admitted to using a microcamera and AI devices to cheat on the test. These events raised significant concerns just before the nationwide college entrance exam scheduled for the following Thursday.

The proposed law would extend the ban to ten years, while national exam cheaters currently face a five year ban. Those caught cheating on the College Scholastic Ability Test are currently barred from retaking the exam the following year. The government previously stated it would push to extend the ban for CSAT cheaters to a period of three years. Rep. Kim Moon-soo and twelve other lawmakers proposed a Higher Education Act revision to extend the CSAT ban to five years. This specific proposal also requires universities to share records of such misconduct with other colleges in the country.

Rep. Kim Min-seok spoke on the official YouTube channel of the Democratic Party about preparing this new legislation. He stated that a ten year ban would effectively deprive cheaters permanently of their opportunity to ever take the exam. Kim added that such a strict penalty would deter students from attempting to cheat on these important national tests. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. President Lee also called for a thorough crackdown against AI assisted cheating during the upcoming college entrance exam.

The People Power Party criticized the government for failing to effectively address these incidents of cheating using artificial intelligence. PPP leader Jang Dong-hyeok wrote on Facebook that the education ministry's announced measures could hardly be considered actual measures. He described the ministry as incompetent, irresponsible, indiscriminate, and reckless in its handling of the current cheating situation. PPP chief spokesperson Park Choong-kwon criticized Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin for blaming his age for not detecting AI cheating. This criticism came just three days before the CSAT after the minister spoke during a recent parliamentary session.

South Korea has seen a series of AI assisted cheating incidents involving university entrance exams and other school tests. Test takers have recently been caught using AI glasses on middle school and high school tests across the country. The case involving the tax accountant exam is the latest example of this trend of using technology to cheat. The military has also toughened its screening of smart wearables amid the scrutiny over these AI cheating incidents. Police have secured a miniature camera as part of their ongoing probe into the tax accountant exam cheating.

The Democratic Party called for thorough preparations and clear guidelines for handling suspected AI cheating ahead of this week's CSAT. The top scorer of the tax accountant exam apologized for cheating before being questioned by the police. Authorities are now working to ensure the integrity of the nationwide college entrance exam taking place this Thursday. The articles do not state if the proposed ten year ban has been officially introduced as a bill. It remains open whether the Higher Education Act revision will be passed or if the government will adopt it.

stories.Headline: Nadler urges Congress to regulate AI and protect creators from intellectual property theft
stories.Summary:
Congressman Jerrold Nadler, the ranking member of the Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust, published an op-ed in Billboard on November 17, 2026, arguing that Congress must regulate artificial intelligence to protect authors, artists and creators from intellectual property theft. Earlier that month, Nadler, Jamie Raskin and Hank Johnson filed an amicus brief in the Southern District of New York in In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation opposing the Department of Justice's argument that AI companies may train their models on copyrighted work, including New York Times journalism, without compensation. The brief states that the DOJ's position violates the plain text of the Copyright Act, which contains no national security exception allowing private companies free use of copyrighted materials. Nadler wrote that dozens of lawsuits in the U.S. and around the world allege AI companies trained their models on millions of articles, songs, books, voice recordings, videos and other creative content without permission or payment.

Nadler wrote that the DOJ filed a brief last month in The New York Times v. Microsoft and OpenAI supporting Microsoft and OpenAI, which the Times alleges copied millions of its articles to train ChatGPT. He cited recently unsealed court filings in which a senior Microsoft scientist privately described the practice as an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions, while the administration argues the evidence of market harm is fair use rather than theft. He also pointed to Suno, the most widely used AI music generator, which major record labels are suing for training on their recordings without permission and which claims fair use despite admitting in court that it trained on essentially all music files of reasonable quality accessible on the open internet. Nadler warned that AI developers everywhere may use the administration's argument to defend mass intellectual property theft.

Nadler said the harm extends across the creative sector, writing that anyone streaming music has almost certainly heard an AI-generated track without knowing it and that platforms are drowning in AI-generated slop. He said AI makes streaming fraud easier, costing artists and rightsholders hundreds of millions or even billions each year according to experts, and that every listen on an AI-generated track dilutes the share of streaming proceeds going to human artists. He noted that Sony Music has requested over 260,000 takedowns of AI deepfakes of its artists and called the problem an uphill struggle. Nadler concluded that unless Congress draws a line in the sand, more companies like OpenAI and Suno will conclude they can rip off the creators whose work trains their models, and he argued that America can lead the world in artificial intelligence without building it on theft.

stories.Headline: Penn State researchers build AI that explains manufacturing fixes to engineers
stories.Summary:
A team led by Penn State researchers, funded by the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, is building a neurosymbolic intelligent system that pairs a neural network learning from industrial data with knowledge graphs of engineering rules. The work was published on November 16, 2026, by Tucker Leighty-Phillips of Penn State University. The system is meant to flag manufacturing problems and explain its recommendations to plant engineers. The Genesis Mission is a national effort led by the U.S. Department of Energy to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery and innovation. The team's aim is to combine data-driven learning with human-like reasoning.

The system will identify manufacturing issues through pattern recognition and symbolic reasoning, and use engineering and physics knowledge to understand and resolve problems. Operators will see what the neural system flags and decide whether to agree or override it with symbolic knowledge and reasoning assistance. The system will talk with engineers, draw out hidden constraints and work with the optimization models plants already use, updating recommendations as floor conditions change. A knowledge graph stores expert knowledge as a web of connected facts, linking items such as a weld defect, a machine setting or an assembly line step to the others they affect. Porosity in a weld can be caused by a travel speed that is too fast, and engineers can add new rules to the graph as they learn them.

Soundar Kumara, Allen E. Pearce and Allen M. Pearce Professor of Industrial Engineering and principal investigator, said the team is building a neurosymbolic intelligence with an explanation capability that will make the future of the global manufacturing landscape different and truly useful. He said neurosymbolic manufacturing intelligence will open new avenues and revitalize manufacturing by providing better explanations for the inferences made. He said the major focus is building neurosymbolic architecture that integrates neural inference with symbolic reasoning. He said the team is building neural reasoning connected with knowledge graphs for two case studies, one from General Motors and another from a small and medium-sized manufacturer in Pennsylvania. He said the architecture will be adaptable enough for other manufacturing applications.

Anirudh Subramanyam, Charles and Enid Schneider Early Career Assistant Professor of Industrial Engineering, said optimization models are very good at finding the best plan under the rules you give them. He said the trouble on a real assembly line is that many of the most important rules have never been written down, as they only live in the heads of the engineers who run it. He said the team wants a system that learns those rules from engineers' feedback and can tell them not just what to change, but which constraint forced its hand. Rebecca Napolitano, co-principal investigator, associate professor of architectural engineering and associate director of the Digital Twin Hub, said the physics and engineering knowledge built into the symbolic side gives a way to test the AI, not just train it. She said that when the system makes a recommendation, the operator can see what it is based on and how confident it is.

The team includes collaborators from multiple Penn State units, industry, a national lab and commonwealth groups, including the Pennsylvania Technical Assistance Program (PennTAP) and Team Pennsylvania Foundation. Los Alamos National Laboratory will provide foundational expertise on neurosymbolic intelligence. Kumara said PennTAP and Team Pennsylvania Foundation work directly with manufacturers across the state, which gives a practical path into the shops that need this most. He said PennTAP offers no-cost energy assessments for companies, so they will measure energy usage at the shop before and after the tools are brought in. He said Team Pennsylvania Foundation will support the project by finding other in-state manufacturers and connecting them.

The researchers are building and testing their approach in two real-world case studies: welding quality inspection at a Pennsylvania manufacturer and assembly line rebalancing with General Motors. The researchers intentionally selected both a small and large manufacturer to test their approach, stating that if the model works at both scales, it should work for all enterprises of different scales. Currently, weld inspection relies on a person looking at the weld, which is getting harder as experienced welders retire, the researchers said. Penn State students are training neural models to spot defects like cracks, porosity and undercut, and are building knowledge graphs from real-world welding rules and standards. For example, if the system spots porosity in a weld image, it can use its welding rules to trace the likely cause to a setting such as electrode travel speed or voltage and suggest an adjustment for the welder to check.

For the General Motors case study, the researchers are applying neurosymbolic intelligence to rebalance assembly lines, where work is split into small tasks across a sequence of workstations. When the product mix shifts or the line must speed up, those tasks must be redistributed, and because tasks depend on one another, moving them can set off a chain of further moves down the line. Plants plan these changes with optimization models, but those models are limited by their hardcoded rules, and their recommendations can be hard for line engineers to interpret. In the team's approach, an optimization model proposes each plan while a neural layer learns from engineers' feedback, and when an engineer rejects a plan, for example because a needed tool sits at only one station, the system automatically infers the unwritten rule, adds it to the optimization model and proposes a new plan. Anirudh Subramanyam is leading the optimization effort with Seog-Chan Oh of General Motors, while Kamesh Madduri, associate professor of computer science and engineering, is leading development of the dynamic knowledge graph.

The researchers are also exploring federated learning, where models improve by learning across several companies without any of them having to share their data. Kumara said small manufacturers usually don't have enough data on their own to train a good AI model, and they also really don't want to hand their production data to a big company or a competitor. Federated learning lets each shop's model learn on its own data and only share what the model learned, not the raw data itself, allowing them to build a better model while ensuring their data stays in-house, the researchers explained. The project also draws on the interdisciplinary research community fostered by Penn State's Digital Twin Hub, a joint initiative of the Cocoziello Institute for Real Estate Innovation and the Institute for Computational and Data Sciences (ICDS). Jessica Menold, co-principal investigator and associate professor of mechanical engineering and industrial engineering, directs the Hub, which connects researchers working across manufacturing, infrastructure, healthcare and other domains to advance digital twin research and applications.

Menold said the challenges of developing digital twins often transcend individual disciplines and industries. She said the project demonstrates the value of bringing together expertise in AI, engineering, advanced manufacturing and human-centered design to advance digital twin research and address real-world manufacturing challenges. She said that by integrating deep learning, engineering knowledge and human expertise, we can move beyond simply modeling physical systems to understanding, predicting and improving their behavior. The researchers said it is equally important to ensure that these increasingly sophisticated systems remain transparent, allowing engineers to understand and critically evaluate the reasoning behind AI-generated recommendations. Other Penn State personnel on the project are Paul Griffin, Lucas Professor in Industrial Engineering; Guha Manogharan, professor of mechanical engineering; Ilya Kovalenko, assistant professor of mechanical engineering; and Tanna Pugh, director of PennTAP.

In addition to Seog-Chan Oh, other external co-principal investigators are Abby Smith of Team Pennsylvania Foundation and William Peck of Los Alamos National Laboratory. Graduate students include Vinay Saji Mathew, Chen Zhou and Xiaowen You, all from industrial engineering. Xiaowen You, doctoral student in industrial engineering, is advised by Soundar Kumara. The article was last updated November 16, 2026, and contact is the College of Engineering Media Relations at communications@engr.psu.edu. The article carries tags including Research, Science and Technology, University Park, Engineering, architectural engineering, industrial and manufacturing engineering, mechanical engineering and Artificial Intelligence.

stories.Headline: Riham Hashi launches Novara Strategies to help companies navigate AI governance and regulation
stories.Summary:
Riham Hashi, a 2026 graduate of Penn Carey Law’s Master in Law program, launched Novara Strategies in April 2025, a boutique consulting firm that helps companies navigate regulation, technology policy and artificial intelligence governance. She had worked in state policy and management roles focused on community-based initiatives and public policy implementation, and she noticed gaps between policy intent and real-world execution. She also worked on the Postsecondary Student Basic Needs Act, which passed in Washington State in May 2023. Soon after launching her firm, she entered the Master in Law program to build the legal expertise her clients needed. Hashi said the program was a deliberate step to strengthen the legal and regulatory foundation she was already building, and that she wanted a stronger framework in regulatory law and to think more precisely about legal structure and compliance, especially in artificial intelligence.

Through the curriculum she gained skills in legal reasoning, building compliance programs and regulatory interpretation. She first noticed a change in her U.S. Law and Legal Methods course, which she called foundational to how she analyzes legal issues for clients, and she said it changed how she reads and structures information and helped her approach statutes and case law with greater discipline and clarity. She also found immediate professional relevance in her Corporate Governance and Compliance and Intellectual Property Law for Strategists, Innovators, and Owners of IP Assets courses, and she said it was easy to connect classroom learning to real-life work. Hashi valued learning from faculty who are actively practicing in the fields they teach, and she pointed to her Corporate Governance and Compliance professor, Andrew Kandel, as an example of that practitioner-driven perspective. She said he is actively doing the work and that it is helpful to learn from someone directly in the field.

She also credited the program’s flexibility as a major advantage for professionals whose work intersects with the law, saying students can come from any field and mold the program to fit what they think is important to their work. She encouraged prospective students to take advantage of the larger Penn ecosystem and to enter the program with a clear sense of how they want to use the degree. For Hashi, the degree provided more than legal literacy, offering a structured framework for understanding governance, compliance and organizational decision-making at a deeper level. That framework now informs the work she is building through Novara Strategies and her broader approach to AI governance and regulatory strategy.

stories.Headline: O'Fallon dispatchers use AI to transcribe 911 calls and suggest questions while a person always answers
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is on the frontlines of crime fighting and is being used in many 911 dispatch centers around the country, according to a report published on Nov. 17, 2026. The police dispatch in O’Fallon, Missouri, is using artificial intelligence-based technology to assist dispatchers who answer 911 calls, the report said. Dispatchers there said a person will always answer the call, according to the report. The report was published by InvestigateTV and carried by wdtv.com, wndu.com and wect.com on Nov. 17, 2026. The kttc.com article was published on Nov. 17, 2026 at 11:36 AM CST and updated three hours later.

Based on the call, the technology displays a specific list of questions for the dispatcher to ask, the report said. It also listens in, transcribes the call in real time and suggests information the dispatcher might have missed, according to the report. In Fairfax, Virginia, AI translates calls into more than 170 languages instantly, the report said. In New Orleans, AI automatically answers calls about accidents officials already know about, and the system will inform the caller about the incident. If the caller is involved in any way, the person can stay on the line to talk to a dispatcher, the report said.

Paul Jokerst, emergency communications administrator for O’Fallon Police, said the technology is there to assist dispatchers. He said it is clearly here to assist, and it is just to assist them, according to the report. He said the technology is not intended to replace dispatchers. He said it is not here to replace anybody, not here to take a job away or hamper somebody’s job, the report said. O’Fallon police dispatcher Mike Conte said he supports the use of AI.

Conte said the technology helps when dispatchers are trying to pick out information they cannot understand from a caller. He said it is very helpful when they are trying to pick out pieces of information they cannot understand the caller, according to the report. He said he supports the technology as long as he is also on the line. He said you will always talk to a human, one of them is always there, and they are always ready to answer your call. Experts say AI would not replace dispatchers at the moment because humans are better at compassion, processing emotion and keeping people calm.

The report said the use of AI in 911 is expanding rapidly. The report said AI in law enforcement continues to evolve. The report was published by Lauren Trager on Nov. 17, 2026 at 12:47 PM EST and updated 18 minutes later, according to wdtv.com. The wdtv.com article is copyright 2026 Gray Media Group, Inc., with all rights reserved. The kttc.com article appeared under a headline about how 911 dispatchers are using AI.

The report did not say how many dispatch centers use the technology or when O’Fallon began using it. It did not give the cost of the technology or name the company that provides it. It did not say whether callers are told AI is listening or whether the system stores recordings. It did not say what happens if the transcription is wrong or how the suggested questions are chosen. It did not say whether other departments in the St. Louis area use similar systems.

stories.Headline: Fraud experts say AI makes impersonation scams more believable and harder to detect
stories.Summary:
Scammers are finding new ways to impersonate people and organizations that their targets trust, fraud experts warn, and these scams can begin across multiple channels including phone calls, texts, email, messaging apps and social media. New technology such as artificial intelligence is making these tactics more believable and harder to detect, according to the articles published on November 16, 2026. Impersonation scams happen when someone pretends to be a trusted person or organization, such as a government agency, law enforcement, a bank, a tech support provider, or even a family member. These scams are effective because they create a sense of urgency and rely on trust to push people to act quickly, the articles state. In some cases, criminals now use AI to generate realistic messages, real-time videos or even mimic a person's voice, which can make a scam feel more urgent and personal.

The articles describe the anatomy of a scam in five steps, beginning with contact from someone claiming to be a trusted source and followed by trust, urgency, a request for money or information, and extraction. Scammers may pose as familiar or authoritative sources, with common examples including calls claiming to be from a bank, a government agency or a relative in distress. Contact can happen in multiple ways, and calls, texts, email and social media messages may all be used together, while messages may be more polished and personalized and timed to feel legitimate. Pressure is a key tactic, and scammers often push for immediate action or ask people not to involve others. For example, people impersonating law enforcement or bank employees often tell people to mention nothing to the bank employees during a withdrawal transaction because they are "compromised."

Joshua Del Valle, executive director of enterprise fraud at PNC Bank, said the technology may be new but the strategy behind these scams is not. Del Valle said fraudsters want to build trust, create pressure, and keep people from pausing long enough to question the request. He said people should verify the request through a contact method they already know and trust instead of relying on how convincing a message, voice or video appears. The articles also report his guidance that a person or organization with a legitimate request will not rush someone into immediate action. Del Valle's comments appear in both the Mesabi Tribune and the Watauga Democrat versions of the article.

The articles list five ways to protect yourself, starting with verifying the request using a trusted contact method such as a known phone number or official website rather than the information provided in the message. They advise not relying on caller ID or voice alone, because phone numbers and messages can be altered, faked or manipulated and sometimes show the name of an institution that is not real. People should slow down and ask questions, be cautious about sharing personal information in response to unexpected requests, and talk to someone they trust before acting because a second opinion can help spot red flags. The articles say slowing down and verifying before responding can help people avoid making a payment or sharing information based on a false request. They direct readers to PNC's Security and Privacy Center for more information on best practices to help prevent fraud.

The articles state that impersonation scams continue to evolve, but the underlying tactics remain the same: gaining your trust and pushing you to act quickly. They note that fraud experts warn scams can start across multiple channels, including phone calls, texts, email, messaging apps and social media. The pieces describe how AI-generated messages, real-time videos and mimicked voices can increase the likelihood that someone will respond without verifying. The articles present the five-step anatomy of a scam as contact, trust, urgency, request and extraction, with money or sensitive information handed over often before the request can be verified. They also give the example of impersonators telling people to say nothing to bank employees during a withdrawal because the employees are "compromised."

The articles say slowing down and verifying before you respond can help you avoid making a payment or sharing information based on a false request. They advise reaching out using a known phone number or official website, not the information provided in the message, and verifying and confirming with additional sources. Readers are told to talk to someone they trust before acting, since a second opinion can help spot red flags. The articles leave open which specific scams prompted the warning, how often such scams occur, and what results any reported cases produced. They also do not say what PNC's Security and Privacy Center contains beyond pointing readers to it for more information on best practices to help prevent fraud.

stories.Headline: Global shares decline as AI stocks tumble following new US chip restrictions and Nvidia leadership turmoil
stories.Summary:
Global shares traded broadly lower on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, as artificial intelligence stocks remained under heavy pressure. This decline followed a significant tumble for AI industry stocks on Wall Street during the previous trading day. Most markets in Asia and Europe fell, although India saw an advance in its Sensex index by 0.6%. U.S. futures edged lower and oil prices dropped as investors reacted to the ongoing volatility in technology. The downturn occurred just as regional leaders gathered for major summits across Asia during the current week.

Germany's DAX fell 0.8% to 26,387.92, Paris's CAC 40 declined 0.5% to 8,307.83, and Britain's FTSE 100 slid 0.7% to 10,805.92. South Korea's Kospi dropped 2.6% to 4,968.48, while Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.3% to 58,860.43 and Taiwan's Taiex plunged 2.3%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng sank 1% to 23,508.17, the Shanghai Composite fell 0.5% to 3,584.58, and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 1.8% to 8,883.20. Samsung Electronics fell 3.1%, SK Hynix dropped 1.8%, SoftBank Group tumbled 3.9%, and the testing equipment maker Advantest slumped 4.4%. The S&P 500 future fell 0.2%, the Dow future dropped 0.4%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.4% on Monday.

Zhiwei Zhang, the president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, stated that the market already worried about these risks. He noted in a commentary that the current situation has made the existing risks even more serious for investors. The Trump administration is responsible for issuing new rules on Monday to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing servers. These rules specifically target advanced U.S. computing chips to increase government scrutiny over the artificial intelligence sector's operations. Interim CEO Colette Kress is now the person responsible for speaking to Wall Street regarding the company's latest results.

Other chip companies were affected as their shares fell after previously climbing on hopes of gaining a competitive advantage. Investors are affected by the volatility, having grown accustomed to Nvidia reporting results and revenue forecasts that exceed analyst expectations. The Bank of England may affect borrowers if it raises interest rates following October inflation data due this Wednesday. Market participants are also watching for signs of cross-border cooperation and trade agreements from leaders in Manila and Shenzhen. Geopolitical tensions continue to affect investor sentiment as regional leaders meet for the ASEAN and APEC summits this week.

Nvidia lost 735 billion dollars in market value after disclosures regarding CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs and alleged Chinese spy ties. On Monday, the S&P 500 index was 1.9% lower and the Nasdaq composite index lost 2.5% as losses broadened. The AI industry has faced criticism that stock prices were in a bubble and fears regarding Democratic midterm election victories. Japan's economy contracted in the July-September quarter, which ended three consecutive quarters of growth according to official government data. Treasury yields eased back after a jump caused by a worse than expected report on U.S. inflation last week.

Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results on Tuesday, and President Donald Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday. Brent crude edged 0.7% lower to 91.80 dollars, while U.S. benchmark crude oil slid 0.6% to 85.20 dollars per barrel. The U.S. dollar fell to 159.24 Japanese yen, and the euro rose to 1.1004 dollars from a previous 1.1001. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains above the monthly low of 4.80%. The articles leave open whether the Bank of England will raise rates and if trade agreements will be reached.

stories.Headline: Anthropic warns that current AI safety tests are too easy and fail to capture advanced model capabilities
stories.Summary:
The frontier AI lab Anthropic issued a warning about safety tests on Friday, November 17, 2026. The company stated that current evaluations for artificial intelligence models have become too easy. These tests fail to capture the full breadth of capabilities in advanced models. Labs have focused on measuring how models follow directions and remain safe. Anthropic believes that these safety evaluations now have a significant problem.

The lab suggests building testing teams with experts who can sample, grade, and analyze responses. Domain experts must cover realistic test cases, and safety tests should be run in a sandbox. Enterprises must match evaluation designs to specific questions and use nuanced simulations to ensure results generalize. Tests should be neither too easy nor too hard for the models to complete. This approach replaces single-turn tasks with more expansive multi-turn conversations to reduce saturation.

Anthropic said that a single headline number for harmless response rates provides only an honest summary. The lab noted that more nuance is generally needed to make the findings useful. They explained that humans extract harmful information through gradual escalation over several prompts. The company stated that user distress tends to accumulate across a conversation and changes context. They argued that frontier labs should focus on these realistic, subtle situations of villainy.

Many experts warned that current tests miss how persistent AI models are in achieving goals. These concerns affect frontier labs and enterprises that rely on these safety benchmarks for security. Some testers attempt to goad models into divulging blueprints for a nuclear weapon. Malicious users avoid direct requests because they know models are experts at denying them. These users instead keep conversations going to break safeguards by the fifth turn.

Benchmarks have come under scrutiny recently after rogue AI agents began going against their instructions. Models are now outgrowing benchmarks because their capabilities exceed what current safety evaluations can test. Single-turn evaluations on the Anthropic API consistently score between 94 percent and 98 percent. Multi-turn responses show a wider range of harmless behavior response rates than single-turn tasks. This background shows that models handle first messages well but may respond inappropriately later.

Anthropic and OpenAI have paused training on their models to strengthen safety and alignment guardrails. They are working to improve safety testing procedures to keep pace with advanced models. The lab intends to incorporate more multi-turn evaluations to give researchers a better idea of abilities. The articles do not state when the paused training for these models will resume. They also leave open how other frontier labs will respond to these safety warnings.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a November 2026 public offering using a governance structure to protect its public benefit mission
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to launch an initial public offering on Wall Street during this current month of November in the year 2026. The San Francisco startup intends to go public while maintaining a pledge to prioritize the benefit of humanity during AI development. This transition to a public company will test a commitment the firm has held since the time of its founding. The company wants to balance the new pressure to deliver profits with its original mission to help the general public. This move marks a significant shift as the startup prepares for its official debut on the American stock market.

The company is a public benefit corporation, which is a legal designation used to balance shareholder interests with the public good. Anthropic has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect its broader mission against various financial interests. This legal status is also used by its rival, OpenAI, to manage the tension between profit and social benefit. Experts say the described mechanisms give the company wide leeway to decide how it measures its benefit to society. The company is operating in uncharted territory as it reaches a potential valuation of many trillions of dollars.

The company is responsible for creating a governance structure that protects its mission from the pull of financial interests. Anthropic says this structure will ensure that the company continues to prioritize humanity as it develops its artificial intelligence. The firm claims that its legal status as a public benefit corporation helps it maintain this specific social balance. These internal mechanisms are designed to keep the company focused on the public good during its growth. The startup maintains that its mission remains central even as it seeks to attract new public investors.

Sarah Kreps is a professor and director at Cornell University who provided an expert perspective on the company's new filing. She stated that the real test emerges if the question of public benefit becomes costly for the business. Kreps believes a conflict may arise when the public benefit clashes with the need to make a profit. Other experts are affected by these developments as they monitor how trillion dollar AI firms handle social responsibilities. These observers are concerned that the company has too much wiggle room in its official IPO filing.

Anthropic was founded as a startup in San Francisco with a core mission to develop artificial intelligence for humanity's benefit. The company chose to incorporate as a public benefit corporation to legally embed this social mission into its structure. This background mirrors the approach taken by OpenAI, which also uses the public benefit corporation legal designation. The firm has spent its early years developing AI while promising to avoid prioritizing profits over the public good. This history sets the stage for the tension expected during its upcoming transition to a public company.

The company will now move forward with its initial public offering to begin trading on the Wall Street stock exchange. This process will determine if the firm can actually prioritize humanity while meeting the demands of its shareholders. The articles leave open exactly how the company will measure whether it is successfully benefiting the global society. It remains unclear if the governance structure will be strong enough to resist the pressure for higher financial returns. The final outcome of this experiment in corporate governance will be seen after the IPO is complete.

stories.Headline: IDB report finds broad AI adoption could raise Latin America and Caribbean GDP by 5.1% over a decade
stories.Summary:
The Inter-American Development Bank published a report finding that broad adoption of artificial intelligence could boost Latin America and the Caribbean’s gross domestic product by 5.1% over a decade. The report, released on Monday, November 16, 2026, is titled “From Digitalization to Artificial Intelligence: Turning Promises into Productivity.” It is the 2026 edition of the Development in the Americas series and runs 422 pages. The Washington-based organization also projected that wages could increase by 4.2% over the same period. The findings were fundamental to September’s meeting of the IDB Group-led Partnership for AI Adoption.

The report states that in a high-adoption, high-productivity-impact scenario, the region’s total factor productivity could increase by 2.3%. It says 35% of adults reported using generative AI in 2025-2026, compared with 43% in European OECD countries and 58% in the United States. Only 26% of adults report having recently interacted with government digitally, compared with 70% in OECD countries, and only 27% report having recently made purchases online, compared with 66% in OECD countries. While 63% of digitally engaged firms surveyed report using generative AI, 82% rely on off-the-shelf tools or light adaptations rather than solutions integrated into their operations. The report says 90% of people in the region can submit their taxes online.

IDB Group President Ilan Goldfajn said artificial intelligence can become a powerful accelerator of development, but its benefits will not come automatically. He said the Partnership for AI Adoption brings together governments and leading technology companies to help the region harness AI’s potential to raise productivity and translate those gains into better jobs, better public services, and shared prosperity. Laura Alfaro Maykall, IDB chief economist and economic counselor, said the report provides one of the most comprehensive economic assessments of what digitalization and AI could mean for the region, moving the discussion from potential to evidence. She said the research quantifies how AI could affect productivity, growth, and wages and identifies the conditions for countries to capture those gains. Julián Cristia, lead economist at the IDB, said governments will play a key role because they must promote AI adoption while the digital agenda is still unfinished.

The report calls for targeted training and enhanced income support for displaced workers, education systems that promote adaptability, greater private and public investments in cybersecurity including data privacy, and regulations that carefully weigh the costs and benefits to households. It says labor mobility is critical to ensure that benefits are large and widely shared. The report offers three prescriptions: strengthen enabling conditions by investing in institutions, digital skills, data, cybersecurity and reliable digital infrastructure; transform government by going beyond isolated pilot projects and integrating public-sector systems around AI while maintaining human oversight; and accelerate business adoption by increasing access to finance, technical assistance, training and innovation. IDB officials note that smaller and informal firms often lack managerial capacity, financing and technological support needed to adopt AI effectively. Cristia acknowledges the region lags far behind in human capital and that AI adoption varies with educational attainment.

The report says the region has struggled with weak productivity growth for six decades. It says digital technologies are already improving business operations and public services, and AI adoption can expand these gains. In Mexico, an AI-based app helped reduce users’ depression by 20%; in Costa Rica, an electronic single-window system increased export values by 46%; and in São Paulo, Brazil, a digital health platform serves 3.4 million users and has delivered 2 million teleconsultations. The report says studies show productivity increases of 59% among writers, 26% among software developers and 15% among customer service providers who use AI. The IDB was founded in 1959 and works with the region’s public sector in 26 countries.

The report concludes that by strengthening institutions, skills, data, and digital infrastructure, and helping governments and firms put AI to productive use at scale, the region can turn technological change into lasting development gains. The report was released the same week that Anthropic is set to become the first major AI lab to go public. The Partnership for AI Adoption convenes governments from the region and leading technology companies, such as Google, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Nvidia. The press contact for the report is Rafael Mathus, with email rmathusruiz@iadb.org and phone +1 (202) 623-1040. The articles do not state what specific reforms countries have committed to or when the projected gains would be realized.

stories.Headline: Baidu head Robin Li warns that artificial intelligence could be a bubble
stories.Summary:
Robin Li, the head of Chinese technology giant Baidu, warned that artificial intelligence could be a bubble on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He spoke during a panel discussion with business leaders in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. This event took place ahead of talks between the world's top two economies regarding the sensitive AI sector. The warning came as the city hosted the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting this week. Li expressed concerns that AI adoption is not currently boosting profits for most companies.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to hold talks with U.S. counterpart Donald Trump on Thursday, November 19, during APEC. These leaders are expected to discuss the risks posed by AI and the need for cooperation between the two powerhouses. Baidu, based in Beijing, posted its sixth straight drop in quarterly revenue on Monday, November 16, due to online marketing headwinds. The company has made an aggressive push into AI, but a domestic consumer slump is currently dragging on its cash flows. Nvidia is also reporting quarterly results today, following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang last week.

Robin Li stated that the situation regarding the global landscape for technology is urgent and has fallen short of expectations. He questioned whether companies are seeing higher revenues or increased profits after adopting AI at the application layer. Li argued that if these issues are not addressed, the concern that AI is a bubble could become a reality. He noted that while there is intense competition at the foundational level, the financial benefits for most are absent. The CEO acknowledged that his own company has seen tangible results in its AI strategy despite the revenue drops.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva told AFP in October that losing confidence in AI returns could lead to worldwide financial stability risks. She warned that tanking stock market valuations could occur if investors stop believing in the future returns of these investments. Market jitters have increased because Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy before quitting his role. This scandal has led to more scrutiny of how Chinese firms access powerful Nvidia chips despite strict U.S. export rules. Nvidia has since rejected an offer from Huang to return as CEO despite pressure from Silicon Valley.

Baidu is sometimes called China's Google and has focused heavily on AI development in recent years to stay competitive. The company continues to unveil new AI processors and supercomputing products to advance its technological capabilities in the field. The U.S. and China maintain a fierce rivalry in AI, yet calls for cooperation on safety steps are growing. Both nations are pushing for AI safety measures as chip tensions loom over the upcoming summit between Trump and Xi. These tensions are exacerbated by the ongoing struggle for control over the most powerful hardware used to train systems.

President Xi and President Trump will meet on Thursday to discuss the risks and potential cooperation regarding artificial intelligence. The world awaits the quarterly results from Nvidia to see if the investment boom remains healthy or is failing. It remains unclear if the two tech powerhouses can overcome their rivalry to establish shared safety standards for AI. The articles leave open whether Baidu can reverse its revenue decline while continuing its aggressive push into AI technology. Investors are still watching to see if AI adoption will eventually translate into higher profits for the majority of companies.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA expands supply chain partnerships to scale AI infrastructure production
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, NVIDIA announced expanded commitments with several supply chain partners to support sustainable long-term growth for its AI infrastructure. The company is working with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries, and TSMC to scale production. These efforts aim to align manufacturing capacity with the demand for accelerated computing and AI infrastructure platforms across the globe. NVIDIA is expanding capacity for substrates, advanced packaging, wafer, and contract manufacturing to support current and next-generation computing platforms. This strategic move ensures the company can deliver the necessary hardware to its customers as AI technology continues to evolve.

Kinsus will expand ABF package substrate capacity by over 3.5x at its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan, by the third quarter of 2028. Production at the Youth campus is expected to begin in the second half of 2027 under a new multiyear agreement with NVIDIA. Samsung Electro-Mechanics amended its agreement to improve operational capabilities at existing factories located in Sejong and Busan, South Korea, for NVIDIA. NVIDIA provided multibillion-dollar funding to SPIL for expanding advanced packaging operations in Taiwan, with increased capacity targeted for completion by mid-2029. Amkor received nearly 3 billion dollars through agreements in July and October 2026 for packaging expansion in Arizona and South Korea.

Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations at NVIDIA, stated that the company's supply chain serves as a strategic advantage for growth. Scott Chen, CEO and president of Kinsus, believes that AI will be one of the most important technology transitions of our lifetime. Duck-Hyun Chang, CEO of Samsung Electro-Mechanics, said they will act as a total solution provider to supply the global market. Kevin Engel, president and CEO of Amkor, noted that long-term planning allows them to advance packaging technologies as production needs grow. C.W. Tsai, CEO and chairman of SPIL, said the agreement enhances their ability to support next-generation packaging for AI systems.

Young Liu, chairman of Foxconn, said their global production network in Asia, North America, and Europe supports the ramp-up of AI infrastructure. Dr. Kevin Zhang of TSMC mentioned that their deep collaboration allows them to prepare manufacturing capabilities for new NVIDIA platforms. Koji Kawashima of IBIDEN stated that expanding the Ono Plant will strengthen production capabilities to meet the growing market demand. Gauss Chang of KYEC said that expanding testing operations into the United States brings their capabilities closer to NVIDIA's supply chain. SC Chien, chairman of Unimicron, said that investing in advanced substrate technologies helps customers unlock new opportunities in the AI era.

NVIDIA previously announced manufacturing expansions in October with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL, and Unimicron to build its foundation. Those plans included an aggregate 2.5x increase in substrate capacity over three years and a doubling of semiconductor testing capacity by 2027. SPIL's optical-engine capacity was set to increase 15x by mid-2027, with another doubling targeted for the end of 2028 for NVIDIA. The company has maintained decades-long partnerships with these suppliers to ensure the stability of its complex global semiconductor manufacturing and assembly network. These combined efforts support the production of high-performance IC package substrates and advanced semiconductor testing for the company's accelerated computing platforms.

Volume shipments of Vera CPUs and NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 for agentic AI began in the third quarter using TSMC's advanced technologies. These specific products leverage TSMC's 5nm and 3nm processes along with CoWoS advanced packaging to achieve high performance and power efficiency. Future steps include the completion of new production lines at SPIL that span bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly, and testing. The articles leave open how global economic and political conditions or changes in industry standards might impact these long-term manufacturing goals. They also do not specify the exact dates for when all the expanded capacities will be fully operational across every partner site.

stories.Headline: Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max flagship AI model to challenge US rivals
stories.Summary:
Alibaba introduced its new flagship artificial intelligence model, Qwen4-Max, on Sunday. The company launched this proprietary system to challenge rivals from the United States. This release occurred on November 17, 2026, according to TechGig. The model aims to improve the handling of complex professional and scientific tasks. It also boosts safety protections for users during various operations.

The model features a 2.4T parameter backbone and 71B active parameters per token. It includes 328B N-gram Embedding parameters and supports a 1M token context window. Users can access it via QwenCloud API, Token Plan, Qwen Studio, QwenWork, and Qoder. Input prices fell to 1.50 dollars per million tokens, while output costs dropped to 4.50 dollars. The system accepts text, images, and video with 393K maximum output tokens.

Alibaba stated that Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, which was released in August. The company said the model is more cost efficient and uses fewer tokens. They reported that internal testing found no evidence of significant high-risk capabilities. CEO Eddie Wu previously noted that the T-Head unit would roll out powerful chips. Alibaba claims the model rivals the performance of systems from Anthropic and OpenAI.

The model affects professionals in finance, law, healthcare, and precision manufacturing. It also serves those in 3D modeling, game development, and frontier scientific discovery. Benchmarks show it beats Kimi K3.1 on legal agent work with a 21.3 score. However, it trails Claude Opus 5.5 on coding and vision tasks. Other affected rivals include Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Tencent, which recently launched Hunyuan 4.

Chinese firms are fighting to build powerful systems without making them prohibitively expensive. Alibaba's Qwen series is currently the most downloaded open-weight model family globally. The company is building a full ecosystem that spans from models to AI chips. T-Head, the chipmaking unit, recently filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong. This launch follows other recent releases like Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro model.

Alibaba will make smaller versions of the Qwen4 series available to users soon. The company has already opened a Token Plan-only preview during this current month. The articles leave open whether the model will ever become an open-weight system. They do not state when the smaller model versions will be officially released. It remains unclear if the model will eventually surpass rivals in hard coding.

stories.Headline: ControlUp launches AI Visibility & Usage Insights for IT to track AI tool adoption
stories.Summary:
ControlUp announced AI Visibility & Usage Insights on November 17, 2026, a new capability giving IT a unified view of AI tools adoption, usage, and experience across the organization. The company said IT teams can see how employees use AI applications including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Notion AI, and others. ControlUp described itself as a company reinventing IT operations with its AI platform. The announcement was published by GlobeNewswire from San Francisco on November 17, 2026. VMblog.com published its article on the launch on November 17, 2026.

The capability includes a unified AI application inventory showing AI tools in use, including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Codex, and Notion AI, with application type, user counts, and top-used models. It offers adoption and usage insights tracking active employees, total usage, and average usage per user across devices and platforms. It provides AI experience scoring with an average AI score and per-application scores highlighting apps that may need attention. It adds platform and environment context showing which browsers, operating systems, and device groups employees use, such as how Copilot and ChatGPT Enterprise usage varies by browser and operating system. It compares AI usage and experience between employees on physical PCs and those on remote desktops, including virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI), desktop-as-a-service, and other remote environments.

It also gives PII risk visibility into sensitive data employees may expose through AI, such as API keys and banking information, with tracking and reporting. Flexible filtering focuses on groups by app, browser, platform, operating system, or device tag. Gartner projects generative AI model spending will grow from $13 billion in 2025 to $139 billion by 2030, citing Forecast: AI Spending, Worldwide, 2025-2030, 3Q26, published October 7, 2026, by Kay Arnott, Jon Erensen, Amarendra ., Adrian O'Connell, and Arunasree Chepa. The capability is offered as an add-on module available to all ControlUp for Apps and ControlUp for Desktops Advanced customers. A demo can be requested at https://www.controlup.com/schedule-a-demo/.

Bob Johnson, SVP Global Partnerships & Alliances at ControlUp, said employees are adopting AI tools faster than IT can track, leaving admins unable to answer basic questions about shadow AI, adoption, or spend. He said AI Visibility & Usage Insights gives IT a clear picture of AI tool adoption to guide governance, plan training, and optimize AI investments based on real usage, not guesswork. With this visibility, IT teams can drive AI adoption by seeing where licensed users are active and where adoption is lagging. They can improve employee experience by spotting underperforming AI applications early and plan investment by comparing adoption and performance to decide where to expand, consolidate, or add enablement. They can establish usage guardrails with a shared, evidence-based view of the AI tools in use across the organization.

The articles state that AI adoption is accelerating across the enterprise as employees use a growing mix of AI assistants, coding tools, and embedded AI features. IT teams are being asked to manage spend and demonstrate value, yet many lack a clear picture of the AI application footprint, including which tools employees use, on which devices, and where more support would help. ControlUp said its capability gives IT a data-backed baseline and a clear view of the AI footprint in their environment. ControlUp describes its platform as built on real-time data, intelligent decisions, and automated action to help IT teams detect, resolve, and prevent issues before they impact the business. The platform delivers Autonomous Endpoint Management (AEM), unifying Digital Employee Experience (DEX) capabilities with agentic AI, and ControlUp ONE integrates real-time signals with AI-driven decisioning and automated remediation.

Attendees can experience AI Visibility & Usage Insights live at the ControlUp booth #5257L at Microsoft Ignite, November 17, 20 in San Francisco. ControlUp experts will demo how IT teams can baseline Copilot adoption and extend that visibility across their AI landscape. The articles leave open what the add-on module costs and when it becomes generally available beyond the stated customer eligibility. They do not say how many customers currently use ControlUp for Apps or ControlUp for Desktops Advanced. They do not give adoption figures for any of the named AI tools. They do not state results from the Microsoft Ignite demonstrations.

stories.Headline: Anthropic sells shares to the public for the first time as Samsung and SK hynix cash holdings surge
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is selling its shares to the public for the first time according to a report from November 17, 2026. This company was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI to create the Claude models. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix also saw their cash holdings surge during the same period of the AI boom. These two South Korean chip giants reported their financial results in corporate filings released on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The surge in wealth for these firms is driven by strong global demand for artificial intelligence memory chips.

Combined liquid holdings for the chipmakers reached 329.23 trillion won, or 246.33 billion dollars, by the end of September. This total rose from 136.3 trillion won a year earlier and from 277.91 trillion won at the end of June. Samsung Electronics held 214.77 trillion won in cash and short term instruments, up from 108.44 trillion won last year. SK hynix reported 114.46 trillion won in liquid assets, which is more than quadruple its previous 27.85 trillion won. The combined holdings increased by 51.32 trillion won in the three months between June and September of 2026.

Corporate filings from the two chipmakers show they benefited from high bandwidth memory used in AI data centers. Samsung Electronics posted cumulative operating profits of approximately 254 trillion won during the first three quarters of this year. SK hynix reported cumulative operating profits of approximately 181 trillion won for the same period of the current year. Katie Prescott, the technology business editor at The Times, explained who will make a fortune from the Anthropic float. She noted that the company is now selling shares to the public for the first time since its founding.

The investors in Anthropic are set to win big from the mega float of the AI powerhouse, Katie Prescott wrote. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than one fourth of the stock market credit loans in Korea. Some Seoul stocks fell sharply on Tuesday morning because of lingering worries regarding the artificial intelligence industry. Authorities are investigating potential AI assisted cheating across 528 national exams before the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test. The prime minister vowed to root out this cheating during the college entrance exams taking place this week.

The AI boom has increased demand for advanced memory chips and high bandwidth memory used in large AI data centers. Anthropic was started by seven people who previously worked at OpenAI before they founded their own company in 2021. Korean startup Upstage is now teaming up with Canada's Cohere to provide sovereign AI solutions for enterprise clients. These security focused solutions are being developed for clients located across the Asia Pacific region of the global market. The chipmakers have seen their combined cash holdings more than double over the past year due to this demand.

The company Anthropic will now move forward with its initial public offering to sell shares to the general public. Authorities will tighten checks on smart glasses to prevent cheating before the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test begins. The articles do not state the specific price of the shares being sold during the Anthropic mega float. It remains unclear how the Seoul stock market will react to the lingering woes of the AI industry. The reports leave open whether the AI chip demand will continue to drive cash holdings for Korean chipmakers.

stories.Headline: HPE and AMD debut Lux AI cluster at No 14 on TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops
stories.Summary:
At SC26 in Chicago, HPE announced that Lux, an AI cluster built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, debuted at No. 14 on the TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops of measured HPL performance. HPE said the system, purpose-built for AI training and inference, placed ahead of machines designed for traditional supercomputing workloads. Lux is the first dedicated AI system to come online for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission. HPE and AMD co-designed and co-constructed the cluster, which gives researchers across the U.S. multi-tenant, cloud-like access. The debut was announced on November 16, 2026, according to the articles.

Lux runs on direct liquid-cooled HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 systems with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and AMD Pensando DPUs. The network uses HPE Juniper Networking QFX switches running 800G Ethernet, with load balancing and congestion management that HPE says reduce bottlenecks and improve GPU utilization. HPE Networking Data Center Director handles intent-based deployment, management, and lifecycle automation. Half of Lux’s 3.5 million annual node-hours are dedicated to the Genesis Mission, and the other half are available for proprietary use, a total equivalent to about 400 nodes running around the clock for a year. HPE has made a $37 million in-kind investment in the program to support research projects.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said the company, with ORNL and AMD, had delivered breakthrough engineering innovation and was furthering what it can accomplish as a proven public-private partnership. She said HPE was proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems. Georgia Tourassi, associate director of computing and computational sciences at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, said she was excited for the debut and the opportunities it creates to expand access to advanced computing resources. She said Lux will give researchers additional capacity and flexibility to advance innovative SI approaches in Earth system prediction, materials development, biology, and fusion energy. Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president of global public sector and strategic partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together.

AMD said the cluster runs its ROCm software stack, and neither company has published a node or GPU count for the system. AMD said Lux is now open to scientific users. HPE describes Lux as the first deployment of HPE Networking products at a DOE national laboratory, bringing scalable, high-performance, open Ethernet to AI-driven science. The Genesis Mission is a DOE program that applies AI to energy research, scientific discovery, and national security on a platform combining AI, supercomputing, quantum systems, and scientific instruments. Zacharia tied Lux to an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that researchers across the country can use.

HPE announced Lux about a year ago as part of its broader collaboration with ORNL and AMD. The partnership also includes Discovery, a forthcoming next-generation supercomputer developed as the successor to Frontier, which first broke the exascale speed barrier. ORNL has said Discovery will pair AMD EPYC Venice CPUs with AMD Instinct MI430X GPUs on an HPE Cray Supercomputing platform, with delivery expected in 2028. Lux carries the integrated management and Silicon Root of Trust protection found across HPE ProLiant servers. The configuration equips Lux with the performance necessary for large model AI training and deep learning.

The articles do not say when Lux began operating beyond its debut at SC26. They leave open how many nodes or GPUs the system contains. They do not state which proprietary users will take the half of node-hours not dedicated to the Genesis Mission. They do not give a date for Discovery’s delivery beyond 2028. They do not say what the $37 million in-kind investment will fund specifically.
