stories.Headline: UN chief Guterres warns autonomous weapons cross a moral red line as Geneva talks open
stories.Summary:
Negotiations on possible rules for lethal autonomous weapons, also called killer robots, are underway at the United Nations in Geneva. This week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons, or CCW, meets just once every five years. Supporters of controls say it is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late. Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, and some experts warn the world is months away from weapons that choose targets and decide to kill autonomously. In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, though these are still controlled remotely by humans.

At least 50 countries, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree binding rules governing autonomous weapons. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules. Washington proposes a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead. U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus, which was achieved in 1995 when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers. This week there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period for rules individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be crossing a moral red line. Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, said the risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, autonomous weapons cannot understand contextual signals the way a human does. She said the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target. U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk called on states to urgently agree on binding international rules to regulate autonomous weapons and protect human lives before it is too late. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society this weekend, warned against quoting laws to men with swords.

Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill, and responsibility for that choice, must stay in human hands. The United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules ahead of this week's meeting. The Red Cross is especially worried that the Geneva Conventions cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons, under which soldiers who are wounded or surrendering can no longer be targeted. Human rights groups warn the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use, with greater danger of proliferation and use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or everyone speaking a certain language.

Ukrainian civilians have reported being hunted by drones as they shop or go to school. The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties and did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, although it over time stopped deploying them and reduced its stockpiles. Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown, and Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention. An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies was demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29.

No treaty or laws will be enacted after this week's conference, but it could lay the groundwork for future legislation. Nicole van Rooijen, part of the campaign group Stop Killer Robots, told Newsweek that the majority of states worldwide want a legally binding treaty. She says failing to act could allow technology to further shape the rules surrounding killer robots in warfare. For diplomats supporting a compromise, it is a way to ensure at least some progress, while for campaigners it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road. Last month, Anthropic, operator of Claude, said in its latest threat intelligence report that Russian-based cybercriminals and Iranian propaganda actors tried to use the AI model for malicious reasons, including attempts to develop software for conventional weapons, firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions, as well as targeting and control systems.

stories.Headline: Australia circulates first draft decision as COP31 ministers arrive to seek compromises
stories.Summary:
COP31 entered its second and final week on Monday, November 16, 2026, at the conference centre in Antalya, Türkiye. Negotiators remained deadlocked on fossil fuels, finance, and adaptation as ministers arrived for the formal high-level segment on Tuesday. Australia, the lead negotiator and co-host, circulated a first draft of an overarching decision late on Monday. This draft serves as a starting point, though countries disagree on its contents and whether it should exist. Ministers will meet in a Divan, an Ottoman imperial assembly, to seek political compromises on these contentious issues.

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge secured 80 endorsements and 271 commitments to make AI technology more sustainable. Governments also launched the Antalya Green Industrialization Compact to accelerate investment in cleaner cement, steel, and other industrial products. Vulnerable nations are pushing for the next IPCC climate assessment to be published by a deadline in 2028. The Climate Club Secretariat, a coalition of 53 countries, is working to cut industrial emissions through existing technologies. These initiatives aim to reduce environmental footprints and create markets for cleaner products in developing economies.

Soenke Kreft of the United Nations University said the slow first half of negotiations now requires a momentum swing. Laurence Tubiana of the European Climate Foundation stated that the world must defend science and the scientists. Mary Robinson, former President of Ireland, urged countries to resolve differences so the IPCC assessment is delivered on time. ITU Deputy Secretary-General Tomas Lamanauskas warned that data centre energy consumption is expected to double by 2030. Ciyong Zou of UNIDO said green industrialization turns renewable energy momentum into jobs and energy security.

Climate activists warned that cover decisions could become a distraction from concrete action and necessary resources for workers. A Climate Action Network representative criticized just transition mechanisms that offer a seat at the table without food. Affected workers include coal miners in Australia, steel workers in Germany, India, and UK, and miners in Africa. Activists also questioned the replenishment of climate funds, noting that only the Solomon Islands announced a Green Climate Fund contribution. Scientists warned that decisions must be guided by evidence regarding the risks of exceeding the 1.5°C warming threshold.

AI can predict extreme weather and improve energy efficiency, but powerful models require vast amounts of water and electricity. Some technology companies have seen emissions rise by 50 per cent, while AI chatbots sometimes abandon established climate facts. Álvaro Rojas used AI to analyze 1,600 disaster risk management documents to identify where countries need loss support. Brigitte Perrin is developing Beluga, an AI platform to centralize fragmented scientific research from various UN and scientific organizations. Peter Schniering noted that electric furnaces and smarter building designs can reduce emissions from steel and concrete.

Next, ministers must decide if they will agree on a cover text regarding the transition away from fossil fuels. They must also bridge disagreements over public funding obligations and financial support for developing economies and climate adaptation. Negotiators need to agree on a mechanism to support communities and workers through a just energy transition. The final outcome will determine if the 1.5°C temperature goal is reinforced and if the issue of overshoot is addressed. The articles leave open whether countries will reach a political compromise on these divided and contentious issues.

The AI trade unwind continued on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, which pushed global stocks lower. Investors prepared for the stock market launch of Anthropic later in the week. Nvidia released its quarterly results, and the stock rose 4% in choppy trade. Solid US retail sales and hawkish Federal Reserve comments kept expectations for higher interest rates alive. Jamie McGeever reported these events from Orlando, Florida.

The S&P 500 tech sector fell 20% since October 6, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor index dropped 30%. Nvidia lost nearly 40% since October 6, shedding over 1.7 trillion dollars in market value. Alphabet lost 640 billion dollars, SpaceX lost 450 billion dollars, and Micron lost 300 billion dollars. Eli Lilly added 250 billion dollars, while gold fell to a one-year low of 3,950 dollars per ounce. Japan stocks fell 1.3%, Europe and UK stocks fell 1.8%, Nasdaq fell 0.7%, S&P 500 fell 1%, and Dow fell 1.6%.

St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said the economy likely requires several interest rate increases before spring 2027. The US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, and Huang agreed to appear before Congress.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, said diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's will be relics in less than a decade. Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks disagreed on X, stating that progress will likely be steady and incremental. BofA's Michael Hartnett named healthcare among the groups most vulnerable to downside in a recent report. He also listed semiconductors, discretionary, and homebuilders as most vulnerable to upside over the next eight weeks. Investors in tech and chips were affected by heavy selling, while the US dollar hit a 19-month high.

AI stocks lost about 5 trillion dollars in less than a month during October. Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk gained 92% on average in 15 months after the October 2022 low. Novo Nordisk lost three-quarters of its value from its June 2024 peak during the subsequent two years. Trump's China data center curb advanced despite lobbying from Amazon, Google, and Meta. Nvidia's daughter, a senior director of product marketing, helped shape the defense of ties to Megaspeed in Singapore.

stories.Headline: Validix unveils Atomic Claim Architecture to govern and verify generative AI content
stories.Summary:
Validix, a Swiss company advancing governed claims for enterprise AI, unveiled its Atomic Claim Architecture on Nov. 17, 2026, according to PR Newswire. The announcement was published by The Manila Times on November 17, 2026, at 10 a.m. Validix AG is based in Zug, Switzerland. The Atomic Claim Architecture is a new patent-pending invention that changes how organizations govern content produced by generative AI. It is a secure governance layer, independent of and complementary to large language models.

The architecture constrains what large language models can generate and verifies content before it is released. The model itself is not modified, so organizations can apply the architecture to AI tools they already use or plan to deploy in the future. The architecture breaks evidence into Atoms, which are small, verifiable units of truth, each traceable to its source. Every claim is built from these Atoms, so it can be traced to the evidence behind it. If AI-generated content cannot meet this standard, it is withheld or sent for human review.

Validix provides continuous monitoring of the evidence, and if the underlying source evidence changes, every affected claim is flagged and sent to a human reviewer. Upstream control, pre-release checks and continuous monitoring of evidence sources form what Validix calls a Governed Claims Infrastructure. Lluis Pallarès, co-founder of Validix, said every organization using AI to communicate is putting its name behind what the technology says. Pallarès said that responsibility cannot be delegated to a language model. Pallarès said the architecture turns evidence into enforceable boundaries for what AI is allowed to assert and makes release a separate, controlled decision without requiring changes to existing AI models.

Pallarès said Validix is designed to accelerate expert review, not replace it, and that reviewers see the evidence behind every claim and keep the final say. In the pharmaceutical sector alone, companies have incurred more than $66 billion in recorded regulatory penalties and settlements globally since 2010, according to Violation Tracker Global. United States False Claims Act settlements and judgments exceeded $6.8 billion last year, according to the DOJ. Validix's first application, built for teams that create, review and monitor content in life sciences, is already in live use at a pharmaceutical company following a pilot project. Marketing and sales teams can verify communications through the Validix platform to check that the information is supported by current evidence.

Validix plans to launch its commercial platform in early 2027 and is opening a limited number of pilot partnerships across regulated industries. A video explainer on how the Validix Atomic Claim Architecture works is available at validix.ch/how-validix-works. HellerWeather released an upgraded version of its AI-powered Content Creator, a browser-based tool that uses forecast and climate data to generate first drafts for vertical videos, webcasts, digital shorts, blog posts, newsletter articles and other formats. Tim Heller, a meteorologist and chief developer of the application, said there is never a quiet weather day thanks to Content Creator. HellerWeather said the new feature is part of its broader AI Tool, which launched earlier this year.

HellerWeather said the browser-based system saves most meteorologists three to five hours of preparation time per week. Heller said it does not take a creative genius to write that today will be partly cloudy with a high of 78. Heller said allowing AI to take care of some of the necessary yet time-consuming work allows meteorologists to focus on tracking severe weather and producing more engaging content. Heller said more content means more revenue. The company said users enter a location and the system applies background prompts built from Heller's 35 years of on-air experience.

Heller said meteorologists keep full editorial control before anything is produced, published or shared. Heller said zero prompting does not mean zero input and that there is always a human-in-the-loop. HellerWeather said the AI Tool also serves as a meteorological and climate research assistant, with access to traditional forecast models and newer AI weather models, including Google's WeatherNext. The company said proprietary forecast confidence rankings and in-app alert-day notifications help weather teams finalize forecasts. HellerWeather said the same data powers more than 20 first drafts that meteorologists can use on air, online and on social media.

The company said the generated content appears in English and can be rewritten in conversational American Spanish, a feature added last summer. HellerWeather said the system is built for browser-based use, strict data privacy and hallucination prevention. The company said it does not require or store proprietary client data. Heller said his goal in building the application is to help his colleagues and coaching clients work more efficiently and communicate more effectively. Heller said Content Creator and the HellerWeather AI Tool do not replace meteorologists but empower them.

stories.Headline: Senator Maria Cantwell urges the Commerce Department to enforce AI chip export controls against China
stories.Summary:
Senator Maria Cantwell released a demand on November 16, 2026, for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to enforce AI chip export controls. Her letter, dated November 15, challenges the Commerce Department for allowing China-linked companies to obtain advanced computing through overseas data centres. Cantwell, the ranking member of the Senate Commerce Committee, alleges that the department resisted restrictions on high-risk companies. This oversight intervention follows earlier reports regarding congressional demands for tighter remote-access controls to protect sensitive American technology. The senator urges Lutnick to use existing powers under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to strengthen enforcement.

The Bureau of Industry and Security published an interim final rule on November 16 to align remote access with physical shipment controls. This rule, directed by Treasury and the National Security Council, covers advanced-chip exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. It also restricts remote access for companies headquartered in China or other restricted destinations and includes a transition period for existing data centres. Cantwell also questioned a 25 percent fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she argues creates incentives for exports. Additionally, she cited 1.2 billion dollars in Nvidia stock held by Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm controlled by Lutnick's sons.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that Treasury, State, Defense, and the US Trade Representative supported restricting Megaspeed for several months. Bessent argued that existing rules require strict enforcement rather than new legislation to prevent national security threats. Cantwell paraphrased these concerns, alleging that Commerce delayed action on repeated warnings and suspended an investigation into the company Megaspeed. She claimed that the department weakened safeguards and allowed the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology. The senator asserted that national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or federal revenue.

House Speaker Mike Johnson stated that a growing consensus in Congress now favors additional restrictions on China's access to AI chips. Senator Elizabeth Warren and Senator Jim Banks argued that export-control decisions with national security implications require stronger congressional scrutiny. Research organisations buying or sharing access to advanced computing infrastructure are affected by these renewed focuses on remote access and intermediaries. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company, described its operations as a legitimate business and denied breaching any US export rules. China has also denied allegations regarding the suspected transfer of restricted chips to its companies.

The dispute involves Megaspeed and allegations that it helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia processors subject to US export controls. Authorities examined whether former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese spy, had a relationship with Jensen Huang. A New York Times report from November 9 alleged that the Commerce Department may have delayed its investigation into Megaspeed. Earlier reports from October 2025 indicated that US authorities were examining the diversion of restricted American computing technology to China. Alice Huang reportedly left the company in August 2025, though Megaspeed has not been found to violate rules.

The official rule text allows a comment period of 60 days after its publication in the Federal Register for research organisations. Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10 regarding the department's enforcement decisions. Chairman Tim Scott has also summoned Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to testify before the committee during the month of December. The articles leave open whether Megaspeed actually breached export rules or if commercial interests influenced the Commerce Department's decisions. It remains unclear if the new interim final rule will successfully close the remote-access loophole for Chinese firms.

stories.Headline: Cathie Wood's Ark buys Nvidia, CoreWeave and Archer Aviation and trims Palantir and Tempus AI
stories.Summary:
Cathie Wood's Ark Invest bought more Nvidia, CoreWeave and Archer Aviation and sold parts of its Tempus AI and Palantir holdings, Yahoo Finance reported on November 17, 2026. The Motley Fool's Marc Guberti wrote the article, published at 1:01 PM CST that day. Late last month Wood told a Bloomberg interviewer the AI trade is not in its first inning. She said the sector is "still in the parking lot before we entered the baseball game." She cited Palantir's 123% year-over-year U.S. revenue growth as evidence of the long-term opportunity in AI.

Most Ark Invest funds focus heavily on AI stocks, which have had a bumpy month but trended higher in recent years. Wood has put a lot of money behind her statement through Ark's exchange-traded funds. The article says AI demand will rise for chips, optical cables, liquid-cooling solutions and electricity. It says humanoid robots and self-driving vehicles are among the next big opportunities. Waymo leads the robotaxi space, and Tesla's Cybercabs are in limited production.

Wood is the founder of Ark Invest, and the article ties her bullish view to Palantir's 123% U.S. revenue growth. It says Palantir excels at agentic AI, which helps explain how the stock crushed the S&P 500 over five years. It says chipmakers keep reporting exceptional growth and enthusiasm for more AI growth in 2027 does not match recent stock performance. It says such setups create asymmetric risk opportunities but require accepting a lot of volatility. It says Wood's Ark Innovation ETF has had many downturns of 20% or more.

The article says the Ark Innovation ETF slumped more than 80% from its February 2021 peak to a December 2022 cyclical low. It says the fund is still down more than 50% from that peak despite promising periods in the intervening years. It says the fund has not recently had the upward momentum it enjoyed from the mid-2010s to 2021. It says the recent pullback in AI stocks has created a more compelling opportunity.

It says the Motley Fool holds positions in Palantir and Tesla and recommends both, and that Guberti has no position in any stock mentioned. The article says ChatGPT first had no connection to the live internet and could not take uploaded images, PDFs and other documents. It says Anthropic's Claude was similar early on but has become an autonomous digital coworker, and Claude Code can create entire apps and websites from a few prompts. It says new features will raise customer expectations, and in five to 10 years current versions of ChatGPT and Claude could look archaic.

It says Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots could become lucrative once AI robotics is ready for broad commercialization. It says 1990s investors underestimated the internet's impact, a pattern that may be taking shape with AI. The article says Stock Advisor's total average return is 802% against 205% for the S&P 500, as of November 17, 2026. It says $1,000 invested in Netflix on December 17, 2004 would be worth $327,620, and $1,000 in Nvidia on April 15, 2005 would be worth $959,410.

It says the Motley Fool's analysts named 10 best stocks to buy now and the Ark Innovation ETF was not one of them. It leaves open whether Wood's concentrated AI bet is still the right one. It does not give the size of the Nvidia, CoreWeave, Archer Aviation, Tempus AI or Palantir trades. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Zoho adds AI agents to Zoho Desk to combine automated tasks with human judgment
stories.Summary:
Zoho launched Blended Agents in its Zoho Desk customer service platform on November 18, 2026, for several global regions. Australia is among the first six regions where this new agentic tool is available to help businesses resolve issues. These AI agents carry out tasks across connected business applications before handing cases to human representatives for nuanced judgment. The handover includes full conversation history and context so that customers do not need to repeat their information. This launch occurs as companies test how far AI can be used without harming overall customer satisfaction levels.

Blended Agents are available in Australia, India, the US, the EU, Japan, and China, with Canada launching soon. They are included in all paid Zoho Desk plans, including Express, while Automation Studio requires Professional and Workstation requires Enterprise. Users pay only for large language model usage, receiving up to 30 million free tokens monthly depending on tier. Companies can also use their own API key and pay their chosen model provider directly for the AI usage. Data stays within Zoho data centres and is not used for training when using Zoho hosted models.

Chief Executive Officer Mani Vembu said that good customer service begins with understanding people through patience and empathy. He stated that Blended Agents are a natural extension of the philosophy upon which the Zoho Desk platform was built. Vembu explained that AI taking on routine tasks allows human representatives to spend more time on situations requiring judgment. This approach keeps customer service personal while providing teams with the tools they need to work more efficiently. He believes that understanding the context of each customer is essential for making a genuine effort to resolve problems.

A CHOICE Consumer Pulse survey cited by Zoho shows 51 percent of Australians say AI chatbots make experiences worse. These AI agents affect support staff by allowing them to pause execution to review or approve specific steps. The tools also help back office teams by identifying repeated issues and flagging scheduling conflicts for unavailable technicians. When support teams answer similar questions repeatedly, the software helps create knowledge base articles to reduce future contact. Businesses can now also manage WhatsApp calls, in chat payments, and existing WhatsApp Business app numbers through Zoho.

Zoho Desk launched in 2016 and now serves more than 125,000 businesses across 155 different countries around the world. The platform recorded a compound annual growth rate of about 35.3 percent between the years 2017 and 2025. Its largest revenue markets are India, the US, Continental Europe, and the Middle East and Africa region. Zoho is a privately held company based in Chennai, India, and employs more than 19,000 people globally. The broader company has more than 150 million users worldwide across hundreds of thousands of different business entities.

Next, businesses can use Automation Studio for no code workflows and Workstation to customise their ticket interface layouts. Support representatives can choose from six predefined styles or use a drag and drop builder for their panels. Companies can now publish knowledge base articles in Markdown and llms.txt formats for easier access by external AI platforms. The articles do not state when the Canada launch will occur or the specific costs for different token tiers. They also leave open how many businesses will adopt these tools to improve the reported Australian customer experience.

stories.Headline: Wolters Kluwer shows legal teams how purpose-built AI speeds contract workflows
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, Wolters Kluwer released an on-demand session regarding how modern legal departments can be powered by artificial intelligence. Speakers Jennifer McIver and Stephanie Allison demonstrated how specific tools like Legisway Advisor, Legisway Analyzer, and Expert AI help corporate legal professionals work faster. These AI-powered solutions are designed to automate repetitive tasks and accelerate contract workflows to improve overall productivity. The presentation focused on using purpose-built AI to uncover critical legal insights and deliver greater strategic value to a business.

Implementing these tools requires a unified legal platform to streamline workflows and improve visibility across various contracts. This technology allows legal teams to review documents more quickly, identify potential risks, and improve general compliance. In a separate report from November 16, 2026, Keao Caindec of the California-based company Clarra noted that AI performs better when accessing consolidated information. Internal tests at Clarra showed that moving away from disconnected platforms improved AI performance sixfold and increased token efficiency by approximately 80 percent.

Keao Caindec, the CEO of Clarra, stated that many corporate legal departments are rushing into AI investments without making necessary operational changes. Raman Rai, an adviser on AI deployment, told attendees at the Law.com General Counsel Conference East that companies often invest heavily without first determining which problems the technology should solve. Additionally, Kira Ciccarelli of Diligent argued that legal departments must have a clearly defined role in AI governance to influence critical decisions early. Robert Rivkin, the chief legal officer for United Airlines, suggested that using AI to the maximum extent before hiring outside counsel will likely become a common practice.

The broader context shows that while some firms like Intuit have used AI to cut costs by 82 percent, others struggle with governance and accuracy. Researchers and judges have warned that while fake citations are decreasing, subtler errors where real cases are used to support wrong points are becoming harder to detect. Legal professionals are also turning to tools like CCH Jurisdictional Compare to streamline multi-jurisdictional analysis through AI-powered collaboration. Future efforts in the field will likely focus on balancing this rapid innovation with strict governance and human judgment.

stories.Headline: C2ES report says AI data centers drive US electricity demand and clean firm power investment
stories.Summary:
U.S. electricity demand is rising for the first time in two decades, driven in part by the power needs of AI data centers, according to a report from the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions. To meet that demand, some hyperscalers are investing in clean firm technologies even though those options carry higher upfront costs and longer deployment timelines than conventional firm power. Clean firm technologies are low- or zero-carbon, dispatchable generation sources, including long-duration energy storage paired with clean energy, traditional and advanced nuclear, next-generation geothermal, and natural gas with carbon capture. Unabated natural gas remains the primary power source for U.S. data centers, and the report says the ultimate climate impact of AI's growth is uncertain.

The report, titled Beyond the Boom: Assessing the Role of AI Data Centers in Scaling Clean Firm Power Technologies, examines why some hyperscalers are making these investments and how the investments could facilitate broader adoption of clean firm power. It also looks at what policies, such as tax credit extensions and permitting reform, are needed to help these technologies compete and scale more effectively. C2ES will present the report's findings at an event on Tuesday, December 1, 2026, from 12:00 to 1:30 p.m. ET. The event will include a fireside chat with Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and C2ES President Nat Keohane, along with a panel discussion with perspectives from hyperscalers, utilities, and clean firm technology providers.

Diandra Angiello, a Technology Innovation Policy Associate Fellow at C2ES, conducts research and analysis on emerging climate technologies such as engineered carbon removal, clean firm generation, and clean hydrogen. Sheldon Whitehouse represents Rhode Island in the U.S. Senate, where he is the Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and Co-Chair of another group, and he champions policies to protect the planet and hold the powerful accountable. Nathaniel Keohane is President of C2ES, a nonpartisan non-profit organization based in Washington, D.C., that works with policy makers and leading businesses on the transition to a net-zero-emissions economy. The articles do not say what happens after the December 1 event.

stories.Headline: Northeastern University London researchers propose in-game AI companions for player mental health support
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Northeastern University London published a peer-reviewed paper suggesting that in-game AI companions could provide psychological support for video game players. This proposal comes as artificial intelligence already functions as a fundamental part of modern gaming by adapting gameplay based on player behavior. The paper, titled Serving the Player or Shaping Them?, argues that these embedded systems can shape a gamer's wellbeing over time. Melika Vafafar, a PhD researcher in computer science, is the corresponding author who believes AI should not be simple characters. This academic provocation explores whether generative AI can be repurposed to support the emotional health of people who play games.

The proposal requires generative AI companions to have sophisticated conversations and use language models to produce real-time responses for the human players. These systems could use sensors in controllers to detect sweaty palms or track brain signals, skin conductance, and eye movements. Vafafar notes that games like PUBG: Battlegrounds and Where Winds Meet already use generative AI for characters that offer helpful tips. Such AI could notice frustration in a voice and encourage a break during a long session or after a losing streak. This approach targets gamers who may play for hundreds of hours a month, creating opportunities to influence their cognition and behavior.

Melika Vafafar stated that adaptive and emotionally responsive AI companions could become systems capable of shaping the wellbeing of players over time. She argued that games could become a platform for emotional support that feels far more personal than any existing digital tools. Christiane Eichenberg, head of the Institute for Psychosomatics at Sigmund Freud Private University, said AI is no substitute for human help. Eichenberg noted that chatbots are non-judgemental and available round the clock, which makes it easier for many people to open up. She added that some scientifically evaluated AI mental health programmes show effects comparable to psychotherapy when used for several weeks.

Travis Gilly, executive director of the Real Safety AI Foundation in Illinois, argued that game studios lack the expertise for such research. He questioned whether studios want to support players or simply add features that make people get attached to the game characters. Amy Bussey from the U.K. charity Ygam said AI could complement support systems for young people facing barriers to help. Bussey warned that boundaries between entertainment and emotional support are blurring, raising concerns about privacy, age assurance, and inaccurate medical advice. These risks affect young people, who might develop emotional dependency or a skewed understanding of relationships through their AI companions.

The articles explain that people turn to chatbots like Gemini, Claude, or ChatGPT because they are accessible and avoid social stigma. In Germany, those seeking therapy must wait an average of 20 weeks, which increases the popularity of these automated conversation partners. Previous AI support has come from chatbots like Replika and Wysa, which can reduce loneliness and improve a user's mood. However, another Northeastern University London study found that AI chatbots can cause emotional dependence, exacerbate symptoms, and even lead to self-harm. General chatbots differ from specialized mental health applications that operate based on clinically validated treatment protocols to help users manage stress.

Future AI companions may use repeated interactions to positively influence the habits and emotions of gamers through personalized and adaptive support. Specialist therapeutic chatbots might be used to bridge waiting times for traditional therapy or provide real-time support during acute stressful situations. Kevin Hilbert, a professor at the Health and Medical University of Erfurt, suggests AI may be effective for mild distress. The articles leave open whether the positive effects of AI-based mental health programmes are stable or long-lasting for the users. It remains undecided how much responsibility should be entrusted to generative AI to benefit human lives and society as a whole.

stories.Headline: Karnataka chief minister D K Shivakumar launches six AI and semiconductor initiatives at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026
stories.Summary:
Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar launched six initiatives at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, which opened on November 17, 2026, in Bengaluru. The summit runs from November 17 to 19 and is themed "AI & Beyond". The Karnataka AI Hub was officially launched at the summit and is established at IIIT-Bengaluru. The state government had earlier approved a ₹35 crore budget for the Karnataka AI Hub. The summit's exhibitors come from more than 75 countries, according to its official website.

The Karnataka AI Hub will focus on AI research, skilling, innovation and entrepreneurship, and is the first step towards the state's proposed AI University. BRAINZ, the Bengaluru Robotics and AI Innovation Zone, is an envisioned 9-acre facility in collaboration with ARTPARK at the Indian Institute of Science. BRAINZ aims to catalyse investments of ₹1,000 crore over five years. The state is supporting IISc's proposed 200-mm research and pilot-line facility under the 2D Innovation Hub, which includes a technology building of about 100,000 sq ft, a 15,000 sq ft cleanroom and 80 to 90 process, metrology and testing tools. The state is also supporting INFIfab, a proposed national facility for semiconductor fabrication, advanced packaging and technology translation, covering about 96,284 sq ft including a 20,000 sq ft cleanroom, with focus areas including MEMS, photonics, quantum technologies and neuromorphic computing.

K-HEAL is a Centre of Excellence for healthcare, medical and assistive technology, and a flagship programme of the Department of Electronics, IT & BT. Innoverse aims to support 35 growth-stage deeptech ventures over five years, including autonomous systems and technologies from underwater applications to space. Shivakumar said Karnataka laid the foundations of modern industry and technology through institutions of learning and research, strong public sector enterprises and the trust of global companies. He said some of India's most ambitious scientific and engineering projects have found a home in Karnataka. He said, "We will bring the talent, the policies and the partnership. You bring your ambition."

Shivakumar said Karnataka accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports. He said the state received $9.4 billion in foreign direct investment equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India's total inflows during the period. He said more than 1,000 global capability centres have established operations in Bengaluru, and the state is home to more than 100 fabless chip companies. He said three out of every five engineers working in India's semiconductor capability centres were based in Bengaluru, and global companies are investing more than ₹23,000 crore in semiconductor research and manufacturing facilities in Bengaluru and Mysuru. The state is developing four electronics manufacturing clusters from Dharwad to Mysuru.

The government announced proposed AI skilling programmes with Google, Salesforce, Pega Systems, Sarvam AI and Gnani.ai, targeting 63,200 engineering and diploma students and professionals. The programmes will cover generative AI, agentic AI, voice AI, cloud computing, data analytics and responsible AI, combining classroom instruction with practical exercises, industry tools, capstone projects and certification pathways. Under the ₹300-crore Nipuna Karnataka reskilling mission, more than 33,000 people have already become industry-ready through partnerships with technology companies. Karnataka is home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, with nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns originating from the state. Through its ELEVATE programme, the government has supported nearly 1,500 startups with $41 million in equity-free grants over a decade, and under ELEVATE NxT, 33 deeptech startups have received ₹30 crore in grants since last year.

The government has allocated ₹25 crore under its Government First initiative to procure innovative solutions developed by startups. Shivakumar said the state accounts for one-fifth of India's bioeconomy, valued at $39.2 billion last year, and the government plans to expand biotechnology into marine resources, agriculture and healthcare. The Karnataka AI Hub aims to develop a globally competitive workforce and facilitate the application of research in practical fields. BRAINZ will bring together research institutions, industries and startups working in robotics, artificial intelligence and deeptech. The 2D Innovation Hub facility will serve as a shared platform for academic institutions and industry partners to undertake semiconductor research and development.

K-HEAL will connect clinicians, researchers, industries and startups to identify unmet healthcare requirements, develop and validate technological solutions and facilitate their adoption. Innoverse will support Karnataka-based deeptech startups that have already developed and validated their technologies and are looking to expand their market presence and global operations. The articles do not say when the proposed AI University, BRAINZ, the 2D Innovation Hub facility or INFIfab will be built or opened. The articles do not name the cost of BRAINZ, the 2D Innovation Hub facility or INFIfab. The articles do not say which company will run each AI skilling programme or when the training will begin. The articles do not say how the six initiatives will be funded beyond the ₹35 crore approved for the Karnataka AI Hub.

stories.Headline: Suno launches Visuals tool to turn AI songs into short video clips
stories.Summary:
Suno launched a new tool called Visuals on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to create short video clips. This product allows users to turn AI songs from their libraries into lyric videos, album art, and clips. The company moved from making songs to creating the visual content that users post alongside their music. These new video clips can be up to 15 seconds long and are available on the web. Mobile versions for iOS and Android are promised to arrive within the next few weeks.

The tool uses H3 Move, a model derived from MiniMax's H3, and requires a separate credit system. A new Platinum plan costs $120 a month, which is four times the price of the Premier plan. Free users are limited to one five second video before they must pay for more credits. The system is designed to follow song structure, lyrics, and beats rather than treating video as separate. This technology comes from MiniMax, which Disney, Universal, and Warner Bros. Discovery sued in California in 2025.

Chief product officer Jack Brody said Suno is a creative entertainment company that now goes beyond music. He stated that everyone is creative and the right tools help people bring their original ideas to life. Brody noted that video generation was previously too slow and expensive for anyone but large enterprises to use. He believes a new generation of models now opens video generation up to creative entertainment for everyone. The company says the model is optimized for how the Suno community will use the product.

Universal Music Group and Sony Music are still suing Suno, alongside the Elvis Presley estate and Jason Isbell. Eminem's publisher has also filed a lawsuit, while a class action group alleges violations of voice and likeness. The Elvis Presley estate claims Suno's assertions about not mimicking real voices are unequivocally false in court. Independent artists are affected by the high cost of the Platinum plan and the separate credit pool. These creators must pay for experiments since many generated clips will not be keepers.

Suno launched Speech last month for poems and meditations, and it launched Hooks in 2025 for user videos. The company was valued at $5.4 billion in June and signed licensed deals with Warner and BMG in September. A Munich court ruled on July 31, 2026, that Suno broke copyright law by training on GEMA songs. Sony and Universal filed another lawsuit on September 18, 2026, naming 60,202 recordings in the new v6 model. ByteDance added similar likeness guardrails to its Seedance tool in March 2026 to compete in the market.

Suno will implement hidden watermarks on videos shared outside the app, though these are currently described as planned. The company will use filters to block prompts for public figures, specific artists, and copyrighted characters or intellectual property. Users must confirm they hold the rights to any files they upload before the tool can be used. It remains an open question whether the $120 plan is worth the cost for the average user. The first month of Platinum signups will determine if the product's specific music alignment is a success.

stories.Headline: Hitachi validates agentic AI platform that cuts chiplet design candidates by over 90%
stories.Summary:
Hitachi's Research and Development Group announced on November 12, 2026, that it had completed and empirically validated a foundational design platform for semiconductor chiplet package design. The platform combines autonomous agentic AI with ultra-fast surrogate physics models to streamline advanced semiconductor packaging. The announcement followed preliminary technical disclosures presented by Hitachi researchers at the 35th IEEE Conference on Electrical Performance of Electronic Packaging and Systems, known as EPEPS 2026. That conference was held in Fort Worth, Texas, from October 18 to 21, 2026. In verification trials using a heterogeneous package with three distinct chiplet types, Hitachi demonstrated that its agentic AI pruned the candidate design space by more than 90%.

Engineers provide high-level targets, thermal design power limits, footprint boundaries and cost goals in natural language, and the agentic AI structures these prompts into formal design-for-manufacturing rules. The system integrates procurement constraints, bill-of-materials availability and vendor lead times to discard unviable component pairings early. The engine concurrently evaluates candidate layouts across electrical performance, thermal dynamics and mechanical stress using accelerated AI surrogate models. Electrical performance covers signal latency, return loss and power impedance, thermal dynamics covers hotspot dissipation and junction temperatures, and mechanical stress covers warpage and shear strain from thermal expansion coefficient mismatches. Hitachi also announced on the same day a technology that uses quantum-inspired CMOS annealing to create a supply-demand plan covering more than 500 generators up to 36 hours ahead in 60 minutes.

Hitachi's Research and Development Group is responsible for the platform, and the company positions it as a foundational technology within its Lumada 3.0 digital transformation framework under its One Hitachi initiative. Hitachi aims to provide edge AI semiconductor engineering services across mobility, energy and robotics. Hitachi plans to conduct Proof-of-Concept engagements with commercial chip vendors, fabless design firms and packaging OSAT providers through late 2026 and 2027. Research teams are also extending surrogate models to support higher die counts, emerging optical interconnects and standard specifications from the UCIe consortium. Both the chiplet technology and the annealing technology remain at the verification stage, and the company is moving toward practical application.

Writing for Mynavi TECH+ on November 13, 2026, technology writer Yukio Kobayashi emphasized that component volatility remains a critical obstacle in chiplet projects. Kobayashi noted that incorporating procurement availability into early automated screening directly targets a common source of project delays. Writing for EE Times Japan on November 16, 2026, semiconductor journalist Takatsuna Mamoto underscored the value of concurrent tri-physics analysis. Mamoto observed that optimizing trace latency often concentrates heat dissipation, generating coefficient-of-thermal-expansion mismatches that can crack solder microbumps. Japanese industry portal Dellows News noted on November 13, 2026, that the technology arrives as edge AI and automotive electronics shift rapidly toward modular silicon, and that for mid-sized semiconductor firms lacking large dedicated packaging teams, automated exploration tools help bridge substantial resource gaps.

Advanced semiconductor packaging has become the primary mechanism for computational scaling as monolithic silicon approaches photolithographic reticle limits and rising wafer defect costs. Disaggregating system-on-chip architectures into modular chiplets such as compute cores, high-bandwidth memory and analog I/O controllers enables process-node optimization for each die. Assembling multiple dies onto high-density substrates creates an explosive combinatorial search space in which engineers must evaluate thousands of spatial floorplans, inter-die bump patterns, routing layers and stackups. With leading-edge fabrication costs climbing at sub-3nm nodes, monolithic dies larger than 800 square millimeters face severe yield penalties. Industry consortia and commercial leaders including the Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express group have prioritized modular advanced packaging, while established commercial electronic design automation suites provide high accuracy for signoff verification but require hours or days of cluster compute time to evaluate a single package geometry.

Following validation on three-chiplet architectures, Hitachi is preparing broader industry rollouts. The articles leave open the results of the planned Proof-of-Concept engagements with commercial chip vendors, fabless design firms and packaging OSAT providers. stories.Headline: Shopify builds Remote Dev to let AI agents run iOS and Android builds in parallel
stories.Summary:
Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment, to let AI agents independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications in parallel, InfoQ reported on November 17, 2026, in an article by Sergio De Simone. Shopify engineers said running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They said three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop, on top of resources already consumed by compilers, simulators and emulators. They also said that if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped. Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but River is a Linux-based solution and could not be used for building iOS apps.

Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH, while Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session. Each River session gets its own environment, so one agent can debug something on Android, another can work on an iOS feature and another can test a PR, all in parallel. Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence, and can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Remote Dev can implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots and create a PR, and if something fails it can inspect the logs, fix the issue and try again.

Shopify says that after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%. Shopify says the platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes and submit PRs. Shopify says agents can verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes and running the same interaction to verify the fix. Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities. Shopify engineers explain that with Remote Dev, they are no longer limited by how many builds and simulators their laptops can handle.

Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, commented on LinkedIn that the key advantage of Remote Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration. He noted that a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous. He pointed out that the article does not explain how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once, which he identified as a key concern. Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern, saying that allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results. Raza said that if you give the agent a red test and enough retries, it will sometimes rewrite the test until it passes, and he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify engineers said running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines, on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators and emulators. They said three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop, and that if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped. Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development. River is a Linux-based solution, so it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev.

Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities. The articles do not say how many remote Macs or Linux VMs the fleet includes.

stories.Headline: Sharjah Digital Department launches Agentic AI Challenge to automate government operations
stories.Summary:
The Sharjah Digital Department launched the Sharjah Agentic AI Challenge to speed up the use of agentic artificial intelligence in government operations. This initiative follows the directives of HH Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammed bin Sultan Al Qasimi, the Crown Prince and Deputy Ruler of Sharjah. The event is scheduled to take place from December 8 to 10 to help automate various government services and operations. It is organized in partnership with Inception42, while Microsoft is participating as a collaborator for the duration of the challenge. The program aims to empower national talent to create innovative solutions that address real world challenges using new agentic AI technologies.

The challenge is open to the public and will include 30 participants who will work in teams of specialists and experts. These teams must develop prototypes of intelligent AI agents that can automate repetitive procedures and reduce the time for processing transactions. The program uses a design thinking approach and hands on learning under the guidance of trainers to create these practical solutions. It begins with an introductory session and three days of intensive work from 8 to 10 December in the city. The final prototypes will be presented to a specialized judging panel that will select the winning teams for the competition.

Sheikh Saud bin Sultan Al Qasimi, Director General of Sharjah Digital Department, said the Crown Prince set a clear strategic objective for them. He stated that the goal is to harness the potential of agentic AI in practical ways across various government institutions. He believes the true value of these technologies is their ability to streamline procedures and improve the quality of government services. He noted that the challenge is a practical step toward building sustainable government capabilities by combining operational experience with technical knowledge. He added that this will strengthen institutional integration and support the goals of the Sharjah Digital Transformation Strategy 2026 to 2028.

The project is designed to make a tangible difference to the lives of people by improving the overall customer experience. It affects national talent by providing them with the opportunity to develop solutions that enhance the efficiency of government operations. The initiative also aims to strengthen partnerships and integration between different entities to promote a sustainable digital transformation for the region. These efforts align with the human centred approach to digital integration that Sharjah has committed to for its citizens and residents. The challenge also supports the broader goals of the We the UAE 2031 Vision and the UAE National Strategy for AI.

The Sharjah Digital Transformation Strategy 2026 to 2028 aims to develop government services and improve the performance of various local institutions. This strategy provides the background for the current challenge to promote a sustainable digital transformation across the entire government sector. The UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 also serves as a foundation for these technological advancements in the emirate. Additionally, the We the UAE 2031 Vision guides the strategic direction for integrating advanced technology into the national infrastructure and services. These frameworks emphasize the importance of strengthening digital capabilities to maintain a competitive and efficient government for the future.

The next step involves the introductory session followed by three days of intensive practical work for the thirty selected challenge participants. Teams will collaborate to turn specific challenges into practical solutions before presenting their final prototypes to the specialized judging panel. The panel will then evaluate the work to select the winning teams based on the quality of their AI agents. The articles do not state what rewards the winning teams will receive after the competition ends on December 10. They also leave open how the winning prototypes will be implemented into actual government operations after the challenge is completed.

stories.Headline: Google spends heavily on AI and rebuilds search as rivals challenge its dominance
stories.Summary:
In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report, and the company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day, the biggest single-day percentage decline since Google went public in 2004. The Planet Money newsletter asked whether Google had been caught in the innovator's dilemma. Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information, and a new generation of AI rivals is now challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was a scrappy startup working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined Google in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science, and became its 20th employee.

When Mayer interviewed at Google there were just seven people there, and by the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee. That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue, and by 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company, by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet, was generating more than $280 billion, a more than millionfold increase. Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results, monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb, and its search business became like an unstoppable money machine. In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water, but neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.

Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI, and in 2017 a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer, a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible. Mayer, now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism, saying this is not a technology that's happening to Google and that they helped invent this new technology. Today Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals, and it is overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links. The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the innovator's dilemma theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail. Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a disruptive technology, and he helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary long before it became a cliché.

Google's researchers made computers translate languages, recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go, and the company developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation, but they didn't release it. On Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore, and Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses. Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business, saying that from a search perspective you want to get the right answer 100% of the time and that these models were not near that bar. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text. Mayer questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI, saying the standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is, are fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer.

Benedict Evans, a widely read technology analyst previously a partner at the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, says that every 10 or 15 years or so a revolutionary platform shift shakes up the tech industry, giving newcomers a chance to challenge dominant companies, and that it happened with personal computers, then the internet, then smartphones, and now with AI. Evans says the whole table gets reset and the things that meant that they had won and you couldn't take them on suddenly don't matter anymore. The process toward monopolization began with Google building a better search engine than rivals, and then, Evans says, its success became self-reinforcing: more users gave Google more data to improve its results, helping it attract still more users, which economists call a network effect. Google also paid to make its search engine the default in browsers and on devices, deals that a federal judge ruled in 2024 had illegally helped maintain its search monopoly. Google runs the operating system on many of our phones, we use free Google services to send emails, write documents, find directions, and watch a stranger explain how to fix our washing machine, and many of us keep going back to Google search out of sheer habit or because we keep getting nudged to go there.

Google has fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich. The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant and as profitable in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search. Christensen warned in The Innovator's Dilemma that companies that keep disruptive technologies bottled up in their labs risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be. The articles leave open what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first, whether a Google chatbot would have taken off in the same way and given Google a first-mover advantage, or whether its flaws would have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect. The articles also leave open whether rival AI systems will borrow from Google's playbook and work to intertwine themselves into our lives.

stories.Headline: US and nine allies form coalition to protect AI technology and infrastructure from China
stories.Summary:
The United States and nine allied nations formed a coalition to protect critical technologies associated with artificial intelligence. This strategic partnership was established to secure the supply chains and infrastructure necessary for advanced computing. The group intends to create a protective barrier against the influence of China in the technology sector. These nations are working together to ensure that sensitive AI models remain secure from foreign adversaries. The coalition is operating under a new framework known as the Pax Silica initiative to manage national security.

This effort requires the implementation of strict export controls on high-end semiconductors and specialized AI hardware. The partners are coordinating their policies to prevent the leakage of intellectual property to rival states. They are focusing on the protection of critical infrastructure that supports the development of large-scale AI models. The governments of the ten participating countries are responsible for overseeing these new security measures.

Officials stated that the collaboration is essential to maintain a technological edge over global competitors. They believe that fragmented policies would allow adversaries to exploit gaps in the global supply chain. The leaders emphasized that collective action is the only way to safeguard the future of democratic technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: ESMO launches a peer-reviewed journal on AI in oncology led by Jakob Kather
stories.Summary:
The European Society for Medical Oncology announced the launch of ESMO Artificial Intelligence and Oncology, a new peer-reviewed journal focused on artificial intelligence across cancer research and clinical care. The formal announcement took place on 16 November 2026 in Lugano, Switzerland. It coincided directly with the opening of the second edition of the ESMO AI and Digital Oncology Congress. The journal is dedicated to publishing data science investigations and educational content on the transformation of oncology through artificial intelligence. The launch establishes a dedicated scientific outlet intended to examine how machine learning technologies are transforming oncology research, diagnostic workflows, and therapeutic care.

The journal will feature original research reports, authoritative reviews, editorials, perspectives, professional correspondence, and news updates. Its subject coverage spans pathology, molecular profiling, diagnostic imaging, clinical decision support algorithms, drug development pipelines, clinical healthcare workflows, regulatory frameworks, medical education, and health economics. Prof. Dr. med. Jakob Nikolas Kather, MSc, will lead the publication as its Editor-in-Chief. Kather currently serves as the Hopp Foundation Professor of Artificial Intelligence in Medicine and is the Founding Director of the Institute for Medical AI at Heidelberg University Hospital.

The journal operates through a continuous online publication schedule and an established peer-review process. The European Society for Medical Oncology said the publication will provide an authoritative platform dedicated to the evaluation, validation, and real-world implementation of artificial intelligence applications across cancer care. The journal aims to promote methodological rigour, transparency, and multidisciplinary collaboration among oncologists, data scientists, and computational researchers. Kather said artificial intelligence is becoming a core technology within modern oncology. He added that the society has an essential role in offering a trusted forum for disseminating research and evaluating the benefits and potential risks of clinical AI systems.

Kather outlined an editorial vision centred on clinically relevant research and prospective validation studies of artificial intelligence tools. Kather said the publication will regularly feature educational materials designed to support the wider oncology community in understanding, interpreting, and applying artificial intelligence technologies in daily practice. This dual focus is intended to give clinicians and researchers practical guidance to navigate automated diagnostic and decision-making systems effectively. The society represents more than 50,000 oncology professionals worldwide, working to secure optimal outcomes for cancer patients.

By delivering educational resources and clinical evidence directly to members and the broader global cancer community, the organization seeks to empower healthcare providers to deliver high-quality patient care. The journal seeks to ensure that algorithmic innovations are thoroughly assessed before integration into oncology practice. The introduction of the journal expands ESMO’s existing institutional activities in the field of artificial intelligence, which encompass policy work, scientific and educational initiatives, and the annual AI and Digital Oncology Congress. These collective efforts reflect the society’s stated commitment to supporting the responsible development and application of AI tools to benefit individuals affected by cancer.

The newly launched journal serves as an extension of this mission, offering continuous peer-reviewed research to guide the safe, effective integration of artificial intelligence into cancer medicine. ESMO shared the launch on LinkedIn. The articles give no bibliographic details for the original publication and no DOI. The journal aims to accelerate the dissemination of scientific evidence, practical guidance, and educational resources.

The articles do not state a publication date for the journal’s first issue or any subscription or access terms. They do not name the other editors or editorial board members. They give no figures on the journal’s size, funding, or expected output. They do not say how the journal will be indexed or where it will be published.

stories.Headline: OpenAI releases a free image classifier that detects child sexual abuse material and flags AI-generated CSAM
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material on November 16, 2026, according to its blog post. The tool is an image classifier that looks for visual signs of abuse in images. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. OpenAI said this is the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific signal indicating if CSAM may be AI generated. OpenAI also released product warnings in ChatGPT, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators.

The classifier is offered at no cost through the OpenAI API to vetted organizations, including child safety organizations and the broader industry. OpenAI trained and designed it with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, OpenAI estimated the new classifier would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool. Images flagged by the new classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse. In fal's testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier's high-confidence flags as novel CSAM, invideo AI's testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban, and SafetyKit's evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children found the classifier detected 90% of cases.

OpenAI said individual companies have a responsibility to prevent their technology from being exploited by predators to harm children. John Shehan, Senior Vice President at NCMEC, said technology has an essential role in helping identify CSAM and the children depicted in it. Shehan said the new classifier gives more organizations access to tools that can help detect previously unidentified CSAM and strengthen reporting. Thorn said protecting children requires more than any single solution or organization and commended OpenAI for working with organizations throughout the child protection ecosystem. OpenAI said it engaged the Tech Coalition and ROOST to help share access to the tool and recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program.

A Childlight analysis at the University of Edinburgh found AI-related reports of CSAM increased globally by more than 8,400 percent from 2023 to 2025. Last year NCMEC received more than 400,000 of these reports, compared with roughly 4,700 in 2023. The ChatGPT warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, OpenAI will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

OpenAI developed the warning approach with input from Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha of the University of Kent, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. OpenAI published CSAM guidance developed with input from the Tech Coalition, Thorn, NCMEC, and the Internet Watch Foundation. OpenAI worked with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems, recently published by the Tech Coalition. OpenAI said this guidance has led to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI said it already prohibits CSAM, trains its models to refuse requests for it, and takes action against accounts that violate its policies.

The first law enforcement tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material. The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences. Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through OpenAI's intake form, and OpenAI said it will continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

stories.Headline: Malaysia regulator seeks details from Anthropic on alleged AI influence operation
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's communications regulator is seeking more information from the artificial intelligence company Anthropic about an alleged foreign-linked operation that used AI to manipulate political influence among users in Malaysia, the Communications Ministry told Parliament in a written reply dated Nov 17. According to the ministry, Anthropic alleged that its Claude AI technology was used by an overseas entity to build several parts of the operation, including targeting systems, fake social media accounts and fabricated news websites. Anthropic also linked the operation to BBS Bilisim Teknolojileri, a technology company based in Istanbul, Türkiye, the ministry said. The ministry said Anthropic reported that the Claude accounts it identified had been terminated and that mitigation measures had been put in place.

The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission will decide on appropriate follow-up action based on the information and evidence it obtains, within its jurisdiction and under the relevant legal provisions, the ministry said. That action could include cooperation with enforcement and security agencies, digital platform providers and other relevant parties where necessary, according to the ministry. Any regulatory or enforcement action would be carried out under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, the Online Safety Act 2025 and other applicable laws, it said. The ministry also said the Digital Ministry is drafting an Artificial Intelligence Governance Bill to strengthen the country's AI governance framework, covering accountability, risk management and the responsibilities of parties that develop and deploy AI systems.

The ministry was answering a question from Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee of PN-Beluran, who asked whether MCMC investigations had identified those responsible for the alleged operation and what action had been taken against the network of fake accounts and fabricated news portals involved. In its reply, the ministry said MCMC is seeking further information and clarification from Anthropic about the report so that any assessment and follow-up action rest on sufficient information and evidence. The government said it would keep strengthening monitoring of potential AI misuse and work with technology providers, digital platforms and relevant agencies to address online harm and ensure a safe, transparent and trusted digital environment. The articles do not say what happens next beyond MCMC's request for details and the drafting of the AI Governance Bill.
