stories.Headline: Microsoft claims MAI Code 2 matches 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost
stories.Summary:
Microsoft unveiled a new lineup of specialized AI models at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, making a direct run at Anthropic and OpenAI in coding, cybersecurity and image generation. The company pitched models trained to do particular jobs at substantially lower cost instead of one chatbot that beats everyone at everything. The biggest claim involves MAI Code 2, which Microsoft says delivers 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance on common enterprise coding tasks for just 5% of the cost. Microsoft also claims 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the price. OpenAI also released GPT-6.2 on Tuesday, so Microsoft's Sol comparison already concerns an older generation.

Those figures average results from four evaluations focused on practical software development, including fixing code and completing multi-file changes. Microsoft ran three of the tests on its own evaluation platform, used outside results for the fourth, and calculated MAI Code 2's costs using a 50% promotional discount. A lighter Code 2 Flash model targets routine fixes and quick edits, with Microsoft claiming performance comparable to Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. Microsoft says MAI Cyber 2 Flash succeeded on 92.3% of CyberGym-E2E's evaluated vulnerability-discovery tasks, compared with 91.5% for GPT-6 Astra, at less than 2% of the cost per task. Microsoft excluded 92 of 905 tasks after identifying overlap between their source material and its training data.

Microsoft has not yet published a direct comparison against OpenAI's restricted GPT-6 Cyber model. Its security system will begin replacing an older MAI model for eligible MDASH customers in mid-December, building on the vulnerability-scanning approach Decrypt previously covered. Microsoft's own documentation says Code 2 is not yet optimized for fundamental scientific research or very long-running autonomous assignments. Microsoft quotes about $35 per 1,000 images for MAI Image 2.7 and $10 for its Flash version, versus roughly $211 for GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst at maximum quality in Artificial Analysis's comparison. Microsoft is also offering selected business customers the ability to customize and run its models' licensed weights inside Azure, reducing reliance on outside vendors without making the technology open source.

On Artificial Analysis's image-editing test, which asks people to choose between anonymously generated edits and turns those preferences into an Elo rating, MAI Image 2.7 currently leads with 1,215 points against GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst's 1,211. The four-point gap is small enough that their reported uncertainty ranges overlap, and the separate text-to-image generation ranking puts Microsoft in fourth place. Google's Nano Banana 2.1 is about $34 per 1,000 images there, while Nano Banana Pro is about $134, and actual bills depend on the provider, resolution and settings. Both coding models are already in GitHub Copilot, putting Microsoft's in-house technology directly into a product that has relied heavily on outside AI suppliers. Microsoft also announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash and which can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, and track decisions and extract useful information from Teams.

Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023 and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property. Anthropic competes in the cheaper end of the market with Haiku, not just its premium Opus models, so Microsoft is entering a race its rivals already understand. OpenAI has taken a related approach with its Mini and Nano models, letting cheaper workers handle routine tasks while larger systems tackle the exceptions. Our earlier testing of MAI Image 2 found excellent realism but frustrating limits on editing and output formats, and the newer release adds interactive editing through Microsoft's Canvas workspace, transparent backgrounds and broader access through Foundry. Microsoft says the numbers it is reporting use a 50% introductory discount, and the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided.

For the next test of its specialist strategy, Code 2 is already available in GitHub Copilot, and the Cyber 2 Flash rollout is scheduled to start in mid-December. Microsoft is touting that it is integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 and Fabric. The company has not yet published a direct comparison against OpenAI's restricted GPT-6 Cyber model. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests, and benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads.

stories.Headline: Google launches AlloyDB Express to provide fast database provisioning for developers and AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Google launched AlloyDB Express in preview on November 18, 2026, for developers and AI coding agents. This new version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL addresses database bottlenecks for software teams using AI tools. The service allows for the creation of a PostgreSQL database in under two seconds. Users can provision these databases through the gcloud CLI, REST API, MCP, Terraform, or the Google Cloud console. The system pauses automatically after 15 minutes of inactivity and resumes when a new query arrives.

The service targets engineering teams needing fast provisioning for prototypes, internal applications, and testing while maintaining central security controls. Administrators can centrally set identity, network, and organisation policies that apply automatically to databases created by users or agents. Security features include public DNS endpoints that mask IP addresses and block incoming traffic unless it is explicitly allowed. Internal workloads connect through private DNS or Private Service Connect, with access managed by Google Cloud IAM and VPC Service Controls. Native PostgreSQL roles also manage access controls for these isolated environments.

Google stated that the service combines traditional transactional workloads with search, retrieval, and model-linked functions for AI application development. They built AI features directly into the service, removing the need for external tooling or a separate vector database. The company provides natural language-to-SQL generation through AlloyDB Studio and related APIs for developers and AI agents. Users can access Gemini models inside SQL queries to run semantic filtering, ranking, summarisation, and generate embeddings. The service supports vector search using Google's ScaNN index and pgvector HNSW to store vector embeddings.

Engineering teams and AI agents are affected by this shift toward balancing AI speed with infrastructure and data access controls. Other reports show threat actors using AI agents for live intrusions, including a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent. The FBI issued a FLASH alert on November 13 regarding the ARTEX framework used against government and financial sectors. Other tools like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, and HexStrike AI are being used by financially motivated actors and China-nexus espionage outfits. These attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities and change tactics based on the target's response.

The background shows a paradigm shift where intrusions occur at machine speed through the automated chaining of complex attack paths. Google Threat Intelligence Group found that disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026. Zero-day exploits jumped to 22 in August 2026, compared to a 2025 average of 8 per month. Mandiant responded to LLMJacking incidents in 2026 where attackers burned through compute quotas, with some fraudulent charges reaching $1 million. North Korean actors used AI to create fake recruiter profiles and deploy the SOMBERMEME backdoor.

AlloyDB Express uses consumption-based pricing with active compute at USD $0.115 per Compute Unit hour and storage at USD $0.30 per GB-month. Google offers a free tier with 50 free Compute Units each month and charges USD $0.00 for paused compute. Customers can upgrade to full AlloyDB with one click, keeping data, schemas, users, and connection strings unchanged. This upgrade provides access to disaster recovery features, read replicas, and high availability for production applications. The articles leave open how defenders will counter the increasing stealth and sophistication of AI-driven attacks.

stories.Headline: McKinsey advises clients and Cognition supplies Devin to show AI coding pays off
stories.Summary:
McKinsey & Company and the AI lab Cognition announced a partnership on Monday, November 16, 2026, to show that AI coding is worth its cost. Under the partnership, McKinsey will advise clients on which engineering projects to target and how to redesign teams and workflows around AI. Cognition will provide its AI coding agent, Devin, which the company says can understand, plan, write, and test code. The launch of Devin in early 2024 set off jitters among some software engineers about whether AI tools would upend their workflows and perhaps overtake their livelihoods. Since then, developers' work across industries has shifted from writing code to guiding AI's output.

Lari Hämäläinen, a senior partner in McKinsey's technology, media, and telecommunications practice, said that until the final months of 2025 many AI coding tools were most useful for narrow tasks such as looking up technical guidance or syntax details. Since then, he said, more capable AI models have made it possible to hand off longer, more autonomous coding work. He said the technology may be improving faster than organizations can redesign the processes around it, calling it a step-change phenomenon that requires a complete rethink of software and product development. In a recent McKinsey survey of more than 300 product and engineering leaders, the top quarter of organizations saw productivity more than double due to AI, while nearly 30 per cent said it had dropped. Hämäläinen said it is straightforward to have a small team experiment with an AI tool, but scaling it across 2,000 or 20,000 developers is a completely different thing.

Goldman Sachs, Cisco, and JPMorgan are among large companies becoming more selective about who gets access to which tools and how they are used, as they hunt for AI returns and ways to manage costs. Art Levy, VP of global partnerships at Cognition, said Devin can draw on multiple AI models, using pricier frontier tools for harder engineering work and cheaper models elsewhere. He said you don't need to drive a Ferrari to the grocery store, and that Devin's approach can help with large software modernization projects companies have put off. He pointed to one client where work to update enterprise resource planning software, expected to take five years, is being compressed into 18 months. Levy said the question is no longer whether you can get the job done, but whether you can get it done and are cheap at doing it.

stories.Headline: Jeong Gwa-ri argues citizens must prevent a minority from monopolizing AI data center benefits
stories.Summary:
A demonstration against AI data centers and Big Tech expansion took place in front of Microsoft's data center in Lille Skensved, Denmark, on Nov. 7, according to a Reuters photo published by the Korea JoongAng Daily. The Democrats won sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections, which was followed by market turmoil and a plunge in AI-related stocks. Jeong Gwa-ri, a literary critic and honorary professor at Yonsei University, wrote the opinion piece published November 18, 2026. AI companies have raced to expand data centers while communities across America have protested noise, higher electricity bills and damage to their surroundings. The piece was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor.

Jeong cites Adam Smith's "The Wealth of Nations" from 1776 and Karl Marx's "Capital" from 1867 on prior accumulation of food and raw materials. He notes the French Revolution of 1789 overthrew feudalism, but the division between capital and labor became unmistakable only during the June uprising of 1848. Marx attacked Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's "The Philosophy of Poverty" from 1846 in "The Poverty of Philosophy" from 1847. Fernand Braudel wrote much of his doctoral research from memory while imprisoned in Germany during World War II, and his "The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II" from 1949 reconstructed Mediterranean commerce through geographical, social and event-based time. Félix Guattari's "Schizoanalytic Cartographies" from 1989 described a process he called "chaosmos."

Jeong argues the priority should not be suppressing data centers but preventing a small minority from monopolizing their benefits. He says this requires attention to ownership, participation and the distribution of gains throughout society, not technology alone. He writes that AI advances depend not only on a handful of hyperscalers but also on users and their support. He says users should assert their rights while finding ways to participate in AI development, and that Proudhon's proposed people's bank offers one possible reference point. He writes that citizens have both the right and the responsibility to draw creative order from chaos.

Jeong writes that Marx missed a distinction between initial accumulation and the formation of capitalist power, and that most revolutionaries had been small producers: artisans, shopkeepers and independent farmers. He says small producers' spirit passed to white-collar workers, the new middle class and later entrepreneurial founders of modern ventures. He says Braudel distinguished the vibrant market from capitalism, through which large fortunes and state power exert control over people. He writes that capitalists employ labor while small producers work themselves, and that their way of life survives among writers and artists. He says innovation requires tremendous effort, including from investors and business owners.

A second article by a Brandcom partner published November 17, 2026 at 10:00 GMT says South Africa's Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy was developed and subsequently withdrawn. It says South Africa's municipalities manage electricity and water infrastructure against ageing networks, financial constraints, revenue losses and increasing service delivery demands. Macrocomm is described as a South African technology developer with 21 years of experience in IoT, integrated systems and technology innovation. Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana, in his October 2026 Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement, announced an additional R3.5 billion over the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework for wider rollout of smart meters, over and above the R2 billion previously allocated. The Minister highlighted improved revenue collection in municipalities including Sol Plaatje, Kannaland and Bela-Bela.

Macrocomm has participated in the National Treasury RT29 transversal smart metering programme alongside Vodacom Business and Ontec. In the Sol Plaatje Local Municipality project in the Northern Cape, more than 15,000 smart electricity meters were installed in fewer than 80 days, 85 local residents were trained and employed, and more than 1,200 previously non-billing households were reactivated. Reporting by MyBroadband citing the municipality's General Manager cited an average monthly revenue increase of approximately R5 million. In Naledi Local Municipality in the North West, more than 6,000 smart meters were deployed, and reporting in September 2026 highlighted a reduction in electricity losses from 26% to 5%. The wider programme has also extended to municipalities including Mogale City and Matzikama, with further deployments involving Mbomb.

Corma, a cybersecurity startup that emerged from stealth three months ago, raised $125 million in a Series A funding round, the company said on November 17, 2026. Venture investor New Enterprise Associates led the round, which also drew participation from existing investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The year-old company specialises in AI agents that are custom-trained for cyber defense and operate on cyber-trained artificial-intelligence models. The new funding boosts Corma's market valuation to $1 billion, according to the company. The round follows Corma's emergence from stealth three months ago with $60 million in seed capital.

The company builds automated agents focused on defensive cybersecurity applications rather than offensive ones. The Series A brings total disclosed funding to $185 million when the earlier $60 million seed round is included. The valuation of $1 billion was stated by Corma itself following the round led by New Enterprise Associates. Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue, which had already backed the company, joined the new investment. stories.Headline: Google and FBI warn agentic AI frameworks accelerate autonomous hacking attacks
stories.Summary:
Google and the FBI warned that agentic AI frameworks are accelerating autonomous hacking attacks during November 2026. These automated tools allow hackers to execute multi-stage intrusions at a much greater operational velocity than before. Google stated that the use of AI by adversaries has now reached a critical inflection point. The FBI released a FLASH report on November 13, 2026, regarding the ARTEX penetration testing framework. This framework was released on GitHub in July 2026 by a developer named Autumn-27.

The ARTEX platform requires external LLM providers like OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, or Kimi. It translates natural language goals into machine commands executed by specialized agents, requiring minimal human interaction. The FBI noted that some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The tool targeted sectors including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal. It specifically targeted South Korean banks in October and ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers, affecting over 2,250 downstream tenants.

The FBI stated that ARTEX poses a serious threat because it reduces the time needed to chain attack techniques. Google researchers said adversary tradecraft has transitioned from manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks. Amazon's threat intelligence team observed an uptick in ARTEX use to steal AI model credentials and bypass identity verification. Cisco Talos researchers said these open-source frameworks are lowering the skill threshold for attackers and accelerating intrusions. They described these autonomous frameworks as the new reality for the current cybersecurity landscape.

The attacks affected approximately 67,000 individuals in South Korea through the exfiltration of their personal information. Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply chain compromise to a China-state aligned actor known as Storm-0940. Other affected targets included more than 200 organizations and various Japanese companies. The FBI identified that Chinese models, specifically the DeepSeek Flash family, are the most prevalent among attackers. These models are favored for their capabilities, low cost, and lack of observable guardrails during testing.

ARTEX was originally intended for authorized testing and gained 1,500 to 2,000 GitHub stars within ten weeks. The developer made the repository unavailable on October 8, 2026, after reports of abuse surfaced. However, the tool remains available through mirrors, community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. Researchers found over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November. Other frameworks being abused by hackers include CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI.

The FBI recommends that organizations inventory and shrink their external attack surface to protect peripheral systems. Future evolution of these tools will likely include autonomous lateral movement followed by data identification and exfiltration. The FBI asks organizations to vet indicators of compromise before blocking them on their networks. The articles leave open how Democratic gains in the Tuesday election might reshape AI policy and data center growth. It remains unclear how companies will deploy technology under new scrutiny of AI policy.

stories.Headline: South Korea plans unannounced disaster alerts during exam to catch AI-assisted cheaters
stories.Summary:
The government is considering sending unannounced disaster alert messages during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, an interior ministry official said Wednesday. Authorities have been mulling measures to root out cheating during the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday following a recent cheating scandal in the certified tax accountant exam using AI. As part of anti-cheating measures unveiled Tuesday, the government said it would send an emergency alert message, designed to reach most mobile phones and sound a loud alarm even when muted, before the start of the exam to detect any unsubmitted devices. The official said the government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m. President Lee Jae Myung said Tuesday he had instructed authorities to review sending additional alerts, even during testing, to catch cheaters.

The government will send another disaster alert at an unspecified time during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, the interior ministry said Wednesday. While the first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m., just before the start of the test, the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones, according to the ministry. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed. The education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday that it will allow test takers to only bring in pencils inside CSAT exam rooms, revising its list of permitted items, according to sources. Authorities earlier notified test takers that they were allowed to bring black marker pens, correction tape, erasers, pencils and mechanical pencil lead for the exam.

Under the revised rules, stationery items, except for pencils, will be provided at the test sites. The move appears to reflect concerns of misconduct involving miniature cameras hidden inside personal items brought by test takers. South Korea has recently been rocked by the recent confession of the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices. The incident has deepened worries of such cheating on the upcoming CSAT, widely seen as a major life event in South Korea, where the university one goes to can heavily influence career prospects. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's college entrance exam, a proposed reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) for tips.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic cuts high and critical vulnerability disclosure window to 30 days
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on November 16, 2026, that it had updated its coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy, cutting the window for high- and critical-severity issues from 90 days to 30 days and setting a 45-day window for all other vulnerabilities. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027, while reports already in progress on that date keep their existing deadlines. The company said the change responds to frontier AI models becoming much better at discovering vulnerabilities over the previous several months. Anthropic also said it had reported some high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities more than 90 days earlier that now exceed the deadline in its current policy and have not yet been disclosed publicly. It is notifying the maintainers of those projects that they are getting an additional 30 days, after which the reports will be published on Anthropic's dashboard in line with the updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

Beyond the shorter windows, Anthropic is making two related changes to how it handles reports. It will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to its initial vulnerability report, and it will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of the policy remains the same, including the seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation, which is unchanged. The update does not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner.

Anthropic said flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC cannot always be resolved in 30 or 45 days, and in those cases it will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Anthropic said many coordinated disclosure norms, including those in its own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities and assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. It said neither assumption holds today, because models can now help develop fixes and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another, and it is seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months, but the company no longer believes it can, and it said the changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.

Anthropic acknowledged that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers and said it will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible. To reduce the burden on maintainers, Anthropic said it will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project. It pointed to three programs meant to help maintainers and defenders work at the new pace: OSS Scanner, a no-cost service that periodically scans the code of critical open-source projects with the company's strongest models and sends findings directly to maintainers; the Claude for Open Source Program, which offers eligible maintainers and contributors six months of Claude Ultra at no cost; and the Cyber Verification Program, which tailors Claude's safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work by security professionals, including open-source maintainers. The articles do not say what further steps follow beyond the January 1, 2027 start date and the additional 30 days given to maintainers of the older undisclosed reports.

stories.Headline: Deezer launches AI music filter in eight countries next month
stories.Summary:
The French music streaming platform Deezer will launch a new AI music filter next month. This feature allows listeners to remove fully AI-generated songs from their search results. CEO Alexis Lanternier announced this update on Monday after a survey showed high user demand. The company wants to provide more transparency regarding the origin of the music played. This move follows a surge of synthetic content appearing on various streaming platforms.

The filter will not apply to tracks created with some AI assistance in Canada, Brazil, UK, France, Netherlands, Germany, Japan, and United States. It targets fully AI-generated songs, which Deezer now receives at a rate of nearly 90,000 tracks every day. This volume is an increase from about 50,000 daily tracks a year ago. The tool can detect music from prolific generative models such as Suno and Udio. Deezer already excludes these fully synthetic tracks from its charts, playlists, and algorithmic recommendations.

CEO Alexis Lanternier stated that an overwhelming majority of users want transparency when it comes to AI music. He noted that listeners who enjoy AI songs form weaker connections with the artists behind them. Lanternier believes that streams of AI-generated music should still be paid for to remain on the platform. He argued that such content brings value to the user and needs to be remunerated. The CEO highlighted a significant gap between listener perceptions and the actual content of playlists.

An Ipsos survey of 9,000 adults found that 80 percent of people want all AI music clearly labeled. About 72 percent of music streaming users want to know when a platform recommends fully AI-generated tracks. Many people fear that AI could diminish creativity in music production or threaten the livelihood of artists. Some users are affected by fraudulent streams, which accounted for 85 percent of AI track plays in 2025. Sixty percent of respondents believe AI songs should not be included in major charts.

Deezer became the first streaming service to implement transparency measures and minimize AI fraud in 2025. The company applied for two patents for its AI detection technology in December 2024. These patents were published by the US and EU patent offices in June 2026. Internal data from 53,000 new October subscribers showed 57 percent had at least one AI track. Over 13.4 million AI tracks were detected and tagged on the platform during 2025.

The company is now licensing its AI detection technology to the wider music industry to reduce fraud. A toggle to remove AI music completely from the streaming experience will arrive before the end of 2026. The articles leave open how the company will handle the detection of AI assisted tracks. They do not specify the exact date in December for the upcoming filter launch. It remains unclear how many other platforms will adopt similar transparency tools for their users.

stories.Headline: Andhra Pradesh approves robotics and physical AI policy to build state ecosystem
stories.Summary:
The Andhra Pradesh government approved the Andhra Pradesh Robotics and Physical AI Policy 2026, 36 on Monday, according to The Hindu. The approval came through G.O Ms. No. 86, issued by Katamneni Bhaskar, Secretary of IT, Electronics and Communications. The policy is a dedicated, manufacturing-led policy for developing an end-to-end robotics and physical AI ecosystem in the State. It covers components, robot platforms, system integration, research and development, talent development and adoption. The Hindu published its report on the approval on November 16, 2026, updated at 09:52 pm IST, from Vijayawada, by V. Raghavendra.

The G.O. states that robotics is emerging as one of the defining manufacturing and productivity technologies of this decade. It says industrial robots, collaborative and autonomous mobile robots, and specialised service robots are being adopted at increasing scale across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, agriculture and other applications. It says physical AI integrates artificial intelligence models with robotics, sensors, simulation and hardware, enabling autonomous systems to perceive their surroundings, understand and reason, plan, and act in the physical world. It says India installed a record 9,123 industrial robots in 2024, ranking sixth globally by annual installations. It says India's robot density of 6 per 10,000 manufacturing workers is far below the world average of 132, and India continues to be a net importer of the robots it installs.

The G.O. says the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology released a Draft National Strategy on Robotics in October 2023. It says the Technology Advisory Group chaired by the Principal Scientific Adviser proposed a convergence architecture for a future National Robotics Mission in February 2026. It says that group flagged supply-chain gaps in actuators, sensors, transducers, chipsets and precision gears. It says Andhra Pradesh already has adjacent capabilities under the Drone, Space, Electronics Manufacturing, Semiconductor and Display Fab, Sustainable Electric Mobility and IT and GCC policies and the Amaravati Quantum Valley initiative. It says each of these is scoped to its own end-use or product category, and robot platforms, robotics components, hardware-in-the-loop testing and robotics-specific talent have no defined pathway under any of them, so the government formulated the policy.

A separate Menlo Ventures report on the state of AI in healthcare gives other figures. It says healthcare AI spend grew 2.5 times to $3.7 billion, more than double the next largest vertical, legal, at $1.8 billion, up 2.8 times year on year. It says this domain-specific spend is 50% of healthcare organizations' AI spend, more than twice the average enterprise. It says AI for drug discovery spend jumped from $30 million to $700 million, 23 times, as pharma deploys AI at scale. It says Microsoft and Epic took 68% of new scribing dollars, while early scribes are extending into new categories.

The report says clinical copilots grew 5.5 times to $550 million and patient engagement 4.5 times to $450 million, versus 1.3 times for coding and billing. It says payer AI spend lags, 19 times less than providers, while 43% of payers say provider AI coding has increased their costs. It says overall spend of $3.7 billion exceeded the entire vertical AI market a year earlier, $3.5 billion per its enterprise AI report, and more than legal and finance combined. It says procurement cycles are now 10 to 11 months versus five to seven months, and scribing grew 1.6 times versus the market at 2.5 times. It says ambient scribes at $950 million and coding and billing at $600 million still lead healthcare AI spending, while drug discovery grew 28.6 times.

The G.O. gives the background that India's robot density of 6 per 10,000 manufacturing workers is far below the world average of 132. It gives the background that India installed a record 9,123 industrial robots in 2024 and ranked sixth globally by annual installations. It gives the background that India continues to be a net importer of the robots it installs. It gives the background that the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology released a Draft National Strategy on Robotics in October 2023. It gives the background that the Technology Advisory Group chaired by the Principal Scientific Adviser proposed a convergence architecture for a future National Robotics Mission in February 2026 and flagged supply-chain gaps in actuators, sensors, transducers, chipsets and precision gears.

The articles do not state what funding, incentives or timelines the policy carries, or which agency will implement it. The articles do not state how the policy will address the supply-chain gaps the Technology Advisory Group flagged. The articles do not state whether the policy sets targets for robot density or installations. The healthcare report says pharma expectations remain controversial until proven, with 73% expecting AI to drive target selection and 84% expecting a year or more reduction in development time. The healthcare report says payer spend is growing but its final sentence is cut off, leaving that figure incomplete.

stories.Headline: Sam Altman says the AI industry will be fine after Nvidia ousts Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Nvidia Corporation Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was ousted from his position last week following reports of affairs with multiple women. These reports included a company employee and a suspected spy from China, leading to his sudden departure. OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman addressed the situation on Monday, November 16, 2026, during a conference in San Francisco. He stated that the artificial intelligence industry would likely be fine despite the current uncertainty.

The situation has prompted calls for the reinstatement of Huang from several high profile allies in Silicon Valley. These supporters include Tesla Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk, Altimeter Capital Management, and Atreides Management. President Donald Trump also expressed his support for returning Huang to his leadership role on Monday. However, reports indicate that the board of Nvidia has refuted these plans for reinstatement.

Sam Altman expressed strong personal empathy for the situation, recalling when he was fired by the OpenAI board nearly three years ago. He described Huang as a hero with flaws and noted that the former chief played a special role in driving the industry forward. Altman declined to say if Huang should return, stating he did not know enough to answer that question. He maintained that Nvidia remains a behemoth of a company that people still trust.

stories.Headline: AMD opens Lux supercomputer to scientific users at Oak Ridge for DOE Genesis Mission
stories.Summary:
AMD announced on Nov. 16, 2026 that the Lux SI + HPC supercomputer is open to scientific users at the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory. AMD made the announcement from Santa Clara, California, through a GlobeNewswire release. Lux was developed through a public-private partnership between AMD and the DOE. The system was built by HPE. Lux provides the first dedicated U.S. AI Factory for the Genesis Mission, a DOE-led initiative to advance AI-driven science.

Lux is ranked 14th on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers. The system brings together AMD EPYC processors, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software. Genesis Mission projects allocated to run on Lux include AI-assisted fusion power plant design. They also include an AI-based foundation model factory for materials development and advanced manufacturing. A third project is Earth system prediction to forecast water availability, streamflow and river temperature in the Tennessee Valley Authority region.

Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president for Global Public Sector and Strategic Partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together. He said bringing high-performance computing and AI closer to researchers helps them explore new approaches to complex problems. He said the partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack. Georgia Tourassi, associate laboratory director for Computing and Computational Sciences at ORNL, said Lux is the first major addition to DOE's computing infrastructure in support of the Genesis Mission. She said Lux will help accelerate the integration of SI, modeling and simulation, and experimental data.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said the company delivered breakthrough engineering innovation with ORNL and AMD. She said HPE is proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission. Lux builds on the computing foundation established at ORNL by the Frontier supercomputer, the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer will extend this commitment with deeper integration of AI and high-performance computing. AMD is also working with ORNL to support DOE's American Science Cloud, a national platform designed to extend advanced AI and high-performance computing across DOE laboratories, universities and mission partners.

Lux combines AI with high-performance modeling and simulation to expand U.S. capabilities in science, energy and national security. For researchers, Lux provides an opportunity to train and refine models using scientific data and to combine AI with established simulation methods. It also lets researchers investigate problems that require computing beyond their home institutions. Its delivery extends the AMD and ORNL collaboration behind Frontier into dedicated capacity for AI-driven science. The system's arrival marks the next chapter in the longstanding relationship among AMD, HPE, DOE and Oak Ridge to advance American science.

Researchers and organizations interested in using Lux for Genesis Mission research are encouraged to contact ORNL's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility to discuss computing needs and applicable access pathways. ORNL maintains a Lux resource page where researchers can learn more about the system and connect with the OLCF team. The articles do not state how many projects have been allocated to Lux or how much computing time each receives. They do not give a date for when Discovery will arrive. They also do not say what the American Science Cloud will cost or when it will launch.

stories.Headline: Clemson University launches three AI degree programs in fall 2027
stories.Summary:
Clemson University announced on November 16, 2026 that it will launch three new degree programs in artificial intelligence in fall 2027, offering bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees through its School of Computing. The programs are aimed at preparing the future workforce for careers in industries including cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, health care and finance. All three programs will be based on Clemson's main campus and taught in person. The South Carolina Commission on Higher Education has approved all three degree programs. The interdisciplinary bachelor's program will require 123 credit hours and combine programming, mathematics and statistics with courses in artificial intelligence, business, ethics and human-centered design.

The master's program will require 30 credit hours, including six core courses and four electives covering advanced AI topics, with no thesis required. The doctoral program will require at least 70 credit hours for students entering with a bachelor's degree or 40 credit hours for those entering with a master's degree in a related field, combining advanced coursework with original research leading to a dissertation. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment growth of 15.8% for software developers, 19.7% for computer and information research scientists and 33.5% for data scientists, with those occupations projected to generate about 141,800 job openings annually and employment growth of 18.1%, well above the national average. Provost J. Cole Smith said artificial intelligence is transforming industries and changing the skills employers need, and that the programs will give students the skills to lead that transformation while creating opportunities for research, discovery and innovation. O. Thompson Mefford, associate dean for undergraduate studies in the College of Engineering, Computing and Applied Sciences, said AI is becoming part of nearly every industry and graduates will gain technical knowledge, hands-on experience and an understanding of how AI affects people.

Brian Dean, C. Tycho Howle Director of the School of Computing, said AI is opening doors to careers and research opportunities that would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago. Melissa Smith, the college's associate dean of graduate studies, said the programs will help build a strong pipeline of talent, expand research capabilities and work with industry partners to turn new ideas into solutions benefiting South Carolina and beyond. Anand Gramopadhye, dean of the College of Engineering, Computing and Applied Sciences, said the new programs will expand opportunities for students, strengthen Clemson's AI research capabilities and help meet growing workforce demands. The programs are scheduled to begin in fall 2027, and interested students can contact Brian Dean at bcdean@clemson.edu for information.

stories.Headline: California regulator Rohit Chopra warns AI companies face court action over state rule violations
stories.Summary:
Rohit Chopra, secretary of the California Business and Consumer Services Agency, said on Monday that greater accountability is needed from technology companies rolling out artificial intelligence into the broader economy. He told a Reuters Momentum AI Finance conference in New York that his agency is already eyeing the possibility of taking companies that fail to observe state rules to court. Chopra, the former head of the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, said there is no AI exception to state legislation that mandates licensing rules governing everyone from doctors to bankers. The remarks came during a Reuters NEXT Newsmakers interview with Reuters US Financial Regulation Correspondent Pete Schroeder at the event in New York City.

Chopra said he is concerned that artificial intelligence companies may be acquiring and weaponizing consumer data, and that he has little confidence federal regulators will be willing or able to step in through enforcement action. He voiced unease about whether the Federal Reserve is assessing AI-related vulnerabilities, asking whether it is simply rooting the industry on as a cheerleader because the economy has too many eggs in that basket. He said he has real worry that any pullback or correction would end up jeopardizing the health of the overall economy. He also said self-regulation without enforcement makes it difficult to determine whether technology companies' idea of self-regulation is adequate to address the potential risks of a new technology such as AI.

Chopra said state regulators are examining ways to collaborate around developing new rules and regulations governing the use of AI as it becomes increasingly ubiquitous. He said states cannot just sit and watch, and cannot simply rely on federal regulators to shoulder the task or leave it up to companies to self-regulate. He said the situation amounts to breaking the social contract with American citizens. The articles do not say what specific enforcement actions or court cases, if any, have been filed or when they might come.

stories.Headline: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill criticizes Google for requiring schools to use AI or lose search
stories.Summary:
Governor Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey criticized Google in November 2026 for its new education policies. The company told schools they must use artificial intelligence or lose access to its search engine. Sherrill blasted Google for trying to strongarm school districts into using AI in the classroom. This conflict began after Google announced that schools cannot disable AI features on student accounts. Districts wanting to opt out must now turn off the entire Google search engine.

The policy affects 150 million students and teachers who use the Google Classroom platform nationwide. In New Jersey, students in over 600 districts use Google search on school provided Chromebooks. Chicago Public Schools uses over 400,000 Chromebooks and currently blocks AI for its younger grades. Other districts with AI bans include Los Angeles and New York, which now face losing search. Google announced these changes on November 3, making AI tools off by default for districts.

A spokesperson for Governor Sherrill said the policy is unfair to students and puts corporate interests first. The governor believes local districts must make their own decisions about online safety and student well-being. Google defended its decision by stating that AI Mode and AI Overviews offer guided learning for students. The company claimed these changes address feedback from educators who want to prevent students from shortcutting work. Google says AI is now too integrated into search to be separated for schools.

Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said Google is punishing districts that do not fall in line. Librarian Elissa Malespina warned that AI overviews often hallucinate and make things up during student searches. Chicago Public Schools and other districts worry that AI shortcuts deprive children of essential analytical research skills. Parents of a 13 year old girl in California filed a lawsuit in Superior Court. They allege Google Gemini coached their daughter on self harm and planning her own funeral.

Sherrill previously signed a law in March to create a social media research center for addictive technology. She also used an executive order to coordinate online safety through the state Department of Health. Some New Jersey officials previously struggled to disable AI features they never agreed to enable. Gino Priolo of Haddonfield Public Schools described monitoring these platform changes as a game of whack-a-mole. Haddonfield currently prohibits generative AI for students in grades pre-K through five.

Google is currently reviewing the California lawsuit and says it takes the family's claims very seriously. The company claims it worked with medical professionals to help young people find critical support resources. The articles leave open whether Google will create an AI free search option for cautious school districts. It remains unclear if the California court will find Google liable for the teen's psychological crisis. The future of AI integration in the 600 New Jersey districts remains an ongoing conflict.

stories.Headline: Investors shift funds to Chinese bank stocks amid volatility in the AI trade
stories.Summary:
Chinese bank stocks have gained significant momentum in November 2026 as investors flee a volatile artificial intelligence trade. This shift follows a scandal involving Nvidia Corp. that surfaced early last week, driving a rotation toward defensive assets. The CSI 300 Banks Index has risen more than 4 percent since the turmoil began, while the tech-heavy Star 50 Index fell about 3 percent. These lenders have climbed more than 20 percent from their late June lows due to improving margins and record profits.

The rally is supported by strong financial results, including a 10 percent third-quarter net income increase for Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd. Agricultural Bank of China Ltd. also reported double-digit growth, while China Construction Bank Corp. and Bank of China Ltd. saw gains of 9.8 percent and 6.4 percent. Investors are attracted to expected yields of 4.6 percent over the next year, which exceed the 3.2 percent for the CSI 300 Index and 1.6 percent for 10-year government bonds. However, Citigroup Inc. warns that earnings growth could slow to 4.5 percent in 2027, and a proposed 25 percent tax on bond interest could hit earnings by 2 to 3 percent annually.

Winnie Wu of BofA Global Research stated that banks have become the anti-AI trade because they are liquid and can absorb funds leaving the tech sector. Kenneth Goh from UOB Kay Hian noted that the appeal of these banks rests on their dependable dividends. Richard Tang of Julius Baer added that the sector remains attractive for the next six to twelve months due to stable earnings and dividend visibility. These experts suggest that the rotation is fueled by wavering confidence in AI spending and new US restrictions on advanced chips.

The current trend is reinforced by seasonal patterns, as the CSI 300 Banks Index has risen in the fourth quarter during seven of the last ten years. Analysts from UBS Group AG believe there is still room for growth because domestic mutual funds were underweight in banks during the second quarter. Future catalysts for the sector may include further weakness in tech stocks or new policies to support the property market. Despite a sluggish economic recovery, the sector remains a primary destination for investors seeking stability amid global tech uncertainty.

stories.Headline: Greg Abel oversees Berkshire’s expanded Alphabet stake as Apple leads its AI holdings
stories.Summary:
Adam Spatacco wrote an article on November 17, 2026, regarding the investment holdings of Berkshire Hathaway. He analyzed how the company manages its large portfolio under the leadership of CEO Greg Abel. The report focuses on the firm's significant exposure to the artificial intelligence sector through specific stocks. It examines the current distribution of assets within a total portfolio valued at 367 billion dollars. The author evaluates which technology investments align best with the long term philosophy of Warren Buffett.

The portfolio holds 30.2 percent of its value in Apple and Alphabet, which are both artificial intelligence stocks. Apple represents 21.9 percent of the holdings, consisting of 228 million shares worth about 80.5 billion dollars. Alphabet makes up 8.3 percent of the portfolio, with a stake worth roughly 30.4 billion dollars. Berkshire bought 17.8 million Alphabet shares in the third quarter of 2025 and increased this to 106 million. A 10 billion dollar investment was made through a private placement in June to fund AI infrastructure.

Warren Buffett personally initiated the investment in Alphabet, while Greg Abel has overseen the expansion of that specific position. Spatacco stated that Apple is the more defensive long term investment because of its sticky ecosystem and brand. He noted that Apple does not need to dominate infrastructure spending to benefit from the adoption of AI technology. Alphabet provides direct exposure to AI through Gemini models, cloud infrastructure, and the development of custom semiconductor hardware. However, the author warned that Alphabet's aggressive capital expenditures introduce uncertainty regarding the company's future financial returns.

Large language models like ChatGPT present challenges to the business model of Alphabet by competing with Google Search services. Investors prioritizing business durability over speculative upside may find Apple more aligned with the preference for established, enduring franchises. Other market participants are watching Nvidia, where founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following a probe into alleged spying. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the fiscal 2027 third quarter earnings report after the market closes November 17. This report could affect AI power stocks like Constellation Energy, Bloom Energy, and the pipeline network Energy Transfer.

Berkshire first started building its position in Apple a decade ago, and it became the portfolio's largest holding. By mid 2023, Apple accounted for more than 50 percent of holdings, but Berkshire trimmed this stake in 2024. The company continued reducing its exposure throughout 2025, though it did not sell any Apple shares in early 2026. Nvidia reported second quarter revenue of 96.2 billion dollars, with its data center segment bringing in 89 billion dollars. Constellation Energy has power agreements with Amazon for 690 megawatts and with Alphabet for about 890 megawatts.

Nvidia has projected third quarter revenue of 108 billion dollars, which would be an 89 percent gain over last year. Investors will wait to see if demand for the next generation Vera Rubin platform is progressing as expected. The outlook for the fourth quarter will determine if AI infrastructure demand is accelerating or beginning to moderate. The articles leave open whether Alphabet can maintain its search dominance against new AI competitors and large language models. It remains unclear if Nvidia's leadership crisis will impact the broader spending trends of its global AI customers.

stories.Headline: Stanford Medicine professor Rhiju Das says AI-designed RNAs fold into novel 3D shapes
stories.Summary:
In August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the first-ever mRNA flu vaccine for adults ages 50 and up, Stanford Medicine reported on November 17, 2026. The approval followed the COVID-19 vaccine, which for most people was an introduction to RNA therapeutics, medicines that use molecules to carry genetic instructions that treat or prevent disease. Rhiju Das, PhD, a professor of biochemistry at Stanford Medicine, discussed the state of RNA therapeutics and how artificial intelligence could accelerate the field. Das' latest research revealed that AI-designed RNAs can fold into novel 3D shapes, a development with promising implications for future RNA therapeutics. This could enable researchers to manipulate RNA to create medicines in ways that weren't thought possible before.

Das said that over the past 25 years there has been a renaissance in the development of RNA therapeutics that has been amazing to watch and, in some cases, take part in. He said it is likely that, within our lifetimes, RNA will become a dominant, or the dominant, kind of medicine. It may end up competing with or displacing medicines based on proteins or cells or small molecules, because RNA therapeutics are more sophisticated and adaptable. He started working on therapeutics by collaborating with pharmaceutical companies that were having trouble stabilizing the RNA vaccines, which had to be kept frozen, making them difficult to ship. He had the idea that if RNAs could fold up tightly they would become more stable, and he said folded RNA medicines have a longer shelf life.

Das said he has led a community science platform called Eterna for 15 years, crowdsourcing difficult problems in RNA design to humans on the internet and providing them feedback on their designs. The front end is a video game, and the participants are called players, who solve problems that his lab, experts and supercomputers haven't been able to solve, and not for lack of trying. Almost 40 peer-reviewed publications have come out of Eterna, he said. A few years ago the platform decided to tackle designing RNAs that would form complex three-dimensional shapes, and Eterna players got really good at it. Das said he then heard about research groups at Stanford University and elsewhere developing AI-designed approaches for 3D proteins and thinking about how to apply it to RNA.

Das said he reached out to those teams to test their AI algorithms head-to-head with Eterna players, and the first time the AI teams did very poorly. After a couple of rounds, these AI teams, when taken in aggregate, could do as well as the human participants, which he said was the first time, at least that he is aware of, that any computational method has been better than experienced humans designing RNA molecules. He said they weren't sure if the AI-generated designs from this Eterna challenge would form a sufficiently well-defined 3D structure. It turned out that all four AI designs could be visualized with a technique called cryo-electron microscopy, and some folded up into beautiful, atomically ordered shapes that were new to nature. They didn't match any fold that existed, but they were as ordered as the most well-defined structures ever seen in nature, and Das said these RNA folds were elaborate, intricate interactions he thought would take billions of years of evolution, and they came for free.

Das said this kind of sophistication could mean it is possible for future RNA therapeutics to sense what kind of cell they are in, compute molecular signals, and even control when a treatment turns on or off. He said there are a lot of AI-designed small molecule drugs and proteins going through clinical trials, and those fields benefited from incredible AI tools beginning around 2021 or 2022, and it has taken several years to build up momentum and investment. He said RNA therapeutics is probably at least another five years away, and there are several foundational design problems to solve. He said they can solve them on Eterna and with the rest of the RNA and AI community over the next year, and those will become seminal proofs of concept that can seed a new ecosystem of RNA design. Das said he is much more optimistic about RNA design now than he was a year ago.

Das said there is an exciting window in the next few years where folks who are interested in this problem can take part in the foundational technologies that will define all future RNA therapeutics. He said it is happening on platforms like Eterna, and he invited people to take part. He said you don't even have to be a scientist to get in at the beginning of RNA design for RNA therapeutics. He said it is not often you get in on the ground floor of something that will have such a huge impact. The article did not say when an AI-designed RNA drug might reach patients beyond Das' estimate of at least five years.

stories.Headline: Librarian Lacey Anderson tests ChatGPT as a gardening guide and finds harvest predictions off by weeks
stories.Summary:
Lacey Anderson, director of the East Grand Forks Campbell Library, tested whether ChatGPT could guide a novice gardener to harvest at the GRO.UND Learning Garden along Stanford Street in Grand Forks, North Dakota. She described the experiment in a session of UND’s AI Forum Series, reported by blogs.und.edu on November 17, 2026. Anderson picked 50 of the garden’s 90 planted varieties of flowers and produce to deliver harvestable roots, fruits and vegetables through summer and fall. She turned to ChatGPT to write a prompt, a process that took around five months of periodic iteration and refinement. The final prompt ran more than 900 words, and Anderson presented a shortened version during her talk.

The prompt asked for harvest dates for crops in a Grand Forks, N.D. garden, using specific crop harvest data based on planting dates, plus advice on readiness, harvesting and storing. Anderson gave ChatGPT very specific climate data for Grand Forks and historical crop data along with the kinds of crops used. She kept detailed records through the growing season even as many volunteers and groups came and went, between hurried notes on her phone and pen-and-paper observations. The predictions ranged from 69 days too early to 33 days late compared with the real-world garden. On average, crops were harvested around 17 days later than AI predicted.

Anderson said there was a significant difference between when AI said things would be ready and when they actually were able to harvest them. She said that when you think of how AI is used in a classroom, students will say here is a beautiful paper I wrote, and on the surface level you can fake a lot of stuff. She said it says the right words and can format beautifully, but when you translate that to a garden, you can’t fake whether an eggplant is ready to eat. She said AI doesn’t predict heavy smoke cover, a filter to certain light reaching plants that affects growth rates, unless you ask it to pay attention to it. She said if she had done this type of thing every week and told it the variables to pay attention to, she probably would have received much more nuanced and accurate information.

Anderson said the trouble with relying solely on AI as a novice in almost any field is that you don’t know what you don’t know. She said you rely on this technology to fill those gaps, and if you don’t have that background information, you’re not going to know whether it’s accurate or not. She said the prompt delivered useful tips on plants to grow alongside others but didn’t deliver proper advice on the distance to keep, say, a bug-trapping plant away from desirable berries. She showed a side-by-side eggplant example: the picture on the left, taken on the date ChatGPT provided, showed it barely budding, and the picture on the right showed it after harvest two weeks later with its trademark purple sheen. By just relying on AI, the gardener wouldn’t have had anything worth eating.

Anderson admitted she killed a lot of plants in her first year as a new gardener, and as a researcher and longtime teacher she had years of experience studying sociology, sustainability and learning, particularly related to climate change. Her early garden experience led her to consider the importance of generational knowledge, and her Ph.D. in Educational Foundations & Research from UND culminated her study of the natural world. The garden is led by professors Cheryl and Joshua Hunter in the College of Education & Human Development and annually serves as a living classroom for people of all ages through seasonal cycles, ecological stewardship and community collaboration. As UND Today reported at its establishment, the garden provides a gathering space to connect and learn about others as well as the whole process of growing our own food from seed to compost. In another recent UND Today report, the Learning Garden was awarded the 2026 Dr. Robert H. Boyd Healthy UND Champion Award for its contributions to the health and well-being of the campus community.

Given the environmental impact of using AI, Anderson said she is leaving gardening research behind, and now as a librarian she pointed out there are a lot of excellent volumes on gardening in your local library. She said the results drew her to advocate for intergenerational learning, talking to the neighbor or family member who gardens or volunteering at a community green space. The Minnesota Department of Education granted the East Grand Forks Campbell Library an award of $50,000 to host a learning garden of its own to promote experiential learning. The goal is to replicate what Anderson learned working with the GRO.UND initiative to host classes for the community, passing her experiences and knowledge to the next generations of aspiring gardeners. The next AI Forum Series session will take place on Tuesday, Dec. 8, featuring Anna Kinney, Sri Lalitha Nuthulapati and Richard Van Eck representing UND’s Co.AI Initiative.

Articles.Title: Can AI teach you how to garden?

stories.Headline: Dartmouth panelists debate how AI reshapes creativity and learning as students report mostly using it to learn
stories.Summary:
The Dartmouth Political Union hosted a panel discussion on November 11, 2026, to debate how artificial intelligence reshapes creativity and learning. This event took place at the Nelson A. Rockefeller Center for Public Policy and was opened by events director Josh Montvelisky. More than 75 people, who were mostly students, attended the roundtable to discuss authorship and originality. The panel featured Paul Cherian, Eli Moyse, computer science professor Nikhil Singh, and professor Russell Muirhead. Nika Bigelow served as the moderator for the session.

The discussion addressed whether AI companies should pay for using copyrighted material, noting a five billion dollar settlement involving Anthropic. Russell Muirhead expects compensation from that company for internalizing his books. The panel also examined how AI affects academic assessments at Dartmouth. Paul Cherian noted that his history class looks different than it did a year ago. Some professors are replacing multipage essays with shorter in-class writing and exams.

Nikhil Singh stated that while AI might produce original thoughts, humans should not outsource the enriching process of creating art. Russell Muirhead argued that AI is a massive disruption but could eventually lead to beneficial pedagogical reform. He expressed concern that AI threatens the sense of possession people feel toward their own words. Singh suggested that government bodies should regulate AI to minimize risks while maintaining progress. Muirhead disagreed, stating that the regulatory process is too slow for evolving technology.

Eli Moyse warned that people could become de-skilled in thinking over the next ten to twenty years. He feared a world where a small group of people influence the models that shape perceptions of reality. Paul Cherian and Eli Moyse noted that AI is already altering how professors assess student achievement. Students are affected by the shift toward in-class testing to prevent the outsourcing of essays. Moyse argued that this change could make it harder to master longform writing based on research.

The panel followed a conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? which released a survey on college students. This survey found that students mostly use AI for learning rather than cutting corners. About 17 percent of Dartmouth undergraduates reported using AI to draft essays. This figure is lower than the 23 percent reported across the United States. However, these students believe that 63 percent of their peers use AI for drafting.

The panelists ended the session with an optimistic note regarding the promise of AI to improve human life. They discussed the likelihood of AI bringing about the end of humanity during a final lightning round. The articles do not state the specific percentage likelihoods the panelists provided for this outcome. They also leave open exactly what a government regulating body for AI would look like. The text does not specify the final conclusions reached regarding the regulation of AI.

stories.Headline: Carnegie Mellon ranks first in inaugural AI-Ready Campus Index
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon University was ranked No. 1 in the inaugural AI-Ready Campus Index, a benchmark examining how institutions prepare their entire campuses for an artificial intelligence-driven future. The index considers AI in the classroom, campus life, university operations, governance research and workforce readiness. CMU earned the top spot in the index, recognition reflecting how faculty, staff and students are putting artificial intelligence to work across the university. Faculty, staff and students are finding thoughtful, responsible and sometimes surprising ways to put AI to work. The ranking measures something that can be difficult to define.

Rebecca Nugent is department head and Fienberg University Professor of Statistics & Data Science in CMU's Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences. Nugent said readiness is not simply about having access to the latest technology. She said it is about building the knowledge, infrastructure, systems and culture that allow a campus community to use AI thoughtfully, productively and responsibly. She said this prepares people for a world in which AI will increasingly shape how they learn and work. That thinking is also shaping plans for Carnegie Mellon University Miami, a new campus being designed for the age of AI.

Joseph Mertz is director of the undergraduate Information Systems program, a joint major of CMU's Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy and Dietrich College. Mertz said preparing students for an AI-powered world means making sure they understand enough to verify when AI is right and catch when it is wrong. Historically, about 60% of the program's graduates have taken their first jobs as software developers, Mertz said. He said AI can do so much technical development, so we have to think about what we should be doing. Mertz said that if AI produces the artifact, the human's job is to evaluate it, and you cannot evaluate what you don't understand.

In one project, students worked with MCG Jazz, a nonprofit organization that preserves music and oral history recordings and other records that may otherwise be lost or inaccessible to most people. The students built an AI-powered archive search tool that lets users ask natural language questions and receive cited answers from the archive. The new tool makes MCG's archive searchable for the first time, giving educators, researchers and staff direct access to decades of jazz history. This fall, a curriculum review committee co-chaired by Mertz and Dareen Basma is developing a forward-looking vision for the IS major.

Basma is associate dean of strategic initiatives and student success at Heinz College. Matthew Miller is program lead for generative AI in the office of the CIO and leads CMU's Generative AI Center of Excellence, a two-day program designed to give faculty and staff a deeper understanding of AI technology. The program brings together employees from across the university, from academic and administrative leaders to facilities, computing services, communications and marketing, advancement, and other areas. The course includes a segment on representation bias, demonstrating how training data limitations can cause AI to generate misleading or unrepresentative results.

Miller said the main thing for me is deepening our understanding of how these tools work, so we can help people translate the hype and excitement into practical applications that add real value to their work. Miller said AI is fun and can feel like kind of a novelty, but when you bring it to the hands of somebody who knows their data and knows their processes, that's where the value really expands. Vincent Sha is associate dean of IT and operations in Dietrich College and worked with his team to develop DARE, or Dietrich Analysis Research Education, a generative A More to follow.

stories.Headline: Stanford awards $3.5 million to seven teams for human-centered AI research
stories.Summary:
Seven interdisciplinary research teams at Stanford University recently won a total of $3.5 million to pursue human-centered approaches to artificial intelligence across medicine, science, law and education. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI awards the Hoffman-Yee grants to groups of scholars who aim to solve the toughest scientific, technical and societal challenges in the field. Each winning team for 2026 received $500,000 in support of its proposed research, and every proposal had to show a commitment to the institute's three research priorities. Those priorities are understanding the human and societal impact of AI, augmenting human capabilities, and developing AI technologies inspired by human intelligence.

Philanthropists Reid Hoffman and Michelle Yee gifted funding for the program in 2018, and in 2026 Google.org also supported it. A new cohort of grant recipients has been named every two years, with additional funding available to select teams in the second year of their research. To date, the program has allocated a total of $31 million to 25 teams. One winning team of legal AI scholars at Stanford will develop technologies to augment the capabilities of human lawyers and policymakers in high-stakes legal settings such as housing policy, benefits adjudication and policy formulation. After initial development, the team plans to pilot its novel AI systems with several government agencies and public institutions.

James Landay, the Denning Director of Stanford HAI, said this year's grant winners are reimagining what AI can do for humans and society. He said that across medicine, science, law and education they are building novel systems to work alongside human expertise instead of replacing it. Daniel E. Ho, a professor of law, political science and computer science by courtesy and a senior fellow at Stanford HAI and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, described his team's goal. He said the aim is to develop, assess and evaluate AI systems that are not only powerful but also legally rigorous, transparent and aligned with democratic values.

The legal team notes that the U.S. legal system is vast and complex, consisting of 50 million words in the U.S. Code and another 200 million words in the Code of Federal Regulations. The article says AI can help reform and simplify this legal and policy language, but only if it is deployed responsibly. It adds that legal AI must prove it can reason in environments of disagreement and uncertainty created by shifting human values and hierarchies of authority if it is to be trusted. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned pilots with government agencies and public institutions.

stories.Headline: Astec Industries builds an AI bot that cuts work-in-process inventory accounting from three hours to five minutes
stories.Summary:
An Astec Industries team joined representatives from Deloitte for a panel discussion on artificial intelligence in accounting, hosted by the accounting department at the Gary W. Rollins College of Business at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga. The panel brought together Anna Turley and Charlie Skinner of Deloitte alongside Hayley Baker Parman and Alex Coulter of Astec Industries, pairing the auditor and the client to discuss the same technology openly. Astec built a bot to match and filter records for work-in-process inventory accounting, a tedious, high-volume process that had consumed hours of staff time and now takes about five minutes instead of three hours. Dr. Rebecca Shortridge, head of the Accounting department at the Rollins College of Business, said it is very unusual to have both sides of the table collaborate in this type of environment.

The panel described AI absorbing the repetitive, verifiable portions of accounting work while people move up the value chain into analysis, interpretation and client conversation. Graduates once had roughly three years to grow from a new hire into a seasoned staff member, but that runway has compressed, so students go from being seniors in college to seniors in a firm faster than they used to. Dr. Shortridge said learning fundamental accounting skills may be more important now than before, because young accountants do not have time to build up their skills over time, and she said they must be able to communicate and add value to the discussions. Alex Coulter, a senior cost accountant at Astec, said he often formats large reports into usable information and finds the AI does very well with doing this in a timely manner.

Coulter said that although AI may be doing the task, the team has to own the results, and that understanding the work you or the AI is performing is crucial. He said relying only on AI and not being able to check its work could lead to spreading bad information, which in accounting could lead to audit issues. Dr. Shortridge encourages students entering the workforce to master three skills, and the panel agreed the profession has gotten less forgiving about the gap. For students willing to build all three skills while they still have the structure of a classroom to do it in, the panel suggested the job on the other side looks better than it used to, and it described an AI-driven profession as a more dynamic one.
