stories.Headline: ERCOT audits large data centers and files grid reports with Texas regulators by December 10
stories.Summary:
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas will file reports on large data centers by December 10, 2026. This audit follows a directive from Governor Greg Abbott to verify projects waiting for grid connections. The process targets data centers and crypto mines to ensure they meet specific state requirements. The Public Utility Commission of Texas will then meet on December 17 to review these findings. This review occurs during a transition of power before a new governor takes office in January.

The Batch Zero process sorts projects of 75 MW or more into three distinct categories. On September 3, ERCOT placed 204 projects totaling 66.4 GW in the base load tier. It put 158 projects totaling 127.9 GW in the studied tier and excluded 373 projects totaling 302.2 GW. The audit examines water reuse, ownership, and whether projects provide their own power or pay their own way. It also includes a community impact review for facilities of 25 MW and above.

Governor Greg Abbott ordered the audit to ensure that failing projects are denied a grid connection. He also told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop processing permits on September 21. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat taking office January 19, 2027, said she would keep approvals frozen. She intends to maintain this moratorium until the Texas Legislature passes new protections for the state. ERCOT general counsel Chad Seely stated the study will miss its April 9, 2027, deadline.

Developers like Skybox Datacenters and Mesquite H2 filed complaints at the commission over their project classifications. Power producers such as NRG Energy and Vistra saw shares fall 14 percent after the recent election. Jefferies analysts noted that slower data center arrivals could lower wholesale power prices for Texas consumers. CoreWeave chief executive Michael Intrator wrote to Hinojosa asking for the responsible completion of permitted projects. These changes affect a pipeline of 474 GW, which is five times the record peak demand.

The Batch Zero process began in June 2026 through a planning guide rule change called PGRR 145. This system was created because data center power requests outran the ability of the operator to study them. Texas currently holds about 23 percent of all planned data center capacity in the United States. The current freeze affects 17 large loads that had completed stability studies and expected to come online. Some developers continue to file projects, including an 8 billion dollar building by Integra in Quanah.

The Public Utility Commission has not committed to acting on the reports during its December 17 meeting. It remains unclear when the Batch Zero process will officially restart or when the permit freeze ends. The Texas Legislature will convene in January 2027 to consider bills that could repeal industry sales tax exemptions. Lawmakers may also introduce requirements for data centers to obtain specific permits from the commission. ERCOT has not yet proposed a new date to complete the delayed Batch Zero study.

stories.Headline: NTT Data CTO Vikram Bharwani argues banks must control data and decisions to use AI
stories.Summary:
Vikram Bharwani, CTO for Banking and Financial Services at NTT DATA in the UK and Ireland, published an article on November 13, 2026, arguing that every major bank will need sovereign AI. He defined sovereign AI not as a bank-owned frontier model or a warehouse full of GPUs, but as the ability to use powerful AI while retaining control of knowledge, actions and decisions. The article appeared on nttdata.com at 06:00:00Z on 2026-11-13, and a second version appeared on 2026-11-14 at 06:00:00Z. Bharwani wrote that banking has spent half a century digitalizing how money moves and how financial services operate. He said AI is now beginning to digitalize something far more complex, namely the judgment behind banking decisions.

Bharwani cited a 2024 survey by the Bank of England and the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, which found that 75% of responding firms were using AI, up from 58% in 2022. He described the reverse information paradox as framed by Satya Nadella, who said that in the AI age the buyer risks giving away knowledge just to use what they bought. Bharwani said a bank's knowledge includes the credit officer's correction, the fraud analyst's rejected lead and the exception an experienced underwriter accepted, with the reasons for those decisions. He said the knowledge layer is more valuable than the model itself, and that a bank can use external models while owning its private evaluations, approved knowledge, feedback and orchestration. He said data residency is important, but a model can run in a bank's own building and still leave the bank unable to explain a decision or switch suppliers.

Bharwani said sovereignty comes down to whether a bank controls its data, can explain decisions, retains what the system learns and can keep operating when something fails. He said an agent's permissions, network access and spending limits need to sit outside the model, and critical actions need approval and an effective way to stop them without it. He said these controls can exist in a public cloud and can also be missing from a private deployment. He said the FCA expects firms to apply existing duties and governance to AI, including consumer outcomes and senior accountability. He said a decision passport should capture inputs, permissions, policy and model versions, tool actions, human interventions and the final explanation, and a bank must recreate that record after changing models.

Bharwani said a mortgage application from someone with irregular income shows what the architecture must do, with AI reconciling payslips and bank statements, finding policy, flagging conflicting evidence and preparing an affordability recommendation. He said the underwriter should see conflicts and assumptions rather than a confident paragraph that hides them, and a declined customer deserves a clear reason and a way to correct the record or seek review. He said an upheld appeal may expose a faulty interpretation, arrears may show whether affordability assumptions reflected risk, and a complaint may reveal that the explanation failed the customer. He said learning should stay in a sandbox, tested against unseen cases, before release under control, and historical lending data can reflect past exclusions while declined applicants create gaps in outcome data. He said the same principle applies to fraud, customer service and operational resilience, and the test is fewer avoidable referrals, lower false positives, faster resolution, sounder decisions and better customer experiences.

Bharwani said banks do not need to own every part of the AI stack but must control their data, knowledge and evaluations, with freedom to change models without losing context. He said banks need clear controls over what agents can do, decision records that survive each technology change and, for critical services, a tested fallback. He said some tasks warrant private inference while others are better served by a smaller model or a clear deterministic rule. He said a bank should start with one material process, establish what a good decision costs today, how long it takes, where it goes wrong and what customers experience, then measure whether AI improves those outcomes. He said cost per token means little if the result is a faster, cheaper mistake.

Bharwani said banks should consider what happens to human judgment as work is automated, asking how junior underwriters learn to challenge AI in five years if it builds every first-pass credit pack. He said they should be given supervised exceptions, simulated cases and access to model traces, and human oversight is meaningless if a person clicks approve without the chance to investigate the evidence. He said powerful AI will be available to everyone, and the real difference will be whether banks turn it into a governed extension of institutional judgment without giving up control. He said a bank can rent a model but cannot rent accountability, and he expects sovereign AI to become part of core banking infrastructure. The articles leave open which specific process a bank should choose first and what the IDC InfoBrief sponsored by NTT DATA concludes.

stories.Headline: Google reports that threat actors use multi-agent AI frameworks to automate vulnerability exploitation
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group reports that state-sponsored and cybercrime groups are using generative AI to increase their operations' speed and scale. These threat actors are adopting multi-agent offensive frameworks to automate the discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities without any human intervention. The group discovered a specific multi-agent framework called exploit_agent on an exposed staging server. This tool was designed to compare web application code, identify flaws, develop exploits, and execute them automatically. The server also contained stolen victim data and scripts for reconnaissance and webshell deployment.

The exploit_agent targeted the education sector and French entertainment and media websites. Attackers use frameworks like Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to reverse engineer patches and weaponize n-day vulnerabilities. Artex is most used by Chinese-speaking groups, while Cairn targeted the US aerospace sector. PentAGI was used for vulnerability scanning in Asia, and HexStrike AI was also observed. Other tools include ZeroHollow for exploit development and Agent Zero for autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation.

Google Threat Intelligence Group stated that these frameworks represent a paradigm shift toward intrusions occurring at machine speed. They noted that automated chaining of complex attack paths allows threat actors to scale their operations significantly. The group observed a Chinese group building its own automated attack framework for likely espionage operations. They also found an end-to-end IaaS platform in August 2026 that automated the entire IO campaign lifecycle. Another commercial contractor developed an AI platform to manage over 100,000 accounts across multiple platforms.

Merlin chief strategy officer Matt Hartman said AI lowers the cost and expertise required for sophisticated cyberattacks. He warned that US water utilities, hospitals, and electric utilities cannot win a manual race against machine speed. Phishing-as-a-Service operators use LLMs, including the Jieyou service active since March 2026, to modify phishing templates. Influence-as-a-Service vendors and political monetization networks use LLMs to scale clickbait and improve long-running influence campaigns. Some actors hunt for LLM credentials in LLMJacking operations, with one case reaching $1 million in abuse.

State-sponsored groups using LLMs include Chinese APTs like Leaky Castle and Iran-linked APT42, also known as Calanque Ion. North Korean hackers, such as Midnight Neptune or UNC1069, use them for cryptocurrency attacks and IT worker activity. LLM Mixers have emerged as illicit marketplaces selling access to frontier and jailbroken models via stolen credentials. Google noted that LLM adoption introduces forensic noise that degrades operational security and stealth for some operators. However, cybercrime actors may accept lower success rates for the increased reach these autonomous tools provide.

Google anticipates that intrusions will become nearly fully agentic as underlying LLMs and tools increase in sophistication. This evolution is expected to reduce human involvement while increasing the stealth and sophistication of malicious activity. Defenders must now nail cybersecurity fundamentals and accelerate the shift toward automated defenses that respond at machine speed. The report serves as an early warning that these capabilities will spread among nation-state and criminal operators. The articles leave open whether improved content quality from AI actually equates to greater impact or success.

stories.Headline: St. Paul student says Turnitin flag gave her a zero as district lacks AI policy
stories.Summary:
A St. Paul Public Schools student wrote in a MinnPost opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, that she received a zero on an English essay that Turnitin flagged as 32 percent AI-generated, dropping her grade to a D on the night before her last day of sophomore year. She said she had earned a 98 percent in the class before that and had not used AI for any part of the essay. When she offered the next morning to rewrite sections with pen and paper, her teacher said that was not necessary because she knew the student's writing style and believed the work was original. The teacher had previously raised concerns about Turnitin, an AI detection tool used by the district.

The piece says the district has no official school board AI policy, although Phil Wacker, the district's high school curriculum supervisor, acknowledged Turnitin's limitations in September 2025, particularly for students whose first language is not English, according to St. Paul Publishing. At that time nearly 30 percent of the district's students were English learners. The SPPS Board of Education recently announced a goal of adopting an AI policy by the end of the 2027-28 school year, with details still vague and the board saying the policy will include expectations for how the district prepares students and staff to use, question, evaluate and create with AI. Wacker said conversations about a policy are happening.

The student argues that administrators, not students, should fix the problem, and that she sees a lack of urgency. She writes that the time spent debating a policy means the conversation will take her class's entire high school career, and that some students use AI and have found ways to avoid detection. Turnitin assigns a score based on the percentage of suspected AI sentences, measuring burstiness, or spontaneity of word choice, and sentence length, and the company claims human writing tends to be inconsistent and idiosyncratic. The student notes that her flagged essay was about how high school writing structure strips individuality from students' work.

stories.Headline: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
stories.Summary:
The Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported a critical inflection point in adversarial AI on November 16, 2026. Threat actors are now deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks to execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. These adversaries include cyber criminals, espionage groups, and those conducting information operations. They use generative AI to compress attack timelines and scale their operations. This shift moves beyond basic prompting toward fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines.

The report identifies open source frameworks called ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI used for autonomous intrusions. CAIRN targets the US aerospace sector, while PentAGI was used against Asian organizations from August to October 2026. CyberStrikeAI uses a Go-based backend API, and HexStrike AI integrates with the Model Context Protocol. Other tools mentioned include ZeroHollow for exploit development and Agent Zero for autonomous code execution. These systems automate the reverse engineering of patches to weaponize n-day vulnerabilities.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group stated that these frameworks represent a paradigm shift toward machine speed intrusions. They noted that while the mechanics of attacks remain the same, the scale introduces new challenges. Google said it is committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly through a multifaceted defense strategy. This strategy includes proactive model-level safeguards and targeted containment protocols to protect infrastructure. They use BeyondZero and an autonomous AI Threat Defense architecture for continuous monitoring.

State-sponsored groups and commercial Influence-as-a-Service vendors are affected by using LLMs to produce synthetic media. Financially motivated actors use LLMJacking to steal credentials and resell access through LLM Mixers. Cyber espionage groups are manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution. Organizations globally are targeted as the barrier to entry for running complex campaigns lowers. Defenders must now deal with a wave of fake LLM-generated exploits that require verification.

The articles state that zero-day exploits averaged 8 per month in 2025 and rose to 11 in 2026. These exploits spiked to 22 in August 2026, while overall disclosures nearly doubled from January to August. Previous research highlighted only nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities before this recent operational deployment. Threat actors now use differential analysis to rapidly weaponize patched vulnerabilities. This process shrinks the patch window for both public and enterprise infrastructure.

Google Security Operations deployed behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect the use of the ARTEX tool. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework to counter LLM-enabled offensive tooling. Experts believe threat actors will continue using these frameworks in global campaigns as capabilities evolve. Future operations are expected to move further along the autonomous scale toward fully agentic intrusions. The articles leave open how stealth will increase as these tools and underlying models evolve.

stories.Headline: Malcolm Myers finds ten AI-exposed companies lose $206 billion in market value since 2021
stories.Summary:
Ten publicly listed companies operating in sectors exposed to artificial intelligence have collectively lost $206 billion in market value since the end of 2021, according to an analysis by Malcolm Myers, who works with marketplace and services platform businesses at EIV. The erosion in market value initially came despite relatively resilient revenue growth, as nine of the 10 companies recorded higher revenues between 2021 and 2025. Their combined revenue increased 47% from $22.2 billion to $32.7 billion over that period, even as investors questioned whether these businesses could withstand AI disruption. The disruption is now becoming visible in their financial performance, with revenue in the third quarter of 2026 declining 23% at Tripadvisor's hotels business, 25% at Fiverr's marketplace, 33% at Shutterstock and 40% at Chegg. The decline in valuations has been particularly pronounced across four segments that Myers noted in his analysis.

In price comparison and travel search, Tripadvisor has lost 77% of its market value since 2021, while LendingTree and TripAdvisor have declined 68% and 67% respectively, as these businesses largely depend on search traffic and referral fees. Booking.com, which facilitates the actual transaction, has gained 20% in contrast to those search-dependent platforms. Shutterstock has lost 97% of its value, while Wix and Adobe have declined 68% and 66% respectively, as AI increasingly enables users to generate content and applications on demand. Freelance marketplaces have faced similar challenges, with Fiverr losing 93% of its value and Upwork falling 72%, as businesses and consumers increasingly use AI to produce digital work they previously outsourced to freelancers. Chegg has lost 98% of its market value as large language models increasingly provide homework answers and educational assistance free of charge, Myers said.

Myers believes not all marketplaces face the same degree of risk, because platforms that aggregate unique supply, facilitate payments and manage fulfillment could prove more resilient as AI agents work alongside these businesses rather than replace them. He also sees an emerging opportunity in AI-native businesses that deliver completed outcomes instead of simply connecting customers with service providers or offering software to complete tasks. Examples include Corgi, which underwrites and issues insurance policies, Lawhive, which provides legal services through an AI-enabled law firm, and Mercor, which organises specialist work to deliver training data and evaluations. Mercor recently completed a $750 million Series D funding round at a $20 billion valuation, less than four years after its launch, and Myers believes the shift towards delivering completed outcomes could create some of the most valuable marketplaces and services businesses over the next decade.

stories.Headline: Urban Legend pays right-wing influencers to promote Nvidia chip sales to China and pro-AI articles
stories.Summary:
Urban Legend paid right-wing influencers to promote Nvidia chip sales to China and pro-AI articles. This activity occurred for more than a year and ended on November 10, 2026. Over 80 influencers on X and other platforms received payments for these endorsements. The marketing firm used a network of about 1,400 different campaigns. These efforts boosted the chipmaker and two dark-money groups in the AI industry.

The campaigns promoted Nvidia H200 chip sales to China and open-weights AI. Build American AI is linked to Greg Brockman, Marc Andreessen, and Ben Horowitz. Innovation Council Action is connected to Trump AI Advisor David Sacks and Jordan Schachtel. Lyceum launched on June 9, 2026, and published four tied policy editorials. Trending Politics marked four of five promoted articles as Sponsored or Sponsored Plus.

Urban Legend declined to comment on the investigation into its influencer marketing practices. One influencer, Kaya Jones, posted a referral link asking others to become paid influencers. Another creator, Ash Saves USA, stated she was helping drive traffic to articles. Lyceum claimed that its publication remains editorially independent despite the promoted content. Upward News did not respond to requests for comment regarding its native advertisements.

The campaigns targeted AI doomers and criticized Anthropic and OpenAI for being woke. These efforts aimed to align AI industry narratives with the Trump administration's goals. Influencers like Donald Trump Jr. and Kash Patel stopped posting these links in November 2024. Readers were affected by undisclosed ads that appeared as organic social media posts. Some promoted articles were written by humans while others were likely AI-generated.

Urban Legend used tracking domains like mycreator.studio, registered on May 29, 2021. The firm paid creators per click or action based on a 2023 agreement. Redirects through exc.to were identified by WIRED Magazine as early as 2021. The company recently registered bitlicustom.com after being questioned about its tracking methods. Most campaigns were unrelated to AI and covered a wide range of topics.

The firm continues to use new domains to track conversions for its clients. It remains unclear who specifically paid for the sponsored articles on Trending Politics. The articles do not reveal the total amount of money paid to influencers. It is unknown if other dark-money groups funded these specific AI campaigns. The full list of the 80 influencers has not been disclosed.

stories.Headline: Trump launches five billion dollar Genesis Mission to advance science through AI
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump launched the Genesis Mission in November 2025 to advance science through artificial intelligence. This government wide effort provides five billion dollars for research and development. It began at the Energy Department and now includes more than 15 federal agencies. The president also issued a second order in June to speed quantum technology development. These initiatives focus on AI, quantum science, and supercomputing to transform engineering.

The Energy Department uses its data, facilities, and computing power to build shared AI tools. It funded nearly 300 projects this year, including nuclear fusion and electric grid simulations. The National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health launched efforts in biology, health, and space. A July report from the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy had 123 pages. Federal agencies spent about 4.2 billion dollars on AI research and development in 2025.

Darío Gil is the undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy. He described AI, quantum science, and supercomputing as the three legs of a stool. Gil stated that 400 million dollars for Genesis is small compared to the 8.4 billion dollar budget. John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, California, called this an inflection point. Sarrao noted that SLAC leads two Genesis projects and is involved in 20 others.

Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University leads a project combining huge datasets from observatories and instruments. She said the idea is conceptually powerful but noted her cosmology grant was reduced this year. Brad Marston, president of the American Physical Society at Brown University, wants all science fields supported. He argued that a balanced approach matters because AI and quantum were once backwaters. Some researchers warn that the AI push comes at the expense of other scientific fields.

Funding cuts and delays have hit public health and climate research during Trump's second term. The 2025 budget law provided some Genesis funding, but other money came from the Energy Department. Quantum technology is less mature, according to Celia Merzbacher of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium. She described quantum computing as being at the first few miles of a marathon. Several projects now involve quantum materials, quantum sensors, and quantum error correction.

The Energy Department's Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop error corrected quantum computers by 2028. Researchers hope that AI and quantum technologies can help each other advance. The articles do not say how the administration will handle future funding trade offs. It remains open whether the balance between core research and AI will be maintained. The reports do not specify when the 123 page federal science report was finalized.

stories.Headline: Xero launches Xforce to help accounting firms build AI workflows
stories.Summary:
Xero announced Xforce by Xero, a team of forward-deployed engineers and partner consultants who work with accounting firms to design their workflows for the artificial intelligence era, in a media release dated Nov. 11. The team will use XeroForce, Xero's APIs and Xero OS, and it will integrate with other software in a practice's technology stack to automate workflows end-to-end, the company said. Xforce is in beta and is being developed with a handful of design partners in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, including Liston Newton Advisory in Australia, Nexia Christchurch and Shepherd Hensman in New Zealand, and Azets and Sumer in the U.K. XeroForce, announced in May, is a natural language custom AI agent builder for the financial workflows of small businesses and accountants, helping practices turn manual tasks into durable, scalable workflows. Xforce brings the expertise of forward-deployed engineers and partner consultants to help accounting firms put XeroForce to work for their practice, their employees and their small business clients, according to Xero. All of Xero's AI innovations, including JAX, its agentic platform, are grounded in what the company calls Accountable Intelligence and sit within the AI-native Xero OS.

More information about Xforce by Xero can be found on the company's website, the article said. The article gave no further dates or figures beyond the Nov. 11 release date and the May announcement of XeroForce. Diya Jolly, president of product and technology at Xero, said that building on positive feedback on XeroForce in beta, Xforce puts experienced experts in the field with firms to help them embed trusted, repeatable and scalable AI workflows. She said those workflows deliver greater consistency and efficiency and give firms time back to reinvest in growing their practice. Jolly said Xero is excited to work with these firms as its first design partners for Xforce, and that together they will explore how AI and automation can make everyday accounting simpler.

She said the shared ambition is to champion clients' success by combining great technology with the personal advice and support that help businesses thrive. Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, chief executive of Xero, said accountants and bookkeepers are being asked to do more with fewer people, and fewer are entering the profession. She said AI can help, but to scale it firms need hands-on support to build it into the way they work. Cassidy said partner consultants provided that support when thousands of firms moved from desktop to cloud, and that Xforce is designed to do the same for AI, with every firm deciding what gets automated on a trusted platform they control. The articles do not say when Xforce will move beyond beta or how firms can join the program.

stories.Headline: Han Seong-sook bans smart devices and deploys extra staff to stop AI cheating in college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Tuesday that the government would activate an interagency emergency response team, ban the possession of smart devices during the exam and deploy additional personnel to test sites to root out AI cheating in this week's college entrance exam. She made the remark during a Cabinet meeting, as concerns deepened that AI-assisted cheating could be used in this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, which is set for Thursday. The concerns followed the confession by the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam that he cheated with the help of AI. Han called such cheating a social evil and said the government would root it out completely.

Han said all smart devices, including smartphones, must be powered off and turned in, and that authorities would thoroughly inspect all glasses and watches worn by test takers. She said items such as collars, sleeves and buttons would also be carefully checked. The government will tighten the management of Wi-Fi networks around the test sites, and all bags belonging to examinees must be stored outside the examination rooms, such as in hallways. Checks will be conducted to ensure that no smart devices are active among the personal belongings stored outside the examination rooms.

Han said the government would deploy additional proctors and apply a zero-tolerance policy to strictly penalize any instances of cheating. She said any suspected case would be thoroughly investigated and met with stern action, including invalidating the exam, revoking eligibility and filing criminal complaints or requesting police investigations. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's exam, including a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or about $75,000, for tips. The article did not say what happens next beyond those measures.

stories.Headline: Banks seek to curb AI debt exposure as backlash against the technology mounts
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times reported on 17 November 2026 that banks are seeking to curb their exposure to debt linked to artificial intelligence, as a public backlash against the technology mounts, though the article itself sits behind a paywall and its full contents are not available. The report carries a headline stating that banks want to limit how much AI-related debt they hold while criticism of the sector grows. No further details, including which banks are involved or what specific measures they are taking, appear in the accessible text. The date of the report is the only precise figure the available material gives.

The accessible portion of the article contains no numbers on the scale of AI debt, no names of institutions beyond the general reference to banks, and no dates other than the publication date of 17 November 2026. It does not say what the banks require of borrowers, what rules or limits they are changing, or how much exposure they currently carry. The only change it signals is a stated intention among banks to curb AI debt exposure in response to a mounting backlash. Nothing in the available text describes a completed action, a decision by a named regulator, or a figure attached to any institution.

The article names no individual as responsible and carries no direct statements from bank executives, regulators or critics, so there is no one whose remarks can be paraphrased. Responsibility for the reported move rests with banks as a group, according to the headline, but the text does not identify which ones. No spokesperson is quoted and no explanation is offered for why the backlash is growing or who is driving it. The accessible material therefore cannot support any account of what was said by anyone involved.

The context the available text provides is limited to the existence of a backlash against AI and a parallel concern among banks about their lending and holdings tied to the sector. It does not say what happens next, whether the banks have set targets, whether regulators are involved, or how the story might develop. Because the articles carry too little to support a longer account, this is a breaking story and further reporting will follow as details emerge. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Democrats win Congress as voters reject data centers over rising power bills
stories.Summary:
Democrats won both houses of Congress during the midterm elections in November 2026. Some candidates won by criticizing the AI boom and the growth of data centers. Voters expressed a strong desire for relief from rising electricity bills. This blue wave occurred as people rejected the proliferation of gigantic data centers. The election results reflect a widespread public backlash against the AI industry.

Voters rejected 40 of 41 local data center measures across 10 different states. A March Gallup poll showed 71 percent of Americans opposed local data centers. Wholesale electricity prices near some centers rose 267 percent over five years. Cornell researchers found operators pay only 38 percent of linked infrastructure costs. The four largest cloud companies expect capital spending of 720 to 740 billion dollars.

Senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan stated that people really hate data centers. Representative Greg Casar wants AI CEOs to testify under oath during hearings. Senator Ed Markey warned executives about the many subpoenas the government will print. Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona called for a day one pause on AI. Senator Bernie Sanders advocated for democratic oversight instead of an outright ban.

Building trade unions view data centers as a bonanza for creating new jobs. Some Republicans distanced themselves from the president because of their own constituents. Voters are concerned about electricity, water, jobs, and various AI doomsday scenarios. Tech leaders have courted President Trump, including Elon Musk who spent 500 million dollars. The Magnificent Seven companies now make up about a third of the S&P 500.

ING estimates that AI investment accounts for 37 percent of U.S. GDP growth. Governor Kathy Hochul of New York froze hyperscale data center permits for one year. Texas Governor Greg Abbott halted new grid connections while pending a necessary audit. Microsoft pledged in January to cover its own power costs for its operations. Meta and Amazon created billion-dollar community funds in August and October of 2026.

The Create AI Act would make a National Science Foundation computing program permanent. The AI Whistleblower Protection Act and AI LEAD Act are other bipartisan bills. OpenAI rebranded its data centers as compute campuses two days after the election. State utility regulators may force data centers to cover their own grid upgrades. It remains uncertain if Democrats can demand accountability from these powerful tech executives.

stories.Headline: NATO cyber agency gives allies OpenAI models and uses up to 300 billion tokens a month
stories.Summary:
NATO's Communications and Information Agency gives NATO's core institutions access to OpenAI's cybersecurity models so they can help protect Allied networks, and the alliance has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens a month. That access comes through Daybreak, OpenAI's program for vetted defenders doing authorized work such as reviewing code, chasing suspicious activity and testing fixes. The exposure sits in software that European institutions run every day, and ENISA, the EU's cyber agency, used OpenAI models to find four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes out for all four. ENISA and CERT-EU reviewed 27 software projects using several frontier models, OpenAI's among them, along with tools such as the Codex security plug-in, and maintainers assessed 88 potential issues and confirmed 95% of them as real.

Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation uses Daybreak to defend civilian infrastructure, and France's ANSSI and national agencies in Germany and Poland also have access. At NATO's 2026 Crossed Swords exercise, run by the CCDCOE, participants built and tested AI agents for cyber operations in Daybreak, with an emphasis on keeping humans in charge. CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help find six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, the operating system on MikroTik's network gear, and its researchers directed the work and checked findings on real systems. MikroTik released fixes, and CERT Polska confirmed they stop the attacks it had seen.

Dr Dylan Browne, the NCIA general manager, said that as the alliance scales adoption it will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models. He said this insight will help NATO optimise costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions. The agency's work therefore ties the technical defense of Allied networks to a closer reading of what the models cost to run and how they compare with rival offerings. The articles do not say what procurement choices or further deployments might follow from that review.

stories.Headline: European leaders meet in Dublin to discuss coordinating US and EU AI safety efforts
stories.Summary:
European leaders including Prime Minister Micheal Martin, Antonio Costa, and Roberta Metsola met in Dublin, Ireland, on November 13, 2026, to discuss artificial intelligence. This gathering highlighted the need for the United States and the European Union to coordinate on AI safety to prevent catastrophic risks. While the Trump administration has shown little interest in this engagement, recent cybersecurity incidents from American frontier labs may encourage narrower cooperation. Progress is more likely to occur through legislatures, specifically by creating a joint AI safety working group within the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue.

This proposed coordination would utilize the Transatlantic Legislators’ Dialogue, which has met twice a year since 1999 to discuss security and trade. The effort would focus on interoperable incident reporting and establishing designated points of contact within regulatory and law enforcement agencies. It would build upon the October 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence and the bipartisan FRONTIER Act currently in the United States. European efforts include the AI Act and the Digital Omnibus, which entered into force in July 2026 to adjust compliance requirements.

The European Parliament's steering committee and a bipartisan US delegation are responsible for managing these legislative exchanges. These officials suggest that focusing on cybersecurity measures first would avoid contentious issues like data privacy or content moderation. They argue that an early dialogue with the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress would ensure that new enforcement measures are compatible. This approach aims to avoid previous failures where dialogues were dismissed as talk shops or seen as attempts to export regulatory regimes.

The current US policy is a patchwork of state laws and voluntary commitments, while the EU uses a formal legal framework. Unresolved questions remain regarding the oversight of restricted models, such as the Mythos rollout by Anthropic through Project Glasswing. Legislators face pressure from constituents to deliver meaningful safety measures that address risks extending across international borders. Future efforts will seek common definitions for incident reporting, drawing on the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act.

Articles.Title: Why Congress and the European Parliament need an AI safety dialogue

stories.Headline: Geetanshu Gulati and Tim Han urge readers to practice preemptive skepticism online
stories.Summary:
The Daily Trojan published an opinion article titled "Everyone should practice a post-AI mindset" on Nov. 17, 2026, written by Geetanshu Gulati and Tim Han. The article argues that readers should employ "preemptive skepticism" as they search for humanity and truth online. It says our generation is living through a technological revolution, and that millennials and Gen Z are often called digital natives or digital pioneers. It states that millennials and Gen Z are the most digitally literate generations, and that everything is done with smartphones nowadays. It gives ordering morning coffee and logging into Netflix or a bank account as examples of smartphone tasks.

The article says the digital world's most daunting thing is its lack of physicality or security, and that there is no such thing as concrete or absolute certification. It says everyone uses the internet and anyone can input information and modify it however they want. It says real information can be modified to mislead audiences, and fake information can be appealing enough to bring out real emotions. It says that with the rise of artificial intelligence-generated content on everyday media platforms, this is easier than ever. The article quotes Jelani Williams, a master's student studying digital social media, saying he has definitely seen a video he thought was AI.

It quotes him saying there are a lot of times he is just skeptical immediately, more so than anything, and asking whether something actually happened. It describes the liar's dividend as a phenomenon in which realistic AI and advanced technology allow public figures to falsely claim that authentic, damaging evidence against them is manipulated. It says the public figure then usually shifts the burden of proof to others, demanding even more concrete evidence despite having just stubbornly rejected the initial facts. It says the internet is permanently changing in ways one can't easily imagine, prompting us to keep engaging, stay up to date and leave marks. The article says people start acting overly intelligent, which makes the internet dangerous, and that one could easily fabricate false information to denounce another.

It says the one attacked could also easily accuse them of falsehood without verification, just because it criticized them. It says that in a world where fake can be mistaken for real and real for fake, simple claims and first impressions do not shift the entire burden of proof onto those presenting them. It says we should evaluate sources, corroborate evidence and demand support for claims of manipulation. It quotes Jelani saying a claim would just have to be backed up really well, and that people have to be taught how to interpret things properly so they understand it is not real. The article says guardrails are starting to be set up for AI transparency, and that the California AI Transparency Act requires generative AI providers to embed machine-readable disclosures in generated content and provide free diagnostic tools.

It says Article 50 of the European Union's AI Act ensures AI systems are developed so users know if they are interacting with an AI system. It says Coalition for Content Provenance and Authority credentials set standards and function as digital labels showing their origin of creation. It says these laws and standards try to keep online content credible and transparent, yet their effectiveness depends on whether companies, platforms and creators follow through. It says these can only be social contracts that lose their meaning if not followed, and that even with penalties in place they are nothing more than retaliatory actions after the consequence that cannot guarantee prevention. The article says one should practice "preemptive skepticism" for every single piece of content encountered, pausing to check where content comes from and what other evidence supports it before deciding whether to trust or dismiss it.

It says one must recognize the liar's dividend of public figures and demand more of their denials. It says skills in actively searching for and verifying the origins of content are a necessary, if not vital, skill for an individual in the post-AI age. It says we are too passive in understanding the changes these technologies bring to our lives, and that not a lot of us get to the nitty-gritty of how they shape behavior and what responsibilities come with using them. It says we often approach new technology as consumers prioritizing convenience, and few of us try to bear the responsibility of deciding what uses are ethical and what limits one should set. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers describe technique to hide malicious payloads in open-weight AI models
stories.Summary:
Researchers described a technique called Lazarus last week to poison open-weight AI models. This method allows attackers to hide malicious payloads inside a few neural network neurons. Microsoft described the resulting compromised model as a sleeper agent for the attacker. These agents can grant an attacker access to the environment of the user. The attack targets models downloaded from the open Internet by unsuspecting users.

The technique requires targeting fewer than 10 dormant neurons late in the processing cycle. These neurons must fire sequentially and stay inactive until they receive a specific trigger. Triggers can be user inputs, tool outputs, or a date read in a terminal. The payload must be small and formatted correctly to function within the model. This differs from MaleficNet, a 2022 technique using code division multiple access.

Briland Hitaj of Confidencial said models are files that almost nobody ever inspects. He noted that malicious models have already appeared on the site Hugging Face. Hitaj explained that neural networks have more parameters than they strictly need for functioning. This allows attackers to nudge weights without visibly changing the behavior of the model. He stated that no scan can prove a model is completely clean.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini of Sapienza University of Rome advised using a defense-in-depth approach. He said users should download models from official sources and compare them to baselines. Organizations are affected because they often give AI agents access to credentials and systems. Mancini suggested monitoring for unusual shell commands or unexpected network connections at system boundaries. He argued for treating model weights like source code or binary files.

McKinsey found that 63 percent of organizations used open-weight models early last year. Another 76 percent of those survey respondents expected to use them more later. These models are popular because they are cheap, auditable, and liked by developers. Qwen 3.8-Max is an open-weight model with 2.4 trillion parameters and 100 million neurons. Researchers have explored storing malicious data in neural networks since at least 2020.

Users should limit AI agent access and require human approval for consequential actions. They must keep production systems and credentials out of reach of the agents. Microsoft says detection requires diffing deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights of the model. The articles leave open how to reliably find triggers chosen by an attacker. They do not state if any sleeper agents have been used outside research.

Articles.Title: 'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: China-linked threat actors use autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations
stories.Summary:
China-nexus threat actors used autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations between August and September. These attackers targeted advanced manufacturing, defense sectors, and various civil and human rights organizations. The malicious activity was tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. This campaign represents the second documented case of China-linked actors using the open source framework called Cairn. The actors conducted twenty-five operations against at least nineteen organizations to achieve unauthorized access or data retrieval.

The campaign targeted seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain firms and three US defense and defense policy organizations. Attackers used Chinese large language models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro to weaponize Cairn. Victims included a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, an education nonprofit, a US teacher's union, and an industry standards body. A defense policy think tank was also targeted through an open back-end registration endpoint on its identity platform. These operations lasted anywhere from twenty minutes to more than fifty hours and occurred simultaneously across multiple organizations.

Unit 42 researchers stated that attackers supplied a target and goal, then Cairn planned and executed the results. They noted that the framework coordinates activities through a shared blackboard where agents write findings as a fact-intent graph. Rickard Carlsson of Detectify said Cairn has a shared record that allows it to build on earlier findings. Tyler Oliver of Huntbase said it does not matter to a victim if a human or AI is behind the keyboard. John Strand of Black Hills Information Security suggested that organizations use continuous attack surface management and cyber deception.

The successful attacks resulted in the theft of dozens of valid credentials and military and government identities. One organization suffered a mass exposure of personal data that exceeded one million records. Attackers created persistent administrator accounts in a production system and modified a live industry standards-ballot document. The victims were affected by password-spraying, brute-forcing of production credentials, and unauthenticated account-creation bypasses on content management systems. Other organizations were targeted through identity and configuration weaknesses and exposed cloud APIs.

The attackers exploited known security gaps including insecure direct object references and mass-assignment privilege escalation. They also used weak and default credentials as well as dated public CVEs to gain initial network exposure. Unit 42 noted that AI is changing the speed, volume, and expanse of attacks but not the complexity. This means that software patching, attack-surface reduction, and identity hygiene remain effective defenses against these AI tools. The articles explain that AI agents can now work with limited supervision to identify and exploit vulnerabilities.

The findings provide a blueprint for how threat actors can weaponize AI tools in future offensive operations. Organizations are encouraged to identify all services exposed to the internet and restrict access wherever possible. Setting up tripwires can detect attackers during reconnaissance and lateral movement before they accomplish their objectives. The articles leave open how other AI penetration-testing frameworks, such as Artex, will be used in future campaigns. It remains to be seen how defenders will adapt to the increasing volume of autonomous AI attacks.

stories.Headline: ICBC Chairman Liao Lin outlines three priorities for banks adopting artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Liao Lin, the Chairman of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Ltd., presented three key priorities for banks using artificial intelligence on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He delivered these insights during his appearance at the APEC CEO Summit to discuss how financial institutions can best capitalize on new technology. The Chairman emphasized that banks must focus on specific strategic goals to successfully integrate these advanced digital tools into their operations. He believes that the current era is being defined by these major transformative technologies.

The strategy requires banks to align their technological advancements with their existing organizational structures to ensure efficiency. Financial institutions must also coordinate their investment cycles to keep pace with the rapid speed of technological change. Furthermore, the Chairman stated that banks must find a careful balance between pursuing innovation and managing potential risks. These three pillars are intended to guide banks as they move from pilot programs into full production.

Liao Lin explained that the Asia-Pacific region offers unique opportunities for AI due to its diverse financial services and vast markets. He also pointed to the highly interconnected industrial and supply chains within the region as a primary driver for growth. The Chairman described artificial intelligence as one of the most significant transformative technologies of the modern time. He suggested that leveraging these regional strengths would allow banks to maximize the benefits of AI adoption.

stories.Headline: Kodivo launches free interactive lessons to help developers direct and verify AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Kodivo launched free, browser-based interactive lessons on November 17, 2026, to help developers work effectively with AI coding agents. The platform's AI Coding path teaches developers how to give agents clear tasks, select the necessary context, and verify the work the agents produce. The lessons include examples and practice questions that show how to turn vague requests into verifiable tasks. One scenario shows an agent changing code for a Save button, after which the saved note disappears when it is reopened.

The lessons present explanations in short, interactive cards that let developers practice the decisions they make while coding with AI. Users can try a lesson without creating an account, and the platform supports connecting external agents such as Codex or Claude Code through MCP. Developers who prefer learning with their own tools can use their own provider account for those connections. The free lessons do not include an external AI subscription or provider usage.

Kodivo is responsible for the platform, and its lessons focus on giving clear instructions and verifying agent output before developers trust the results. The stated aim is to improve developer proficiency in AI-assisted coding workflows. The lessons teach that verifying a requirement means following the interaction through saving and reopening, rather than solely inspecting the code. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress oversees a cautious shift in AI funding strategy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is likely to recalibrate its aggressive financing strategy following a change in leadership. Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026, leading to this shift. Colette Kress has served as interim CEO since the resignation of Huang. The company is now expected to take a more cautious investment approach. Financial partners continue to discuss funding arrangements for various artificial intelligence companies.

The $500 billion initiative announced August 10 involves Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR. Nvidia may backstop 25 percent of transactions, which equals 125 billion dollars. An OpenAI data center in Ohio saw guarantees reduced from 250 billion to 105 billion dollars. Apple data center guarantees were cut from 500 billion to under 250 billion dollars. These specific guarantees are separate from the broader third-party capital initiative.

Interim CEO Colette Kress has overseen finances since 2013 and maintains a cautious stance. Former CEO Jensen Huang stated that the days of acting as a blank check are over. Huang told partners in Berlin they must build structures to raise their own funding. He suggested that companies seeking GPUs should collect upfront payments from their own customers. This approach aims to reduce the industry's total dependence on Nvidia's financial support.

UBS estimates that over 50 billion dollars in liquidity could disappear from the market. AI startups and neocloud companies with limited financial resources are directly impacted by this shift. These companies rely on guarantees to secure data centers and AI chips upfront. Low profitability and rising interest rates could make it harder for them to operate. Morgan Stanley expects future capital to concentrate on large customers with stronger credit profiles.

PitchBook reports Nvidia made 129 global investments this year, compared to 49 in 2023. This activity accounted for 27 percent of all global venture investment activity this year. The company projected 70 percent revenue growth for fiscal 2028 during a presentation in August. Previous adjusted gross margins were 75 percent, with third quarter guidance set at 74 percent. Wall Street expects third quarter revenue of 109.1 billion dollars and earnings per share of 2.47.

Nvidia will release fiscal 2027 third-quarter results on November 17 and hold an earnings call. Investors will watch the rollout of the Vera Rubin platform and its revenue contribution. The company will provide written commentary on results at 6:20 a.m. Korea time, November 18. A $3 billion investment in Perplexity and talks with other startups remain under consideration. The articles leave open how rising memory prices will impact the company's gross margins.

stories.Headline: Uber's legal AI agent cuts contract review time by over 20 per cent at 91 per cent accuracy
stories.Summary:
Uber's Legal Redlining Agent has cut the average contract review time by more than 20 per cent while reaching 91 per cent accuracy in its AI-generated decisions, the company said in a report dated 17 November 2026. The system sits directly inside Microsoft Word, where it analyses proposed contract changes and assesses the legal risks they carry. It then recommends policy-aligned responses by drawing on retrieval-augmented generation, historical lawyer feedback and deterministic rules. Lawyers stay responsible for reviewing and approving every recommendation the agent makes. The agent spots edits made by external parties, works out their intent and compares the changes against legal policies.

It suggests whether a clause should be accepted, rejected or modified, and it writes comments explaining each recommendation. Uber began building the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025. An initial RAG setup pulled relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide the language model's responses, and a later feedback loop captured lawyers' decisions, reasoning and final edited text. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions down to about 20 candidates, and a second language model-based filtering stage checks their relevance.

Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life set to 365 days, gives priority to recent decisions. The architecture pairs a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph, while OpenSearch stores vectorised legal rules and historical feedback and Redis keeps session state for follow-up questions. A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and can override the model's recommendations. Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix invests 1.4 trillion won to support domestic chip suppliers and fund Trinity Fab
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix announced on Monday that it plans to spend 1.4 trillion won, or about $1.05 billion, over the next five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment. The South Korean chipmaker said the programme is meant to strengthen its supply chain as competition intensifies in the AI chip market. The company also gave details of a jointly funded testing facility called Trinity Fab, which will cost 874.6 billion won and will sit at its semiconductor complex in Yongin, south of Seoul. Smaller suppliers will use the facility to test products under conditions similar to commercial chip production lines, and it is scheduled to begin operations in May 2027.

SK Hynix will put 443.2 billion won into Trinity Fab, the central government will contribute 373.6 billion won and local governments will add 57.7 billion won. The facility will be housed within the first chip plant at the Yongin cluster, where the company plans to invest 600 trillion won to build four fabrication plants. The supplier support programme covers four stages, namely research and development, testing, mass production and sales, and its aim is to help smaller companies overcome financing and technology challenges. Under the research support programme, SK Hynix will provide up to 50 per cent of initial development costs in advance and will compensate suppliers for work done even if a project does not meet its targets. SK Hynix and financial institutions will further provide 2 trillion won in financing, backed by the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation.

SK Hynix is responsible for the investment and for the Trinity Fab partnership, which it runs with the central government and local governments. The company said the programme is intended to assist smaller companies in overcoming financing and technology challenges, and it will pay suppliers for work undertaken even when a project falls short of its targets. The articles do not name any individual executive or give any further direct comment from the company. The context the articles give is intensifying competition in the AI chip market, which the investment is meant to address by bolstering the supply chain. The articles do not say what happens after the five year programme or after Trinity Fab opens in May 2027.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix to invest $1.05 billion in chip supplier support

stories.Headline: IBM chairman Arvind Krishna plans $10 billion quantum investment and predicts AI will displace 10 to 20 per cent of jobs
stories.Summary:
IBM spends approximately $3 billion every year in India, and the company plans a $10 billion global investment in quantum computing over the next five years, according to Chairman and Chief Executive Arvind Krishna, as reported by TechGig on November 17, 2026. Krishna also predicted that artificial intelligence could displace 10 to 20 per cent of jobs over the next decade, with the business process outsourcing industry likely to face the biggest reductions in employment. IBM has continued to expand its workforce in India, hiring an estimated 5,000 to 10,000 people over the past year, and it is increasing recruitment in chip design, software development, testing, site reliability engineering, and AI. Nearly half of the code written at IBM is already generated by AI, Krishna said, and he predicted that programmers would evolve into system engineers who tell AI what to write rather than writing code themselves.

Krishna estimated that AI could add around $500 billion to India's gross domestic product by the end of the decade, and he urged the country to accelerate AI adoption across businesses and government rather than focusing disproportionately on developing large language models. IBM research indicates that over 90 per cent of Indian enterprises recognise AI's potential, but more than 75 per cent have made little progress in adoption, a gap that reflects challenges in data readiness, skills, and willingness to redesign business processes. Unlike earlier technologies, AI delivers full benefits only when it is integrated across entire business processes, according to the article. IBM is working with the Andhra Pradesh government and Tata Consultancy Services to establish a quantum computer in Amaravati by early 2027, and Krishna expects quantum computing to generate significant revenues by 2028-29 as commercial and scientific applications emerge.

Krishna favoured a light-touch approach to AI regulation, arguing that excessive government intervention could undermine innovation, and he said existing laws already address several potential harms associated with the technology. He advised the Indian government to scale existing initiatives in semiconductors and AI deployment before pursuing additional technology bets. Krishna predicted that open models would account for 80 per cent of all AI tokens before the end of the decade, which could limit the pricing power of a small number of large model providers. He also warned businesses against becoming overly attached to existing products and models as technological change accelerates, according to the report.

stories.Headline: Fractal evaluates 20 to 25 startups for acquisitions to strengthen enterprise AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
Fractal is evaluating 20 to 25 startups for potential acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering, according to a Reuters report cited by TechGig on 17 November 2026. The company is looking to strengthen its enterprise AI capabilities ahead of an expected scale-up in enterprise AI adoption. CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said the merger and acquisition focus is on acquiring specialised engineering talent. The company also aims to strengthen relationships with large cloud computing firms and frontier AI labs. Fractal is open to deals worth up to ₹1,000 crore, with a preferred acquisition size of $50-100 million, Velamakanni said.

The company evaluated around 800 potential targets over the past 12 months. Fractal reported record revenue from operations of ₹956.5 crore in Q2 FY27, up nearly 20 per cent year-on-year, while net profit more than doubled 139 per cent year-on-year to ₹79.2 crore in the same quarter. Earlier in November, Fractal acquired Geneva-based analytics firm PricingOne for 1.32 million Swiss francs ($1.57 million), which Velamakanni described as an acqui-hire providing a foothold in Europe. Velamakanni expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper. He noted the cost of fixed intelligence from a foundation model could fall 93 per cent over a year.

This shift should make large-scale AI deployment compelling for enterprises, with impact becoming meaningful as early as FY28. Fractal aims for acquisitions that accelerate its ability to build and deploy complex enterprise AI solutions. The company reorganised its business in April around three pillars: AI-led Transformation, AI Foundations, and AI Work & Workforce. This structure enhances its enterprise AI offerings and builds capabilities in agentic AI governance. The articles do not say when any acquisition might be completed or which specific startups are in talks.

Articles.Title: Fractal seeks AI acquisitions for enterprise AI scale-up

stories.Headline: Henna Virkkunen hosts Brussels Apply AI Summit and presents first startup award
stories.Summary:
Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels on 17 November 2026, the European Commission has announced. They will discuss how artificial intelligence can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector, according to the press release. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will host the summit and present the first Apply AI Startup Award to three European start-ups.

The award recognises innovative European startups and scaleups developing AI solutions in the strategic sectors, the Commission said. Alongside the in-person event, an online conference platform will run from 16 to 20 November, allowing an additional 2,500 participants to join part of the summit. The Apply AI Summit marks one year since the adoption of the Apply AI Strategy, which sets out how to speed up the use of AI in Europe’s key industries and the public sector. It concludes the first European AI Innovation Month, running from 14 October to 17 November 2026, organised by the European Commission in partnership with the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union.

Virkkunen, as Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, is responsible for hosting the summit and presenting the first Apply AI Startup Award to the three winning European start-ups. The Commission organised the European AI Innovation Month in partnership with the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union. The press release does not say what the three start-ups said or name them. The articles give no further statements from the hosts or participants.

The summit is tied to the Apply AI Strategy, which the Commission adopted one year before the event and which sets out how to speed up the use of AI in Europe’s key industries and the public sector. The articles do not say what happens after the summit beyond the online platform running until 20 November. More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korea and other allies sign a security pact to protect AI technologies and supply chains
stories.Summary:
South Korea joined the United States, Japan, and other allies on Sunday, November 16, 2026, to sign a security pact for artificial intelligence. This agreement, known as the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, aims to protect critical AI technologies and supply chains from hostile actors. The move occurred just before U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this Wednesday and Thursday in Shenzhen. The pact is part of a larger State Department initiative called Pax Silica, which seeks to help allied supply chains withstand shocks.

The declaration was signed by the United States, Korea, Japan, Australia, Israel, Britain, India, Singapore, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. It requires these nations to safeguard sensitive technologies that could provide a military or intelligence advantage if stolen or illicitly transferred. Participating countries plan to establish working groups, including one dedicated to creating economic hubs that attract AI investment. Jacob Helberg, the U.S. under secretary of state for economic affairs, expects Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden to sign the agreement this week. Second Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jin-a signed the document in person as the head of the Korean delegation.

Jacob Helberg described the declaration as historic because partners agreed to treat the security of technology and infrastructure as a shared responsibility. He noted that chip design, equipment, and shipping ports are often located in different countries, necessitating this joint approach. While some view the bloc as an effort to isolate China, a source familiar with the matter stated that the text does not single out any specific country. Victor Gao, vice president of the Center for China and Globalization, warned that using recent scandals to pressure China would be a total miscalculation.

The timing of the pact coincides with a tariff truce between Washington and Beijing that lasts until January 10, 2027. Upcoming talks in Shenzhen may focus on a trade-off between Chinese rare earths and American AI technology. Tensions have also risen following allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. These concerns about technology leaks have led to bipartisan calls in Washington for stricter export controls on AI chips. If no deal is reached this week, China may use its control of rare earths to pressure the United States.

Articles.Title: Seoul joins U.S.-led AI pact as Washington rallies allies before Trump-Xi talks

stories.headline_source: Seoul joins U.S.-led AI pact as Washington rallies allies before Trump-Xi talks

stories.Headline: New Jersey assembly committee advances bills to regulate AI in insurance and tenant screening
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced legislation to regulate artificial intelligence in insurance, housing and the workplace at a November 16, 2026 meeting of the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee. The committee took up bills limiting AI use in insurance claim denials, regulating automated tenant screening and imposing new requirements on electronic monitoring of employees. Lawmakers also considered measures requiring greater transparency from data center developers. Assemblyman Chris Tully (D-Bergenfield), the committee chairman, said the legislation reflects the need to protect consumers as AI becomes more widely used. The proposals drew concerns from businesses about higher costs and restrictions on emerging technology.

One bill, A5494, would prohibit certain uses of artificial intelligence in denying homeowners, automobile and flood insurance claims. It advanced with Assemblyman Chris DePhillips (R-Wyckoff) abstaining and every other committee member voting in favor. A second bill, A5495, would regulate automated tenant screening systems used to evaluate prospective renters. It also advanced with DePhillips abstaining and the remaining committee members voting in favor. The committee held a discussion-only hearing on A4981, which would regulate AI-based electronic monitoring systems used in employment and public services.

Assembly members Heather Simmons (D-Glassboro) and Cody Miller (D-Monroe) are sponsoring that proposal, along with 16 other Democratic co-sponsors. Tully said AI systems can improve efficiency and tackle fraud, but that people must be protected from automatic denial by algorithms. He said that when a major decision affects someone's life, there must always be a human in the loop. Tully said mandating human oversight establishes common-sense guardrails to use these powerful tools responsibly. DePhillips said he abstained on both bills because proponents and opponents did not seem that far apart and he saw an opportunity for both sides to collaborate.

Assemblyman Balvir Singh (D-Burlington) said he felt like he was learning to ride a bike while riding it. Assemblywoman Carmen Morales (D-Bloomfield) defended the insurance proposal as a consumer protection measure and said it really is about transparency. Insurance industry representatives raised concerns that the restrictions could limit their ability to use new technology and leave companies at a competitive disadvantage. Nicholas Kikis, vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, did not take a position on the tenant screening bill but warned that AI has made it increasingly difficult for landlords to detect fraudulent applications. Kikis pointed to income verification, saying documents landlords previously could verify with relative ease can now be altered using AI.

Jeff Kolekowski of the New Jersey Builders Association raised similar concerns without taking a formal position on the bill. Anthony Russo of the Commerce and Industry Association of New Jersey said the monitoring bill would add a high cost to companies that invent those technologies and that they would have to pay to have it approved. Russo said that if the bill goes through, it just adds to the cost of doing business. Jack Ramirez of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association said the bill's definition of artificial intelligence was too broad and could subject ordinary business tools to additional regulation. Eric Richards, legislative affairs coordinator for the New Jersey AFL-CIO, said AI has the power to change the very nature of work and that without oversight AI companies pose tremendous risk to working people.

Richards said the bill puts clear common-sense ground rules for how AI can be used in the workplace and makes sure an employer can't spy on you when you're off the clock. A5224 would require data center developers to disclose certain information to the public and elected officials before preliminary site plan consideration under the Municipal Land Use Law. S4304, sponsored by State Sens. Linda Greenstein (D-Plainsboro) and Brian Stack (D-Union City), would prohibit agreements intended to conceal certain information about data center developments, and its Assembly counterpart is A2774. Greenstein said that if you don't play by the rules of open government, you don't get to build in New Jersey, and that confidentiality agreements could prevent residents and local officials from learning the full extent of a project's electricity demands and environmental effects.

Chris Sotiro of the Climate Revolution Action Network said the developers are not interested in transparency but are interested in hiding. A2774 advanced with bipartisan support, with DePhillips, the only Republican present at the hearing, voting in favor, and Assemblyman Greg McGuckin (R-Toms River) was absent. Earlier this year, Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation sponsored by Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Summit) that redirected $250 million in unused data center tax credits to the New Jersey Economic Development Authority. The measure passed the Legislature with nearly unanimous support.

The hearings illustrate the competing pressures facing lawmakers as they try to establish protections for consumers, tenants and workers without imposing restrictions that businesses say could discourage innovation or make new technologies more expensive to use. The articles do not say when the full Assembly or Senate might vote on the bills. The articles do not say what happens to A4981 after the discussion-only hearing. More to follow.
