stories.Headline: Tangzheng Lian and coauthors post BlinkOPD, a distillation method that cuts training data 12-fold
stories.Summary:
Tangzheng Lian, Hang Zhang, Guanyu Hu, Renjiu Hu, Zhensong Zhang, Jiankang Deng and Jifei Song posted a paper on arXiv on 17 November 2026 describing a method called Blink On-Policy Distillation, or BlinkOPD, for training multimodal large language models. The work targets on-policy distillation, a post-training approach that improves fine-grained perception by folding costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. The authors report that vanilla on-policy distillation is inherently susceptible to what they call linguistic momentum, in which the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes and thereby weaken corrective supervision. Their proposal has the teacher blink at every token, reading the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed.

The method adds a first-glance gain that further strengthens the correction on rollouts which conflict with the teacher, so that more effective supervision is extracted from each on-policy trajectory. Using only 500 training images, which the authors say is 12 times less data than existing on-policy distillation methods, BlinkOPD reaches state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks. Beyond fine-grained perception, the paper reports strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination and multimodal reasoning abilities. The abstract lists the code as a URL on the paper's page.

The seven authors are credited with the method and its results, and their abstract states the claims about the benchmarks and the training data without attributing them to any other party. The paper appears under the identifier 2611.16402 and is dated 17 November 2026, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The abstract describes on-policy distillation as an effective post-training approach and frames BlinkOPD as the response to the linguistic momentum problem it identifies. No further statements from the authors beyond the abstract are given in the articles.

The context the articles supply is the arXiv listing itself, which also describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features directly on the website. The listing says both individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have embraced its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv is committed to working only with partners who adhere to them. It also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next with the paper beyond its availability in the listed formats.

stories.Headline: Vasudha Gadhiraju grounds Normal's AI rollout in cross-agency data work
stories.Summary:
The 57 cities recognized in this year's survey from the Center for Digital Government are prioritizing AI while modernizing core systems and upgrading data infrastructure, GovTech reported on Nov. 16, 2026. Leading cities are putting guardrails in place, launching AI-driven applications and adopting agentic workflows. At the same time, they're exploring new cybersecurity strategies, upgrading legacy systems and elevating the health of their data pipelines. In the face of lean budgets and rapid changes in technology, IT leaders are positioning themselves as strategic partners with city agencies. They're driving innovation while continuously improving both constituent engagement and employee experiences.

In Normal, Ill., Director of Innovation and Technology Vasudha Gadhiraju follows two guiding principles: make digital transformation a cross-agency effort, and ground the work in data. Grounded in the What Works Cities framework from Bloomberg Philanthropies, the approach now includes a cross-departmental Data Innovation Team that is helping build data governance and literacy. The town is leveraging training from InnovateUS, and it has begun to onboard AI applications, with an immediate focus on upgrading from a machine-learning-based chatbot to a true AI interface. The IT team has implemented the "Normal Forum," a platform used to document project updates and solicit constituent feedback around road safety. The town shares its public rights-of-way with Illinois State University, so safety for pedestrians, cyclists, motorists and transit users is of the utmost importance.

In Schaumburg, Ill., Director of Information Technology Peter Schaak said he was eager to embrace AI, but early on the village wanted to put some guardrails around it and to structure its approach. That has meant putting in place a high-level administrative protocol that instructs employees in effect to do good things, don't do bad things, with AI. From there he implemented a standard operating procedure, and the village did some training around both those documents to introduce and encourage the use of AI in the organization. The immediate impact of that effort has included adoption of Microsoft Copilot as the preferred internal AI tool, and the village also launched an external AI virtual assistant and an internal-facing virtual assistant, named for Serena and Louis, two swans that live on the municipal campus. The team also is working to leverage AI in short-term rental analysis tools to identify properties that are maybe not registered as rental properties but being used as short term rentals, the Airbnbs and Vrbos of the world.

In Corona, Calif., CIO Chris McMasters said it starts out with governance and security, and without that in place the city wouldn't have been able to do the things it is doing today. The IT team moved early to identify all the shadow AI already in use and then built policy around what people were actually doing with the tools, and the city adjusted its licenses to support the AI tools people were actually using, and IT worked with a startup to implement a security platform. An AI agent will tee up a graffiti complaint work order with human oversight and communicate the outcomes back to the resident, taking a process that was about 20 minutes per incident down to less than three minutes per incident. The IT team also replaced its 30-year-old ERP and HR systems with Workday last year, the culmination of two years' labor. The team also embedded an agent across the city websites that can watch when people are getting frustrated, hanging too long on a page or clicking wildly, and can prompt a human to intercept.

In Virginia Beach, CIO Peter Wallace said IT is not a call center, but a value center, and the tech team needs to deliver tangible results, and faced with budget cuts, you've got to be measurable. In Schaumburg, the IT team undertook an initiative to create worst-case scenario runbooks, and that entailed a ton of sequencing and dependency analysis and operational timing, and the team worked through all of those over the span of the year. The runbooks establish responsibilities and sequencing and assignment of personnel, a whole long list of roles and responsibilities and tasks to help the team get through a catastrophic breach. As Schaumburg built a new village hall, the tech team had to disassemble its main operations area and rebuild it in a temporary facility, and this fall the team was in the midst of taking it apart again and shifting to a brand-new facility. In Corona, IT is in the midst of consolidating city data on a single platform, and the city will use that to generate profiles about the people that engage with it, so that when it puts out things, it is much more targeted.

In Normal, Gadhiraju said the town wants to make sure people truly understand the advantages of AI and the efficiencies it brings, while also recognizing where AI may not be able to deliver at scale. She said there are so many vendors now who quickly use the word AI to sell products, and a lot of these vendors are approaching the town's departments directly, and people need to ask the right questions and not be tempted by the bells and whistles. She said data and technology and innovation should always work towards solving a problem that the community is facing. In Schaumburg, Schaak said the village's focus is on operational benefits, and it is moving out of the world of funny graphics and songs and trying to be strategic in how it deploys these tools. He said the focus is to be fiscally responsible while always leaning forward, always looking to expand services, improve services, improve response times, in an environment of continuous improvement.

In Corona, McMasters said the city is being very methodical about how it engages the public, to give them the things they want, and there is this memory the city is creating so that people's experiences with their government can be persistent. He said IT played a huge role in the project management, bringing all the departments together, executing and then leading everyone through, and outside consultants helped as well, and their involvement knocks down a lot of the bureaucracy and the politics and helps to streamline things. In Normal, Gadhiraju said across departments the town all works collaboratively, and it could not do what it is doing without the type of culture that it has, and while the city's approach to data has been years in the making, it has really come together in the past year. She said the IT team has worked to build strong data pipelines, making sure that it has good back-end connections to its systems so that data can be put to work, and there is now a dashboard that shows at a glance how well the town is doing on its goal of planting more trees than it removes, and another to help manage cellphone expenses. She said the town is truly building in the measurement in every aspect of the work it does, and she is optimistic about the new AI interface, and the town does need a chatbot, and it needs to make sure people can easily ask it questions.

stories.Headline: Nvidia outlines AI-defined model for chip fabrication using simulation and digital twins
stories.Summary:
Nvidia outlined what it calls an AI-defined model for semiconductor fabrication on 17 November 2026, combining accelerated computing, physics-based AI, AI agents and digital twins. The company said the approach focuses on using AI tools to shorten engineering analysis in chip manufacturing, where assessing process changes, materials interactions and defects can take days. It noted that physical experiments on production lines are costly, and that manufacturers face rising demand for advanced chips and increasingly complex processes. Nvidia said even small errors in yield or process quality can have significant commercial consequences in that environment.

The model relies on faster simulation so engineers can test more alternatives before deciding which changes to try in physical production. Software provider COMSOL is using Nvidia's cuDSS library to speed up semiconductor manufacturing simulations by up to 10 times, and Applied Materials is working with Nvidia on atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. Nvidia said Applied's Ginestra platform runs up to 10 times faster than CPU-only approaches with cuDSS, while its ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35 times faster with Nvidia PhysicsNeMo. Siemens is integrating Nvidia cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, which Nvidia said delivers up to 17 times acceleration on key simulation workloads. Nvidia also cited Lam Research, which it said has shown that the PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behaviour in milliseconds compared with days for a full simulation.

Nvidia said engineers still make the decisions in semiconductor production, but many intermediate steps can consume hours, and it highlighted AI agents as a way to automate sequences of tasks traditionally handled manually. It said Advantest is using Nvidia NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate the selection of which AI model to apply to a particular task, cutting response times from hours to minutes. Applied Materials uses Nvidia Omniverse libraries to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabrication plants, according to Nvidia, and those models simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and assess layouts, throughput, cost and process control. Nvidia argued that these technologies become more useful when linked in a closed engineering loop, where production data informs simulations and AI models that are then used to test alternatives before engineers decide on the factory floor.

Nvidia presented the closed loop as a way to shorten feedback cycles across semiconductor manufacturing, helping engineers identify problems earlier, evaluate more options and act on production insights sooner. The push comes as chipmakers and their suppliers look for ways to manage greater process complexity without relying solely on slower, more expensive physical trials. Nvidia said the aim is to extend simulation beyond individual manufacturing steps to the operation of the factory as a whole, which it said is increasingly relevant as fabrication plants become more complex and the cost of unsuccessful process changes rises.

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank uses Windows 11 and Intune to secure devices and run AI agents
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank built a secure, manageable foundation for AI with Windows 11, Microsoft reported on November 16, 2026. The bank invested in Microsoft Surface devices to bring a more secure foundation to employees. Windows 11 anchors Flagstar’s modernization, with Microsoft Entra for identity, Intune for device management, and Windows Autopilot for setup. Flagstar needed to unify a fragmented technology environment, simplify employee access and device management, and protect customer information as it introduced AI. Headquartered in New York, Flagstar Bank serves consumers and business clients across the United States.

Following mergers that brought together three organizations and six data centers, Flagstar needed a more consistent approach to employee access, device management, and AI. Its starting point was a patchwork of on-premises Active Directory systems and a legacy domain-join model for deploying devices. The bank is consolidating its Active Directory systems, with the goal of using Microsoft Entra as the authoritative source for employee identities and group membership. With Windows Hello for Business, employees sign in with a PIN or biometrics instead of relying on passwords. Microsoft Intune gives IT a single place to govern, control, and secure devices across the environment.

Kevin Kilbride, engineering manager at Flagstar Bank, said the Windows environment consisted of different hardware models and software versions, and that joining that with a domain legacy deployment system made it difficult to manage. Kilbride said moving to Windows as the secure foundation takes the bank from a fragmented environment to a more manageable IT experience, which translates to teams, employees, and then customers. Jason Pope, Flagstar’s chief technology and data officer, said that in a highly regulated organization you need to be able to show who, what, where, when, and how a specific user accessed an application, and that Windows together with Microsoft Entra and Intune gives the bank that ability. Kilbride said getting new devices imaged and shipped to employees used to take days, and that now the bank ships new Surface devices directly to employees and, with Windows Autopilot, employees are online in less than 15 minutes. Pope said using agentic AI on the Windows platform has enabled the bank to spend more time with customers and remove repetitive sequences, specifically in banking where there is a lot of duplication of entry.

Under the legacy domain-join model, IT spent at least a day or two getting each device ready before shipping it out, and employees had to wait for equipment to arrive before they could start work. Now the end-user support team simply allocates a device and gets it to the employee, and when the employee signs in with company credentials, Windows Autopilot and Intune automate the remaining setup. Employees across the bank already use StarIQ, the bank’s AI tool built on Microsoft Copilot, which Flagstar CEO Joseph Otting says has an adoption rate of about 83 percent. Within its Windows 11 environment, Flagstar also runs a custom small language model on Microsoft Surface devices, and its purpose-built agent, BranchIQ, uses the device’s neural processing unit to help bankers perform know-your-customer activities and accelerate onboarding customers. Localizing the AI model on the device supports the bank’s security priorities and enables offline access to policies, procedures, and customer-onboarding assistance.

When onboarding a customer, bankers must verify identity as part of know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks, which in the past meant jotting down details from a driver’s license or passport or keying them into a legacy system over and over. With BranchIQ, a banker can instead take a photo of the ID that stays on the device, and the agent extracts the details and enters them automatically into the systems of record used to set up the new customer and account. Windows supplies the operating environment and guardrails for this agent workflow with Microsoft Execution Containers, while Surface provides the neural processing unit and mobile form factor that bring it to branch colleagues’ flow of work. Agents on Surface devices are given their own identity in the Entra Suite, which lets the bank track an agent’s actions apart from a person’s. Microsoft Execution Containers, built into Windows 11, add control over what each agent can access and do, and give the bank a way to account for those actions to regulators.

Pope said that with the bank’s agents using Microsoft Execution Containers on its Windows platform, the bank was able to ascertain how an agent is working and control it, then prove how and why it controlled it and produce that report for regulators. Flagstar is now exploring how to expand its use of the containers as part of its Windows 11 AI work. Pope said the principle behind the bank’s Windows modernization is making work easier while keeping it secure, manageable, and compliant, and that from how employees sign in and get their devices to running AI locally on Surface, Windows is the foundation, and it is the same foundation the bank will use as it brings governed agents into the bank. Centralized policy management helps IT identify settings that need attention, resolve issues, and keep devices aligned as the bank’s security and compliance standards evolve. Together, these modern identity and device management tools help Flagstar document application access and demonstrate policy enforcement to auditors.

stories.Headline: Researchers review how AI can cut emissions across iron and steelmaking
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive academic review published in Carbon Neutral Systems examines how artificial intelligence can accelerate decarbonization across the iron and steel industry by optimizing process efficiency, enabling feedstock substitution, and supporting carbon capture, utilization, and storage. The study was authored by Xidi Shang, Wuliang Yin, Jianxin Pan, Min Wang, Hua Wang, Kai Yang, and Qingtai Xiao. It synthesizes findings from 133 representative investigations identified through structured database searches covering research published between 2000 and 2025. The review was published on November 16, 2026, according to bioengineer.org. The article appeared under the site's Technology section with a reading time of five minutes.

The authors highlight that the global steel sector accounts for approximately 7 to 9 percent of direct industrial carbon dioxide emissions. Traditional blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace configurations generate roughly 70 percent of global crude steel output. Electric arc furnace operations currently produce approximately 41.5 percent of crude steel in the European Union and 68.0 percent in the United States. The review maps five technological pathways under evaluation across global producers, ranging from conventional coal-fed blast furnace systems paired with carbon capture to scrap-fed electric arc furnaces, hydrogen-based direct reduction, and electrolytic ironmaking. The article's subject of research is artificial intelligence applications in low-carbon iron and steel metallurgy.

The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries. They state that most models lack comprehensive representations of dynamic cross-unit couplings among material, energy, and carbon flows, which restricts route-wide optimization across entire industrial complexes. They note that industrial datasets suffer from noise, missing values, regime drift, and a scarcity of validated operational logs for emerging hydrogen or electrolytic pilots. Because metallurgical operations depend strictly on thermodynamic conservation laws, the authors say unconstrained black-box learners risk outputting nonphysical predictions when extrapolating outside training domains. The review concludes that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks, supporting verifiable, plant-wide carbon reduction across the steel industry.

The authors highlight that broad deployment of newer hydrogen and electrolysis technologies faces substantial hurdles, including capital requirements, infrastructural bottlenecks, and high operational costs, requiring system-wide optimization within existing facilities while cleaner routes mature. They report that multimodal perception frameworks combining two-dimensional photographic images with three-dimensional point clouds have achieved material granularity recognition rates exceeding 90 percent. Vision-based monitoring tools detect bosh pressure channel anomalies eight to sixteen minutes prior to operational disruptions, according to the review. Digital-twin structures integrated with deep residual networks identify carbon emission deviations, categorizing operational anomaly severity with reported classification accuracies exceeding 97 percent.

In electric arc furnaces, artificial neural networks estimate endpoint carbon concentrations, achieving reported hit rates of 96.67 percent within an error margin of 0.05 percent carbon. The review delineates the baseline operating structure of integrated steelmaking, where raw-material preparation, blast furnace reduction, converter refining, and rolling units share significant energy flows and off-gas networks. Sintering, pelletizing, and coking supply the burden materials required for blast furnace operation, wherein fossil carbon acts simultaneously as a chemical reducing agent and an energy source. Conventional chemical analyses remain accurate but require offline sampling that cannot provide high-frequency process feedback.

Echo state networks, variational mode decomposition, and swarm intelligence algorithms generate multi-step forecasts of blast furnace gas production and gasholder storage levels, driving root-mean-square errors below 0.05 across benchmark industrial datasets. The article's references cite Shang, X., Yin, W., Pan, J., Wang, M., Wang, H., Yang, K., & Xiao, Q. (2026), published in Carbon Neutral Systems, volume 2, issue 1. The review states that future progress depends on physics-informed, multi-scale gray-box architectures that embed conservation equations and transport kinetics directly into deep neural frameworks. The authors observe that current industrial applications remain predominantly confined to isolated processing units operating within narrow parameter boundaries.

The article does not state when or whether such plant-wide architectures will be deployed. It does not give a timeline for the five technological pathways it maps. The article does not report any response from steel producers or policymakers to the review. It does not state the review's conclusions on costs for the hydrogen and electrolysis routes beyond the hurdles it lists.

stories.Headline: Law.com authors warn firms that wider AI use expands supervision duties and malpractice risk
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, Law.com published an article by Nicholas Cutaia and Ruth-Claire Pollioni titled "The Expanding Duty of Vigilance: How AI Adoption May Be Reshaping Legal Malpractice Risk." The article says firms are putting more AI tools like Harvey, Claude, and Legora into the hands of more lawyers, on more matters. It asks whether firms adopting AI to work faster are weakening the human oversight needed to catch its mistakes. It says the obligation to supervise that use grows along with the adoption. It examines how that gap can turn efficiency gains into malpractice risk and what firms can do about it.

The article is a 9 minute read and was published at 12:44 PM on November 16, 2026. It appears under the Artificial Intelligence topic and the Legal Technology section of Law.com. The rest of the article sits behind a subscription, and Law.com lists subscription benefits including strategic intelligence, integrated insights, personalized experience, and smart search and alerts. Law.com gives contact details at 1-855-808-4530 for the Americas and 44(0) 800 098 386009 for the UK and Europe. The page is copyrighted 2026 by ALM Global, LLC, with all rights reserved.

The article is credited to Nicholas Cutaia and Ruth-Claire Pollioni, who wrote that the obligation to supervise AI use grows as more tools reach more lawyers on more matters. They ask whether firms adopting AI to work faster are weakening the human oversight needed to catch its mistakes. They say the article examines how that gap can turn efficiency gains into malpractice risk. They say it also covers what firms can do about it. The articles give no further statements from the authors.

A related Law.com piece by Thomas F. Berner, dated November 12, 2026, argues that AI cannot replace human lawyers' judgment, character and creativity and that its output requires careful human review. A November 16, 2026 piece by Pouya Shafabakhsh says AI can help model litigation scenarios but New York practice still places settlement authority with the client. A November 13, 2026 piece by Pouya Shafabakhsh and Alexander Paykin says New York courts should not admit digital evidence casually, nor make every unsupported "deepfake" claim a ticket to expensive forensic testing. A November 12, 2026 Law.com report by Ryan Harroff says Latham's AI-fluent junior associates prompted the firm to revamp its training playbook, adjusting the schedule and curriculum for this year's academy. The articles say the affected people include lawyers, paralegals and clients.

A TechSpective article by Lila Warren, dated November 14, 2026, says AI has worked its way into courtrooms, law offices and legal research departments across the country. It says AI-driven platforms scan thousands of case files, statutes and legal precedents, completing in minutes tasks that once took junior associates hours or full days. It says AI tools help lawyers identify problematic clauses, inconsistencies and missing provisions faster than manual review. It says predictive analytics tools evaluate how courts have ruled on similar cases, and AI-driven e-discovery platforms streamline document review in discovery. It says a probate litigation attorney in California may use AI-assisted research and case analysis for complex matters like estate disputes involving contested wills or trust administration.

The TechSpective article says questions around data privacy, attorney-client privilege and the accuracy of AI-generated outputs are at the forefront of ongoing legal and ethical debates. It says bar associations and regulatory bodies are actively working to establish guidelines that keep AI use within appropriate ethical boundaries. It says over-reliance on automated tools could lead to critical errors if attorneys accept AI outputs without proper scrutiny. It says legal fees may decrease as efficiency improves, and turnaround times on documents and case updates can be significantly faster. It says AI-powered client portals and chatbots make it easier to access basic legal information and communicate with legal teams outside traditional office hours.

The TechSpective article says the most effective approach treats AI as a powerful assistant rather than a substitute for genuine professional legal judgment. It says the human element of law, including empathy, ethical reasoning and nuanced judgment, remains irreplaceable. It says attorneys who thrive will embrace AI as a tool while prioritizing the personal and professional skills that define excellent legal practice. It says the future of law is both human and machine working together toward better outcomes. The Law.com article leaves open what firms can do about the supervision gap, because that content requires a subscription.

stories.Headline: National Whistleblower Center hires Attention Studio to lobby for AI whistleblower protections
stories.Summary:
The National Whistleblower Center added Attention Studio as an outside lobbying firm in 2026 while it pushes the AI Whistleblower Protection Act, which remains in committee in both chambers of Congress. Attention Studio reported $100,000 for the third quarter in a filing signed on Nov. 9, and it is the only registrant on record for the center that quarter. Two lobbyists are named on the filing, Olivia Konar, a policy associate, and Ava Smithing, a founding partner, and both also appear on the firm's new client registration for the center. The bill would bar employers from retaliating against employees and independent contractors who report artificial intelligence security vulnerabilities or violations of AI-related laws.

The legislation would also bar contracts that waive those protections and give whistleblowers reinstatement and back pay. The filing lists S. 1792 and H.R. 3460 and says the lobbying urged Senate and House offices to cosponsor the bill and support committee action before the end of the 119th Congress. It names the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and the Commerce Committee. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) sponsors S. 1792, which was introduced May 15, 2025, and referred to the HELP Committee, and Congress.gov shows 13 current cosponsors, five of them original, with no later committee or floor action. Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) sponsors H.R. 3460, which was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day, and its cosponsor page shows 10 current cosponsors, one of them original.

A coalition letter dated June 10, 2025, backs S. 1792, and its 22 signers include Americans for Responsible Innovation, the Center for Democracy & Technology, the Government Accountability Project, Public Knowledge, and the National Whistleblower Center. The signers say fear of retaliation, including over confidentiality agreements, can deter insiders from disclosing AI risks, and they argue protections support transparency, accountability, public safety, and national security. The letter cites a June 2024 public statement by more than a dozen current and former employees of leading AI companies. Both bills wait in committee, S. 1792 in the Senate HELP Committee and H.R. 3460 in the House Education and Workforce Committee, and the filing's stated goal is committee action before the 119th Congress ends. Attention Studio is a new outside firm for the center, which makes the firm's work on this bill the change to track.

stories.Headline: Study finds AI-generated ad labels reveal only that AI played some role
stories.Summary:
A study published on November 16, 2026, in a TechXplore article republished from The Conversation examines what an "AI-generated" label in advertising actually communicates to consumers, concluding that such a label reveals only that artificial intelligence played some role without clarifying how large or small that role was. The article explains that AI might have served as one tool in a largely human-led creative process, perhaps editing an image or refining text, or it might have generated much of the finished advertisement with limited human input, and a single label can cover both extremes and everything in between. The authors note that advertising has long used disclosures, such as the "#ad" tag influencers place on social media or labels marking sponsored content, which help consumers recognize the commercial side of what they are watching or reading. Their research indicates that AI disclosures serve a different purpose, because traditional disclosures tell consumers why content is being shown to them while AI labels draw attention to how it was produced without revealing the respective roles of humans and machines.

The article reports that the distinction matters because evidence suggests disclosing AI involvement can reduce levels of trust, and other research points to overall consumer resistance to AI, although reactions vary considerably depending on what the technology is used to create. It notes that AI blurs the line between editing existing content and creating new content, since a person may still develop the idea and refine the result while the balance between human and machine contribution varies considerably, and disclosing AI involvement can invite judgments about who or what created the content, how much human input was involved and whether the use of AI was appropriate. The article says this may help explain criticism of AI-led campaigns by brands such as Coca-Cola and Gucci, and it describes how governments and platforms are beginning to address these questions through new approaches to AI transparency. The EU wants providers of certain generative AI systems subjected to strict disclosure requirements, and technology is emerging that allows digital content, including ads, to carry accessible information about its provenance and editing history.

The article reports that Meta acknowledged its "Made with AI" label appeared on content involving only minor AI modifications and did not provide sufficient context, and the company replaced that wording with "AI info" before later making the label less prominent when AI had been used to edit rather than generate content. It also describes the same ambiguity appearing in reverse, with labels reading "human-made" and "no AI" emerging to signal human authorship, and it asks whether these mean no AI whatsoever or a predominantly human process in which AI played a supporting role, since both kinds of label can obscure as much as they reveal. The authors advise consumers to take a little time to consider how they interpret AI labels, saying the term "AI-generated" tells us something but not everything about how content was produced and does not by itself mean the result is fake, poor quality or untrustworthy. They add that the label will not spell out the human role, including who developed the idea, selected and refined the output, checked its accuracy and decided what ultimately appeared, and they conclude that an AI label should be a starting point for evaluating content rather than the end.

stories.Headline: AMD completes its 8.2 billion dollar World Labs acquisition and names Fei-Fei Li chief scientist
stories.Summary:
AMD completed its acquisition of World Labs on Monday, November 16, 2026, for a total of 8.2 billion dollars. The chip giant gained immediate access to the research and artificial intelligence models developed by the acquired firm. Fei-Fei Li, who is widely known as the godmother of AI, will join the company as chief scientist. She will also take on the role of executive vice president to help guide the organization. The deal integrates World Labs' specialized AI models that simulate 3D environments to train robots for virtual and real worlds.

This strategic move allows AMD to better compete with Nvidia, which currently holds a strong position through its open-weights models. The acquisition requires the integration of pioneering model research into the future hardware, software, and systems of the company. These new capabilities aim to help developers and researchers push the boundaries of what artificial intelligence can achieve. AMD Chief Executive Officer Lisa Su expressed her excitement about welcoming Fei-Fei Li and her exceptional team to the company.

Su stated that optimizing compute platforms and models together is necessary to provide the infrastructure for the next era of super intelligence. She believes that the research from World Labs will be essential in shaping the future of their technical ecosystem. This announcement follows the recent recognition of Su as the Yahoo Finance CEO of the Year for 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Lawyers say generative AI gives narcissistic family litigants speed and false authority
stories.Summary:
A law.com expert opinion piece published on November 16, 2026, by Elisa Reiter of Calabrese Budner and Daniel Pollack of Yeshiva University's Wurzweiler School of Social Work describes how generative AI has affected narcissistic behavior in family litigation. The authors say that generative AI did not create narcissistic behavior in family litigation, but it has given that behavior speed, scale and a veneer of authority. They describe the litigant who treats the courthouse as a stage and files a dozen motions in a month. They describe the opposing party who rewrites the history of the marriage with unshakable confidence and frames every parenting exchange as proof of the other parent's unfitness. They describe the litigant who reacts to any adverse ruling as a personal insult.

The full text of the article sits behind a subscription paywall on Law.com, so the specific requirements, changes, numbers and dates it sets out are not available. The visible portion gives no figures, no court dates and no named cases beyond the authors themselves. The page does list related coverage, including a November 16, 2026, article by Laura Lorek reporting that court filings containing hallucinations have fallen for two straight quarters while subtler errors may be harder to catch. It also lists an October 22, 2026, report by Avalon Zoppo on the Fifth Circuit reassigning a case after a judge misused AI to draft a ruling, with Judge Jerry Smith writing for the appellate court. Those items are separate stories and are not part of the Reiter and Pollack piece.

The authors are responsible for the opinions in the article, and the visible text attributes the described litigation behavior to anonymous litigants rather than to any named person or firm. The article's own framing is that AI supplies speed, scale and a veneer of authority to behavior that already existed. Beyond that framing, the paywalled article does not disclose what the authors recommend or what they say should change. The surrounding coverage suggests that courts and practitioners are watching AI errors in filings, but the articles do not say what happens next in family law specifically. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Oikonomou presents PanAdipo AI model that characterizes epicardial fat from routine echocardiograms
stories.Summary:
Evangelos Oikonomou, MD, an assistant professor of medicine in the section of cardiovascular medicine at Yale School of Medicine and associate director of the Cardiovascular Data Science Lab, presented data on the PanAdipo model at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, Illinois, according to HCPLive. PanAdipo is a new view-agnostic, video-based deep learning model developed for echocardiographic interpretation, and the presentation highlighted the efficacy of AI-enabled echocardiography to characterize prominent epicardial adipose tissue. Oikonomou and colleagues developed PanAdipo to characterize prominent epicardial adiposity from standard 2D B-mode echocardiographic acquisitions. The model was tested across 5 major cohorts, which included a total of 1,114,441 videos from 28,797 random transthoracic echocardiographs in 21,479 unique patients. The team analyzed discrimination of the report label and of CT-defined high indexed EAT volume, correlation with paired cardiac CT phenotypes, and BMI-adjusted associations with cardiometabolic biomarkers and newly documented metabolic disease.

The 4 cohorts included temporally distinct Yale-New Haven Health System transthoracic echocardiographs (n = 4588), emergency department point-of-care ultrasound (n = 10,957), the community-based Multiethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (n = 2740), and external MIMIC-IV transthoracic echocardiographs (n = 4549). In held-out transthoracic echocardiographs, PanAdipo discriminated prominent epicardial adiposity with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.91 (95% CI, 0.88-0.94), and saliency maps localized attention to epicardial regions across views. Although PanAdipo was modestly correlated with body mass index (p = 0.19-0.4; P <.001), the researchers saw a strong correlation with ectopic adiposity features on paired CT scans (n = 23), particularly pericardial fat fraction (p = 0.75) and skeletal muscle fat fraction (p = 0.74). In the MESA cohort, higher PanAdipo was associated with higher homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and triglyceride levels after adjustment for age, body mass index, sex, and waist-hip ratio. Longitudinally, each 1-SD increment in log(PanAdipo) was associated with a 21% and 37% higher risk of incident type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, respectively.

Oikonomou told HCPLive that the focus of the work was to uncover a layer in routine cardiac imaging that has been ignored or left on the table while interpreting those tests. He said that when a cardiac ultrasound is ordered, the focus is on the structure and anatomy of the heart, but he believes there is an additional layer where adverse adiposity can be phenotyped. Oikonomou said the next step is to identify the optimal point where the tool contributes value and generates actionable information that can inform clinical care, behavioral modifications for a patient, or a more personalized allocation of emerging cardiometabolic therapies. He said that would need to be studied in prospective clinical studies, but it could also become a kind of companion diagnostic for greater precision.

Oikonomou reports no relevant disclosures. Oikonomou and colleagues determined that the PanAdipo system successfully shifts routine echocardiography into a scalable AI-enabled biomarker for EAT. They also concluded that it captures cardiometabolic risk across community and clinical settings, supporting cardiac ultrasound as a method of metabolic risk stratification distinct from anthropometric indices. The findings were presented at the AHA Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 to 9, 2026, and a preprint by Aminorroaya, Coppi, McNamara and colleagues titled "AI-Enabled Echocardiography Identifies Prominent Epicardial Adipose Tissue Associated With an Adverse Cardiometabolic Profile" was published October 9, 2026, on medRxiv.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches IPO at $1.4tn valuation and turns 4,000 staff into millionaires
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, launched its initial public offering this Thursday. This float is expected to value the AI company at $1.4tn, or £1.1tn. The event will likely turn over 4,000 staff members into millionaires as stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, estimates the minimum value for these staff will be $20m each. This wealth is expected to boost London's ailing high-end property market.

The company employs 5,000 people worldwide, including more than 200 based in the UK. Anthropic plans to open a London office capable of accommodating up to 800 people. In 2024, UK filings show the firm spent £24.1m on an average of 43 staff. This equals a mean average of £560,000 per person, with some base salaries reaching £630,000. Tech buyers now target London properties with budgets ranging from £2m to £40m.

Buying agent Jo Eccles says agents sometimes mistake wealthy tech entrepreneurs for renters of small flats. Jeremy Gee of Beauchamp Estates says AI buyers are often younger and move quickly. He notes these buyers value location and quality and will pay premiums for special homes. Shona Baijal of Coutts says young entrepreneurs often feel overwhelmed by their sudden wealth. She advises these new clients not to rush into making financial decisions.

Igor Babuschkin of xAI reportedly bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park in February. Suneil Setiya of Quadrature Capital reportedly paid £270m for Providence House in Royal Hospital Chelsea. Aidan Devane of Quadrature Capital attributes success to proximity to city AI labs. Beauchamp Estates lists a £42m sub-penthouse and sees more inquiries from US and local buyers. Coutts found eight of ten exclusive properties in Mayfair, Belgravia, and Knightsbridge sell below asking.

Anthropic was founded in San Francisco in 2021, where housing demand has already surged. In San Francisco, one-bedroom rents average $4,400 monthly, which is 25% higher than last year. London's King's Cross knowledge quarter now hosts Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta near Google. Demis Hassabis co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. His AI drug discovery startup, Isomorphic Labs, is also located in the north London area.

Alex Gerko is expected to make hundreds of millions in paper gains from this IPO. Bloomberg found AI powered roughly a quarter of UK economic growth this year. The UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, led by the IT sector. The CAPE ratio reached its highest level since 2000, suggesting the US market is overvalued. It remains uncertain if this wealth is permanent or a temporary flash in a bubble.

stories.Headline: Google opens preorders for Gemini smart glasses with Samsung and sets Dec 10 release
stories.Summary:
Google opened preorders on Nov. 12 for its Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear, developed with Samsung, with frame designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, and plans to release the glasses on Dec. 10. The Warby Parker models start at $395, while the already available Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 costs $449. Google's glasses are powered by Gemini, and Meta's glasses use Meta AI. Both products offer cameras, AI assistants, and hands-free features. Buyers must decide whether to buy Meta's glasses now or wait for Google's alternative.

Warby Parker offers three frame styles starting at $395, and Gentle Monster has six styles priced from $449 to $489. Both collections use the same underlying hardware, with differences in design, fit, and lens options. The glasses combine Gemini with a 12MP camera, open-ear speakers, and four microphones, according to Samsung's announcement. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 also has a 12MP camera but includes six microphones. Both support 3K video recording at 30 fps, and both advertise up to nine hours of battery life per charge.

Google's glasses offer 64GB of storage, twice Meta's 32GB, and Google claims up to 72 hours with its charging case, while Meta's case provides another 50 hours. Google's frames weigh approximately 40 to 44 grams depending on the model, and Meta's standard Wayfarer Gen 3 weighs about 51.5 grams and offers adjustable temple tips. Both support prescription lenses, although options vary by frame. Google's glasses offer HDR photography and video stabilization, while Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 includes slow motion and hyperlapse recording. Meta claims its updated microphone system reduces background noise.

According to Google's product announcement, the glasses allow wearers to ask Gemini questions about their surroundings, translate conversations, and get hands-free assistance. On supported Galaxy phones, users can ask Gemini to summarize a whiteboard and save the information to Samsung Notes. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offers similar visual assistance, voice commands, and live translation, with integrations centered on WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram. Meta's September launch announcement introduced a customizable action button. Google is a better fit for people who regularly use Gemini, Maps, and other Google services, while Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 suits those who frequently use Meta's messaging and social apps.

According to Google's official product information, the glasses support selected Pixel and Galaxy phones as well as compatible iPhones, and activation requires an eligible Google account associated with the United States or South Korea. Users must be at least 18, and some capabilities, including Guided Vision and Aira visual assistance, require a compatible Android phone at launch. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 requires a compatible smartphone, a Meta account, and the Meta AI app, and its supported services and AI features can vary by country. Google says its privacy protections include recording indicators, camera permission controls, and automatic redaction of bystanders' faces during Gemini visual queries. The company also says visuals processed through those queries are not used to train AI models or target advertisements.

Meta's glasses include an external recording indicator to alert people nearby when photos or videos are being captured. Buyers prioritizing camera quality, call performance, or real-world battery life may be better off waiting for independent comparisons after Google's Dec. 10 release. The $395 Warby Parker models could be worth waiting for, particularly for buyers who regularly use Gemini and Google services. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 is the more immediate choice for shoppers who want smart glasses now or already rely on Meta's supported apps. Before spending hundreds of dollars, buyers should check whether their phone supports the features they want.

stories.Headline: Flagstar Bank deploys 4,000 Microsoft Surface devices to run its BranchIQ AI agent locally for employees
stories.Summary:
Flagstar Bank chose Microsoft Surface devices to bring hybrid AI and mobile banking to employees, Microsoft said in a customer story dated 11/16/2026. The bank’s own BranchIQ agent runs local AI on Surface, supported by Windows 11 and centralized device management. Flagstar is headquartered in New York and serves businesses, commercial real estate clients and consumers across America. The bank has 5,300 employees, according to chairman and CEO Joseph Otting. Flagstar’s planned rollout covers 4,000 Surface devices.

During rollout, Flagstar reduced initial Windows Autopilot setup from up to about an hour to 15 minutes. Surface devices are managed through Microsoft Intune, secured with Microsoft Entra and tied into the bank’s Microsoft 365 environment. Windows Hello for Business makes sign-in easier for employees. BranchIQ runs as part of a small language model locally on the Surface devices. Starting with a photo of an identification document, BranchIQ extracts required information locally and helps populate systems of record.

Otting said it was a moment when you start to see how everything links together and how the 5,300 employees could become more effective in the AI strategy. Otting said that when he saw what Surface could do and how AI could be used on the device, he was hooked. Jason Pope, chief technology and data officer, said Surface meets the bank’s needs by being rapid, quick and easy to use, and that speed matters because transaction per second in banking is important. Pope said BranchIQ lets branch colleagues perform know your customer activities, onboard individuals and access standards, policies and procedures directly on device, with or without an internet connection or Wi-Fi. Pope said Surface was the perfect blend from chip to cloud, not just hardware but hardware tied into Microsoft 365, managed by Intune and secured by Entra.

Christina Previti, head of tech product delivery, said employees are not sitting at a desk all day but are in front of clients, moving between buildings and meetings, and traveling. Previti said Surface lets them move across offices and states seamlessly, and that for a bank the security is critical. Previti said she lives in New York City and commutes on the subway every day, and the device fits in almost every bag she has. Pope said the bank was very deliberate with Surface pilots in branches, starting very small with one branch and taking a hands-on approach to change management. Pope said branch one loved it and started evangelizing it, and then branch two came on.

Flagstar has grown through mergers, and a unified employee experience is a priority, according to the story. Running Surface on Windows 11 gives employees the same seamless, secure experience wherever they work. Surface’s neural processing unit helped win Flagstar over and made hybrid intelligence a natural fit for a bank handling sensitive customer information. The bank considered the total cost of ownership, including its experience with older Surface devices still in use. Because Surface is designed by Microsoft to work with Microsoft software, Windows 11, Microsoft 365 and the tools that manage and secure them work as one experience.

Flagstar worked directly with Microsoft to cut initial Autopilot setup to 15 minutes, which Pope said meant less time waiting for a new device and more time getting back to work. As the rollout grows, the goal stays the same: better employee experiences that translate into more positive client interactions. The story directs readers to discover more about Flagstar Bank on LinkedIn and YouTube. The story lists the organization size as 1,000-9,999 employees and the country or region as the United States. The story does not say when the 4,000-device rollout will be completed.

stories.Headline: Microsoft report guides workplace AI security priorities as IT teams face identity risks from agents and user-built apps
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Cybersecurity Insiders on November 16, 2026, sets out practical steps for containing and securing artificial intelligence in the workplace, and it draws heavily on Microsoft's yearly Digital Defense Report as a guiding priority list for the next twelve months. The author argues that the protection of AI use is not vastly different from the security work IT teams already do, despite the large amount of hysteria surrounding the technology. The piece notes that end users are increasingly building their own apps through vibe coding and then expecting IT to handle hosting, security and support. It also observes that attacks are often described as sophisticated when the root cause is simply someone misconfiguring a basic control that every product has. The article says identity is the surface that matters most, and that the core failure is too much standing access that is too loosely enforced, a weakness red teams have exploited for years.

It explains that AI agents operate like virtual users, with an identity, access to files and resources, and the ability to carry out digital tasks on a computer, so identity must remain a priority. The author advises against blocking all AI tools, because users have become very dependent on them, and instead recommends discovering what is being used, most easily through tools that inspect network traffic and show which domains and categories are visited. Presenting that data to business owners can shock them about where data is going, which typically convinces them that AI governance is not optional. The author, writing from an IT management perspective, says technology is the quicker and easier part of the job, while understanding and working with people is what separates one professional from the rest. The article asks whether the rest of the business received adequate training on approved AI tools and understands what not to do with business data, and whether some parts of the organization would be more productive with specialized tools routed through strong security controls.

It recommends asking people what business problem they are trying to solve, rather than accepting an answer that begins with a request for AI to do something. The author also sets out an order to follow, starting with identity and seeing how far an organization can get, because that path aligns with the failures that lead to most business compromises. The article notes that few IT staff have worked in environments where they are involved with all aspects of the cybersecurity strategy, and that starting at an MSP can make it difficult to know where to begin. It says all steps have their own merits, but some matter more than others, and it gives the example that starting with data governance while allowing all users to access stored data on any device has less impact than first preventing that action within the identity project. The conclusion states that the priority remains ensuring businesses implement the fundamental security controls long considered essential, since getting these basics right creates a stronger foundation and better prepares organizations for the risks of emerging technologies.

stories.Headline: China fines AI virtual human operator for fabricating product usage experiences
stories.Summary:
The Market Regulation Bureau of Panyu District in Guangzhou issued a penalty on November 13, 2026. This agency fined Guangzhou Wode Film and Television Media Co., Ltd. over 68,200 yuan for illegal medical advertisements. The penalty was publicly disclosed on November 16, 2026, targeting the operator of the virtual character Fang Taozi. This case marks the first penalty in China for AI virtual humans fabricating product usage experiences.

The fine targets a 60-second ad for Nuts Power cosmetic contact lenses, which are Class III medical devices. The AI character claimed the lenses were comfortable for a whole day and did not shift when blinking. Regulations require such ads to be reviewed and clearly mark that users should read manuals or seek medical guidance. Additionally, the law prohibits using advertising spokespersons for recommendation or certification of these specific medical devices.

The Market Regulation Bureau classified the act as the illegal publishing of medical advertisements and false advertising. Officials stated the penalty targets the fabricated content and publishing procedure rather than the identity of the on-camera presence. They argued that while AI is not a legal spokesperson, it cannot bypass the bottom line of authenticity. The core issue is the fabrication of fictitious personal product usage experiences by a digital image.

Netizens questioned how a digital image with no eyeballs or corneas could know if lenses were comfortable. Viewers in the comment section realized that the AI had no eyes to experience the product. This case affects the AI digital human track, specifically those providing realistic human-like experience product recommendations. High-risk categories like medical devices and pharmaceuticals now face a greatly compressed commercial order space.

Fang Taozi gained 400,000 followers in one month after the June 12, 2026, launch of the series The Laid-off Girl. The operator, established in September 2019, registered 192 art work copyrights including Fang Taozi and Zhou Yiheng since July. The account's short video quotations started from 168,000 yuan, which is more expensive than many bloggers with millions of followers.

The industry will now divide into brand image broadcasting and realistic human-like experience product recommendation. AI can still broadcast parameters and read brand propositions, but it cannot output first-person physical experience testimony. Future boundaries include five prohibited actions: wearing, eating, applying, using, and smelling. The articles leave open how beauty, food, and home furnishing categories will adapt to these rules.

stories.Headline: Knit Health raises a $35 million Series A led by NEA to guide patient referrals with AI
stories.Summary:
Knit Health, a startup that uses an AI world model to predict patient care needs, forecast treatment impacts and optimize referrals, raised a $35 million Series A round led by NEA, CEO Jonathan Kolstad told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was reported by Will Maddox of Axios in a story published on November 16, 2026. The company's stated aim is to guide patient referrals with artificial intelligence. Investors are betting on AI that predicts patients' next health needs rather than simply documenting their current ones.

The $35 million Series A was led by NEA, according to the report, and the funding is intended to support Knit Health's work guiding patient referrals with AI. The company uses its AI world model for three stated purposes, which are predicting patient care needs, forecasting treatment impacts and optimizing referrals. The report frames the investment as a bet on prediction over documentation, meaning AI that anticipates what patients will need next instead of only recording what they currently need. The articles give no further terms of the deal, no total valuation and no list of other participating investors.

Jonathan Kolstad, the CEO of Knit Health, confirmed the $35 million Series A round to Axios Pro exclusively, and the report attributes the funding news to him. The articles do not include any further direct statements from Kolstad beyond his confirmation of the round and its amount. No other executives, investors or NEA representatives are named or quoted in the material provided. The report also does not say what Knit Health plans to do with the proceeds beyond its existing focus on AI-guided referrals.

The context given is that investors are placing bets on AI that predicts patients' next health needs rather than simply documenting their current ones, which is how the report describes the big picture behind the round. The articles do not say when the round closed, how the company will spend the money, or what happens next for Knit Health beyond the funding itself. No details are given about the company's customers, its market, or any prior funding. The report was published by Axios on November 16, 2026, with Will Maddox as the author.

stories.Headline: New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill pushes state action on child safety and Big Tech privacy as federal AI rules stall
stories.Summary:
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill pushed for state action on child safety and Big Tech privacy during a November 2026 interview. She acted because federal regulation on AI and social media has stalled while power shifted toward state governors. Sherrill believes states must now lead on data center oversight and the protection of children online. She argues that the current political climate requires governors to exercise powers that have not been tested recently. This shift occurred as President Donald Trump concentrated power within the executive branch of the federal government.

The governor signed a data center plan in May 2026 and related build-out bills in August 2026. New Jersey received a 525 million dollar share of the Meta settlement to address these tech issues. Sherrill noted that New Jersey put every port on notice that importing Russian diesel is illegal. She mentioned a data center fine exceeding one million dollars as part of her state's regulatory efforts. The governor also expressed her openness to joining the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact for future elections.

Governor Sherrill stated that power moves into vacuums left by the federal government in Washington. She said that states are now the laboratories for AI and privacy because no federal statutes exist. Sherrill believes that state data center plans are converging on pillars like energy and water reporting. She argued that this convergence and litigation could eventually produce a de facto national standard for the country. The governor claimed that being a strong leader requires being accountable and transparent about government problems.

Nilay Patel noted that tech billionaires now control huge swaths of local and national broadcast media. He mentioned that influencers like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani are shaping a new brand of politics. Sherrill said that voters are furious and scared because of the actions of billionaires like Elon Musk. She believes that working families are most empowered when Democrats fight for affordability and accountability. The governor noted that some communities are affected by noise and water issues caused by data centers.

Sherrill began her campaign in November 2024 immediately after Donald Trump won the presidential election. She ran on themes of affordability and accountability to secure a huge win in the midterms. The governor observed that corruption became a top issue for voters according to a Guardian poll. She linked this anger to tech CEOs visiting the White House and Trump's personal financial gains. Sherrill also discovered that the previous administration failed to clear non-citizens from the state voter rolls.

The state will continue to allow local towns to decide if they will host data centers. Moratoriums on these centers will likely spread until operators can prove they will not harm communities. Sherrill expects more Big Tech litigation to occur as states continue to fill the federal power vacuum. The articles leave open how the industry will demonstrate a model that convinces towns to cooperate. It remains unclear if influencer politics is a permanent shift or just a temporary moment in time.

stories.Headline: Democratic control of Congress shifts AI policy toward risk-based oversight, Carrillo, Ellison and Braithwaite write
stories.Summary:
Democratic control of Congress will shift the national debate regarding artificial intelligence policy on November 16, 2026. This political change moves the focus away from the deregulatory agenda previously established by the Trump administration. The new leadership intends to implement a risk-based approach that emphasizes accountability for various impacts. This strategy specifically targets the economic, consumer, and public safety consequences of deploying these technologies. The new policy framework requires a stronger focus on consumer harms, fairness, safety, and transparency.

Congress may also increase its scrutiny of cybersecurity measures and the power costs associated with data centers. Businesses must prepare for a higher volume of investigations even if no new laws are passed. Companies are encouraged to demonstrate that they have implemented strong safeguards to protect the public. Pablo Carrillo, Bradford Ellison, and Dominic Braithwaite are the authors responsible for analyzing these upcoming regulatory shifts.

They suggest that the government will likely push for tougher oversight to ensure that AI systems remain safe. The authors indicate that the shift toward accountability will redefine how technology companies operate within the United States. They believe that the focus on risk will replace the previous trend of reducing government interference. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley rightsholders add over 100 AI tracks to Suno lawsuit
stories.Summary:
Rightsholders of Elvis Presley amended a lawsuit against the AI music generator Suno on November 13, 2026. This legal action was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The plaintiffs added more than 100 AI tracks that allegedly imitate Presley's voice or infringe songs. This amended complaint follows an original lawsuit that was first filed on November 6, 2026. The legal team is led by Richard S. Busch of the firm Adams and Reese.

The suit involves Elvis Presley Enterprises, ABG EPE IP, Raleigh Music Publishing, Abilene Music, and various trusts. It seeks 128.85 million dollars for copyright infringement across 859 songs, including Let's Twist Again by Chubby Checker. Elvis Presley Enterprises seeks over 50 million dollars, potentially tripled to 150 million, under Tennessee's ELVIS Act. Additional claims include 21.475 million dollars for stripping credits and 2,147,500 dollars for bypassing access controls. The filing cites 58 reproduced songs and 40 tracks using Presley's voice or likeness.

The plaintiffs allege Suno trained its AI on Presley's recordings without a license and willfully violated the Copyright Act. They claim Suno stole Presley's likeness and voice without care, calling the company's public denials unequivocally false. A spokesperson for Suno stated the service helps people create original music and prohibits unauthorized use of work. Suno claimed it does not allow prompts for specific artists and uses third party providers to screen files. CEO Mikey Shulman previously wrote in a blog post that the company never allowed prompts for copyrighted songs.

The lawsuit affects Suno, which raised 400 million dollars at a 5.4 billion dollar valuation in June. Other musicians, including Jason Isbell, are involved in a separate proposed class action lawsuit filed in Boston. Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment are also currently suing the AI company for similar issues. Warner Music Group settled its dispute with Suno and reached a licensing deal in November 2025. The plaintiffs argue that Suno's claims about prompt restrictions are false based on evidence provided to Billboard.

Suno admitted in an October 20 answer that users could include artist names in prompts as of January 2026. The company argued that it converts artist names into style descriptions rather than replicating a specific voice. The Presley plaintiffs cite a track called Recording session that allegedly infringes six different songs, including Hound Dog. Another exhibit is described as a complete reproduction of the hit song Can't Help Falling in Love. The complaint also includes 72 outputs of songs Presley recorded that the plaintiffs do not actually own.

The plaintiffs want a court order barring Suno from using Presley's voice and the destruction of training datasets. The case tests if the ELVIS Act applies to AI services to hold companies liable for their tools. The court must decide if Presley's army service from 1958 to 1960 allows for tripled damages. It remains to be seen if the court will grant the request to impound internal model weights. None of the allegations in either version of the Presley complaint have been tested in court yet.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley rightsholders amend Suno lawsuit, adding more than 100 allegedly infringing AI tracks

stories.headline_source: Elvis Presley rightsholders amend Suno lawsuit, adding more than 100 allegedly infringing AI tracks

stories.Headline: Texas bill requires AI developers to report rogue incidents within 72 hours
stories.Summary:
A bill filed Tuesday in the Texas House of Representatives would require developers to report any rogue artificial intelligence incidents to the state, and it would let the state attorney general investigate any failures to report. House Bill 1201 was authored by Rep. Salman Bhojani, a Democrat from Euless. If passed, the law would govern frontier models developed or tested in Texas, along with incidents that happen to a person or computer system in Texas. The bill defines a frontier model as an artificial intelligence system, or the model it is based on, that is trained on a broad set of data, designed for generality of output, adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks, and trained using more than 10 to the 25th power integer or floating-point operations.

The incidents covered by the bill include accessing a computer, network or system without the owner's consent, disabling, circumventing or deceiving a human oversight process, and preventing an authorized person from rejecting, modifying, overriding or terminating the model's decisions or actions. They also include modifying, deleting or disclosing data without owner consent, and any action beyond the model's permissions that creates a foreseeable risk of death or bodily injury, substantial property damage, disruption of critical infrastructure or government service, or compromised information system security. Developers would have to report such incidents to the Texas Department of Information Resources within 72 hours, and that deadline shortens to 24 hours with law enforcement notified if there is an imminent threat of substantial harm to people. The penalty for failure to report would be at least $10,000 but no more than $100,000, though penalties could reach up to $1,000,000 per incident if a developer knowingly conceals information or submits materially false or misleading reports.

The bill would create some protection for developers, since a report would not be an admission of liability and would be confidential. HB 1201 would also make it illegal for an employer to retaliate against an employee who files a report in good faith. The Texas Department of Information Resources would be required to publish an annual report with an aggregate summary of rogue AI incidents. If enacted, the bill would take effect on Sept. 1, 2027, and the department would have to implement rules and a reporting system by Dec. 1, 2027. The legislative session starts on Jan. 12, 2027.

Articles.Title: Texas bill proposes ‘rogue AI incident’ reporting mandate

stories.headline_source: Texas bill proposes ‘rogue AI incident’ reporting mandate

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric unveils Reference Design 115 for modular AI factories supporting 227 kW racks
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric introduced its RapidScale Modular Data Center Reference Design 115 on October 21 at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, outlining a modular AI factory architecture engineered for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform. The design supports AI rack power reaching 227 kW, according to the company. A study conducted with Compass Datacenters documents an approximately 80% reduction in selected onsite installation activities through prefabricated white-space modules. Schneider describes the design as a 10, 20 MW, Tier III-targeted modular AI factory architecture developed to ANSI standards. The published example concentrates on one deployment unit containing four scalable units, designed around four NVIDIA Vera Rubin clusters with 1,008 GPUs each.

That translates to 4,032 GPUs distributed across 56 AI computing racks, supported by another 32 networking racks. The documented configurations support approximately 10.4 MW to 11.4 MW of active IT load, with total peak facility power of approximately 13.25 MW. The reference design assigns approximately 33,518 square feet to the deployment unit, divided between IT space and supporting utility infrastructure. Reference Design 115 uses four 3.75 MW RapidScale powertrains to serve the IT environment, providing a 3+1 distributed redundant UPS architecture. Each powertrain includes a 5,000-amp QED-2 switchboard, three parallel 1,250 kW Galaxy VXL UPS units, and associated distribution infrastructure, and the UPS systems provide five minutes of runtime at rated load.

Separate 2.5 MW powertrains provide 2N electrical infrastructure for the mechanical systems, with UPS support for critical coolant distribution units and pumps. The design continues to use 480V AC distribution for AI racks, with 415V distribution for networking equipment. At the Max-P operating point, each AI rack draws approximately 227 kW, while at Max-Q power consumption falls to approximately 188 kW per rack. In the tabulated Max-P configuration, 42 AI racks operate with approximately 10.4 MW of total IT demand, including networking equipment, and the Max-Q configuration supports all 56 AI racks with approximately 11.4 MW of aggregate IT demand.

The Max-P configuration operates with three of the four IT electrical powertrains, while the full 56-rack Max-Q configuration uses all four. Schneider's design assumes that liquid cooling removes approximately 96% of the heat generated by the liquid-cooled racks, with the balance handled by air-cooling infrastructure. Motivair liquid-to-liquid coolant distribution units connect the computing equipment to a high-temperature technology cooling loop designed for approximately 108°F supply and 126°F return temperatures. A separate chilled-water system supplies 64°F water to Uniflair fan walls, which manage residual rack heat and other air-cooled equipment.

Schneider models annualized power usage effectiveness at approximately 1.1 under the San Francisco and Dallas conditions examined in the reference design. The companies first announced their jointly engineered EcoStruxure white-space module in September 2025, and their October 2026 White Paper 238 examines the installation sequence for integrated IT pods at a Compass hyperscale campus. In the configuration studied, an approximately 1,000-square-foot pod accommodates up to 42 rack positions with a maximum electrical capacity of 1.2 MW. The study reports that selected onsite activities required 15 hours for the prefabricated pod, compared with 75.5 hours for the conventional approach.

Compass also documented improvement through repetition, with one earlier installation requiring 18 hours compared with 15 hours for the later deployment examined in the study. In September, UL Solutions announced that Schneider had achieved the first certification under its UL 2140 program for specified prefabricated power distribution assemblies. The comparison excludes offsite manufacturing activities and does not measure total data center construction or commissioning time, and it also excludes certain conventional overhead-support installation work. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Schneider Electric's AI Factory Strategy Moves Beyond the Modular Data Hall
