stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could erase many jobs forever and urges lawmakers to act
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the 71 year old cofounder of Microsoft, published a 6,000 word essay earlier this year titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical,” in which he warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out careers over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. In the essay he called for certain jobs to be “human reserved” and said AI will take on work in law, customer service, medicine, software and manufacturing, adding that many jobs will disappear forever. He wrote that the transition to the AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history and that the world is not preparing adequately for that transition. He also said that if the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.

The warning arrives alongside new figures on job losses, as Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported on November 5, 2026, that AI has been cited in 121,401 job cut announcements so far in 2026, which is approximately 20 percent of all cuts. Gates had already raised his concerns in September, when he appeared on NBC News’ Meet the Press with Kristen Welker and was asked whether AI is powerful enough to end all of humanity. He responded that AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths and that there has never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools. He added that self regulation is not enough and that legislation needs to be passed, with politicians and law enforcement offering safeguarding and monitoring.

The essay sets out Gates’ view that the coming shift will be turbulent and that choices made now are critical, and it calls for some roles to be set aside for humans rather than left to machines. His September remarks place the responsibility for safeguards on lawmakers and law enforcement rather than on the industry alone, since he said self regulation is not enough. The Challenger, Gray & Christmas count of 121,401 AI cited job cut announcements in 2026, about 20 percent of all cuts, gives a measure of how far the disruption has already gone. The articles do not say what steps, if any, governments or companies have taken in response to his call for legislation.

stories.Headline: Beyond detection: How artificial intelligence is transforming clinical dental hygiene practice - RDH
stories.Summary:
Marianne Dryer, MEd, RDH, and Andrea Fisher, MSML, RDH, wrote an article published by RDH on Nov. 17, 2026, about artificial intelligence in clinical dental hygiene practice. The article says AI can enhance radiographic interpretation and help hygienists identify periodontal changes more consistently. It says visual AI tools can make complex findings easier for patients to understand, supporting codiagnosis and treatment acceptance. It says voice-assisted charting and integrated AI can strengthen documentation, workflow efficiency, and longitudinal periodontal monitoring. The article says dental hygienists make hundreds of clinical decisions every day that influence patient outcomes.

The article says advanced imaging platforms can detect subtle changes in crestal bone height, quantify radiographic bone loss, and compare findings over time. It says accurate classification still depends on clinical attachment level, probing depths, bleeding on probing, recession, furcation involvement, mobility, medical history, and an understanding of disease activity. It says studies show less than 16% of periodontal charts are recorded to completion. It says bleeding on probing affecting 30% or more of the mouth is consistent with generalized moderate gingivitis. It says concerns about insurance coverage and reimbursement often limit use of the preventive CDT code 4346 for scaling in the presence of generalized moderate to severe gingival inflammation.

The article says the dental hygienist remains responsible for interpreting findings within the context of the patient's clinical presentation, risk factors, and overall health. It says AI should never be viewed as a substitute for comprehensive periodontal assessment. It says AI can identify patterns and highlight areas of concern but cannot independently determine etiology, classify disease, or establish an individualized treatment plan. It says comprehensive periodontal assessment, classification, patient education, treatment planning, and clinical judgment remain the responsibility of the dental hygienist. It says AI does not determine treatment or coding.

The article says AI bridges a communication gap by converting complex diagnostic information into clear, visual representations. It says color overlays, highlighted areas of bone loss, and side-by-side comparisons of previous radiographs transform abstract findings into meaningful conversations. It says patients are more likely to accept treatment when they understand what clinicians see. It says incomplete records may affect diagnostic consistency, treatment planning, communication among providers, and insurance reimbursement. It says AI-assisted radiographic interpretation, along with comprehensive depiction of CAL and disease activity, will support early coverage for D4341 and D4342, nonsurgical scaling and root planing.

The article says AI is far more than a technology trend and is an emerging clinical tool. It says AI's greatest value lies not in replacing clinical expertise but in enhancing it. It says some AI platforms function as standalone applications that analyze radiographs or identify patterns of disease. It says others are fully integrated into practice management and imaging systems, allowing clinicians to access AI-generated insights without disrupting their clinical workflow. It says one of the fastest-growing applications is voice-assisted AI.

The article says dental hygienists should consider how technology supports patient care, documentation, and communication rather than asking which AI platform is best. It says the most valuable systems integrate seamlessly into existing workflows, improve efficiency without increasing administrative burden, and enhance rather than replace clinical decision-making. It says AI should simplify the clinician's day while strengthening the patient experience. The article ends mid-sentence in the text provided, at voice-enabled periodontal charting. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel superintendent Mark Bedell asks parents to weigh banning or embracing student AI use
stories.Summary:
Anne Arundel County’s public school system faces a decision soon on whether to ban students’ use of artificial intelligence or embrace it, The Baltimore Banner reported on 11/17/2026 at 5:30 a.m. EST. Superintendent Mark Bedell has been asking parents to tackle that question, along with what to do about cellphone use in schools, at a series of community meetings. Bedell organized the meeting series because he pledged to listen to community members’ feedback before making any AI policy recommendations of his own. The last two meetings were planned for this week, with families invited to gather on Tuesday at Annapolis High and on Thursday at Meade High from 6 to 8 p.m.

The roughly three dozen parents who gathered Thursday night at Southern High in Harwood expressed a mix of excitement and fear about the new technology. The draft AI policy under consideration by Anne Arundel’s school board is light on specifics. It requires AI tools to be vetted for educational value before adoption and emphasizes that the technology may not replace employees’ duties. It also directs the district to establish expectations, conditions and limitations for students’ use of AI. The board is set to update and finalize the policy next month.

Bedell said Thursday during the meeting at Southern High in Harwood that the district will learn how to adjust to this AI era, even though it has everyone a little nervous. Bedell conceded in an interview that he doesn’t know how to give older students access to AI and prevent them from using it to cheat. He said the district has always been able to figure out how to put guardrails in for new technology, but for this technology it just hasn’t figured it out yet. He said a few themes have emerged from the meetings he’s attended, with many parents asking the district to teach students how to use AI safely. Others have asked for AI to be banned outright for children in elementary and middle schools, just as cellphone use at school is banned for those grades.

Other parents have begged Bedell to keep AI out of their children’s schools altogether. Attendee Tamara Bauer said she loves AI and uses it often in her personal life, and the district’s priority should be teaching students to use AI safely and appropriately. Bauer is a mom of two and the principal at the Center of Applied Technology South, an Edgewater high school offering job training, and she attended with her son Levi, a fifth grader who was the youngest kid there. Bauer said that when Levi needs help with his math homework, she sometimes scans his worksheets and feeds them into an AI model, asking it to explain step by step how to find the answer rather than show her the answer.

She then helps guide her son to do the work, and she said a child working alone would be less deliberative. Hillary Klemmt, a parent affiliated with the Schools Beyond Screens coalition, which advocates for evidence-based education technology policies, asked why the district is rushing to embrace AI blindly and why it is using children as guinea pigs when there is so much at stake. A procession of speakers who testified at a board meeting last month all had the same message: Ban it. Some parents argued AI can’t and shouldn’t be avoided, even though students may use it to cheat, while others said it stifles creativity and has no place in schools.

The Banner’s related coverage included a report on Oct 23, 2026, that Anne Arundel parents and teachers urged the school board to restrict AI in classrooms. Another related report on May 5, 2026, covered what to know about Anne Arundel schools’ trial run with AI-powered weapons detection. Jessica Calefati, an education investigative reporter at The Baltimore Banner who covers the Anne Arundel County schools and Maryland’s child welfare system, wrote the story. The final two meetings were scheduled for Tuesday and Thursday from 6 to 8 p.m., at Annapolis High on Tuesday and Meade High on Thursday.

The school board is set to update and finalize the draft AI policy next month. Bedell has not yet outlined his own AI policy recommendations, which he pledged to make after listening to community feedback. The articles do not state what the board will decide or when Bedell will present his recommendations. The articles do not state how many meetings Bedell has attended or how many people testified at last month’s board meeting.

stories.Headline: Nigerian lawmakers and experts urge AI regulation to curb digital misinformation at Abuja forum
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers and communication experts called for stronger safeguards against digital misinformation at the 2026 World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on Monday, warning that misuse of artificial intelligence and social media could undermine public trust and weaken democratic institutions. Tajudeen Abbas, speaker of the house of representatives, was represented by Julius Ihonvbere, the house majority leader, and said misleading information could spread faster than institutions could respond. He said technology improves access to information but has also increased the capacity to misinform, manipulate and distort public discourse. Abbas urged public relations and communication professionals to promote public understanding, institutional credibility and democratic participation, and said responsible communication is a condition for the effective functioning of democratic society.

Abbas said artificial intelligence offers opportunities in research, information access and efficiency but could also be used to generate falsehoods, impersonate public figures and manipulate democratic debates. He urged public institutions to communicate accurately and transparently, asked the media to uphold independence and verification, and called on technology companies to take responsibility for misuse of their platforms. He said the proposed Abuja Declaration should establish common principles around accuracy, transparency, freedom of expression, institutional accountability and ethical AI use. Osita Izunaso, senator representing Imo west and chairman of the senate committee on capital market, called for regulation of artificial intelligence to prevent its misuse. He urged social media users to verify information before sharing it and warned against treating everything published online as factual.

Kete Omenugha, the first female vice-chancellor of Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University, called for communication ethics to become a compulsory course in Nigerian universities, irrespective of students' disciplines. She cited an incident in which a false WhatsApp voice note claiming examinations had been postponed by two weeks caused some students to stop preparing and travel home. She also warned against the use of AI to create offensive caricatures of lecturers, vice-chancellors and fellow students, saying many people carry scars all through their lives. Emmanuel Dandaura, vice-president of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations, urged practitioners to move beyond publicity and persuasive content to embrace strategic leadership, ethical conduct and institutional accountability. He warned that artificial intelligence had made deception cheaper, faster and increasingly convincing.

Dandaura said in a presentation titled "Redefining Public Relations: Nigeria's Gold Proposition for a Changing World" that the value of practitioners should lie in sound judgement, accountability and moral courage rather than merely producing persuasive content. He said machines can produce persuasive content better, so the enduring value of public relations must lie in judgment, accountability, moral courage and the ability to counsel institutions toward responsible conduct. The forum highlighted the need for responsible communication, ethical use of AI and stronger regulatory frameworks to address the spread of false and manipulative narratives. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the proposed Abuja Declaration.

stories.Headline: Mavria raises $130M at a $1B valuation to build factory-made AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Mavria, a Houston, Texas-based company that enables factory-built data center infrastructure for the artificial intelligence industry, has raised $130 million across pre-seed and seed funding rounds at a $1 billion valuation. The latest round was led by Paradigm, with participation from AMP public benefit corporation, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier, and Dream Ventures. The company plans to use the capital to secure critical supply chains, expand manufacturing capacity and expand its workforce. Mavria was founded by a team with backgrounds spanning energy, software, manufacturing and infrastructure development, and its co-founders previously worked together at the U.S. Department of Energy.

The company's first product, Terrain, is a factory-built data center platform that integrates power, cooling, controls, and information technology pods into a standardized system. It uses repeatable manufacturing processes intended to reduce deployment timelines, improve cost predictability, and simplify procurement, designed for frontier AI laboratories, cloud providers, and data center developers. Terrain 01, Mavria's first data center system, is currently in production in Houston. Adam Blake, co-founder and CEO of Mavria, wrote on the company's blog post that the team believes in rapidly deploying infrastructure as a product rather than custom-building every project.

Blake is an American energy and software entrepreneur who joined the U.S. Department of Energy in early 2025 as a senior adviser to Energy Secretary Chris Wright, where he also led the agency's Department of Government Efficiency team. His responsibilities included implementing a federal directive to streamline regulatory pathways under the Atomic Energy Act, with a target of bringing three new non-commercial nuclear reactors to criticality by July 4, 2026. During his tenure at the department, Blake and his co-founders identified constraints in America's aging power grid and industrial supply chains as significant obstacles to meeting the growing infrastructure demands of artificial intelligence. The founders believe that America's ability to expand its industrial base will become increasingly important to its competitiveness in artificial intelligence.

Paradigm is a technology investment firm led by Matt Huang and Alana Palmedo that invests in companies developing technologies across artificial intelligence, robotics, cryptocurrency, and other emerging sectors. Founded in 2018, the firm manages more than $11 billion in assets and invests across stages and geographies, from early-stage financing to public markets. Its portfolio investments include drone delivery company Zipline, aerospace and defense company True Anomaly, payments platform Stripe, prediction market Kalshi, Hyperliquid, and financial services firm Citadel Securities. The firm has offices in San Francisco, New York, and Washington, D.C.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans to launch an initial public offering to raise billions of dollars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to launch its initial public offering this week to raise significant capital. CEO Dario Amodei pitched the debut at JPMorgan headquarters in Manhattan on November 13, 2026. The company seeks to raise $64.4 billion through the IPO and $26 billion via private placement. This event follows a period where AI startups captured 86 percent of U.S. venture capital. The reported valuation for the company is $1.4 trillion, which is lower than the $2 trillion originally floated.

The deal involves investments from Google, Microsoft, and chip giants like Nvidia, Broadcom, and Micron. Other investing firms include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Advanced Micro Devices. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner aims to invest $5 billion, five times his largest previous IPO investment. These figures emerge as AI deal value globally reached $521.4 billion over the trailing twelve months. This growth occurs despite a 21.6 percent drop in the total count of AI deals.

Dario Amodei promoted the firm's public debut to an audience at the JPMorgan Chase headquarters. Brad Gerstner told CNBC that he views the company as a cornerstone compounder for a long time. Mike McLelland of Clearstead stated that successful exits provide more confidence in the realization story for investors. He noted that companies are staying private longer and strategic exits have been relatively muted recently. This follows Google's $32 billion purchase of Wiz in 2025, which was its largest acquisition ever.

Jake Miller of Opto Investments noted that thousands of smaller infrastructure and data service companies are affected. Venture capital funds returned 17.8 percent in the first half of 2026, benefiting these linked firms. However, private credit and buyout funds have lagged, with returns of 2.6 percent and 1.4 percent respectively. Private credit suffered due to fears that AI could render some software companies uncompetitive. Private equity funds have also struggled to sell portfolio companies at a profit this year.

Venture capital had a five-year return of 6.19 percent, trailing its ten-year annual average of 13 percent. AI captured $355.9 billion of U.S. venture dollars in the first half of 2026, per Clearstead. Infrastructure funds returned 4.2 percent in the first half of the year, driven by data center needs. In Texas, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a moratorium for new data center permits during midterm elections. A CEO scandal at Nvidia has also added risk to the broader AI financing sector.

Market reception to the shares may set the tone for the next leg of the boom. Juan Mier of PitchBook expects venture returns to moderate in the third quarter as public valuations adjust. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act could increase permitting speed if the legislation is passed. Investors are now becoming more discerning, with some focusing on early-stage Seed, Series A, and Series B companies. The articles leave open whether political pressure will successfully slow new data center development.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Advances Biological Digital Twins While Validation Limits Regulatory Adoption
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is transforming biological digital twins across every level of biological organization, according to a theoretical analysis by toxicologist Thomas Hartung published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and reported by bioengineer.org on November 18, 2026. The analysis examines how deep learning, transformer architectures, foundation models, and physics-informed neural networks have elevated biological simulation beyond static systems of differential equations. Biological digital twins maintain internal states coupled to physical counterparts through continuous data assimilation rather than functioning as generic classifiers or open-loop simulations. Across five nested scales, from single-cell multi-omics to the environmental exposures of entire populations, these architectures show capacity to model human biology without surrogate animal species. Hartung argues that technical ingenuity alone cannot secure regulatory trust without agreed credibility standards, independent prospective testing, and formal governance of self-updating algorithms.

The analysis establishes four foundational commitments that exclude conventional simulations, software dashboards, and static pattern predictors. A biological digital twin demands specificity, binding its computational state to a distinct biological instance such as a single patient or an individual organ-on-chip rather than an average population category. It requires continuous data assimilation, an iterative loop where telemetry, biosensor readings, or longitudinal omics samples update the model to track physical drift over time. The twin must encode mechanistic constraints from biological principles rather than statistical correlations alone, and it demands empirical testability with refutable predictions and quantified uncertainty. Representations lacking any criterion, including frozen neural networks, open-loop simulations, or decorative avatars, fail this definition and cannot serve as dependable regulatory instruments.

At the cellular level, representation learning and foundation models fuse multimodal single-cell measurements into dynamic latent manifolds. Single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer, scGPT, and scFoundation learn compressed representations across tens of millions of cellular profiles, separating technical batch artifacts from genuine biological signals. This manifold enables virtual perturbation experiments simulating cellular trajectory shifts under novel pharmacological compounds, gene knockouts, or environmental toxicants. In exploratory toxicology, virtual cells reorder experimental pipelines, nominating informative hypotheses for bench testing while reducing reliance on early rodent toxicity screens and primary animal cell cultures. General foundation models serve as shared infrastructure rather than digital twins until conditioned on specific cell populations and coupled to incoming experimental data.

At the in vitro level, computational twins model engineered cell cultures, microfluidic devices, and organoids, which Hartung identifies as the most technologically mature tier. The DigiLoCS liver-on-chip framework separates intracellular metabolism, passive permeability, and compartment partitioning, predicting clinical drug clearance distributions more accurately than conventional lumped single-compartment methods. Emerging organoid twins incorporate biophysical priors and active learning to forecast therapeutic responses and drug resistance in patient-derived cancer tissues, offering alternatives to patient-derived xenograft rodent models. Coupled with laboratory automation, closed-loop organoid systems can predict responses, execute robotic perturbations, and update internal states within hours. Mathematical unidentifiability, where multiple unmeasured parameter combinations yield identical observable outputs, remains a persistent challenge requiring targeted, standardized physical measurements rather than algorithmic expansion alone.

At the organ level, digital twins confront fluid dynamics, biomechanics, barrier transport, and electrical propagation across anatomical structures. Investigators deploy physics-informed neural networks to bypass the computational cost of traditional finite-element modeling without large-animal studies in dogs or pigs. By penalizing violations of physical conservation laws within loss functions, these networks act as rapid surrogate models executing organ-scale biomechanical simulations in near-real time while maintaining physical plausibility outside training domains. A three-organ microphysiological platform linking gut, liver, and placental tissues investigates maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics during pregnancy, addressing conditions where animal testing routinely misleads because reproductive toxicity and placental transfer diverge sharply between rodent models and humans. Derived from the Virtual Physiological Human tradition, these hybrid architectures integrate mechanistic physical principles with machine learning for auditable, trustworthy organ-scale safety assessments.

At the individual patient level, the Virtual Human Twin integrates multimodal health records, wearable telemetry, high-resolution imaging, and personal omics into an individualized clinical forecast. Personal twins enable clinicians to compare therapeutic regimens, evaluate dosing schedules, and anticipate adverse drug reactions in silico prior to clinical administration. In cardiology, personalized models calibrated to patient-specific electrophysiology and anatomical imaging have simulated arrhythmic activation pathways to guide catheter ablation procedures before surgery. In oncology, hybrid twins simulating tumor microenvironments assist clinicians in navigating heterogeneous malignancies without relying on animal xenografts. The review cautions against hype surrounding all-encompassing digital human replicas claiming to forecast a patient's entire lifespan, noting that current clinical twins are narrow decision-support instruments that must contend with data harmonization challenges, physiological drift across aging, and algorithmic biases disadvantaging underrepresented demographic populations.

At the population level, digital twins aggregate individual profiles to analyze community disease dynamics, conduct in silico clinical trials, and evaluate environmental hazards across the human exposome. While genetics reveals inherited susceptibility, the exposome maps the modifiable totality of environmental exposures including diet, occupational chemicals, and airborne pollutants. Exposome twins link external exposure monitoring, biokinetic internal dose modeling, molecular pathway alterations, and clinical endpoints to guide precision prevention strategies rather than producing unverified correlations. Statistical mining and generative modeling of historical control databases enable virtual control groups for toxicity studies, curtailing the sacrifice of concurrent control animals, an application recognized in a March 2026 draft qualification opinion from the European Medicines Agency regarding non-Good Laboratory Practice rat dose-range-finding studies. In human trials, synthetic cohorts extend clinical evaluations into hard-to-enroll populations such as pregnant women or rare-disease patients, provided researchers apply rigorous counterfactual reasoning and target-trial emulation to prevent confounding and spurious certainty.

Despite computational demonstrations across all five biological scales, the review stresses that independent scientific validation and regulatory credibility, not algorithmic novelty, represent the binding constraints on the discipline. Most published twin frameworks remain retrospective demonstrations conducted by original developers rather than prospectively verified methods evaluated across independent laboratories. Because biological digital twins are inherently adaptive systems that continuously assimilate fresh data and update internal parameters, traditional validation frameworks treating assays as frozen, one-time tests are structurally inadequate. Hartung advocates next-generation validation, an iterative and risk-proportionate methodology evaluating methods across five dimensions: technical reliability, biological relevance, predictive performance, applicability domain, and data integrity. Twin credibility must be assessed against human-relevant biological mechanisms rather than concordance with historical animal tests, which themselves frequently suffer from poor reproducibility and limited predictive accuracy for human outcomes, and validation must operate as an ongoing, modular case-building process evaluating mechanistic backbones and adaptive learned components independently.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Advances Biological Digital Twins While Validation Limits Regulatory Adoption

stories.Headline: Ha Jung-woo tours Daejeon AI research sites to discuss K-Moonshot and K-Factory industrialization
stories.Summary:
Standing vice chairman Ha Jung-woo of the National AI Strategy Committee visited several research sites in Daejeon on November 17, 2026. He toured the National AI Science Research Center, Daejeon Tipstown, and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology to discuss industrialization. This trip followed previous regional visits to Daegu-North Gyeongsang and Gangwon that took place during October. Ha met with various officials from academia, industry, and research to review ways to apply artificial intelligence in the field.

The committee is focusing on the K-Moonshot project, which uses AI across twelve mission areas including nuclear fusion, semiconductors, and new drugs. This effort is supported by the National AI Science Research Center, which was established in May to integrate AI into the entire research process. Additionally, the government is promoting K-Factory, an intelligent unmanned factory system that utilizes digital twin technology and robots. Ha reviewed the KAIROS platform at KAIST, which is an unmanned operating system built with domestic technology to control logistics and humanoid robots.

Ha Jung-woo and other officials discussed the necessity of strengthening industrial competitiveness to help South Korea become one of the top three AI powers. During a talk concert at Innovate Korea 2026, Ha exchanged views with Yoon Kuk-jin, Jin Yohan, and Hong Won-hwa regarding corporate survival and future talent. He also spoke with investors and startups at Daejeon Tipstown, a facility established in 2021 that currently hosts thirty companies. The participants focused on the tasks required for entering global markets and exporting the K-Factory system overseas.

stories.Headline: US governors implement diverse AI regulations and data center policies
stories.Summary:
Various US governors and governor-elects implemented diverse AI regulations and data center policies during the 2026 midterm election cycle. These leaders took varied approaches to the AI boom and the infrastructure needed to power it. Some officials viewed the technology as an economic opportunity, while others focused on safety and regulation. The debate included issues like deepfakes, environmental impacts, and the rapid expansion of data centers. Voters decided if these issues would play a role in the outcome of the elections.

California governor-elect Xavier Becerra proposed expanding AI literacy and using AI for government audit and transparency tasks. Outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom and New York Governor Kathy Hochul explored an AI kill switch to disable advanced systems. In 2025, Alabama Governor Kay Ivey banned Chinese platforms DeepSeek and Manus from state devices and networks. Colorado's new bill on automated tools takes effect January 1, 2027, after Governor Jared Polis repealed Senate Bill 24-205. Delaware Governor Matt Meyer signed legislation in 2025 launching an AI regulatory sandbox for corporate and health technologies.

Governor Kay Ivey stated that generative AI is a monumental step for government service but requires careful study. Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders wrote that Arkansas cannot afford to be left behind as AI changes how people work. Governor Matt Meyer described his regulatory sandbox as a way to combine innovation with transparency and public trust. Governor Ron DeSantis wrote that his AI Bill of Rights defends Florida families and children from potential harms. Governor Katie Hobbs described her goal as ensuring AI strengthens rather than undermines the state economy.

Local residents pushed back against data center projects over potential energy costs and environmental impacts. Goldman Sachs economists predict Democratic wins may lead to short-term moratoria affecting 45 percent of planned US capacity. Alaska governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins supports a temporary moratorium until developers cover their own energy and infrastructure costs. Alabama governor-elect Tommy Tuberville also campaigned for developers to pay their own electricity, water, and infrastructure costs. Florida governor-elect Byron Donalds believes local governments should decide if data center facilities belong in their towns.

The AI boom has slowly become a flash point in US politics across the political spectrum. Governor Mike Dunleavy argued that Alaska has an arctic advantage that reduces cooling costs for server racks. Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders joined RAISE US, an initiative launched by Eric Holcomb and Gina Raimondo. Governor Jared Polis previously signed a consumer-protection law in 2024 to stop AI-driven algorithmic discrimination. Governor Ned Lamont launched the third phase of the Tech Talent Accelerator in February to expand AI education.

Governor-elect Phil Weiser suggested that former coal towns could be potential areas for geothermal-powered data centers. Governor Katie Hobbs created an AI steering committee in 2025 and launched a government tool in 2026. Governor Ron DeSantis signed a bill to prevent residents from paying for hyperscale data centers through utility bills. Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders urged Congress to remove the AI regulatory moratorium from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill. The articles leave open how federal action will evolve as states move ahead with their own rules.

stories.Headline: Law students sue Tribhuvan University over AI detection rules that reject theses
stories.Summary:
Law students including Vivek Chaudhary filed a writ petition in the Supreme Court of Nepal on 17 November 2026 against Tribhuvan University over its use of foreign AI-detection software. The petition challenges provisions of the university's Anti-Plagiarism Software Management and Operation Rules, 2080. Students say theses, seminar papers and clinical reports built over months of work were rejected on the estimated AI report shown by the private foreign software Turnitin. The petitioners named the Government of Nepal, the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the Ministry of Education and Sports, the Ministry of Defense and Tribhuvan University as respondents. The students say they were punished without even the minimum opportunity to present their defense.

The complaint centres on clause 10(3) of the Tribhuvan University Rules 2080, under which theses, seminar papers and clinical reports are rejected solely on the estimated percentage shown by software such as Turnitin and iThenticate as likely AI-generated. The petition seeks an order of mandamus quashing the provision, plus an interim order and priority from the court to secure the students' academic future. It asks for a mandamus to repeal the controversial provision and to create scientific and transparent standards for the use and regulation of AI. The petition cites the Tribhuvan University Act, 2049, arguing the university exceeded its general rule-making authority by creating prohibitions and punitive consequences, including rejection of theses, not present in the act. It also cites Article 28 of the Nepal Constitution and the Personal Data Protection Act, 2075.

The petitioners argue that no prevailing law in Nepal defines AI plagiarism and that there is no official government standard or software to identify it. They say information from the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers clarified that no separate act or regulation specifically addressing AI has been issued in Nepal. Under the Nepal Government's Work Allocation Regulations, they say, jurisdiction to regulate AI lies with the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. They argue the regulation seriously violates the principles of natural justice because it gives no mandatory prior opportunity to present a defense, question the software's errors and conduct independent technical testing. They say the university council's regulation, made beyond the scope of the act, is entirely voidable.

The petition states that the software reports themselves admit that similarity does not mean plagiarism. Students say parts flagged as AI by Turnitin showed as human-written or zero percent AI on other detection software such as ZeroGPT and Grammarly. The petition says the software collects students' names, email addresses and thesis details, plus keystrokes, deleted parts, IP addresses and digital activities during writing, and stores them on external servers indefinitely. It says students face serious risk of phishing attacks, email spoofing and identity theft from sending sensitive personal information and intellectual property to foreign company servers without legal authority and explicit consent. As key evidence the petitioners presented the official stance of the University of Virginia in the United States and a 2026 study by researchers at the University of Florida concluding that commercial AI detectors are flawed and unsuitable for academic evaluation or action.

The petition cites general legal principles and precedents from the Supreme Courts of India and the Philippines stating that plagiarism requires malice, deliberate intent and the theft of another person's original creation. It argues that since artificial intelligence does not claim ownership or copyright, plagiarism in the traditional sense is not objectively applicable to the use of AI-generated content. It cites international judicial precedents and scientific studies confirming that AI detection tools cannot be considered conclusive evidence. The petition claims Tribhuvan University and other educational bodies made mandatory the use of private software like Turnitin and iThenticate to check the originality of students' theses, seminar papers and clinical reports. It argues these software give automated results as likely AI-generated based solely on probability, with high technical errors and false positive rates.

Tribhuvan University spokesperson Nabin Bhandari clarified that theses cannot be copied verbatim and that the software will automatically detect it if done so. He expressed the view that anti-plagiarism testing is essential to prevent one person from stealing another's thesis and to make research original. He said such a system is necessary to prevent thesis duplication. The petition requests an interim order, stating that depriving students of research or examinations based on results from flawed and unscientific technology will cause irreparable damage. The articles leave open the court's response to the petition and any hearing date.

stories.Headline: Massachusetts lawmakers file bills to ban algorithmic rent pricing statewide
stories.Summary:
Massachusetts state Rep. Lindsay Sabadosa, a Democrat from the 1st Hampshire district, and state Sen. Cindy Friedman, a Democrat from the 4th Middlesex district, filed bills in the House and Senate to outlaw algorithmic rent pricing in the state. The Joint Committee on Housing reported the bills out favorably in March, and the proposals now sit before the Committee on Ways and Means. The bills respond to rent-pricing software, often called revenue management software, that many of Massachusetts’ largest landlords use at their properties. The software draws on nonpublic leasing data from nearby properties to recommend how high rents can go. Landlords using such programs have been accused of unfair pricing, intentionally leaving units vacant and colluding with others to reduce competition.

The bills would ban rent-pricing algorithms in Massachusetts, and the session ends Jan. 5. The biggest industry player is Texas-based RealPage, which claims on its website that its customers outperform competitors who do not use the service by up to 7%. RealPage’s algorithm analyzes nonpublic data from landlords using its software, including listed rent, the actual price tenants agree to after discounts and lease length, for new leases and renewals. The software also accesses data on a unit’s future demand and occupancy, including inquiries and applications from prospective tenants. A 2023 report by the Metropolitan Area Planning Council found that 21% of Greater Boston properties sold between 2004 and 2018 were purchased by an investor or speculator, and a 2025 study by the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy found that 8.9% of residential parcels nationwide are owned by a corporation.

Sabadosa compared traditional rent-setting to selling a used car, where the seller checks prices for the same or similar models and sets an asking price accordingly. She said the algorithm is a much more sophisticated way of looking at all the rents than trying to understand the maximum the market will bear in a given community. She said that for someone just trying to make money it is surely a great idea, but for thriving communities where people can afford to live it is a terrible idea, because it is constant upward pressure that pushes everybody out. Friedman said the problem is that it is distorting the market and called it kind of immoral, saying people are taking rental places where people can live and need to live off the market. Friedman said it becomes much more insidious much faster than a landlord going through Zillow or Redfin.

Demetrios Salpoglou, CEO of the real estate platform Boston Pads, said frequent price fluctuations he sometimes sees on the website cause unnecessary issues for renters and landlords. He said he has seen out-of-state landlords rely too heavily on algorithms without understanding neighborhood nuances, and has heard from confused consumers or their agents about a unit’s price changing twice daily. He said it is like over-engineering a Hyundai and calling it a Porsche, and that he has never really had a landlord say the rental software is incredible. Salpoglou said most small- and mid-sized or independent property owners he works with use real-time pricing data on his platform and may lower rent near the lease date but otherwise rarely change prices unexpectedly. He theorized corporate landlords may use the software to satisfy obligations to owners and investors, which he called, in the nicest way he could say it, a CYA.

In 2024 the U.S. Department of Justice and several states, including Massachusetts, sued RealPage and some of the largest landlords in the country, alleging the practice illegally decreases competition. In November of last year RealPage and the DOJ reached a settlement requiring the company to stop using non-public competitor data in price recommendations, not to use active lease data to train its models and to remove or redesign features that limit price decreases. RealPage did not admit wrongdoing and said in court documents that it continues to believe the use of non-public data led to more efficient and procompetitive pricing and reduced vacancies. Massachusetts and other states continued their case, and two landlord defendants, Greystar Management Services and LivCor, have settled, while the case against RealPage, Camden Property Trust, Pinnacle Property Management Services and Willow Bridge Property Company is ongoing. Attorney General Andrea Campbell said in January 2025, when the state joined the case, that her office will seek to hold accountable those who betray renters’ trust and undermine a fair and competitive housing market.

Neither Sabadosa nor Friedman was optimistic the state legislation would pass this session, and Friedman said she thinks the proposal could make it into larger housing-related legislation next session. New York was the first state to ban the technology, with the prohibition taking effect in December 2025, and California and New Jersey have since followed suit. RealPage sued New York seeking to overturn the law, arguing it violated the company’s First Amendment rights to free speech and dissemination of information, and in late September a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking the law while the case plays out. New York Attorney General Letitia James has appealed the decision. Sabadosa said one advantage of Beacon Hill being a little slow-moving is seeing the laws pass in other states and the immediate legal challenges, and that they are looking at what the courts identified as issues and redrafting to be responsive.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities in Congress push for AI laws targeting data centers and model safety
stories.Summary:
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will likely press for various AI laws. These lawmakers seek to regulate data centers, frontier model safety, and cybersecurity. They also want to protect workers' welfare, civil rights, and national security. These efforts follow midterm elections where AI concerns played a seminal role. Some legislation may move during the lame-duck session to restrict chip exports.

Sen. Mark Warner introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July 2026. Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the No Harm Data Centers Act in April 2026. In September 2026, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The Senate voted 73 to 25 on November 9 to advance that act. Rep. Jay Obernolte introduced the FRONTIER Act in June 2026 for model safety.

Sen. Mark Warner proposed the SAFE AI Act and the AI AGENT Act. He also suggested the National Workforce Transition Fund and the PHD Talent Act. Rep. Jay Obernolte said developers must take specific steps to ensure model safety. Rep. Ayanna Pressley urged Democrats to prioritize the AI Civil Rights Act. The Congressional Black Caucus vowed to ensure civil rights protections in AI laws.

Voters are affected, as 56 percent cited AI as a major voting factor. Over 40 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by these voters. Rep.-elect William Lawrence campaigned on opposing local data center development and pausing AI. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel campaigned on requiring notice before AI-driven layoffs at large employers. Rep.-elect Scott Wiener proposed reviving the U.S. Digital Service to advise federal agencies.

Public perception of data centers is negative regarding environmental and energy impacts. Recent AI agent-enabled cyber breaches have increased the focus on cybersecurity issues. Competition with China remains a high priority for national security and AI policy. Some lawmakers want to prevent the release of AI superintelligence and recursive self-improvement. Others seek to protect critical infrastructure from quantum computing and foreign national security adversaries.

Congress may include the AI Overwatch Act in the National Defense Authorization Act. This would require licenses for the export and transfer of certain integrated circuits. The Chip Security Act is another bill that may be included in that act. The articles leave the scope and timing of laws uncertain due to divided government. It remains to be seen which specific proposals can actually become federal law.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy proposes a temporary moratorium on city AI use
stories.Summary:
Portland Council President Jamie Dunphy proposed a temporary moratorium on the City's use of artificial intelligence on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, asking for a pause on new contracts and AI expansion. Dunphy's proposal will go before Portland City Council on Dec. 3, and if approved, new contracts and plans to expand the use of AI in City operations would pause. The pause would last until the city implements new privacy infrastructure and guardrails. Dunphy cited the increase in software and services with embedded AI sold to the City to express his concern for the speed with which governments are being pushed to use and accept AI. The proposal would align with the executive order Gov. Tina Kotek recently signed ordering the State to establish parameters and proceed with caution before implementing AI.

Dunphy said emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, meaning the city cannot simply go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code. He said his goal is to protect public privacy, security, and civil rights while the administration makes the City's Data and Privacy Office fully operable and adopts comprehensive legislative guidelines. Dunphy said he understands the desire by private companies to rush to adopt these technologies to reduce costs and increase efficiency, but the government is not beholden to profit-driven shareholders. He said the city must move more intentionally, that its job is to serve the best interest of the public, and that this means considering the impacts on real people. Dunphy said that is not the city being slow, but taking time for critical thinking.

Dunphy added that the Data and Privacy Office established in March is not yet operational, meaning the City cannot yet review technology contracts with expertise or clear Code guidelines. Co-founder of AI Portland Megan Notarte told KOIN 6 News that she knows the city of Seattle has a responsible AI use policy, so if she were to provide a more educated view she would look at what Seattle is doing. Notarte said she thinks there are probably ways of moving forward that maybe are not a moratorium for the year. Portland residents can submit written or verbal testimony regarding the City's approach to AI on the city's website. The articles give no further comment from other officials or groups, and they do not name which residents or organizations are affected beyond the City and the public.

The articles state that the Data and Privacy Office was established in March, and that it is not yet operational. They state that Dunphy cited the increase in software and services with embedded AI sold to the City as the source of his concern. They state that the proposal would pause new contracts and plans to expand the use of AI in City operations until new privacy infrastructure and guardrails are in place. They state that the proposal aligns with Gov. Tina Kotek's recent executive order ordering the State to establish parameters and proceed with caution before implementing AI. They state that Notarte pointed to Seattle's responsible AI use policy as a model worth examining.

The proposal goes before Portland City Council on Dec. 3, where members will consider whether to approve the pause on new contracts and AI expansion. If approved, the pause would hold until the city implements new privacy infrastructure and guardrails and the Data and Privacy Office becomes fully operable. Residents can submit written or verbal testimony on the City's approach to AI through the city's website before the council takes up the proposal. The articles do not say what the council will decide, how long the moratorium would last if approved, or when the Data and Privacy Office is expected to become operational. The articles also do not say what specific contracts or expansion plans would be affected, or what the State's parameters under Gov. Kotek's executive order will contain.

stories.Headline: Nexus Legal Group launches simplified AI WebTracker plans for law firms
stories.Summary:
The Nexus Legal Group LLC announced on November 16, 2026, simplified plans for AI WebTracker, its AI-powered prospect intelligence platform that identifies people actively researching legal help in a firm's practice areas and markets, including people visiting competing law firm websites, and delivers them in a fresh feed every morning. The platform is now offered in two plans, Self-Serve and Done-For-You, and every plan includes lead scrubbing before a firm's team reaches out. The launch targets two of the largest drains on law firm marketing budgets, which are ad spend that reaches people who never call and per-lead fees paid to lead-generation companies for contacts that may be shared with other firms, outdated or unqualified. Each lead in the feed shows who the person is, why they entered the feed, which competing firms they viewed, and where and when they were active, down to the ZIP code, and firms export these audiences directly to their ad platforms and CRM. The Self-Serve plan includes the daily prospect feed, audience exports to ad platforms and CRM, and built-in scrubbing, with the firm's own team running its ads, while the Done-For-You plan adds full Nexus Lead Validation and Database Scrubbing, audiences and Nexus-designed, firm-approved ad creatives uploaded to ad platforms the firm already owns, such as Google, Microsoft Bing and Meta, ongoing feed tuning, and a monthly report, review call and dedicated Nexus contact.

Every plan includes TCPA Real-Time Scrubbing, Do Not Call Lookup, Phone List Scrubbing and the Name Recognition Algorithm, and the Done-For-You plan adds the Nexus Lead Validation and Database Scrubbing upgrade, which runs Scammer Scrub, TCPA Lookup and Scrubbing, and DNC Lookup and Scrubbing on a firm's monthly leads and uploaded lists, with each record marked Validated, Review or Do Not Contact and given a time-stamped Validation Record. AI WebTracker is a flat monthly subscription that is never tied to leads, cases or outcomes, there is no setup fee, and firms can cancel with 30 days' notice. Firms pay their ad platforms directly and keep ownership of their ad accounts and the audiences they build, and the ad budget is paid from the firm's own ad account, never handled by Nexus. An optional Nonprofit Outreach and Intake Support add-on is available with either plan and provided with Legal Support Cases, Inc. under a separate agreement. Rob Parker, Managing Partner of The Nexus Legal Group, said firms are being squeezed from both sides, paying more every year to bid on the same keywords as every competitor in town and paying lead vendors for names that too often turn out to be wrong numbers, recycled lists or people who already hired someone.

He said AI WebTracker lets a firm see who is actually researching its type of case, in its own markets, before that person picks up the phone. He also said a firm should not pay more because a vendor sent more names, and that with a flat subscription the feed grows the firm's own audience every day and the firm keeps what it builds. AI WebTracker is designed for personal injury, mass tort, trucking and commercial vehicle, wrongful death and other practice areas where speed and geography decide which firm signs the case, and law firms can book a demo and receive pricing at WebTrackerLeads.ai. The company notes that AI WebTracker uses licensed data sources, that being identified in the feed is not consent to be contacted, and that scrubbing and Lead Validation reduce risk but do not guarantee compliance and are not legal advice. The Nexus Legal Group describes itself as a legal marketing and technology company that helps law firms find, reach and sign high-value cases, and its media contact is team@nexuslegal.group and 855-925-1035.

stories.Headline: Democratic Congress prepares AI safety and testing bills as Trump administration favors deregulation in 2027
stories.Summary:
The articles report that federal artificial intelligence policy is likely to divide along institutional lines in 2027, according to a November 17, 2026 analysis by Kevin Edgar and Michelle Tanney of BakerHostetler published on JD Supra. The Trump administration will continue to emphasize American technological leadership, infrastructure development and regulatory restraint, while the Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to focus more heavily on safety, accountability, consumer protection and the costs associated with AI. When the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, AI policy is likely to look markedly different from the federal approach of the past two years. Democratic control of the House and Senate will give the party significant authority over the congressional agenda beginning Jan. 3, 2027. Current reporting indicates that Democratic lawmakers are preparing proposals addressing advanced-model testing, AI-related harms and the costs associated with AI deployment and development.

Congressional oversight may move faster than legislation, and new congressional leadership will control committee agendas, hearing calendars and subpoena authority. Pending legislation identifies the controls Congress may expect, including independent testing of frontier models, incident reporting, government oversight and human-controlled shutdown capabilities. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act would create a federal oversight regime for frontier AI and independent assessment of certain developers' safety practices. H.R. 9925, the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or FRONTIER Act, was introduced in July by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., with bipartisan cosponsors. H.R. 9917, the AI Kill Switch Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, would require covered entities to maintain technical capabilities to shut down certain covered technologies.

Sen. John N. Kennedy, R-La., subsequently introduced S. 5417, the AI Emergency Button Act, which likewise would require developers or operators of advanced AI systems to incorporate a human-controlled shutdown capability. Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan proposed pausing the training and release of the most powerful AI models until federal safeguards are established, prohibiting the development of superintelligent systems and recursive self-improvement, and creating a Cabinet-level agency empowered to inspect AI laboratories, block dangerous model releases and order shutdowns. In November, the Department of Justice announced a Super Intelligence Task Force focused on misuse of advanced technology by foreign and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct. The DOJ specifically identified regular reporting of risks and incidents and vigorous internal controls over advanced AI systems as areas of focus. Proposals such as the Clear Liability for Artificial Intelligence Misconduct (CLAIM) Act from Rep. Trahan would create new federal remedies specifically addressing harms caused by AI systems.

Regulatory fragmentation may persist, because presidential veto authority, Senate procedural requirements and continuing disagreements over the appropriate scope of AI regulation make enactment of a comprehensive federal statute uncertain. Companies should therefore prepare for overlapping federal oversight, executive action, state regulation, agency enforcement and private litigation rather than presume that a single national framework will emerge. A congressional committee need not establish probable cause before issuing a subpoena, unlike federal law enforcement seeking a search warrant. Congressional investigations can develop rapidly, encompass conduct that is not itself unlawful and unfold publicly alongside legislative and political debate. Companies should not wait for a subpoena to assess their readiness, and organizations facing potential congressional scrutiny should identify the internal personnel responsible for responding to congressional inquiries.

For much of the past two years, federal AI policy has largely been developed through executive action rather than comprehensive legislation. The Trump administration's approach culminated in a federal effort to challenge state AI laws viewed as inconsistent with a uniform, minimally burdensome national framework. Democratic lawmakers have already used letters, information requests and other minority-party tools to examine AI companies and their practices. Existing consumer protection, antidiscrimination, privacy, intellectual property, product liability and other laws may already apply to conduct involving AI, depending on the technology, use and resulting harm. Organizations should therefore remain responsible for the accuracy, reliability, confidentiality and integrity of work produced with AI assistance.

The articles state that the change in congressional control will not necessarily produce entirely new areas of scrutiny, and that what will change in 2027 is the authority behind those inquiries. The incoming Senate will include members who campaigned on substantially more aggressive restrictions in the development of advanced AI. The articles state that the resulting tension may shape federal AI policy even if Congress does not enact comprehensive legislation. The articles state that the emerging divide may be less about whether AI should be governed than about how. The articles leave open which AI bills ultimately become law.

stories.Headline: Scott Loughlin says AI agents on personal devices test whether BYOD programs can survive
stories.Summary:
Employees who use personal devices for work are increasingly running artificial intelligence agents that can read work email, open files and act across applications without a person at the keyboard, and Scott Loughlin, a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader in Washington, DC, wrote in a Bloomberg Law column published on November 16, 2026, that this raises the question of whether bring-your-own-device programs can survive agents in their current form. In a Gartner survey conducted in early 2026, 88% of employees with an enterprise AI tool also used personal AI tools for work, and those tools will likely increasingly include AI agents. Loughlin wrote that the core controls of a BYOD program, a company-managed container for work apps, monitoring of corporate systems and the ability to remotely wipe work data, were designed for apps that people operate and may not work as well for devices running AI agents. Because an agent works inside the employee's logged-in session, company records may show the employee doing what the agent did, and the agent's history and memory sit in the provider's cloud under the employee's account, beyond the reach of a remote wipe. Loughlin wrote that none of this requires hacking, but the exposure is real and no new AI statute is needed to create it, with personal data given to an unapproved agent raising issues under the GDPR and US state privacy laws, protected health information entered into a personal agent possibly being a HIPAA breach, and routine flows of source code or pricing undercutting trade-secret protection.

He wrote that EU law restricts the scope of employee monitoring and may require works-council consultation, and that US laws can limit employers' access to employees' personal accounts. He described three models likely to be applied role by role: access-only BYOD, in which personal devices reach corporate data only through a managed browser, app or virtual workspace; a sanctioned agent, in which an enterprise agent lets the organization control the agent even when it does not control the device; and company-owned devices for people in the most sensitive roles. He noted that the May 2026 guidance on agentic AI from CISA, the NSA and other governments recommends giving agents their own short-lived credentials and requiring human approval for high-impact actions. Loughlin recommended that organizations assign ownership at the leadership level, naming an accountable executive, adding personal and unsanctioned agents to the enterprise risk register and reporting on them to the board committee that oversees cybersecurity risk. He also recommended revisiting the BYOD agreement to address which agents may touch company data, employee disclosure duties, a narrow commitment to preserve and produce work-related agent data, and offboarding certification that connectors are revoked and work-related memories deleted, covering phones and tablets and calibrated to local employment and privacy law.

He advised updating legal-hold and e-discovery playbooks to add agent prompts, outputs, logs and memory to custodian questionnaires and hold notices, mapping roles and controlling the connection points where the law allows, updating incident response with scenarios for a hijacked or misused personal agent, and aligning related policies so they cross-reference each other. Loughlin wrote that organizations that plan ahead will be better positioned to demonstrate reasonable governance to regulators, courts and customers, and that agent risks are developing quickly enough that organizations are changing their BYOD programs in the short term before settling on a longer-term model. He wrote that it is a good idea to make the sanctioned path easier than the personal one and to focus controls on the connection points the organization owns. He wrote that BYOD rests on the premise that a company can manage the risk of devices it does not own, that agents using employees' credentials on those devices test that premise, and that BYOD is unlikely to disappear but programs are likely to change.

stories.Headline: Judicial codes of conduct bar judges from using AI to make decisions
stories.Summary:
Judicial codes of conduct forbid judges from using artificial intelligence to make decisions, but some judges have turned to the technology for administrative tasks and academic purposes, according to a Law360 report published on November 16, 2026. The report, written by Steven Lerner, said hurdles still remain before more judges adopt AI in their work. The article did not name any judges, courts or specific tools involved in the reported use. It also did not give figures on how many judges have used AI for administrative or academic work. The report said the judicial codes of conduct bar judges from using AI to make decisions, which limits how far the technology can go in court work.

It said some judges have used AI for administrative tasks and for academic purposes despite that restriction. The article did not describe which administrative tasks or academic uses the judges have pursued. It also did not say what specific hurdles are holding back wider adoption. The report gave no dates, numbers or names beyond the publication date and the author. The article did not identify any official, court or agency as responsible for the reported hurdles, and it did not include any statements from judges or other people about the issue.

No one was quoted in the available text, so there are no remarks to paraphrase. The report did not say who sets or enforces the judicial codes of conduct it described. It also did not say whether any court has issued guidance on AI use by judges. The available article did not provide context on how many judges currently use AI or how the reported hurdles might be addressed.

It did not say what happens next, whether rules might change or whether more judges are expected to adopt the technology. The report ended without naming any next steps, hearings or proposals on the issue. Because the articles carry too little for a longer story, no further details can be added beyond what is known. stories.Headline: Judge Wise lets memory price collusion lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron proceed
stories.Summary:
A class action lawsuit over memory price manipulation will proceed after Judge Noel Wise of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California dismissed the joint motion to dismiss filed by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron on November 14. The ruling, a 20-page document, rejected the three manufacturers' attempt to end the case. The lawsuit was first filed on June 25 this year. Mark Garciagire, an ordinary consumer living in Pasadena, California, joined 16 other plaintiffs and entrusted the boutique law firm Bathaee Dunne to sue the three major memory manufacturers in federal court. The 17 plaintiffs include ordinary consumers who buy RAM modules from Amazon and Micro Center, as well as small distributors such as PC assembly stores in Florida.

The three parties must submit an official response before December 7 and are required to hand over internal production capacity schedules, executive correspondence and meeting minutes during the subsequent discovery phase. The plaintiffs accuse the three giants of colluding to control production since October 2022, leading to a 697% surge in the price of regular DRAM contracts within 18 months. They presented shopping receipts in the 118-page indictment. The three companies together hold over 91% of the global DRAM market share. This is the first time in DRAM history that a class action lawsuit over price hikes during the AI cycle has crossed the motion to dismiss stage and entered the evidence discovery phase.

Judge Wise became a federal prosecutor through the U.S. Department of Justice's Honors Program in her early years and later spent ten years presiding over complex civil litigation trials in California courts. In response to the claim that the old case would repeat itself, she only replied: "This court does not think so." Facing the defense lawyers' "eagles watching each other" theory, Judge Wise refuted along the same metaphor: in nature, eagles may watch each other when hunting, but they will never fly together in a neat formation. She dismissed the motion to dismiss because the plaintiff presented "additional factors" sufficient to meet the threshold at this stage. The plaintiff's lawyer Brian Dunne's team was also prepared early.

The defense lawyers referred to the period from the end of 2022 to the beginning of 2023 as the "DRAM Winter". In the first quarter of 2023, Samsung's semiconductor division suffered a huge loss of 3.51 billion U.S. dollars, SK Hynix lost 2.61 billion U.S. dollars, and Micron posted a net loss of 5.833 billion U.S. dollars for the entire 2023 fiscal year. The lawyers argued that production cuts were for self-rescue, and shifting production to HBM was to chase the AI trend. They cited the Chicago School's "oligopoly interdependence theory", which successfully convinced judges in a similar lawsuit back in 2018. The plaintiff pointed out that on October 26, 2022, SK Hynix took the lead in cutting DRAM production capacity, and only three weeks later, Micron followed suit immediately.

In January 2023, Samsung executives even publicly stated that "we will never artificially reduce production of memory chips", but on April 7, 2023, Samsung suddenly made a 180-degree turn and joined the production cut camp. According to TrendForce's calculation, by the first quarter of 2026, the output value of a single wafer for DDR5 64GB RDIMM has surpassed that of HBM, and its profit margin is also higher than HBM. In the third quarter of this year, the global total DRAM revenue soared to nearly 200 billion U.S. dollars, a year-on-year surge of 369%, but the actual total shipment capacity of the entire industry only increased by 4%. The lawsuit revealed that Samsung and SK Hynix forcibly raised the price of server memory sold to Google and Microsoft by 60% to 70% within one quarter, and refused to sign long-term multi-year contracts. By the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, Micron's single-quarter revenue surged to 54.23 billion U.S. dollars, and its Non-GAAP gross profit margin soared to 87%, surpassing NVIDIA in one go; its full fiscal year net profit reached 84.97 billion U.S. dollars.

In the second quarter of 2025, the three parties all shut down or significantly cut the production lines of low-cost DDR4 for regular PCs; Samsung and Hynix also simultaneously stopped selling old DRAM manufacturing equipment to the second-hand market. On December 3, 2025, when consumer-grade memory prices hit a record high, Micron suddenly announced the shutdown of Crucial, its well-known consumer brand that had been in operation for 29 years. By January 2026, the three parties launched almost identical "customer review mechanisms" in the same month, using nearly copy-pasted questionnaires to interrogate distributors and OEMs. Apple CEO Tim Cook publicly complai

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Asian investors sell off AI stocks ahead of Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO
stories.Summary:
Asian investors sold off artificial intelligence stocks on Sunday, November 15, 2026, as they reduced their exposure to the volatile tech sector. This market movement occurred because investors are cautious ahead of a crucial week for the boom in artificial intelligence technology. The selloff caused benchmark stock indexes in Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan to slump, with the Taiex plunging more than 4 percent. US Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.5 percent after the cash index dropped 1.2 percent on the previous Friday. These actions reflect a fragile market sentiment as traders await several major corporate and economic events scheduled for the coming days.

Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, while Claude chatbot maker Anthropic prices its initial public offering on Wednesday and debuts on Nasdaq Thursday. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the former chief financial officer, must now shore up investor confidence following the resignation of Jensen Huang. Huang left the company last week after revelations of extramarital affairs, leaving a leadership void at the signature AI bull market stock. LSEG data shows Nvidia lost 1.9 trillion dollars in market capitalisation since early October due to concerns over debt-fuelled AI buildouts. Additionally, Democrats won the US midterm elections earlier this month, which threatens to bring more stringent regulations on data-centre expansion.

Interim CEO Colette Kress is responsible for managing the company, but media speculation suggests Jensen Huang might discuss a possible comeback. The Financial Times reports that Nvidia has approached Rene Haas, the CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, for the leadership role. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the company needs to find a leader outside the firm. Elon Musk stated on X on Saturday that Nvidia would lose critical deals if Huang is not at the helm. These figures believe the leadership crisis is a primary driver of the current pressure on the artificial intelligence trade.

Investors in Asia are the most affected by the current slump, though European markets have remained more resilient during this volatility. The lower concentration of AI shares in Europe has bolstered the continent's appeal as a haven, with futures rising in Germany. US consumers are also in focus as earnings from Home Depot, Lowe's, Target, and Walmart provide insight into their resilience. Retail sales data on Tuesday will further clarify the economic state of the consumer during this period of tech market instability. Market participants are now watching to see if the AI trade can recover from this recent series of shocks.

The AI boom has been led by a four-year tech-led bull market, but sustainability concerns have grown since early October 2026. Inflationary pressures have raised market bets to about 8 percent for a supersized half-point interest rate hike in December. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will speak in San Francisco on Monday about how AI will reshape the entire US economy. The Federal Reserve is also under scrutiny following hawkish comments from officials regarding the current state of national inflationary pressures. These background factors have created a tense environment for investors who are weighing tech growth against broader economic risks.

The Federal Reserve will release the minutes of its October policy meeting on Wednesday, and several Fed speakers will talk this week. Markets will monitor the retail sales data and the specific earnings results from Nvidia to determine the next direction for stocks. The debut of Anthropic on the Nasdaq will serve as another major test for the current sentiment regarding AI investments. It remains open whether Jensen Huang will return to the company or if Rene Haas will be appointed as CEO. The articles leave it unclear how the new tech boom will evolve and on what specific timetable it will progress.
