stories.Headline: AI token sales rise as China shifts focus toward AI inference and edge computing
stories.Summary:
AI token sales rose during the Double 11 shopping festival in November 2026. Large model token packages were sold through e-commerce shelves and livestreaming rooms. This trend coincided with a boom in artificial intelligence inference across China. Chip manufacturers also shifted their layout strategies to focus on inference. These changes affected the entire upstream and downstream of the industrial chain.

JD.com saw token package sales increase 20 times month-on-month during a November 2 livestream. Tmall sold 100,000 Qianwen Office membership cards in half an hour on November 2. China Center for Information Industry Development reported inference data exceeded training data by June. Daily average token calls surpassed 175 trillion, which is 1000 times higher than early 2024. Intel and Qualcomm showcased AI PCs and edge solutions at the China International Import Expo.

Wang Zhicong of Intel China said computing power will shift toward the inference side. He stated that AI capabilities must be deployed collaboratively between the end and the cloud. Qualcomm's Wan Weixing said end-side AI is evolving toward agent experiences like task orchestration. UCloud's Liu Hua believes cloud service delivery units are shifting toward the token. Wang Jiandong suggested that token measurement calibers and billing disclosures should be standardized.

Consumers are affected by varying model capabilities and unclear refund rules for token quotas. Some users reported server congestion and disconnection when using unofficial AI transfer stations. These gray market hubs may cause privacy leakage, data outflow, and malicious implantation. MediaTek and NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip now reaches users via ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI. AMD's Michael Nordquist noted that agent PCs have shipped over 500,000 units.

The industry is moving from cloud-based models to local replacement of cloud tokens. AMD released the Ryzen AI Max PRO 400 series in September 2026 for local models. This processor can run 300-billion-parameter models without needing any cloud offloading. The Tmall AI Space Station now hosts models from Qianwen, Zhipu, MiniMax, and Qoder. JD.com launched an AI software recharge hall featuring DeepSeek, Volcano Engine, and JD Cloud.

Intel may implement green computing power warehouses in the first half of next year. These warehouses will convert green power into inference tokens for distribution via networks. Qualcomm used the Snapdragon X2 series processors for agent AI PCs at its summit. The articles leave open how the government will regulate unregulated gray market hubs. stories.Headline: Policy chief Ha Joon-kyung chairs emergency meeting on AI exam cheating
stories.Summary:
The Presidential Office scheduled a response meeting for the afternoon of November 15, 2026, to address artificial intelligence assisted exam cheating. Policy Chief Ha Joon-kyung chaired this emergency session after fraud was uncovered in the national tax accountant examination. This urgent government action occurred just four days before the College Scholastic Ability Test on November 19. The meeting followed the admission of a top scorer who used generative AI to cheat on professional exams. This individual turned himself in to the police on the same day the meeting was announced.

The cheating involved a subminiature camera, a smartphone, and generative AI during the 63rd tax accountant examination's first and second rounds. Person A also admitted to cheating on the first round of the certified public accountant examination. The government is now accelerating efforts to tighten supervision for the upcoming College Scholastic Ability Test. There are mounting concerns that students might use advanced electronic devices like smart glasses to cheat. These measures aim to prevent similar fraud from occurring during the high stakes national college entrance test.

Presidential chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun held a briefing at the Chunchugwan press center in Cheong Wa Dae. Lim stated that the Presidential Office views the AI cheating matter as being extremely serious. He explained that the office had been working hard to prepare measures because the college exam was next week. Lim noted that the policy chief would lead the meeting to address potential cheating in multiple professional exams. He emphasized that the government is deliberating countermeasures to ensure the fairness of these national tests.

Critics argue that management systems for all national qualification examinations need a full review because proctors failed to detect the cheating. Students taking the College Scholastic Ability Test are directly affected by the government's plan to tighten exam supervision. The public is concerned about the integrity of professional certifications after the top tax accountant scorer admitted fraud. This incident has highlighted vulnerabilities in testing rooms that were previously thought to be secure from electronic devices. The government's response reflects a need to protect the fairness of the competitive national examination system.

President Lee Jae-myung instructed the government at a Cabinet meeting on November 10 to concentrate all capabilities on tackling various crimes. This led to the Public Safety Plus Project, which targets crimes threatening daily life and the socially vulnerable. Priority areas include motiveless violent crimes, relational crimes, scams, drugs, illegal private lending, digital sex crimes, and disinformation. The project also targets unfair practices such as real estate crimes and corruption tied to local collusion. These initiatives aim to create tangible outcomes that the public can feel regarding their overall safety.

The government will conduct an intensive review of every ministry's crime response and performance by the end of the year. Specific measures include creating safety patrol units and introducing life sentences without parole for certain serious crimes. Lim Kwang-hyun stated that the government will detect warning signs early to prevent harm and protect victims. The articles leave open the specific technical methods the government will use to detect smart glasses during exams. They also do not specify the exact penalties that will be applied to the tax accountant cheater.

stories.Headline: Singapore assesses impact of US AI chip export rules on local data centres
stories.Summary:
Singapore is currently assessing the impact of a new US rule regarding AI chip exports. The US Commerce Department announced this measure on November 16 to target China's remote access. This crackdown targets data centres in South-east Asia to prevent the circumvention of existing technology restrictions. The rule aims to stop Chinese firms from using remote computing arrangements in third countries. It could potentially end the current boom of data centres across the South-east Asian region.

The rule adds Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil to a list of countries subject to export restrictions. It takes effect 90 days after being gazetted in the Federal Register and requires Commerce Department licences. Exemptions are provided for American cloud hyperscalers like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services, but not local operators. The rule targets servers, electronic assemblies, and advanced computing integrated circuits rather than naming specific brands like Nvidia. Narrow exemptions are granted to social media companies and online retailers such as TikTok and Sea Limited.

The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information issued a statement. They said they are studying the details carefully and engaging affected companies to understand the potential business impact. The ministries are also talking to US authorities to facilitate trusted access for companies based in Singapore. They stated that Singapore is a trusted hub and does not condone violating the laws of other countries. They intend to safeguard the business environment and act against those who flout the law.

Paul Triolo of DGA Group said the rule makes it difficult to service large Chinese generative AI companies. He noted that removing Chinese customers complicates economics because hyperscaler-level clients drive critical revenue and debt servicing. Data centres in Singapore must now audit clients to ensure they are not shell companies from China or Macau. They must also check for links to jurisdictions under US arms embargoes, including Russia and Iran. Triolo believes the rule is unlikely to be rolled back due to strong political momentum.

The US is concerned that Chinese giants like Tencent, ByteDance, and Alibaba have unrestricted cloud access to advanced chips. This issue became public on November 8 after news of an affair between Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. Alice Huang is a former Megaspeed executive and a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to be in China. Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO on November 12, and Alice Huang was banned from Singapore. Authorities are now scrutinising Megaspeed and Super Micro for potential violations of laws and false declarations.

President Donald Trump will visit Manila for the ASEAN summit from November 17 to 19 and meet Xi Jinping. The US may impose broader trade restrictions if countries tolerate evasion of these new AI chip export rules. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick hold opposing views on China's access to advanced AI chips. Trump affirmed this split on November 16, stating that both friendly and aggressive views toward China are acceptable. It remains open whether these controls will drive regional players toward Chinese alternatives or sovereign third-stack solutions.

stories.Headline: Nebius plans $40bn to $45bn 2027 infrastructure spend as CEO Arkady Volozh warns site delays hit Microsoft capacity
stories.Summary:
Nebius announced on November 12, 2026, a planned capital spending outline of $40 billion to $45 billion for 2027, according to CASRAI. The AI Insider reported on November 16, 2026, that the neocloud company warned delays at third-party sites are weighing on its AI infrastructure buildout. CEO Arkady Volozh said building at this scale is hard and that Nebius is not immune to industry-wide delays. Capacity for Microsoft at a Vineland, New Jersey, site run by DataOne has slipped, with just over half now due by year-end and the rest in Q2 2027. Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571%, but cut its 2026 forecast to $3 billion, and shares fell 17%.

The 2027 plan projects between $40 billion and $45 billion in infrastructure spending to expand global GPU clusters and data centre operations. The plan follows a revision of the full-year 2026 capital expenditure target to approximately $27 billion. Nebius aims to surpass one gigawatt of operational power capacity across its facilities. The Microsoft contract is worth up to $19.4 billion and allows Microsoft to terminate affected service and impose penalties for missed dates. A primary bottleneck occurred at a 300-megawatt data centre facility in Vineland, New Jersey, operated by partner DataOne.

Chief product and infrastructure officer Andrey Korolenko attributed the delay to DataOne winding down temporary generation faster than expected as it moves to Bloom Energy fuel cells. Volozh said Nebius is not immune to industry-wide delays. Nebius said Microsoft has been part of the planning. Chief revenue officer Marc Boroditsky said deals with Microsoft and Meta included large prepayments. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez said prepayments and contract-backed financing should cover up to 85% of 2027 spending.

CASRAI said management indicated roughly 75% to 85% of the projected capital outlay will be covered by customer prepayments on qualifying long-term contracts and asset-backed credit facilities secured against investment-grade commercial commitments. Site commissioning faced regulatory scrutiny from the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection regarding temporary natural gas generation units, prompting an accelerated transition to permanent Bloom Energy fuel cells. The resulting timeline revisions pushed commercial activation for certain capacity blocks from late 2026 into the first half of 2027. Nebius expects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion. The neocloud commercial model is predicated on multi-year, multi-million-dollar take-or-pay agreements backed by substantial upfront cash prepayments.

Nebius operates within the rapidly expanding category of specialised GPU neocloud providers, offering high-density compute clusters distinct from traditional general-purpose hyperscale cloud architectures. Recent transactions with major industry partners, including multi-billion-dollar capacity agreements with Microsoft and Meta, underscore how hyperscalers are leasing wholesale capacity blocks from specialized operators. To mitigate counterparty and operational risks inherent in third-party development, Nebius is shifting future capacity additions toward owned-and-operated sites. The company's expansion roadmap focuses on scaling proprietary sites, including a second facility in Mäntsälä and new development in Lappeenranta, Finland, alongside domestic US campus developments in Missouri and Alabama. As facilities expand to multi-hundred-megawatt scales, the environmental footprint and power grid interactions become critical operational factors.

Very few academic institutions possess the balance sheet flexibility or procurement authority to enter into multi-year capacity prepayment arrangements, leaving research groups at a structural disadvantage when seeking direct access to leading-edge GPU architectures. As major hyperscalers contract large tranches of neocloud capacity wholesale to satisfy commercial enterprise commitments, spot and on-demand GPU capacity for academic researchers becomes increasingly scarce and volatile in pricing. Research teams undertaking compute FLOPs estimation for grant proposals must frequently adjust computing budgets upward to account for shifting cloud pricing tiers. For universities, managing access to scalable research data infrastructure increasingly requires hybrid strategies that combine campus-level clusters, national consortium allocations such as the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and structured institutional cloud agreements. Research computing administrators must ensure external cloud compute deployments comply with institutional research data management policies and data sovereignty requirements.

stories.Headline: Former Wall Street regulator warns AI bubble will burst and cause recession by 2028
stories.Summary:
A former top Wall Street regulator said in mid November 2026 that the artificial intelligence bubble will likely burst and cause a recession by the 2028 election, according to CNN. The warning came as a survey reported by the Chosun Ilbo on November 15, 2026 found that 87% of Wall Street experts cite AI as a major risk. The two reports together frame a market that has risen sharply on AI enthusiasm while professionals increasingly flag the danger. The CNN report identifies the speaker as Wall Street's former top cop, a reference to a senior enforcement official, though the supplied text does not name the person.

The CNN account says the expected burst would be severe enough to tip the economy into recession before voters go to the polls in 2028. The Chosun Ilbo figure of 87% is the share of Wall Street experts who named AI as a major risk in the survey it reported on November 15, 2026. Both dates fall in November 2026, which places the warnings roughly two years before the 2028 election. The articles give no further numbers, no specific forecast dates beyond the election, and no named companies or individuals beyond the former official described in the CNN headline.

Responsibility for the warning rests with the former enforcement chief, who according to CNN expects the bubble to pop and drag the broader economy down with it. The Chosun Ilbo survey places the concern among a large majority of Wall Street experts, who see AI as a major risk rather than a purely positive force. The former official's view, as CNN frames it, is that the run-up resembles a bubble that cannot hold. The experts surveyed by the Chosun Ilbo did not, in the supplied text, offer a single unified prediction beyond flagging the risk.

The context is a market that has climbed on AI optimism while a growing share of professionals warn of a correction, and the CNN report ties that correction to a possible recession before 2028. What happens next depends on whether the bubble deflates gradually or bursts suddenly, and the articles do not say which outcome they expect beyond the former official's warning. The Chosun Ilbo survey suggests the concern is widespread rather than isolated to one voice. Neither article, in the text provided, gives a timeline for the burst beyond the 2028 election horizon.

stories.Headline: Ramaphosa leads South African delegation in Silicon Valley to study AI development and adoption
stories.Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived in California in the United States of America on Saturday, 14 November 2026, for a working visit to Silicon Valley, where he is leading a high-level, multi-stakeholder South African delegation to gain insights into the global artificial intelligence ecosystem and to inform South Africa's approach to the development, adoption and application of AI. The delegation comprises representatives from government, academia, business, research institutions, technical experts and university students, which the Presidency says reflects the country's commitment to an inclusive, collaborative and multi-stakeholder approach to harnessing the opportunities presented by AI. The programme includes engagements with leading technology companies, investors, researchers, academics and AI experts, as well as technology demonstrations and knowledge exchanges, which provide an opportunity to explore developments in frontier AI, robotics, data infrastructure, cloud computing, digital innovation and the practical application of AI across various sectors. A key component of the visit is engagements with leading academic institutions, focusing on the implications of AI for technology, security, the economy, business and the labour market, as well as emerging developments in robotics and technological research.

The programme also features the South Africa AI Opportunity gathering, under the theme Building the African AI Economy: Infrastructure, Investment and Innovation, which brings together South African and international stakeholders to explore how South Africa can position itself as a competitive AI hub on the African continent. Discussions there focus on AI infrastructure, data centres, computing capacity, energy requirements, investment opportunities and the growth of a competitive start-up ecosystem, while other areas of engagement include the application of AI in government and industry, law enforcement and public safety, AI safety and security, governance, skills development and the future of work. The delegation also engages with technology and infrastructure companies to gain insights into emerging technologies, investment trends and developments shaping the global AI ecosystem, and these interactions seek to identify opportunities for investment, knowledge exchange, skills development and the strengthening of South Africa's technological capabilities. The Presidency says AI presents significant opportunities to improve productivity, strengthen public service delivery, stimulate economic growth and support the creation of new industries and employment opportunities, with potential applications in South Africa including health, education, criminal justice, public administration and public procurement.

The visit provides an opportunity to learn from countries and institutions at the forefront of AI development, understand the associated risks and challenges, and consider how South Africa can develop an enabling policy, regulatory and skills environment to support responsible AI adoption. It also promotes South Africa as an investment destination, showcases progress in economic reforms, including through Operation Vulindlela, and highlights opportunities for investment in the country's digital economy, research capacity and innovation ecosystem. South Africa seeks to harness the transformative potential of AI while safeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection and responsible AI governance, ensuring that technological advancement contributes meaningfully to inclusive economic growth and development. The President is accompanied by the Ministers of Finance; International Relations and Cooperation; Science, Technology and Innovation; Trade, Industry and Competition; Communications and Digital Technologies; Electricity and Energy; Small Business Development; and the Presidency, as well as South Africa's Ambassador to the United States of America, and media enquiries are directed to Vincent Magwenya, Spokesperson to the President.

stories.Headline: Claroc finds Grok Build exposes corporate data for thousands of users
stories.Summary:
Security firm Claroc discovered that Grok Build exposed corporate data for thousands of users recently. This vulnerability was caused by default sharing settings and a flawed URL design. The platform is operated by SpaceXSI, which is the new name for xAI. The breach occurred because the system used capability based access control. This method relies on the secrecy of the URL to restrict access.

The system generates randomized subdomains ending in grok.me, such as failing chassis traders. Claroc found 37,571 online subdomains, and 35,578 of these exposed data without a login. The default sharing permission was set to anyone with the link. This design allowed passive DNS services to collect hostnames and reveal application addresses. These flaws affected 24 internal applications created by SpaceXSI and X employees.

Claroc notified SpaceX about these security findings on November 8 but received no response. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI removed links to its 24 internal apps after an inquiry. However, Claroc stated that no access restrictions were implemented for applications created by other users. The company noted that private access should be the default for all platforms. They urged companies to require security reviews for all AI generated software.

The breach affected Fortune 500 companies, defense contractors, and a Peruvian construction company. The construction firm exposed medical records for 3,784 workers on an occupational health dashboard. Tesla exposed the names, productivity, and bonuses of 22 mechanics in a performance report. A U.S. Navy contractor lost personnel rosters, and an IT firm exposed a hardware bill. A Norwegian Finnish aerospace group exposed explosives inventory and handling procedures at a U.S. facility.

Vibe coding allows non developers to build software using natural language and simple prompts. Other platforms like Lovable, Bolt, and Replit may also be vulnerable to passive DNS searches. Moltbook previously exposed 1.5 million tokens, and Cal AI exposed 3.2 million user records. Red Access found 5,000 exposed assets across Lovable, Base44, Replit, and Netlify in early May. Meta Muse suspended its sharing feature on October 20 after a similar discovery.

SpaceXSI has removed its own internal apps, which now display an app not found message. The articles leave open whether other users have secured their specific application visibility settings. It remains unclear if SpaceXSI will change the default sharing permissions for all Grok Build users. The reports do not state if the affected defense contractors or Fortune 500 firms were notified. No timeline is provided for fixing the underlying passive DNS vulnerability.

stories.Headline: UCIe Consortium releases 4.0 specification to integrate memory and improve chiplet system efficiency
stories.Summary:
The UCIe Consortium released version 4.0 of its chiplet interconnect specification on November 12, 2026. This new standard extends the role of the organization into system management and memory connectivity. The update moves the technology from connecting individual dies to coordinating complete multi-chiplet systems. It introduces the UCIe.mem protocol to bring memory into chiplet architectures. These changes address critical needs for bandwidth, power, security, and reliability.

The UCIe.mem protocol provides approximately 2.5 TB/s of bandwidth per millimeter of die edge and 93.75% data efficiency. An optional power profile reduces link consumption by 30% to 80% at 64 GT/s. An enhanced bump map increases shoreline bandwidth density by 20% and area density by 10%. The specification includes Trusted Reporting of Chiplet State and bidirectional integrity-protected management channels. Automotive features include optional error notifications and link-health monitoring for vehicle electronics.

Debendra Das Sharma, an Intel senior distinguished engineer, chairs the consortium and identifies shoreline space as a major constraint. Samsung Corporate Vice President Cheolmin Park serves as the president of the organization. The consortium develops specifications and supports interoperability but sells no processors and reports no product revenue. Sharma notes that AI models require growing memory bandwidth, particularly for inference systems retrieving model weights. The organization collects membership dues to support its ongoing technical development.

Honda R&D and Mirise Technologies expressed support for the new automotive reliability and monitoring additions. Cadence's Arif Khan expects designers to combine these standardized interfaces with specialized fabrics at different levels. Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari identifies verification across protocol boundaries as a continuing engineering challenge for designers. AI accelerator designers are affected and need measured silicon results to determine actual system-level performance. ISVs and CIOs must monitor how these configurations affect model capacity and product availability.

The consortium began in March 2022 with founding companies Intel, AMD, Arm, ASE, Google Cloud, Meta, Microsoft, Qualcomm, Samsung, and TSMC. It incorporated in August 2022 and added Alibaba and Nvidia to its board, eventually exceeding 150 members. Intel and Synopsys demonstrated the Pike Creek cross-foundry test chip in 2023 to show progress. GUC announced a UCIe PHY implementation on TSMC N3P in March 2025 with 32 Gb/s per lane. Rebellions identifies its Rebel-Quad NPU as a UCIe-Advanced implementation.

AMD expects production chiplets with native UCIe 1.1 connectivity for Versal RF-series adaptive SoCs in late 2027. The industry will look for further silicon announcements and compliance results during 2027 and 2028. It remains open whether these specifications will change AI processor economics or create a hardware inflection point. Future evidence depends on validated silicon, interoperable memory controllers, and commercial products under production workloads. The actual gains will depend on chiplet placement, process compatibility, and specific operating conditions.

stories.Headline: Meta runs JiTTests in production to catch risky code changes before merge
stories.Summary:
Meta has moved its Catching Just-in-Time Tests, known as JiTTests, from a research prototype into its production infrastructure, according to a report published on 16 November 2026. JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change, so that a failing test becomes concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. The Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026, and the method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper titled "Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta." The system runs on Meta backend code with hundreds of millions of lines, and the research paper analyzes 22,126 generated tests. The system runs overnight on spare capacity and selects the previous day's risky diffs using a mechanism similar to Meta's Diff Risk Score.

Two diff-aware workflows produce candidate tests: the dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy and treats it as a mutant of its parent, while the intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary, then lists risks and builds a mutant for each. An LLM-as-Judge ensemble scores each failing test using the test code, failure trace, diff and inferred intent, and a Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment called RubFake adds deterministic checks that flag patterns such as reflection, broken mocks and not-implemented exceptions. A human-on-the-loop step decides whether to contact an engineer based on the combined ranking, and the rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. The research team reports that diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests and 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs, while dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%, and Meta's earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%.

Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate at full scale, which is self-reported, and privacy SEV occurrence is down 20%. The initial deployment confirmed only 8 of 41 reported catches, or 19.5%. The judge models named in the paper are Llama3.3-70B, Gemini 3 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4, and the system is not publicly available. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper "Harden and Catch," and the team concedes that executing code takes more computational steps than having an LLM or agent read the diff and leave comments. The team argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss, and the bottom line the report gives is executable proof of a bug before merge, with the caveat that the numbers are internal and self-reported.

stories.Headline: A man surnamed Han admits using AI smart glasses to cheat on national accountant exams
stories.Summary:
A thirty four year old man surnamed Han admitted on Sunday that he cheated on national exams using generative artificial intelligence. He confessed on a YouTube channel that he used electronic devices to cheat during the first round of the tax accountant exam. Han also admitted to cheating on the second round of that exam and the first round of the certified public accountant exam. He turned himself in to the police after facing allegations that he used AI equipped smart glasses to commit fraud. This scandal has sent shockwaves throughout the nation and exposed a lack of safeguards against AI assisted misconduct in South Korea.

Han scored 397.5 out of 400 in the April first round exam, with perfect scores in three subjects and one missed finance question. Three months later, he scored 663 out of 800 in the second stage written examination and was named the overall top scorer. The Ministry of Finance and Economy moved to suspend his certification, while the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency Public Crime Investigation Unit investigates. Policy Chief Ha Joon Kyung chaired a meeting on November 15, four days before the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test. Two proctors were assigned to the classroom where Han took the test, but they did not detect his fraudulent behavior.

Prime Minister Han Seong sook called for comprehensive measures to protect the fairness and credibility of state examinations during a Monday meeting. She stated that those who worked hard to prepare for exams should not be disadvantaged by the cheating of other candidates. The Prime Minister added that such misconduct should not undermine public trust in competitive examinations and required measures before and after tests. Presidential chief of staff Lim Kwang hyun told reporters on Sunday that the government was working to find solutions for the crisis. A presidential official stated that the office is taking the matter very seriously because the college entrance exam takes place next week.

Kim Yong jae, the 2018 top scorer, said that earning a perfect score in even one subject is virtually impossible for candidates. He noted that candidates have only 80 minutes to answer 80 accounting questions, suggesting the top scorer was either a genius or cheater. The Financial Services Commission came under fire for failing to detect the cheating, while the public expressed growing concerns over exam integrity. Other national certification examinations were held before the tax accountant exam, raising questions about whether cheating occurred in those other tests. The scandal affects the credibility of state administered exams and the trust of students who prepare honestly for these competitive tests.

The articles state that the nation has focused too much on competing for AI leadership and too little on necessary institutional safeguards. There was a widespread belief that AI is inherently beneficial, creating a gap between technological ambition and the actual institutional preparedness. The editorial argues that after the fact responses are insufficient and that the nation is unprepared for the age of artificial intelligence. Proctors lacked the tools and technology needed to identify AI assisted cheating, making it impossible for them to notice the misconduct. The government has belatedly scrambled to introduce measures in response to the scandal as the college entrance exam approached on Thursday.

Officials are now discussing preemptive detection measures and advanced technologies capable of thwarting AI assisted misconduct before the nationwide college entrance exam. The Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education held a training session on November 11 regarding a smart glasses cheating prevention guide in Yongsan gu. The government is working to find solutions to ensure that no more AI assisted cheating occurs during the upcoming scholastic ability test. It remains questionable whether the nation is prepared to build the necessary infrastructure to detect such high tech fraud in the future. The articles leave open whether other national certification exams were compromised by similar AI tools before the confession of the man.

stories.Summary:

Eason Zhang previously served as a strategic consulting partner at a global firm. He founded a fintech enterprise after leaving that consulting role in 2015. The startup combines Silicon Valley AI technology with Hong Kong financial business resources. CTO Steve brings experience from Silicon Valley entrepreneurship to the technical architecture. A chief scientist from a Silicon Valley laboratory serves as an expert consultant.

stories.Headline: FAA officials say the new SMART AI system did not cause the airline ground stop
stories.Summary:
The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA's new $875 million AI-powered system, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there's no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system. The top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday. The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn't caused by the SMART system, any product of ASI or its integration with FAA and ATC. The timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. That office sends recommendations to the FAA's command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration. SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams, including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics, into one platform. SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers, three days before the ground stop.

The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system's recommendations. According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals. SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.

Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as large, rectangular boxes, according to the fact sheet, which doesn't reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through. To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time, allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas. No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools. SMART, however, is not, at least not yet, set up for AI to be in charge of flight control, rather it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails. The Oct. 13 letter said the nation's front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART's development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process. The letter said the use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information. Mike O'Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that's doing the work. O'Donnell said the FAA cannot afford to be wrong on this.

O'Donnell said it's good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they're not giving wrong information to controllers based on what AI has come up with. He said there's got to be a way to verify and validate what it's doing to make sure that it's not the wrong information. He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI until we know for sure that it's proven itself time and time again, and that's going to take a while. The AI system's launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country, and the National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees, and in an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the AI does the math and the computation, but the human operator makes the decision and is the decider and the judge.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prepares a $60 billion IPO this Thursday despite AI market fears
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is preparing to launch a massive initial public offering this Thursday despite significant instability within the artificial intelligence sector. The company that created the Claude chatbot intends to sell stock to the public during a period of rising financing costs and market volatility. This blockbuster financial move could potentially raise more than 60 billion dollars, which would rival the June offering from SpaceX. The company is pressing ahead with the sale even as investors worry about a possible bubble and political shifts.

The offering comes as Anthropic faces substantial financial pressure, including 6.2 billion dollars in existing debt and a lack of profitability. The company has committed to spending 900 billion dollars on computing and infrastructure in the coming years, with 70 billion dollars due in the next twelve months. Nvidia has agreed to purchase approximately 10 billion dollars of stock following the IPO, although the chip designer recently saw its own stock drop 4 percent. This volatility follows the sudden departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a 15.5 percent plunge for CoreWeave on October 14.

Company officials acknowledged in financial filings that their current debt levels are substantial, yet they are moving forward to secure capital. They are likely betting that selling shares now is better than waiting for newly elected Democrats to take office in January. These politicians have vowed to crack down on the industry and may support a national moratorium on new data centers. Additionally, new Democratic governors in Texas and Georgia have promised to stop the construction of new data center facilities.

The timing is critical because demand for public offerings can vanish quickly, as seen when U.S. debuts dropped from nearly 400 in 2021 to only 71 the following year. Anthropic may also be seeking a competitive advantage by beating its rival, OpenAI, to the public market. Current market measures suggest shares are trading at 40 times their long term earnings, which is higher than levels seen before the 2008 financial crisis. This high valuation could allow the company to fetch top prices for its shares this week.

stories.Headline: Artist Olivia Tai collects confessions about using AI to write personal messages
stories.Summary:
Olivia Tai, an artist who has repeated a project called the Confession box more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, set up a purple box on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square that held dozens of secrets written by passersby. A sign on the box read “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret,” and among the confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages. The confessions included “I had AI write my breakup text,” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text,” and “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”

Tai said calling the project a confession suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty, but they used it anyway. The question the project raises is whether using a chatbot for personal messages crosses a line, and whether it is ever acceptable to use AI to write a holiday card, a birthday message, a love letter or wedding vows. Danielle Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia who conducted vignette-based experiments as part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who had not. Hass said everyone felt guilty and that the driver of this relationship was dishonesty, with people feeling like they were manipulating others.

Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK, said his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy, even when they are honest about their AI use. Claessens noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes, but something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off. He said what people really want in social relationships is for others to put effort in, because it shows as a signal that you are invested in the relationship. Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it is appropriate and when it is not.

Newman suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide, asking whether you would be comfortable telling your partner you used AI to write your wedding vows, and said personal messages do not need to be perfect because part of what makes them authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect. Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who does not share a native language, or people with learning disabilities such as dyslexia who could use it for help. Hass said she believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she is glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages. Hass said guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings and to show us where we are supposed to be human.

stories.Headline: Fluke study finds 78 percent of data center operators hit electrical disruption in past year
stories.Summary:
Fluke Corporation published a study on November 17, 2026, finding that 78 percent of data center operators experienced electrical or power-system issues contributing to disruption, delays, downtime or serious near-misses in the past year. The study was announced from Everett, Washington, and distributed by GlobeNewswire. Fluke said the global race to build and expand AI data centers could face a major setback. The research raised questions about whether the infrastructure behind the AI boom can deliver on the industry's ambitious growth plans. Operators are racing to secure additional grid capacity while weaknesses inside data centers threaten to delay new AI workloads and disrupt existing operations.

Only 33 percent of operators say their electrical infrastructure is fully ready for higher-density AI workloads. 34 percent say electrical skills shortages have delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity. 29 percent say power-quality issues have reduced their ability to deploy or operate AI/GPU workloads. 29 percent report that electrical problems are only identified after performance or equipment failure, or downtime, has occurred. Fewer than half of operators, 45 percent, report real-time visibility across critical electrical systems.

Parker Burke, President of Fluke Corporation, said the industry has spent years asking where the power will come from. He said the findings show the focus should also be on how effectively data centers can use the power they already have. He said the electrical infrastructure inside data centers is becoming a critical bottleneck as AI drives unprecedented demand for computing capacity. He said that without addressing this last-mile challenge, the industry risks having the power to expand but not the infrastructure to deliver. Burke also said grid constraints are largely outside an operator's control, while what is within their control is how effectively they monitor, maintain and manage the electrical infrastructure they already have.

Six in ten operators, 60 percent, say recruiting qualified electrical technicians has become more difficult. Three-quarters of operators, 76 percent, say access to sufficient power and grid capacity is moderately or severely limiting their ability to expand. Operators report an average 12-month wait to secure additional grid connection or power capacity for AI and GPU-related expansion. The study was commissioned by Fluke on behalf of Censuswide and surveyed 1,300 data-center industry operators and professionals across six countries: the US, UK, Germany, France, India and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Censuswide is an international market research consultancy headquartered in London, with offices in New York, Dubai, Bristol and Glasgow.

Fluke Corporation was founded in 1948 and describes itself as the world leader in compact, professional electronic test tools and software for measuring and condition monitoring. Fluke customers are technicians, engineers, electricians, maintenance managers and metrologists who install, troubleshoot and maintain industrial, electrical and electronic equipment and calibration processes. The study examined the power, infrastructure and workforce challenges facing the industry as AI demand accelerates. The findings suggest the challenge is no longer simply securing power from the grid but ensuring data centers have the infrastructure and expertise to turn that power into reliable computing capacity. Burke said greater visibility into electrical systems and a proactive approach to maintenance will be increasingly important as operators look to maximize existing capacity, reduce disruption and support growing AI demand.

Fluke said data center operators can improve electrical reliability through regular electrical testing, power-quality monitoring, thermal inspections and preventive maintenance. Fluke said poor power quality can cause equipment malfunctions, overheating, unexpected shutdowns and downtime, and that voltage fluctuations, harmonics and electrical disturbances can affect the reliability of critical data center systems. Fluke said operators can help reduce the impact of electrical skills shortages by investing in technician training, standardized testing procedures and diagnostic tools that make electrical troubleshooting more efficient. Fluke said it provides electrical testing and measurement tools, power-quality analyzers, thermal imaging cameras and condition-monitoring solutions for data center environments. The articles leave open which specific operators or countries accounted for the reported issues and near-misses.

stories.Headline: Complaint filed against education minister for dereliction of duty over AI cheating
stories.Summary:
Lee Jong-bae, a former Seoul city council member from the People Power Party, filed a complaint against Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The complaint was submitted to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency following remarks Choi made during a National Assembly education committee session on Monday. Choi stated that it would be difficult for authorities to detect every instance of cheating involving artificial intelligence. This legal action occurred just before the College Scholastic Ability Test, also known as Suneung, which was scheduled for that Thursday.

The complaint alleges that the minister committed dereliction of duty by failing to implement effective countermeasures against AI-assisted cheating. Lee Jong-bae argued that the government could have prevented such misconduct by installing radio detectors in test rooms or postponing the Suneung. These demands come after several high-profile cheating incidents, including a case where the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam used a miniature camera. Public anxiety has increased due to these events and other reports of AI glasses being used in schools.

Lee Jong-bae claimed that Minister Choi consciously abandoned his official duties despite knowing the limitations of the current monitoring system. He urged the police to conduct a thorough investigation and strictly punish the minister for his perceived negligence. The former councilor believes the government possesses the necessary tools to stop AI cheating but has failed to use them. He maintains that the minister's admission of difficulty in catching cheaters proves a lack of adequate preparation.

The situation reflects a broader national scramble to crack down on AI-assisted cheating before the annual college entrance exams. Other recent reports indicate that students in middle and high schools have been caught using AI glasses this year. The government has vowed to maintain zero tolerance against such academic dishonesty to protect the integrity of national tests. Police are currently investigating the tax accountant exam case after the top scorer turned himself in and apologized.

stories.Headline: AI analysis of one echocardiogram clip plus H2FPEF score identifies 78% of hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF cases
stories.Summary:
Researchers applied an artificial intelligence model called EchoGo HF to resting echocardiograms from 280 outpatients who had been referred for suspected heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and each patient also underwent exercise hemodynamic testing as the diagnostic gold standard, according to research published in the November 2026 issue of the Journal of Cardiac Failure. Adding the AI analysis of a single routine echocardiogram clip to the H₂FPEF clinical score identified 78% of patients with hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF, compared with 48% using the score alone. The AI model added the most value for patients with low or intermediate H₂FPEF scores, the group where diagnosis is hardest, so the authors tested a two-step strategy of calculating H₂FPEF first and then applying AI only when the score is inconclusive. An AI-detected HFpEF result also independently predicted elevated filling pressures and reduced exercise capacity, which suggests the model reflects disease severity as well as diagnosis.

The November issue, focused on artificial intelligence in heart failure, also includes a study in which investigators used clinical notes from 599 patients seen in cardiology clinics to optimize a large language model, OpenAI's o1, that classified the documented reason for non-prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors with 84.7% accuracy. Physician-attributed factors were the most common theme at 28.7% of notes, and the leading specific reasons were deferring the decision to a future visit at 15.4% and the physician judging the patient low-risk or unlikely to benefit at 7.4%. A review in the same issue maps current AI applications across the heart failure care continuum, including AI-enabled ECG and imaging for opportunistic detection of low ejection fraction, HFpEF and structural heart disease, risk stratification based on electronic health records, clinician decision support, remote medication titration and wearable monitoring. The review's authors conclude that the strongest evidence favors AI built into active clinical workflows that guide targeted testing, treatment optimization and follow-up, rather than AI used only to send passive alerts.

In their Editor's Page, guest editors Jonathan W. Cunningham of Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School, Elena Donald and Nir Uriel of Columbia University Irving Medical Center, and Ankeet S. Bhatt of Kaiser Permanente San Francisco Medical Center wrote that heart failure's population burden is growing and outcomes are worsening while the number of heart failure physicians is flat and training spots go unfilled, and that AI could help close that gap. They wrote that promise alone is insufficient and that AI, like any innovation intended to change clinical care, must be rigorously studied to understand where it adds value, where it does not and how it can be implemented safely and effectively. The editors called on the heart failure community to move past retrospective and in silico demonstrations of model performance and instead want prospective studies, including randomized trials where feasible, that test whether AI tools improve clinical decisions, treatment delivery, outcomes, equity and clinician workload. They wrote that AI researchers will continue to advance these tools but that clinicians and patients must lead their translation into care, and the complete November 2026 issue is available online now.

stories.Headline: Africa Tech Festival opens in Cape Town to advance AI development across the continent
stories.Summary:
The Africa Tech Festival 2026 officially opened on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, in Cape Town, South Africa, to advance digital transformation. This event focuses on positioning the African continent to seize various opportunities that arise in the current age of artificial intelligence. Organizers brought together leaders from the technology and telecommunications industries, along with investors, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and innovators, to explore emerging technologies. These participants gathered to foster new partnerships and advance digital development across the continent during this influential and large technology event. The festival aims to help Africa move from being a consumer of foreign solutions to a developer of its own technologies.

The 29th edition of the festival runs through Thursday at the Cape Town International Convention Centre under the theme Powering Africa's Digital Transformation. More than 13,500 attendees and 2,000 companies from over 130 countries joined more than 450 speakers and 350 exhibitors at the venue. Six content pillars guide the event, including Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Startups, Digital Transformation, and Telecoms and Connectivity, for all participants. The schedule includes keynote speeches, panel discussions, technical masterclasses, investment forums, roundtables, networking opportunities, and specialist industry sessions for the attending guests. An exhibition also features various startups and providers of AI solutions from across the telecommunications and technology sectors for the attendees.

South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile delivered a virtual opening address where he urged African countries to shape the global AI landscape. He stated that the continent must become an exporter of emerging technologies instead of remaining a consumer of solutions developed elsewhere. Mashatile argued that digital transformation is fundamentally about human development and must be inclusive and people-centered to ensure a prosperous future. He called for active participation in developing and governing these technologies to ensure they advance the developmental goals of the continent. The Deputy President also urged African countries to build their own capabilities by drawing on local talent to solve regional challenges.

Mashatile warned that millions of people could be left behind due to infrastructure gaps, skills shortages, and high connectivity costs. He noted that inadequate broadband access remains a significant barrier that must be addressed to make digital transformation truly inclusive for all. The Deputy President highlighted the African Continental Free Trade Area as a key opportunity to establish a single digital market across Africa. He argued that closer regional integration would help drive inclusive growth, investment, and innovation through harmonized regulations and stronger cross-border collaboration. To realize this, he said the continent must enable interoperable payment systems and trusted data flows between the different African nations.

The articles describe the Africa Tech Festival as one of the largest and most influential technology events currently held on the continent. This event covers key areas ranging from entrepreneurship and digital infrastructure to the growth of the broader African digital economy. Mashatile outlined five priorities, including investing in human capital, building future-ready infrastructure, and strengthening the innovation ecosystems found across the continent. He also emphasized the need for responsible digital governance and cybersecurity to build trust while deepening regional integration and continental cooperation. These priorities are intended to translate the digital potential of the continent into broad-based prosperity for all of its people.

The festival will continue through Thursday with various sessions designed to turn high-level discussions into tangible progress for the African people. Mashatile called for bold investment, decisive action, and stronger partnerships to build a more connected, competitive, and inclusive future for generations. He believes Africa will compete in the age of AI by creating solutions with global relevance rather than through simple imitation. The articles leave open how specific countries will implement these five priorities or how the single digital market will be established. They do not state which specific companies are exhibiting or provide the exact outcomes of the various investment forums and roundtables.

stories.Headline: Marsh's Schnur links AI tools to a doubling of client cyber incidents
stories.Summary:
Marsh reported that its clients filed 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October, which is more than double the 48 incidents recorded in the final two weeks of May, according to data the insurance broker released and Reuters reported on November 17, 2026. Meredith Schnur, who leads the US and Canada cyber practice at Marsh Risk, told Reuters in an interview this week that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities, and she said AI could be attributed to a significant number of the incidents. She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, combined with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors driving the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. Schnur said AI is not a peril but an amplification of risk in all areas, and she said the technology lets attackers find and exploit longstanding vulnerabilities such as unpatched software, exposed systems and weak identity controls at a much faster pace. The rise in reported incidents requires businesses and their insurers to contend with attacks that spread faster and reach more targets, because AI tools that are becoming more widely accessible let attackers scale their operations with fewer resources.

GlobalData expects global cyber insurance premiums to rise 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026, before growth accelerates to 10% in 2027 to reach $18.3 billion, as businesses respond to rising attack frequency. The Marsh figures compare the final two weeks of October with the final two weeks of May, and the 105 incidents more than double the 48 recorded in the earlier period. The report ties the increase to AI adoption and to slower containment and response times, and it says the wider availability of AI tools is widening the pool of potential targets and putting pressure on businesses. Schnur, the US and Canada cyber practice leader at Marsh Risk, is the person the articles identify as explaining the data, and she attributed a significant share of the incidents to AI in her interview with Reuters this week. She said the signs that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities are happening, and she described AI as an amplification of risk in all areas rather than a peril in itself.

She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, together with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors behind the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. The reporting was by Noor Zainab Hussain and Manya Saini in Bengaluru, with editing by Shilpi Majumdar, and the story was published by Reuters and carried by Insurance Journal. The context the articles give is a cyber insurance market that GlobalData expects to grow faster over the next two years as businesses respond to rising attack frequency, with premiums reaching $16.6 billion in 2026 and $18.3 billion in 2027. The articles do not say what Marsh or insurers will change in response to the data, and they do not describe any new policy terms or claims figures beyond the incident counts and the premium forecasts. What happens next, according to the articles, is continued growth in cyber insurance premiums at a faster pace over the next two years, driven by the rising frequency of attacks that the Marsh data shows.

stories.Headline: Tencent releases Hy4 flash to provide cost efficient AI for professional workflows
stories.Summary:
Tencent announced the release of Hy4 flash on November 17, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, to power high speed and cost efficient AI deployment. This new model is the latest addition to the Hy model family and is designed to support everyday professional productivity workflows. The company developed this tool to provide a stronger balance of intelligence and efficiency for real world tasks for its users. It aims to deliver exceptional cost performance while maintaining strong intelligence and practical utility across various types of professional digital work. The release follows the launch of Hy4, which joined the ranks of leading open source AI models on November 4.

Hy4 flash has 224 billion total parameters, including 64 billion Engram parameters, with only 12 billion active parameters and 1M token context length. It costs US$0.070 per million input tokens, US$0.281 per million output tokens, and US$0.003 per million cached input tokens for its users. The model is available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom, QQ, ima, and Marvis, with OpenRouter integration coming very soon. From now until November 30, users can access the model for free on WorkBuddy or get 50 percent off via TokenHub. It uses hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram features, with a KV cache size 1/24 of Hy3 and 1/6 that of Hy4.

The Tencent Hy team made specific engineering choices across the pipeline to achieve this level of cost performance and strong practical utility. They used megakernel, 4-bit quantization, and DFly techniques to reach decoding speeds that exceed 150 tokens per second for low cost deployment. The team built an internal benchmark called WorkIndex based on typical WorkBuddy tasks to focus on deliverable quality and task turnaround time. They stated that reinforcement learning was used to cut the average end to end task output tokens by 50 percent for efficiency. The team recommends Hy4 flash for everyday tasks like deep research, document processing, PowerPoint generation, simple front end displays, and computer use.

Internal WorkBuddy users participated in a blind evaluation of 259 tasks in 27 categories to test the effectiveness of the new model. These 85 users reported satisfaction levels close to Claude Haiku 5.5, while noting the shortest task completion time among all models. The model slightly outperforms Hy4 Preview, which has 770 billion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, in overall effectiveness for users. Per task costs are 1/13 of Hy4 Preview, 1/20 of Hy4, and 1/8 of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max tier peak hour pricing for tasks. Users are directed to the more capable Hy4 for complex tasks such as long horizon software engineering to ensure the best results.

Tencent was founded in Shenzhen, China, in 1998 and has been listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong since the year 2004. The company is a world leading internet and technology firm that develops innovative products to improve the quality of life for people. Its communication and social services connect more than one billion people globally to help them stay in touch and access transportation. The business also covers financial technology, including payment, credit, wealth management, and insurance sectors, to support partners and their digital upgrades. Additionally, the company publishes some of the most popular video games and high quality digital content to enrich interactive entertainment experiences globally.

Tencent Hy plans to open source Hy4 flash with frequent iterations to continuously improve its practical utility and efficiency for real world work. The company will continue to push the boundaries of intelligence while delivering exceptional cost performance for its various professional AI tools. Hy4 previously ranked second among Chinese models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and first among open source models on Agent Arena. The articles do not state the specific date when the open source version of Hy4 flash will be released to the public. They also leave open the specific details regarding the upcoming integration with OpenRouter and any future pricing changes after November 30.

stories.Headline: Family physician Mara Gordon uses an AI scribe on her phone to draft notes but reviews and signs each one
stories.Summary:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., wrote in a piece published November 17, 2026, that a reader asked whether to worry about an artificial intelligence scribe recording private medical conversations. The reader said her doctor had started recording office visits with an AI scribe and that she said yes when asked if she was comfortable. The reader said that in hindsight she felt a little freaked out. Gordon wrote that AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Gordon wrote that doctors use them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

Gordon wrote that she first asks the patient if they are comfortable using the service. Gordon wrote that if the patient says yes, she starts recording using an app on her smartphone, usually set down on the desk in the exam room. Gordon wrote that the scribe uses "automatic speech recognition," which records the conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. Gordon wrote that sometimes, when a family member accompanies the patient, the app needs to distinguish between three or more voices. Gordon wrote that when the visit ends, the recording is transcribed and a large language model geared toward medicine converts the raw transcript into a medical note.

Gordon wrote that the notes follow a standard format specific to the specialty and the type of visit. Gordon wrote that the notes reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making. Gordon wrote that she is ultimately responsible for the content of the AI-generated note and always reads them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them. Gordon wrote that when the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, she almost always ends up editing them to make her clinical decision-making more clear.

Gordon wrote that she talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego who specializes in clinical informatics. Gordon quoted Kim saying that an overburdened doctor seeing too many patients has an AI tool offered that seems like a great solution but no time to adequately review everything. Gordon quoted Kim saying the note goes into the chart and another AI tool reading the notes propagates errors throughout the chart. Gordon wrote that she comes across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time and that it is hard to know how much is related to AI and how much to human error. Gordon wrote that many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients, and that health equity advocates fear this means unequal access that could further widen health disparities.

Gordon wrote that she has been an eager adopter in her own primary care practice. Gordon wrote that she uses an app on her phone that records her conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record. Gordon wrote that it saves her time and helps her focus more fully on her patient, so she can make eye contact rather than stare at the computer screen. Gordon wrote that she shares her patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship. Gordon wrote that she worries corporate health systems will pressure doctors to use time saved with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients, and that artificial intelligence might one day put her out of a job.

Gordon wrote that there are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Gordon wrote that most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, though some use a desktop computer or a separate recording device. Gordon wrote that she uses her personal smartphone, as do many physicians she knows, and that she once got notification pings from her book club's group chat while recording a patient visit, which made her put the phone in "do not disturb" mode. Gordon wrote that conversations are not stored on her device but uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note, and that most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time. Gordon wrote that HIPAA means the program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy, and that the software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step, encrypting it, controlling access, protecting against data breaches, and being liable if data is leaked.

Gordon wrote that she recently saw a patient with metastatic cancer who did not believe he had cancer despite multiple conversations with her, his oncologist, and his surgeon, and that she had even, with his permission, called his spouse. Gordon wrote that the AI scribe did not get this tricky situation right and that the note simply said the patient had been misdiagnosed rather than reflecting the nuances of the conversation. Gordon wrote that she often catches other errors, like mistaking a patient's gender or age, and that the scribes are known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not," where the difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe companies delete recorded conversations within a set period of time as a security feature, to protect patient privacy and protect doctors from lawsuits, and that there is widespread concern the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits. Gordon wrote that some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could assess the quality of AI-generated notes or study physician-patient communication, and that for now recordings of regular appointments, unless a patient is enrolled in a research study, are not used for research.

Gordon wrote that most of her patients readily agree to the AI scribe, but occasionally patients worry the data isn't really secure or could be used to identify them in the future. Gordon wrote that if a patient doesn't want the AI scribe, she just takes notes on the computer while they talk, as she did for years before the scribes became available. Gordon quoted Kim saying AI is "just everywhere" and it would be impossible to separate it, and that software relying on machine learning is used for billing, clinical decision-making, and communication between the doctor's office and patients. Gordon wrote that AI is often used in risk calculators, like tools that estimate a patient's risk of heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure, and in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis based on vital signs and lab values. Gordon quoted Kim saying it is basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you."

Gordon wrote that she asked Kim, a primary care doctor like her, whether AI would replace them in the coming years, and whether an AI scribe that could ask the same questions she does could generate a treatment plan as good or better than the one she recommends. Gordon wrote that Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care, possibly for the better if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer. Gordon wrote that the article ends there, leaving Kim's ultimate answer about replacement unstated. Gordon wrote that readers can send health questions to thrive@npr.org. Gordon wrote that she is happy to have robots help with her administrative tasks but still takes pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence.

stories.Headline: ROBOTERA deploys humanoid robots across China Post network in Guangdong to tackle labor shortages
stories.Summary:
Beijing Xingdongjiyuan Technology Co., Ltd., known as ROBOTERA, deployed humanoid robots across the China Post Group Guangdong Branch network on November 17, 2026. This initiative represents the most geographically extensive use of embodied intelligence robots within the logistics sector to date. The rollout covers 11 postal hubs located in eight different cities across Guangdong Province. These specific locations include Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Dongguan, Jiangmen, Shantou, Shanwei, Jieyang, and Heyuan.

The project requires the integration of robots into high-volume sorting and cross-regional logistics coordination tasks. These humanoid systems utilize a self-developed five-finger dexterous hand for flexible handling and offer multiple power options for continuous operation. Since a pilot began at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026, the robots have induced more than 1,500 parcels per hour. This technology allows human employees to shift their focus toward quality control, operations coordination, and robot maintenance.

ROBOTERA and the China Post Group Guangdong Branch are jointly responsible for implementing this large-scale industrial productivity project. The company stated that its AI-native, full-stack technology approach helps translate embodied intelligence into new industrial productivity. They explained that the robots fill capacity gaps by performing strenuous frontline tasks during peak shopping seasons. This strategy addresses persistent labor shortages and high workforce turnover in the labor-intensive logistics sorting industry.

Guangdong serves as a demanding environment for validating robotics because it is the largest province in China by express parcel volume. The integrated solution has already been adapted for various parcel types and sorting configurations in East China. These systems include adaptive speed control and irregular-item rejection to prevent collisions and jams. ROBOTERA intends to continue working with industry partners to bring embodied intelligence into more real-world workflows.
