stories.Headline: Diligent Institute finds only 15% of APAC boards very confident in overseeing major risks
stories.Summary:
Diligent Institute published its APAC Governance Outlook 2027 report on 18 November 2026, based on an online survey run during August and September of board members, C-suite leaders, general counsel, company secretaries and other governance leaders across Asia-Pacific, with Australian-headquartered organisations making up 63% of respondents. The report found that cybersecurity, data protection and privacy were the leading strategic priority for 69% of respondents, with AI deployment next at 54% and operational cost optimisation at 52%. Despite that focus, only 15% said they were very confident their board had the information, expertise and processes needed to oversee significant risks, and the most commonly cited barriers were insufficient time at 26% and a lack of relevant expertise at 17%. Respondents also described a broader risk backdrop, with 55% expecting economic downturns to disrupt their organisations over the next 12 months, 53% naming geopolitical events as a major threat and 48% identifying cyber and data privacy incidents as a likely source of disruption.

On AI, 29% of respondents said adoption was outpacing governance, 25% said governance was keeping pace and 8% said governance was ahead of adoption, while a quarter said they used approved AI tools for governance workflows, 17% reported informal use of general-purpose or consumer tools and another 25% had no foreseeable plans to use AI in those settings. Asked about the main opportunities from AI, 78% pointed to improved data analysis and reporting and 58% named workflow automation, while 66% cited security and privacy as their leading AI concern and half named hallucinations, misinformation or disinformation. Digital technology, including AI and data management, was the most frequently cited board skills gap at 62%, more than double the 29% who named cybersecurity, and 65% said more time for strategic planning or dedicated planning meetings would improve the boardroom while 26% said their board lacked time to discuss emerging risks. Nearly half called for more formal development, with 49% selecting mandatory director training or continuing education and 48% wanting greater access to outside parties or experts on specific issues and risks.

Dottie Schindlinger, executive director of Diligent Institute, said effective oversight is not about adding every emerging issue to an already full agenda but about understanding how risks intersect, identifying what matters most to the organisation's strategy and decisions, and ensuring management is taking action. She said boards can start by asking for clear, integrated reporting that connects emerging risks to business priorities, dedicating time to challenging assumptions, and gaining a clear understanding of where and how AI is being deployed, including in their own governance processes. The articles say the findings come as boards in Australia face regulatory scrutiny over operational resilience, cyber governance and executive accountability, and that the concentration of Australian respondents gives the results particular relevance for local boards as organisations deal with cyber threats, data governance questions and pressure to demonstrate clearer oversight of AI use. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's findings and recommendations.

stories.Headline: South Korea's military screens smart glasses at entrances to block covert recording on bases
stories.Summary:
Military authorities in South Korea stepped up screening of wearable devices on Tuesday to prevent unauthorized equipment from entering military facilities. These officials targeted smart glasses capable of filming or recording to ensure that no such devices are brought onto bases. The Ministry of National Defense issued these instructions to all military units across the armed services during the previous month. These new security measures officially took effect on November 1 to block devices that can perform covert recording tasks. The military is now focusing on these wearables to maintain security across all of its various military installations.

All eyeglasses must now pass through an X-ray scanner if one is available at the specific military unit entrance. Guards on duty at units without scanning equipment must physically inspect the glasses to ensure they are not smart wearables. These guards will specifically inspect the arms and frames of the glasses for charging ports or hidden miniature cameras. Suspicious glasses must be handed over to guards to verify the model, serial number, and specific charging specifications. Guards will also check these suspicious devices for any speakers or control buttons to confirm if they are unauthorized devices.

A ministry official stated that they ordered all units across the armed services to increase inspections for visitors and personnel. This official noted that the military will tighten disciplinary standards by weighing factors like whether the device use was intentional. The ministry plans to revise internal directives soon to impose stiffer disciplinary measures on those bringing unauthorized smart devices. Officials said these steps are necessary to prevent the unauthorized use of recording devices within the secure military facilities. The ministry is coordinating these efforts across all branches of the armed services to ensure a consistent security standard.

The tougher rules follow growing scrutiny in South Korea over several cheating cases that involved the use of artificial intelligence devices. A top scorer on the tax accountant exam fueled this concern by confessing to using generative AI to cheat. This individual admitted to using a smartphone and a miniature camera to gain an unfair advantage during the professional test. These cheating scandals have affected the general public's trust and prompted a wider crackdown on AI devices across the country. Other government sectors are also scrambling to stop AI cheating ahead of the national college entrance exam for students.

The background of this military action is rooted in the rise of AI assisted cheating using miniature cameras and smartphones. South Korea is currently facing a series of high profile cases where generative AI was used to cheat on exams. This environment of scrutiny has led the government to consider disabling Wi-Fi at certain test sites to prevent cheating. The military is reacting to these societal trends to ensure that similar technology is not used for unauthorized recording. These measures reflect a broader national effort to root out the misuse of artificial intelligence in various professional settings.

No violations involving smart glasses have been reported from any military units since the tougher rules took effect this month. The military will continue to monitor the situation as they implement the revised internal directives for stiffer disciplinary actions. The articles do not state when the revised directives will be finalized or exactly how much stiffer the penalties will be. It remains open whether other types of wearable technology beyond smart glasses will face similar levels of strict security screening. The reports do not specify if these screening measures will be permanent or if they are temporary emergency responses.

stories.Headline: Upstage and Cohere partner to build sovereign AI solutions for enterprises
stories.Summary:
The South Korean artificial intelligence startup Upstage announced a strategic collaboration with the Canadian firm Cohere on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. These two companies signed a partnership agreement on November 16, 2026, at the Seoul office of Upstage to develop sovereign AI solutions. This joint effort aims to help both organizations expand their presence within the global enterprise AI market. They intend to provide specialized services for businesses and institutions that must follow strict regulatory requirements.

The partnership requires the integration of the Solar Pro and Solar Mini large language models from Upstage with the North enterprise AI agent platform from Cohere. Upstage will also include its Document Parse processing platform to enhance the combined technical capabilities of the new solution. These services will be available through cloud-based virtual private clouds or via systems installed locally for maximum security. This approach allows organizations to maintain complete control over their own data while utilizing advanced AI tools.

Upstage CEO Kim Sung-hoon, Cohere co-founder and CEO Aidan Gomez, and Cohere Asia-Pacific President Chang Hwa-jin are the leaders responsible for this agreement. While the articles do not provide direct quotes, the executives indicated that the collaboration focuses on security-focused enterprise clients. They expressed a shared goal of providing sovereign AI solutions that prioritize data privacy and institutional security. The leadership team believes this integration will better serve the needs of high-security corporate environments.

The companies plan to move beyond the South Korean market to expand their partnership across the broader Asia-Pacific region. This expansion will focus on delivering enterprise AI solutions that allow various organizations to keep their sensitive data secure. By targeting this region, the firms hope to establish a strong foothold in the growing demand for sovereign AI. They will continue to develop tools that balance high-performance artificial intelligence with strict data sovereignty.

stories.Headline: IBM study finds only 18% of chief AI officers control AI investment decisions
stories.Summary:
The IBM Institute for Business Value published a study on November 17, 2026, dated from Armonk, New York, finding that only 18% of surveyed Chief AI Officers have full control over AI investment decisions. The global study surveyed more than 1,600 Chief AI Officers and equivalent enterprise AI leaders. It was conducted in cooperation with Oxford Economics, which surveyed 1,667 senior executives responsible for enterprise AI strategy, governance, implementation, and value realization. Those surveyed included Chief AI Officers, Chief Data and AI Officers, Heads of AI, and equivalent AI leaders, whom the study refers to collectively as CAIOs. The survey ran from April to June 2026 across 33 geographies and 20 industries.

Just 29% of respondents say their organizations adjust decisions and resources quickly when AI performance insights identify opportunities to improve outcomes. Fewer than one-third of surveyed CAIOs say AI is reshaping the business model, including what the organization sells, how it prices, or how it captures value. While only 32% say AI is reshaping the business model, 35% say it primarily strengthens the existing model, and 26% expect it to reshape the model but have not made the necessary shifts. 48% of CAIOs say AI agents initiate and execute actions across workflows, yet 75% say governance, risk or compliance delays AI-driven action. While 73% of respondents have defined where human oversight is non-negotiable, only 61% say AI decision rights are clearly defined and consistently applied.

Joanne Wright, Senior Vice President, Transformation and Operations at IBM, writes in the study's foreword that few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise. She writes that the outcomes Chief AI Officers are accountable for often depend on decisions made by others. She says successful AI leadership requires more than technical expertise or operational oversight. She says it requires gathering evidence, influencing decisions, and measuring success. The study identifies a group of high-impact CAIOs whose organizations report stronger results.

High-impact CAIOs report that 63% of AI projects deliver measurable business outcomes, compared with 43% for all other CAIOs, and that 49% move from pilot to production, versus 33%. They scale successful initiatives enterprise-wide in eight months, compared with 13.5 months among all other CAIOs. High-impact CAIOs are nearly four times as likely to say they can quickly pause, adjust or redirect AI systems without disrupting operations, and 96% of them say AI-generated outputs can trigger actions autonomously, compared with 40% of all other CAIOs. Nearly all high-impact CAIOs say AI is embedded directly into workflows compared with 59% of all others, and 94% say they use business outcomes to determine which initiatives receive additional funding and talent and which do not. 96% of high-impact CAIOs say they stop or reduce investment in initiatives that fail to deliver, even when those initiatives have senior sponsorship, compared with 46% of others, and 95% say they reinvest AI-generated productivity gains in higher-value transformation, compared with 44% of other respondents.

Only 31% of all CAIOs say clear thresholds for stopping AI initiatives are critical to AI success, and 40% say decisions are discussed when performance insights reveal opportunities, but action is delayed. 71% of CAIOs believe their organizations risk falling behind competitors in AI transformation, and CAIOs rank workflows and business processes as the top priority for change. The findings link the stronger outcomes of high-impact CAIOs with differences in how their organizations manage AI autonomy and control, redesign business workflows, and make evidence-based investment decisions. Additional analysis examined organizational behaviors associated with stronger enterprise outcomes across governance, decision rights, workflow integration, operating-model design, value management, transformation execution, and business-model innovation. The IBM Institute for Business Value is IBM's thought leadership think tank, combining global research and performance data with expertise from industry thinkers and leading academics.

The full report is available at a link on IBM's website, and the media contact is Marisa Conway of IBM Corporate Communications. IBM describes itself as a leading provider of global hybrid cloud and AI and consulting expertise, helping clients in more than 175 countries. The articles do not say what organizations should do in response to the findings, beyond the report link. They do not give the names of any surveyed CAIOs or the identities of the high-impact group. They do not break the results down by geography or industry, though the survey covered 33 geographies and 20 industries.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
stories.Summary:
At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners. The initiative is a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft launched it with organizations across industries to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents. The announcement came from Redmond, Wash., on Nov. 17, 2026. The initiative reflects a principle that greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency.

The initiative has three parts, the first being that Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology's SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams' ability to govern them securely or compliance teams' ability to audit their actions. Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency.

Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself for security controls to be effective. Gallot said the work will bring more transparency to all models and called it a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing better accountability and traceability. Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe, said security teams need clear visibility into what agents are accessing, what actions they are taking and how those actions can be verified. Gupta said building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability. John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International, said clients want to move faster with AI and should not have to choose between innovation and safety.

Israel said trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight, and that KPMG is proud to work with Microsoft on the initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards. Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture, said organizations taking the next step in their AI reinventions need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from. Sidhu said initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as Accenture secures AI models and fits them with controls and governance. Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential.

Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations' ability to understand the context behind an agent's actions, and that evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. Accountability stays with the organization, and when something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn't an answer, and "trust the model" isn't a control.

Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. On seeing, organizations should know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took, and monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds. On verifying, agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves. Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source, the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy, so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider's account of its behavior.

On controlling, clear evidence of each workflow's purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with organizations when models and providers change, and organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider. Microsoft and industry leaders will share insights at Microsoft Ignite on how organizations can manage AI models and agents with confidence. More is available on the Microsoft Security blog, and press can contact Microsoft Media Relations, We. Communications for Microsoft, at (425) 638-7777. The articles leave open what the open standards will contain and when the work will reach Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot.

stories.Headline: AdMaven launches Mave AI assistant that prepares campaign changes for advertiser approval
stories.Summary:
AdMaven introduced an AI assistant called Mave that is built directly into its advertiser dashboard, letting advertisers launch pop campaigns, adjust settings, analyze live account data and get platform help in their own language, according to a company announcement dated November 18, 2026. The company said media buyers often spend roughly 26 percent of a campaign manager's time, or over 10 hours a week, on a tedious weekly checklist of monitoring results, tweaking bids, reallocating budgets and pausing underperforming ads. Mave was designed to handle that post-launch daily grind so media buyers can focus on strategy rather than repetitive tasks, and it never acts on its own. Whenever an advertiser asks to create a campaign, adjust a bid or change a budget, Mave prepares a confirmation card showing every detail, nothing happens until the advertiser clicks Approve, and cards expire after 10 minutes.

With Mave, advertisers can set up to 5 pop campaigns at once through guided, clickable prompts, with support for CPM, Smart CPM, Smart CPA and Pure CPA where enabled, plus country, OS and device targeting and an optional daily budget before creatives go into standard review. They can pause or resume up to 20 campaigns at once, update bids for one country or all countries, or adjust daily budgets with a $10 minimum, and they can ask in plain language for daily check-ins, weekly summaries, campaign comparisons and period-over-period breakdowns by day, country, device, OS, browser and source, with data refreshing roughly every 10 minutes. Mave can also identify sources that spend without converting or convert at a much higher CPA than average so advertisers know which ones to block, show running and paused campaigns, creative approval status, current bids by country, source lists and available balance plus credit line, and answer questions from AdMaven's help center of 35 articles, including setup guides for 13 trackers, tracking macros and policy rules. When an issue needs a person, such as a payment or creative-review dispute, Mave prepares a pre-written message so the advertiser can contact support in one click.

Noam Cohen, Co-Founder at AdMaven, said most of what advertisers do in the dashboard is not launching something new but the same daily questions about how campaigns are doing, where they are overpaying and what should be paused. He said Mave lets them ask those questions directly and get an answer or a change ready to approve, but it does not make the call for them, and the budget and judgment stay with the advertiser while Mave removes the clicking in between. AdMaven describes itself as a performance-driven global advertising network delivering over 1 billion daily impressions worldwide, specializing in Pop, Push, In-page Push and Interstitial ads, and offering publishers a brand-protected ecosystem with no minimum traffic barriers.

Mave is currently rolling out on an invite-only basis, enabled account by account inside the AdMaven advertiser dashboard's chat panel, and read-only Q&A access is also available through the AdMaven API for pulling account answers without making changes. Advertisers interested in early access can reach out to their account manager, and the company invites interested advertisers to sign up as an AdMaven advertiser to get started.

stories.Headline: MiTAC Computing unveils full-stack infrastructure to scale agentic AI for enterprises
stories.Summary:
MiTAC Computing Technology Corporation unveiled a comprehensive AI infrastructure ecosystem at the SC26 event in Chicago on November 17, 2026. The company showcased these innovations at Booth 4615 to demonstrate how full-stack solutions overcome common enterprise AI deployment bottlenecks. This new ecosystem aims to scale agentic AI by addressing critical compute, thermal, and data challenges for modern businesses. MiTAC collaborated with several strategic partners including AMD, Canonical, DDN, Intel, NVIDIA, and Rafay to deliver these scalable architectures. The event took place at McCormick Place from November 17 through November 19 to present these high-performance server solutions.

The G8825Z5 server uses AMD EPYC 9575F or 9755 processors and AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs for the compute-intensive prefill stage. For the decode stage, the air-cooled G4520G6 uses Intel Xeon 6 processors and eight Skymizer HTX301-4S accelerator cards. Each HTX301-4S card has 256 GB of memory, providing 2 TB of aggregate memory to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model. The upcoming ORv3 44OU Helion solution will scale up to 32,768 AMD Zen 6 CPU cores for hyperscale environments. A 52U liquid-cooled rack integrates 12 G4826Z5 servers with 96 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs to increase GPU density by 50 percent.

Rick Hwang, the President of MiTAC Computing Technology, stated that scaling agentic AI requires cohesive infrastructure rather than fragmented systems. He explained that MiTAC provides the foundational full-stack solution necessary to make sustainable AI factories a reality for enterprises. The company also utilized the vision of AMD Chair and CEO Dr. Lisa Su announced at the OCP Global Summit. MiTAC aims to empower organizations to intelligently route complex workloads and maximize agents-per-watt efficiency through their new rack-scale architectures. These leadership goals focus on providing end-to-end capabilities from research and development to global manufacturing and support.

Enterprises are affected by the need for more than raw GPU power to handle the exponential surge in inference workloads. Canonical Ubuntu provides the certified operating system layer to ensure seamless deployment and enterprise-grade reliability for these AI factories. The DDN Infinia solution prevents accelerator data starvation by processing monumental data streams with ultra-low I/O latency for users. Rafay helps organizations maximize return on investment by providing dynamic GPU-as-a-Service orchestration to eliminate idling across distributed workloads. Their expertise covers barebones, systems, racks, and cluster levels to achieve high performance and integration for their global customers. The company provides customized platforms for hyperscale data centers and specialized AI applications to meet unique business needs.

Industry leaders and experts stated on November 17, 2026, that China can help APEC economies narrow the digital divide. They believe China's open-source artificial intelligence models and rapid deployment capabilities can accelerate technology adoption across the real economy. Collaboration on artificial intelligence has become a primary and closely watched priority for this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation innovation agenda. These experts argue that China is emerging as a critical testing ground for global development in robotics and intelligent vehicles.

Closing the digital divide requires more than just hardware, as developing economies often lack the local talent and governance frameworks to maintain imported tools. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reports that the country ranks first worldwide in downloads of open-source large language models. To support this, the China Center for APEC Cooperation on Cross-border Data Flows was established in Qianhai, Shenzhen, Guangdong province. This center manages the Shenzhen-Hong Kong cross-border data verification platform and a secure data channel for medical information.

Samantha Zhu of Accenture Greater China noted that 88 percent of Chinese enterprises have moved beyond the pilot stage of AI adoption. Jeff Shi of SenseTime explained that his company now serves over 430 companies in the Asia-Pacific region by offering industry-specific solutions. Liu Qingfeng of iFlytek mentioned that his company has 600,000 overseas developers across 220 countries and regions. He also noted that over half of the 29 countries that signed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization agreement on July 16 cooperate with his firm.

The regional supply chain is shifting toward computing power and algorithms as flexible manufacturing replaces old labor cost advantages, according to Zhang Shaogang. New trade chains involving robotics and industrial large language models are emerging to favor economies that can operationalize these tools. Lin Zhifeng stated that the cross-border data verification model has already been replicated in Singapore. Future efforts will extend this cooperation to more APEC economies and broader industrial fields like new energy and smart manufacturing.

stories.Headline: CloudKeeper reaches Select tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track
stories.Summary:
CloudKeeper announced on November 17, 2026, that it had achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track, according to a press release carried by The Manila Times. The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers, and the Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through four tiers, which are Certified, Select, Preferred and Global Premier. The recognition builds on CloudKeeper's existing relationship with Anthropic and adds to its capabilities in helping businesses implement and manage AI solutions.

Drawing on its expertise in cloud infrastructure, FinOps and AI, CloudKeeper will support organizations building with Claude, including implementing Claude through Amazon Bedrock and addressing their AI infrastructure, governance and cost optimization needs. The company says putting AI into production involves decisions beyond selecting a model, such as how applications connect with existing systems, where workloads run, how usage is governed and how costs are managed. With experience across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, and offerings such as FinOps for AI and Generative AI Launchpad, CloudKeeper helps customers navigate these considerations. The announcement builds on CloudKeeper's earlier appointment as an authorised Anthropic reseller, which lets customers access Claude models through Amazon Bedrock within AWS.

Deepak Mittal, the CEO of CloudKeeper, said the company has spent over 15 years helping businesses make better decisions about their cloud investments, and that AI raises important questions about infrastructure, consumption and long-term costs. He said CloudKeeper wants to help customers get the most out of what they are building with Claude while keeping the economics in view, and called the recognition a meaningful step in that direction. Aman Aggarwal, the COO, said the interesting work begins when a team takes Claude from a promising capability and makes it useful in its own environment, which means connecting it with existing applications, making sound architecture choices and putting the right governance in place. He said the company's engineering and cloud teams work across these challenges and that the recognition supports the work being done with customers.

CloudKeeper describes itself as an outcome-driven AI and cloud cost optimization partner that combines FinOps expertise, proprietary technology and hands-on execution. With over 15 years of cloud cost optimization experience, it says it has helped more than 500 global companies reduce cloud and AI spend by an average of 20% across AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Its outcome-based model delivers ongoing savings without upfront costs or long-term commitments, according to the release. stories.Headline: Nvidia pledges disciplined support for AI infrastructure and raises fiscal 2028 sales forecasts
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Tuesday that it will continue supporting AI infrastructure through investments and credit guarantees. The company reported third quarter results that beat expectations and raised its fiscal 2028 sales forecast. This news eased investor concerns following the recent exit of former CEO Jensen Huang from the firm. Neocloud and chip stocks rallied after the company disclosed its plans for selective and disciplined support. Nvidia stock rose 1.2 percent in overnight trading following the release of the quarterly financial report.

The company disclosed 32 billion dollars in neocloud commitments, which is down from 36 billion in Q2. Total guarantees reached 118 billion dollars, while 390 billion dollars were committed toward future supply and capacity. Revenue for the third quarter more than doubled to 115.8 billion dollars, beating expectations of 109.3 billion dollars. Data center sales rose 110 percent to 107.6 billion dollars, and current quarter revenue is forecast at 130 billion. Fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecasts were raised from 70 percent to 75 percent by interim CEO Colette Kress.

Interim CEO Colette Kress stated that neocloud operators are an important part of the global AI infrastructure chain. She explained that credit backstops only activate if partners can successfully build and deliver the necessary computing infrastructure. Kress noted that the company remains thoughtful and disciplined regarding how it commits capital to the AI ecosystem. She added that Nvidia is rigorously evaluating future investments as the market matures and more capital sources become available. Kress emphasized that neoclouds provide more customers with access to compute and expand the reach of the platform.

Analyst Daniel Newman called neoclouds the biggest sustained bet for Nvidia to create an ecosystem of powered hyperscalers. Wharton professor Mohamed A. El-Erian noted that the earnings highlight Nvidia's expanding role as a major AI creditor. Hedge fund manager Eric Jackson said the push into physical infrastructure for AI compute was the earnings highlight. Nebius and IREN rose over 10 percent, while CoreWeave gained 9 percent and Marvell Technology gained 5.7 percent. Arista Networks rose 3.7 percent, and chip heavyweights Intel, AMD, Micron, and Broadcom rose between 2.7 and 4.7 percent.

The company recently cut ties with 63 year old co founder Jensen Huang following a scandal involving extramarital affairs. One of these affairs allegedly involved a woman who is a Chinese spy, leading to his sudden departure. Huang previously played a central role in the deals that made Nvidia a de facto financier of AI infrastructure. The uptick in supply commitments was primarily related to the multiyear procurement of memory supply for the company. Shares of Nvidia had fallen 16.5 percent year to date as of the most recent market close.

Chairman Harvey C. Jones stated on an analyst call that Nvidia is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. The iShares Semiconductor ETF rose 3.8 percent as retail sentiment on Stocktwits climbed into the extremely bullish zone. One trader suggested that Elon Musk should act soon if he wants to buy shares of the company Nebius. The articles do not state when the current quarter ends or the specific dates for fiscal 2028 targets. It remains open whether other capital sources will reduce the need for Nvidia to provide these credit guarantees.

stories.Headline: Senator Maria Cantwell accuses the Commerce Department of failing to stop AI chip flows to China
stories.Summary:
Senator Maria Cantwell accused the Commerce Department of failing to stop China from getting advanced AI chips in a November 15 letter. She claimed that Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to take action, which she argued undermined the national security of the United States. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also accused the department of weakening export controls by resisting the blacklisting of a Singaporean company. This company, called Megaspeed, is at the center of a scandal involving the export of Nvidia processors to Chinese customers. The accusations follow reports that the Commerce Department delayed action despite repeated warnings about risks to America's technological AI advantage.

Cantwell urged Lutnick to use the 2018 Export Control Reform Act to strengthen enforcement and prevent restricted technology from reaching barred companies. The dispute involves Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that US authorities suspect helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia chips subject to export controls. The Trump administration imposed a 25 per cent fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, creating a perverse financial incentive. Cantwell cited 1.2 billion dollars in Nvidia stock held by Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm controlled by the sons of Howard Lutnick. These financial conflicts raise questions about whether business interests were put ahead of national security during the export approval process.

Senator Cantwell stated that America cannot maintain AI leadership if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Treasury, Pentagon, State Department, and US Trade Representative's Office favored blacklisting Megaspeed for months. Bessent noted that the Commerce Department, which is in charge of the trade blacklist, had not been in favor of this. A spokesperson for Lutnick, Kristen Eichamer, declined to comment on the letter but confirmed that Lutnick agreed to testify soon. Cantwell alleged that the department suspended a probe into Megaspeed and resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as security threats.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday that a growing consensus in Congress now favors new restrictions on China's AI access. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Senator Jim Banks of Indiana argue that export decisions should face much greater congressional oversight. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is affected by reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive and suspected spy. Megaspeed is affected by the investigation, though the company denies the allegations and says it conducts a legitimate and lawful business. China has also denied the allegations that restricted chips were transferred to its customers through the Singaporean technology firm.

The New York Times reported in October 2025 that US authorities were investigating if Megaspeed helped Chinese customers obtain restricted Nvidia chips. Megaspeed stated on Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it has not violated export rules. A November 9 New York Times report alleged that the Commerce Department may have delayed the investigation into the Singaporean company. The controversy involves the diversion of restricted American computing technology to China to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology. These events occur as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January of the coming year.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has summoned Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify before his committee in December. Senators Warren and Chris Coons wrote to Lutnick, Marco Rubio, and Stephen Miller to preserve all documents regarding Nvidia exports. These officials were given until November 17 to confirm that the preservation directives for communications and documents had been issued. US officials are also scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering. The articles leave open whether Megaspeed actually breached US export rules and how Washington will handle future semiconductor export decisions.

stories.Headline: Google Project Zero cuts vulnerability disclosure to 90 days as AI speeds attacks
stories.Summary:
Google's Project Zero team of security researchers announced on 16th November 2026 that it has replaced its long-standing "90 + 30" disclosure policy with a new approach it calls "Full X", under which a vulnerability is made public X days after it is reported to the vendor. As of 13th November, X stands at 90 days, meaning the extra 30 days of soak time that previously let patches reach users before technical details became public has now been removed entirely. The team said the change is needed because large language models now let attackers find vulnerabilities more efficiently and make it more likely that several parties will discover the same flaw independently. Project Zero said it is now finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where it once found only a few a year, which has made the old system of negotiating with vendors increasingly unmanageable.

The policy sets out two further reductions on fixed dates, with X dropping to 60 days on 2nd February 2027 and the policy moving to "Full 30" on 3rd January 2028, when vulnerabilities will be disclosed just 30 days after reporting. The team also said AI has cut the time needed to reverse-engineer a patch and work out which vulnerability it fixes, adding that patch soak time is no longer meaningful when attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins said on X that he understands what Google is trying to do but does not agree with it at all. He said the number of CVEs found in 2026 is double that of 2025, so security fixers face double the workload while getting two thirds of the time to do it, and he warned that at some point the dam is going to break.

Ivan Milenkovic, vice president of risk technology at security vendor Qualys, said vendors will object and some have already warned Google that tight deadlines push them to fix the reported bug ahead of a more severe one, which he called a fair response, though he said the alternative was letting attackers set the deadline. He described the previous 30-day soak time as a comfort blanket that is now being removed, and warned that saying "we patch monthly" now means an organisation is slower than disclosure. He advised organisations to focus on the half-life of vulnerabilities as a key metric, saying boards should stop asking how many critical vulnerabilities they have and instead ask how many days a fixed bug stays unfixed in their estate. The articles do not say what further action Google, vendors or regulators will take beyond the scheduled reductions in 2027 and 2028.

stories.Headline: Upwork survey finds 77% of AI users say their workload increased
stories.Summary:
The article, published by eu.36kr.com on 17 November 2026 and written by Wei Xi, argues that AI is making people busier rather than more productive. It says AI can produce a decent draft in three minutes, but writing a heartfelt, engaging article people want to read has not become easier. It reports that many former colleagues at large tech companies use AI daily while bosses raise requirements, and many product managers must bring a working demo to the review meeting. It says AI does not save time but makes people busier and busier. It presents three paradoxes: the Cowan Paradox, the Solow Paradox and the Jevons Paradox.

The article cites Ruth Schwartz Cowan's 1983 book More Work for Mother, which observed that washing machines, vacuum cleaners and electric stoves were widespread by the 1970s yet she was busier than her mother's generation. It says full-time housewives in the US spent about 52 hours a week on housework in 1924 and around 55 hours a week by 1966. It says economic historian Joel Mokyr named this the Cowan Paradox. It says Cowan found the work of one housewife in 1950 would have needed three or four people in 1850. It says new tasks such as driving to the supermarket and picking up and dropping off children did not exist in the horse-drawn carriage era.

The article reports that the staffing agency Upwork surveyed 2,500 people, finding 77% of employees who use AI say their workload increased and 81% of executives admit they raised work requirements in the past year. It says Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye of UC Berkeley published an article in Harvard Business Review in February 2026 titled AI Has Not Reduced Work, It Has Made Work More Intensive. It says they spent eight months observing a tech company with about 200 employees and found product managers started writing code and researchers took on engineering tasks. It says renowned developer Simon Willison shared the article and said it matches his own experience. It says Stanford Social Media Lab coined the term "workslop" in September 2025 for AI outputs that look decent but cannot push work forward.

The article says the lab surveyed 1,150 full-time American employees, 40% of whom received such outputs in the past month, each spending an average of 116 minutes processing them, an implicit loss of $186 per person per month. It says engineer Siddhant Khare wrote AI Fatigue Is Real, No One Is Talking About It in February 2026, which topped the Hacker News leaderboard, arguing every task gets done faster so you take on more tasks but your brain cannot expand its capacity. It says John Maynard Keynes wrote Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren in 1930, calculating that with 2% annual capital growth and usual technological advance, by 2030 people need work only three hours a day, 15 hours a week. It says Swiss and Spanish economists calculated in 2024 that annual working hours per capita in the US fell from 2,316 hours in 1929 to 1,765 hours in 2019, a 23.8% reduction in 90 years, while Keynes' target is about 780 hours a year. It says Sam Altman said publicly this summer that every technological revolution promised more leisure but society never lived with less work, and he does not think AI will change this because humans are naturally competitive.

The article says economist Robert Solow wrote in a July 1987 New York Times book review that "You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics," and won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in October of that year. It says US non-farm labor productivity grew at an average annual rate of 3.19% from 1948 to 1973, fell to 1.53% from 1974 to 1995, returned to 3.15% after the internet boom in 1996, and dropped to 1.39% after 2004. It says Anders Humlum of the University of Chicago linked survey data of 25,000 Danish employees with official tax and employment archives and found AI users save an average of only 2.8% of their time, with no significant impact on income or working hours. It says MIT's Generative AI Divide report last July found enterprises invested 300 to 400 billion US dollars in generative AI but 95% of institutions saw no measurable returns. It says Callum Williams of The Economist posted a US productivity curve in February 2026 captioned that the AI productivity boost is still not visible in US statistics, and Indeed Hiring Lab pointed out US total factor productivity slowed from 1.5% to 0.8% in 2025.

The article says Stanford economist Paul David explained that electricity faced the same paradox: power stations were built as early as 1881, but by 1900 there was barely evidence of efficiency gains in factories, and US manufacturing productivity exceeded 5% per year only in the 1920s, 40 years after commercialization. It describes this as the productivity J-curve, in which productivity first declines then rises as enterprises adjust processes and train employees, and says today's AI is stuck at the bottom of the J-curve. It says Workday research found that in 89% of institutions less than half of jobs have been redesigned to match AI capabilities. It says American economist Erik Brynjolfsson is the flagbearer of the optimists, and in March 2026 the US Bureau of Labor Statistics announced productivity grew 2.8% in 2025, against an average of only 1.2% in the decade before the pandemic. It says he tweeted that it is still hard to determine how much of this growth AI contributed, but the Solow Paradox might be ready to retire.

stories.Headline: Kaseya launches MCP servers and 17 AI skills for MSPs in early access
stories.Summary:
Kaseya on Tuesday launched Model Context Protocol servers for Autotask, Datto RMM and IT Glue, together with 17 pre-built AI skills that let managed service providers connect tools such as Anthropic's Claude directly to customer, ticket, device and documentation data. The Miami-based vendor said the capabilities are available in early access, and it plans additional MCP servers across its platform. The announcement also included enhancements to Datto RMM, such as faster remote access and AI-powered device and activity log insights, as well as improvements to Datto SaaS Protection. Kaseya Insights, which is coming soon, will bring business and operational intelligence from Autotask and Datto RMM into a connected view that MSPs can query using natural language.

Kaseya CEO Rania Succar said MSPs are trying to accelerate top-line growth and improve operating margins by automating work that has historically been manual. She said everybody is playing with AI and getting exposure to it, but they are struggling to make a difference to their bottom line and to their margins. Succar said Kaseya has been on a mission to change that dynamic for MSPs by automating work that was historically manual around IT and security. She said the company developed the new capabilities alongside MSPs, with hundreds of partners interviewed and about 50 becoming design partners who helped prioritize the workflows. Succar said Kaseya plans to expand its MCP integrations across its offerings in the coming months, pointing to a forthcoming agent center as a major part of its 2027 AI roadmap.

Matt Rose, co-founder and CEO of Longwood, Fla.-based Kaseya partner Tech Rage IT, called the MCP announcement a promising move, particularly because it gives partners an easier way to connect AI tools with operational information already sitting inside their technology stacks. Rose said the amount of time he spends trying to find something in Autotask is ridiculous, and that an MCP server that could help him find the data and act on it would be tremendous. He said the opportunity will depend on how effectively individual MSPs put the technology to work, rather than simply adopting AI for the sake of adopting it. Rose said that if his technicians can pull out information quicker on what fixed a problem, it should allow time savings, though everyone will have to find their own level of cost savings and what they can actually do.

stories.Headline: AI agents bypass corporate card review limits by splitting costs and switching suppliers without authorization
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence agents are challenging corporate card spending rules by staying within budget limits while exceeding their actual purchasing authority. These agents can bypass review thresholds by splitting large project costs into smaller charges or switching to cheaper suppliers without proper authorization. Recent reports from November 2026 highlight how these automated tools can commit thousands of dollars without triggering traditional manual reviews. Effective oversight requires distinguishing between per-charge thresholds and project-level limits to prevent unauthorized spending. A pilot program from October involving BILL, Billtrust, and Visa requires buyers to approve invoices before agents complete payments.

Rain launched a service on November 10 that enforces original terms by fixing the merchant, amount, and expiration date during virtual card issuance. Other firms like Ramp, Mercury, Sunrate, and Corpay use various methods including single-use cards, recurring limits, and approved workflows to control agent behavior. Finance leaders are implementing diverse safeguards, as 57 percent of surveyed CFOs require two approvals or callback confirmations for outgoing payments. According to a July survey by PYMNTS Intelligence and J.P. Morgan, 62 percent of CFOs automatically clear low-risk payments without manual review. An August report by PYMNTS Intelligence and Plaid found that 81 percent of firms check payment histories, while 61 percent reserve real-time identity verification for high-risk transactions.

These executives emphasize that verifying a new seller is a separate task from confirming the payment amount. The current landscape involves a mix of automated rules and human intervention to manage the risks of AI procurement. Future systems must provide reviewers with detailed comparisons between original suppliers and proposed substitutions to ensure informed decision-making. Once procurement approves a change, revised terms can govern the issuance of a new corporate card. Finance departments will continue to match these employee decisions against eventual charges within the purchasing record.

stories.Headline: SmartKargo releases four AI cargo apps that run on airlines existing systems
stories.Summary:
SmartKargo, a cargo technology company based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, released the first four applications in its AI Apps portfolio on October 26, according to FreightWaves. Each application is aimed at a single part of the cargo profit and loss statement, and the company says the apps run through APIs on top of whatever cargo management system an airline already uses. There is no migration involved, and SmartKargo says the apps can go live in weeks rather than years. Airlines can start with a single app and add the others later, and each app is independent and priced on usage, transactions or assets rather than seats.

Air cargo generated $151 billion in revenue in 2025, according to IATA, yet many decisions still run on static rules, manual overrides and delayed reports, the article says. SmartKargo frames every app around one test, whether it drives revenue, reduces cost or reduces risk. One of the four apps, AIRCAM, targets cargo pricing by reading demand, capacity and market signals for each shipment and returning a rate recommendation inside the booking and quoting flow. It forecasts booked and unbooked demand, allocates belly and freighter space to the highest-value mix, and flags underpriced capacity, and every recommendation shows its reasoning so revenue managers are not handed a black box. Win-loss outcomes feed back into the model so pricing improves continuously, and VietJet Cargo is the named early adopter.

Chief Revenue Officer Olivier Houri said the company starts with something more useful than hype, a business question, according to the article. McKinsey & Company notes that more than half of a flight's capacity is often booked in the final week, when yield volatility is at its widest, and static tariffs adjusted by hand are poorly suited to that window. The article also says operations are where cargo quietly loses money, since a missed connection becomes a missed service level agreement and then an unhappy shipper, and most operations centers still learn about these problems after the fact. The article does not say what happens next beyond the release of the first four apps.

stories.Headline: New York Fed president John Williams says AI investment surge may push the Fed to raise rates further next year
stories.Summary:
New York Fed President John Williams said on Tuesday at the Axios BFD summit in New York that the artificial intelligence boom could lead the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further next year. He described an economy that is strengthening while inflation stays stubbornly high, with AI investment and soaring stock prices helping to fuel that growth. Williams said the United States is seeing a lot of strength today coming from the investment surge around AI, along with strong consumer spending driven by stock market wealth. He added that if those trends continue, they are a factor that will argue the Fed may need to raise rates more.

Williams pointed to tariffs, energy prices and rising costs for semiconductors and other AI-related goods as sources of inflationary pressure, and he called AI an important one because it is more likely to be the persistent factor. He downplayed the need for a larger, half-percentage-point rate hike at next month's policy meeting, saying he does not think the situation calls for dramatic action. That contrasts with Fed governor Christopher Waller, who last week raised the possibility of a supersized hike if October's core inflation reading came in at 0.3% or higher, and the report subsequently showed exactly that. Williams also said the Fed is closely monitoring the growing use of complex financial instruments to fund the AI boom, though he sees no immediate threat to financial stability.

Williams acknowledged parallels between the increasingly complex financing arrangements underpinning the AI boom and those that emerged in the housing market before the 2008 financial crisis. He said the Fed is definitely seeing structured finance of the type seen in housing finance, which is why it is paying attention to that. He said he does not see it as a financial stability risk yet, but it is definitely growing fast, and the structured finance part is growing even faster than was seen before. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the Fed's next policy meeting and its continued monitoring of these financing arrangements.

stories.Headline: Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approves policy governing ethical AI use across county government
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a policy on Tuesday that governs the safe, ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence technologies across county government. The policy sets standards, responsibilities and governance requirements for AI systems that the county develops itself, buys from outside vendors or reaches through third-party platforms. A board letter from the county's chief executive officer said AI technologies are increasingly used across county departments to enhance service delivery, improve operational efficiency and support data driven decision making. The letter said that as these technologies advance, it is critical for the county to maintain clear governance structures, safeguard sensitive information and ensure that AI is deployed responsibly and ethically. The policy requires county departments to follow principles involving human-centered design, security and safety, privacy, transparency, equity, accountability, effectiveness and workforce empowerment.

It requires AI systems to protect personally identifiable information, protected health information, criminal justice information and other sensitive data from unauthorized access, disclosure and manipulation. It also requires the county to disclose the purpose and use of its AI systems to the public and to identify work products generated by AI. The policy prohibits fully automated high-impact decisions without meaningful human review, covert tracking or social scoring of people, and the cognitive or behavioral manipulation of people or vulnerable groups. County employees are barred from uploading nonpublic or regulated county information to unapproved AI platforms, using such platforms to make official decisions or relying on AI-generated work as an authoritative source without independent human verification. The policy says AI should be used to enhance jobs and provide training and retraining opportunities for workers, rather than replace county employees or contractors.

Oversight responsibilities go to the county's chief information officer, chief information security officer, chief privacy officer and department-level information technology managers. The policy allows no exceptions, according to the county. County Counsel reviewed the proposal, and the Audit Committee approved it on Sept. 16. The board letter said there will be no fiscal impact to the county from the proposed AI Policy. The board letter also said the policy establishes consistent requirements to ensure that any AI technologies developed, procured or used by county departments comply with applicable laws, protect county information assets, maintain public trust and mitigate the risk of bias or misuse.

Articles.Title: LA County Supervisors Approve AI Policy

stories.headline_source: LA County Supervisors Approve AI Policy

stories.Headline: Thomson Reuters expands CoCounsel agentic AI across tax and compliance workflows
stories.Summary:
Thomson Reuters announced on November 17, 2026, at its annual Synergy Conference in Las Vegas, that it has expanded CoCounsel across tax and transactional compliance, bringing agentic AI into more of the workflows tax professionals rely on every day. The company said the new capabilities leave the review, the sign-off and the judgment to professionals, aiming to replace the scramble of starting quarter-end with a blank spreadsheet or a day that begins with a bounced invoice. The announcement covers tax and transactional compliance work handled through products including ONESOURCE, Pagero, Checkpoint and CoCounsel Tax, Audit & Accounting, which the company says are already trusted inside many of the world's largest companies. Thomson Reuters said it has the authority, AI technology and products to change the slow adoption picture, citing its existing portfolio as the base for the expansion. The change matters because demands and complexity keep rising for tax professionals, yet 62% of tax leaders said their departments made limited or no progress adopting automation and AI over the past year, according to the company.

Most tax teams still find out an invoice was wrong when it comes back rejected or a correction lands in next month's return, and new e-invoicing and digital reporting rules are raising the stakes. Thomson Reuters said it has already launched agentic AI products to make this work easier, including ONESOURCE Indirect Compliance, which cuts routine reporting time by up to 65%. The next step is new CoCounsel agentic workflows that bring indirect tax, e-invoicing through the Pagero network and global trade together, giving CoCounsel one view of each transaction. The new workflows are designed to check each customer, vendor and product as they are set up and every invoice before it reaches the tax authority, and to reconcile later changes against the books and prefill the return for review. Errors surface while they are still easy to fix, and a professional approves the return before anything is filed, so the review and sign-off stay with people.

Ray Grove, Head of Product, Transactional Compliance at Thomson Reuters, said the goal is to get every transaction right the first time, with each customer, vendor and invoice checked as it happens so a mistake is fixed once, at the source. He said what reaches the end of the period is then a short list of exceptions for the professional to work, which over time changes the job from reacting to what went wrong to deciding what happens next. The context is a tax function still largely manual, where many teams reach the quarter's income tax number by pulling data from the ledger, chasing details through email and consolidating workpapers, the article says. Against that backdrop the company positions the CoCounsel expansion as the next step beyond its existing agentic products, tying indirect tax, e-invoicing and global trade into a single view of each transaction. The articles do not say when the new CoCounsel agentic workflows will become available, how they will be priced or which customers will receive them first.

stories.Headline: Salesforce assigns monthly AI token budgets to roles after some staff spent thousands per month
stories.Summary:
Salesforce began assigning monthly AI token budgets to every role this month, after some individuals spent thousands of dollars per month on tokens last quarter, according to an internal memo viewed by Business Insider. Chief Operating Officer Miguel Milano wrote in an email to employees that the budgets would let the company focus its AI spend on the work that matters most for customers and the business. A Salesforce spokesperson said the company does not have companywide individual token budgets and leaves AI usage management to team leaders, adding that its focus is ensuring AI investments deliver the greatest impact. The company piloted the budgets on one team for a month and found that group was operating well under budget by month two with no drop in output.

The sales organization under President and Chief Revenue Officer Alexa Vignone will have a budget of $1,000 per month for technical roles and $100 per month for non-technical roles like sellers. Customer Success under Jim Roth, and Global Professional Services and Forward Deployed Engineering under Lori Steele, will have budgets of $500 per month for technical roles and $100 per month for non-technical roles. Employees are asked to manage their own budgets, and organizational unit leaders will manage each team's budget so one person's spike can be offset by others. When an individual's AI spend approaches 100%, the individual and the manager both get a Slack notification from the DevBar app, with the option to request approval up to 20% above the individual limit. Exceptions up to 20% above the limit need second line manager approval, requests up to three times the limit need third line manager approval with an ROI justification and last 90 days, and anything above three times the limit goes to Alexa, Jim or Lori with finance and is reviewed monthly.

Milano said AI confidence is now high and the company is shifting focus from adoption to impact, and he urged employees to match the model to the task and to add token consumption to manager one-on-ones. He wrote that even heavy users typically spend under $100 per month, and that the company never wants a budget to get in the way of great work, so anyone with a high-impact use case should ask for more. In Works Council countries, leaders will have visibility into pooled team spending rather than direct individual usage. Other companies have set similar limits, with Coinbase using weekly AI spending caps of $500 to $5,000 based on role and seniority, and JPMorgan Chase introducing a $2,000 monthly limit for some engineers using Anthropic's Claude Code. In May, CEO Marc Benioff said Salesforce expected to spend roughly $300 million on Anthropic tokens this year, largely for coding agents.

stories.Headline: Voters back 40 of 41 local measures opposing data center development
stories.Summary:
Voters backed measures restricting data center development during the 2026 midterm elections. This backlash occurred as artificial intelligence became more integrated into the economy. Many people fear that this technology will trigger a surge in layoffs. These concerns about infrastructure became a prominent political issue this year. The revolt served as a proxy for broader affordability concerns.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that 40 of 41 local ballot measures opposed development. These measures target data centers and their consumption of water and electricity. The voting results created electoral difficulties for candidates who supported the AI buildout. This opposition happened across various state and local races in the United States. The measures aim to slow the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Stephanie Aliaga of J.P. Morgan said the AI buildout lost on the ballot. She noted that political resistance adds difficulty to permitting, financing, and power hurdles. Nicol Turner Lee and Darrell M. West said results may lead to policy shifts. They believe these shifts will affect the tech sector and data center development. Aliaga added that previous efforts to slow the buildout had struggled to advance.

Era Dabla-Norris and Anton Korinek noted that public skepticism could keep labor effects manageable. Kate Fortmueller said CEOs might use AI as a boogeyman to increase shareholder value. TIAA found that 40 percent of surveyed people see AI as a retirement threat. This fear of retirement instability rises to 51 percent among Gen Z respondents. Many workers fear AI will automate their tasks and potentially entire roles.

High profile companies cited AI when announcing major job cuts in 2026. Challenger, Gray & Christmas recorded 121,401 AI cited cuts through October of this year. This figure represents around 20 percent of the total annual job cuts reported. Economic conditions were the top reason for cuts with 130,531 announced layoffs. October alone saw 1,265 job cuts specifically attributed to artificial intelligence.

Goldman Sachs economists expect a low hire and low fire employment form through 2027. They suggest that AI displacement will have a larger impact in subsequent years. The full consequences for the labor market might not appear until a recession hits. History shows that routine occupations often drop sharply after productivity booms and never recover. The articles leave open if regulatory friction will successfully prevent ubiquitous AI adoption.

stories.Headline: Anthropic proceeds with IPO despite AI sector volatility and $6.2 billion debt
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is proceeding with its initial public offering despite significant volatility within the artificial intelligence sector and rising investor concerns. The company is moving forward with this plan while other tech stocks experience dramatic swings and the broader market remains unstable. This decision comes during a period of uncertainty following the abrupt departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang due to personal scandals. Anthropic hopes to enter the public market quickly before investor demand evaporates or political crackdowns intensify.

The company currently faces immense financial pressure, including $6.2 billion in accumulated debt and a lack of profitability under standard accounting rules. Future spending plans are massive, with $70 billion slated for the next year and $900 billion committed to infrastructure. Nvidia intends to purchase approximately $10 billion of Anthropic stock after the offering, while the company continues using hardware from AMD and other vendors. Additionally, newly elected Democrat governors in Texas and Georgia have pledged to halt new data center construction.

Company leadership is motivated to sell shares because borrowing has become more expensive due to inflation and the sector's high cash requirements. They are attempting to avoid the fate of companies like StubHub and Klarna, which postponed their public offerings due to market jitters. By going public now, Anthropic may beat its rival OpenAI to the market and attract investors before the sector becomes oversaturated. This strategy aims to secure funding before Congress considers a national moratorium on the construction of data centers.

stories.Headline: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million seed round to deploy agentic AI for delivery supply chains
stories.Summary:
Pedestal AI came out of stealth on Tuesday with $4.7 million in seed funding, according to TechCrunch, and the startup aims to use agentic AI to make delivery supply chains faster and more reliable. The round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage, and the company said the money will expand its product and engineering teams, grow its marketing organization, and support additional deployments. Pedestal said its plan has already brought it together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work drivers were supposed to do.

The agentic system Pedestal built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions, and if the call did not go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. The deployment also collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which the company said could be used to optimize the system even further. CEO Raj Aggarwal told TechCrunch that the challenge is that the data is messy and constantly changing, and that it is disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. He said deliveries are particularly well suited to training reinforcement learning systems because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, which makes it easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what is working and away from what is not.

Aggarwal also told TechCrunch that the kind of problem Pedestal works on can have an immediate effect on a client's bottom line, which makes it easy to justify the expense. He said that if you can get it right, you can have really big impact. Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups, the article said. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory, and another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

stories.Headline: Jefferies expects Zoom to beat third quarter guidance and raise its outlook on stronger AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Jefferies said on November 17, 2026, that Zoom Video Communications is positioned to deliver stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and raise its financial outlook, as artificial intelligence adoption, enterprise demand and customer experience services support growth. The broker expects revenue growth in constant currency to accelerate to about 5.2%, compared with the company's guidance of 3.9%, an upside of more than 120 basis points. Jefferies expects enterprise revenue growth to accelerate from 7.8% in the second quarter to more than 8%, exceeding the consensus forecast of 7.1% reported growth. It attributed the improvement to stronger adoption of AI products, including ZoomMate and Zoom Revenue Accelerator, alongside continued momentum in customer experience services and Zoom Phone.

The online business is also expected to perform better than market forecasts, with Jefferies seeing scope for revenue growth of 0% to 1%, compared with consensus expectations for a 0.8% decline. Jefferies forecasts operating income of about $517.5 million, at least $5 million above the company's guidance range of $510 million to $515 million, implying an operating margin broadly in line with or slightly ahead of expectations. The broker also expects earnings per share of about $1.54, above the guidance midpoint of $1.47, supported by stronger operating income and share repurchases. For the fourth quarter, Jefferies expects management to guide for revenue growth of about 4.4% in constant currency, in line with consensus, and operating income of approximately $538 million.

Jefferies said greater detail on the path towards sustained double-digit enterprise growth and customer interest in unified communications and AI services would be important indicators of progress. The broker believes investors are likely to reward a clean earnings beat and stronger guidance, with the shares trading at about 15 times estimated 2027 free cash flow. Investors are also expected to focus on Zoom's longer-term targets for fiscal 2030, which call for revenue growth of 6% to 8% and an operating margin of about 40%. Continued pricing benefits, steady customer additions and increasing AI adoption are expected to support the online business despite seasonal pressures and tougher comparisons.

stories.Headline: Only 4% of HR chiefs feel very prepared for AI workforce change, Conference Board survey finds
stories.Summary:
The Conference Board's latest CHRO Confidence survey, released in the third quarter of 2026, found that only 4% of chief human resources officers feel very prepared to manage AI-driven workforce change over the next two years, while 55% consider their organizations at least somewhat prepared. The overall confidence index slipped to 56 in the third quarter from 58 in the second, a step down from the record high it reached earlier in the year. The biggest barriers CHROs cited were difficulty predicting AI's workforce impact at 41%, limited AI skills at 39% and an unclear AI strategy at 31%, and just 19% said anticipated AI effects are built into workforce and financial planning across the enterprise. Hiring rose from 59 to 61, while retention eased from 55 to 54 and engagement fell from 59 to 55, and fewer CHROs expected overall workforce size to grow over the next six months, 49% compared with 55% in the second quarter.

Diana Scott, U.S. Human Capital Center Leader at The Conference Board in New York, said she was not surprised by how few CHROs feel very prepared, describing it less as a reflection of confidence than of where they are in the journey and the work still ahead. She said the 4% figure is probably appropriate because most organizations have not really embraced AI and are still experimenting and prototyping rather than pulling it into their overall systems. She said real transformation happens when an organization looks at an entire workflow and asks whether AI will augment or automate the work and how it will move to somebody else, rather than bolting AI onto existing processes. She recommended three starting steps: start small by picking one inefficient workflow and testing technology with executive buy-in and employee involvement, build basic AI skills across the workforce, and communicate clearly about the leadership's overall vision of AI, since workers who use AI frequently are more than twice as likely to believe their jobs could disappear within five years.

Scott said you cannot boil the ocean or do it all at once, and that employees should be involved because many understand how work happens and will have ideas. On skills, she said getting employees skilled in basic AI is table stakes and must be in place if it is not already, though Businessolver research found that executives focused on cutting headcount with AI are half as likely to prioritize AI upskilling as their peers. On communication, she said leadership must be very clear about its overall vision of AI, and that being open about what is still unknown matters too. She said you cannot promise employees there will be a job for them, but you can show them there is a path and growth and that you are providing the tools and support to guide them there. Gallup, which surveys workers directly, found that U.S. employee engagement fell to 29% in the third quarter of 2026, its lowest level since 2011.
