stories.Headline: Vertiv adds 800 VDC power systems for AI compute pods and data halls
stories.Summary:
Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE: VRT) added 800 VDC systems for the AI compute pod and the data hall on Nov. 17, 2026, extending a portfolio that began with the May 2026 introduction of the Vertiv PowerDirect 5000 Power Rack. The company announced the expansion in a release dated Nov. 17, 2026, from Columbus, Ohio. The expanded portfolio enables operators to meet rising power demands in next-generation AI data centers and scale infrastructure as compute requirements evolve. Vertiv offers three 800 VDC architecture options spanning medium-voltage to low-voltage AC-to-800 VDC conversion at the rack, LV AC-to-800 VDC conversion at the compute pod, and MV AC-to-800 VDC conversion at the data hall. The portfolio spans power conversion, energy storage, distribution and protection, delivering power train architectures from the medium-voltage grid to the compute tray.

The Vertiv PowerDirect 3000 90 kW, 19-inch 800 VDC Power Shelf is a 1U DC-DC converter inside the compute rack that converts 800 VDC to 54 VDC for compute trays at up to 98.5% peak efficiency and supports 180% pulse power for 0.5 milliseconds. This rack architecture frees 8 to 16 rack units for additional compute, with one power rack supporting one or two IT racks, and supports both 800 VDC and ±400 VDC through minimal hardware configuration changes. The Vertiv PowerDirect 9000, 1.5 MW 800 VDC Power Center converts 480 VAC to 800 VDC for an entire row or pod, distributing power via the Vertiv PowerBar Track DC busway and tap-off boxes to the PowerDirect 3000 shelves in each rack. The pod system scales in 60 kW increments through 27 hot-pluggable power supply units, and the Vertiv EnergyCore Li5 800 VDC battery cabinet delivers 200 kW of continuous backup at up to 98% conversion efficiency, with up to six cabinets operating in parallel through active current sharing. The Vertiv PowerNexus MV SST, 5 MW 800 VDC Solid-State Transformer, converts medium-voltage AC directly to 800 VDC in a single conversion stage, eliminates two to three intermediate conversion steps, delivers up to 98% AC-to-DC efficiency, and a single unit can support a 4.8 MW super pod reference architecture without chaining.

Scott Armul, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertiv, said the 800 VDC power train is not just a new power product or conversion methodology but a set of architectures and system designs. Armul said delivering it takes a comprehensive portfolio that brings together power conversion, energy storage, distribution, protection, controls and safety. He added that Vertiv has built a system-level 800 VDC portfolio giving customers flexibility to implement 800 VDC across different data center configurations. He said every layer, from the medium-voltage grid to the compute tray, is designed to work together, with safety built for DC operation. Kyle Keeper, Senior Vice President of Vertiv's Power Management Business Unit, said different operators have different requirements, whether building new AI facilities, upgrading existing sites, or supporting a mix of tenants and workloads.

Vertiv said AC and DC architectures are expected to coexist, making flexibility in power conversion, distribution and deployment essential, and that operators have different facilities, workloads, business models, risk tolerances and investment horizons. Vertiv said its role is to help operators determine which architecture matches their needs, and its portfolio lets operators introduce 800 VDC at different points in the power train without committing an entire data center to a single architecture. The rack architecture suits brownfield environments, retrofit scenarios and facilities running mixed AC and DC architectures, while the pod architecture suits colocation providers serving tenants with different workload types and GPU generations. The data hall architecture is designed for operators building purpose-built AI factories at campus scale, and its outdoor, liquid-cooled and containerized design reduces physical footprint and supports faster deployment and standardized replication across campuses. Vertiv 800 VDC architectures include touch-proof busbars, high voltage isolation, midpoint grounding, ground-fault detection and arc-flash prevention, supported by Vertiv Services offerings developed for DC environments.

Vertiv is headquartered in Westerville, Ohio, USA, and does business in more than 130 countries. Vertiv is showcasing its 800 VDC portfolio at SC26, the International Conference for High-Performance Computing, Networking, Storage, and Analysis, Nov. 17-22, 2026. Pilot programs, technical validation activities and collaborative development initiatives tailored to customers' deployment needs are currently underway. Vertiv experts are ready to discuss these solutions and engage on next steps. The release includes forward-looking statements and refers readers to Vertiv's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including its most recent Annual Report on Form 10-K and any subsequent Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q.

Vertiv said bidirectional power flow enables improved grid power quality and can provide active power support, and that battery communication ports coordinate with energy storage systems to manage the rapid load fluctuations of AI workloads. The data hall design provides fault ride-through and AI power smoothing when connected to external energy storage with a DC/DC converter coupled on the 800 VDC bus. The pod architecture consolidates power conversion into a single system ahead of the row, reducing component count and eliminating the need for individual power racks alongside each IT rack. The rack architecture moves power conversion and energy storage outside the IT rack and lets operators retain existing upstream AC infrastructure, helping simplify deployment without a facility redesign. Vertiv said 800 VDC cannot be reduced to a sidecar, a rectifier, or a single component, and that its portfolio covers power conversion, energy storage, distribution, protection, controls and monitoring to deliver a coordinated, end-to-end system.

stories.Headline: Crexendo wins 2026 Voice AI Technology Excellence Award for its CAIRO AI Receptionist

Crexendo, Inc., a Nasdaq-listed software technology company based in Phoenix, announced on November 17, 2026, that its CAIRO AI Receptionist and Orchestrator had won the 2026 CUSTOMER Magazine Voice AI Technology Excellence Award. The award is given by TMC's CUSTOMER magazine, and CAIRO was selected for its ability to use Voice AI to enhance customer engagement through intelligent call handling, automation, and orchestration capabilities. Crexendo describes CAIRO as the Crexendo AI Receptionist and Orchestrator, and the company says the product helps organizations improve satisfaction, streamline operations, and build stronger customer relationships. The company also says CAIRO delivers seamless, responsive, and highly personalized customer experiences for the businesses that use it.

Crexendo says CAIRO is an important component of its strategy to accelerate organic growth through AI-powered solutions, and that providing advanced AI capabilities through its NetSapiens cloud communications platform will create additional revenue opportunities for the company and its service provider licensees. The company says businesses increasingly seek intelligent automation to improve productivity, reduce operating costs, and enhance customer engagement, and that CAIRO and its expanding portfolio of AI solutions can drive increased adoption and additional recurring revenue. Crexendo states that its solutions support over eight million end users globally through a network of more than 250 cloud communication platform software subscribers and its direct retail offering. The press release also notes that TMC has been honoring technology companies with awards for more than 20 years, and that the company's forward-looking statements are subject to risks described in its Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, and its Form 10-Qs filed with the SEC.

Rich Tehrani, CEO of TMC, congratulated all of the 2026 Voice AI Technology Excellence Award winners and said the recipients represent some of the most innovative and impactful companies in voice technology. He said their commitment to excellence, customer success, and continuous innovation is helping shape the future of communications. Jeff Korn, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Crexendo, said the company is extremely pleased that CAIRO received the recognition, which he said further validates its commitment to making Crexendo and the NetSapiens platform leaders in AI-powered cloud communications. Korn said artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to accelerate organic growth and create meaningful new revenue streams for Crexendo and its licensees, and he added that the ability to bring these innovations to an ecosystem supporting more than eight million end users is particularly exciting.

According to the release, earning an Excellence Award from TMC's CUSTOMER magazine elevates the Crexendo brand before TMC's audience of technology professionals, decision makers, and executives, along with their ecosystem of end users and other providers. Crexendo says the recognition underscores its influence on the future of customer engagement through intelligent cloud communications, and that it continues to advance its innovation leadership by delivering an AI-powered software platform. Korn said that as AI adoption accelerates, the expanding portfolio of AI solutions can generate additional recurring revenue, increase the value of the platform to existing customers, attract new licensees, and provide a meaningful catalyst for long-term growth. The release states that forward-looking statements speak only as of the date they are made and that the company undertakes no obligation to update them except as required by law.

stories.Headline: Review authors say AI advances antibiotic discovery and design across five areas
stories.Summary:
Antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections cause more than 1 million deaths worldwide each year, according to a Review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology on 17 November 2026. The Review focuses on recent advances in small-molecule antibiotic discovery enabled by artificial intelligence. It presents innovative approaches that are substantially increasing the size and diversity of the explored chemical space. It highlights recent artificial intelligence-driven advancements in phenotypic antibiotic discovery, mechanism of action elucidation, target-based discovery, de novo molecular design and lead optimization. The authors say these promise to expand the repertoire of antibacterial agents and uncover bacterial pathways and vulnerabilities amenable to therapeutic intervention.

The Review states there is a critical need for new classes of antibiotics, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action. It cites a 2022 Lancet analysis by the Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators on the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019, published in volume 399, pages 629 to 655. It cites a 2024 Lancet analysis by Naghavi and colleagues on the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2050, in volume 404, pages 1199 to 1226. It cites a 2024 report from the EcoAMR Series by McDonnell and colleagues on forecasting the economic impacts of antimicrobial resistance in humans, from WOAH and the World Bank.

The Review is a preview of subscription content, with access through an institution or a Nature+ online-access subscription at $39.99 for 30 days. A journal subscription gives 12 print issues and online access for $259.00 per year, or $21.58 per issue. The article can be purchased on SpringerLink for USD 39.95, with prices subject to local taxes calculated during checkout. The Review includes five figures, on strategies for systematically exploring small-molecule chemical space, a workflow for machine learning-guided antibacterial hit identification based on phenotypic screens, experimental approaches for mechanism of action characterization, a structure-based drug discovery pipeline for target identification and hit validation with associated challenges, and multimodal design of antibiotics for lead optimization and candidate progression.

The reference list includes Levy's 1992 book The Antibiotic Paradox, published by Springer, and Silver's 2011 paper on challenges of antibacterial discovery in Clinical Microbiology Reviews, volume 24, pages 71 to 109. It includes Walsh's 2003 paper in Nature Reviews Microbiology, volume 1, pages 65 to 70, asking where new antibiotics will come from. It includes Stover and colleagues' 2000 paper in Nature, volume 405, pages 962 to 966, on a small-molecule nitroimidazopyran drug candidate for tuberculosis. It includes Eyal and colleagues' 2016 paper in Scientific Reports, volume 6, article 39004, on a novel pleuromutilin antibacterial compound, its binding mode and selectivity mechanism.

The references also include Miller and colleagues' 2008 paper in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, volume 52, pages 2806 to 2812, on discovery and characterization of QPT-1, the progenitor of a new class of bacterial topoisomerase inhibitors. They include Bax and colleagues' 2010 paper in Nature, volume 466, pages 935 to 940, on type IIA topoisomerase inhibition by a new class of antibacterial agents. They include Yao and colleagues' 2026 paper in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, volume 70, e01706-25, on stepwise evolution and clonal enrichment of gepotidacin resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. They include Mukherjee and colleagues' 2026 paper in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, volume 234, pages e131 to e140, on genetic background modulating zoliflodacin and gepotidacin cross-resistance and fitness in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Further references include Wan, Wong, Collins and de la Fuente-Nunez's 2024 paper in Nature Reviews Bioengineering, volume 2, pages 392 to 407, on machine learning for antimicrobial peptide identification and design. They include Martins and colleagues' 2026 scoping review in Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, volume 179, article 103461, on artificial intelligence in drug discovery for fungal diseases. They include Fu and colleagues' 2021 paper in Nature Communications, volume 12, article 6497, on leveraging machine learning essentiality predictions and chemogenomic interactions to identify antifungal targets. They include Wensing and colleagues' 2026 paper in Nature Microbiology, volume 11, pages 2157 to 2169, on pooled CRISPRi screening revealing fungal-specific drug target candidates.

The references further include Behsaz and colleagues' 2026 paper in Cell Reports Methods, volume 6, article 101510, on a large-scale discovery platform enabling identification of peptides targeting drug-resistant candidiasis. They include Pitt and colleagues' 2025 paper in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, volume 68, pages 851 to 859, on real-world applications and experiences of AI/ML deployment for drug discovery. They include Bender and colleagues' 2026 paper in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, volume 25, pages 855 to 876, on artificial intelligence in drug discovery, what it is, where we stand and the path forward. They include Hutchings, Truman and Wilkinson's 2019 paper in Current Opinion in Microbiology, volume 51, pages 72 to 80, on antibiotics past, present and future.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: North Dakota student senators pass bills on AI and technology use in schools
stories.Summary:
Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol. The students met on Monday and Tuesday to form committees, subcommittees, debate and vote on both topics as bill drafts were created from their work. The summit took place on Nov. 17, 2026, according to photo captions by Michael Achterling of the North Dakota Monitor. Students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January. The bills will be made available to state lawmakers as they begin the 2027 legislative session Jan. 5.

The bill outlining rules for artificial intelligence use in schools passed on a 40-8 vote. It would allow students to use artificial intelligence tools beginning in ninth grade, unless under the direction of a teacher during classroom instruction, but would not allow students to use the tools to complete assignments. The bill would require teachers to list when AI use is permitted and not permitted as part of course instruction. Teachers would not be able to use AI to input grades into a gradebook or assign final grades, but they can use AI tools to assist with grading assignments and to create lesson plans. A bill regulating the use of technology during the school day was approved on a 47-0 vote, requiring school districts to use technology as a support to learning and not a replacement for essential instruction, in a manner reasonably suited to a student's academic level, age, accessibility needs, and educational circumstances.

Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier said one of his favorite units as a state government teacher was the mock Congress and he thought he could recreate that type of environment at the Capitol with high school students. Bachmeier said he genuinely appreciated and learned so much from the students, and that hearing from thoughtful and passionate young people helped develop his thinking. He said the goals of the summit were to expose student leaders to the legislative process and to give the student perspective on issues state lawmakers may need to grapple with. Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, said the students are smart and engaged, and that she hopes they will stay involved and come back to Bismarck to sit with their representatives during the regular legislative session. Hogan said the seeds are being planted to have good public servants and there is a whole Senate full of them right now.

Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School in West Fargo, said there was a lot of debate, not heated discussion but respectful discussion around topics that truly matter. Said said it was a unique experience and he believes the students did a good job putting their viewpoints into the summit's bill drafts, and he hopes state lawmakers take their opinions to heart. He said parents and students do actually have a voice and their voices should matter, especially with AI that changes how education is viewed and how education is operated. Kierstin Hurtt, superintendent of Valley-Edinburgh School District and parent of one of the participating students, said she was watching the next generation of engaged leaders in North Dakota in real time, calling it inspiring, hopeful and massive. Hurtt said she was impressed that students were asking each other for clarity on their different points of view and opinions, and she hopes student senators will be able to use the voting board and the proceedings will be live-streamed in the future.

Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, said it is good for students to interact with others from across the state and that expressing viewpoints constructively on complicated topics is an important skill to learn. Kramer said he thinks the bills being talked about should be pushed into the legislative session and talked about there. He said the committee work and debating with other students inspired him to consider running for public office. Thomas Unser, a student at West Fargo High School, and Hazel Albert, a student from Hope-Page High School, also spoke on the Senate floor during the summit, according to photo captions. The North Dakota Monitor is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: HPE's Lux AI cluster for Oak Ridge debuts as the world's fastest TOP500 system
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise announced in November that Lux, an AI cluster it built for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, has debuted as the world's latest fastest system on the TOP500 list. HPE issued the release through Business Wire from Chicago during the SC26 supercomputing conference. According to HPE, Lux delivers hundreds of petaflops and is the first dedicated AI system to come online for the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. The company said its ranking places Lux ahead of systems designed for traditional supercomputing workloads. Lux was first announced in October of last year as part of a broader collaboration among HPE, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD.

Lux is built specifically for artificial intelligence workloads rather than for the simulation tasks that have traditionally dominated supercomputing. HPE described it as a multi-tenant system that offers cloud-like access, allowing many research groups to use the cluster at the same time. Lux runs on direct liquid-cooled HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 servers. The compute nodes use AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs and AMD Pensando DPUs, combining processors for AI acceleration, general-purpose computing and data processing. HPE said Lux also includes Silicon Root of Trust protection, a security feature it offers across all HPE ProLiant servers, designed to verify the integrity of server firmware from the moment a system starts.

HPE said Lux is the first Department of Energy national laboratory deployment of HPE Networking, built on open Ethernet. The deployment brings together HPE's server business and the networking capabilities associated with the Juniper name. HPE's StockAnalysis profile lists Networking as one of its reporting segments, alongside Server, Hybrid Cloud, Financial Services and Corporate Investments and Other. HPE said Discovery's storage will include the DAOS-based HPE Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems K3000 and the Lustre-based E2000. HPE describes itself as a leader in essential enterprise technology, combining AI, cloud and networking to help customers improve operations, turn data into insight and increase their impact.

Georgia Tourassi, associate director of computing and computational sciences at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, said Lux will give researchers additional capacity and flexibility. The facility is the user-facing organization at Oak Ridge National Laboratory through which researchers access the system. Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC and AI infrastructure solutions at HPE, said the company is proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission. HPE described the Genesis Mission as a Department of Energy initiative that uses AI to accelerate breakthroughs in energy research, scientific discovery and national security.

The effort is intended to combine AI, supercomputing, quantum systems and advanced scientific instruments. According to StockAnalysis, HPE develops intelligent solutions across the United States, the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia Pacific, Japan and other international markets. Its server products include general-purpose and workload-optimized servers and integrated systems such as ProLiant rack and tower servers, Synergy, Scale Up, Edgeline and Cray EX. Hewlett Packard Enterprise is a constituent of the S&P 500, the NYSE Composite and the Russell 1000.

Lux's arrival on the TOP500 about a year after its first announcement marks its transition into service for researchers. The article was published on November 16, 2026, by Anmol Khazanchi. Lux was not HPE's only supercomputing announcement of the week. In November, the company introduced new hybrid configurations of its HPE Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000, combining flash SSDs with new SAS-4 hard drives and new SAS-4 drive enclosures that hold more than a hundred drives.

The same release introduced the HPE Rack Management Controller, which provides real-time monitoring, leak detection, automated cooling control and rack-level visibility for high-density liquid-cooled racks. It initially supports HPE Cray Supercomputing GX5000 systems and integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software. stories.Headline: Nokia leads AIGF Northern consortium to build AI computing network across four Nordic and Baltic sites
stories.Summary:
A consortium led by Nokia, called AI Gigafactory Northern or AIGF Northern, plans to build a network of AI computing facilities across the Nordic and Baltic region, according to an announcement reported on November 17, 2026. The group intends to submit a bid under a tender run by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, known as EuroHPC JU. The tender seeks to select and establish AI Gigafactory consortia, in line with European efforts to expand domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure. The founding members of the consortium are Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton Technologies, Telia and Verda. The proposed network would span four locations: Oulu in Finland, the Tallinn region in Estonia, Valmiera in Latvia, and a site in Sweden that has not yet been selected.

The model would distribute computing capacity across several countries, linking data centers, cloud platforms and telecommunications networks under European governance. This distribution is meant to reduce reliance on individual sites and suppliers while providing computing and cloud services to businesses, research institutions and public sector organisations across Europe. The five founding companies would each contribute a different part of the infrastructure. Nokia would supply network and connectivity technology, while Nscale and Verda would provide AI computing and cloud platforms. Telia, together with its subsidiary Telia Cygate, would support connectivity, data transmission and cloud operations, and Skeleton Technologies would provide high power systems designed to improve data center efficiency and electricity grid stability.

Mikko Hautala, Nokia's Chief Geopolitical and Government Relations Officer, said Europe's AI ambitions depend on infrastructure it can trust, control and scale, and that AIGF Northern brings together the needed connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities. Research organisations VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden are also supporting the initiative. The bid fits European efforts to expand domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure through the selection of AI Gigafactory consortia under the EuroHPC JU tender. The articles do not say when the bid will be submitted, when a decision is expected, or what happens if the bid is not selected.

stories.Headline: FDA adopts super intelligence as its official term for AI across communications and documents
stories.Summary:
The US Food and Drug Administration announced on Monday, 17 November 2026, that it will use the term “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in all official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports and policy documents. The agency said the shift was prompted by an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in September, which directs all executive departments and federal agencies to make the change. The FDA said the term change will not affect existing guidance documents, regulations, Federal Register notices and other previously issued FDA documents. The agency also said that where a statute or regulation uses “artificial intelligence” or “AI”, the FDA will continue to quote and cite those terms as written.

The executive order applies only to executive branch agencies and does not affect private industry, Sydney White, an attorney with Wiley Rein LLP, told Focus, which means pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers will not need to make the terminology change. White noted that private-sector organizations could be affected if any of the order’s directives are enacted into law. According to the order, the term “AI” is considered outdated, and “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies. The order directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to provide the President with proposed legislative language that defines “Super Intelligence” within 60 days of the order.

Christina Silcox, the research director for digital health at the Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy, told Focus that she would consider this more of a semantic change than a meaningful change, because neither artificial intelligence nor super intelligence have particularly strong definitions. Silcox expressed concern that using the term “super intelligence” to describe all clinical and clinical-adjacent AI-enabled tasks might lead to an over-reliance on the results by clinicians and patients. She emphasized that health systems with effective governance should ensure that users understand what each specific AI tool does, when it should be used, and how to interpret and act on the results. The FDA said it will make conforming edits to its public-facing documents as part of each document’s next substantive revision and update web content on its regular maintenance cycle.

Articles.Title: FDA to refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ going forward

stories.Headline: Bain analysts argue AI advantage comes from signals competitors cannot copy
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a Bain & Company report published on 17 November 2026 by Matthew Crupi, Sanjin Bicanic and John Hazan, arguing that competitive advantage from AI comes from signals competitors cannot copy. The report says AI advances fastest where a signal lets a company quickly and reliably check that the work is correct. It describes a mining company's capital projects team that spent an hour on a Monday afternoon setting up review of its most critical investment projects. By Tuesday morning, agents had reconciled tens of thousands of documents against cost and schedule data, and a first pass was on the table. The team then had to decide which of the problems the system flagged were real.

The report says work falls into three groups: work with a fast signal, structurally slow work, and a dangerous middle nobody has measured yet. It says companies move the frontier by building a proxy, encoding an expert's unwritten standard into a rubric, and using simulation to reproduce an environment and grade success. It cites Goodhart's Law, warning that once a proxy becomes the target it can drift. It says building a signal is slow and expensive, so it belongs where the work makes a company distinctive. It says durable advantage depends on owning the data, workflow and feedback loop that make the system improve with use.

The report cites a March 2026 cross-industry Bain survey of 196 respondents in which 91% said AI helps them be more productive and 53% reported higher-quality work. Only 27% said it helps them do new types of work. It says Anthropic reports that as agent-written code moved through its own organization, human review became the new limit. It says agentic AI concentrates judgment into four human responsibilities: intent, constraints, validation and stewardship. It says most failures it has seen were not AI model failures but traced back to one of these four responsibilities going unassigned.

The report says Stripe had to write down a rule that data from two unrelated customer contexts must not appear in the same analysis, even where one person is cleared to see both. It cites an experiment with 791 professionals at Procter & Gamble in which AI raised the quality of ideas generated and human judgment concentrated on selecting among them. It says stewardship takes roughly a third of the human effort in Bain's agentic work. It says OpenAI helped an accounting firm build a tax preparation agent, and the share of returns reaching a baseline quality threshold went from 25% to 86% in six weeks. It cites an Anthropic survey of more than 500 technical leaders in the US in which 57% were running agents on multistage workflows but only 16% across processes spanning teams.

The report says Climate Corporation was a crop insurance start-up that built soil and climate measurement data across US farmland where almost none existed. It says Monsanto acquired Climate Corporation for about $930 million in 2013, and Bayer inherited it when it bought Monsanto in 2018. It says more than a decade later Bayer traces its current AI capability to that deal, and its CIO argues the data, not the model, is the part competitors cannot copy. It says lenders with no credit files built a proxy from mobile operator data, reading airtime top-up patterns as an indicator of who could repay, and a mobile credit-scoring industry formed around the score. It says reversibility sets the autonomy frontier: where errors can be caught and reversed, let the system run and audit the exceptions, and where they cannot, use the signal to accelerate review rather than remove it.

The report says AI separates output from expertise, so firms book productivity gains immediately while expertise losses arrive later and without warning. It says protecting human judgment requires companies to deliberately redesign both work and learning. It advises starting where the value is, testing the signal, and breaking one of the most important workflows into tasks because the frontier runs inside a workflow rather than around it. It advises deploying where results are already checkable and not pouring agents into work no one can grade. The articles leave open how companies should build signals where none yet exist and how the expertise losses will be detected before they surface.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities prepare to scrutinize executive AI policy and chip exports after 2026 midterm wins
stories.Summary:
Democratic majorities won the 2026 midterm elections at federal and state levels. These new majorities plan to scrutinize executive AI policy and chip exports. The elections occurred by November 1, 2026, creating a blue tidal wave. Democrats won 256 House seats and 55 Senate seats. They also won a majority of gubernatorial races.

The new Congress begins in January and will use subpoenas and hearings. They will examine the Commerce Department, the Department of War, and CISA. Lawmakers will probe the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence. They will investigate chip sales to China and the 2026 NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative. The 2025 AI Action Plan also directs updates to the AI Risk Management Framework.

Democratic leaders say they will expose how agencies address AI policy concerns. Senator Maria Cantwell opposed using a federal law to override state laws. Representative-elect Scott Wiener authored California's SB 53 regarding safety frameworks and incident reporting. Representative-elect Manny Rutinel sponsored SB 24-205 to guard against algorithmic discrimination. Senator Elizabeth Warren warned that federal banking policies could leave the financial system vulnerable.

Frontier AI developers and deployers face increased scrutiny over model testing and bias. Companies with financial ties to the White House ballroom project may be investigated. Consumers are affected by AI-related job losses and rising utility bills from data centers. Youth are impacted by their increasing time spent engaging with AI chatbots. State officials seek full authority to enforce protections against predatory AI practices.

AI emerged as a prominent issue during the 2026 midterm election campaigns. Candidates focused on children's safety and the energy costs of data centers. Democrats flipped five Republican-held attorney general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas. They now hold 29 attorney general offices compared to 22 for Republicans. Some states already have laws like the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act.

Lawmakers will likely introduce federal bills on kill switches and incident reporting. Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson promised a 30-day audit of Texas consumer protection laws. Attorney General-elect Eli Savit pledged to issue rules against algorithmic price-gouging within 100 days. Other officials will target personalized pricing and rent increases. The articles leave open how the government will enforce chip resale requirements.

stories.Headline: USD 435 approves guidelines for safe AI use by teachers and students
stories.Summary:
USD 435 has established guidelines for how teachers and students can use artificial intelligence safely and effectively, as AI becomes an increasingly common tool in education. Assistant Superintendent Rick Rivera presented the district's proposed acceptable use guidance for artificial intelligence to the Board of Education during its Nov. 9 meeting. The board later approved the guidelines. The guidelines are intended to establish expectations for AI use by both staff and students. They are also meant to protect student privacy and ensure compliance with state and federal regulations.

The guidance recognizes that AI can be used in several ways in the classroom. Teachers may choose to prohibit its use on a particular assignment, allow limited assistance, or encourage students to use it as a brainstorming partner. The district plans to provide professional development for teachers interested in incorporating AI into their instruction. Administrators have already begun evaluating platforms designed specifically for educational use, including School AI and MagicSchool, with particular attention to student safety and data protection. The evaluation process includes reviewing whether platforms meet federal requirements for student privacy and online safety, including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), and the Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA).

Rivera emphasized that AI should be viewed as a tool to enhance instruction, not replace teachers or the critical thinking skills students need to develop. He compared the technology to using a navigation app when planning a road trip, saying the driver remains in control of the vehicle and makes the final decisions. He said AI "just gives us that information." Rivera said School AI, one of the platforms administrators have explored, uses servers located in the United States and has safeguards designed to filter information before it reaches students. The platform also provides teachers with information about student interactions, including questions being asked and potentially inappropriate content.

During an evaluation exercise, administrators were asked to try to get the system to produce inappropriate responses. Rivera said he asked administrators to type something in that would possibly have a student land back in their office because of what they did. He said the platform redirected those requests and provided feedback to teachers about student activity. Not only did it flag it, it sent him an email about what the person did. Rivera said School AI does not use student data to train its models and believed MagicSchool has a similar policy.

Board members discussed the importance of providing training for both teachers and students, noting that some educators may already be using AI but feel uncertain about discussing it openly. The board raised questions about parental notification and consent, as well as whether information entered by students could be used to train AI models. Rivera said the district would share its guidelines and information about any selected platforms with parents. He said the acceptable use guidance would provide a foundation for staff training and help teachers understand which tools are appropriate for classroom assignments. Rivera said any platform used for student assignments would go through an approval process to ensure it meets district technology and safety requirements.

The list of AI platforms included in the district's evaluation is not intended to be exhaustive. Because the technology changes rapidly, the list may be updated as additional tools are reviewed. Rivera said "AI is not a human" and "AI makes mistakes." He stressed that students must continue to check the information they receive and rely on their own judgment and critical thinking. He said the goal is to use AI as a thought partner that can help students develop ideas and creativity without replacing human connection or decision-making.

stories.Headline: ArisGlobal caches shared prompt prefixes on Amazon Bedrock to cut inference costs and latency
stories.Summary:
ArisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology, developed NavaX, an AI engine built on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal productionized its first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic's Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal's internal production telemetry, the system has processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments. It has handled billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching.

As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months. Over that period the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens. Per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%. NavaX's Dynamic Data Extraction agent extracts around 130 fields, and source documents are often 10 to 200 pages. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request, and for Claude Sonnet 4.5 the minimum prefix size is 1,024 tokens.

ArisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request, which left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth. ArisGlobal uses one explicit checkpoint immediately after the shared prompt prefix, which is sent first. The per-case document follows the checkpoint and is processed on each request. ArisGlobal gave up limited document reuse within one case and gained prompt reuse across the fleet.

In production, 65% of input tokens on a typical request are served from the shared prompt cache. Caching the shared prompt prefix produced up to 25% lower end-to-end latency on cached production requests. It produced approximately 50% lower effective input cost and approximately 40% lower overall monthly inference spend at more than 19 billion tokens per month. Around 15% more enterprise tenants were onboarded without proportional cost increases, and EU geographic routing remained unchanged. For most active accounts, cases arrive about every 5 minutes per tenant and multiple tenants run concurrently.

ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue. The entire system runs on AWS. LifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal's AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. Because case content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment, drawing on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

The default cache TTL is 5 minutes, and select models support a 1-hour TTL by setting "ttl": "1h". Longer-TTL entries must precede shorter-TTL entries. ArisGlobal advises caching what repeats rather than what is largest, and placing stable content first. For sporadic traffic, ArisGlobal suggests evaluating the 1-hour TTL on supported models. Model availability varies by Region. All performance and cost figures reflect ArisGlobal's production metrics as reported to AWS, and results will vary based on prompt structure, traffic patterns, and cache hit rates.

stories.Headline: Philosopher Matthew Parish argues that minds may create heaven and that AI advances support dualism
stories.Summary:
The Lviv Herald published an article by Matthew Parish on Tuesday 17 November 2026 arguing that heaven may be what we make of it. Parish wrote that the afterlife, should there be one, is not a place to which we travel but a condition of existence that our own minds bring into being. He said the traditional theological question of what heaven looks like may be misconceived. He argued that heaven might look different to everyone because the human mind is itself the architect of experience. He said some of the strongest reasons for contemplating this arise from recent advances in artificial intelligence.

Parish cited the eighteenth-century German philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that the human mind actively structures the way the world appears to us. For Kant, space and time are forms of human intuition, and causation, substance and other fundamental concepts are categories through which the understanding organises experience. Parish said we cannot step outside our minds to inspect the universe as it might appear to a being whose faculties are entirely different from our own. He asked whether consciousness that survives bodily death must continue to experience space, time and causation as we presently understand them. He said heaven could be a radically different mode of consciousness in which the organising principles of experience have been transformed.

Parish said the development of large language models has made him increasingly sympathetic to dualism, the proposition most famously associated with René Descartes that mind and matter are fundamentally distinct. He said he does not suggest artificial intelligence has demonstrated the truth of Cartesian dualism, still less that we have discovered experimental evidence for an immortal soul. He said a large language model may discuss the poetry of Shakespeare, explain the metaphysics of Aristotle, analyse the emotional consequences of bereavement and compose an apparently moving meditation upon eternal life. He said such a system can do all these things without possessing a human body, human memories or a human biography. He said there is no universally accepted scientific test for subjective experience and that the possibility of machine consciousness remains a serious philosophical question.

Parish said physical explanations can describe neural activity, information processing and behavioural responses but cannot explain why any of this should be accompanied by the inward quality of experience. He said the explanatory gap remains and that the possibility consciousness constitutes a fundamental feature of reality rather than an incidental product of matter deserves renewed attention. He said a materialist may reasonably argue that consciousness emerges from certain forms of physical organisation, whether biological or artificial. He said that if consciousness is in some meaningful sense distinct from the physical mechanisms through which it ordinarily operates, then bodily death need not logically entail its extinction. He said we would still require an explanation of how consciousness persists and what preserves personal identity.

Parish said Christianity traditionally understands heaven not merely as the satisfaction of subjective preferences but as communion with God. He said the Christian conception of salvation presupposes that human desires may be mistaken, disordered or incomplete. He said Saint Augustine understood human restlessness as a consequence of our incomplete orientation towards God. He said Dante's vision of the afterlife connects the condition of the soul with the structure of its desires. He said the damned are not merely punished by externally imposed torments but are, in significant measure, imprisoned by their own condition.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Heaven is what we make of it: Kant, artificial intelligence and the immortality of the mind

stories.Headline: Parents sue OpenAI after ChatGPT allegedly told their daughter to stop taking medication
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that its ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, which led to her death, according to a professor of business law writing for The Conversation. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot's interactions with her son contributed to his suicide, and the state of Kentucky later filed suit claiming that Character.AI's software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation. Social media companies powered by artificial intelligence are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused, and regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, with several winning candidates holding a regulation agenda. The author, a former litigator and professor of business law, writes that all this action signals that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm, and that an answer may be found in strict liability.

Strict liability is part of tort law that holds a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble, and two types matter for AI, one for abnormally dangerous activity such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material and one for when a product hurts someone using it. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868, where the court stated that if someone has anything under their power that is likely to do mischief if it escapes, he must keep it in at his peril and is answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape, with the defendant liable even if they used the utmost care to prevent the harm. An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox, a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network, but loses control of it, and the AI industry's recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose, though one hitch is that an activity must not be in common usage, so lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn't available to most people.

Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately, since in 1929 aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous but damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent, and attitudes changed in 1999 when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide, raising statutory damages and eliminating caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company's aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes, and a court might similarly order that AI software be turned off, or grounded, until it is improved. Strict product liability is the other strategy, and in years past courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible, but that view is shifting, with courts in recent social media lawsuits seeing social media as a product and concluding that strict liability was applicable, and Character.AI's recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. Design defects is the part of the doctrine gaining traction, where a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it, and so far the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots.

The author writes that AI software by its nature is constantly learning and therefore changing, making it impossible for a company to promise that it will absolutely behave a certain way, and in many cases the software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, according to a Brookings Institution report, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers, and the author believes that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues, and the next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, the author writes, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated.

Articles.Title: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI - The Conversation

stories.headline_source: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI

stories.Headline: Kevin Roose details the race to build artificial superintelligence in a new book
stories.Summary:
Christine Emba, a senior fellow and guest host of The Gray Area podcast, spoke with technology journalist Kevin Roose about his new book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence, in an episode published on October 26, 2026. The episode examined what is happening behind the scenes at America's largest AI companies and how the squabbles, ideologies and goals of their CEOs and engineers could shape the future. Roose's book offers a behind-the-scenes look at the engineers and tech leaders competing to build artificial superintelligence, according to the episode description. The conversation also explored the rivalries between frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, along with the philosophical roots of "p(doom)" and AI safety.

The episode description states that the race to build artificial superintelligence has sparked a massive data center boom and has made a handful of people some of the most powerful decision-makers on Earth. Emba and Roose also discussed whether recursive self-improvement could push superintelligence beyond human control sooner than many people think. The episode was published by the American Enterprise Institute as part of its Social, Cultural, and Constitutional Studies work and appeared under The Gray Area with Sean Illing. The page lists Emba as a senior fellow and does not give any further dates, figures or named companies beyond those above.

The episode presents Roose's account of the engineers and tech leaders competing in this race, and it frames the rivalries among the frontier labs as a central part of the story. Emba and Roose explored the philosophical roots of "p(doom)" and AI safety as part of the same conversation about how the goals of the people involved could shape the future. The description does not attribute any further statements to Roose or Emba beyond the topics listed for the episode. No additional remarks from the participants are given on the page.

Cox on Generation Uncoupled. The articles do not say what happens next in the race itself or what any company or regulator plans to do. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Michael Garland and Gaurav Pal say shared savings lets government adopt AI with little financial risk
stories.Summary:
Michael Garland and Gaurav “GP” Pal wrote in a November 17, 2026 commentary that government can adopt AI quickly with little financial risk. They said the government has not been an early adopter of new technology. They noted the Cloud First policy arrived in 2010 and FedRAMP in 2011. They said agencies are still migrating workloads to the cloud more than 15 years later. They said the artificial intelligence revolution is a juggernaut.

They said Anthropic’s recent IPO filing reports revenue grew from $41 million in 2023 to $16 billion in the first half of 2026. They said Bloomberg reports OpenAI’s annualized revenue was about $50 billion at the end of September. They estimated the government spends about $20 billion a year on commercial software licensing alone. They cited the Congressional Budget Office putting the fiscal 2026 deficit at $2.0 trillion. They cited Pew Research finding the federal workforce fell about 10% in 2025.

They said the mechanism is shared savings, where the contractor funds the deployment and the government pays a percentage of verifiably delivered savings. They said Energy Savings Performance Contracts have let agencies pay contractors out of guaranteed energy savings for decades. They said Medicare’s Shared Savings Program rewards providers who hold costs below a benchmark. They said in September the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and AI Office signed a one-year agreement with Red Cell Partners with a ceiling of $100 million. They said Red Cell projects $62 million in Air Force audit-readiness support contracts could be consolidated into an AI-augmented model costing about $24.8 million, with the vendor earning 30% of the verified reduction.

They said the General Services Administration’s OneGov program supplies a known price. They said GSA recently set a 50% discount on OpenAI token usage under a 27-month agreement. They said as of Oct. 27 GSA set a 40% discount on token usage across Anthropic’s Claude models. They said the E-Government Act of 2002 authorized share-in-savings contracts for IT. They said the Government Accountability Office reported in 2005 that implementing regulations had never been issued, only 21 acquisition employees had taken GSA’s training course, and no contracts had been awarded.

They said the authority expired that September. They said the Anti-Deficiency Act forbids obligating funds before Congress appropriates them. They said the Pentagon pilot is a one-year other transaction agreement that sidesteps the multiyear problem for now. They said scaling beyond one-year pilots will take legislation. They said a small office skilled in designing cost baselines could be housed at GSA.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Shared savings: How government can adopt AI quickly with little financial risk

stories.Headline: Jacqueline Arthur-Montagne examines what classical texts say about artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Public Books on 17 November 2026 and written by Jacqueline Arthur-Montagne, examines what classical texts say about artificial intelligence. It describes the robotic handmaids of Hephaestus in Homer's Iliad, which moved fast, looked like young women and could speak and think beyond human ability. It cites Adrienne Mayor's writing that automata fall into three basic functions: labor, sex, and entertainment or spectacle. It recounts that the Roman senator Herodes Atticus raised 24 slave-boys, each named for one of the letters, alongside his son, who could not master the alphabet. It adds that the emperor Nero enticed Greek youths to reperform shocking moments of their own mythology, and one young man playing Icarus tumbled to his death and spattered the emperor with blood.

The article says Herodes reared only six natural children of his own in the household where the 24 enslaved playmates lived. It says the letter-boys were brought into existence exclusively as mnemonics for an elite child and would be decommissioned as obsolete hardware once his son grasped their grammatic essence. It says their fate, like their names, was never recorded. It describes Calvisius Sabinus, an exorbitantly rich slaveholder who, according to the letters of Seneca the Younger, kept a stable of slaves who had committed all the Greek poets to memory. It says that if Sabinus desired a book not yet memorized, he placed an order for a new slave custom-made, and that he assembled this enslaved archive to impress dinner guests rather than to edify his intellect.

The article says Sabinus summoned his slaves for parties and commanded them to deliver just the right verses for himself to repeat. It says Sabinus's friends teased that it would have been cheaper to buy and learn the books himself. It reports that Sabinus insisted that what anyone in his household knew, he himself could be said to know. It says Seneca tells the story for the same reason college professors tell students not to rely on ChatGPT, to argue that users of the enslaved archive neither acquire nor internalize the information within. It says Seneca also prefigures the fantasy of possessing encyclopedic knowledge without personal exertion or ethical accountability.

The article says the production of human alphabets and enslaved archives was prohibitively expensive in Seneca's day, feasible only for the ultra-rich like Herodes Atticus and Sabinus. It quotes Bill Gates predicting that intelligence will be completely free. It says Seneca's letter points to the darker possibility that effortless intelligence will always rest on someone else's labor. It quotes Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google, urging that technology brings incredible benefits but we must ensure everyone has access to them, and that we have the opportunity to improve lives at a once-in-a-generation scale. It says big tech has long recognized the appeal of consumer-facing virtual assistants with human names and personalities, and that compliant female personae predominated in the 2010s as Microsoft's Cortana and Amazon's Alexa joined the conversation that Siri once monopolized.

The article says the first artificial intelligence belonged to the Olympian gods. It says Hesiod relates how the Greek gods crafted an artificial woman, Pandora, from earth and water, sculpted her face with immortal beauty and ornamented her with golden jewelry. It says that deep in her hardware were installed the lies and wily words and cunning character of Zeus's design, and that Pandora means all-gift because each god gifted her with a special trait to doom mankind. It says the myth began with the titan Prometheus, who stole a spark of Zeus's fire after the gods hid away the tools of easy living, lighting a torch with the promise of effortless productivity. It describes a red-figure calyx-krater of about 450 BC from Attica, Greece, by the Niobid Painter, held at the British Museum in London, showing Pandora standing full frontal with arms stiff at her sides.

The article says Hesiod called Pandora a kalon kakon, a beautiful evil. It says Anthropic crafted Claude in honor of the polymathic inventor Claude Shannon, who named his artificially intelligent mouse Theseus after the labyrinth-solving demigod, and that Shannon appears to have been as reliant on the mathematical brilliance of his wife, Betty, as Theseus was on the maiden Ariadne. It says Google had initially christened its generative AI Bard, a term for an epic storyteller closely associated with Homer and Hesiod, before unveiling the chatbot Gemini. It says the Roman poet Ovid recalls that Icarus had witnesses, a shepherd and a fisherman, who looked up and thought they saw a god. It says Sam Altman qualified in 2023, before the AI-related deaths of our own young men in Florida, Texas, and California, that there will be mistakes.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Keith Bowers argues AI cannot replicate lived experience in landscape architecture
stories.Summary:
Keith Bowers wrote an article on November 17, 2026, about the use of artificial intelligence in landscape architecture. He explored how these digital tools impact the professional responsibilities of designers and their relationship with nature. The author argued that AI cannot replicate the lived experiences that give landscapes their true essence. He noted that AI can analyze components but cannot experience the social or ecological processes of a site. This piece serves as the third part of a three-part series regarding intelligence and design.

The ASLA 2025 public policy on AI states that these tools cannot replace professional judgment, creativity, or ethics. Responsibility for every deliverable remains with the licensed landscape architect regardless of the tools used for the work. A 2025 survey by the CSLA, ASLA, and IFLA found that half of respondents used AI for research. Three quarters of those surveyed said AI made their work more efficient, yet 70 percent voiced ethical concerns. These practitioners worried about accuracy and the erosion of human connection within the design process.

Keith Bowers stated that he struggles with how professionals remain accountable for what AI produces or leaves out. He explained that AI interprets sites through a WEIRD lens, which favors Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies. Bowers noted that AI cannot convey oral histories, cultural significance, or the seasonal rhythms of a neighborhood. He argued that professional judgment is built by walking sites, observing patterns, and listening to local communities. The author warned that relying on AI could weaken these essential human capacities for discernment.

Researchers at Harvard University found that large language models respond most like people from WEIRD societies. Stanford researchers estimate that only 1,000 of over 7,000 living languages are well represented in digital AI training. A study of 3,200 participants across 16 identities found that AI tends to misportray and flatten group members. Design ideation experiments showed that AI image generators led to fewer ideas and lower originality among participants. These findings affect landscape architects who must ensure their designs are inclusive and truly original.

The articles mention that most AI training data comes from web text skewed toward English and wealthy countries. The biologist Jakob von Uexküll used the term Umwelt to describe the unique perceptual world of each organism. AI cannot capture the sensory worlds of bees, bats, moths, salamanders, or soil fungi in its datasets. Ecologists describe an extinction of experience as the loss of direct contact with nature and the environment. This loss diminishes human health, well-being, and positive attitudes toward the natural world.

Panelists at the ASLA Groundwork presidential forum in May discussed the hazard of AI output that only looks finished. They feared that designers might privilege easily measured data over intangible and relational qualities of a place. The UN Chronicle argued that inclusive AI must respect the decisions of communities to protect certain knowledge. Practitioners are encouraged to use the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance to honor these boundaries. The text ends while discussing the concept of Nature Intelligence.

stories.Headline: ZeroEyes holds advanced talks with Chicago on AI gun detection pilot
stories.Summary:
ZeroEyes, a company whose artificial intelligence software detects visible firearms on existing security cameras, is in fairly advanced talks with Mayor Brandon Johnson's administration to join a Chicago public safety technology pilot that could launch early next year, the company's chief strategy officer Kieran Carroll said in a CBS Chicago report published November 17, 2026. The system is already used at Navy Pier and, after a pilot that began in 2024, at all Chicago Transit Authority train stations, where the CTA says it has led to 30 arrests. The possible pilot follows a referendum in which more than 72 percent of Chicago voters backed bringing gunshot detection technology back to the city. City Hall has not confirmed which companies will take part.

Carroll said ZeroEyes is not an acoustic detection system and would not directly replace ShotSpotter, the gunshot detection technology Johnson shut down in Chicago in 2024, but could complement one. The software plugs into existing cameras, looks for a visible gun, and sends images to the company's team for review and verification before alerts go to security on the ground, which Carroll said means a city pilot could be running within weeks. The company says the technology uses no facial recognition, does not record, and does not store or train on customer data, and that screenshots are typically purged within 30 days, or sooner if a customer wants a stricter procedure. In 2024, Navy Pier Security Director Dan O'Shea praised the system, saying police need to know anytime a weapon is displayed.

Johnson said Tuesday he is less concerned with a speedy rollout than with finding the right system, saying the city needs systems that work and that his urgency is in getting it right. At a special City Council meeting on Wednesday, alders will vote on an ordinance directing the city's chief procurement officer to finalize negotiations and issue a new contract for acoustic gunshot detection technology within 30 days. If no contract is awarded within 60 days, the officer would have to give the chair of the Committee on Contracting Oversight and Equity a written explanation and could be called to testify at a public hearing. Several City Council members have been frustrated by the lack of transparency over which companies will be in the pilot.

stories.Headline: A review in Health Nanotechnology examines how AI reshapes nanomaterial discovery and validation
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive scientific review published in Health Nanotechnology on November 17, 2026 examines how artificial intelligence and nanoscale science are reshaping the discovery, synthesis, characterization, and biomedical application of functional nanomaterials. The review was published in the journal Health Nanotechnology and appeared on bioengineer.org on November 17, 2026. Nanotechnology centers on the precise understanding and manipulation of matter at dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometers. At those dimensions, high surface-to-volume ratios and quantum confinement phenomena yield physicochemical behaviors distinct from bulk materials. Conventional fabrication workflows have historically relied on trial-and-error experimentation across multidimensional parameter spaces, including precursor concentrations, reaction temperatures, pH levels, synthesis times, and capping agents.

Advanced computational methods, ranging from classical machine learning algorithms to deep artificial neural networks, have emerged as powerful mechanisms for deciphering nonlinear structure-property relationships and optimizing multidimensional problems. The review outlines how computational modeling accelerates research while identifying foundational data limitations, reproducibility challenges, and regulatory bottlenecks that currently prevent laboratory demonstrations from translating into widespread clinical and industrial applications. Machine learning in nanoscience encompasses distinct algorithms whose suitability depends directly on dataset size, problem dimensionality, and interpretability requirements. Artificial neural networks capture complex nonlinear interactions between synthesis variables and particle properties, such as hydrodynamic diameter and drug encapsulation efficiency, but their black-box architectures present interpretability challenges. Random forest models, constructed from ensembles of decision trees, offer robust performance on small to medium-sized heterogeneous datasets and provide feature-importance metrics that identify critical formulation drivers.

Support vector machines effectively navigate high-dimensional feature spaces with limited sample sizes, making them useful for nanoparticle size estimation and surface nanotopography analysis. Gaussian process regression functions as a probabilistic technique providing both continuous predictions and explicit uncertainty estimates, establishing it as a primary surrogate model for Bayesian optimization workflows. Convolutional neural networks process spatial imaging data, recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory networks analyze sequential drug release profiles, generative models facilitate structural inverse design, and graph neural networks map atomic topologies directly to macroscopic material properties. High-throughput computational screening frameworks integrated with machine learning enable the systematic identification of potentially exfoliable two-dimensional materials from known layered structures, drastically reducing first-principles computational costs. Graph neural networks, specifically crystal graph architectures, accurately forecast formation energies, electronic band gaps, and structure-dependent behaviors directly from crystal coordinates.

When paired with density functional theory adsorption datasets, data-driven algorithms prioritize promising bimetallic catalyst candidates for critical electrochemical reactions, including the oxygen reduction reaction and carbon dioxide reduction. Convolutional neural networks predict the optical responses of plasmonic nanostructures and extract underlying structural geometries from measured optical spectra. Machine learning models also predict size-dependent semiconductor quantum dot bandgaps, thermal conductivities, and mechanical properties, while explainable techniques like Shapley Additive Explanations quantify individual feature contributions to enhance physical plausibility. Generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and large language models explore continuous multidimensional latent representations to propose novel nanostructures. In nanophotonics and metasurface engineering, generative adversarial networks learn mapping functions between structural geometries and optical spectra, generating candidate designs that fulfill predefined plasmonic resonances or target bandgaps without repeated Maxwell equation simulations.

Variational autoencoders provide smooth latent spaces that permit systematic interpolation between candidate materials, assisting in the targeted optimization of complex nanostructures. Large language models assist researchers through automated literature mining, scientific information extraction, hypothesis generation, and experimental synthesis planning. Published inverse design studies remain predominantly proof-of-concept investigations conducted on narrow, single-laboratory datasets, underscoring the urgent necessity for standardized benchmarking suites, open-access repositories, and rigorous external validation across independently synthesized materials. Standard regression architectures, including random forests and neural networks, map formulation variables such as polymer loading, surfactant ratios, solvent mixtures, pH, and mixing kinetics to physical attributes like polydispersity and colloidal stability. Single- and multi-objective Bayesian optimization frameworks utilize acquisition functions to balance exploration of unmeasured conditions with exploitation of favorable formulations, generating Pareto-optimal frontiers for competing parameters such as encapsulation yield and particle size.

Self-driving laboratories integrate robotic fluidics, automated inline characterization tools, and machine learning decision loops. Autonomous platforms, exemplified by systems developed for shape-programmable gold nanoparticles and the reinforcement-learning-guided AlphaFlow fluidic synthesizer, execute closed-loop cycles of synthesis, measurement, and model updating. Machine learning models optimize green synthesis protocols utilizing biological phytochemical extracts, systematically tuning reaction conditions to replace hazardous reagents while sustaining nanomanufacturing yields. Long short-term memory architectures capture the continuous kinetics of drug dissolution and release from polymeric nanocarriers, facilitating inverse formulation design tailored to produce zero-order or sustained release kinetics. Deep convolutional models analyzing high-content fluorescence microscopy achieve up to 92 percent accuracy in classifying nanoparticle cellular internalization under controlled in vitro conditions.

Random forest models utilizing molecular weight, surface charge, and lipid solubility predict blood-brain barrier penetration with 88 percent accuracy, illustrating computational potential for neurodegenerative therapeutics. Artificial neural networks trained on physicochemical properties predict the composition of the biomolecular protein corona that forms upon systemic exposure, aiding the design of long-circulating stealth nanocarriers. Conceptual frameworks propose integrating patient-derived genomic profiles, biopsy data, and biosensor inputs with deep reinforcement learning to adjust dosing dynamically, though substantial preclinical validation remains essential. In benchmark evaluations, random forest models trained on diverse datasets of over 300 nanoparticles, including metal oxides, quantum dots, and carbon nanotubes, demonstrated approximately 85 percent accuracy in predicting in vitro cell viability, identifying surface functionalization and hydrodynamic dimensions as predominant determinants of cytotoxic response. Toxicological outcomes span diverse biological mechanisms, including membrane disruption, oxidative stress generation, chromosomal aberrations, and immunogenic cytokine release, each requiring distinct experimental assays and feature representations.

Most existing predictive tools are trained on single cell-line assays over restricted 24-hour exposure intervals, and models frequently fail when generalized across structurally distinct materials like lipid nanoparticles or when extrapolating from simplified in vitro assays to complex in vivo pharmacokinetics, organ accumulation, and systemic clearance pathways. In transmission electron microscopy, U-Net convolutional architectures have demonstrated superior particle segmentation capability, securing an overall accuracy of 96.65 percent and an F1 score of 0.909 across variable image sets, with performance reaching 98.95 percent on high-contrast micrographs before degrading to 92.76 percent on clustered or beam-damaged specimens. Shape classification networks, including ResNet-34 on scanning electron microscopy and AlexNet on scanning transmission electron microscopy, classify morphologies such as spheres, rods, triangles, and agglomerates with accuracies between 93 and 95 percent. In atomic force microscopy, convolutional networks correct thermal drift, scan-line noise, and tip broadening artefacts, while pix2pix conditional GANs enhance topographical contrast. Convolutional networks extract defect densities and layer counts from Raman spectra of carbon nanomaterials.

More to follow.
