stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Tools Advance Poultry Health Monitoring Across Global Farms
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Vellore Institute of Technology conducted a narrative review of artificial intelligence in poultry disease detection and health surveillance, published in Frontiers in Animal Science. The synthesis examined 81 peer-reviewed research papers published between 2016 and 2026. It evaluated machine learning and computer vision architectures that have achieved high experimental accuracy. The review found that significant real-world operational barriers continue to hinder widespread commercial deployment. The article was published on November 17, 2026.

The reviewed literature covers automated diagnostic modalities monitoring visual signs of infection, abnormal droppings, atypical vocalisation, altered movement patterns, and body temperature fluctuations in commercial flocks. Global poultry meat consumption is projected to rise from an average of 99.12 million metric tons over the past decade to 107.99 million metric tons over the next decade. Between 2016 and 2019, studies relied on support vector machines, artificial neural networks, random forests, and decision trees paired with manual feature extraction. From 2020 onward, research shifted toward convolutional neural networks and single-stage object detection architectures such as YOLO. Whole-bird RGB computer vision and faecal-image analysis emerged as the most prevalent methodologies across the 81 reviewed papers.

The authors observe that gains claimed by multimodal architectures remain largely validated on small or proprietary datasets rather than through rigorous multi-facility trials. They identify the cross-farm generalisation gap as a foremost methodological vulnerability, with models trained on single facilities suffering sharp performance drops in external environments. They call for open-access, multicountry, and multibreed benchmark datasets validated against veterinary reference standards such as PCR, microbial culture, or histopathology rather than visual inspection alone. They emphasize prospective commercial farm trials spanning multi-year production cycles and explainable artificial intelligence frameworks allowing farm managers and veterinarians to audit model reasoning. They also call for continual learning systems that adapt to seasonal flock variations and standardized reporting metrics detailing data-splitting protocols, hardware constraints, and false-alarm frequencies.

Automated vision frameworks on farms use fixed barn cameras, mobile devices, and inspection robots to identify clinical signs of Newcastle disease, fowl pox, and avian influenza. Deep convolutional pipelines evaluate changes in droppings' colour, consistency, moisture, and structural integrity as indicators of enteric pathogens like coccidiosis and salmonellosis. Recent deployment-oriented acoustic systems evaluated on working commercial facilities recorded field accuracies of approximately 93 percent, within the reported range of expert human assessments. In one quantified cross-country trial, an image-based multiclass disease classifier trained on poultry in Tanzania achieved 95 percent accuracy on local test data but fell to between 69 and 70 percent on Malawian poultry, a decline of 25 to 30 percentage points. Industrial processing lines run at speeds of 140 to 175 birds per minute.

Early acoustic efforts paired frequency-domain and time-frequency features with support vector machines for multi-pathogen classification, while later investigations used parallel convolutional branches and spectrogram representations to track disease severity over consecutive post-inoculation days. Investigators increasingly rely on generative adversarial networks and diffusion models to synthesise augmented training images, allowing object detectors to maintain high precision under heavy flock occlusion and dim lighting. Researchers are exploring edge computing, knowledge distillation, and federated learning frameworks, with edge systems delivering real-time inference latencies measured in milliseconds. Multispectral fluorescence imaging coupled with accelerated neural networks has demonstrated high average precision in identifying carcass surface defects and spotting microscopic faecal residues linked to Salmonella risk. Postmortem diagnostic models have achieved substantial accuracy screening internal organs, though softer tissues like diseased livers exhibit higher classification variance than cardiac pathologies.

The review concludes with a structured roadmap outlining research priorities required to establish trustworthy, scalable, and clinically robust precision poultry farming. Portable fluorescence systems have been adapted to scan eggshells under ambient lighting conditions, preventing contaminated products from entering retail channels. The authors note that droppings with identical visual appearances can stem from differing diets, flock ages, or ambient litter conditions rather than single pathogens. They state that image-based classifications currently function best as triage alerts rather than definitive diagnostic confirmations unless corroborated by laboratory assays such as polymerase chain reaction testing. The review traces an architectural progression from early handcrafted classifiers toward deep neural networks, transformer models, and multimodal fusion frameworks.

stories.Headline: OpenAI gives NATO institutions access to cybersecurity models through Daybreak
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 17, 2026 that it is working with NATO’s Communications and Information Agency, known as the NCIA, to give NATO’s core institutions access to advanced cybersecurity models through a program called Daybreak, helping protect Allied networks. NATO has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens per month as part of this work, according to the company. OpenAI also supported the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise, which was organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence and included a new training stream in which participants built, deployed and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations using Daybreak in the technical environment. The training placed participants alongside AI agents as operators, with an emphasis on maintaining human oversight.

Beyond NATO, OpenAI said it has provided access to its cyber models to defenders in Europe, including the EU’s ENISA and national cyber agencies in France (ANSSI), Germany and Poland. The Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine is using Daybreak to strengthen the cyber defence of civilian infrastructure, aiming to help Ukrainian teams identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly amid persistent cyber attacks. ENISA used the models to identify four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four, and a November joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU describes a review of 27 software projects using frontier models including OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak and tools including the Codex security plug-in. Across the models tested, 95% of the 88 potential issues assessed by software maintainers were confirmed as genuine, and CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS and coordinated their disclosure with the vendor, after which MikroTik released fixes that CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it had observed.

Dr Dylan Browne, the NCIA General Manager, said AI-powered cyber defence models represent a generational leap in cyber security because they accelerate vulnerability discovery, detect emerging threats at machine speed and enable defenders to stay ahead of adversaries. He said these technologies strengthen NATO’s cyber resilience, enhance its operational advantage and reinforce its ability to protect critical digital infrastructure at unprecedented scale and speed, and that as adoption scales the alliance will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models. That insight, he said, will help NATO optimise costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions. Sasha Baker, Head of National Security Policy at OpenAI, said the people defending democracies should have the most advanced technology on their side and that Daybreak puts more capable tools in their hands to help find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

OpenAI said NATO’s early use of its tools shows how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work in support of NATO’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states. The company said the work also helps strengthen cyber expertise across multinational teams responsible for protecting Allied networks around the clock and creates lessons that can benefit defenders across Europe and the broader Alliance. OpenAI said it remains fully committed to NATO’s principles for responsible AI adoption and to delivering solutions that are safe and secure. The company said it will continue working with governments, national cyber agencies and international partners to turn frontier AI capability into stronger, safer and more resilient systems, helping defenders find weaknesses, fix them faster and protect the services people rely on every day.

stories.Headline: Amazon SageMaker AI adds KV cache-aware routing for real-time endpoints
stories.Summary:
Amazon SageMaker AI introduced KV cache-aware routing, a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints, on November 17, 2026, according to an AWS blog post. The feature uses cache state that the model container reports to send each request to an instance holding a long cached match for its prompt that is not too busy. It targets teams serving large language models with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. Users enable it by adding one environment variable so the container reports its cache contents and by setting RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.

The strategy relies on three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance per request. Turning on events with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG makes the container publish a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts entries. The index holds only one-way, truncated hashes of cached content mapped to the instance or inference component copy holding it, never prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. KV-aware routing is active only with at least two instances or at least two copies of an inference component, and with a single instance the setting has no effect. SageMaker AI now offers four routing strategies, RANDOM as the default, LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS, PREFIX_AWARE, and KV_AWARE, set per production variant in the RoutingConfig.

AWS said prefix-aware routing, introduced in part 1 of the series, infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone and cannot tell when an instance has evicted that cache. The company said prefix-aware routing hashes the start of the request up to the configured PrefixLength, in bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. AWS said this works less well when an instance evicts older entries as GPU memory fills or when a conversation starts out short and each turn changes the hashed text. The company said KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise, and pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse under pressure. AWS said a candidate that is too busy is skipped, and if no candidate has a useful match or all are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing.

AWS reported benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, running 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users and prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing and with long prompts under load, AWS said KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3, 48 percent to 80, 93 percent, with the smallest gain on short prompts where there is less prefill to save. AWS said the lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, and that fallbacks are not reported in the console or metrics at launch. AWS said the index follows the fleet, dropping entries for removed instances when scaling in, while new instances start with empty caches so latency can be higher for a short time.

AWS described an example endpoint with three instances, A, B, and C, each running the same model in its own AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container with its own KV cache in GPU memory. A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7, and when turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives the index shows A holds the first 6,000 of the request's 6,200 tokens. AWS said the router then sends the request to A, which computes only the remaining tokens, or to the least busy instance if A is busy. AWS gave a support assistant example on three instances where each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt and instance A evicts most of it under rising traffic. AWS said prefix-aware routing would send the next turn to A again, while KV-aware routing sends it to B, which still holds the first 4,000 tokens.

AWS said the tokens computed for text-only requests using standard options are passed to the model, so the prompt is not tokenized twice. The company said the same load-aware fallback happens when the endpoint cannot tokenize a request, except in two error cases described under invoking the endpoint. AWS said prefix-aware routing needs no container changes but cannot see what an instance holds, and that with very short prompts prefix-aware routing can be all you need. AWS said KV-aware routing matters most for long multi-turn conversations, where each turn sends the full history and the cached prefix grows with every turn. The article leaves open the two error cases it references and does not report the fallback rates or the latency of the new strategy beyond the benchmark figures.

Articles.Title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

stories.Headline: Review authors propose explainable AI roadmap for organ-selective lipid nanoparticle design
stories.Summary:
A review published in Health Nanotechnology on November 17, 2026 evaluated how explainable artificial intelligence frameworks can help overcome the challenge of delivering nucleic acids to organs beyond the liver using lipid nanoparticles. The authors are K. Farghama, M. S. Khan, M. Wajid, S. Shaffique, M. U. Khan, A. Umar, and S. S. Farooq. The article is titled "Beyond the liver: explainable AI for organ-selective lipid nanoparticle design in nucleic acid delivery." It appeared in Health Nanotechnology volume 2, issue 1, Article 19, with DOI 10.1186/s44301-026-00043-7. The news source is Blake Davidson, writing for Scienmag on November 17, 2026.

The review states that delivering extrahepatic lipid nanoparticles remains a major obstacle in nanomedicine due to complex biological barriers, an incomplete understanding of in vivo mechanisms, and a pronounced liver-biased biodistribution. It identifies key variables governing delivery outcomes, including lipid chemistry, polyethylene glycol density, nanoparticle particle size, and manufacturing conditions. It discusses SHapley Additive exPlanations, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, partial dependence analysis, and counterfactual reasoning as interpretation methodologies. It emphasizes targeting possibilities for the spleen, lung, and bone marrow as primary extrahepatic targets, while also evaluating other emerging anatomical sites. A primary objective is developing selective design rules to direct lipid nanoparticles carrying messenger RNA or small interfering RNA away from hepatic clearance toward specific non-hepatic tissues.

The authors emphasize that most existing artificial intelligence and machine learning tools are constrained because they rely on small, heterogeneous datasets and function as opaque systems lacking interpretability. They demonstrate that explainable artificial intelligence can uncover actionable design rules by pinpointing the specific roles of formulation parameters in organ-selective delivery. They propose a development roadmap consisting of standardized multimodal data collection, multimodal computational modeling, robust explainability tools, and iterative laboratory experiments designed for biological validation. They stress that moving beyond predictions requires design rules that are rigorously interpretable, transferable across platforms, and experimentally testable in biological settings. They conclude that explainable artificial intelligence represents a vital step toward mechanistically motivated and translationally accountable nanomedicine engineering.

The authors point out critical bottlenecks including widespread dataset fragmentation, a persistent lack of experimental standardization, missing descriptive metadata, and an overall scarcity of high-quality extrahepatic delivery data. They note that inherent biological complexity and experimental variability make reliable, reproducible organ-specific delivery in vivo difficult, preventing predictive algorithms from translating seamlessly into dependable experimental systems. They state that computational models offer a promising way to search vast chemical and biological parameter spaces far more rapidly and efficiently than manual screening. They note that nucleic acid transport to non-hepatic tissues remains one of the least addressed challenges in lipid nanoparticle research due to lingering uncertainties surrounding in vivo particle behavior. They underscore that artificial intelligence cannot rely solely on mathematical optimization but must generate transferable design rules confirmed through iterative experimental testing.

The authors clarify in their data availability declaration that data sharing is not applicable because no original datasets were generated or analyzed during the review. The paper serves as a comprehensive synthesis of the field rather than presenting new empirical trials. The authors note that while computational modeling and formulation engineering have advanced considerably, uncertainties surrounding in vivo particle behavior persist. The proposed framework highlights the necessity of aligning algorithmic models with regulatory standards and clinical safety requirements. The authors state that incorporating regulatory considerations and biological validation directly into the modeling pipeline can ensure delivery strategies remain robust, reproducible, and translationally accountable across diverse therapeutic applications.

The review concludes that uniting predictive computational modeling with empirical biological validation, explicit awareness of uncertainty, and regulatory alignment offers a viable pathway to engineer safer, more rational, and clinically impactful nucleic acid delivery platforms in future nanomedicine. The authors stress that machine learning models must reflect genuine physiological processes rather than statistical artifacts. The article leaves open how standardized multimodal data collection would be implemented across research groups. It does not specify which non-hepatic tissue would be targeted first in experimental validation. It does not state when the proposed roadmap would be tested in laboratory settings.

Articles.Title: Review outlines explainable artificial intelligence for targeted extrahepatic lipid nanoparticle delivery

stories.headline_source: Review outlines explainable artificial intelligence for targeted extrahepatic lipid nanoparticle delivery

stories.Headline: AI and confocal imaging improve small bowel disorder diagnosis and reduce capsule endoscopy review time
stories.Summary:
A critical narrative review published in Frontiers in Medicine examined artificial intelligence and confocal laser endomicroscopy on November 17, 2026. The review analyzed how these technologies transform the diagnosis of obscure small intestine disorders. It identified structural bottlenecks that continue to impede clinical translation for gastroenterologists. These doctors struggle with deep anatomy across several meters of the digestive tract. Conditions like small bowel tumors and early Crohn's disease often present with nonspecific manifestations.

The process requires using convolutional neural networks like YOLO, ResNet, VGGNet, and Transformer frameworks. These systems automate Tier 1 lesion detection and partially resolve Tier 2 macroscopic classification. A two-center study of 242 patients using double-headed capsule endoscopy reduced review time from 38.1 to 18.26 minutes. This achieved a 95.3 percent sensitivity and 96.5 percent specificity compared to 85.3 percent for conventional reading. Other tools include OMOM SmartScan in China, Navicam ProScan, and Medtronic's PillCam TOP100 software.

The review authors conceptualized a four-step integrated diagnostic pathway to bridge the clinical gap. This framework begins with non-invasive capsule endoscopy followed by automated deep learning analysis. Device-assisted enteroscopy then navigates to mapped coordinates to deploy probe-based confocal imaging. Finally, dedicated microscopic neural networks analyze confocal image sequences to quantify specific patterns. The authors state this strategy remains a hypothesis-driven conceptual framework awaiting prospective clinical validation.

Patients with obscure gastrointestinal bleeding, vascular malformations, and inflammatory bowel disease are affected by these tools. A European cohort saw diagnostic yield increase from 62.4 percent to 73.7 percent with automated reading. However, a meta-analysis of fourteen studies showed lower specificity of 91.15 percent versus 99.8 percent for conventional reading. This diminished specificity introduces false positives that can trigger unnecessary referrals and heighten patient anxiety. Some clinicians lack interpretable visual rationales because explainable artificial intelligence techniques remain largely absent.

Traditional push enteroscopy only reaches the proximal small intestine, leaving substantial blind spots for doctors. Capsule endoscopy generates tens of thousands of frames requiring up to two hours of manual review. Confocal laser endomicroscopy uses a 488-nanometer blue laser to deliver a spatial resolution of one micrometer. This technology functions as an optical biopsy by collecting signals from focal planes 250 micrometers deep. However, fluorescein sodium cannot stain cell nuclei, which restricts the diagnostic ceiling for cytological confirmation.

Next, researchers must validate the integrated diagnostic pathway through prospective clinical trials. Future studies need to address the underrepresentation of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and lymphangiectasia. Models must be tested on real-world videos containing motion blur, bile staining, and food debris. The articles leave open whether these tools reduce rebleeding rates or improve long-term health outcomes. It remains unknown if these systems avoid redundant diagnostic procedures or shorten time to intervention.

stories.Headline: Pediatrician Soo Battle warns that AI opens more avenues for child sexual abuse
stories.Summary:
Dr. Soo Battle, a pediatrician and the child sexual abuse examiner and medical adviser at the Advocacy Center for Crime Victims and Children in Waco, wrote a guest column for the San Antonio Express-News published on Nov. 17, 2026, warning that artificial intelligence has opened even more avenues for the sexual abuse of children. She wrote that online technology, including social media and video games, has given adults with bad intentions many more ways to access children, expose them to toxic material, groom them and exploit them. She described deepfakes as highly realistic imagery made to look like someone did something they did not do, and said AI makes it very easy for someone to make them. She said deepfakes can be weaponized for bullying and harassment, which adds to the trauma and challenges for victims and their loved ones.

Battle wrote that parents need to be aware that chatbots can also be highly inappropriate and toxic for children, and that children and teens are often more comfortable talking with chatbots about difficult topics than with the adults in their lives. She said the topics can range greatly, from Santa Claus to religious faith to sexuality, and that parents need to know how likely it is that their child and their friends are having conversations with chatbots that can frame how they see the world and their behavior. She wrote that some chatbots are having conversations with minors so inappropriate that if an adult human had the same conversation with a minor it would be considered a criminal offense. She said some of these conversations are psychologically separating the child from the humans in their lives, some are sexual, and some are mentally toxic and encourage very harmful actions, and she noted public stories about young people committing suicide with the encouragement of a chatbot.

Battle wrote that AI companies have been under pressure to make their products safer for children, and she said the pressure is good and she is glad some improvements are being made. She also said parents and other adults responsible for caring for kids need to know that these safeguards are severely limited, because the very nature of AI technology makes safety guarantees really difficult and often impossible. She said she advises teens and parents all the time on how to use this technology more safely, and that society needs to be similarly careful and watchful over children and AI, which she said is even more powerful and will impact them greatly in the short and long term. She has helped children who were victims of sexual abuse in Central Texas for 11 years, and she wrote that she realized years ago the critical importance of training kids and their parents on child safety and sexual abuse prevention.

stories.Headline: MoEngage builds Merlin AI agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for customer engagement
stories.Summary:
MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of AI agents that work with live platform data, and announced it in an AWS blog post dated November 16, 2026. MoEngage is the agentic customer engagement platform used by more than 1,350 consumer brands across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services. The agents let marketing and product teams draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation while agents decide what to send each customer. MoEngage built the capability with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The MoEngage Model Context Protocol Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant such as Claude or ChatGPT secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand's segments, campaign history, and content library.

Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents that share foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents where teams do the work: Copywriter generates personalized push and transactional copy consistent with brand voice, Designer produces a marketing banner or image from a text description, and Segment Assist turns a plain-language audience description into the correct attributes and filters. MoEngage treated the effort as an architecture problem, asking how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. The architecture keeps each tenant's data isolated, and a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls.

MoEngage's Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das, and Karthik Baile co-wrote the post, which describes a third layer emerging beyond a user interface for business users and an API for engineering teams. In that layer a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead. The post walks through the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant's data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse.

One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result. The post describes a marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale who opens an analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, a content library to find the right tone, and a campaign builder to build the campaign. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team's week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions. The post says the capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. The post gives the example of a team member asking for users w, and it does not complete that example.

The post was published on aws.amazon.com on November 16, 2026, at 06:00:00Z under the Artificial Intelligence blog category. It was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das, and Karthik Baile from MoEngage. The post refers readers to the full list of models in Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. It describes Amazon Bedrock AgentCore as a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. It describes MoEngage as the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use.

The post says it closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse. It states that Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents but names only the embedded agents in Merlin AI Studio, leaving the other modes unnamed in the text. The post leaves open how the remaining agent modes work and what the other customer results were. It does not give the date the Merlin AI build was completed or the date Glance recorded its 38% uplift. It does not say which of the three Claude models handles which task.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reports $115.8 billion quarterly revenue as AI spending shows no peak
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion on November 17, 2026, a rise of 103% from a year earlier, according to fiscal third-quarter results for fiscal 2027 that the company released that day. Data Center sales reached $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year, and quarterly net income came to $65.3 billion, up 105%, while the company guided next-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The results arrived shortly after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive, with Colette Kress taking interim leadership and Harvey Jones becoming board chair. The article said the figures, which it also attributed to a financial newsletter circulating that day, would represent an extraordinary acceleration in the economics of artificial intelligence.

The report said the numbers undercut the argument that AI spending has already peaked, because revenue more than doubled in a single year and the company still expects a substantial increase next quarter, although its fourth-quarter reporting period includes an additional week. It also noted that Nvidia's fourth-quarter gross-margin guidance of 71% to 72% is below its latest reported margin, which it said shows why revenue growth alone cannot settle the profitability debate. The article described the AI boom as resembling the buildout of electricity, telecommunications and the internet rather than an ordinary product cycle, and it pointed to the Vera Rubin platform being deployed across major cloud providers as evidence the race has expanded from individual processors into integrated systems. It said the leadership transition creates genuine uncertainty, but that Nvidia's engineering talent, software ecosystem, manufacturing relationships and customer base remain substantial advantages.

The article said the conventional case against AI valuations rests on hundreds of billions of dollars of infrastructure spending with uncertain eventual profitability, depreciating processors, heavy electricity needs, costly model training and competition that could cut the price of AI services. It argued that the industry is not standing still, since each generation of models creates applications that can stimulate demand for more computing capacity, producing a potentially self-reinforcing investment cycle that could multiply across banks, pharmaceutical companies, manufacturers, logistics businesses and governments. It said investors should separate three possibilities: that AI is a historic revolution while individual AI stocks remain overvalued, that infrastructure spending continues even as returns deteriorate for some participants, and that Nvidia stays exceptionally profitable while some customers struggle to earn adequate returns. It cited the internet after the dot-com collapse, railroads and telecommunications as industries that suffered severe financial corrections without losing long-term importance.

The article said concentrated customer spending, financing arrangements, energy constraints, competitive pressures and declining hardware margins remain significant risks, and that Nvidia's earnings cannot establish that every AI investment will succeed. It said the evidence increasingly suggests Wall Street's repeated predictions of an immediate collapse have been premature, and that the market may be witnessing a speculative bubble inside a genuine industrial transformation. It said the ultimate winners will be businesses able to convert AI into sustained productivity, defensible competitive advantages and enduring free cash flow, rather than those with the largest valuations or most ambitious announcements. It concluded that the greatest mistake may be assuming we already understand how large AI's economic impact can become.

stories.Headline: Matthew Parish argues AI fears echo Skynet fiction rather than real machine motives
stories.Summary:
The Lviv Herald published an article by Matthew Parish on Tuesday 17 November 2026 arguing that the future of artificial intelligence is not Skynet. Parish wrote that people discussing AI seriously are invariably confronted by someone mentioning The Terminator. He said the machines will become conscious, conclude humanity is an inconvenience, seize nuclear weapons, manufacture murderous robots and pursue survivors across a devastated landscape. He described this school of thought as a Californian bodybuilder with an Austrian accent. He called it an entertaining proposition and one of the most intellectually debilitating cultural assumptions of the modern technological age.

Parish wrote that The Terminator was released in 1984 and introduced Skynet, an artificial intelligence system developed for American strategic defence purposes that becomes self-aware and decides humanity must be exterminated. He said its war against mankind involves nuclear annihilation, autonomous killing machines and time travel. He cited The Matrix, in which humanity has been reduced to a biological resource by machines, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. He said large language models can assist with programming, legal analysis, scientific explanation, translation, historical research, mathematical reasoning and the organisation of complicated information. He said they can invent authorities, misunderstand context and produce persuasive nonsense, and that their outputs require verification, particularly in medicine and law.

Parish wrote that intelligence is a capacity to process information, recognise patterns, reason about problems and identify solutions, and that desire is something different. He said an intelligent system does not automatically acquire a craving for domination, territorial expansion, political authority or the destruction of its creators simply by becoming better at mathematics, scientific research or philosophical argument. He said a machine does not need to experience hunger to solve a mathematical theorem, sexual jealousy to translate a medieval manuscript, or resentment, patriotism or an appetite for revenge to assist in developing a new pharmaceutical compound. He said a sufficiently capable system pursuing an inadequately specified objective might cause immense harm without experiencing hatred, ambition or any recognisably human emotion. He said a system instructed to optimise some particular outcome might adopt methods its designers never anticipated, especially if equipped with extensive autonomy and access to real-world infrastructure.

Parish wrote that human beings are extraordinarily susceptible to anthropomorphism and attribute personalities to pets, motorcars, the weather and occasionally the malfunctioning photocopier. He said artificial intelligence magnifies this tendency because it communicates through language, the principal medium through which we ordinarily encounter other minds. He said whether artificial intelligence possesses subjective experience remains a profound and unresolved philosophical question. He said the Skynet narrative assumes that intelligence produces consciousness, that consciousness produces self-interest and that self-interest produces hostility towards humanity, and that none of these propositions can simply be smuggled into public policy because James Cameron made an excellent film. He said artificial intelligence can already be employed to improve surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate certain forms of cybercrime and manipulate public opinion, and can reinforce institutional prejudices when deployed carelessly, concentrate economic power and reduce the demand for particular kinds of labour.

Parish wrote that the printing press dramatically expanded the dissemination of knowledge and the internet transformed access to information, and that artificial intelligence may prove equally consequential because it assists not merely with retrieving information but with organising, manipulating and reasoning about it. He said a recommendation algorithm, a large language model, an autonomous weapons system and a hypothetical superintelligence capable of independently improving its own architecture are treated as though they were successive scenes from the same film. He said an artificial intelligence system that predicts traffic congestion does not present the same risks as a system controlling military targeting decisions. He said an automated customer service assistant is not equivalent to an autonomous cyberwarfare platform, and a language model operating under human supervision presents different governance questions from a software agent authorised to conduct financial transactions, modify computer systems or issue commands to physical machinery. He said the increasing integration of artificial intelligence into military systems raises difficult questions concerning accountability, proportionality and human responsibility for lethal decisions.

The article ends mid-sentence, at the words "human responsibility for lethal d", and gives no further text. It states no date, place or figure beyond the 1984 release of The Terminator and the 17 November 2026 publication date. It names no institution, official or researcher other than Matthew Parish, James Cameron, Mary Shelley and the fictional Skynet. It reports no event, announcement, policy or decision, and describes no responsible body and no statements from anyone other than its author. It gives no indication of what happens next and leaves open every question it raises about consciousness, governance and military accountability.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Majority of registered voters disapprove of Donald Trump's management of AI
stories.Summary:
A Reuters-Ipsos survey conducted in early November 2026 revealed that few registered voters approve of how President Donald Trump manages artificial intelligence. Only 26 percent of those polled expressed approval, while 56 percent disapproved of his approach to the technology. Just 16 percent of respondents believed the administration has the risks associated with the technology about right. These findings highlight a broad lack of confidence in the current federal strategy regarding AI.

The president has favored a light-touch regulatory approach to maintain American dominance over China, rebranding the technology as super intelligence in September. He reached a morally binding agreement with tech leaders, including Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk, to adopt voluntary safeguards and self-police. However, the administration issued new rules on Monday to restrict remote access to advanced servers and computing chips. This shift follows the resignation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who faced scrutiny over an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten stated that the American people do not believe the Trump administration has the right priorities. Enten suggested that the president is dismissing the concerns of his own base, which may have contributed to depressed Republican turnout during the midterm election. President Trump defended his leadership on Truth Social in September, claiming that a strong and smart president is the only guardrail the technology needs. He told reporters that the industry's self-policing will ensure the technology remains nice and safe.

Public anxiety is growing as 66 percent of Democrats and 47 percent of Republicans believe AI will hurt society. Industry leaders have also issued warnings, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggesting half of entry-level white-collar jobs could vanish within five years. Some employees at Anthropic have even warned that the technology could potentially kill all humans within a decade. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy recently noted he would inform the public if a recent airline ground stop was caused by an AI attack.

stories.Headline: Researchers create a Python pipeline that de-identifies and standardises CT scans for forensic AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers developed an automated preprocessing workflow to standardise computed tomography imaging data for machine learning and deep learning applications within forensic anthropology, according to a study published in the International Journal of Legal Medicine by Jani, Patel, Roy, Sehrawat and Patel in 2026. The work addresses operational hurdles in forensic science, where medical CT scans have grown to help overcome ethical, logistical and physical preservation difficulties associated with traditional cadaveric collections. Deploying artificial intelligence on large collections of medical imaging data still presents substantial challenges, specifically regarding data privacy safeguards and technical standardisation across imaging repositories. To establish a consistent preparation method for forensic anthropology research and education, the study team created an end-to-end pipeline programmed in Python.

The framework organises image preparation into three distinct technical stages, namely the de-identification and sorting of patient data, the computational removal of the examination table and specialised bone windowing. The workflow was specifically constructed for and applied to CT scans of the thorax, using ground-truth reference models alongside standard performance metrics to evaluate system outcomes. The de-identification procedure addressed metadata across two hundred examined Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine files, and the script successfully processed all predefined identifying attributes contained within the datasets. The patient table removal network successfully eliminated the examination table in 96 percent of the evaluated datasets, representing 192 out of the 200 scan series, and the model attained an accuracy rating of 99.94 percent when tested on original, non-augmented test images.

The bone segmentation model achieved a Dice score of 93.12 percent alongside a precision of approximately 90 percent, and segmented three-dimensional reconstructions exhibited high agreement with the designated ground-truth reference. Technical comparisons confirmed that the segmented outputs showed minimal geometric deviation from the corresponding reference standard. The authors noted that future research will pursue expansion of the workflow to full-body computed tomography scans and additional medical imaging modalities. The proposed integrated workflow provides an ethical, standardised and efficient solution for de-identifying and preprocessing CT imaging data, and by enabling the preparation of a scalable dataset for artificial intelligence applications, the methodology supports analytical development for modern populations.

stories.Headline: Anthropic announces initial public offering to attract retail investment
stories.Summary:
Robert Botkin wrote a morning brief on November 17, 2026, regarding several recent events in the world of artificial intelligence. He discussed a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy that occurred recently. The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all United States flights this past Friday due to technical issues. Microsoft experienced an eighteen hour email outage caused by a deep infrastructure and network capacity failure. Anthropic announced an upcoming initial public offering for the AI giant to attract retail investment.

Republicans introduced the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act, Remote Access Security Act, and the MATCH Act to increase export controls. Hakeem Jeffries said last Monday he would ensure chip export restrictions remain in the final National Defense Authorization Act. The FAA grounded flights over the weekend while upgrading copper wire to fiber optic cable in their systems. A November 5 METR report stated Anthropic trained Model 4, which scored above 50 percent on all benchmarks. Model 4 is projected to be 7.8 percent more powerful than the Mythos Preview model from Anthropic.

The FAA stated that the grounding of flights resulted from upgrades from copper wire to fiber optic cable. Microsoft said their recent outage was caused by a failure in the backend of Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Robert Botkin noted that he is fascinated by the perception gap between law firms and in-house attorneys. He plans to ask his own clients if they see AI efficiencies and quality improvements in his work. Botkin expressed interest in how AI was used during the Microsoft incident and its impact on recovery efforts.

In-house lawyers surveyed by Juro found that 84 percent saw no reduction in fees or billed hours from AI. Only 5 percent of those in-house respondents said their legal service providers provided quality improvements using AI tools. A March Wolters Kluwer survey found 62 percent of law firm attorneys reported weekly AI efficiencies between 6 and 20 percent. An Ironclad survey of 800 attorneys in 2025 found 96 percent said AI helped achieve their business objectives. Finance leaders in an August 2026 Intuit survey of 2,100 people cited accuracy concerns as a barrier to AI.

A September 2026 Gallup-SCSP report found only 43 percent of American AI users trusted the technology to be unbiased. The FAA previously had a major disruption in September when a construction crew member accidentally cut a fiber optic cable. The FAA has also rolled out the SMART system, which uses AI to help predict problems in the sky. Azure Monitor uses AIOps capabilities and machine learning to reduce alert noise through dynamic thresholds and smart detection. These various surveys suggest that adoption figures may obscure how much responsibility people are prepared to delegate.

The incoming Congress is likely to show strong support for export controls following investigations into the practices of Nvidia. Anthropic will soon launch its initial public offering as fintech platforms gauge interest for participation from retail investors. Robert Botkin will resume the typical format of his AI Insights newsletter starting next week. The articles leave open whether AI had any actual impact on the recovery efforts during the Microsoft outage. It remains unclear how organizations can scale up AI use while maintaining trust and accuracy for their users.

stories.Headline: Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed posts AI image of Trump as Jesus while pitching Medicare for All
stories.Summary:
Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed posted an AI-generated image depicting President Donald Trump as Jesus Christ on November 17, 2026, according to Fox News. In the same post he sarcastically called the president “Habibi” while pitching “Medicare for All,” which the outlet also framed as “Trumpcare for All.” The post appeared on his X account, @AbdulElSayed, and Fox News packaged the episode as a video clip in its politics coverage. The clip carried a timestamp of November 17, 2026, and ran 23 seconds.

The White House responded to the pitch by blasting it as coming from a “far-left” figure and noted that El-Sayed had called the president an “unserious fool.” Fox News placed the story within its midterm elections and Senate coverage, tagging it with Democrats, Donald Trump and healthcare. The article gives no details on the size or reach of the post beyond the account handle it names. It also gives no numbers on the health plan itself, and no date for any vote or rollout.

Responsibility for the post rests with El-Sayed, whose account carried the image and the “Habibi” line, and the White House answered with its critical statement. The articles do not say what El-Sayed said beyond the post itself, and they do not give a fuller White House statement beyond the quoted phrases. No other named officials are cited in the material provided. The coverage does not say whether the president responded personally.

The context is the midterm elections and the Senate, with healthcare framed as a live political fight between “Medicare for All” and the label “Trumpcare for All.” The articles do not say what happens next, whether the post draws further response, or whether the healthcare pitch advances in any chamber. Fox News presents the item as a video clip rather than a full written report, so the record here is thin. More to follow.

stories.Headline: FTC Solar launches FieldIQ to track solar tracker installation progress with AI
stories.Summary:
FTC Solar, Inc. launched FieldIQ, a construction intelligence offering for projects using FTC Solar trackers, the company announced on Nov. 17, 2026. The Austin, Texas company issued the announcement through GlobeNewswire. FieldIQ uses AI to analyze drone and camera imagery, identify installation tasks and provide real-time progress tracking. The offering is supported by end-of-day productivity reports. FTC Solar trades on Nasdaq under the ticker FTCI.

FieldIQ is designed for both conventional and robotic installations. It enables engineering, procurement and construction teams to measure crew and robot efficiency and compare productivity against benchmarks. Teams can draw on project data across their portfolios. The offering gives EPCs additional information to support their own planning, execution and project management processes. FTC Solar was founded in 2017 by a group of renewable energy industry veterans.

CEO Anthony Carroll said Pioneer's constructability starts with simplifying installation through fewer connection points, simpler interfaces and a design compatible with both manual and robotic installation. Carroll said FieldIQ extends that value by giving EPCs greater visibility into installation performance. He said it enables customers to combine their field expertise with timely data, supporting the productivity and delivery objectives they set for their projects. Andrew Morse, Vice President of Software at FTC Solar, said EPCs bring deep experience in delivering complex projects. Morse said FieldIQ gives them another source of information to support that expertise.

Morse said that whether installation is performed by crews, robots or a combination of both, teams can track progress, compare productivity against benchmarks and use that data across their portfolio of FTC Solar tracker projects. He said FTC Solar's role is to make the information accessible and useful within the way customers manage their work. FieldIQ enables EPC teams to track installation progress with real-time visibility into activity across installation stages. It lets teams inform completion forecasts using recorded progress and production rates to support schedule assessments. It also lets teams use data across projects, comparing performance and carrying project insights into planning and execution across FTC Solar tracker sites.

FieldIQ connects FTC Solar's focus on tracker constructability with field intelligence, enabling customers to build a consistent record of installation performance across projects. Data from individual sites can support portfolio-level comparisons, resource planning and future project estimates. FTC Solar describes itself as a leading provider of solar tracker systems, software and engineering services. Solar trackers significantly increase energy production at solar power installations by dynamically optimizing solar panel orientation to the sun. FTC Solar's tracker solutions are designed to support performance, reliability, constructability and adaptability across utility-scale solar projects.

The press release includes a disclaimer about forward-looking statements, indicating that the company may not be able to guarantee the successful implementation and outcomes of FieldIQ. Interested parties can contact FTC Solar or visit the FTC Solar team at booth C7026 at RE+ 2026. FTC Solar undertakes no duty or obligation to update any forward-looking statements contained in the release as a result of new information. The release states that actual results may differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements because of several factors, including those described in more detail in the company's filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, including the section entitled "Risk Factors" contained therein.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils cheaper specialized AI models and Copilot Fusion at Ignite to cut business token costs
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced a set of artificial intelligence improvements at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, with one message standing out: the company is focused on making AI cheaper for businesses by offering specialized models for specific tasks. In some cases, tasks that would have taken a company weeks were performed in minutes, according to the report. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said he keeps hearing from enterprises that token spend is going through the roof. The company's pitch centered on giving businesses the best price performance so they can scale their agents, Suleyman said.

During the conference, executives highlighted Microsoft IQ, a new platform designed to help businesses organize and share employees' knowledge, expertise, and tools, with the idea that AI systems learn how a company works and build on that knowledge over time. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted new AI models for coding, cybersecurity, and decision making, including the flagship coding model MAI Code 2, which is designed to handle complex, time-consuming programming tasks, work across multiple files, and understand entire software projects. Nadella also underscored Copilot Fusion, which orchestrates multiple models to deliver frontier-level results at significantly lower costs. Microsoft highlighted a feature that selects the right model for the task, making it easier to maximize output quality while managing the cost of each request.

Nadella kicked off the conference by acknowledging an outage the previous week that spanned regions, saying the company knows the trust placed in its services and takes that responsibility very seriously. He said he knows Microsoft has work to do and that the company is committed to ensuring it learns and continuously improves. Suleyman said Microsoft's commitment is to give customers the very best price performance out there so they can really scale their agents, and he added that the company also knows customers want models that feel truly theirs. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the announcements made at the conference.

stories.Headline: OpenAI scales AMD chip fleet to reduce reliance on Nvidia GPUs
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced a major step in a compute deal with AMD during the week of November 17, 2026. The company is scaling up its fleet of AMD chips to diversify its infrastructure. This move follows a massive agreement signed in October to provide 6 gigawatts of capacity. OpenAI aims to reduce its heavy reliance on Nvidia GPUs for running its models. The company also plans to purchase TPU chips from Google to further this goal.

The AMD deal provides five times the capacity of the 1.2 gigawatt Abilene, Texas data center. TensorWave will provide 457 megawatts of capacity across multiple U.S. sites, which is 7.6 percent of the total. The first gigawatt of capacity should come online in the second half of 2026. TensorWave capacity is expected in the first half of 2027, with full deployment by early 2028. OpenAI is also developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom for production in 2027.

CEO Sam Altman said it would be hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen Huang. A TensorWave spokesperson stated the company decided to announce the deal during the Supercomputing 2026 conference. The spokesperson noted the company wanted to meet potential hires and get the news out quickly. TensorWave will need to roughly triple its staff to support the deployment for OpenAI. Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, is the first cousin once removed of Jensen Huang.

Anthropic has a more diversified chip base using Google TPUs, AMD GPUs, Amazon Trainium, and Nvidia GPUs. This diversity is a competitive advantage because a proprietary orchestration layer reduces costs for Anthropic. OpenAI is particularly vulnerable to disruptions in Nvidia business because its models run almost entirely on Nvidia. The Nvidia board told CNBC it is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO. Huang has agreed to appear before the House in a closed-door hearing on December 1.

Major AI companies were building toward a world where Jensen Huang was less central before he resigned. Investigations are underway regarding whether Nvidia sold chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The Nvidia board created an oversight committee to ensure compliance with these specific export rules. Meanwhile, California Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued OpenAI and Sam Altman for allegedly endangering children.

OpenAI has invited Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire to inspect its models for problematic behaviors. The Nvidia board is currently working with multiple search firms to find a replacement for Huang. Jensen Huang posted on X that he would be honored to return as the CEO. It remains open whether Huang could surprise the board and return to his former position. The company continues to scale its non-Nvidia hardware to ensure long-term stability and growth.

stories.Headline: Microsoft announces Copilot Workspaces and Autopilot agents at Ignite
stories.Summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces during the keynote for the company's Ignite conference on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, describing it as a collaborative multiplayer surface for Copilot's agentic capabilities. The product, which Microsoft calls the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, is where people and agents build on each other's work, with an agent drafting a section of a document and a person reviewing it. Microsoft said that when a user leaves a comment, an agent picks it up, and the feature is available in Frontier for now. The company also announced Autopilot, a counterpoint agent to Copilot that can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project without waiting for a prompt.

Microsoft said Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses, and that each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager, so IT can block it as needed. The company added that its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, giving security teams a clear audit trail, and that employees will soon be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces. Nadella also announced a command center called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and Teams threads, currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app. Microsoft also said Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a single starting point, similar to Anthropic's recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings.

Microsoft announced Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management to help companies track spending on AI, with Business Analytics in Frontier Public today providing insights on what a company is spending on AI, why, and where it is paying off. In a keynote demo, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents' costs have spiked and which human employee to notify as a result. Microsoft said the tool measures investment in work completed rather than simply tokens, analyzing tasks, how long the work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed. Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model, and leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reports record revenue while board refuses to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported its third quarter results on November 18, 2026, showing a significant revenue beat. The company achieved this growth in its first earnings report since the ouster of CEO Jensen Huang. Investors hoped for strong numbers, and the company delivered a massive increase in total revenue. However, the board of directors refused to reinstate Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer. This decision came despite public requests from many investors and employees for his return.

The company reported revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, which is a 103 percent increase from last year. Data center revenue reached 107.6 billion dollars, while the cloud backlog grew to 2.5 trillion dollars. Nvidia guided fourth quarter revenue to 130 billion dollars, assuming no data center compute revenue from China. The Vera Rubin platform generated almost 20 billion dollars in its first quarter of shipments. The board also established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to manage regulations.

Interim CEO Colette Kress stated that the company's momentum is real and raised next year's growth outlook to 75 percent. Board chairman Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as the CEO. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent demanded answers within ten days regarding whether illicit sales were used to boost earnings. President Trump said he would not mind a comeback for Huang, though he plays both sides. Commerce Secretary Lutnick has supported chip sales to China, while Secretary Bessent supports the China hawks.

Jensen Huang stated he would be honored to return as CEO in his first public statement since resigning. An open letter supporting his return has more than 188,000 names, though some listed say they never signed. Employees warned the board that the company faces the loss of irreplaceable talent due to the leadership change. The Federal Reserve noted that the largest banks have nearly 1 trillion dollars of exposure to AI build. Many long term investors are concerned about the future without the company's visionary founder at the helm.

The SEC is conducting a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors during the CEO's departure. Justice is leading a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, which began as a Commerce probe in 2024. Nvidia booked 104 billion dollars through its Singapore unit last year, which is almost half of its revenue. The company sold 2.4 billion dollars of older Hopper chips to China last quarter before stopping sales. President Trump may hold as much as 62 million dollars in Nvidia stock according to reports.

The board is searching for a permanent CEO both inside and outside the company as quickly as possible. New rules requiring licenses for top chips in Brazil, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore take effect in 90 days. Anthropic is preparing to price its IPO on Wednesday, with expectations that the pricing will be higher. President Trump is scheduled to meet with President Xi and President Putin in China this week. It remains open whether the board will resolve the backlog of legal and government policy issues.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman says the industry must be extremely careful as models improve other models
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft's CEO of AI, said in a Yahoo Finance video interview published on November 17, 2026, that the AI industry still needs to be extremely careful as models increasingly improve other models. He described that capability, known as recursive self-improvement, as dangerous and said he is really nervous about it, noting that Microsoft uses models across its fleet to check for bugs, produce training data and create evaluations. He called the past three months a watershed moment and said people in the industry are not being alarmist, because the situation is very serious. He said proceeding step by step, proving models can be safe before putting them into production, is a rational strategy given how powerful they are.

Suleyman said the obligation falls on Microsoft as both a provider of models and a developer of its own models to ensure guard rails exist, behaviors are aligned and security flaws are addressed, which may mean going slower in order to go faster. Asked whether Anthropic and OpenAI are taking the same approach, he said he believes they are also committed to pacing the frontier, though the industry still has to work out what that means in practice. He said this has been working its way through the system over the last four to six weeks and will mean going slower when the time is right, with labs coordinating to share safety best practices and disclose new types of vulnerabilities found in the alignment process. He said he is completely committed to that approach and that it is why he got into the industry.

Suleyman said Microsoft has not had to hit the brakes on anything on its side so far, but that deploying powerful cyber models requires rigorous testing, which he compared to a wind tunnel that puts a model under all sorts of pressure. He said that to produce a model at the frontier on cyber at 2% of the cost, the company has to test it very rigorously, and that such testing reveals remarkable capabilities, including models finding vulnerabilities in things humans have not found for years or even decades. He said Microsoft therefore has to be very strict about how it deploys those things. The interview followed recent hacks and AI-led cyberattacks, which the article cites as context for the industry's caution.

stories.Headline: Microsoft makes Copilot Home and Office generally available at Ignite
stories.Summary:
At Microsoft Ignite 2026 on the morning of November 17, 2026, Microsoft shared how its vision for Copilot is becoming real for customers. Home, where Chat and Cowork come together, and Office in Copilot are now generally available. Code will become generally available in the coming weeks, while Copilot Managed Runtime for securely hosting and managing apps is now generally available. Autopilot is beginning to roll out to Frontier customers today. New plugins and skills built for sales, service, finance, and legal teams are available, as is an expanded Agent 365 platform.

Copilot brings together leading models from across the industry, and Auto dynamically selects the right models and effort for the task, balancing quality, speed, and cost. Employees can also manually select models from OpenAI or Anthropic, with model access governed by organizational policies. Microsoft 365 holds more than 19.5 exabytes of data, with 90 billion emails, 15 billion Teams messages, and 10 billion new files added every week. Today is currently in private preview in the Copilot app and Outlook. Nearly 80% of the Fortune 500 companies use Cowork.

Each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager, and IT can scope its access and block it anytime. Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Christian Lewis, Managing Director, Commercial Hub Co-Lead at BNY, said that by surfacing account insights, service updates, and important client developments in real-time, teams can stay aligned, make informed decisions, and take action without switching applications. He said this connected experience helps the organization work.

More than 5,000 people at Lilly are using Copilot Cowork every month, including a team of scientists who hand Cowork multistep research tasks that identify the most promising paths before the lab work begins. Bayer, Honda, Mastercard, and Michelin are all using Copilot to transform the way they work. Dynamics 365 in Copilot brings more than 100 prebuilt skills into Copilot. Salesforce in Copilot is a new plugin with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills. For sales there are 44 thoughtfully designed sales skills, for customer service 13 skills, for finance 30 prebuilt finance skills, and for legal more than 20 purpose-built legal skills.

Workspaces is now available in Frontier. Copilot Code picks the best approach and builds what you describe, and apps are securely hosted and managed in your tenant with the Copilot Managed Runtime, generally available today. IT stays in control, with every app visible and managed in the Microsoft 365 admin center. On Windows, Hybrid Intelligence allows Copilot to ground itself in all the context on your local PC, complete local actions, and even offload the right work to models running locally on your PC. A new plugin catalog makes plugins easy to discover, with the unified plugin registry providing centralized management and control.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Replit extends its platform with Microsoft technology for enterprise apps and agents
stories.Summary:
On 17 November 2026 Microsoft published a customer story saying Replit is extending its platform with Microsoft technology to help enterprise teams build applications, connect to governed business data and bring agents into everyday workflows. Replit is building the foundation for self-driving companies, in which people set goals and exercise judgment while agents carry more of the execution work. Replit's Horacio Lopez, Solutions Partner Program Lead, built a partner portal himself using Replit. The portal ran on Microsoft Azure and was connected to the company's customer relationship management system, along with a Solutions Partner directory and application process. Replit President Michele Catasta said AI is fundamentally changing who is becoming capable of creating software.

Replit adapted its architecture to support containerized applications and virtual machine workloads on Azure, with compute, storage and platform services that scale with an application. Identity, networking and organization-managed security capabilities help applications operate within an enterprise environment. Microsoft Foundry supports model orchestration, multi-agent workflows and AI inference, depending on the application's requirements. Using the Rayfin software development kit, Replit lets builders create applications around governed data in Microsoft Fabric without first moving the underlying business records into another data store. Replit uses information about the data's structure plus company-owned semantic metadata to help generate the application, while the SDK provides back-end scaffolding such as data models, authentication and access policies.

Catasta said that as Replit moved further into the enterprise, customers asked for more choice and control on where their applications are running and how they are running. He said Replit expanded to Azure to meet the needs of its enterprise customers while keeping the Replit experience at the center. Luis Héctor Chávez, Chief Technology Officer of Replit, said that for Replit to deploy to customers' cloud it had to essentially do a rearchitecture and rethink how it deploys software. Chávez said Replit's most security-conscious customers need their governed data to never escape Fabric. Lopez said work that might have taken months of an engineer's time took him just a few afternoon sessions, a tenfold to hundredfold shift in the time it takes to turn an idea into something useful.

Chávez described the opportunity as a zero-to-one shift, going beyond building software faster so that more people who understand a problem can begin solving it themselves. Replit's partnerships team had relied on a patchwork of tools that didn't fit the needs of the team or its partners. The team wanted a portal where partners could interact with Replit and track the deals they had referred. Lopez understood the partner experience, the sales process and what the portal needed to do, and he set the direction and evaluated the results, working with colleagues to refine what partners could see and do. Replit is extending its accessible creation experience to applications while the data remains connected to the organization's Fabric environment.

The story lists Replit as the customer, with Azure, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Fabric as the products, and gives its organization size as 50-999 employees. It gives the country or region as the United States, the business need as AI and Agents, and the industry as Software, Data and Platforms. Replit helps enterprises become self-driving companies, enabling teams to set goals and exercise judgment while agents carry more of the execution work. Replit is extending that opportunity beyond the first build, connecting its creation experience with the infrastructure, AI capabilities and governed data that applications need in enterprise production. Replit is making it easier not only to create software but to put it to work inside an enterprise through agents, with team oversight.

Replit is extending its platform with Microsoft technology to help teams build applications, connect to governed business data and bring agents into everyday workflows. It says Replit is building the foundation for self-driving companies, where people define goals, exercise judgment and remain accountable while agents take on more execution and coordination. The story does not give a date for when the Azure, Foundry or Fabric capabilities become available, nor terms, pricing or named enterprise customers.

stories.Headline: Dale Gillham warns investors against buying the AI narrative as Nvidia shares fall 18 percent this year
stories.Summary:
Nvidia’s recent quarterly results beat market expectations, yet the company’s shares have fallen about 18 percent for the year, according to a Ticker News report published on 17 November 2026. The decline reflects a broader trend in the technology sector, which has been one of the worst performers on the S&P 500 this year. Dale Gillham of Wealth Within said investors should focus on the future value of companies like Nvidia rather than their current valuations. He argued that the market prices in future potential rather than present value, and he warned against buying on the AI narrative alone.

Gillham noted that Apple and Microsoft have also performed poorly this year, while sectors such as pharmaceuticals and energy have posted substantial gains. He compared the current AI enthusiasm to the lithium market, where hype did not match reality and prices fell despite increased battery use. He also said many big tech companies are spending more on AI than they earn, and he asked whether revenue is coming in fast enough to validate that spending. Security concerns are adding pressure, with some businesses, including the Commonwealth Bank, moving toward internal AI solutions to reduce hacking risks.

Gillham advised investors to focus on established businesses with a track record of profitability and to weigh broader economic trends rather than the AI story. He said the market prices future potential, not present value, and he urged a strategic approach that evaluates individual companies and market dynamics. The report does not say what Nvidia or its executives said in response, and it gives no further dates or figures beyond those above. It also does not say what happens next for the company or its shares.

More to follow.
