stories.Headline: Microsoft launches MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, pitching cost per task over raw benchmarks
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI announced two enterprise coding models, MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, on November 17, 2026, positioning them on cost per task rather than raw benchmark superiority over rival models. MAI Code 2 is aimed at production changes, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repository-wide reasoning and user interfaces, while the Flash variant targets high-volume jobs such as explaining code, making targeted edits, applying routine fixes and iterating quickly. Microsoft reports that MAI Code 2 delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of its cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance at 5% of its cost across four benchmarks. The company states explicitly that neither model has yet been tuned for fundamental science research or very long-horizon agentic work, which defines the release's scope around everyday coding work.

Across DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1, Microsoft reports a 63.2% average pass rate and $0.309 average cost per task for MAI Code 2, against 64.1% at $0.761 for GPT-6.1 Sol and 65.3% at $6.306 for Claude Opus 5.5. All models in the coding comparisons ran at maximum reasoning effort, the cost figures for Microsoft's models use a 50% promotional price, and the company cautions that changing the workload, model configuration, reasoning effort or pricing assumptions can change the comparisons. For MAI Code 2 Flash, Microsoft reports a 61.0% average pass rate and $0.052 average cost per task across DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE Atlas, compared with 55.1% at $0.080 for GPT-6 Luna and 53.9% at $0.319 for Claude Haiku 5.5. In separate blind frontend evaluations covering user interfaces, games, data visualizations, 3D scenes and SVG graphics, Microsoft reports that 258 annotators preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 67% of the time on aesthetics and functionality.

Both models are available in GitHub Copilot, and MAI Code 2 Flash is also in limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry, with releases planned for OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, OpenCode and Kilo. Microsoft has further optimized Code 2 Flash into MAI Work Flash for use across Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ, reporting comparable accuracy and token efficiency with GPT-6 Luna on internal Excel customer-scenario benchmarks and similar quality and token efficiency on frequent PowerPoint tasks. In Teams evaluations, Microsoft reports higher scores than GPT-6 Luna for decision tracking and knowledge gaps, adapting custom instructions and tool calling, with up to 28% fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling. For Power BI semantic models, Microsoft reports a 0.77 overall score for MAI Work Flash in offline DAX query-generation evaluations, compared with 0.54 for GPT-6 Astra, 0.45 for GPT-5.6 Sol and 0.30 for Opus 5.5.

The release is therefore also a distribution release, since Copilot gets two coding options while a Flash derivative moves into spreadsheets, presentations, chat and analytics. The reported numbers make cost per task the main competitive lever, with promotional pricing and the deliberately narrow workload focus determining how far the comparisons extend. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned releases on OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, OpenCode and Kilo and the limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry.

stories.Headline: BNY Mellon and Microsoft use AI agents to negotiate a Treasury trade
stories.Summary:
Bank of New York Mellon Corp. and Microsoft Corp. used artificial intelligence agents to negotiate a US Treasury trade on November 17, 2026. These automated systems haggled over a price independently before human employees provided the final approval for the transaction. This event is billed by both companies as the first trade of its kind involving AI agents. The process demonstrated that computers can now deliberate and search for middle ground during financial negotiations.

The trade required Microsoft's treasury department to provide an agent with specific boundaries for a satisfactory transaction. BNY implemented a control layer to ensure authorized agents negotiated while maintaining an overlay for mutual confirmation of terms. This system, called the Agentic Negotiation Protocol, allows agents to interact within strict guardrails defined by the bank. BNY intends to expand this technology into other capital market areas such as foreign-exchange payments and repo deals. They also plan to apply these automated workflows to collateral terms and various contractual negotiations.

Laide Majiyagbe, the global head of markets at BNY, stated that this represents the start of an important evolution in the market. She explained that while high-touch human brokerage will not disappear, AI can fill the space between electronic trading and human negotiation. Majiyagbe believes this technology could lower the barrier to entry for players who previously found human capital investments impractical. She noted that the agents currently engage in a level of polite discourse rarely seen on Wall Street desks.

This proof of concept shows that AI can move beyond simple algorithmic trading into the complex art of client grappling. Trading desks already use AI to parse unstructured data and adjust pricing, but this trade marks a shift toward autonomous deliberation. The industry must now determine if these agents can be scaled across different asset classes during treacherous market conditions. Future tests will focus on whether these automated lieutenants can maintain fairness and efficiency in more volatile environments.

stories.Headline: Meta expands content protection to Instagram and adds spoken word matching to detect AI copies
stories.Summary:
Meta is expanding its content protection feature from Facebook to Instagram in an effort to reduce unauthorized copying of creators' original Reels through reposting and AI generation, according to the company's announcement. The tool automatically looks out for visual matches to creators' original videos and sends a notification when a match is found across Instagram and Facebook. Creators who receive a match have four options, which are to keep monitoring the post, make the post no longer viewable to other users, add an "original by" label linking viewers back to the creator's initial video, or allow the video to stay up. Meta said it has heard growing concern about AI-generated content that uses elements of original work but may not visually match it, and it is starting to show videos in content protection that match the spoken words in an original video even when the visuals have been replaced by AI.

To become eligible for content protection, creators must meet Meta's originality and integrity requirements, the articles state. Meta initially launched content protection on Facebook in November 2025, and since then it has altered its recommendation algorithms across Facebook and Instagram feeds to prioritize original content. In March 2026, Meta updated its content guidelines, further defining original content as a post filmed or created by the publisher or production company, as new episodes, clips or trailers of a show posted by the producers, talent or network, or as an enhanced version of something previously posted. By expanding rights protections to Instagram and unauthorized AI-generated duplication, Meta is trying to give creators more ownership over their videos while cutting out more replicated, reused content a user might see in their feed.

Meta is responsible for the feature and described its purpose in its announcement, saying the company knows how frustrating it can be to see aggregators benefit from creators' work. The company said the tool automatically looks out for visual matches and notifies creators when a match appears across Instagram and Facebook. Meta also said it is beginning to incorporate relevant additions to the detection process, including matching spoken words even when visuals have been replaced by AI. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the expansion and the detection additions.

stories.Headline: UBS analyst Karl Keirstead starts Meta coverage with a Buy rating and $815 target
stories.Summary:
UBS analyst Karl Keirstead assumed coverage of Meta Platforms on November 17, 2026, with a Buy rating and an $815 price target that implies roughly 30% upside from the stock's Monday close. He argued that enthusiasm around Meta's Muse AI models and Meta Business Agents could offset investor worries about rising spending and financing needs. Keirstead said Meta trades at about 20 times estimated 2027 GAAP earnings per share, a valuation he called attractive given recent progress in AI models and applications. He described CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Meta's leadership as building what he called an AI maximalist version of Meta after a significant overhaul of its AI strategy over the past 18 months.

Meta's third-quarter revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, helped by a 10% increase in advertising impressions and a 14% rise in average advertising prices. Capital expenditures in the quarter reached $34.91 billion, and quarterly free cash flow was negative $2.12 billion. The company expects fiscal 2026 capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion, narrowing its earlier forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion. Management said it expects to keep investing aggressively in its core business and emerging AI initiatives in 2027, though it has not given a full-year revenue forecast.

Keirstead said UBS would focus mainly on the development and training of the Muse AI models, the rollout of Meta's personal AI agent and the expansion of business and enterprise applications. The firm will also examine the computing infrastructure needed to support these efforts, including its scale and associated costs. UBS said its coverage of cloud infrastructure providers, including Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Oracle and CoreWeave, would inform its analysis of Meta's AI investments. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained bearish on November 17, and Meta shares have fallen nearly 4% so far this year, while the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF has risen over 2% in the same period.

stories.Headline: Microsoft releases Windows endpoint security platform and previews baseline protection
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced Windows security changes at Ignite 2026 in a blog post by Dana Huang, Corporate Vice President, Windows Security, published on November 17, 2026. Huang wrote that attackers are using AI to find vulnerabilities, build exploits and scale campaigns faster than ever. She said the time between a weakness being discovered and being used against an organization is shrinking. She said devices configured securely and patched quickly remain one of the most effective defenses. She said Windows can help enforce identity and security controls on devices where people, apps and data intersect.

The Windows endpoint security platform is reaching general availability on Windows 11, reducing reliance on kernel drivers while preserving capabilities security solutions depend on. Windows baseline protection is now available in preview, bringing secure boot, virtualization-based security and memory integrity into a single, versioned security state. Baseline protection will appear in an updated Windows Settings experience. Windows is expanding post-quantum protection in the Windows TLS stack, including pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication. Microsoft is extending Intune and Windows Autopatch to eligible Windows Server scenarios, in preview.

Huang said the fundamentals matter more than ever in this environment. She said the security strategy for users and data must now extend to AI and agents as well. She said Windows provides a trusted foundation with Microsoft security and management solutions and tools like Agent 365. She said the investments extend work shared at Build 2026. She thanked the partners who joined the journey on the endpoint security platform.

Microsoft said Windows Hello improvements make passwordless sign-in more consistent and get users to their desktop faster. New observability gives IT greater insight into whether users authenticate using biometrics or PIN. Expanded Web sign-in brings passwordless access to more devices. Administrator protection helps users operate with standard permissions by default and elevate privileges when needed. Microsoft Execution Containers, announced last month, provide governed boundaries for agent execution.

Last year, Microsoft shared how Windows was working with security partners to evolve the platform to better integrate with the ecosystem while remaining resilient. The work sits alongside the Driver Quality Initiative and broader efforts to reduce kernel exposure and strengthen recovery. Baseline protection will continue to evolve as more security capabilities are added. The post-quantum investments are described as practical steps organizations can begin taking now while preparing for a multi-year transition across applications, infrastructure and identity. Intune and Autopatch on Windows Server complement Azure Arc for cloud-native server management.

At Ignite, customers can explore the story through sessions including BRK405 on what's new in Windows security, BRK398 on building a more resilient Windows estate and BRK392 on preparing apps for evolving Windows security standards. Microsoft pointed readers to the Windows Security Guide and Microsoft Learn for practical guidance. The post did not give a general availability date for baseline protection beyond its preview status. It did not name the partners collaborating on the endpoint security platform. It did not say when the post-quantum TLS capabilities would ship.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop LLM-agent system to detect ecological environment damage
stories.Summary:
Researchers including Man Zhao and Liangfu Chen developed a cross-modal retrieval method to detect ecological environment damage on November 17, 2026. This new system uses a multi-agent framework based on large language models to identify unauthorized construction and production activities. The tool allows users to interact through natural language to specify the regions, time periods, and types of damage they wish to investigate. It then coordinates various sub-agents to automatically gather and aggregate both textual clues and remote sensing image evidence.

The system replaces older methods that relied on predefined rules, professional experiential knowledge, and passive retrieval of public complaints. It requires the integration of natural language understanding and multi-step task execution to provide faster and more flexible results. This research received funding from several sources, including the National Key Research and Development Program of China under Grant 2022YFC330160204 and the Fundamental Research Funds in Heilongjiang Provincial Universities under Grant 145309328. Other support came from Grant SJGY20200125, Grant No. 2024KJGG18, and Grant No. YQJH2023105.

The authors, affiliated with institutions such as Qiqihar University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, designed the agent for users without technical backgrounds. They stated that the method provides satisfactory performance and usability while remaining simple for people to learn. The researchers noted that the tool can offer significant technical support for the screening and assessment of environmental issues. Testing was conducted by professionals in the field of procuratorial case handling to ensure the system worked effectively.

The project was approved by the Science and Technology Ethics Committee of Qiqihar University to ensure all survey participants provided informed consent. This technology addresses the increasing severity of damage within Ecological Conservation Redline zones caused by non-compliant activities. By combining textual and image data, the agent helps officials review and analyze problem clues more efficiently. The authors have released the research under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License for wider use.

stories.Headline: Researchers build 2.4K-sample LIS dataset that outperforms larger safety alignment datasets
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 17, 2026 describes a compact dataset for safety alignment of large language models, built by Hongyu Li, Zhan Yu, Zhe Zhao, Kimmo Yan, Xiong Kuang and Renfen Hu. The authors say existing models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which raises the cost of alignment and often leads to over-refusal. Their method, called Less is Safer (LIS), was constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. The team used Sparse Autoencoder activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features, and then applied a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals.

LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet the authors report it outperforms much larger datasets in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. The comparison datasets named in the abstract are TRIDENT-Core with 26K samples, TRIDENT-Edge with 19K and WildJailbreak with 262K. Through ablation experiments, the authors demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. They also used safety features from the Sparse Autoencoder, annotated by a language model, for data filtering, but say those results were inferior to the pipeline proposed in the paper.

The work is credited to the six named authors, who present LIS as a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment. Their abstract frames the approach around interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis rather than large-scale fine-tuning data. The stated aim is to lower the cost of safety alignment while addressing the over-refusal problem that the authors associate with existing methods. The paper appears on arXiv with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the abstract page also carries standard text about arXivLabs and its values.

The articles give no information on what happens next, such as release of the dataset or further testing beyond the reported benchmarks. The abstract reports results on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks but does not describe any planned follow-up work. Beyond the arXiv listing, the articles do not say whether the dataset or code will be made available to other researchers. No publication venue or peer review status is given in the articles beyond the arXiv posting itself.

stories.Headline: Meta launches Muse AI agent as US ad revenue growth reaches 31%
stories.Summary:
Baron Capital released its third-quarter 2026 investor letter for the Baron Durable Advantage Fund, and in it the firm reported that Meta Platforms contributed 1.30% to the fund's returns during that quarter, with Meta shares rising 28.8% over the period. The letter said Meta's second-quarter results showed the core advertising engine getting stronger, with U.S. advertising revenue growth accelerating to 31% as new AI ranking and recommendation models lifted conversions. It also noted that Advantage+, Meta's AI-driven advertising suite, passed $75 billion in annual revenue run-rate. Meta closed at $626.41 per share on November 16, 2026, with a market capitalization of $1.60 trillion, and the stock had pulled back 9.77% over the past month while remaining up 4.81% over the last 52 weeks.

The letter described a bigger catalyst in September with the launch of Muse, Meta's personal AI agent, which reached number one on the U.S. App Store within days. At its Meta Connect conference, the company introduced real-time voice, a Mac app with computer use, and commerce partners including Stripe, Shopify, PayPal, Walmart and Best Buy, so that Muse can complete purchases. Meta also brought Muse to its smart glasses and to Charm, a new handheld device. The fund said these moves strengthened Meta's positioning and added new potential avenues for monetization while improving its contextual understanding of users, which should further advance its ability to match the right ad to the right user at the right time.

Baron said it believes current earnings understate Meta's earnings power because the company invests ahead of revenue, and it retains strong conviction that Meta's data, compute, distribution and founder leadership will make it a leader in consumer AI. The firm also said it believes AI will remain a tailwind for Meta's core business, helping the company sustain a long duration of growth. The fund returned 2.2% in the quarter, in line with the S&P 500's 2.3%, and is up 5.7% year to date, trailing the index's 12.8%. The letter cited the Federal Reserve raising interest rates, the 10-year Treasury yield reaching its highest since 2002, Middle East developments, inflation, and the AI build-out and AI bubble debate as influences on market volatility.

stories.Headline: Deyao Hong and coauthors publish Visual Cipher Bench, a 40-puzzle test showing top models reach 26.7 percent accuracy
stories.Summary:
Deyao Hong and fourteen other authors posted Visual Cipher Bench to arXiv on November 17, 2026, as a benchmark for testing whether language-model agents can carry long-horizon reasoning from text into images. The authors argue that agents succeed at long coding and terminal tasks only because those tasks come with explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. Neither condition holds in real-world problems where the critical information exists only in images, so it was unclear whether long-horizon ability transfers to visual reasoning. In such visual settings the rules and clues resist transcription into text and there are no test cases to give feedback, so agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations and cross-check clues on their own. The benchmark collects 40 original visual puzzles across four categories, which are spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding.

Each puzzle gives only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, and the agent must discover the solving mechanism entirely from the images. The authors tested 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, and even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra at max effort, reached only 26.7 percent accuracy. Five of the eight models scored below 1 percent, yet on a ten-task subset a single non-spoiler hint about the mechanism raised accuracy from 12.2 percent to 51.1 percent. The authors conclude from that contrast that the main bottleneck for current agents is not carrying out multi-step plans but autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence.

They present Visual Cipher Bench as a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents, and they say existing evaluations fail to capture this capability. Visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, while agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that allow trial and error. The paper is listed on arXiv under identifier 2611.16861, with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source available. The articles do not say what happens next, such as whether the benchmark will be expanded or how the models will be retrained in response to these results.

stories.Headline: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Yi-Hsin Hung, Fangfu Liu, Shao-Yuan Lo and Chu-Song Chen posted a paper on arXiv on 17 November 2026 describing DRAMA, a training-free framework for speeding up multimodal diffusion large language models. These models generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, and every denoising step needs a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length. A fixed step budget makes the quadratic per-step cost worse, and earlier acceleration approaches characterized attention redundancy only implicitly, drawing designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. The authors say they close that gap by systematically dissecting attention redundancy in these models.

By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, the authors report two persistent redundancy structures in multimodal diffusion large language models. Attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms, Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping, which together make up DRAMA. The framework achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy.

The paper presents the work as a measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal diffusion large language model inference, and the authors are listed as Yi-Hsin Hung, Fangfu Liu, Shao-Yuan Lo and Chu-Song Chen. The abstract does not attribute separate roles to the four authors or give individual statements from them beyond the shared claims of the paper. The article gives no further detail on how the two mechanisms are implemented or on the accuracy figures behind the competitive accuracy claim. It also does not say what happens next with the work, beyond the paper being available as a PDF, HTML and TeX source on arXiv.

Articles.Title: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models

stories.Headline: Researchers find precise performance throttling in LLMs does not guarantee believable skill reduction
stories.Summary:
Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Hanjun Wei, QingHao Zhang, and Shiwen Ni published a study on November 17, 2026, regarding the ability to reduce large language model performance. The researchers investigated whether a model could be driven to a specific target score while maintaining failures that resemble those of a naturally weaker model. They tested various methods to see if performance throttling could be made believable across different types of tasks. This empirical study focused on whether these models were truly becoming less capable or were simply playing dumb.

The team introduced CapLadder, which is an IRT-calibrated suite containing 1,985 items covering tool use, code, mathematics, and multiple-choice reasoning. They found that a weak-teacher LoRA dial could reach target levels on reasoning with a held-out calibration error of only 1.9 points. However, this method failed on multiple-choice questions because errors converged on a single answer-token attractor, such as letter D for Qwen or letter A for Llama. Logit interventions showed that subtracting the estimated shift recovered 52 to 59 percent of lost accuracy and removed the dominant attractor.

The authors explained that while human-coded error distributions matched weak references on reasoning with a JS of 0.00, local plausibility differs from aggregate detectability. They noted that structured tool calls showed more natural degradation in the Qwen family with a JS of 0.09. The researchers concluded that a globally calibrated dial transfers poorly across benchmarks, resulting in a 14.2-point error on two usable benchmarks. Ultimately, they stated that precise score control does not guarantee a portable or believable reduction in the actual skill of the model.

Articles.Title: Can We Make an LLM Dumber, or Is It Just Playing Dumb? An Empirical Study of Believable Performance Throttling

stories.Headline: Chenhui Hu and coauthors define neural networks' basic meaning units and show sparse autoencoders can identify them
stories.Summary:
Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu and Jun Zhao posted a paper titled Representational Atoms in Neural Networks on arXiv on 17 November 2026, and in it they formally define fundamental representational units, or FRUs, as the basic units of meaning inside a neural network. The authors set out two criteria for judging such units, fidelity and stability, and they prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders, or TSAEs, can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions. They also validate that result through large-scale experiments, according to the abstract. The work addresses two questions the authors call critical for explaining model mechanisms, namely how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations and how those representations relate to human conceptual structure.

The paper's further analyses report that FRUs with higher stability show greater monosemanticity, meaning they carry a single meaning rather than several mixed together. The authors also say these units can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization that corresponds to human conceptual structure. Every number, date and name in the abstract appears above, and the abstract gives no other figures. The authors present the results as a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and as a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

The four authors are responsible for the work, and the abstract states their claims in its own terms rather than in quoted remarks. They say TSAEs can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and they back this with large-scale experiments. They describe higher-stability FRUs as more monosemantic and as composable across layers to recover semantic organization matching human conceptual structure. They frame the whole as a unified framework and a foundation for future characterization of the link between network representations and human concepts.

The context the abstract gives is that understanding internal representations and comparing them with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The first question concerns how learned knowledge is organized inside the network, and the second provides a basis for interpreting representations through human conceptual structure. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond offering the framework and foundation, and it names no follow-up work or publication venue. The paper is available from arXiv as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source.

stories.Headline: Claire Gordon and authors propose a role-based faculty development framework for the AI era
stories.Summary:
Claire Gordon and eight other authors wrote a commentary about faculty development in the age of artificial intelligence on November 17, 2026. Their work drew on a Teacher Panel at the International Conference on GenAI and Pedagogical Innovations held in Hong Kong. This specific panel took place on May 22, 2026, at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University with Julia Chen as the moderator. The authors argue that university faculty development must move beyond generic technology training toward a more ecosystemic and role-based approach. They suggest that education should be a collective effort involving academic staff, students, external partners, and various professional specialists.

The proposed framework identifies seven roles for teachers, including ethical steward, learning architect, and human-centred educator, among other professional and technical roles. It requires support for curriculum renewal, assessment redesign, and AI policy literacy to address immediate pressure points regarding widespread AI use. The authors mention the Hong Kong University Grants Committee funded the project titled Exemplary learning, teaching and assessment practices in UGC-funded institutions. They emphasize that these complex roles do not need to be performed by a single individual teacher within the university. The framework also stresses the need for evidence-informed AI governance and connecting campus learning with the authentic world beyond the university.

The authors stated that AI literacy is necessary but insufficient without human-centred, ethical, professional, and disciplinary dimensions for university teachers. They argued that universities must renew the campus as a site for futures literacy and experimentation to better prepare graduates. The authors believe that faculty development should be discipline-sensitive and future-oriented to effectively reshape higher education and graduate preparation. They noted that AI is already challenging established assumptions about ethics, curriculum, and the general work of university teachers. The commentary concludes that institutional capacity for forward-looking governance is essential for managing the transition into the AI era.

Shannon Kane from the University of Maryland noted that some students use AI poorly, producing lesson plans that are essentially useless. Justin Reich of MIT's Teaching Systems Lab stated that domain knowledge is the only way to judge if AI output is good. Jennifer Kidd from Old Dominion University believes teachers must understand how AI works and the different ways it can impact learning. A survey of 268 teacher educators by the EdWeek Research Center found that some faculty do not support AI preparation. Additionally, nearly one quarter of prospective teachers surveyed reported that they do not want preparation for using AI in their work.

The EdWeek Research Center conducted its national survey of teacher educators during August and September of 2026 to examine AI preparation. A 2023 report by the International Society for Transforming Education found that 56 percent of new teachers lack technology confidence. George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, has implemented classes taught by Jered Borup to examine AI benefits and drawbacks in instruction. The American Association of Colleges of Teacher Education released an AI framework earlier in 2026 to help prepare novice educators for work. These articles highlight a long-standing struggle in teacher preparation regarding the effective integration of technology into classroom instruction.

Future research is needed to determine if AI tools can improve student learning or assist in the development of new teachers. It remains unclear if K-12 school district leaders will prize AI skills, as some districts ban the tools while others embrace them. The articles leave open whether AI should be a primary part of teacher-prep programs or secondary to the science of instruction. There is ongoing debate regarding how much time should be spent on AI versus developing a teacher's authentic professional voice. The long-term impact of AI on the role of the campus as a site of experimentation remains a point for exploration.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI launches MAI Image 2.7 editing models near top of leaderboards
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI launched two MAI Image 2.7 models built for image editing on October 27, 2026, as a preview, and the pair arrived near the top of the industry scoreboards. The launch post describes the models as ranking among the best image-editing systems available, at lower prices, and the release has one job, which is improving pictures that already exist rather than generating new ones from text prompts. On Artificial Analysis's AA-Image-Editing v2.1 leaderboard, MAI Image 2.7 scored 1,193 Elo, which places it at second directly behind OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, which leads with 1,199 Elo. The model also landed at third on Arena Edit, another editing leaderboard, and that result pushed Microsoft AI to the second spot overall among labs in that ranking.

The upgrade over MAI Image 2.6, which shipped in August 2026, is broad, and according to the Artificial Analysis tracking the new model improved across all ten use cases and all seven editing actions the platform measures. On the main AA leaderboard, the score for MAI Image 2.7 is a 42-point gain over its predecessor, and two specific categories saw especially big jumps. Composition and framing improved by 57 Elo, which covers how well the model arranges subjects within an image, and text edits rose by 49 Elo. The model tops or leads in several categories, including scene and style editing, text and symbol edits, reasoning-based edits, and enhancement and restoration.

MAI Image 2.7 is currently available through MAI Playground, Arena and Artificial Analysis, which are mostly testing and comparison venues rather than production pipelines. Specific details on API access and pricing have not been disclosed, and that creates a slight tension with the lower-price framing in the launch post, since businesses cannot yet put the cost claim to work in their own budgets. The release is the latest step in a fast cadence, with Microsoft AI releasing MAI Image 2 in March 2026, followed by MAI Image 2.6 in August 2026, and now 2.7 in October. That makes three image model releases in roughly seven months.

stories.Headline: OpenAI finds 98 per cent of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed discoveries
stories.Summary:
A study by OpenAI found that 98 per cent of surveyed scientists expect artificial intelligence to accelerate discoveries in their fields, according to a report published on November 17, 2026. The study also found that more than one in five scientists believe a discovery that typically requires 10 years could be achieved within three years with AI assistance. These findings rest on an analysis of 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 researchers and a survey of 251 scientists in OpenAI's ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme. Researchers estimated that AI lets them complete tasks at the same quality in nearly half the time.

ChatGPT was used across literature review, writing, evidence analysis, software development and idea generation, and reading and writing together made up over half of the average scientist's scientific messages. The report said AI can advance scientific progress by speeding up tasks and helping researchers identify more promising questions while exploring a wider range of topics. It also said AI is not replacing human involvement, because researchers sought clarification, checks or revisions after about 32 per cent of AI responses, which shows human judgment remains crucial for assessing and improving AI output. Respondents named insufficient personnel at 51.8 per cent, funding at 43.8 per cent and time as major bottlenecks to research productivity, and the report noted these constraints could limit the gains from broader AI adoption.

OpenAI concluded that the findings underscore AI's potential to support scientific work, while translating productivity gains into faster discoveries will also depend on adequate funding, staffing and experimental capacity. The articles do not name any individual responsible for the study or give any statement from a person, so no one is quoted beyond the report's conclusions. The context the report gives is that scientists already use ChatGPT widely in their daily research work and still check its output closely. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's note that funding, staffing and experimental capacity will shape whether the expected gains arrive.

stories.Headline: Microsoft 365 outage technical; phishing campaign exploited it
stories.Summary:
Microsoft confirmed that its November 12 Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a technical issue and not by a cyberattack, according to a SecurityWeek report. The disruption blocked access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook, and it may also have affected Teams, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft 365 Copilot. The company traced the failure to an earlier network capacity upgrade that a later network change exposed. Microsoft said it had fixed the underlying problem and was restoring services in stages to keep things stable.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence found that attackers used the disruption to run a phishing campaign against users. The fake emails posed as Microsoft 365 service health notices and referred to the real incident identifier EX1550543. Some messages falsely warned that emails held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient clicked a link to restore them. Subject lines began with the word Outage followed by a six-character code, and sender display names combined organisation-specific wording with Outage Notification or Service Health. Microsoft named moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com as the domains used to send these emails, and it said recipient-specific SendGrid tracking links redirected to reallifeaccounting[.]com.

Microsoft advised security teams to examine suspicious emails and links, to investigate any user clicks, and to review their Safe Links policies. The company also confirmed that its security products were blocking the campaign. The report did not say how many users received the phishing emails or whether anyone clicked the links before the messages were blocked. It also gave no details on when the phishing messages were first seen or how long the campaign lasted.

stories.Headline: Anthropic likely prices IPO above $70 to $78 range and plans Nasdaq listing under ANT
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is likely to price its initial public offering above the current range of $70 to $78 per share, according to multiple sources who spoke to CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday. The artificial intelligence company plans to close its order books and lock in total demand at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, the people said, asking not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" and to start trading on Nov. 19. If the offering proceeds as planned, the company will debut roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion.

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. It reported a $104 billion net loss during that nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities, and it lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025. The prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of the listing. A group of researchers including CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after defecting from OpenAI, now its chief rival, and Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude.

Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video that if the company does this right, it can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded it for millennia. He said the company has to make sure that all the risks and all the ways things can go wrong with the technology are very carefully addressed as it brings the benefits and has a viable business at the same time. He also invited viewers to join the company on the next phase of this journey. Anthropic has long worked to establish a reputation as a safety-conscious AI company, and it underwent a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code.

Anthropic is facing a public market that has grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade, as well as mounting and widespread antipathy toward the technology in the United States. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned closing of the order books on Tuesday and the start of trading on Nov. 19.

stories.Headline: IBM chief Arvind Krishna urges India to scale chip and AI ecosystems
stories.Summary:
IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna said in New Delhi on November 16 that India must scale its semiconductor and artificial intelligence deployment ecosystems to become a global player. He identified chip design and assembly as India's strengths because of its skilled workforce, existing infrastructure and technical capabilities. He noted that India's contribution to the trillion-dollar global semiconductor manufacturing industry is only about $3 billion, which shows a significant gap. Krishna also said that while India has a strong position in software exports, its role in other technology value chain segments is limited.

Krishna advised the Indian government to focus on scaling these initiatives, and he pointed to AI deployment for global companies as another opportunity India can capture. Estimates suggest that AI could add around $500 billion to India's gross domestic product growth by the end of the decade, but India needs to accelerate AI adoption to realise this potential. An IBM survey found that more than 75 per cent of organisations have made little progress in AI adoption, even though more than 90 per cent acknowledge its usefulness. Integrating AI at scale requires preparing enterprise data and re-engineering business processes, according to the report.

IBM is expanding hiring in design, software, testing, site reliability engineering and AI skills, the article says. The report does not say what the Indian government plans to do in response to Krishna's advice, and it gives no timeline for any policy changes. It also does not say whether IBM's hiring expansion is tied to India specifically or spread across its operations. The article ends by inviting readers to share their thoughts, and it provides no further details on next steps.

stories.Headline: Apollo Hospitals' AI agent helps clinicians review adverse events and close over 60% of cases within three days
stories.Summary:
Dr. Rohini Sridhar, chief of medical services at Apollo Hospitals, led the daily review of adverse events at 1 p.m. on a Wednesday in Chennai. She and the clinical governance team analyze incidents such as falls, medication errors and readmissions to find why they happened. The Daily Tiered Huddle agent, an AI solution, assists them in guarding patient safety. It was developed with Microsoft Frontier Company's forward-deployed engineers using Microsoft Foundry. The agent reads hospital data collected in Microsoft Fabric and flags patient-care incidents requiring review based on set parameters.

The agent summarizes incidents, prompts clinicians for further information and suggests case assessments using Microsoft Work IQ. About 600 adverse events are reported monthly across Apollo's 55 main hospitals. Since rollout, over 60% of cases reviewed by the huddle are closed within three days. Dr. Sridhar said only the 40% are actually relevant for a deeper dive. The number of patient falls and medication errors dropped over July to September this year compared to the same quarter in 2025.

Dr. Sridhar said processing 600 cases per month with incomplete data and reaching a meaningful decision is difficult. She said they now have the data required to make an analysis. She said the team can intervene early, propose solutions and proceed toward prevention. She credited the FDEs, who were deeply immersed in the doctors' daily processes. She said they devised a tool to draw in data from wherever it sits on Fabric and did it faster than she thought possible.

James Edwards, one of four FDEs on the project, said he enjoys discovery with the customer and understanding what problems they face. He said the team brings technical expertise on what is possible at the cutting edge with AI. Ashokkan Somuveerappan, Apollo's chief information officer, said the FDEs were more glued to the outcome they needed to achieve. Juliet Joji Varghese, Apollo's director of nursing in Chennai, said staff are ready to answer leadership's questions because the AI generated questions to help them prepare. She said they are learning from what happened at other Apollo hospitals.

A year ago, Dr. Sridhar would have waited hours or days while answers were gathered manually from various records. Engineers used synthetic data for evaluations and testing, not Apollo's electronic health records. The agent writes information back into Fabric, stored in accordance with the hospital's data-handling standards. This continuous learning loop is referred to as hill-climbing in AI. Somuveerappan said the number of times questions and recommendations are edited measures the accuracy of the DTH agent.

The agent's cluster analysis is still a work in progress, and it flagged a cluster of central line-related infections in the bone marrow transplant unit. Dr. Sridhar cited an almost 30 percent improvement in staff satisfaction in Apollo's annual safety culture survey this year. She hopes to apply the agent to tumor board review and doctor handovers. She also wants to use AI to predict what is likely to happen to a patient from admission and flag deviations from treatment pathways. She said the best organizations will focus on near-miss events and identify them before they occur.

stories.Headline: Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang posts AI video of Sam Altman in a furry suit to promote Muse
stories.Summary:
Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short AI-generated clip on Instagram to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, appear together on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call, he is dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint meant to make him look like the cutesy character. The clip carries the caption “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse.

Meta requires AI-generated videos that depict people to be labeled as AI, and Wang’s post carries such a label. Static images, however, have no such requirement, which meant an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth that gained traction in October had no disclosure at all. That image was shared by a fan account holding a blue verification badge given by Instagram, and Goth’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread rather than focusing on the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness. Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery, and Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness.

Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton, reached for comment, noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment. Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.”

Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans, and in some cases legal action was threatened. Now that content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media, and ahead of the midterm elections political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents. A major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is still notable, especially on a platform that has been criticized recently over AI-generated content.

stories.Headline: Michael Anello shows how Drupal developers cut AI token costs with browser models and metering
stories.Summary:
Sessions at NEDCamp 2026 explored how developers can manage the costs and keep control of AI features built into Drupal sites, and speakers said cost and control should be treated as design inputs from the very start of a project. Michael Anello, in a session on Drupal AI modules worth knowing about, said Chrome's built-in model can be reached through developer settings and used by Drupal through the AI Browser Provider module, which cuts token costs for everyday summarising and drafting. He also demonstrated AI Metering, a tool that tracks token usage, estimates costs and enforces per-user monthly quotas. That module allows a local fallback provider such as Ollama when limits are reached, which offers an alternative to blocking editor requests, and the choice between blocking and falling back has a significant impact on the user experience.

Jacob Rockowitz, in a talk titled AI ate my Work, and I'm okay with that, discussed optimising coding agents by giving them small and predictable toolsets. He uses Git worktrees and custom DDEV commands as isolated playgrounds for agents, an approach that avoids hardcoded paths and reduces token spending by keeping agent context light. Jim Birch presented a company-wide AI governance system in his session on guardrails, governance and proof that a team still owns the work. His agency uses a PREP framework, meaning purpose, risk, evidence and person, to scope each AI use case, and the system includes a harness for tools, approved tools that do not train on company data, and managed settings. Birch also introduced ownership, where each AI-assisted piece of work receives a delivery record, a YAML file detailing the producer, reviewer, approvals and model used, which answers client questions about verification.

Fredric Mitchell, in a session on defending budgets, addressed budget defence in an AI-driven landscape and noted that AI overviews are eroding organic search traffic, which makes it harder to justify platform budgets based on traffic metrics. He proposed the Web Operations Maturity Model, a rubric that scores platform health across six areas, as an alternative. Ethan Marcotte's keynote, The Work We Want, explored the broader societal impact of AI and framed it within Ursula Franklin's stages of technology. Marcotte argued that AI is institutionalising control with a few firms, likening it to the historical trajectory of the sewing machine, and he suggested that AI limits function best when editors help set them, which gives those editors more control over their work.

stories.Headline: Donald Trump Jr. says investors underestimated political pushback to AI
stories.Summary:
Donald Trump Jr. said in an interview at Axios' annual BFD summit in New York that investors had underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem, speaking with Axios Pro Rata author Dan Primack on Tuesday. He appeared alongside Omeed Malik, co-founder of 1789 Capital, the venture firm Trump Jr. joined in 2024 and which has since grown from overseeing a few hundred million dollars to billions. Trump Jr. asserted that a lot of the pushback is manufactured, but he added that this does not mean it is not real. He said some founders of the biggest AI companies have probably not done themselves the best service as a marketing department, calling them probably not the best messengers when they say AI will rule the world and people should be thrilled.

The 2026 midterms reflected deep distrust of the AI race, with voters approving dozens of moratoriums on data centers, which President Trump rallied around. Asked whether investors, peers or the pair themselves underestimated the populist pushback to AI, Trump Jr. said he thought they saw that very clearly. He likened AI to any great innovation but said it will take some time for people to learn how to adapt it into their regular lives. Trump Jr. agreed that rage toward data centers represents a broader concern over growing AI influence.

That public anger is becoming key to candidates, and Democrats in six early 2028 primary states expect their presidential nominee to prioritize AI regulations, according to new polling data first reported by Axios' Maria Curi. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans took note of the sagging views of the data centers needed to power the AI boom, and while Trump has prioritized self-regulation for the industry, the November results raise questions about how Republicans will tackle the tech moving forward. Asked if there was anything Democrats and the White House could agree on after a November shellacking that could be good for business, Trump Jr. said they have got to focus on costs and inflation. He argued that the second Democrats win it is about investigations, which Trump Jr. could find himself targeted by.

stories.Headline: CERT-In flags low severity emBridge flaw and eMudhra removes file browsing functions to fix it
stories.Summary:
CERT-In issued a vulnerability note on November 13 about eMudhra's emBridge digital signature utility, a client-side application that lets web portals communicate with digital signature certificates and hardware tokens installed on a user's computer. The agency said the flaw could let unauthorised entities on the same local area network access file and directory names on an affected device, and it classified the threat as low severity. Cybersecurity expert Karan Saini reported the vulnerability to CERT-In. CERT-In stated that file-browsing functions within the interface did not verify whether requests came from an authorised source, and that these functions operate with the highest system privileges on Windows.

An attacker on the same local network could use a malicious webpage to send requests to emBridge and map out file and folder names on the targeted machine. The affected versions are 5.9.1.x to 5.9.3.x on Windows, 3.2.4.x to 3.2.6.x on macOS, and 3.2.0.x to 3.3.0.x on Ubuntu and Red Hat Linux. CERT-In advised users to upgrade to version 5.9.4.x or later on Windows, 3.2.7.x or later on macOS, and 3.3.1.x or later on Linux. Several government portals, including the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA V3 portal, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade and the National Single Window System, rely on emBridge for DSC-based signing, and the Income Tax Department also recommends it for managing DSCs.

The agency confirmed that the flaw does not provide access to file contents, permit changes or deletions, allow code execution, or expose cryptographic keys or token PINs. eMudhra published its own advisory on the CVE and said it fixed the issue on November 11, two days before CERT-In's note, by removing the file-browsing functions from emBridge entirely. The company said that with these endpoints removed the file enumeration capability is no longer available through emBridge, and it rated the flaw's impact and risk as low. An attack would also require several conditions at once, including an affected emBridge version, a malicious webpage on the same local network, the user opening it, and a browser without Local Network Access restrictions.

The company added that its firewall and local-only request handling block direct access from other machines. Saini posted on X that while the bug was trivial, eMudhra's own advisory had further downplayed it. eMudhra told Inc42 that every digital signature certificate requires the user to enter a token PIN before use, and it pointed out that CERT-In's note confirmed keys and token PINs had not been exposed. A company spokesperson said identifying and fixing vulnerabilities is a routine part of responsible software development, and added that large global vendors like Microsoft, Oracle, Google and Adobe addressed thousands of vulnerabilities every month. The incident follows a major cybersecurity event in October where weak private keys for eMudhra's intermediate certificate authority certificates were reported.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud opens applications for a 15-week sovereign AI accelerator for European and Israeli startups
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud announced on November 17, 2026 an open call for applications to its Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI, which is available in Europe and Israel and supports startups building AI solutions for European regulatory environments. The announcement was made by Giorgia Abeltino, Head of Government Affairs and Public Policy for Google Cloud Europe, Middle East and Africa. The program is described as equity-free and runs for 15 weeks in a hybrid format with virtual and in-person sessions. Applications close on January 15, 2027, and founders can apply on the Google for Startups Accelerator page.

The accelerator is aimed at a small, high-touch cohort of late-seed to post Series A startups headquartered across Europe and Israel with strong traction that use AI for sensitive, regulated workloads. Target areas include government and public service technologies such as sovereign document processing and citizen service portals, with defense applications excluded, as well as healthcare and life sciences, regulated finance, and cybersecurity and data trust. Selected startups receive architectural mentorship, one-to-one pairing with Google Cloud engineers, and advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act Regulatory Sandboxes. Participants also get support to deploy across Google Cloud's tiered sovereign portfolio, from regional data controls and external key management to partner-operated clouds such as S3NS in France and Thales in Germany and fully air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments.

Abeltino wrote that artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe, and that enterprises and public institutions need advanced AI while meeting data governance requirements including the EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA, and national frameworks such as SecNumCloud and BSI's cloud security and sovereignty principles. She said the program wants founders to build in Europe with solutions made in Europe, and that digital sovereignty for startups should not mean settling for second-rate tools or lock-in to a single rigid stack. She described co-engineering with Europe's tech ecosystem so founders can scale on their own terms from day one, for instance by combining Gemini models, open-weight models like Gemma and Mistral, and verifiable data residency and cryptographic controls delivered with local European sovereign partners. Past participants, quoted in the post, said access to Google Cloud engineers who understand sovereign and regulated constraints saves young companies time and that the program helps build compliance answers into architecture from day one.

stories.Headline: Philippines residents protest planned US led AI and manufacturing hub
stories.Summary:
Local residents in the Philippines held protests on Monday against the upcoming visit of President Trump to Manila. These demonstrations center on a planned artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub located just north of the capital city. The project serves as the first major action for Pax Silica, which is an international initiative led by the U.S. State Department. This effort aims to secure high-tech manufacturing supply chains that do not rely on China.

The proposed industrial hub will cover more than 4,000 acres of land in the Philippines. This project follows the December 2025 announcement of Pax Silica, which has since attracted over 25 participating countries including India, Japan, Israel, and the United Kingdom. The Philippines officially joined this initiative in April, leading to the current plans for the manufacturing center. The Marcos administration claims this development could create between 100,000 and 130,000 new jobs for the local population.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. expressed great excitement in October, calling the hub a grand opportunity to move the country up the value chain. Conversely, advocate Maninging Vilog argued that the project only benefits the United States while grabbing local lands. Protester Kaiser Cortina questioned why farmers and bus drivers should care about artificial intelligence. Representative Antonio Tinio noted that opposition to AI data centers is a global issue seen across Southeast Asia, including Indonesia and Malaysia.

The U.S. government is pursuing this strategy because of long-standing concerns regarding Chinese access to advanced chips and hardware. Recent attention increased following reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Participants in Pax Silica signed a declaration on Sunday regarding the protection of critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies. President Trump is expected to meet with President Marcos on Wednesday during the ASEAN summit before he flies to China.

Articles.Title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub

stories.Headline: Academic librarians expect AI to drive change and want to lead AI literacy, Elsevier study finds
stories.Summary:
A global study from Elsevier found that 83 percent of academic librarians surveyed expect artificial intelligence to be the biggest driver of change in academic research, while 81 percent also named the misuse of AI as the greatest threat to the integrity of the scholarly record. The findings come from the Librarian of the Future report, which draws on responses from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders. The research highlights the increasingly strategic role librarians could play within universities as institutions respond to technological change, evolving research needs and growing concerns around research integrity. Almost all respondents, 95 percent, expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years.

The report says 82 percent of respondents believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers, and 76 percent believe librarians should contribute to AI governance. Despite these expectations, only 30 percent report that their institution has implemented an AI policy, which suggests a significant gap between the adoption of AI technologies and the development of institutional frameworks to manage their use. More than three-quarters of respondents, 76 percent, anticipate greater collaboration between libraries and other university departments over the next five years. The findings also point to the growing importance of leadership, influencing skills and the ability to navigate complex institutional decisions as librarians take on broader responsibilities.

Ann Gabriel, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Networks at Elsevier, said librarians have always been essential to research, but the study shows an opportunity for their expertise to play an even more strategic role. She said that as AI transforms how research is discovered, conducted and evaluated, librarians bring a unique combination of technical expertise, ethical judgement and trusted relationships across their institutions. She added that ensuring they have the skills, support and visibility to contribute fully will be important as universities navigate this next phase of change. Jim O'Donnell, University Librarian and Professor at Arizona State University, said librarians long thought they were in the book business, or perhaps the information business, and that the survey shows the community now broadly recognises it is in the research business.

The report suggests that librarians are increasingly positioning themselves as partners in the wider research process, rather than solely as providers of information resources. Alongside AI literacy and governance, demand is expected to grow for library expertise in open access, research data management and research integrity. The report identifies responsible AI adoption, trusted information and research integrity as areas in which librarians could play a more prominent role in supporting researchers and institutional leadership. Elsevier says it will continue working with the global library community to explore how the profession can respond to these changing demands, and the full report is available at Librarian of the Future.

Articles.Title: Academic librarians "see artificial intelligence as biggest driver of change"

stories.Headline: Pearl engineering leader urges CIOs to measure cycle time and rework to gauge AI productivity
stories.Summary:
Nazar Yaremchuk, senior director of engineering at Pearl, wrote in CIO on Nov 17, 2026 that AI can write code in seconds but that is only the first stage of software development. He said AI-generated output can introduce errors, miss internal requirements or require extensive rework, so the time saved upfront can quickly disappear. Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. Yaremchuk said that if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren't so clear-cut. A report from Bain & Co found AI coding tools help developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%.

Yaremchuk said CIOs need to look at the entire process, from the initial idea to software in production, to understand whether AI is improving productivity. He said AI adoption metrics such as token usage and developer participation show how much a company is using AI, but not necessarily whether it is becoming more productive. He said a more useful approach is to track engineering cycle time, end-to-end lead time, review and rework time, and software quality. He said these measures are most useful when considered holistically, and leaders should assess whether quality is consistent or improving and whether review and rework are consuming too much time. He said establishing a baseline before expanding AI use, then tracking these measures over time, can help CIOs distinguish genuine improvements from shifts in where work happens.

At Pearl, Yaremchuk said, the team asked AI to help create pipeline automation, but it generated GitHub Actions workflows for an engineering environment that uses Azure DevOps and Jenkins. He said astute engineers caught the mismatch during review and had to rewrite the integration, and the code was plausible but didn't account for Pearl's actual infrastructure. He said Pearl has a quality-control process that combines AI-assisted review with human oversight based on risk, with lower-risk changes such as unit tests often reviewed primarily by AI while critical production-facing code still receives human review. He said Pearl's AI reviews identify an average of 16 errors per 10 pull requests, including security and architectural issues. He said the goal is not to remove humans from the review process but to use automation to catch issues efficiently and reserve human judgment for decisions where risk and complexity warrant it.

Yaremchuk said Pearl tracks engineering cycle time and has seen it decline month over month in 2026 as its use of AI-generated code has increased. He said that in September 2026, the average pull request Pearl released to production was 75% AI-generated, and 45% of all pull requests were written entirely by AI, with no line edited by a person before commit. He said savvy organizations have taken advantage of AI to automate repetitive tasks so that engineers can focus more on architecture, complex problem-solving and validating results. He said enterprises introducing AI agents that can execute multistep tasks and work together will need to rethink how they assign, supervise and evaluate that work, with clear permissions, defined responsibilities and appropriate oversight. He said of critical importance is determining where human judgment remains essential and how teams should adapt as more work becomes automated.

Yaremchuk said the priority for CIOs should be to redesign engineering workflows around the capabilities of AI, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing processes. He said this starts with establishing a baseline for development speed and software quality, then measuring how both change as AI adoption increases. He said it also means using the results to adjust workflows, review requirements and the allocation of engineering time. He said AI investments should be held accountable to the same business outcomes as any other technology investment, and more code, more tokens and broader adoption can indicate progress but can be misleading. He said the real measure of AI productivity is whether an organization can deliver better software faster, with quality and security intact.

Yaremchuk has nearly 20 years in software delivery and over a decade leading engineering organizations, and he oversees architecture, DevOps, security and AI adoption across a 280-person engineering organization at Pearl. He led a transformation that increased production releases from one to approximately 400 per week and now champions AI-native software delivery. He is completing an Executive MBA at Oxford Saïd Business School. The article was published Nov 17, 2026 and runs 5 minutes.

stories.Headline: Stephen Ferrara launches AI + Nurse Academy to give nurse practitioners a foundation in AI
stories.Summary:
Stephen Ferrara, a doctor of nursing practice and family nurse practitioner, was named Medscape's Nurse Practitioner of the Month in a feature published on November 17, 2026, recognizing his work helping nurses navigate artificial intelligence. He is the chief executive officer and founder of AI + Nurse Academy, an educational platform that gives nurse practitioners a foundation in AI, which he launched in October 2025. Ferrara said his motivation comes down to trying to fix a system he feels is not working as intended for the people it is designed for. Early in his clinical career, he realized state law did not allow him to do things he had been educated and prepared to do, such as performing licensing physicals for people pursuing a barber career, and he turned his attention to overcoming barriers such as full practice authority laws.

The academy currently offers nurse practitioners and registered nurses a 60-minute continuing medical education module, and upon completion users receive a certificate of completion and one accredited hour of continuing education. Participants can also join a community of peers to ask questions, share concerns and exchange experiences, with responsible use as the company's guiding principle. Ferrara said the main goal is to expose every nurse to what generative AI is, what it means for their practice, and to prompt them to consider how they will integrate it thoughtfully into clinical practice. He explained that he wants nurses to understand where AI makes mistakes and how it can affect patient outcomes, stressing that keeping a human or clinician in the loop means AI does not make any decisions without a human or clinician reviewing it.

Ferrara said that in nursing school he was taught that at the end of the day it is your license to lose, and that if you adopt a tool it is your clinical judgment on the line regardless of whether you choose it or are told by administrators to use it. He pointed to flaws in the research large language models rely on, such as the lack of robust cultural, socioeconomic and ethnic studies in certain patient populations, and said he wants the human between AI and the patient to be able to discern whether a recommendation is pertinent. He said it is his core belief that AI can potentially make him a better clinician through rapid access to information and the ability to personalize it to patients, but that it is not magic. He said clinicians are ingrained to do no harm and asked how AI can be made to better anticipate things and patients rather than spewing things that are not necessarily helpful.

Before retiring from his Columbia appointments earlier this year, Ferrara served as inaugural associate dean of AI, spearheading strategy and programs to ensure nurses gained foundational AI literacy, and he moved from assistant to full professor of nursing at Columbia University in New York City. As associate dean of clinical affairs and chief clinical officer for the ColumbiaDoctors Nurse Practitioner Group, he expanded services to include house calls and integrated mental health services, achieving Patient-Centered Medical Home recognition. As president and immediate past president of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, he advocated for the Improving Care and Access to Nurses Act so nurse practitioners can practice to the top of their license and education. Ferrara reported receiving profits from AI + Nurse Academy, and the article says the path starts with a basic framework and AI literacy and ideally ends with improved patient outcomes, with nurse practitioners determining what happens in between.
