stories.Headline: Guardian and New York Times executives warn AI search cuts reader traffic at Seoul conference
stories.Summary:
Katharine Viner, editor-in-chief of The Guardian, and Hannah Yang, executive vice president and chief growth and customer officer at The New York Times, spoke on Monday at the KPF Journalism Conference 2026 in Seoul. The event was held by the Korea Press Foundation at the Korea Press Center in Jung District, central Seoul, under the title "Navigating the Next Decade of Journalism." Viner gave the keynote speech and warned that AI-driven "zero-click" search is the biggest risk the Guardian faces right now. Yang described the same threat from the other side of the paywall, saying search engines and social media now send publishers less traffic. Both executives said the answer lies in putting journalists closer to readers and building relationships a chatbot cannot replicate.

Viner said her fear is that people end up with an agent that gives them a daily summary in the style of the Guardian rather than taking them to the Guardian. Yang said AI chatbot use for news had doubled in a year in Korea, Greece and Spain. Viner said the Guardian asked readers to pay voluntarily instead of erecting a paywall, and they gave more than 125 million pounds, or $165 million, in the last financial year. She said the Guardian has close to 200,000 monthly unique browsers in Korea, which per capita makes it one of the paper's biggest audiences in Asia. Yang said The New York Times launched a digital paywall in 2011 and now has 13.8 million subscribers, more than 10 times its print peak of 1.3 million.

Viner said that in 2016 the Guardian was losing a huge amount of money and faced pressure to put up a paywall, which would have meant only people with money could access it. She said the voluntary model "shouldn't work, but it does," and that the Guardian is trying to attach its journalism to individuals and learn from influencers. Yang said The Times boiled its strategy down to "a simple five-word business plan: Make journalism worth paying for." She said The Times made news more trustworthy by bringing people closer to the humans reporting it, with reporters sharing video and their experience on the ground ahead of this year's U.S. primary elections, and that "AI can't do that." Viner credited the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian and has no shareholders to pay, and contrasted it with Jeff Bezos's interventions at The Washington Post.

Yang credited the New York Times' "very patient owners," the Sulzberger family, and a journalism-first culture, and said she deliberately does not know which articles drive subscriptions because she does not want that to influence what the newsroom covers. Lee Kyong-hee, deputy editor of Content Division One at the JoongAng Ilbo, which publishes the Korea JoongAng Daily, asked what The Times would do with only a tenth of its budget. Yang suggested smaller outlets build on their differentiating factor, asking "What is your crossword, right? What are your recipes?" and acknowledged a subscription-led model "may not be the model in Korea. Maybe not now." David Buttle, co-lead of the Spur Coalition, said the British-based nonprofit launched in February has more than 100 members in 25 countries and "exists to force a fair licensing market into existence."

Buttle said the coalition is meant to last only while that market takes shape, and once publishers can protect their work from unauthorized use and set licensing terms, it will have no reason to exist. Thibaut Bruttin, director general of Reporters Without Borders, said journalism is "at a tipping point," facing five crises at once: violence against reporters, the global appeal of strongmen, the power of tech platforms, the collapse of the industry's economics and falling public trust. Bruttin said leaders around the world were studying U.S. President Donald Trump's approach to the press, and that Trump "was elected because he undermined the public's trust in the press." He said 71 percent of the deals AI companies have struck with news media are with British, U.S. and Canadian outlets, so the problem is the diversity of the news media, not the survival of English-speaking media. Bruttin said he was convinced the press would survive but warned it "could become like jazz music," still around but serving only "a small elite."

Yang said people are just finding news in other places, and that it is important not to confuse the waning of the link-based web with the idea that the public is any less interested in news. Viner said the Guardian gives its journalism away while The New York Times charges for it, yet both brought the same warning to Seoul. The conference's panel of Korean media figures pressed Yang on how The Times' lessons apply in a market where most news is read free on portals. Bruttin said he sees a vast majority of the news media in financial trouble, with no positive solutions or deals being presented by tech companies. The articles do not say what the conference's organizers plan next, whether the Guardian or The Times will change their models, or how the Spur Coalition's licensing push will proceed.

Articles.Title: Guardian, New York Times sound alarm as AI pulls readers away

stories.Summary:
The Financial Times published an article on 17 November 2026 under the headline "The AI sell-off makes sense. Staying bearish may not," but the accessible portion of the page contains only subscription offers and site navigation. No details of the sell-off, the companies involved, the figures behind it or the identity of the author appear in the available text. The article's argument, as its headline states, is that the sell-off is understandable while remaining bearish may not be, but the body of the piece is locked behind a paywall. Nothing in the accessible material says what happened, who did it or when beyond the publication date.

The page offers no numbers, dates or names connected to the story itself, only the pricing of the FT's subscription plans. Readers are offered a trial for one dollar over four weeks, after which the standard rate is seventy-five dollars per month, alongside other plans priced at forty-five dollars and sixteen point ninety-nine dollars per month. The article sits behind that paywall, so its claims about the AI sell-off and about bearish positioning cannot be checked against the text. The accessible page also carries a copyright notice for THE FINANCIAL TIMES LTD dated 2026 and a note that market data is delayed by at least fifteen minutes. No person is named as responsible for the article in the accessible text, and no spokesperson or author is quoted anywhere on the page.

The only statements available are the headline itself and the subscription terms, neither of which explains the reasoning behind the bearish warning. Because the body of the article is unavailable, there is nothing to paraphrase about what the author or anyone else said. The context of the sell-off and what happens next are likewise absent from the accessible material. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Korea reports six smart glasses cheating cases in national exams as Samsung opens AI eyewear preorders
stories.Summary:
Six cases of cheating involving smart glasses were reported in national qualification exams in Korea this year, and the top scorer on a national tax accountant licensing exam admitted to cheating with generative AI, telling police on Tuesday that he had used a miniature camera. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which administers the tax accountant exam, said it would consider inspecting all eyeglasses worn by test takers and introducing radio signal detectors to prevent cheating. The Korea Radio Promotion Association, under the Ministry of Science and ICT, is developing a dedicated detector that can identify AI glasses through Bluetooth signals. On Thursday Samsung Electronics opened preorders for its Intelligent Eyewear lineup, developed with Google, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, and the Gentle Monster collection is already sold out.

Global AI glasses shipments rose 263 percent year-on-year in the first half of this year, and display-less models that look more like conventional eyewear accounted for 96 percent of total shipments, according to the market tracker Counterpoint Research. In an Oct. 15 survey of 600 respondents by the Gyeonggi Research Institute, 92.2 percent said cheating with AI glasses in exams could become a serious social problem. The same survey found a double standard, with 56.2 percent saying they would use the glasses' recording functions themselves while only 26.8 percent said they would be comfortable with strangers recording videos around them. Counterpoint said growing public concerns over privacy and cameras are new challenges, and that these headwinds could introduce greater uncertainty and weigh on market growth in the near term.

Samsung said an external LED indicator lights up when the glasses take photos or record video, and the camera is automatically disabled if the LED is covered or fails to work properly. One AI industry official said the recent cheating controversy involved a miniature camera and earphones, but the backlash appears to be spilling over into the entire smart glasses market, and that a few isolated cases could attach a negative stigma to technology built to make life more convenient. Another industry official said every company developing smart glasses is working to address privacy concerns and prevent misuse, but they all share the same worries about the current situation. Professor Park Han-woo of Yeungnam University's Department of Media and Communication said society encourages people to embrace AI on the one hand while failing to give sufficient guidance on how far its use should go, and that institutions must provide clear and specific guidelines reflecting the changing technological environment.

Industry officials said the market has growth potential but fear that rapidly spreading cheating concerns could cement negative perceptions ahead of widespread adoption. The second industry official said government regulations on AI glasses would likely be introduced eventually, and that it is important to strike a balance between addressing public concerns and allowing the industry to develop new devices. He compared the situation to the concerns seen when smartphones were introduced, saying it would be difficult to hold back technological progress. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea said it would consider the inspection and detector measures, while the Korea Radio Promotion Association continues developing its Bluetooth-signal detector.

stories.Headline: LangChain raises a $300 million Series C led by CapitalG at a $3 billion valuation
stories.Summary:
LangChain, an AI agent management startup, raised $300 million in a Series C funding round led by CapitalG, the company announced on Friday, November 13, 2026, according to TechGig. The round included participation from Singapore's GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP and Sapphire Ventures, and it values the company at $3 billion. That figure is more than double the $1.25 billion valuation LangChain held a year earlier, when it raised $125 million. LangChain began in 2022 as an open-source project that addressed tasks early large language models found difficult, such as web searching and API calls, and it later shifted its focus to managing AI agents. The funding supports LangSmith, the company's agent management software, which is designed to be model, cloud and ecosystem agnostic so that businesses keep ownership of their intelligence.

LangChain reports 7,000 LangSmith customers, including startups Harvey, Rippling and Clay as well as enterprises Nvidia, Toyota and Salesforce. In a separate deal reported by Axios, Operand, which uses AI to do due diligence for private equity firms, raised $31 million across a seed round and a Series A led by Khosla Ventures at a $220 million valuation. Operand CEO Ram Gorthi told Axios Pro exclusively that the company focuses on non-traditional data sources to help firms get an edge and on AI to process a higher volume of data. Mirendil, an AI lab founded by former Anthropic researchers, announced a $1 billion Series A led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital on Thursday, November 12, 2026, but its release names no valuation, according to TechTimes.

The training bill the company cites, less than $10 million in compute, covers only its smallest model, and the company says agents wrote over 99% of the code for that model. The round arrives 141 days after Mirendil's $200 million seed at a $1 billion valuation, and no independent evaluation of any Mirendil model has been published. Bloomberg reported in September that the company was in talks to raise up to $1 billion at a $5 billion valuation, with Kleiner Perkins leading and Andreessen Horowitz in discussions to participate, but no source reviewed confirms the final terms match that report. For context, TechTimes notes that typical 2024 U.S. medians were about $3.1 million for a seed round and $12.4 million for a Series A. The articles do not say what happens next for LangChain, Operand or Mirendil beyond the funding announcements themselves.

stories.Headline: President Lee orders tip rewards and tech records law to curb AI cheating on college exam
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's college entrance exam, including a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or about $75,000, for tips and a proposal for legislation that would require tech companies to provide records for investigations. Lee remotely presided over an emergency meeting Tuesday evening while visiting the Philippines, hours after Prime Minister Han Seong-sook unveiled a series of measures to prevent AI-assisted cheating earlier in the day. The government's response follows a cheating scandal involving the top scorer on this year's national tax accountant exam, which heightened concerns that similar methods could undermine fairness in the country's high-stakes college entrance exam. During the meeting, Lee said the measures announced by the prime minister should be thoroughly reviewed, taking into account all criticisms and opinions, to address any shortcomings and ensure they are effectively implemented on the ground.

The measures announced earlier Tuesday include deploying 8,400 additional proctors, tightening inspections of students' glasses and clothing, sending emergency alerts before the exam, restricting public Wi-Fi access around testing centers and strengthening penalties for those caught cheating. Lee ordered officials to review additional measures ahead of Thursday's exam and proposed a reward system offering at least 100 million won to those who report admissions cheating involving advanced technology, with additional payments based on the number of individuals implicated. He also called for a system under which individuals involved in coordinated cheating schemes could receive reduced or waived penalties if they voluntarily report the violations, and he ordered that an additional emergency alert be sent at an unpredictable time during the exam to help identify unauthorized electronic devices. Lee also instructed the Education Ministry to provide stationery, including erasers and correction fluid, at testing centers to prevent such items from being misused to conceal cheating devices.

Lee reviewed the government's arrangements with major global technology companies to secure evidence in suspected cases of students photographing exam questions and using AI to obtain answers, and he called for legislation requiring technology companies to provide relevant records at the government's request, including in cases involving suspected violations during this year's exam. In a post on X, Lee wrote that he had instructed officials to pursue legislation requiring the submission of records related to unlawful requests for exam answers upon government request, starting with this year's exam. He also wrote that surely even the boldest test-taker would not risk getting caught because their communication device went off in the middle of an exam. Lee wrote that cheating using advanced technology is tantamount to stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of students who have worked hard to prepare for the exam, and he said the government would mobilize its full capabilities with a wartime sense of urgency to eradicate this theft of exam scores and ensure that honest test-takers are not harmed.

stories.Headline: Seoul dentistry student Lee Jin-woo livestreams solving Suneung Korean section to rebut AI cheating claims
stories.Summary:
Lee Jin-woo, a 33-year-old first-year dentistry student at Seoul National University, announced on Instagram that he will livestream himself solving the Korean-language section of Thursday's Suneung exam, according to a Korea Herald report published on Nov. 17, 2026. He recently drew attention after earning perfect scores on both multiple-choice sections, reading comprehension and logical reasoning, of the LEET held in July for 2027 law school admission. The exam, introduced in 2008 as the country moved from the traditional bar examination to a law school system, tests reading comprehension, logical reasoning and aptitude for legal studies rather than knowledge of law, and it also includes an essay section that individual law schools may consider. Reports noted that Lee was not the first person to achieve a perfect LEET score, since a legal professional who ranked first nationwide in the 2013 exam also earned full marks.

Suspicions that Lee used AI to cheat arose after he showed his test booklet during an interview with YouTuber Mimiminu, who is known for college entrance exam preparation content. The booklet showed corrections to his answers for questions 25 through 29, with his initial choices matching the correct answers to questions 24 through 28, leading some to speculate that he may have shifted answers by one question while copying them from an external source, possibly AI. The fact that the corrections appeared on the test booklet itself, rather than on the answer sheet where such mistakes typically occur, fueled further suspicion, and Lee explained that he misread the questions' requirements after losing concentration toward the end of the exam. He has also faced allegations of falsifying past Suneung score reports, because the reports he posted on social media for the exams he took in 2012, 2017, 2023 and 2025 all bore his current name, which he adopted after a legal name change, while he had used a different name while attending Korea University before enrolling at Seoul National University. His reported scores show a dramatic improvement over the years, from grades of 6 to 8 across subjects on the nine-grade scale in his first Suneung in 2012, to 7 in Korean language, 1 in math and 4 in English in 2017 with grades of 2 to 3 in the remaining subjects, to grades of 1 or 2 in major subjects by 2023, and to the top grade of 1 in every subject in last year's exam. An official from the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation, which administers the exam, told Newsis that score reports generally retain the name used at the time of registration unless it was formally changed through administrative procedures.

Lee aims to dispel the mounting suspicions by solving Suneung questions live under conditions more challenging than those faced by regular test takers, and while the Korean-language section normally allows 80 minutes for 45 questions, he plans to answer 56 questions in just 65 minutes, covering both elective subjects, Speech and Writing and Language and Media. He told a local news outlet that the livestream is intended to quickly verify his abilities using newly released exam questions that could not have been leaked in advance. The livestream will run on his Instagram account from 9:30 a.m. to 12:20 p.m. Thursday at the Daechi IDA Admissions Research Institute in Gangnam-gu, Seoul, with Korean-language instructors from Megastudy and Daesung MyMac and news reporters in attendance. The allegations come amid mounting concern over AI cheating, including a recent confession of AI-assisted cheating by the top scorer on the tax accountant qualification exam, and President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's college entrance exam, including a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or about $75,000, for tips.

stories.Headline: Samsung and Google sell out all 16 Intelligent Eyewear models in early preorders
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and Google saw all 16 models of their jointly developed Intelligent Eyewear listed as sold out on Gentle Monster's Korean online store as of Monday, four days after preorders opened in South Korea and the United States. Several of the models sold out within hours on Thursday, according to Gentle Monster, and reservations for a public preview in New York have also filled up. The glasses, built with the South Korean fashion eyewear brand Gentle Monster, are scheduled for release on Dec. 10 in South Korea and the US. Neither Samsung nor Gentle Monster has disclosed how many pairs were available or ordered, so it is impossible to tell whether the glasses are a breakout hit or simply in short supply.

The glasses cost between 650,000 won and 700,000 won in Korea, a starting price of about $490, and they pack Google's Gemini AI assistant into Gentle Monster's distinctive frames with Samsung's hardware engineering. Samsung has made comfort a selling point since unveiling the glasses in July, claiming they would be lighter than most competing AI eyewear, and the finished models weigh between 39.6 and 43.9 grams. That is roughly 7 to 10 grams lighter than the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which weigh around 48 to 51 grams. Wearers can ask Gemini about what they see, translate conversations, take photos or get directions without pulling out a phone, and because there is no display in the lenses, Gemini responds through speakers, with Samsung claiming up to nine hours of battery life.

Meta already holds a dominant lead, as its Ray-Ban smart glasses helped it capture 94 percent of global shipments of displayless AI glasses in the first half of 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. With comparable camera resolution and battery life, Samsung and Google will have to make their case through Gemini's capabilities and comfort. Google is also emphasizing privacy, saying bystanders' faces are obscured before images reach Gemini, and recording is disabled if the external camera indicator is covered. Samsung and Google have separately partnered with US eyewear retailer Warby Parker, whose six variations of Intelligent Eyewear start at $395 and will initially be available in the US.

stories.Headline: Samsung plans AI TV that pauses video when viewers leave the room
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics plans to reveal a new artificial intelligence television during the CES 2027 trade show in Las Vegas. This event will take place from January 6 to January 9 of next year to showcase the latest technology. The device, which is tentatively called TV-I, will use artificial intelligence to monitor the movements of people in the room. It can automatically pause a video when a viewer leaves the couch and resume playback when they return. This system aims to turn the television into a living room companion that understands the interests of the user.

The new television will allow viewers to search for clothes or restaurants appearing on the screen without using a phone. This builds upon the Click to Search feature from 2025 TVs that lets users ask questions using a remote button. Samsung has already partnered with Amazon in the United States to make advertisements on Samsung TV Plus directly shoppable. This service has grown to reach more than 100 million monthly active users across the entire world. The company is also considering the debut of its first humanoid robot at the same January electronics show.

Lee Won-jin, the president and head of the Visual Display Business, is leading this shift toward service revenue. He previously served as the head of Google Korea and was appointed to lead the TV business in May. Lee wants to move the division away from simply selling hardware to making money from content and shopping. This strategy follows a surprise leadership change that occurred before the regular year-end reshuffle of company executives. The company believes that relying solely on device sales is no longer a sustainable way to turn a profit.

The shift comes as TrendForce expects global television shipments to drop 0.8 percent to 194.65 million units this year. Long replacement cycles and slow demand are creating a difficult market for manufacturers of electronic screens. Low prices from Chinese competitors and the rising cost of components have added further strain to the industry. Samsung is now betting on steady income from existing customers through advertising and digital services. Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong recently visited the Robotics eXperience Business Office to check on the progress of the robot business.

stories.Headline: Kim Jina meets Jacob Helberg in San Francisco to discuss AI and economic cooperation
stories.Summary:
Second Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jina met with U.S. Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg and discussed cooperation in artificial intelligence and broader bilateral economic ties, Seoul's foreign ministry said Tuesday. The talks took place in San Francisco on Monday local time, according to the ministry. Kim attended the Pax Silica Retreat in San Francisco on Sunday, where she took part in government-level discussions and public-private exchanges on AI and economic security. Kim signed the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity at the retreat. Kim also met with Qatari Minister of State for Trade Affairs Ahmad Al-Sayed in San Francisco on Monday to discuss bilateral ties and ways to expand cooperation in investment, AI and other areas.

Kim emphasized South Korea's broad capabilities across the AI value chain and its readiness to work with the United States and other partner countries. She explained the objectives of South Korea's AI Basic Act and outlined plans for major projects involving semiconductors, data centers and physical AI, including efforts to match companies for cooperation. The retreat brought together representatives from 13 countries and the European Union, while 10 of them signed the San Francisco Declaration, including South Korea, the U.S., Japan, Australia, India and Britain. The declaration calls for cooperation to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure and promote super intelligence-led growth. Launched in December 2025, Pax Silica is a consultative platform among like-minded countries aimed at promoting cooperation in AI and economic security.

Helberg asked about Seoul's AI policy direction and plans for major projects, and proposed encouraging greater collaboration between companies from the two countries. The two sides agreed to strengthen cooperation in AI and other advanced industries and encourage business collaboration in various areas, including semiconductors, data centers and physical AI, the ministry said. The officials also discussed ways to promote bilateral trade and investment and deepen cooperation in strategic industries, and agreed to continue consultations on ways to advance bilateral economic cooperation. Kim called for Washington's support for the successful implementation of South Korea's investment projects in the U.S., announced last month. She stressed the importance of ensuring stable visits by Korean businesspeople to facilitate the investments and called for working-level discussions on ways to improve investment conditions.

Al-Sayed expressed interest in South Korea's major projects involving semiconductors, data centers and physical AI. The two sides agreed to continue close communication to advance cooperation in trade, investment, AI and others. The ministry said the Kim and Helberg talks took place on Monday local time in San Francisco. Kim and Helberg posed for a photo in San Francisco on Nov. 16, 2026, in a photo provided by Seoul's foreign ministry. Kim spoke with Al-Sayed during their meeting in San Francisco on Nov. 16, 2026, in a photo provided by the foreign ministry.

The ministry said Tuesday that the Kim and Helberg meeting took place in San Francisco on Monday local time. The retreat where Kim signed the declaration was held in San Francisco on Sunday. The articles were published by Yonhap News Agency on Nov. 17, 2026, and Nov. 16, 2026. The ministry provided photos of Kim with Helberg and with Al-Sayed, both dated Nov. 16, 2026. The articles list related coverage on a Pax Silica Summit in Washington and a senior U.S. official's praise of South Korea's chip production.

The articles do not say what South Korea's investment projects in the U.S. announced last month involve. They do not name the three countries and the European Union that did not sign the San Francisco Declaration. They do not give the date of the Kim and Helberg meeting beyond Monday local time or the date of the Al-Sayed meeting beyond Monday. They do not say what the working-level discussions on investment conditions would cover or when they would occur. They do not say what follow-up steps the two sides planned after agreeing to continue consultations.

stories.Headline: China-linked Vapor Panda group uses AI tools to target Korean foreign policy organizations
stories.Summary:
A China-linked hacking group known as Vapor Panda targeted Korean diplomacy and foreign policy organizations using artificial intelligence tools. These cyberattacks occurred between October 17 and October 29, 2026, and some of the attempts were successful. The group used an AI agent-based penetration testing tool called Artex to scan for vulnerabilities in web applications and interfaces. This campaign was separate from other attacks against the Korean financial sector that took place during the previous month.

The Vapor Panda group targeted more than 200 organizations worldwide, including security agencies in Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and Latin America. They also attacked United States companies in the financial, defense, nuclear energy, semiconductor, and pharmaceutical sectors. The hackers primarily used the Chinese AI model DeepSeek to power Artex, though they may have used other paid subscriptions. This automation allowed the group to target hundreds of organizations simultaneously while potentially reducing the overall cost of the operations.

Adam Meyers, the senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike, reported these findings during a briefing on Tuesday. He stated that AI does not create a new form of attack but instead increases the speed and scale of existing methods. Meyers noted that automating processes previously done by humans has lowered the barriers for carrying out these cyberattacks. He emphasized that organizations can still defend against such threats by maintaining round-the-clock monitoring and sufficient visibility into their security environments.

stories.Headline: Han Won-seok tells police he used a hidden camera, smartphone and small monitor to cheat on the tax accountant exam
stories.Summary:
Han Won-seok, who has admitted to cheating on this year's tax accountant certification exam, told police that he used a small monitor alongside a miniature camera and a smartphone to aid him during the test, according to news reports on Tuesday. In a written confession, Han reportedly said he used a hidden camera to photograph the exam questions, sent them to a generative AI model through his smartphone to get the answers, and then viewed the responses on a separate monitor roughly the size of a smartphone. Earlier speculation had said that he may have used a tiny earpiece to receive the answers, and the exact type of monitor he used remains unclear. Han answered 159 of 160 multiple-choice questions correctly in the first round of the exam in April, and he achieved perfect scores in three of the four subjects, including introductory tax law, where other candidates scored an average of just 30.18 points out of 100. The cheating scandal came to light on Sunday when Han confessed to his actions in a video posted on the YouTube channel of his attorney, Lee Don-ho, after his exceptionally high scores sparked suspicions among other test-takers.

Han told reporters at around 9:17 a.m. as he arrived at the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency's investigation headquarters in Mapo-gu, western Seoul, that he was truly sorry to those who prepared for the exam and those involved, and that he would not hide what he did and would tell the truth to investigative authorities. Police are conducting forensic examinations of the devices Han submitted as part of an investigation into whether any accomplices were involved. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which oversees national qualification exams, said two proctors were stationed in the room where Han took the exam, and he was seated in the middle of the second row during the first round and the middle of the front row during the second. As more details emerged about the equipment used in the scheme, criticism mounted over how the cheating went unnoticed by exam supervisors, with one user writing on the online community DC Inside that even if the devices were small, they were still about the size of a smartphone except for the tiny camera, and asking where he could have hidden them.

Amid growing concerns over AI-assisted cheating, police have set up a special task force to crack down on exam fraud, and authorities also plan to investigate a growing number of online posts circulating on social media and internet forums in which users claim to have cheated on exams using AI, news reports said. The scandal has also cast suspicion on others who passed the same exam as Han, raising questions about whether more cases of cheating may have gone undetected. In response, the Korea Association of Certified Tax Accountants plans to introduce new tests during mandatory practical training to assess newly certified tax accountants' skills without AI assistance and identify those who may have cheated on the exam. The association said it would do everything it could to ensure that those who obtained their certifications through cheating are not allowed to practice as tax accountants and represent taxpayers.

stories.Headline: Mullin says an expert blames AI for recent system outages while Duffy calls the situation a head-scratcher
stories.Summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he spoke with an unnamed technology expert who blamed artificial intelligence for the series of system outages over the past few days, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the situation a head-scratcher. Several cyber mishaps have occurred since last week, including issues with Microsoft systems, a nationwide ground stop due to a telecommunications error, several major online banks and banking services experiencing system failures, and an issue with United Airlines's system. The scenarios happening in tandem have caused concern that America's technological infrastructure is at risk. Mullin told Fox News that he spoke with a technology expert, whom he clarified was not SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who suspected AI could be attempting to fix problems when added to older systems.

Mullin said the expert told him these programs are not designed to work as fast as AI, so when a program able to write code goes in, it self-fixes, and as it starts self-fixing itself it is like doing a change order on a house, where changing one thing starts everything else changing. He described that ripple effect as causing systems to be overrun that were not designed to run as fast as AI technology is today. Mullin again clarified there is no evidence that the outages affecting aviation, banking, and Microsoft are the result of a cyberattack. He said he could tell with 98% certainty that this is not a cyberattack, noting that no one is out there taking claims for it and that they are not seeing the traffic or the footprints going in and out, so nothing points to it being connected other than what the cyber guy briefed him on about three hours earlier.

Duffy also recognized the apparent pattern of technology failures but mainly discussed the issues facing aviation, saying he was just learning about the issues facing United Airlines while pointing out the banking and Microsoft incidents occurring in the same time span. He said the United problem is not an FAA systemwide problem but that it is a head-scratcher, and that as of right now he does not know the root cause of United. Duffy said he asked the FBI to come in just to make sure to put people at ease that this was not a hack, and he said he thinks it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error. The Department of Transportation has said the flight stoppage Friday evening was due to a disruption caused by an L3Harris contractor upgrading a telecommunications line from copper wire to a fiber-optic cable, and that as the contractor installed the new router, the new technology is claimed to have overloaded the air traffic control system, leading to the ground stop.

stories.Headline: OpenAI offers a free classifier to vetted groups and pauses ChatGPT for 24 hours on flagged abuse attempts
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced a new image classifier on Monday, November 16, 2026, at a press briefing in Washington, DC, according to The Verge’s coverage. The tool detects potential child sexual abuse material, including AI-generated imagery. OpenAI is offering free access to vetted organizations. The announcement has two halves: a detection tool for investigators and platforms, and new friction inside ChatGPT for users who try to find abusive material. OpenAI said it will also give developers guidance on detecting this type of content and train law-enforcement personnel on using AI in investigations.

OpenAI said the classifier can tell AI-generated abusive imagery apart from authentic imagery involving children. Access is free for vetted organizations, and OpenAI has not said how many groups are receiving access. OpenAI said new ChatGPT warnings will interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and direct users toward specialist help. When the warning triggers, OpenAI said it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. OpenAI said it reports all identified CSAM on its platforms to NCMEC.

OpenAI attributed the wording in coverage to the company as a whole, and the coverage includes no direct quote from an individually named OpenAI representative. OpenAI frames the tool around efficiency, saying a classifier that ranks and flags files can shrink investigators’ exposure and speed the path to cases where a living child needs help. OpenAI says its Stop It Now helpline regularly hears from people who report that an AI chatbot sent them there, though OpenAI has not published a count of those contacts. OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. The public coverage does not establish the classifier’s official product name, a release price beyond the free tier for vetted groups, technical accuracy, model specifications, training-data details, or how many organizations are receiving access.

The Internet Watch Foundation, a UK hotline, reported 3,440 AI-generated CSAM videos in 2025, up from 13 in 2024. IWF classified 65% of those videos, or 2,233, as Category A, the most severe tier under UK law, and 30%, or 1,027 videos, as Category B. Childlight data reported on November 16, 2026 put referrals of AI-generated material to the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children at about 4,700 in 2023 and more than 400,000 in 2025, an implied two-year change of about 8,400%. Google and Microsoft have long offered hash-matching, content classifiers, and reporting or moderation tools, Meta uses automated detection, hash databases, human review, and NCMEC reporting, and Thorn’s Safer platform gives trust-and-safety teams tools to detect, review, and report CSAM. Small nonprofits and under-resourced police units stand to gain the most from free access, but only if the vetting process is quick enough for them to use.

For most of the past two decades, the fight against online child abuse imagery rested on a shared database model in which platforms hashed known files and compared uploads against them. A hash catches a file someone already identified but fails on a freshly generated image that no one has seen. A classifier can flag new material, which is why synthetic abuse pushes the industry toward models. Classifiers produce false positives and false negatives, and hashes mostly do not. OpenAI’s distinct move is the bundle, pairing a free classifier for vetted groups with developer guidance, police training, and user-facing warnings inside its own product.

The public coverage does not explain how removal of a flagged conversation interacts with preservation for investigators. Whether the tool reliably separates synthetic from authentic imagery is the open question, because OpenAI has not published accuracy figures in the coverage reviewed. Readers should expect child-safety groups to ask for a model card, an audit path, or both, and the sources reviewed for this story contain no evidence that either is public. How often each layer of OpenAI’s stack fires is not public. More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korean law and accounting firms launch AI compliance certification service
stories.Summary:
Three South Korean law and accounting firms launched a new AI compliance-certification service on November 17, 2026. This professional service was developed by D&A LLC, LIN LLC, and Deloitte Anjin LLC to assist companies. These organizations want to help businesses assess and demonstrate their adherence to domestic and international rules. The firms created this tool as companies expand their use of artificial intelligence across various operations. The certification process requires an evaluation of corporate AI management frameworks against several specific regulatory requirements.

It measures these frameworks against the South Korea AI Basic Act, the EU AI Act, and various international standards. The service assigns compliance grades to companies based on how well they meet these legal obligations. These grades are intended to help businesses defend themselves against potential litigation over AI-related harm. The developers of this service believe that public certification can bolster the legal defenses of companies using this technology.

They stated that the tool helps firms demonstrate compliance with newly introduced artificial intelligence rules and existing business regulations. By obtaining these grades, companies can show they have taken necessary steps to manage risks. This approach allows businesses to prepare for future regulatory changes while maintaining their current technological growth. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google gives Japan early access to its latest AI model to boost cybersecurity
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 17, 2026, that it will provide the Japanese government and major infrastructure providers with early access to its latest artificial intelligence model. This strategic move aims to strengthen the national cybersecurity posture of Japan as the country faces a significant increase in digital attacks. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian traveled to Japan on November 16 to discuss these security measures with various government officials. The initiative is designed to help the nation defend its critical systems against an AI-fueled surge in malicious activities.

The program requires the deployment of frontier AI technology to identify and mitigate threats across essential infrastructure networks throughout the country. By granting early access to these advanced models, Google intends to help Japan manage the risks associated with sophisticated cyberattacks. This collaboration focuses on providing the tools necessary to protect sensitive data and maintain the stability of vital public services. The integration of these AI capabilities will allow security teams to respond more quickly to emerging vulnerabilities in their software.

Thomas Kurian is the executive responsible for overseeing this expansion of cyberdefense support during his recent visit to Tokyo. He met with government representatives to coordinate the delivery of these high-level AI tools to the appropriate agencies. While the specific details of his remarks were not fully disclosed, the visit emphasized the need for stronger partnerships between tech leaders and national governments. The goal is to ensure that Japan has the most current technology to combat the evolving nature of global cyber threats.

This development occurs as Japan continues to grapple with a sharp rise in unauthorized external access to its critical systems. The country has recently experienced security breaches, including an incident involving the Fugaku supercomputer, which highlighted existing gaps in security spending. These events have prompted Japanese officials to seek more advanced models from various technology firms to secure their digital borders. The partnership with Google represents a critical step in the broader effort to modernize the nation's defensive capabilities.

stories.Headline: Foreign investors return to Indian stocks as capital rotates away from AI shares
stories.Summary:
Indian stocks experienced a rapid rebound on November 17, 2026, as foreign investors returned to the market. This surge occurred because global investors shifted their focus away from artificial intelligence shares and responded to falling oil prices. These combined factors encouraged a significant rotation of capital back into Indian equities after a period of selling. The market recovery followed a trend of volatility affecting several other major Asian stock exchanges.

The shift in investor sentiment resulted in nearly $9 billion in foreign investor inflows into the Indian market. This financial movement was further supported by the results of the United States midterm elections and a decrease in global oil costs. Previously, these stocks had been sold off due to widespread concerns regarding headwinds created by artificial intelligence. The current rebound indicates a strategic hedge as investors move away from AI-related assets.

Market analysts suggest that the recovery is driven by a global rotation away from technology shares that were previously overvalued. Foreign investors are now taking a fresh look at Indian stocks to diversify their portfolios against AI risks. While specific officials were not named, the trend reflects a broader reaction to geopolitical and economic shifts. The inflow of capital suggests a renewed confidence in the stability of the Indian economy.

Articles.Title: Indian stocks stage rapid rebound as AI hedge accelerates

stories.headline_source: Indian stocks stage rapid rebound as AI hedge accelerates

stories.Headline: Utah tests AI that diagnoses acne and prescribes treatment without a doctor visit
stories.Summary:
Utah is running a first-of-its-kind experiment to test whether artificial intelligence can safely deliver health care, including diagnosing patients and prescribing medication without a patient seeing a doctor, according to KUTV. The state's Office of AI Policy is overseeing pilot programs with seven companies testing different applications of AI in health care, and one of those companies is Nolla Health, which operates the Nolla Derm app. That app allows patients to receive an acne diagnosis and prescription without ever seeing a doctor face-to-face, the station reported on November 16, 2026. Patients older than 18 and not pregnant can download the app, pay a subscription fee and upload five pictures of their acne, after which the trained AI system makes a diagnosis and recommends treatment. Dr. Zaid Fadul, chief medical adviser for Nolla Health, said the AI can prescribe only from a list of five to eight approved generic medications commonly used to treat acne, and the app prescribes Nolla Derm creams rather than oral medications.

During the first phase of the pilot, Fadul and a second physician must review and approve every prescription before it goes to a patient, and if the AI performs well in that stage the program can advance to later stages giving the technology more autonomy. Utah's Office of AI Policy said the pilot programs will go through three stages and can operate for a maximum of three years, with independent evaluators selected by the state but paid by the participating companies determining whether the technology is safe and appropriate before it advances. Current laws governing patient safety and privacy apply to all the pilot programs, and Utah law currently allows only humans to practice medicine. Zach Boyd, director of the Utah Office of AI Policy, said Utah does not have enough doctors and other health care professionals to meet growing demand, and the goal is to find out whether AI can take on some routine clinical tasks so physicians can focus on more complex issues such as cancer.

Boyd said he does not believe AI will replace doctors anytime soon and acknowledged that AI will make mistakes, just as human providers do, but he said the technology will have to perform at least as well as a human provider before the state allows it to advance. Fadul said acne medication is relatively low-risk and a good way to test AI prescribing for patients who often struggle to get a timely dermatologist appointment, adding that he wants to increase access to physicians rather than replace them. Michelle McOmber, president of the Utah Medical Association, questioned whether AI should be placed between doctors and patients, saying it is not appropriate to take the physician out of the loop when prescribing medication, though she said AI could help doctors with paperwork and administrative tasks. If the pilot programs are successful, their results could help guide the state in making regulatory changes, according to the report.

Articles.Title: Utah tests if AI can safely diagnose patients, prescribe medication - KUTV

stories.Headline: Taiwan dollar weakens as AI boom earnings stay in foreign accounts
stories.Summary:
The Taiwan dollar has begun sliding toward its weakest exchange rate since 2016, which contradicts the usual rules of currency trading. This unexpected decline occurred despite the island experiencing its longest streak of double-digit quarterly economic growth in nearly 40 years. The current situation is driven by a massive boom in artificial intelligence that has generated immense wealth. Huge amounts of export earnings are piling up in foreign accounts rather than supporting the local currency.

The economic strength of the region is evidenced by the fourth-largest current-account surplus currently found in the entire world. Two major companies, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co., are central to this growth. These two industry giants combined to bring in roughly 140 billion dollars in sales during the third quarter alone. This massive influx of capital from the AI sector should normally lead to a much stronger national currency.

Market analysts are confounded because the overwhelming evidence on paper suggests the currency should be increasing in value. They note that the paradox exists because the earnings from the AI boom are not being converted back into the local dollar. The disconnect between the strong economic performance and the weak currency remains a significant puzzle for traders. No specific officials have provided a formal explanation for why these funds are staying abroad.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Taiwan’s currency paradox: How an AI boom left its dollar behind

stories.headline_source: Taiwan’s currency paradox: How an AI boom left its dollar behind

stories.Headline: OpenAI partners with NATO to provide Daybreak AI cybersecurity tools
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on 17 November that it is partnering with NATO to give the transatlantic alliance cybersecurity tools from its Daybreak platform and to help it investigate potential cyberattacks, according to a statement released during the NATO Edge tech and digital defence conference in Izmir, Turkey. The ChatGPT maker said the deal gave NATO access to the advanced AI of Daybreak for uses ranging from reviewing software and investigating suspicious activity to validating vulnerabilities and developing and testing fixes. The company said its AI can help review software, investigate suspicious activity, validate vulnerabilities and speed up cyber defence across Allied networks. NATO said the tools will improve cyber resilience and protect critical digital infrastructure, at a moment when debate is growing around the world over the role AI should have in warfare.

OpenAI said it was fully committed to NATO’s principles on responsible adoption of artificial intelligence and on using the technology safely and securely. The company said NATO’s early use of OpenAI tools shows how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work in support of the alliance’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states. It also said the deal helps strengthen cyber expertise across multinational teams responsible for protecting Allied networks. OpenAI has already partnered with the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, known as ENISA, and with national cybersecurity agencies in France, Germany and Poland, and Ukraine also uses the US tech firm’s tools against cybersecurity threats to civilian infrastructure.

Dylan Browne, director-general of the NATO Communications and Information Agency, said in the statement that AI-powered cyber defence models represent a generational leap in cybersecurity. He said they accelerate vulnerability discovery, detect emerging threats at machine speed and enable defenders to stay ahead of adversaries. For NATO, he said, these technologies strengthen cyber resilience, enhance operational advantage and reinforce the ability to protect critical digital infrastructure at unprecedented scale and speed. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the announcement and the stated aims of the partnership.

Articles.Title: Defence alliance NATO partners with OpenAI on cybersecurity

stories.Headline: Experts say anti-AI trade and stable rupee draw foreign capital into TCS and Infosys
stories.Summary:
Major frontline Indian IT stocks including TCS, Infosys and HCLTech have seen significant price corrections and are now available at attractive valuations, according to stock market experts quoted in a Livemint report published on 17 November 2026. The report said experts believe smart global capital has started rotating out of overcrowded global AI plays and into Indian IT services as a hedge against overheating in Western tech stocks. It said the anti-AI trade and a stable Indian rupee are expected to fuel demand for IT shares and help long-term investors meet their goals. The report also said IT stocks are favourites of foreign institutional investors and that a stable rupee is expected to attract smart money moving out of bond and currency markets.

Avinash Gorakshkar, founder of Avinash Mentor Research, gave three reasons for treating IT stocks as long-term value picks: the anti-AI trade, a setback to Donald Trump's Republican Party in the US midterm elections, and the stable Indian rupee. He said FIIs are switching money from the bond market into emerging markets including India, and he advised investors to look at large-cap IT stocks, especially TCS and Infosys, because of their big exposure to US and European markets. He said these companies are expected to benefit from improved trade with the US after the India-EU trade deal and the midterm poll setback. Anuj Gupta, a SEBI-registered market expert, said the choice between TCS and Infosys depends on whether an investor prefers defensive scale and margins or higher dividend yields and a lower valuation multiple.

Gupta said TCS suits investors looking for a stable, lower-risk compounding core with superior free cash flow and industry-leading operating resilience during uncertain global demand cycles. He said Infosys suits investors looking for a higher dividend income stream of about 4.5 per cent and a slightly cheaper valuation relative to its earnings power. Mahesh M Ojha, vice president of research and business development at KC Securities, said Infosys has strong support at ₹1,125 and ₹1,112 and faces a hurdle at ₹1,163, with a break above that level expected to take the stock to ₹1,200. He said a fall below ₹1,090 could take Infosys down to ₹1,075.

Ojha said TCS has strong support at ₹2,378 and faces a hurdle at ₹2,440, and that breaking above ₹2,440 could take the stock to ₹2,500. He said a fall below ₹2,378 could take TCS down to ₹2,316. The report carried a disclaimer saying the story is for educational and informational purposes only and that the views and recommendations are those of individual analysts or broking companies, not Livemint. It advised investors to check with certified financial experts before making any investment decisions.

stories.Headline: Anthropic targets $1.33 trillion valuation as it prepares to go public
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering that could make it one of the most valuable companies to ever go public. According to a report by The Wall Street Journal published on November 17, 2026, the maker of the Claude chatbot is targeting a potential valuation of $1.33 trillion or more. This move comes during a period of intense investor interest in AI firms and recent developments involving the chipmaker Nvidia. The company has already reached a valuation of $965 billion following several massive funding rounds.

This transition to a public company follows a rapid climb in value that began in 2021 with a $124 million Series A round at a $461 million valuation. Subsequent rounds included a $580 million Series B in 2022, a $450 million round in 2023, and a $750 million round that pushed the value to $18 billion. In 2025, Lightspeed Venture Partners led a $3.5 billion round, while Iconiq later led a $13 billion round valuing the firm at $183 billion. Early 2026 saw GIC and Coatue Management lead a $30 billion round, followed by a $65 billion Series H in May 2026.

The Series H round was led by Sequoia Capital, Greenoaks, Dragoneer, and Altimeter Capital, with Amazon contributing $5 billion. Other early investors included Jaan Tallinn and Sam Bankman-Fried, though the latter's stake was sold during bankruptcy proceedings. According to the company's IPO filing, annualised run-rate revenue grew from $47 billion during the Series H round to about $81 billion by the end of October. PitchBook data indicates that more than 300 entities, including sovereign wealth funds and venture capital firms, have invested in the company.

stories.Headline: India plans AI and machine learning as core pillars of its VISTAR statistical overhaul
stories.Summary:
The article, published by The Hindu on November 18, 2026 at 07:00 am IST and written by Santosh V. Perumal, examines balancing AI-driven estimates and ground-level evidence in official statistics. It reports that AI and Machine Learning are positioned as core pillars in the newly approved Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research (VISTAR). The article states that VISTAR is set to overhaul India’s official data architecture. It notes that the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) seeks to use AI/ML algorithms to ingest, clean, and harmonise high-volume, alternative digital data. The piece warns that this could expose the country’s statistical system more to the risks of synthetic data, which is AI generated, simulated or hybrid.

The article states that VISTAR proposes increasing the number of major surveys from 43 to 59 during the 16th Finance Commission cycle. It reports that the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) for 2025 collected information from more than 6.7 lakh establishments across 24,153 surveyed first-stage units. It mentions that recent moves to introduce MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) on UPI may lead to higher cash transactions. It cites the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe 2025 Framework on Responsible AI for Official Statistics, which emphasises fairness, accountability, transparency and validity. It refers to Gauss-Markov’s BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator) principle as a key benchmark for estimation under specified statistical assumptions.

The article states that MoSPI seeks to use AI/ML algorithms to address the primary bottleneck of data silos. It reports that the World Economic Forum (WEF) said in a special publication in 2025 that synthetic data is becoming an essential tool in the data ecosystem, addressing many of the limitations of real-world data, from data scarcity to privacy. It notes that the WEF specifically highlights “model collapse”, in which repeated training on synthetic outputs can progressively degrade the diversity and quality of model-generated information. It states that the WEF said public scepticism about data authenticity grows as synthetic content proliferates, even for organic data. It reports that the WEF said this “liar’s dividend” threatens societal trust and is worsened by poor disclosure or traceability practices.

The article states that a statement reading “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war” was signed by 350 technology and industry leaders. It reports that the signatories included Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, and Bill Gates. It states that the statement warns of scenarios including loss of human control over machine optimisation goals. It notes that economists, international agencies, and state governments may challenge the numbers if they lack an empirical audit trail. It reports that possible consequences could be the misallocation of public resources, distortion of economic indicators and the erosion of public confidence.

The article states that the distinction between observation and estimation is fundamental in statistics. It notes that an estimate, however sophisticated, cannot automatically substitute for evidence collected from the ground. It reports that synthetic data is artificially generated using statistical algorithms, mathematical models or AI/ML techniques and is designed to reproduce the patterns, relationships and distributions found in actual datasets without necessarily reproducing the original observations. It states that synthetic data need not be rejected in toto since it has legitimate applications in research, privacy protection, testing algorithms and exploring scenarios in situations of scarce observations. It notes that India’s informal economy has put the statistical system in a tight spot as a vast part of economic activity remains outside organised corporate structures, formal accounting systems and regular digital reporting.

The article states that the challenge is to ensure that AI does not substitute for ground-level evidence. It reports that India must factor in human oversight, ground verification and source transparency while preserving statistical independence, taking a cue from the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe 2025 Framework. It states that primary surveys must be the bedrock of official statistics. It notes that model-generated estimates must be separately identified from actual survey-based estimates. It states that the broader objective should be producing estimates that are unbiased, reliable and supported by evidence.

Articles.Title: Balancing AI-driven estimates and ground-level evidence in official statistics

stories.Headline: Karnataka chief minister D.K. Shivakumar announces state aim to become global hub for AI, deep tech and semiconductors
stories.Summary:
Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar announced on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, that the State aims to become a global hub for artificial intelligence, deep tech and semiconductor manufacturing, speaking at the inauguration of the 29th Bengaluru Tech Summit, themed “AI and Beyond,” at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre. He told an audience of international delegates, industry leaders, scientists and investors that Karnataka was drawing on its progressive policies, research institutions and skilled workforce to lead the next phase of global technological innovation. The Chief Minister said the State already contributes two out of every five dollars India earns from software and services exports, roughly $173 billion in 2025, and that in the first half of FY 2025-26 it attracted $9.4 billion in FDI equity inflow, or 26.7% of India’s total. Bengaluru hosts more than 1,000 Global Capability Centres, with over 30 new ones bringing in more than $1 billion in investments during 2025 alone, and the city is home to over 24,000 recognised startups and nearly 40% of India’s unicorns.

To support deep-tech ventures, Shivakumar described several State interventions, including ELEVATE NxT, which gives grants of ₹1 crore to deep-tech startups and has disbursed ₹30 crore in equity-free funding to 33 ventures since 2025, while the broader ELEVATE initiative has backed nearly 1,500 startups with $41 million in grants over the past decade. The deep-tech accelerator Innoverse will guide 35 growth-stage companies toward industrial-scale operations over the next five years, and the Government First initiative allocates ₹25 crore to procure innovative solutions directly from startups. He said Bengaluru houses nearly half of India’s AI and machine-learning talent, and that the State is establishing India’s first government-driven AI University with a central AI Hub, a Centre of Excellence at IIIT-Raichur to deploy AI across 13 north Karnataka districts, and the proposed Bengaluru Robotics and AI Innovation Zone for prototyping and manufacturing. Under the ₹300-crore Nipuna Karnataka mission, over 33,000 people, including women returning from career breaks, have already been reskilled alongside global tech firms.

In hardware and electronics, the Chief Minister said Karnataka is moving from chip design to full-scale manufacturing, accounting for one-fifth of India’s electronics exports and hosting over 100 fabless chip companies and three-fifths of India’s semiconductor capability centre engineers, while global firms are investing over ₹23,000 crore in semiconductor facilities across Bengaluru and Mysuru. He outlined plans to expand the State’s bioeconomy, valued at $39.2 billion or one-fifth of India’s total, through a Marine Biotechnology Policy, the Krishikalpa Centre of Excellence, an institute for genome editing and gene therapy, the Charaka med-tech centre, an AI in Biotechnology hub and 11 new commercial incubators. Inviting global partners to collaborate, he said Karnataka would bring the talent, policies and partnership and asked them to bring their ambition, adding that what lies beyond AI the State wants to build there with them. Summit participation has grown from 57 countries in 2025 to over 75 this edition, with exhibitor numbers nearly doubling.

stories.Headline: ANU vice chancellor K Gangadhara Rao urges students to embrace AI and digital skills for jobs

Gangadhara Rao, the Vice-Chancellor of Acharya Nagarjuna University, told students on Tuesday that they should embrace artificial intelligence and digital skills to improve their employment opportunities. He spoke at the College Summit 2026, which the Magic Bus India Foundation organised together with the university on its campus in Guntur. At the same event, ANU Rector R. Sivarama Prasad said skill development and partnerships between industry and academia would improve students’ employment prospects. The summit showcased eight AI-based websites and applications developed by 16 professionals trained under the Magic Bus programme. The Ratan Tata Innovation Hub in Anantapur identified three of those projects as having potential for enterprise development and expressed interest in taking them forward.

The event also featured a panel discussion on preparing young people for employment, and college principals, placement officers, industry representatives and programme alumni attended the summit. RTIH CEO R. Hafeez Basha took part in the event, according to the report. Representatives of Acharya Nagarjuna University and the Magic Bus India Foundation exchanged a memorandum of understanding on the university campus in Guntur on Tuesday. The report was published on November 17, 2026, and updated the same day at 10:21 p.m. IST.

Rao said students should acquire skills that are relevant to industry requirements, and he tied AI and digital skills to better employment opportunities. Prasad said skill development and industry-academia partnerships would improve students’ employment prospects. Basha’s participation is recorded, and his organisation expressed interest in carrying three projects forward, but the report gives no further statement from him. The articles do not say what the memorandum of understanding requires or what changes it makes.

The context given is a push for industry-relevant skills and closer ties between universities and employers, presented at a summit that also displayed student work. The articles do not say what happens next beyond RTIH’s stated interest in the three projects and the signing of the memorandum.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen with an xhigh reasoning level
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, 2026, its third new model in six weeks. The model introduces an xhigh reasoning level, the first reasoning level above high on a Gemini model. It scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, one point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), and four points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (high). With default high reasoning it scores 51, just behind GPT-6.1 Sol (xhigh, 52) and Claude Opus 5.5 (high, 52).

Hydrogen has a 1M token context window and accepts text, image, video, and speech input with text output. It offers four reasoning levels: low, medium, high, and xhigh. It is priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens getting a 95% discount at $0.075. At xhigh it costs about 32% as much per task as Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) but about 2.5 times as much as GPT-6.1 Sol (max). Cost per task falls from $3.16 at xhigh to $1.87 at high, while medium costs $0.80 and low $0.29, scoring 41 and 27 on the Intelligence Index.

Artificial Analysis reported that Hydrogen has strengths in visual reasoning and non-hallucination. On GDP.pdf it scored 33% all-pass on medium reasoning, a tied first place, and on AA-Omniscience it had an 8% hallucination rate, compared with 43% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and 52% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). On AA-Briefcase, graders rated its presentation above other Gemini models, including Carbon. It was weaker on agentic terminal work, scoring 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 50% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, against 64% and 53% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and 56% and 58% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max).

Artificial Analysis said xhigh reasoning helps on science tasks, lifting Terminal-Bench-Science from 41% at high to 50%, but makes no difference on Terminal-Bench 4.0, which stays at 54%. Science scores range from 46% in earth sciences to 53% in physical sciences. Hydrogen has an output speed of about 200 output tokens per second, and at high, medium, and low reasoning effort it sits on the Time per Task versus Intelligence Pareto frontier, meaning no models are both more intelligent and have a lower time per task. Artificial Analysis congratulated the Google DeepMind team on the launch.

stories.Headline: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents raise code output 30 percent but slow reviews 49 percent
stories.Summary:
Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton found that firms adopting AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, while finished work did not measurably rise and code review took 49 percent longer. The working paper covered 718 firms and 725,938 workers. The current version is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper. The study ran from January 2021 to March 2026.

The paper's tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent and pull requests rose 23 percent. Finished work, counted as Jira issues resolved, moved by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. Time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase.

The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used an AI review tool, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent.

The authors say timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee's firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months. The authors acknowledge that larger firms adopted earlier and control for firm size. They say any hidden difference would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee's code only once a week.

The engineer said that after some outages caused by AI-generated commits, new rules required senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms' own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as "Co-authored-by" lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison. The authors tested whether engineers shifted to larger tasks by labeling a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extending those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model.

Harvey's workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss "commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work" and that its tool produces the research and a first draft "in a matter of hours." Cooley's Oct. 8 announcement says its redaction agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court. Neither announcement reports a measure of the review stage. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases.

More to follow.
