stories.Headline: Cal athletics posts AI-generated Big Game graphic with wrong scores and misidentifies Immortal 21
stories.Summary:
Cal’s athletic department posted multiple Big Game social media graphics with egregious errors on Nov. 17, 2026, and the Cal Football account posted the first graphic depicting the Stanford Axe. The image included game scores dating back to 1899 even though the actual Stanford Axe only has scores dating back to 1933, the first year it was used as a game trophy. The graphic posted completely inaccurate scores for the entirety of the series, with the wrong team winning in the wrong seasons, “Stamford” winning one and “Caanford” winning another. It included game scores for 1943 to 1945 when the rivalry was halted for World War II, and no updates at all past 1985. Most egregiously, the graphic had the wrong score for the 1982 game immortalized by “The Play,” the Bears’ five-lateral, game-winning kickoff returned for a touchdown that saw the Stanford band storm the field amid the runback.

When Stanford is in possession of the Axe, the school switches the score on the trophy to say “Stanford 20-19” because they object to the ruling on the play, but this graphic said “California 31-20,” a score that has never happened in the history of the rivalry. Cal deleted the graphic after a few hours after fans dogpiled the post, and the school put up a new version later on Monday showing the correct Axe trophy with all of the correct scores on it, though parts of the trophy aren’t very easy to read because of a glare. The glare mostly obscures the 2010s, when Stanford had a dominant run in the rivalry. Almost immediately after that gaffe, a second embarrassing gaffe was uploaded by the Cal Athletics account. In a post discussing the history of the Big Game, Cal celebrated “The Immortal Twenty-One,” the Cal students who stole the Axe in 1899 and kept it in a bank vault for 31 years.

There’s only one big problem with that: the “Immortal 21” is actually a group of Stanford students who stole the Axe back from Cal in 1930, not the Cal students from 1899. Cal Athletics left that post up for nearly a full day before deleting it on Tuesday morning. The errors come seven months after Cal reorganized its athletic department and moved the marketing, creative and communications units away from the school and into an external company called Strawberry Creek Studios. In announcing the restructure, the school said the move will “create a continuous stream of authentic storytelling that connects communities and student-athletes, and transforms engagement into meaningful revenue for Cal Athletics and UC Berkeley.” What Cal didn’t announce at the time was that the move came weeks after workers in the Cal athletic department had voted to unionize.

David Covucci, who runs the FOIAball newsletter, a journalistic outlet that uses public records to uncover stories in college athletics, reported last week that the entire University of California system’s communications, marketing and sales professionals filed to form a union with UC-UAW, and nearly 82% of the 1,600 workers voted pro-union. The union was certified on March 23, giving them immediate union protections even as negotiations were just getting started. But in April, as Cal announced the Strawberry Creek Studios, Cal laid off the entire athletic department’s workforce as part of the restructuring, and the school could only say affected employees were “encouraged to apply for these newly defined opportunities.” According to Covucci’s reporting, 17 workers laid off were part of the new union, which received no warning about the impending changes. The union responded by filing an “Unfair Practice Charge,” which Covucci obtained, against the school for the layoffs, alleging the school did not properly allow the union the chance to bargain with the school over the layoff decisions.

In effect, Cal Athletics did what Covucci described as a “union-busting” tactic to create a new content studio to try to drive more revenue to the department. The Strawberry Creek Studios announcement quotes Cal football general manager Ron Rivera as saying the move will allow Cal to “be better equipped to execute the vision of our football program and entire athletic department.” The Cal football team is 3-7 on the season and is likely to miss a bowl game for the first time in four years. Ahead of the biggest rivalry game the school has, Cal has posted two graphics with significant errors in them, one of which clearly appears to have been AI-generated, and only got deleted after fans noticed and brought attention to it online. The first graphic immediately led to accusations of artificial intelligence-generated slop.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen to strengthen AI cooperation and manage technology risks
stories.Summary:
President Xi Jinping and other regional leaders gathered in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday for the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting to discuss artificial intelligence. This event follows previous discussions in San Francisco in 2023, Lima in 2024, and Gyeongju in November of last year. The current meeting aims to strengthen cooperation regarding the adoption of AI and the management of its associated risks. These efforts seek to ensure that economies at various stages of development can share the benefits of new technology.

The process requires translating regional commitments into practical support to prevent a widening digital divide among member nations. This involves implementing the APEC Artificial Intelligence Initiative for 2026 to 2030, which emphasizes bridging gaps in capacity. It also builds upon a July statement from the APEC High-Level Forum on AI in Chengdu regarding secure deployment and responsible adoption. Specific goals include creating shared computing power resources, joint training programs, and mutual recognition of AI standards.

Nicolas Miailhe of the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council stated that the divide involves the capacity to choose and manage technology. He suggested that China could contribute by sharing its experience in deploying AI for manufacturing, logistics, and trade. Zhang Jingjia from Nankai University noted that while AI can narrow gaps, the concentration of data and talent in leading economies could reinforce existing advantages. Sun Chenghao of Tsinghua University proposed using voluntary pilot projects to help small businesses manage cross-border trade documents.

The regional cooperation focuses on areas that individual economies cannot address alone, such as costly infrastructure and differing data rules. Experts believe that moving from broad principles to concrete actions will allow every member economy to participate in the AI wave. The current framework is designed to carry this work forward into the host year of Vietnam in 2027. Future success depends on providing working tools and skills on the ground rather than just producing official texts.

Articles.Title: Forum presents opportunity for AI cooperation - China Daily

stories.headline_source: Forum presents opportunity for AI cooperation

stories.Headline: Professors Li Jia and Zhang Dandan say AI speeds up workers but not profits without organizational redesign
stories.Summary:
Professors Li Jia and Zhang Dandan discussed the disconnect between individual worker speed and corporate profit during an October 30 employers' summit in Singapore. A survey of nearly 9,000 executives across seven countries, conducted by the Bank of England, Bundesbank, and the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, found that 78 percent of firms use AI. Despite this widespread adoption, these executives estimated that the technology added only about 0.2 percentage point annually to labor productivity growth over three years. While employees are completing reports and emails faster, these technical gains have not yet translated into significant revenue increases for their employers.

Realizing these benefits requires a total organizational redesign rather than simply purchasing more software subscriptions to fix bottlenecks. A Microsoft experiment involving 7,137 knowledge workers at 66 companies showed that frequent users saved 3.6 hours on email, but meeting times remained unchanged. Individual speed is evident, as a study of 5,000 customer service agents showed a 14 percent increase in resolved issues, while consultants worked 25 percent faster. However, productivity lags when executive decision making only improves by 10 percent despite a 65 percent time saving in reviewing financial information. A 2024 Procter and Gamble experiment with 776 employees demonstrated that AI could help technical and marketing staff better integrate their work.

The authors argue that management must identify where saved time goes and focus on product innovation to drive growth. Research by Tania Babina on public firms in the United States suggests that AI investment boosts sales and employment through new offerings rather than lower costs, with returns appearing after two or three years. Large firms currently benefit more than small ones, as Singapore's SME adoption is roughly 23 percent compared to 70 percent for larger companies. The professors suggest that governments should provide subsidies and credible evaluations to help smaller firms overcome their lack of resources. They conclude that while software is easy to buy, the scarce and necessary capability is the ability to reorganize work.

Articles.Title: Commentary: AI Is Speeding Up Workers, but Not Boosting the Bottom Line - Caixin Global

stories.headline_source: Commentary: AI Is Speeding Up Workers, but Not Boosting the Bottom Line

stories.Headline: Attackers breach Fireworks AI twice and push malicious Cursor extensions to about 5,000 users
stories.Summary:
Attackers launched a supply chain attack against Cursor after compromising the AI inference platform Fireworks AI twice during October. The breach was discovered on October 29, and the threat actors used stolen credentials to push malicious copies of the Claude Code extension. These modified versions, numbered 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, were available through the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace for approximately 11 hours. The attackers gained entry by stealing a Cursor access key from Fireworks, which allowed them to access unredacted credentials and internal SaaS tools.

The incident requires users who installed the tampered extensions to follow a specific security notice, as simply uninstalling the software may be insufficient. Cursor estimates that at most 5,000 users were affected by the malware, which was served via a cache rather than the Open VSX marketplace source. The breach exposed archived non-production source code, limited customer support data, email conversations, product usage metrics, and some user credentials. This security failure also impacted other companies, as both Uber and Notion disclosed data breaches resulting from the same Fireworks AI compromise.

Cursor officials stated that the malicious activity occurred entirely within their own environment and that Anthropic was never hacked. They explained that the attackers used exfiltrated secrets to place unauthorized copies of the extension directly onto the marketplace cache. The company believes the situation is now contained, noting that no further attacker activity has been detected since November 1. They urged affected customers to take the necessary remediation steps to ensure their systems are fully secure.

Articles.Title: Cursor Supply Chain Attack Started at Fireworks AI - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: Kyndryl survey finds 78% of UAE leaders say sovereignty rules strengthen security
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl released the UAE findings from its third annual Readiness Report on 16 November 2026, drawing on a survey of 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries, including 100 in the UAE. The report found that 78% of UAE business leaders say sovereignty requirements strengthen security by increasing control over critical systems, compared with 69% globally. It also found that 52% of UAE leaders significantly changed their AI strategy in the past year, compared with 48% globally, and that 73% say they are deploying AI in workflows beyond pilots. Nearly three-quarters of UAE leaders, 73%, describe their core IT estate as mostly or fully modernized, in line with 71% globally, while only 1% call their environment mostly legacy, compared with 5% globally. The findings show that 72% of UAE business leaders say full operational control over their technology is worth paying 10% or more extra for, compared with 68% globally, while 73% say dependence on foreign technology providers is an acceptable risk that can be managed through contracts and safeguards, compared with 61% globally.

On sovereignty actions, 39% of UAE organizations reviewed who can access sensitive data, 37% updated data governance policies for residency requirements and 34% evaluated vendor lock-in risk. The transition to scale remains uneven, with 51% of UAE leaders still saying they are in the experimentation phase and 64% saying they have more technology pilot projects than they can realistically scale. Concern about cyberattacks stands at 39% in the UAE against 58% globally, yet average complete readiness across external risks is 25% in the UAE, broadly in line with the global figure of 24%. Maged Wassim, Vice President and Managing Director of Kyndryl MEA, said UAE business leaders are advancing AI adoption with a clear view of what they want to keep control of. He said the findings suggest control and global partnership are not in competition, because leaders want the oversight to protect critical systems and the reach of a global ecosystem.

He said the opportunity now is scaling AI, and that focusing on people, technology and governance can help organizations do that with confidence. Kyndryl describes itself as the world's largest IT infrastructure services provider, offering advisory, implementation and managed services to thousands of customers in more than 60 countries. The report says sovereignty considerations now extend beyond where data is stored to how systems are managed, who can access sensitive information and how organizations manage technology dependencies. The findings suggest that maintaining this oversight may help organizations manage technology dependencies while retaining the flexibility to work with different providers. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's release.

stories.Headline: Vultr expands Chennai operations into network engineering and developer relations and plans over 300 more hires
stories.Summary:
Vultr is expanding its presence in Chennai beyond data centre infrastructure into global network engineering, security and developer relations, Kevin Cochrane, its Chief Marketing Officer, told Dataquest in an interaction published on 16 November 2026. The company started with its first three regions in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, initially providing core cloud compute for cloud-native engineers building and deploying web applications. It is now extending that infrastructure with GPUs to support the transition towards AI-native engineering. India is Vultr's largest footprint outside the US. Vultr's developer relations team, comprising around 40 people, is based in India.

Before its recent Chennai expansion, Vultr had around 75 employees across India, and in the last few months it has hired more than 100 people in Chennai. It expects to hire over 300 more in the coming months, spanning systems reliability, DevOps, security operations, networking, server engineering and data centre operations, as well as sales and marketing. Network optimisation and network engineering across Vultr's 34 data centre regions worldwide are now being based in Chennai. Vultr has more than 2,00,000 customers worldwide. Vultr currently has four regions in India, compared with nine in the United States and nine in Europe.

Cochrane said Vultr's investment in India goes well beyond data centre capacity. He said the developer relations team in India creates educational programmes, content and documentation and manages the worldwide developer community, including hackathons and user groups. He said enterprises are bringing build systems and test environments closer to their engineering teams in India because that is where the teams are based. He said geopolitical uncertainty is pushing enterprises to distribute workloads across multiple regions for resilience. He said data sovereignty matters for AI workloads, citing a model developed using Indian healthcare data as an example of organisations wanting the associated workloads and data to remain within India.

Cochrane said Vultr sees an explosion of interest in demand for core CPU computing, with demand approaching a one-to-one ratio between CPUs and GPUs. He said Vultr offers a public cloud platform combining CPU and GPU computing, and its partnership with AMD brings together EPYC CPU processors and Instinct GPU accelerators in the same infrastructure. He said Vultr started with AMD for the Chennai cluster because there was customer demand for its MI355X GPUs, and that it does have Nvidia capacity in India and will bring in more. He said the Chennai facility is already connected to its power supply and will not affect the existing power grid.

He said Vultr is working with Supermicro on energy-efficient racks and using liquid cooling, whose closed-loop system keeps water consumption very low. Cochrane said that until recently enterprises did not fully understand how to use AI effectively, and that innovations such as Model Context Protocol, which allows AI agents to connect with enterprise systems and access data to perform tasks, are changing that. He said Vultr has seen a dramatic transformation in just the past three months. He said a significant part of the team in India is involved in site selection for future data centre capacity and infrastructure expansion.

He said the expansion will be distributed across India and it is highly likely Vultr will establish additional regions in the country. He said Vultr cannot disclose the potential locations at this stage. He said continued economic growth will require investments in electricity generation and grid resilience. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Rackspace raises 2026 revenue outlook and targets 20 to 22 megawatts of AI capacity by end of 2027
stories.Summary:
Rackspace Technology reported on November 16, 2026 that its third-quarter revenue fell 9.3% to $609.1 million, while its Public Cloud segment declined 17.2% over the same period. Despite that revenue decline, the company's adjusted EBITDA rose 8.5% to $75 million, and the company raised its 2026 revenue outlook. The company also said it expects to operate 20 to 22 megawatts of AI computing capacity by the end of 2027. Rackspace signed a multi-year deal to provide Blacksmith with 2 megawatts of compute and storage capacity in Northern Virginia, with deployment expected to start in early 2027.

Rackspace said the 20 to 22 megawatts of AI capacity could potentially generate $420 million to $460 million in annualized revenue when fully deployed and utilized. The company and Together AI signed a non-binding letter of intent to explore enterprise AI services and a joint sales strategy, and any offerings depend on further agreements and customer needs. Rackspace and HFS Research also surveyed 502 enterprise AI leaders, finding that 33% met or exceeded their AI business case while 96% reported major governance gaps. The articles do not say who at Rackspace is responsible for these figures or what executives said about them.

The articles give no named executive comments, so no one is quoted on the revenue outlook, the AI capacity targets or the Blacksmith deal. The survey of 502 enterprise AI leaders is the only finding the articles attribute to the company alongside HFS Research, and it concerns governance gaps rather than the financial results. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the stated expectations, which include deployment of the Blacksmith capacity starting in early 2027 and operation of the AI capacity by the end of 2027. Any Together AI offerings depend on further agreements and customer needs, according to the articles.

stories.Headline: AI removes code scarcity and makes human judgment the next constraint in software delivery
stories.Summary:
The article, published by ET CIO on 16 November 2026, says artificial intelligence has removed the scarcity of code in software delivery. It says AI now moves code generation, testing, documentation, prototyping and analysis through much shorter cycles. It says lower effort and cost are expanding production capacity and bringing more choices around priority, technical fit and trust. It says human judgment is emerging as the next constraint in AI-enabled software delivery. It says every technological breakthrough removes one constraint and exposes another.

The article says that for much of the digital era, building software required significant time, talent and investment, which kept engineering capacity limited. It says that ability to create software was a source of competitive advantage. It says features left in backlogs, workflow automations, customer experiences and new digital products can become more feasible as those economics change. It says greater production capacity puts more weight on where it is directed. It says more possibilities bring more decisions around priority, business value and the outcomes worth pursuing.

The article is by Saravana Kumar Dharmarajan and was updated on 16 November 2026 at 08:00 AM IST. It says companies need to implement effective governance frameworks to manage the intricacies of AI-generated results. It says organizations can maximize resource efficiency and turn software surplus into significant achievements by aligning technology investments with tangible benefits. It says the answer about where value lies will influence how organizations use the additional capacity AI makes possible. It says judgment, business context, decision quality, architecture, trust, attention and accountability carry more of the load as organizations gain this ability.

The article says the evolution of artificial intelligence is reshaping software delivery, emphasizing enhanced decision-making over traditional methods. It says attention will turn toward delivering business value and quality outcomes with an increase in organizational capacity. It says technology organizations have traditionally linked delivery capacity with output. It says more developers, larger teams and higher velocity gave organizations the ability to build more.

It says lower barriers to software creation have led to an increase in the value of the capabilities that guide what gets built. The article says agentic AI refers to systems that can understand context, reason, make decisions and take action. It says AI agents need access to real-time, relevant and trusted data and the ability to work across applications and workflows. It says they must operate within appropriate security, governance and human oversight frameworks.

It says their deployment must be connected to clear and measurable business outcomes. It says the question is becoming what the enterprise needs to put in place for AI to act safely, intelligently and at scale. The article says the question is no longer simply what AI can do. It says the challenge now is building the foundations to scale AI securely and responsibly, with real-time data, trusted intelligence and a clear focus on measurable business outcomes.

It says the article was read by 1097 industry professionals. It leaves open what scarcity comes next and where value lies when software becomes easier to create. It does not say what governance frameworks companies should adopt. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Coinbase's D'Agostino calls AI IPO bitcoin drain argument reasonable as Anthropic nears Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Coinbase's head of institutional strategy, John D'Agostino, said on the Milk Road podcast on Monday that the case for upcoming artificial intelligence IPOs drawing risk capital away from bitcoin was a reasonable argument, according to an article published on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He made the comments as Anthropic prepares to go public, with its shares expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. D'Agostino said he was not convinced the drain had done lasting damage to bitcoin. He said that what he looks for in such situations is a breakdown in market structure, with market participation falling sharply and concentrating among a single type of participant, and that he did not see any of that.

D'Agostino said he saw nothing structurally different from four to five months earlier, when everybody was extremely bullish. He described bitcoin as a commodity comparable to gold or crude oil, so its sharp swings did not worry him, and he pointed to crude oil, which once traded below zero, as the world's most important commodity. Such drops upset people who bought at the top, he said, but they do not devalue the asset. Bitcoin's price was up 0.3% during the past 24 hours, and on Stocktwits the retail sentiment around BTC remained in the neutral zone while chatter around it stayed at high levels over the past day.

On why companies have been slow to go public on-chain, D'Agostino said a company that lists purely on-chain could become the next Nvidia, the next Anthropic, the next Tesla or the next Coinbase, and that this was possible. For now, he said, most companies were sticking to traditional listings because they do not have to change, since bankers can promise heavily oversubscribed offerings and crypto cannot yet match that. He said the industry should stop dismissing skeptics, describing them as not stupid, as people who disagree and act rationally given their position. Larger companies will move only once on-chain trading makes up a meaningful share of their volume, such as 10, 20 or 30%, he said.

The comments come as Anthropic prepares for its Nasdaq debut, and Tom Lee had said retail investors may be cashing out of crypto ahead of the listing. The article cited other coverage, including a Wall Street Journal report that investors might be ditching bitcoin for the Anthropic IPO and a MarketWatch report that bitcoin was below $68,000 and could fall further if investors cash out to buy into the offering. D'Agostino's remarks were reported by Anushka Basu, who has no position in any of the stocks mentioned in the article.

stories.Headline: IFF uses AI to streamline its strawberry flavor portfolio across countries
stories.Summary:
Food and beverage companies are using artificial intelligence to help decide which recipe changes to test first, Food Ingredients First reported on 18 November 2026. International Flavors & Fragrances used AI to streamline its strawberry flavor portfolio across several countries. AKA Foods said developers at South African supplier TDC report saving 10 to 15 hours a week after adopting its tool. Cargill teams use predictive modeling to consider how reducing sugar or increasing protein could affect taste, texture, and mouthfeel. Nestlé said its recipe optimization tools help product developers balance taste, nutrition, cost, and sustainability.

IFF launched Concept Muse, an AI tool for developing early-stage food and beverage concepts, the week before the article. AKA Studio connects formulation, sensory, regulatory, and production data in one place, according to AKA Foods. Seventeen people across two sites at TDC now use AKA Studio to find and reuse previous work. Wageningen University & Research researchers advise manufacturers to test AI tools on reformulations with known results. Eirini Pegiou, a food technology researcher at WUR, points to hybrid modeling, which combines data-driven AI with mechanistic models and scientific knowledge of food ingredients and processes.

Benjamin Mattei, vice president of intelligence and digital transformation at IFF, said the process can be lengthy and complex, but with the right data and AI tools the portfolio was optimized and rationalized much faster while maintaining or enhancing local consumer preferences. David Sack, CEO and co-founder of AKA Foods, said a typical case is an ingredient cost spike or supply shortage where a replacement is needed without hurting the sensory profile. Sack said you still have to make it, feel it, and taste it. Renee Boerefijn, senior director of R&D for Cargill's indulgence category, said ingredients interact and a change that improves one attribute can affect another. Boerefijn described the predictive model as a decision-support tool that helps experts decide what to test but does not make the decision for them.

Boerefijn said equipment, processing conditions, raw-material variation, and the demands of an existing production line can all affect the finished product's taste, texture, and consistency. She said a solution needs to meet food safety and regulatory requirements, work reliably under real operating conditions, and make commercial sense. A Nestlé spokesperson said final decisions remain with its scientists and product developers. Pegiou said models may perform well under familiar conditions but struggle to predict outcomes for new ingredients, formulations, or processing conditions that differ from their training data. Pegiou asked whether the model has been tested on independent datasets beyond the data used to develop it.

IFF uses formulation, chemistry, sensory, and consumer data to help its flavorists identify promising options for tasting and consumer tests. Sack said TDC previously kept its formulations and findings in a master spreadsheet only a few people knew how to interpret. Givaudan has used AI to make fragmented consumer research easier for its flavor teams to access. Pegiou said valuable knowledge often resides in the experience of food technologists rather than in structured, accessible datasets. Cargill uses lab and plant data to consider manufacturing requirements before settling on a formulation.

WUR researchers Jack Yang and Jos van den Puttelaar describe a small intervention that the article does not set out in full. The article does not say how the strawberry flavor portfolio work at IFF turned out in consumer tests. It does not give the results of any validation of the AI tools on independent datasets. It does not say when Concept Muse will be used more widely or what it costs. It does not say what Nestlé products the recipe optimization tools have been applied to. More to follow.

stories.Headline: IAASB publishes first guide on applying quality management standards to AI audit tools
stories.Summary:
The International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board published new guidance on 11 November 2026 explaining how existing quality management standards apply to artificial intelligence tools used in audit and assurance engagements. The 24-page document, titled Guide 1: Common Conceptual Foundation, is the first instalment of a planned four-part series from the board. The guidance focuses on AI tools used to design or perform procedures for obtaining audit and assurance evidence. It addresses responsibilities at both firm and engagement level, the lifecycle of AI tools, and considerations for identifying and assessing quality risks.

The guide discusses several potential risks associated with AI-enabled audit tools, including hallucinations, automation bias, limited transparency, missing information, changes in performance and widespread errors. It gives an example involving the extraction of non-standard terms from contracts, where a tool may omit important details without indicating that information is missing. The IAASB confirms that audit firms and engagement partners retain their existing responsibilities when using AI, even when the technology performs a substantial part of an audit procedure. Firms remain responsible for determining whether tools are appropriate for their circumstances, including when those tools are supplied by a global network or external technology provider. The guide also addresses human oversight, explaining that effective involvement may depend on whether individuals have the necessary competence, sufficient time, relevant information and authority to challenge or override AI outputs.

The IAASB plans to publish the remaining guidance in stages, with firm-level quality management before AI tools are deployed due in January to February 2027. Engagement-level use and oversight is scheduled for April to May 2027, and an integrated edition covering all four guides, including monitoring and remediation after deployment, is planned for July to August 2027. The timetable is subject to IAASB approval, and the board emphasises that the guides are non-authoritative and introduce no new requirements. They explain how firms can apply existing standards, particularly ISQM 1 and ISA 220 (Revised), to AI-enabled technological tools. Guide 1 is currently a pre-final version and may be revised as the remaining guidance is developed.

stories.Headline: Genesis AI raises $500 million to scale its Eno general-purpose robot
stories.Summary:
Genesis AI SAS announced on November 17, 2026, that it raised $500 million in a Series A round led by Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse. The round also drew the venture capital arms of Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Zoom Communications, Samsung Electronics and Ericsson, along with former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt and other tech executives. The Paris-based company builds a general-purpose robot called Eno, which moves on a wheeled base rather than legs. That base can adjust the robot's height through a mechanism of two large panels joined by a hinge, letting Eno adapt its configuration to each task.

Eno runs on a custom artificial intelligence model called GENE, which Genesis says is easier to train than traditional robotics-optimized neural networks and can produce higher output quality. Because training data must match the robot it controls, Genesis modeled Eno's palms and fingers on the human hand so the robot can learn from demonstrations of people performing tasks by hand. The hands have 20 degrees of freedom against the human hand's 27, and they are covered in a soft material designed to mimic skin. Genesis has released demo videos showing the system playing the piano, cooking and solving a Rubik's Cube, and it says that versatility lets Eno work in industrial settings and homes alike.

Co-founder and chief executive Zhou Xian said the company is working to build the world's best general-purpose robot and that building everything itself lets it improve the entire robot faster in one closed loop. He said the funding will accelerate efforts to deploy the robots in the real world at scale. Genesis will use the capital to hire more AI researchers and roboticists and to step up its training data collection in a bid to expand the model's capabilities. The company has not said when Eno will be commercially available or how the new funding will be spent beyond those hiring and data efforts.

stories.Headline: Micron pauses work on a 4.5 billion dollar high bandwidth memory plant in Taiwan
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology paused work on a planned facility in Taiwan, according to a report dated November 6, 2026. This company is the only large memory maker based in the United States and trades on Nasdaq as MU. The report stated that the project was valued at roughly US$4.5 billion for the construction. This specific site was meant to produce high-bandwidth memory and DRAM for the global market. The news arrived while the market for high-bandwidth memory remains unusually tight for many buyers.

The paused project in Taiwan required roughly US$4.5 billion to produce high-bandwidth memory and DRAM. Micron announced on November 12, 2026, that executives would attend upcoming investor events to meet shareholders. One such event is the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas, on November 18 at 10:50 a.m. Mountain Time. The report from November 6, 2026, is the primary source for the details regarding the facility pause.

No available source identifies the meaning of a reference called US-Li mentioned in a headline fragment. Micron has not provided a confirmed reason for the pause or a statement on the length of time. The company did not tie the decision to policy, cost, or demand in any attributable on-record statement. Executives are scheduled to appear at the TomorrowX Summit, but the notice was routine corporate scheduling. This notice did not mention the Taiwan facility or suggest a response to the November 6 report.

Management may be pressed on spending, timing, and supply during the upcoming public appearance in Texas. AI server builders and gamers who feel DRAM pricing effects are among those affected by the pause. Buyers have little spare room because SK hynix locked up over half of 2027-28 HBM4 capacity. Toolmakers and contractors may reshuffle their schedules, which could potentially speed up the timelines of rival chipmakers.

Local governments in Taiwan may need to revisit hiring targets, infrastructure plans, and various project incentives. The pause removes a future flexibility point for moving capacity between HBM and ordinary DRAM production. The memory industry is a cyclical business where prices rise during shortages and fall when capacity floods in. Three companies, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, dominate the global supply of DRAM and high-bandwidth memory.

High-bandwidth memory is scarce because it consumes more wafer area than standard DRAM and adds yield risk. Counterpoint reported third-quarter growth at 369 percent, which was driven by rising prices and AI memory demand. A federal judge recently allowed a DRAM price-fixing suit to proceed, though it is unrelated to this. Analysts will parse the November 18 appearance for hints about the direction of the company's capital spending.

Investors want to know if the pause is a total cancellation or just a temporary timing delay. It remains open whether Micron will add this lost capacity at other sites or change customer commitments. The articles leave open whether the company will change its outlook on its share of the HBM market. No source has established the identity of US-Li or its connection to the memory maker.

stories.Headline: Lam Research’s Chin Hock Toh says advanced packaging drives AI scaling through industry collaboration
stories.Summary:
Chin Hock Toh of Lam Research wrote about how advanced packaging is becoming a critical technology for scaling artificial intelligence on November 16, 2026. This shift allows the integration of compute, memory, and connectivity into next-generation systems to overcome performance and efficiency challenges. Advanced packaging now serves as a primary innovation engine rather than just a supporting function for semiconductor manufacturing. The process helps chipmakers integrate multiple technologies into optimized systems that deliver greater performance than traditional monolithic chip approaches. This evolution is reshaping the roles of various players across the entire semiconductor ecosystem to meet AI demands.

The technology requires high-bandwidth memory, chiplets, hybrid bonding, and 3D integration to solve the memory wall and rising thermal demands. Lam Research has invested in these areas for over 15 years and has shipped more than 500 SABRE 3D systems. The company recently opened a dedicated Panel Center of Excellence in Salzburg, Austria, to support future panel-level packaging productivity. These processes include TSV formation, electrochemical deposition, TSV etch, and wafer-to-wafer stacking for leading foundries and memory manufacturers. Such advancements are necessary because AI systems depend on how efficiently data moves between processors, memory, and networking components.

Chin Hock Toh, the director of Technical Program Management for Advanced Packaging at Lam Research, stated that no company can solve AI scaling alone. He explained that the industry's center of gravity is moving from chip design toward a more comprehensive system design approach. Toh noted that advanced packaging expertise is now a strategic capability rather than simply a manufacturing service for the industry. He emphasized that future progress depends on collaboration among chipmakers, foundries, memory suppliers, equipment providers, materials companies, and research institutions. Lam Research collaborates with leading universities and imec to accelerate the commercialization of these next-generation packaging technologies.

Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers, known as OSATs, are affected as they move beyond traditional assembly roles to become strategic enablers. These OSATs now help customers navigate complex packaging architectures, heterogeneous integration, and the scale-up of manufacturing for AI systems. The industry is also affected by the need for new materials and more precise manufacturing techniques to manage defects and yield. Designers are affected because they must now combine specialized components into tightly integrated systems to improve flexibility and power efficiency. These changes are driven by the enormous compute power and memory bandwidth required by modern AI workloads.

For decades, the semiconductor industry followed a formula of making transistors smaller, faster, and more energy efficient to achieve progress. However, the AI era is changing the definition of scaling by emphasizing integration as much as transistor density. Heterogeneous integration allows the combination of multiple semiconductor technologies into a single package to achieve higher performance and design flexibility. High-bandwidth memory specifically provides the necessary data flow to feed modern AI accelerators efficiently. This background shows that the industry is shifting toward system-level design to overcome existing computing constraints.

The industry will next explore panel-level packaging to enable larger package formats and higher productivity for future heterogeneous integration architectures. Future AI progress will depend on the ability to integrate more compute, memory, and intelligence into highly optimized systems. Lam Research continues to invest in panel-level processing technologies to support this transition for its customers. The articles leave open how long the adoption of panel-level packaging will take to become a standard industry practice. They also leave open how specific geopolitical tensions or trade regulations might impact the future sale of these equipment technologies.

stories.Headline: Silicon Box starts basic design for its first plant outside Singapore in Novara
stories.Summary:
Silicon Box’s planned packaging and test plant in Novara, Italy, has entered the basic design phase, with construction set to start in 2027, according to a press release from the company. The milestone was reached together with the design and engineering firms Stantec and Drees & Sommer, both of which were appointed in 2025. A week earlier, on 9 November, the project was formally presented at the site in Agognate, outside Novara, with a symbolic laying of the foundation stone. The project, which Silicon Box calls Vulcan Project, represents an investment of EUR 3.2 billion and will be the company’s first production site outside Singapore.

The plant will integrate chiplets from different manufacturers into a single package that works as one chip, processing them on large square panels rather than round wafers, which Silicon Box says gives higher output at lower cost. The target markets include AI, supercomputing, electric and autonomous vehicles, robotics, mobile devices and space technology, and Silicon Box says its team in Singapore has so far shipped more than one billion units with the technology. The investment is backed by EUR 1.3 billion in public funding, which the Italian government manages through its investment agency Invitalia under the national semiconductor programmes that form part of the EU Chips Act. The European Commission has also granted the project Open EU Foundry status, and the plant will cover a 60-hectare site and is expected to employ around 1,600 people at full capacity.

According to Silicon Box’s COO, Jae Hak “JH” Yee, the design phase is where the experience from Singapore will be built into the new plant. He said the Singapore facility has shown that advanced panel-level packaging can run at high volume and at high yield, and that the task now is to build that same discipline into Novara from the first drawing. Stantec coordinates the project and is responsible for the office building, outdoor areas, infrastructure, water and power supply, and permits. Drees & Sommer designs the production and utility buildings, including the cleanrooms.

Silicon Box describes the Novara plant as the first of its kind in the EU, and it will be the company’s first production site outside Singapore. The basic design phase follows the formal presentation at the site in Agognate on 9 November, and construction is set to start in 2027. The plant is expected to employ around 1,600 people at full capacity on a 60-hectare site. The public funding of EUR 1.3 billion is managed by Invitalia under the national semiconductor programmes that form part of the EU Chips Act.

stories.Headline: Tiny Corp opens second tinybox red preorder at $89,000 after first batch sells out
stories.Summary:
Tiny Corp began taking preorders on November 5, 2026 for a desktop machine called the tinybox red that holds four of AMD's Instinct MI300X data center accelerators, and the first batch of 25 units at $60,000 sold out within three days. The cards inside are refurbished, they come without warranties, they are capped at 500W each, and they are linked only over PCIe 5.0. A breakdown posted by the AI Quanting account on X noted that the store page already showed the machine as out of stock a few days after the listing went live. Tiny Corp has now opened preorders for a second batch of 50 units at $89,000, which is about 48% above the launch price and roughly $29,000 more per box.

On paper the machine offers 768GB of GPU memory, 21.2TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth and 10.44 PFLOPS of FP8 compute, which are exactly four times AMD's own per-card figures of 192GB of HBM3, 5.3 TB/s and 2.61 PFLOPS of dense FP8. The listing quotes the dense number rather than the 5.22 PFLOPS AMD lists with structured sparsity, so the published specification is the more conservative one. The host is a 32-core water-cooled AMD EPYC Genoa platform with 192GB of DDR5 RAM, a 1TB boot drive, four 1TB drives in RAID 0, two 10GbE ports and an OCP 3.0 slot. Two standard 1,700W ATX power supplies feed the 54V the GPUs need through a converter, so the box runs on one 220V circuit or two 110V circuits, and Tiny Corp claims it stays under 50dB.

Tiny Corp is the company behind the machine and it is the party taking the preorders, while the account AI Quanting on X is credited with spotting that the first batch had sold out. Tiny Corp says the second batch will be delivered in Q1 or Q2 2027, though it stops just short of committing to either date as a firm timeline. The company also claims the box stays under 50dB, which would make it far quieter than the rack servers MI300X cards normally live in. The cards themselves are refurbished and come without warranties, which is part of how four data center accelerators fit into a desktop box.

The context is that MI300X cards normally live in rack servers, and Tiny Corp has squeezed four of them into a box that runs off ordinary wall power. The first batch sold out within three days at $60,000, and the second costs nearly 50% more than the former. The second batch of 50 units is now on preorder at $89,000 with delivery penciled in for Q1 or Q2 2027. Beyond that shipping window, the articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Nasha Fitter helps build Citizen Health AI tool Ari to aid caregivers
stories.Summary:
Nasha Fitter helped develop a company called Citizen Health that uses an AI system called Ari, and she spoke with News 3 ahead of the HLTH USA 2026 conference about providing tools for caregivers looking after a sick relative. The system is designed to help caregivers organize medical records, track symptoms, prepare for appointments, and navigate insurance and benefits. Fitter turned her daughter's rare disease diagnosis into a mission aimed at helping millions of families, and National Caregivers Month is observed in November. Fitter said most families feel very intimidated when they are talking to specialists and feel unprepared because they do not know what questions to ask.

Fitter said Ari does all that work by preparing the families and giving them questions, then taking the questions back and starting to piece things together. She said the system has a longitudinal history of the patient, so it is able to see things your doctor might miss. The articles give no other numbers, dates or names beyond the HLTH USA 2026 conference, News 3, Citizen Health, Ari and Nasha Fitter. The articles do not say what the tool requires from families or what it changes for them beyond organizing records, tracking symptoms, preparing for appointments and navigating insurance and benefits.

Fitter is the mother who helped build the tool, and she described how Ari prepares families with questions and pieces information together from a longitudinal history of the patient. She said families feel intimidated and unprepared when talking to specialists, and she said Ari does that work for them. stories.Headline: Preferred Networks taps Samsung Foundry and Semifive to build 3D-IC AI inference chip
stories.Summary:
Japanese AI company Preferred Networks has chosen Samsung Foundry to manufacture the logic chips for its next-generation AI inference semiconductor, the MN-Core L2000, with South Korea's Semifive acting as turnkey partner. The two companies disclosed the collaboration on the 17th at SC26, the supercomputing trade show held in Chicago. Tokyo-based PFN is responsible for the processor architecture and logic design, while Semifive handles design implementation, memory supply, packaging, testing and mass production. The chip uses a 3D-IC structure that stacks the compute chip and DRAM vertically, which the companies describe as the first commercial application of such a design. Tape-out, the handoff of the completed design to manufacturing, is targeted for the first quarter of 2027, and the L2000 series is the successor to the MN-Core L1000, which is scheduled for launch in 2027.

According to PFN, the new chip targets more than double the memory bandwidth of the L1000 by creating hundreds of thousands of data pathways between the compute chip and the DRAM. Because the memory is attached vertically, components such as the interposer needed to connect chips side by side are eliminated, and the company expects manufacturing costs to fall as well. Vertically stacking chips still poses challenges, since heat dissipation is difficult and securing manufacturing yields is tricky, and industry observers expect considerable process tuning before 3D-IC reaches a stable mass-production stage. Cho Myung-hyun, CEO of Semifive, said 3D-IC is a next-generation solution that can overcome the supply constraints of HBM, and that starting with the collaboration with Japan's PFN the company will lead commercialization of next-generation AI semiconductors. He has previously described the technology as offering wider bandwidth and lower power consumption than bundling eight HBM4 chips.

The collaboration is a case of the foundry-to-design-IP alliance in the AI semiconductor supply chain being reshaped around a Japanese customer. With HBM procurement emerging as a bottleneck, the attempt to secure bandwidth through vertical memory stacking has now been connected to an actual mass-production line. That development is expected to make the push to reduce memory dependence a new variable in the competition for design services and foundry orders. Semifive plans to expand the technology's application beyond data-center AI chips to robots and smart devices.

stories.Headline: Bulloch County correctional officers give students an AI-generated coloring page that parents criticize
stories.Summary:
Parents are raising concerns about an AI-generated coloring page that children took home from a career day at an Effingham County school, according to WTOC. Bulloch County correctional officers handed out the coloring sheet, and parents posted the first page online saying it has racial undertones. Andrell Fields, a concerned parent, said the picture shows a Black male inmate performing manual labor with a white correctional officer standing over him. Fields also highlighted the messages of “Teamwork” and “Hardwork,” and said the two figures are not working collaboratively because of the manual labor the inmate is pictured doing.

Fields has a son who does not go to Guyton Elementary and did not receive the coloring page, but she said she would be upset if her child came home with the material. She said she would not show her Black son that this is his place in society, his only place in society. Dal Cannady, Bulloch County’s communications director, said the officers made the pages themselves using AI. He said the sheets are not part of the county’s regular educational materials or usual school presentations, and that the two officers who presented used AI to create and print the images.

Fields said the county’s explanation that officers used AI makes the situation worse rather than better. She said people are teaching AI every day in everything they do, and if that is what AI is perceiving, it says a lot about the human race. She said that does not make her feel any better and actually concerns her even more. Fields said elementary-level children are impressionable and she wants all parties involved to pay attention to the messages they are communicating to students.

Fields said people have to be careful what they put out there to youth, whose minds absorb everything, especially African American youth. She said someone could have taken a second look at the page and asked how it would be perceived. WTOC has asked Effingham County Schools about the coloring page and is waiting to hear back.

stories.Headline: Unemployment Labs finds restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips in six Chinese AI models
stories.Summary:
Unemployment Labs found that restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips were used in six Chinese AI models. This U.S. nonprofit research organization published its findings in a report on November 12, 2026. The analysis suggests that major Chinese companies accessed cutting-edge hardware despite strict U.S. export controls. These findings indicate a potential gap in the semiconductor restrictions targeting China on national security grounds. The research was led by Will DePue, who previously worked as a researcher for OpenAI.

The report analyzed six models released since April, including DeepSeek V4-Flash, V4-Pro, Moonshot AI Kimi K3, K3.1-Pro, MiniMax M3, and Ant Group Ling-3.1-Flash. DeepSeek V4-Flash and MiniMax M3 matched B200 and B300 series characteristics, while others matched GB200 and GB300 series with Grace CPUs. Blackwell launched in February last year, and the Rubin chip went on sale in July this year. The Trump administration allowed H200 exports but blocked Blackwell and Rubin chips from entering China. The researchers estimated that 12,000 Blackwell GPUs were used, costing over 500 million dollars for final training.

Will DePue and his team used digital forensic techniques to analyze numerical patterns and initialization fingerprints in model weights. They stated that they reproduced initialization patterns of DeepSeek V4-Flash on a B300 chip and Kimi K3 on a GB200. The researchers cautioned that their figures are rough estimates based on assumptions about data volumes and GPU utilization. They explained that the traces were insufficient to determine where the GPUs were physically installed during the process. They added that the findings do not prove that Chinese companies directly violated U.S. export control laws.

Industry experts suggested that Chinese firms might have smuggled chips through third countries or rented them from Southeast Asian data centers. The report affects four major companies, which are DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and the Ant Group. Some experts believe these firms skirted sanctions to build their advanced artificial intelligence systems. The findings highlight how China may have gained access to hardware despite the stringent U.S. government restrictions. These experts have long raised the possibility of using workaround routes to obtain restricted Nvidia computing power.

The Blackwell chip is an advanced AI accelerator that the U.S. government restricts from export to China. A recent internal scandal at Nvidia involved Alice Huang, who allegedly had an improper relationship with former CEO Jensen Huang. Alice Huang is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China through a Singapore entity called Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary. Jensen Huang was removed from his post on November 12 amid these allegations and other internal company issues. Some reports suggest that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, may have been a Chinese spy.

It remains to be seen if the U.S. government will introduce additional measures to target potential circumvention routes. The report does not independently establish how the Chinese companies obtained access to the restricted Blackwell hardware. It is unclear if the Blackwell GPUs played a central role throughout the entire training process for these models. The analysis does not prove whether the hardware used for initial weights was used for subsequent training runs. The researchers have not established the exact physical location where the chips were used for these projects.

These financial efforts coincided with a rise in global market shares for the company's flagship smartphones, televisions, and semiconductors. The semiconductor business unit led overall earnings growth, recording sales of 356.3358 trillion won.

The facility investment plan requires 52.7509 trillion won, or 93 percent of the total, to be concentrated within the semiconductor division. This funding aims to strengthen next-generation memory technologies and expand production capacity for advanced system semiconductor processes. The company also signed a foundry supply agreement with Tesla worth 16.54 billion dollars that lasts until 2033. Market shares grew to 22.1 percent for smartphones, 29.5 percent for televisions, and 38.3 percent for DRAM.

Company officials stated that these investments are necessary to prepare for a mid-to-long-term increase in demand for AI infrastructure. They noted that the expansion of the AI ecosystem and premium products helped increase the market share of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Flip 8. The company also highlighted the importance of mass producing HBM4 and 1c-nanometer DRAM to maintain its top position in the memory market. They are currently expanding cooperation with major clients including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Hong Kong Techtronics, and Supreme Electronics.

The company continues to secure a stable customer base by signing multi-year supply contracts with global big tech and AI cloud firms. It also maintains a strong intellectual property portfolio, having registered 8,411 patents in South Korea and 8,470 in the United States this quarter. stories.Headline: Nvidia accepts CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and appoints CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 11, and the company announced this decision the following day in November 2026. This leadership change allows Samsung Electronics to benefit as the artificial intelligence semiconductor market diversifies beyond the dominance of Nvidia. Analysts believe the departure of Huang marks a turning point that will accelerate supply chain diversification and expand the market. Samsung is poised to emerge as the biggest beneficiary of this changing ecosystem as Nvidia's near monopoly shows signs of weakening. The shift encourages customers to seek alternative suppliers for the high bandwidth memory needed for artificial intelligence chips.

The transition requires Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, to serve as the interim CEO of Nvidia during this period. KB Securities projected on November 16 that non-Nvidia customers will account for 65 percent of Samsung's HBM shipments by 2027. In 2027, global HBM demand is projected to be 38 percent for Nvidia, 37 percent for Google, and 13 percent for AMD. Other customers are expected to account for 12 percent of the global demand for high bandwidth memory in that year. Samsung's HBM shipments to Nvidia are estimated to be 35 percent by 2027 as the broader AI ecosystem diversifies.

Kim Dong-won, the head of research at KB Securities, said uncertainty regarding leadership encourages customers to diversify their supply chains. He stated that demand for AI accelerators is expanding beyond GPUs to include custom chips known as application specific integrated circuits. Kim noted that the AI empire will only grow larger despite the departure of the leader he called the king. He expressed confidence in the growth prospects for Samsung because it possesses the broadest customer base outside of the Nvidia ecosystem. These changes are expected to expand the memory supplier base and increase the HBM used in each individual chip.

Google, Amazon, and AMD are rushing to commercialize their own AI accelerators, which directly affects the demand for memory products. These companies are key customers for Samsung Electronics and are expanding their presence in the artificial intelligence accelerator market. The growth of the ASIC market also drives demand for server DRAM and other high capacity memory products for Big Tech. Google's Tensor Processing Units and AWS Trainium are specific examples of custom chips that are driving this structural market shift. This diversification reduces the global reliance on any single company and increases the strategic value of memory semiconductor suppliers.

The articles explain that the AI inference market and in-house chip development by Big Tech are accelerating the adoption of ASICs. Processing-in-Memory technology is emerging as a growth driver because it performs computing operations within memory to improve overall computing efficiency. This technology reduces data transfers and eases communication bottlenecks that typically exist between GPUs and the memory storage components. Samsung Electronics showcased its next-generation LPDDR5X-PIM product at the FMS 2026 conference held in the United States last August. LS Securities suggested that this evolution could lead to a re-rating of corporate valuations for the memory semiconductor industry.

Industry attention is now focused on whether Samsung Electronics can successfully capitalize on this structural shift to increase its market share. The market expects the AI chip landscape to move gradually away from the near monopoly previously held by the Nvidia company. It remains open whether the interim leadership under Colette Kress will stabilize Nvidia or further accelerate the entry of competitors. The articles leave open how the notebook PC slump, expected to last until mid-2027, will interact with these AI shifts. Future growth depends on the continued expansion of the ASIC market and the adoption of in-memory computing by Big Tech.

stories.Headline: Media Nov Records files a copyright strike that removes Samantha Shokin's folk song recording from YouTube
stories.Summary:
Media Nov Records filed a copyright strike against musician Samantha Shokin last month. This action removed Shokin's recording of a Bulgarian folk song from YouTube. The company claimed ownership of the recording to trigger the takedown. Shokin had uploaded the song to YouTube several years ago. The recording had gained 125,000 views before the strike occurred.

The strike affected the song Bre Petrunko, which is in the public domain. Media Nov Records lists addresses in Marina Del Rey, Los Angeles, and the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland. Corporate papers show the company was founded last year with shareholders in Turkey. The company operates 500 YouTube channels featuring AI art and looping electronic beats. Some videos include Douyin watermarks and AI generated women.

Media Nov Records told 404 Media it works with various artists and partners. The company claimed its AI identifies music across platforms to ensure accurate protection. They initially told Shokin that emails from her and Loopmasters went to spam. They later asked Shokin for original audio files and recording evidence to prove ownership. Finally, they retracted the claim because the video had not generated revenue.

Samantha Shokin said she felt vindicated but unhappy that a journalist was needed. Loopmasters, which sold her voice in a Folk Legends pack, tried helping her. Copyright lawyer Alfred Steiner said the company likely used AI to file shotgun takedowns. He noted that filing requests for rights not owned can lead to liability. Steiner stated that fly by night entities are often difficult to pin down.

Shokin first recorded the song during the pandemic and uploaded it to SoundCloud. Her voice later appeared in songs with millions of hits after Loopmasters sold samples. Philip Koutev popularized a version of the song in 1963, but the Smithsonian holds that copyright. Media Nov Records claimed to exist since 1996, but web records only start last year. YouTube uses automated systems that often automatically approve copyright claims.

YouTube reinstated the video after Media Nov Records withdrew the complaint. The company stated the retraction was not a waiver of any held rights. Media Nov Records said it intends to initiate legal proceedings regarding the copyright dispute. The articles leave open whether the company will actually pursue these legal actions. stories.Headline: University of Chicago uses $3.1 million NIH grant to build synthetic pediatric head image database
stories.Summary:
The University of Chicago received a $3.1 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to create AI tools that generate a database of pediatric head images, the university announced on Nov 17 2026. The project will be led by Antonio Porras, PhD, Associate Professor of Neurological Surgery, and his team. The team will partner with Children's National Hospital in Washington, DC, Children's Hospital Los Angeles and the University of Southern California, and Children's Hospital Colorado and the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. The research team will use one of the largest curated datasets of clinical images from pediatric patients. The team will develop new generative AI tools to create realistic synthetic images at all ages and stages of cranial development.

Hospitals cannot always share craniofacial images from real patients with other institutions for research because of concerns about patient privacy. The project will develop a publicly available synthetic data platform with representative images of both healthy children and those with craniosynostosis, a condition where sutures in an infant's skull fuse prematurely before the brain is fully formed. The grant is one of the first projects underway in the newly launched Section of Computational Neurosurgery at UChicago, which brings together expertise in neurosurgery, artificial intelligence, and data science. Porras is scientific director of the section, the first of its kind in the nation, in partnership with clinical director Rohaid Ali, MD, Assistant Professor of Neurological Surgery. The section collaborates with neurosurgeons, computer scientists, engineers, data scientists and other researchers across the university.

Porras said the team has not been able to share this data in the past, but advances in new pediatric-centric AI methodologies are starting to allow synthetic datasets that do not compromise privacy. He said the team is learning to synthesize scientifically accurate and realistic datasets so others can develop their own research projects to advance understanding about craniofacial development. Mohamad Bydon, MD, Ginni & Mark Rometty Chair of the Department of Neurological Surgery and Stahl Professor of Neuroscience, said AI and computational capabilities are important tools that advance treatment of pediatric and adult diseases of the brain, spine, and peripheral nerves. Bydon said images are a window into a patient's condition and the project creates a paradigm to study and predict outcomes and ultimately have more effective surgeries and treatments. Ali said not everyone works at a large, high-volume academic medical center or has access to experienced surgeons who have done thousands of these procedures.

Ali said the datasets are going to help guide surgeons everywhere to perform procedures in the most effective way possible. Ali said the implications are hugely beneficial for all medical fields, not just neurosurgery, and that reliable synthetic data based on imaging will have translatable potential across a whole host of surgical and disease pathologies. Surgeons can treat craniosynostosis with procedures to reopen prematurely fused skull bones in infants, giving the brain enough room to develop normally. Such procedures require careful planning, assessing the current shape and structure of the skull and projecting how it will develop after surgery. Because children are growing so quickly at this age, their skulls may change even in the few weeks between initial imaging scans and when they can have surgery.

Access to a robust dataset of how a child at the same stage is expected to develop will allow surgeons at more hospitals, large and small, to better prepare for procedures by comparing their patients to reference data without taking additional images and exposing kids to more radiation unnecessarily. Porras said the first goal of the project is to develop a complete dataset of images for healthy children and next build a repository of images for patients with craniosynostosis, both before and after surgery. The team will then develop a publicly available data-sharing platform with a graphical interface that other surgeons can use to evaluate their own patients, without the need for specialized technical data skills that may not be available at all institutions. Porras said the team will be able to objectively and quantitatively evaluate the specific anomalies of these children when they are diagnosed, and forecast how they will develop. Porras said this will allow surgeons to evaluate the differences and similarities between the outcomes from different surgical approaches, so for the first time they can help plan the optimal thing to do for each patient.

The article was provided by the University of Chicago and subjected to News-Medical.Net's review protocols, and the site states modifications may be made to the article's style and length. The article was posted on Nov 17 2026 and was last updated on Tuesday 17 Nov 2026. The article states the editing team highlighted verified accuracy, scholarly review, sourcing from a reliable authority, and scrutiny for errors. stories.Headline: Google and Mandiant report that cyber criminals now deploy autonomous AI tools to run multiple stages of attacks
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group released its GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold report on Monday, November 16, 2026, and the report was developed with the cybersecurity firm Mandiant. The research draws on incident response investigations, global threat actor tracking and security monitoring, and it found that cyber criminals have moved beyond using AI to assist with individual tasks. According to the report, threat actors are increasingly deploying autonomous tools that can carry out multiple stages of cyber attacks, using large language models to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits and execute attacks at machine speed. Researchers found that attackers are increasingly using open source, multi-agent frameworks to automate activities that were previously done by humans, sometimes with no human help at all.

One public sector example cited in the research is the late-summer exploitation of PaperCut print management software, which is used by more than 70,000 organizations, including universities, libraries and government agencies. In August, attackers exploited two vulnerabilities that, when combined, allow unauthenticated remote code execution, and four days after the initial vulnerability disclosure there was a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations, likely using large language models. By the numbers, the Cloud Security Alliance reported that the attack reached 48 countries and 395 organizations, including 204 compromised instances in the education sector. Attackers have not changed long-standing access methods such as using compromised credentials and exploiting unpatched systems, but what has changed is speed and scale, with high-velocity attacks that leave visible forensic trails.

Researchers say hackers are now more sophisticated when using AI, and they expect attacks to involve even less human intervention and to become harder to detect. The report attributes the shift to threat actors building full attack frameworks rather than relying on simple prompts, and it points to machine-speed execution as a defining feature of the activity. The articles do not name individual attackers or identify who is responsible beyond describing them as threat actors tracked by Google and Mandiant. The articles do not say what specific steps organizations should take next or what further action Google or Mandiant plans.

stories.Headline: Gary Blank says state agencies use AI to cut regulatory text and taxpayer letters
stories.Summary:
Newly elected governors have an opportunity to use artificial intelligence in their state agencies to reduce friction in the economy and be better stewards of taxpayer dollars, according to a column by Gary Blank of the Pioneer Institute. Blank wrote that some state agencies have already begun quietly using AI to transform operations and public services outside of political debates about regulation, data centers, layoffs or scary uses. He argued that agencies using AI only for efficiency just get faster bureaucracies, while smarter use could change the work itself. As an example, he said an AI tool could help a constituent complete a transaction without needing to call a call center employee.

A recent Pioneer Institute study shows that diverse agencies can develop creative use cases in larger and smaller states with deep technology industries or broad economies, Blank wrote. A handful of states provide well-designed AI-powered chatbots that help people find information, answer questions and guide transactions such as transferring an out-of-state driver's license, applying for a grant, starting a business or paying taxes, and the chatbots are available in multiple languages 24/7. Nevada incorporated AI into its tax agency to draft taxpayer letters, and the agency reports calls fell 52% in two years. Maryland and other states are developing AI tools to support new work requirements that take effect soon, especially with recipient outreach and paperwork, and California uses the technology to reduce mispayments in unemployment and welfare programs.

Blank wrote that state regulations, rules and required reports have piled up and become confusing, and AI can help states sift through them to find provisions that are out of date, duplicative, hard to understand, conflicting or outside national norms. He said the tools recommend changes for agencies to consider, and any changes go through the preexisting process in that state for public input. Ohio, Oklahoma, New York, Texas and Virginia have done this in different ways, and in Ohio the government reported the AI tool found a total of 17.4 million words of regulation, which it then cleaned and reduced by 12.6%. The state estimates streamlining the regulations saved 60,000 hours of labor over a decade.

Blank wrote that AI is unlike other technologies and transformative use cases may require organizational changes far beyond new IT software. He said federal, state and local governments should learn from each other and the private sector about how to use AI, and they should be more open about results and cost-benefit information. He added that sometimes applications should be retired and that annual use case inventories could be part of the solution. All federal agencies are required to publish how they use AI, yet few states do so, and Blank wrote that a few agencies demonstrate that with smart use of AI governments can both be more frugal and achieve greater outcomes for the people they serve.
