stories.Headline: AI tools help defenders find software flaws at scale but fixing them lags
stories.Summary:
In August, researchers found flaws in the PHP programming language, which underpins roughly 70% of the world’s websites, that could’ve allowed hackers to steal data or install malware on a huge scale. The flaws prompted a warning from the National Security Agency and a global effort to patch the bug. Other flaws have recently been found in systems ranging from Linux to OpenSSL to FreeBSD. Project Glasswing, a cybersecurity initiative started by Anthropic PBC, found more than 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July alone, many of critical severity. Anthropic independently found thousands more.

Project Glasswing granted select companies and security researchers access to a specialized version of the Claude AI model. An AI tool that Microsoft Corp. tested on the Linux kernel earlier this year took, on average, about 22 minutes and just $3.60 to verify each suspected flaw. A report by Google’s threat-intelligence team found that monthly vulnerability disclosures roughly doubled over the first half of the year. Only about 0.2% of all those found had actually been exploited by hackers. One study found that companies fully fixed only 26% of known-to-be-exploited vulnerabilities last year.

The Bloomberg editorial board wrote that such reports may sound like portents of a future AI apocalypse but are in fact cause for guarded optimism. The board said many of these flaws have been lurking undetected for years, and discovering and patching them makes the broader system safer. It said AI-assisted defenders are proving especially adept at finding weaknesses in widely used software that traditional testing has missed. The board said problems in PHP had been evident as early as 2024, but it took AI to grasp their full significance. It said AI is transforming the economics of security research.

The board said defenders can now use agents to scan for weaknesses at unprecedented scale and speed and to scour places like old libraries and codebases that once would’ve been too costly or impractical to investigate. It said defenders appear to have at least a temporary advantage, and there’s little evidence criminals have achieved widespread success. It said the immediate challenge for cybersecurity pros will be to advance from finding flaws to fixing them. It said top AI models are quickly getting better at writing patches, yet deploying them widely and at the requisite speed remains a problem. It said at many organizations, 30 to 60 days remains the norm for critical flaws.

The board said the White House should expand its efforts to get frontier AI cyber capabilities to as many vetted defenders as possible while modernizing the existing vulnerability management process. It said federal procurement rules should insist on secure automated updating and other software best practices, along the lines of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s “Secure by Design” pledge. It said Congress must invest in defending critical infrastructure, including essential open-source projects. It said it isn’t hard to imagine a day when the entire defensive process unfolds behind the scenes, seamlessly and automatically, with internet users blissfully unaware. It said getting from here to there could be an eventful journey.

The editorial was published by the Marin Independent Journal on November 16, 2026, and by the Duluth News Tribune on November 14, 2026. The Marin Independent Journal credited the piece to the Bloomberg editorial board and said it was distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC. The Duluth News Tribune ran it as an Other View and listed its office at 222 W. Superior St, Duluth, MN 55802. The Duluth page also carried a link to a Local View item titled “JFK’s visit to Duluth before assassination not his only time here.” The articles leave open how quickly patches can be deployed widely and whether defenders’ temporary advantage will hold.

stories.Headline: Zhi Chen and Zi Huang edit a plant science AI collection that seeks submissions until 19 July 2027
stories.Summary:
The journal npj Science of Plants has opened a collection titled Artificial Intelligence in Plant Science: From Understanding to Sustainable Production, with a submission deadline of 19 July 2027, according to the collection page. The collection is edited by Zhi Chen of the University of Southern Queensland in Australia and Zi (Helen) Huang of the University of Queensland, also in Australia. It supports and amplifies research related to Sustainable Development Goals 2, 12 and 13, which cover zero hunger, responsible consumption and production, and climate action. The page states that articles will be displayed once they are published, so no research papers have appeared in the collection yet.

The collection seeks interdisciplinary work on artificial intelligence for the study, monitoring, improvement and management of plants, spanning the pathway from fundamental plant understanding to sustainable production. Listed topics include automated phenotyping, crop growth and yield modelling, AI-assisted breeding, and detection of plant diseases, pests and environmental stresses. Other areas cover remote and proximal sensing with RGB, multispectral, hyperspectral, thermal, fluorescence, depth and LiDAR data, plus integration of imaging, genomic, phenotypic, environmental and management information. Methodological topics include computer vision, multimodal learning, self-supervised, few-shot, zero-shot, continual and transfer learning, and foundation, vision-language and generative models, along with explainable, trustworthy and resource-efficient approaches. The collection also welcomes precision agriculture, decision-support systems, agricultural robotics, resource optimisation, controlled-environment agriculture, digital twins and predictive modelling, as well as datasets, benchmarks and digital research infrastructure.

The page says that translating AI capabilities into reliable scientific and agricultural outcomes requires approaches that account for biological variability, heterogeneous data, limited annotations and changing environmental conditions. It states that close collaboration between plant scientists and AI researchers is therefore essential to develop methods relevant to plant science and robust beyond individual experimental settings. Contributions should demonstrate clear relevance to plant science and provide validation appropriate to their research questions and intended use, and studies addressing generalisation, interpretability and robustness are welcome across all areas. The journal notes that APC waivers are available and can be allocated upon acceptance on an ad-hoc basis, with enquiries directed to the Journal Publisher, Aicha Hanna.

stories.Headline: AI models scan filings and court records to map cross-border holding chains
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is changing how institutional investors and international founders handle cross-border due diligence and asset protection, according to an article published by Rebellion Research on November 16, 2026. The article says specialized AI models now scan corporate filings, shareholder registers and court records at the same time to map complex holding chains across three or four countries and languages. Automated Know Your Customer workflows trace ultimate beneficial owners through multiple tiers of holding companies, giving compliance teams an instant visual map of control and voting rights instead of manual cross-referencing of PDFs. Continuous screening algorithms monitor global watchlists and adverse media in real time and alert users when a counterparty's risk profile shifts, which the article says cuts onboarding delays and lowers data-entry errors.

The article says moving intellectual property, equity stakes or liquid securities into an international holding vehicle requires strict adherence to local statutory rules, because courts and tax authorities look past paper registrations to where real management decisions happen. It advises confirming that a chosen jurisdiction offers predictable commercial courts and clear creditor-protection laws, and keeping independent bank accounts, local accounting records and formal board minutes separate from operating businesses. For banks, it lists four checks: proof of economic substance such as physical operations or qualified directors, documented source of wealth through audited statements or tax filings, clarified intercompany flows of royalties, dividends or management fees, and updated beneficial ownership records ready for annual reviews. The article also warns that algorithms struggle with legal nuance and might flag a legitimate restructuring involving three jurisdictions or a newly formed trust as suspicious.

The article attributes guidance to the U.S. Mission to ASEAN, which it says highlights AI-driven threat analysis and fraud prevention as ways to strengthen cross-border defenses, and to IMTF, which it says shows financial institutions pairing automated tools with human-in-the-loop oversight for transparency and accountable decision-making. It cites Astra Trust offshore services as an example of specialists who align corporate formation, board governance and cross-border compliance across financial centers. The article's stated position is that licensed fiduciary professionals should verify statutory compliance and oversee governance while automated platforms handle repetitive KYC checks and watchlist monitoring around the clock. It concludes that software alone cannot replace the legal standing that properly licensed corporate service providers bring to multi-jurisdiction structures.

stories.Headline: Northwest Arkansas Community College plans MIT partnership to create employer-specific AI training
stories.Summary:
Northwest Arkansas Community College announced last week that it plans to enter a one-year letter of intent with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Pathways for AI Training and Hiring program, according to a news release from the college. NWACC, which is described as Arkansas' largest community college, is planning to work with MIT to establish artificial intelligence training for employers in the region. The PATH program is a workforce development initiative that helps individuals find jobs as artificial intelligence becomes more prominent. The program specifically focuses on helping two-year colleges like NWACC create artificial intelligence training programs.

NWACC is seeking businesses based in the region that hope to better prepare employees as the use of artificial intelligence grows, the release states. If the new curriculum is successfully established and implemented, unique coursework will be designed for each participating employer, according to the release. The letter of intent states that success will be measured by whether the institutions can identify a significant workforce need and determine a credible, responsible and sustainable way to address it together. Officials from NWACC and MIT met in July for a workshop that also included regional business leaders, and the workshop aimed to identify sought-after skills related to artificial intelligence across different industries.

Dennis Rittle, president of NWACC, said in the release that as the region's leader in artificial intelligence education and workforce development, it is the college's responsibility to keep looking for ways to best prepare the Northwest Arkansas workforce for the AI economy at home and around the world. He said the PATH team from MIT is outstanding at helping learners, regardless of background, secure jobs in the growing AI economy. He said the two organizations will look to develop hyper-local, industry specific AI training to solve actual workforce needs. He also said he is deeply grateful for the trust PATH has placed in NWACC and excited for the opportunities it brings to the businesses and workforce of Northwest Arkansas.

stories.Headline: Inc42 identifies five emerging AI startups focusing on infrastructure and autonomy
stories.Summary:
Inc42 published a curated list of five emerging AI startups in November 2026. The editorial team selected these companies for their focus on infrastructure, autonomy, and measurement. These startups build tools for inference routing, semantic video intelligence, autonomous commerce, AI-native CRM, and pipeline generation. They aim to help enterprises run AI models more efficiently, reliably, and at scale. The list is not a ranking and is presented in alphabetical order.

BLUE, founded in 2023 in Bengaluru, uses a codec to cut storage by 90 percent. Kily was founded in March 2025 in Bengaluru by Sankalp Mehrotra, Anurag Singh, and Sharad Chitlangia. Revspot, founded in 2024 in Bengaluru, raised 4.8 million dollars in a Series A round. RouterPlus was founded in 2026 by Alok Bishoyi and Lakshmi Narayana for LLM routing. Superleap, founded in 2024 in Bengaluru, was started by Subham Kumar Boundia, Alok Maurya, and Saurabh Maheshwari.

Kunal Kislay leads BLUE, which turns CCTV feeds into a searchable intelligence layer for enterprises. Kily uses Core Decision AI to manage marketplace listings and pricing for over 50 brands. Revspot created Spot, an AI growth agent that generates qualified pipelines for high-ticket B2C businesses. RouterPlus matches requests to models like Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, and DeepSeek using customer evals. Superleap uses SuperOS, SuperSense, and SuperAgents to rebuild the CRM category as a revenue operating system.

Britannia and Hindustan Petroleum use BLUE, while Kily works with ITC, Unilever, Mondelez, and Coca-Cola. Revspot serves over 50 customers in real estate, education, automotive, and wealth management sectors. RouterPlus helps teams manage API keys and contracts while shifting from closed to open-source models. Superleap counts Razorpay, Aakash Education, Cars24, and MediBuddy as customers for its AI-native revenue system. These tools affect businesses struggling with the trade-off between intelligence, speed, performance, and cost.

Indian boardrooms previously focused on which large language model to adopt for their enterprise needs. Now, the priority has shifted toward the cost of running these models and inference spending. Recent funding includes 20.7 million dollars for AuxoAI, 66 million dollars for Blacksmith, and 2.3 million dollars for QwikBuild. Spill Games also raised 10.5 million dollars for AI-led mobile gaming in late October. Investors are now betting on companies that deploy existing models rather than new frontier models.

The global video analytics market is projected to reach 33.61 billion dollars by 2031. The AI sales agent market is estimated at 3.4 billion dollars in 2026 and 15.8 billion by 2033. The AI model router market is estimated at 100 million dollars in 2025 and 4.1 billion by 2035. The global CRM market is projected to reach about 321 billion dollars by 2034. The articles leave open how these specific startups will scale within these growing global markets.

stories.Headline: China showcases AI and robotics to world leaders at a summit in Shenzhen
stories.Summary:
China is hosting world leaders in the city of Shenzhen this week. US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin are attending a global economic summit. The city is presented as a high-tech wonderland powered by artificial intelligence. This event showcases China's home-grown innovation and robotics to the visiting dignitaries. The city is touted as the origin story for a high-tech future.

The summit highlights a city where drones deliver dinner and driverless taxis play music. Humanoid robots at DexForce Technologies serve coffee and play chess for visitors. The city is located in south-eastern China and is close to Hong Kong. It has evolved from a fishing village to a hub for electric vehicles. Some coffee costs 30 yuan, while breakfast noodles cost under 3 yuan.

Engineer Huang Shihua says that Shenzhen is a miracle for young people. He believes that robots will serve humanity by taking on dangerous tasks. Huang claims that AI can foster equality and help emerging economies catch up. He compares the opportunity in Shenzhen to the dreams found in America. He hopes that AI will help the entire world become one family.

A construction worker says that life is hard and factories have relocated. A delivery driver in his 40s says the city is no longer a place to thrive. Ms Lu earns 200 yuan per day delivering food inside the SEG plaza. A taxi driver says his house is worth a third of its original price. Canadian and Vietnamese tourists call the drone delivery technology amazing and great.

Shenzhen grew from a fishing village into one of China's wealthiest cities. It manufactured cabbage patch dolls, then televisions, iPhones, and now advanced humanoid robots. The city is central to the bold vision for China held by Xi Jinping. However, the second-largest economy faces a property crisis and sluggish consumer spending. Many manufacturers have downsized or moved to find cheaper labour for production.

Gig work now supports 200 million workers, or 40 percent of the urban labour force. Job agent Li Xiaohe offers temporary factory jobs paying around 22 yuan an hour. Some drones now fly at night to warn people not to cause trouble. The articles leave open how many workers will fit into the AI future. They do not say if the property market will recover its original value.

stories.Headline: Researchers at Guangxi Medical University outline a machine learning roadmap for mapping cardiac regeneration barriers
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University conducted an analysis published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. The analysis establishes that the adult mammalian heart has virtually no capacity to regenerate lost cardiomyocytes after injury. Machine learning algorithms applied to high-dimensional biological data offer a systematic strategy to map regulatory networks governing repair. The authors caution that direct experimental validation of artificial intelligence in cardiac regeneration remains scarce. They position their work as a methodological roadmap rather than a synthesis of settled clinical conclusions.

Heart failure is the terminal stage of numerous cardiovascular conditions and a principal cause of mortality globally. Its escalating disease burden is driven by population ageing. After myocardial infarction, most adult cardiomyocytes withdraw permanently from the cell cycle. This leads to permanent scar formation, progressive ventricular remodelling, and irreversible loss of contractile function. Adult zebrafish retain lifelong regenerative capacity, and neonatal mice have a brief window of complete myocardial regeneration that closes during the first postnatal week.

The authors state that the adult mammalian heart keeps its regenerative machinery strictly restrained. Previous cell-based therapies, including bone marrow-derived cell and cardiosphere infusions, yielded only modest clinical efficacy in trials and meta-analyses. This was due to poor graft survival, inefficient engraftment, imprecise control over lineage fate, and active suppression by the hostile host microenvironment. The biological barriers span transcriptional circuits, post-translational protein interactions, and spatial cell-to-cell communication networks. Single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and high-throughput proteomics each illuminate distinct facets but cannot alone resolve integrated biology in sparse, heterogeneous datasets.

Deep learning architectures, variational autoencoders, and graph neural networks are being deployed to model multi-omics layers jointly. Frameworks such as Weighted Nearest Neighbour, Graph-Linked Unified Embedding, and scGPT project modalities into unified latent spaces. Unsupervised dimensionality reduction including Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection and SC3 clustering identifies atrial, ventricular, and conduction-system cardiomyocyte populations. BayesSpace, GraphST, and Tangram combine spatial adjacency matrices with transcriptomic profiles to map border-zone niches. The authors emphasize that spatial co-localisation and computational neighbourhood enrichments establish descriptive statistical associations rather than proven causal mechanisms.

Delivery of transcription factors GATA4, MEF2C, and TBX5 converts fibroblasts into cardiomyocyte-like cells in vitro and enhances ventricular function in animal models of myocardial injury. The Hippo-YAP pathway, Neuregulin1 and ErbB4 signalling, Meis1 expression, and metabolic shifts away from fatty acid oxidation control cardiomyocyte cell-cycle exit and re-entry. The review identifies a persistent gap: proteomic and phosphoproteomic validations lag substantially behind transcriptional and genetic manipulations. Interpretable machine learning applied to spatial transcriptomics revealed macrophage-niche programmes driving pathological fibrosis, and targeted in vivo gene silencing using lipidoid nanoparticles attenuated myocardial fibrosis in mice after infarction. An artificial intelligence model trained on thousands of cardiac fibrosis publications mapped ten nodal pathways, confirming that fibroblast-specific deletion of Jak1 and Jak2 prevents pressure-overload fibrosis.

Monocle, diffusion pseudotime, and CellRank leverage RNA velocity and Markov chains to predict cell state transitions. Applying standard trajectory inference to adult cardiac regeneration is limited because regenerative cells exhibit extremely low basal proliferation, leaving few intermediate states. Cardiac repair involves non-linear jumps such as dedifferentiation, proliferation bursts, and redifferentiation that violate assumptions of continuous progression. Longitudinal spatiotemporal profiling of the injured adult heart remains exceptionally scarce. An artificial intelligence agent analyzing single-cell maps encompassing 1.8 million cardiac nuclei nominated a small-molecule activator of mitochondrial biogenesis that conferred cardioprotection in experimental models, and quantitative proteomics showed glutathione peroxidase 4 downregulation drives cardiomyocyte ferroptosis.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Framework Integrates Multi-Omics Data to Target Cardiac Regeneration Barriers

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh forms a task force to study AI's impact on jobs and the economy
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh convened a conference in San Francisco on Monday, November 16, 2026, to examine how artificial intelligence affects the economy. He gathered technology executives and economists to discuss whether this revolution could cause massive job displacement for white-collar workers and lower the prices of services. The event served as a public forum for Warsh to explore these questions through his newly assembled task force on productivity and jobs. While he offered no immediate conclusions regarding interest rates, the findings from this group could eventually inform future monetary policy.

The Federal Reserve is currently contemplating raising interest rates in December to slow price increases caused by vast spending from AI firms. This occurs as the AI lab Anthropic prepares to price shares for an initial public offering on Wednesday, potentially raising 64 billion dollars at a 1.4 trillion dollar valuation. Meanwhile, voters in the November 3 midterms passed several state-level measures to slow the construction of essential data centers. Warsh is utilizing a task force including venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, and Stanford economist Chad Jones to provide outside expertise.

Chairman Warsh suggested that AI might create a service-sector version of the China shock, which followed China joining the World Trade Organization in 2001. He noted that while that event lowered prices for goods, it caused the loss of one million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall. Marc Andreessen expressed optimism about the technology but argued that heavy government regulation in healthcare and education might prevent rapid job displacement. Former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo called the anti-data center trend a very troubling sign that would be bad for the country.

The three task force members must now assemble their perspectives into a formal report for the chairman within the next few months. After this report is submitted, the Federal Reserve will debate the results to decide if they should shape official monetary policy. The central bank must determine if AI will lead to medium-term disinflation, which might eventually require the Fed to lower interest rates over the long term. Because the technology is racing ahead, the institution may need to reach a conviction on these answers sooner than originally planned.

Articles.Title: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means

stories.Headline: Reliance Jio stops new claims for its free Google AI Pro subscription
stories.Summary:
Reliance Jio has stopped accepting new claims for its free Google AI Pro subscription, which gave eligible users up to 18 months of access to Google's premium Gemini features. The redemption window ran from October 30, 2025, to October 29, 2026, according to terms and conditions listed on Jio's website. Jio's support page now says the offer is unavailable on new recharges or plan upgrades. The offer initially covered users over the age of 18 on unlimited 5G plans priced at ₹349 or above. Starting February 11, 2026, Jio temporarily extended eligibility to users on plans priced at ₹299 or above that offered 1.5 GB of data per day.

Users who activated the offer can continue using the subscription for up to 18 months from activation, provided they maintain an eligible recharge plan. Eligible users could activate the subscription, valued at ₹1,950 per month, through the MyJio app. Subscribers were required to maintain an eligible recharge plan throughout the subscription period to retain access to the benefits. Jio reserved the right to suspend access if users failed to maintain the required plan. The development comes a year after Reliance Industries Ltd, through its AI arm Reliance Intelligence, partnered with Google to accelerate AI adoption in India by offering free Google AI Pro access to Jio users.

Announcing the partnership, RIL said the 18-month subscription would provide access to Gemini 2.5 Pro through the Gemini app, higher limits for image and video generation using Nano Banana and Veo models, expanded access to NotebookLM, and 2 TB of cloud storage, among other benefits. The company valued the combined package at ₹35,100 per user. Beyond the consumer-facing offering, the partnership also positioned Reliance Intelligence as a strategic Google Cloud partner in India, with plans to expand access to Google's proprietary AI hardware accelerators, or TPUs, for local organisations. Inc42 has reached out to Jio for further details on the development, and the story will be updated on receiving a response.

Separately, Jio Platforms is in talks with the Indian Space Research Organisation, Skyroot Aerospace, and other domestic launch providers for its proposed constellation of 1,600 satellites in low Earth orbit. The company is exploring whether it can carry out the programme in India, from satellite design to launch and operations. It is also in discussions with SpaceX. Jio Platforms listed on the BSE and NSE on October 28 at ₹1,358 apiece, a 21.4% premium to its issue price of ₹1,119. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹8,387 Cr in Q2 FY27, marking a 13.7% increase from ₹7,379 Cr in the year-ago quarter.

Sequentially, net profit grew 8% from ₹7,764 Cr in Q1 FY27. Operating revenue rose 11.4% YoY and 3.3% sequentially to ₹40,475 Cr in the quarter under review. The offer was the consumer-facing part of Reliance's AI partnership with Google, which also covers the distribution of Gemini Enterprise and access to Google's AI chips for Indian organisations. The redemption window ended on October 29, 2026, a year after the offer launched. Eligible subscribers could activate the offer through the MyJio app.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers say AI cuts drug discovery timelines to 12 to 18 months and costs by up to 40%
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping drug discovery by compressing timelines from a historical average of five years to as little as 12 to 18 months, according to a narrative review published on November 16, 2026. The review examines how machine learning, deep learning and advanced computational frameworks address high attrition rates and massive capital requirements in conventional pharmaceutical research. Researchers are shifting from reactive, descriptive analyses to proactive, predictive modeling that guides experimental design and uncovers non-obvious relationships between molecular structures and disease mechanisms. Modern drug discovery draws on unprecedented volumes of biological data from next-generation sequencing, proteomics and metabolomics platforms. Machine learning and deep learning have become essential for extracting meaningful insights from this biological big data.

The review says AI reduces development costs by up to 40% while compressing timelines to 12 to 18 months. Machine learning supports quantitative structure-activity relationship modeling and prediction of absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity properties. Convolutional neural networks analyze cellular phenotypes and 3D molecular structures, graph neural networks treat atoms as nodes and bonds as edges, and transformers enable context-aware modeling of protein sequences and SMILES strings. DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts 3D structures from amino acid sequences with accuracy approaching X-ray crystallography and has generated over 200 million predicted structures. AlphaFold 3 models complex assemblies containing proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules and ions, and diffusion-based tools like RFdiffusion enable de novo protein design.

The review attributes these advances to researchers integrating machine learning, deep learning and computational frameworks across the pipeline. It says AI-driven biomarker analysis groups patients to develop personalized medicine approaches considering individual genetic and molecular profiles. Machine learning algorithms identify optimal patient populations, predict treatment responses and design adaptive trial protocols that adjust based on interim results. The review states that explainable AI and uncertainty quantification methods such as Bayesian deep learning attempt to address the black-box nature of deep learning models. It says balancing complexity with interpretability remains an ongoing trade-off.

Public databases support computational modeling, including PubChem with data on more than 322 million chemical compounds, the Cambridge Structural Database for crystallography, DrugBank for pharmaceutical information and metabolomics databases like HMDB. Relay Therapeutics and Nimbus Therapeutics used AI models to design selective inhibitors for FGFR2 and TYK2 and moved them into clinical trials with greater speed. Insilico Medicine's AI-driven, end-to-end pipeline for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis moved from target identification within fibrotic pathways to generative molecular design and faster clinical testing. Researchers designed the antibody AU-007 to target the interleukin-2 pathway, activating anti-tumor T cells while preventing cytokine release syndrome. Other platforms identified PVRIG for the antibody COM-701 and mapped receptor networks for HMBD-001.

Computational models predict patient-specific neoantigen epitopes to guide personalized immunotherapies such as EVX-01 for melanoma and GRANITE-001 for solid tumors. An AI-designed HIV vaccine candidate was discontinued, which the review cites as an experimental setback in translation. Drug repurposing advanced dexmedetomidine into Phase 3 trials for agitation in Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia, evaluated talabostat for prostate cancer and identified bevantolol to reduce chorea in Huntington's disease. The NLM-Chem corpus contains 150 full-text articles annotated with approximately 5,000 chemical entities, supporting automated text-mining pipelines. Domain-adapted transformer models such as BioBERT and SciBERT achieve high relation-extraction accuracy, and architectures combining Relation BioBERT with bidirectional long short-term memory networks detect and categorize drug-drug interactions.

Biological datasets often suffer from missing values, experimental variability and systematic biases that can impact model performance and generalizability. Algorithmic bias, particularly when models are trained on datasets that fail to represent diverse populations, risks creating disparities in medical outcomes. Large-scale training and high-performance computing resources often remain inaccessible to smaller institutions and organizations in developing countries. The field lacks standardized, large-scale benchmarks and rigid evaluation protocols, and inflated performance claims often result from data leakage or inconsistent data splitting. Federated learning offers collaborative research that preserves patient privacy by training models across decentralized data sources without sharing raw sensitive information, and digital twins could enable in silico clinical trials simulating how populations might respond to new drug regimens.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Significantly Accelerates Drug Discovery and Molecular Development Timelines

stories.Headline: Dreamteam raises $53 Mn to build an AI-native CRM platform
stories.Summary:
Dreamteam, an AI-native customer relationship management platform cofounded by former Freshworks executives, emerged out of stealth mode and raised $53 Mn, nearly ₹498 Cr, in a strategic funding round from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest, as reported by Inc42 on November 16, 2026. The startup did not elaborate how it plans to utilise the funds. Founded in 2025 by former Freshworks executives Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy, Dreamteam is building an AI-powered CRM platform. Its four AI agents help enterprises track commitments, flag pipeline risks and automate routine sales workflows. The startup claims its AI platform pulls data and context from customer conversations, emails and Zoom interactions to enable AI coworkers to automate regular work.

Dreamteam claims to already cater to hundreds of companies across industries such as AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing and consulting. The platform also allows businesses to create custom apps and dashboards using natural language without writing code. Going forward, Dreamteam said it plans to focus on expanding its use cases across the entire customer lifecycle, including prospecting, onboarding and upselling. The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian AI startups. As per Inc42 data, homegrown AI ventures raised $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q2 2026, up 265% year on year.

Together Fund cofounder and partner Girish Mathrubootham said CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption. He said he had worked alongside Dreamteam's founders since day one as their vision for an AI-native CRM took shape. He said their deep CRM expertise and proven record of scaling enterprise software make them uniquely positioned to lead this reinvention. Venture capital and private equity firms remain bullish on startups that help enterprises put AI to work across business functions. Just last month, US-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith bagged $66 Mn in its Series C round led by Sequoia Capital.

Prior to this in October itself, another enterprise AI startup AuxoAI raised $20.7 Mn in its Series A funding round led by NTTVC. Fractal Analytics CEO Srikanth Velamakanni also recently reportedly said the AI analytics company is in discussions with 20-25 AI startups for potential acquisitions. At the heart of all this is the growing Indian enterprise AI ecosystem, which is projected to become a $71 Bn opportunity by 2030. The articles do not say when the round closed or what valuation it gave Dreamteam.

stories.Headline: Researcher maps four decades of AI growth in echocardiography research
stories.Summary:
An investigator conducted a bibliometric analysis of artificial intelligence research in echocardiography and published the results in the Journal of Cardiovascular Imaging. This comprehensive study mapped worldwide growth in the field by evaluating literature spanning more than four decades of cardiovascular imaging. The researcher analyzed 2,682 peer-reviewed and conference documents published between 1984 and November 10, 2025. These documents collectively accumulated 35,083 citations across global scientific databases. The analysis revealed a dramatic surge in publication volume and citation visibility following 2018.

The study required a dual-source search strategy querying both Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection through November 10, 2025. Scopus provided 2,472 documents, while the Web of Science supplied 1,928 records, resulting in 2,682 unique publications after deduplication. The research tracked 1,509 original research articles, 534 conference papers, and 300 review articles. In 2024, there were 572 records, and 2025 saw 573 records before the data collection ended. The analysis focused on diseases like heart failure, valvular heart disease, coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital heart disease.

The investigator stated that citation metrics measure scholarly visibility rather than translational effectiveness, diagnostic rigor, or patient safety. They noted that unadjusted observational comparisons reflect scholarly attention rather than underlying methodological quality or independent causal effects. The researcher explained that reliance on two databases may have underrepresented non-English literature and unindexed regional validation studies. They also mentioned that bibliometric databases remain susceptible to positive publication bias regarding successful algorithmic benchmarks. The author concluded that future research must transition toward rigorous multicenter prospective trials.

The study found that the United States led productivity with 1,404 publications, followed by China with 784 and the United Kingdom with 512. The Mayo Clinic ranked first in institutional output with 142 publications, while the University of California had the highest average citations. Top investigators included Francisco Lopez-Jimenez with 55 publications, Zachi I. Attia with 54, and Paul Andrew Friedman with 52. Open access publishing and dedicated funding were associated with higher citation counts for the researchers involved. The United States and United Kingdom formed the most productive partnership with 237 co-authored papers.

Echocardiography has been the most widely used clinical cardiac imaging modality since Inge Edler and Carl Hertz introduced ultrasound in 1954. Over subsequent decades, ultrasound instrumentation incorporated technological advancements that expanded daily procedural workloads and created highly complex diagnostic studies. Traditional manual acquisition and interpretation encountered structural limits under growing demands for precision cardiovascular medicine. Artificial intelligence emerged as a transformative methodology to provide computational solutions for automated view classification and myocardial quantification. These tools also offer diagnostic classification and structured electronic reporting across various clinical settings.

Future efforts must prioritize algorithmic explainability and dataset diversity across different ultrasound equipment platforms. Researchers need to integrate these technologies directly into clinical guidelines and real-world cardiovascular care. The study suggests a shift from retrospective single-center model development to more rigorous prospective trials. The articles leave open how these tools will specifically impact patient safety and diagnostic rigor in practice. They also leave open the exact timeline for the full integration of AI into standard clinical guidelines.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Accelerates Microbial Biosynthesis of Functional Bio-Based Nanomaterials
stories.Summary:
Microbial biosynthesis has emerged as an environmentally friendly alternative to traditional physicochemical nanoparticle production techniques, offering a versatile platform for generating functional nanoscale materials under mild reaction conditions. Conventional production routes, including chemical reduction, sol-gel processing, and laser ablation, routinely rely on hazardous reducing agents, toxic organic solvents, and high energy inputs that create environmental hazards and leave harmful surface residues. Microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, algae, cyanobacteria, and actinomycetes circumvent these issues by deploying enzymatic pathways, metabolic by-products, and active biomolecules to reduce metal precursors and stabilize nanoscale structures. Recent synthetic evaluations demonstrate that these biogenic nanomaterials possess superior biocompatibility and surface functionality compared with their chemically manufactured counterparts. However, translating microbial synthesis into industrial production has long been impeded by complex biological dynamics, unstandardized parameters, and erratic batch-to-batch variation, prompting researchers to integrate artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-driven materials informatics across every stage of the fabrication workflow.

Microbial nanomaterial generation operates through distinct biological mechanisms, primarily categorized into intracellular and extracellular pathways, alongside specialized biomineralization processes. In intracellular routes, metal cations traverse microbial cell envelopes through dedicated ion channels or electrostatic interactions with surface carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, undergoing reduction via intracellular enzymes, reduced cofactors such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, and thiol-bearing molecules like glutathione. Although intracellular synthesis yields smaller, highly monodisperse nanoparticles, product harvesting requires cell lysis that complicates downstream recovery. Extracellular synthesis circumvents this limitation by secreting reductive enzymes, extracellular polymeric substances, and redox-active metabolites into the surrounding culture medium, facilitating direct particle nucleation and capping without cellular disruption. Concurrently, biomineralization allows organisms such as magnetotactic bacteria to synthesize single-domain magnetic crystals of magnetite or greigite within membrane-bound magnetosomes, producing structures with tight size distributions and permanent magnetic dipole moments under strict genetic regulation.

The biochemical diversity across microbial classes dictates the morphology, yield, and catalytic activity of the resulting nanoparticles. Bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Escherichia, and Shewanella offer rapid growth and accessible genetic manipulation, using redox enzymes like nitrate reductase to yield metallic and metal oxide architectures. Fungi provide exceptional biomass yields and robust extracellular secretion rates, releasing high volumes of enzymes and secondary metabolites that simplify downstream purification while generating silver, gold, and zinc oxide nanoparticles. Photosynthetic microalgae and macroalgae utilize light and carbon dioxide to produce polysaccharides, polyols, and pigments that drive phyco-nanotechnology, yielding crystalline structures under sustainable cultivation regimes. Cyanobacteria contribute distinct phototrophic pathways that continuously supply reducing equivalents, whereas actinomycetes, particularly Streptomyces species, leverage diverse secondary metabolite profiles to assemble antimicrobial silver and gold particles with unique surface functionalization.

Despite the inherent flexibility of biological systems, native microbial synthesis remains exquisitely sensitive to extrinsic and intrinsic cultivation parameters. Small fluctuations in metal precursor concentrations, ambient pH, reaction temperatures, dissolved oxygen levels, nutrient feeds, and agitation rates trigger profound shifts in particle size, crystal structure, dispersity, and overall stability. For instance, alkaline reaction environments alter the ionization state of functional groups and boost biomolecular reducing capacity, favoring smaller, more uniform nanoparticles. Elevated temperatures accelerate reduction kinetics up to the threshold of thermal protein denaturation, while microbial physiological status during the logarithmic growth phase provides peak metabolic activity for efficient nucleation.

Because these environmental parameters exhibit complex, multidimensional interactions, traditional one-variable-at-a-time experimentation and standard response surface methodologies fail to resolve nonlinear interdependencies, leaving bioprocess optimization labor-intensive and frequently unrepeatable. Artificial intelligence and machine learning models are fundamentally transforming this landscape by replacing trial-and-error laboratory cycles with predictive modeling. Supervised learning algorithms, including artificial neural networks, support vector machines, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting regressors, can map multi-parameter inputs directly to nanoparticle size, yield, and morphology. Hybrid algorithmic frameworks, such as neural networks coupled with particle swarm optimization, have successfully isolated precursor concentrations, feed rates, and agitation speeds as primary drivers of particle dimensions.

Furthermore, convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and transformer-based architectures automate feature extraction from electron microscopy and spectroscopy imagery, quantifying structural properties without subjective operator intervention. Integrating these predictive algorithms with high-throughput multi-omics profiles, spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, allows researchers to anticipate cellular states and systematically dial in desired nanomaterial specifications with minimal experimental iteration. Beyond primary synthesis, post-synthetic surface functionalization is critical for adapting microbial nanomaterials to demanding technological environments, as native biomolecular capping layers alone rarely satisfy rigorous industrial or clinical benchmarks. Polyethylene glycol coatings provide steric hindrance that limits non-specific protein adsorption, extending circulation half-lives and preserving structural integrity even under extreme thermal stress.

Natural biopolymers like chitosan introduce reactive amine groups that promote mucoadhesion and support covalent drug conjugation, while targeted protein functionalization utilizing antibodies, transferrin, and cell-penetrating peptides enhances receptor-mediated uptake in pathological tissues. Researchers are also constructing hybrid nanocomposites by embedding biogenic nanoparticles within bacterial cellulose scaffolds or coupling them with graphene oxide and reduced graphene oxide sheets, achieving synergistic mechanical strength, superior electrical conductivity, and amplified catalytic performance. Stimuli-responsive functionalization represents an advanced frontier in biogenic material engineering, enabling dynamic structural and functional adaptations in response to environmental triggers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google rolls out Tasks AI assistant to users in India with Gemini 4 Hydrogen
stories.Summary:
Google has begun rolling out its new agentic AI assistant Tasks, formerly Gemini Sparks, to users in India, the company announced in a blogpost. Josh Woodward, the vice-president of Google Labs and the Gemini app, wrote the post announcing the rollout. The service comes bundled for free with Google's new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. Woodward said the update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India. Tasks was reportedly initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, an agentic AI helper.

The new feature will enable users to assign tasks to the AI assistant, including making calls, booking appointments, comparing products, making payments and completing purchases. Gemini can draw on information already available within Google services, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, files and payment cards, to carry out tasks on a user's behalf. With Tasks, Gemini can call businesses, wait through hold periods, identify available appointment slots and add bookings to a user's calendar. Under the hood, Gemini uses the agent payments protocol (AP2) to enable Tasks to make purchases online. Google said it plans to integrate the universal commerce protocol (UCP) into Gemini to further streamline the checkout experience.

Woodward said the update is rolling out free of charge across the six markets using the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. Google said it is working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to enable tokenised card transactions via Tasks. However, the big tech juggernaut did not specify whether partnerships extend to India too. Google has also invited app developers to join its Connected Apps Platform, which could pave the way for Indian consumer, fintech, travel tech and foodtech brands to build task-based third-party integrations with the assistant. Unlike Gemini's Chat that only generates responses to a user's queries, Tasks goes one step further and enables the chatbot to perform basic functions.

India's inclusion in the initial rollout gives Google a large market to test consumer adoption of the personal AI assistant feature. Adoption will depend on the availability of supported merchants, payment methods and third-party apps in the country, and there appears to be no clarity on this front. These features could make Gemini Tasks a channel for online shopping, bill payments and routine purchases. The launch is part of a broader wave of big tech giants rolling out personal AI assistants to capture the masses. In September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg showcased the company's new offering called Muse, which allows an AI agent to send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously.

Prior to this, OpenAI also introduced Dots that can draft board meeting decks, conduct background research, and handle multi-step project management. xAI has also been developing Grok Bot, which sees cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. Microsoft is also pursuing agents, built on OpenClaw, which can function as digital teammates. Back home, Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform, launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps. Tasks was subsequently expanded to the US-based subscribers of the Google AI Ultra tier.

With the rollout, Google could be looking to expand the role of AI assistants beyond answering questions to embedding them in daily life. Google is now rolling out this feature for free in six markets. To further scale the rollout, Google has invited app developers to join its Connected Apps Platform. The articles leave open whether the card partnerships with American Express, Mastercard and Visa extend to India. The articles also leave open the availability of supported merchants, payment methods and third-party apps in the country.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sarvam AI launches Token Factory inference engine to provide enterprises with local model access in India
stories.Summary:
Sarvam AI launched its Token Factory inference engine on November 18, 2026, to provide enterprises with local AI model access. This new offering allows users to run workloads on GPUs located in India through a single API. The unicorn aims to capture the local inference market by offering high speeds and low latency. It uses a three-tier caching architecture to rival the performance of global inference leaders. The company targets enterprises that must follow strict data residency mandates for their sensitive information.

Token Factory hosts Sarvam's 105B model and open-weight models from Google, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi in India. BFSI customers can access dedicated GPU capacity and on-premises inference deployments to ensure their data remains secure. Other providers like Krutrim have hosted DeepSeek models since last year, and OpenAI offers GPT-6 Luna workloads. Anthropic provides in-country inference for select Claude models through Amazon Bedrock to compete in the region. These diverse options create a crowded arena for any company offering local AI inference services.

Sarvam claims that hosting global models on Indian infrastructure supports data residency for local enterprises. The company believes that clients will pay for multi-model flexibility and the security of sovereign infrastructure. However, critics argue that relying on foreign open-weight models might dilute the push for homegrown AI. They question if the company can truly champion sovereign Indian AI while hosting overseas models. Sarvam must now invest in GPUs and software to maintain its competitive edge against giants.

Global AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic have opened offices in India to ramp up local investments. Anthropic saw a 15X increase in Indian downloads from July to September, while ChatGPT downloads fell 21%. Despite this, OpenAI revenue from in-app purchases in India grew 70% during the third quarter of 2026. The broader AI ecosystem is expected to contribute 1.7 trillion dollars to India's GDP by 2035. These trends show that India has become a major battleground for the world's leading AI companies.

Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas now plans to file for a US IPO by the first quarter of 2027. He previously stated the company would not go public before 2028, but growth has exceeded his expectations. Perplexity reached an annual recurring revenue of 1 billion dollars, beating its previous projection of 750 million. Meanwhile, Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq this week, and OpenAI has filed confidentially. These moves indicate a broader trend of major AI firms seeking public listings in the US.

The articles leave open whether Sarvam can outpace global giants or if its playbook arrived too late. It remains unclear if the company can successfully woo enough clients to justify its GPU investments. The future of the Indian AI market depends on how enterprises balance sovereign needs with global model power. Other stories mention a grooming brand called H.I.M. and Urban Company's 2,500 crore rupee placement. FirstCry and Lorazzo also face various growth targets and market opportunities through the coming years.

stories.Headline: CtrlS Datacentres targets 4.4 GW of data centre capacity by 2030
stories.Summary:
CtrlS Datacentres is targeting 4.4 GW of data centre capacity by 2030, the company said in an interview published by Analytics India Magazine on 16 November 2026. Rahul Dhar, President of Global Data Centre Operations, Enterprise Colo Delivery, Programme Management and Energy R&D at CtrlS Datacentres, gave the interview to AIM. CtrlS recently announced a ₹10,000 crore investment in Bihar to set up a 150 MW AI factory in Bodh Gaya. The company is also expanding its presence in Bihar with a ₹400 crore data centre in Patna. CtrlS’s Patna data centre currently has 12 MW of IT capacity, with scope to scale up as demand increases.

The strategy is to bring infrastructure closer to customers, particularly content-based businesses that need to serve users in smaller cities, Dhar said. Dhar said the new facility would support demand for digital infrastructure in Bihar and eastern India. CtrlS plans to establish more than 20 edge data centres across tier-2 and tier-3 cities over the coming years with improved fibre connectivity. It currently operates 19 data centres across 10 cities, including Lucknow, Noida, Kolkata and Gandhinagar, and operates a containerised data centre in Bhubaneswar. Hyperscalers constitute the largest source of demand for CtrlS, although the company also serves nearly 40 Indian public and private sector banks.

Nikhil Kamath, Co-founder of Zerodha, and entrepreneur Sreeram Reddy Vanga recently invested a combined ₹250 crore in CtrlS Datacenters. Canadian Pension Plan Investment Board also invested around ₹7,000 crore in the company earlier this year. Dhar attributes investor interest in CtrlS to its focus on hyperscale campuses, advance planning for high-capacity grid power, and modular designs. CtrlS is building greenfield data centre campuses for hyperscalers in Hyderabad and Mumbai. It is also in discussions with neocloud companies seeking capacity, and expects to deliver against its existing commitments over the next 12, 24 months.

This year, the central government introduced a 21-year tax holiday for foreign companies providing global cloud services using India-based data centres. Dhar said it won’t affect CtrlS’s existing demand, which is driven by domestic customers as well as global technology companies. He said that even with the tax holiday and a possible influx of foreign investors, Indian colocation providers have a good order book in hand. Dhar said India needs to shorten the period for forecasting data centre power requirements and speed up approvals for power transmission lines and fibre networks. Utilities and government departments typically seek power consumption on 7, 8 year horizons, he said.

Dhar said the projection that typical governments or power or utility departments ask for can be reduced to three to four years. Data centres are growing from facilities with capacities of around 5, 8 megawatts to campuses ranging from 10, 100 MW. Dhar said operators are bulk consumers of power, so they need better planning or better awareness among various government departments on how much power they need, at what time and at which location. He also called for faster right-of-way approvals to lay fibre networks and transmission lines, particularly when operators acquire land on city outskirts. CtrlS is providing inputs to government bodies and industry associations, including the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, NASSCOM and the Confederation of Indian Industry, on India’s recently proposed data centre policy.

Several states, including Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra, have already introduced data centre policies. According to Mordor Intelligence estimates, India consumed about 150 billion litres of water in 2025 to cool about 1.5 GW of data centre capacity, a figure expected to more than double by 2030. CtrlS uses closed-loop chillers to limit water loss and is reusing treated wastewater at one of its Mumbai facilities to reduce dependence on fresh water. The company also owns and operates a nearly 100 MW captive solar farm in Nagpur, with the power fed into the grid to offset consumption at its Mumbai data centres and similar initiatives planned for other locations, including Hyderabad. CtrlS also operates its facilities at a power usage effectiveness of around 1.4.

Dhar said CtrlS is prepared to support customers deploying liquid-cooled infrastructure, including GPU providers and cloud companies. He said all of CtrlS’s data centres are rated tier-4 data centres, and the company uses external certification and has introduced an Integrated Command and Control Centre in Hyderabad to monitor infrastructure centrally. The centre supports predictive analysis and preventive maintenance, and CtrlS is also applying AI to infrastructure monitoring, including CCTV systems, to improve responses to operational issues. Dhar said data centre operators will need to keep adapting their facilities to changing chip technologies, power densities and cooling systems as AI workloads increase infrastructure requirements. The article was published on 16 November 2026.

Articles.Title: Inside CtrlS’s Massive 4.4 GW Bet on India’s AI and Data Centre Boom - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Ethics professor Domènec Melé argues AI shapes habits and desires but cannot replace human wisdom or communion
stories.Summary:
Dr. Domènec Melé, an emeritus professor of business ethics at IESE Business School and an emeritus member of the Royal European Academy of Doctors, published an article titled “Christian Spirituality and Artificial Intelligence: Discernment in a Global Technological Economy” in the journal Religions on 27 October, the academy reported on 16 November 2026. In it he reflects on how artificial intelligence and new technological environments affect the spiritual development of human beings. He writes that artificial intelligence has shown it not only expands human capabilities but also shapes habits, desires, attention and forms of relationship. He argues that processing information or generating plausible responses is not the same as wisdom, which requires integrating knowledge with experience, moral judgement and an orientation towards worthy ends.

Melé holds that fluid and personalised interaction may simulate attention or empathy but does not amount to communion, because communion requires reciprocal presence, vulnerability and the capacity for self-giving between persons. He notes that in an economy rewarding engagement or productivity, optimising means does not automatically settle which ends are worth pursuing. He says artificial intelligence can reduce repetitive burdens and broaden access to knowledge or assistance, but replacing activities whose value includes human participation, such as teaching, care, professional judgement or personal accompaniment, carries risks. He also warns of an unequal distribution of human presence, since those with greater resources may keep access to teachers, doctors or advisers in person while others increasingly receive automated substitutes.

The article further underlines the material footprint of the technology, noting that although it may appear immaterial to users, artificial intelligence depends on data centres, chips and electricity grids whose consumption of energy and water is considerable. Melé does not advocate rejecting technology or absolutising it, and he suggests technical creativity can be understood as a form of participation in the care and development of creation, while the power it confers is a responsibility entrusted to human beings rather than absolute dominion. In a context of concentrated infrastructure, data and capital, he argues that the social doctrine of the Church offers criteria of dignity, the common good, subsidiarity and solidarity to keep individuals and communities from becoming passive recipients of decisions taken elsewhere. He concludes that progress is genuinely human when directed towards the integral development of persons and, within the Christian horizon, towards communion with God and with others.

Over the past 30 years Melé has researched and written extensively on business and economic ethics, corporate social responsibility, Christian social ethics, spirituality in management, management philosophy and humanistic management. He has published more than 70 book chapters and scientific articles in journals including the Journal of Business Ethics, Business Ethics Quarterly, Business Ethics: A European Review, Business and Society Review, Philosophy of Management and Humanistic Management Journal. He is also the author of several books that have become reference works in humanistic economics, among them “Ethics in Business Management”, “Anthropological Foundations of Business Management”, “Business Ethics in Action. Seeking Human Excellence in Organizations”, “Christians in Society” and “Ethics in the Family Business”, the last co-authored with fellow READ emeritus member Miguel Ángel Gallo.

stories.Headline: Dreamteam raises $53m to build AI-native CRM with four AI sales teammates
stories.Summary:
Dreamteam has raised $53 million across its seed and Series A rounds to build an AI-native customer relationship management platform that uses multiple AI teammates to manage sales workflows and customer relationships. The funding was led by Together Fund and Accel, with participation from Premji Invest, according to an article published by Analytics India Magazine on 17 November 2026. The company says more than 100 companies across 13 countries currently use its platform. The money will help Dreamteam expand the platform, which aims to reduce the manual work involved in maintaining traditional CRM systems.

The platform currently offers four AI teammates, each assigned a specific sales function. Rachel acts as a market analyst who researches prospects and their companies, while Sally manages deals and follow-ups. Raj monitors sales pipelines and identifies potential risks, and Alex handles CRM configuration based on business requirements. The four agents operate through a shared system called Company Brain, which keeps customer information from calls, emails and meetings, so the agents can access previous conversations, customer priorities and outstanding commitments instead of working independently. The system is also designed to update CRM records as customer relationships and business requirements change.

Anand Venkatraman, co-founder and CEO of Dreamteam, said AI finally gives the company a way to change the foundation of CRM. He said Dreamteam learns from the work a team is already doing, keeps the context alive and gives every salesperson skilled AI teammates that can reason over it and move work forward. Dreamteam argues that conventional CRMs, where representatives manually record interactions, update deal information and track follow-ups, often fail to capture important details from customer conversations. The company says its agents operate within company-defined policies, pricing rules and approval limits, that emails require human approval before being sent, and that users can inspect the sources behind recommendations and correct information stored by the system.

Dreamteam plans to expand the agents' responsibilities beyond individual sales tasks to manage broader customer journeys, including lead generation, renewals and account expansion. It also envisions its agents eventually communicating with buyers' AI systems to exchange requirements and handle routine business interactions.

stories.Headline: Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud partner to expand AI education across over 1,000 Indian schools and colleges
stories.Summary:
Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud announced on 17 November 2026 that they will partner to expand AI education across more than 1,000 public and private schools and colleges in India, combining hands-on learning programmes with industry-aligned certifications. The initiative will pair Accenture LearnVantage's learning programmes with Google Cloud's unified AI stack to set up AI Labs in schools and Centres of Excellence in higher education institutions. The programmes will cover foundational AI literacy, applied generative AI, agentic AI and AI engineering, with the stated aim of preparing students for emerging technology roles. The partnership will also introduce structured learning pathways for students and educators, supported by Google's AI tools and personalised coaching through Gemini.

At the school level, the two companies plan to establish AI Labs powered by Google Gemini that introduce younger students to foundational AI concepts in controlled learning environments where they can experiment with AI tools and develop practical skills. For higher education institutions, the partnership plans Centres of Excellence, centres and academies that will serve as hubs for applied learning, innovation and industry collaboration, giving students access to modern tools, expert mentorship and opportunities to work with emerging technologies. The curriculum will include generative AI and agentic AI literacy, applied generative AI and agentic AI programmes, an AI developer programme and AI engineering, and students who complete the programmes and assessments will receive certifications. The platform will also offer guided learning pathways, multilingual voice capabilities and AI-driven content to make learning more accessible, and institutions will be able to explore customised offerings, including degree programmes, aligned with changing industry requirements.

Anurag Bansal, Managing Director of Accenture LearnVantage for Asia Oceania and the Middle East, said in a statement that the future of learning will be shaped by how learning pathways and talent creation for careers are reimagined as those careers continue to evolve. The collaboration will also support Accenture LearnVantage's existing national AI initiatives, including the National AI Olympiad and AI Infinity, which aim to encourage AI literacy and introduce students to careers in emerging technologies. The announcement was published by Analytics India Magazine on 17 November 2026, the same day the outlet listed a related story on HCLTech partnering with Cohere to target sovereign AI markets. The articles do not say what funding the initiative involves, how institutions will be selected or when the labs and centres are expected to open.
