stories.Headline: Amagasaki by-election candidates use AI-generated faces on posters as officials confirm no legal grounds to remove them
stories.Summary:
A city council by-election in Amagasaki, Hyogo Prefecture, on November 15, 2026, drew 12 candidates for one vacant seat, and at least four of them displayed posters with AI-generated faces rather than their own photographs. Former prefectural assembly member Hikoharu Konishi acknowledged that four candidates had used artificial images, and the Amagasaki City Election Administration Commission confirmed at least four posters were suspected of using generative AI. In one case, officials said the man depicted on the poster of candidate Hiroyoshi Hara was not Hara himself, and an election official who had met Hara said the person shown looked completely different. The controversy emerged during a closely contested race in which voters also chose a mayor on November 15, with incumbent Kazumi Matsumoto winning a second term and Hiromi Ikeshita securing the council seat. Some posters depicted men with tattoos on their arms, while others showed attractive, distinguished-looking older men alongside simple campaign messages.

Japan's Public Offices Election Act has regulated posters through requirements on dimensions and identification of responsible parties but has not required candidates to use photographs of themselves. After the July 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, when campaign poster boards displayed sexually explicit images of women and other material unrelated to candidates, lawmakers revised the law to require candidates' names to be clearly visible and to prohibit material damaging another person's reputation or violating public morals. The amended law contains no provision requiring a candidate's actual face to appear on a poster, and election authorities said they had no legal grounds to order the posters removed. Under the publicly funded election campaign system, public funding for poster production in the Amagasaki by-election was available up to approximately 610,000 yen per candidate, depending on reimbursement conditions. Each of the four candidates received enough votes to qualify for the return of the 300,000 yen deposit required to stand in the municipal election, though all four were defeated.

An Amagasaki election official said the commission could not intervene simply because a photograph or image was misleading, citing freedom of political activity and freedom of expression. Konishi, who with his secretary had submitted the candidacy registrations on behalf of the four individuals, reportedly responded that he found officials' requests for identity verification unpleasant. Speaking on behalf of candidate Koichi Sato, number 12, on November 14, the final day of campaigning, Konishi told voters the posters were the ones everyone in Amagasaki had been talking about and asked whether people genuinely felt suspicious about the images. He confirmed to Kansai Television that the images were produced using AI, saying of Sato's poster, "This was made with AI," and calling it "an image." Konishi said production costs were matters to be settled between candidates and contractors, that he had followed the Public Offices Election Act properly with the election commission's approval, and that outsiders should not make a fuss.

One Amagasaki resident said the artificial appearance immediately discouraged closer examination of the candidates' messages, and another said it made them wonder how committed the candidates really were and that it was difficult to sense any sincerity. Another resident said candidates should not engage in such unusual practices, while another questioned whether the individuals were seriously attempting to win office. Reporters searched Amagasaki for campaign vehicles and tried to contact the individuals by telephone but could not locate them or obtain interviews. Ono Planning Office, a local poster production company that has worked on more than 1,000 campaigns, restricts AI use to image correction and set its own guidelines in November. Company representative Satsuki Ono said AI can create a completely different face from the original material, that this is no longer simply correcting a photograph, and that charging nearly 600,000 yen for posters made with AI for practically nothing and paying only for printing could yield a substantial profit.

Election consultant Takuma Ohamazaki said that normally someone who runs for election incurs expenses and finishes with a financial loss, and that in this case he suspected some people may have ended up making money. Ohamazaki also warned that increasingly sophisticated AI could make future cases far harder to detect, saying the cat-and-mouse game between technological advances and the Public Offices Election Act will continue. Legal experts said Japan's election legislation has historically been designed to regulate specific, identifiable practices, making it difficult to anticipate abuses from new technologies, and that restrictions on political expression must be balanced against democratic freedoms including the right to participate in elections and communicate political messages. There has been no confirmation that the four candidates or their associates improperly received public funds or profited, and the allegations remain suspicions rather than established wrongdoing. Similar concerns circulated on social media, where users questioned whether obtaining publicly funded poster payments might have been one motivation for entering the election.

Further changes to the Public Offices Election Act are scheduled for March 2027, including a requirement to disclose when AI has been used in election-related materials. The planned disclosure requirement has drawn criticism because it carries no penalties for violations and does not necessarily require detailed explanations of which elements of an image were generated or altered. Experts questioned whether a simple declaration that AI was used would provide meaningful protection against misleading campaign imagery. Without clearer definitions of prohibited conduct or enforceable penalties, they warned, candidates may continue exploiting gaps between rapidly developing technology and election regulations. The Amagasaki controversy has highlighted a broader challenge facing Japan's democratic system.

Articles.Title: AI-Generated Election Posters Spark Controversy in Japan - News On Japan

stories.headline_source: AI-Generated Election Posters Spark Controversy in Japan

stories.Headline: City leaders at Global AI Cities 2026 set out five priorities for making AI and digital infrastructure resilient
stories.Summary:
At Global AI Cities 2026, more than 300 local government leaders from over 50 cities gathered in Manchester to discuss artificial intelligence and digital resilience. The event was organised by Global Government Forum and co-hosted by Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Sarah Wray reported on the conference for Global Government Forum on 16 November 2026. The discussions were captured in the report Making AI work for people and places: Five priorities for cities. The report draws on insights from the event and includes examples from Romania, Westminster and Alberta.

The report sets out five priorities for cities, including fixing the fundamentals and prioritising according to criticality. It also calls for governing AI throughout its lifecycle and making digital infrastructure itself resilient. The report says resilience depends on people and partnerships as well as technology. Global AI Cities 2027 is to be held in Manchester on 24-25 May. The report is available to download.

Alexandru Georgescu, senior researcher at Romania's National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics, said local authorities are not actually ready for AI in itself. He said generative AI and large language models are not comparable to traditional software and need new processes and new cybersecurity practices, including adversarial testing and red-teaming. He said many large organisations are not ready to do this, let alone local administrations that probably have not budgeted for it. He said cities are agglomerations of critical infrastructures that serve wider regions and become targets for criminals, rogue states or state-sponsored organisations. He concluded that many local authorities are not adequately prepared and do not have the level of support they need from central authorities.

Gurpreet Muctor, chief data and technology officer for Westminster City Council, said a late 2025 cyber-attack took five months to recover from and forced the shutdown of all systems. He said the attack was perpetrated by somebody who impersonated a council employee and was still a manual process, not an AI attack. He said AI increasingly adds a new layer to that threat in the form of deepfakes that can impersonate council workers, politicians or senior officials. Richard Henderson, corporate chief information officer for the Government of Alberta, said many local governments make it too easy for hackers because they are not getting the fundamentals right. He said Alberta built AI-assisted tooling to scan 400 million lines of government code for vulnerabilities, work he estimated would have taken a human 125 years of development time.

Henderson advised cities not to wait for the most advanced tools and said they can probably build their own reasonable facsimile relatively quickly for not a significant amount. He said the only way to survive the deepfake threat is through good governance and protocols, such as an agreed challenge phrase to ascertain that someone is genuine. Georgescu said there is too much focus on the cutting edge when good enough is often adequate for both attackers and defenders. He said his institute prioritises based on criticality, identifying which systems would cause the greatest harm if compromised and hardening those first. He highlighted the most basic AI-related risk as someone pasting citizen data into a public LLM to save time, and said the human factor and security culture matter.

Georgescu said there is not enough talk about the lifecycle of AI products and systems and how decommissioning will be handled. He warned of AI agents stuck in systems and attached to data that an adversary could exploit long after the department that built them has moved on. Henderson said staff are not interested in waiting for discussions about AI and will use it whether organisations like it or not. One senior leader at the summit described facing a pandemic, a major snowstorm and an energy blackout, which highlighted the difference between having technology and having resilience. The city is now strengthening resilience through a city brain supported by AI, improved cybersecurity, closer partnerships with telecom providers, resilient government buildings, district-level citizen refuges with power and connectivity, and new platforms providing real-time information on infrastructure.

The articles do not state what specific measures, funding or deadlines follow from the report's five priorities. They do not name the city whose leader described the succession of crises. They do not give the outcome of the Westminster attack beyond the five-month recovery and system shutdown. They do not say what action, if any, Romania's central authorities have taken in response to Georgescu's comments. They do not give details of the Global AI Cities 2027 agenda beyond its dates and location.

Articles.Title: AI’s double-edged sword: why cities must prioritise digital resilience - Global Government Forum

stories.Headline: HCLTech and Cohere partner to build sovereign AI solutions for enterprises and governments
stories.Summary:
HCLTech and Cohere announced on 17 November 2026 that they have partnered to build and deliver sovereign artificial intelligence solutions for enterprises and governments. Under the agreement, HCLTech will become one of Cohere's preferred global systems integrator partners in Canada and Germany. The two companies plan to combine Cohere's sovereign AI platform and models with HCLTech's professional services and AI implementation capabilities. They also intend to extend the partnership to other markets beyond Canada and Germany.

The initial development work will focus on insurance, financial services, and manufacturing, according to the companies. Potential applications include jurisdiction-aware claims assessment, secure analysis of sensitive financial data, and faster access to technical documentation. The partnership will use Cohere's models and its North agentic AI platform, alongside domain-adapted models and retrieval and reasoning capabilities. The companies said the solutions would be deployed in customers' preferred environments to address data residency, security, and regulatory requirements.

Phil Blunsom, Chief Technology Officer at Cohere, said organisations should not have to choose between the benefits of AI and control over their data. He said the partnership with HCLTech would help customers tackle complex, industry-specific challenges while meeting their security, governance and data sovereignty requirements. HCLTech Executive Vice President and Canada Country Head Dave Chopra said the partnership would combine Cohere's platform with HCLTech's local presence in Canada to help organisations adopt AI. The companies also said both hold ISO 42001 certification, the international standard for AI management systems.

Cohere was co-founded by Aidan Gomez, Nick Frosst, and Ivan Zhang in 2019, and Gomez was the youngest co-author of the landmark Google research paper that invented the Transformer architecture powering generative AI. The agreement follows HCLTech's October partnership with Anthropic to expand enterprise adoption of agentic AI through its Claude models, which included plans for a dedicated Anthropic business unit and a Centre of Excellence. HCLTech has also pursued sovereign AI initiatives in India, and in February HCLSoftware partnered with Sify Digital Services to develop a sovereign AI stack for Indian enterprises.

stories.Headline: Instructure launches Foundry venture and Athena AI study coach for Canvas
stories.Summary:
Instructure has launched Instructure Foundry, a standalone venture focused on AI development for education, and its first project is Project Athena, an AI study coach designed to work with Canvas, according to an announcement reported on 17 November 2026. The venture brings together small teams to develop and refine new products with input from educators and institutions, while Instructure continues developing its existing platforms, including Canvas, Mastery and Parchment. Project Athena is being built to give students study support based on material already in their Canvas courses, using course content, assignments and upcoming assessments to generate personalised quizzes, study guides and coaching prompts. Athena will connect to the learning environment through a read-only link governed by existing student permissions, and Instructure said student conversations with the tool will not be used to train external AI models.

In the United States, Hinds Community College is involved in the initiative following an initial pilot, and the project is expected to extend access to its 7,000 students. The tool is intended to give students extra support outside classroom and tutoring hours, and by drawing on a student's own course context in Canvas it is expected to identify gaps in understanding and adjust prompts as learning progresses. Instructure said the structure is intended to help it move faster on emerging technologies without affecting the stability of products already used by schools, universities and vocational education providers.

Shiren Vijiasingam, Chief Product Officer at Instructure, said AI has changed what is possible, with small teams now able to build and test new ideas faster than before, and he said Foundry gives those teams space to iterate on emerging solutions rapidly while core products continue to get sustained investment. He said Project Athena represents what Instructure believes responsible AI in education should look like, grounded in learning science, connected to the learning environment and built to support understanding through skill mastery, and he said it will coach toward mastery rather than answers. Zach Pendleton, Chief Architect at Instructure, said the pace of change has outrun the conventional roadmap, and he said investors have provided incremental funding so the venture does not compete with investment the core products need. He described Instructure as running two tracks, one that serves and scales what it has built and one that explores what is next.

The launch reflects a wider debate in education over how institutions should use AI while protecting student information, maintaining academic integrity and keeping educators central to teaching, and providers in Australia and elsewhere have been weighing whether to adopt new tools within systems they already use or through separate applications. The announcement comes as education providers seek AI tools that can be integrated into existing platforms rather than used as standalone consumer applications, which creates pressure on software companies serving the sector to show both speed of development and controls around privacy, security and educator oversight. Athena is under development and is being created with educators and institutions, and as the first project to emerge from Foundry it will test whether tightly integrated AI study support can gain traction with institutions seeking more direct control over how students use generative AI.

Articles.Title: Instructure launches Foundry & Athena AI study coach - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Los Angeles schools survey parents, students and staff to shape generative AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District is distributing a survey to parents, students and staff to help inform its policy on generative artificial intelligence in schools, LAist reported on November 16, 2026. The district wants to hear from community members about how the technology should be used in classrooms across the system. The survey is meant to gather input that will shape the district's formal policy on generative AI. The report was published by Elly Yu, who covers early childhood issues for LAist. The survey follows a surprise moratorium that LAUSD implemented in September on student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for this school year.

Before that moratorium, district policy allowed students 13 and older to use the technology under supervision. The school board has an ad-hoc committee on generative AI that examines the new technology and what its role should be in the classroom. The committee was formed as part of a resolution that was passed to limit screentime in the district. The ad hoc committee is scheduled to meet four more times this school year, on Dec. 9, 2026, Jan. 20, 2027, March 3, 2027 and April 7, 2027. The committee plans to make policy recommendations that the full board could vote on.

The survey of parents, students and staff is intended to help inform the district policy that emerges from that process. The committee's work and the survey together will feed into the recommendations the board may eventually consider. The context is a district still working out how generative AI fits into its classrooms after the September moratorium paused student use on school-issued devices. The ad-hoc committee's four remaining meetings this school year give the board a schedule for turning community input into recommendations it could vote on. The survey gives parents, students and staff a way to weigh in before those recommendations take shape.

Articles.Title: LAUSD wants to hear from parents about how the district should use AI - LAist

stories.Headline: Pronto Software marks 50 years with accelerated AI investment and security-first ERP roadmap
stories.Summary:
Melbourne-based ERP company Pronto Software is marking 50 years in business, using the anniversary to highlight an accelerated investment in artificial intelligence that it has been developing since 2021, when it began exploring machine learning before speeding up its roadmap after generative and agentic AI emerged. Managing Director and CEO Chad Gates, who has led the company for a decade and joined 21 years ago, said the rapid pace of development has forced software providers to reconsider how they build and deliver products. Pronto has taken what it describes as a deliberate, security-first approach, building its own GPU infrastructure within Pronto Cloud and hosting large language models internally while still allowing connections to external models so it is not dependent on a single provider. The architecture is designed around authentication, permissions and access controls so that AI agents and connected systems cannot access information or perform actions beyond their authorised capabilities.

Gates said the company took the position early that it would provide a high-trust model, describing AI as a capability rather than a technology and saying the data is where the value lies rather than the AI itself. He said customers are primarily concerned with two issues, security and productivity, wanting to know how AI can improve efficiency while worrying about exposing sensitive information or investing in technology that fails to deliver returns. Pronto has operated debt-free since its inception, and Gates said its independent ownership structure and local presence remain competitive advantages against large multinational providers, particularly with owner-operated customers who can speak directly with staff. He said the technology will change dramatically but the truth should never change.

Looking ahead, Gates said AI will fundamentally change how employees interact with ERP platforms, potentially reducing the need for traditional interfaces filled with screens, forms and menus as staff increasingly rely on AI assistants and agents to retrieve information, generate reports and interpret business data through conversation. He suggested future product development could become less reliant on building dedicated screens for every new feature, with AI generating interfaces and reports when users need them. He identified agent-to-agent communication as another significant area of development as businesses deploy larger numbers of autonomous agents, raising questions around coordination, permissions and the management of data and workflows. Quantum-safe encryption is also a priority, with Gates warning that advances in quantum computing combined with increasingly capable AI systems could create considerable security challenges that providers need to prepare for before the technology becomes mainstream.

Gates believes the scale and speed of change now underway will exceed anything the business has experienced previously, and he said the challenge will be continuing to innovate while maintaining the security, reliability and customer relationships that have underpinned the company's longevity.

Articles.Title: Pronto Software marks 50-year milestone with AI-focused ERP roadmap - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: EU science and ethics advisors urge public AI evaluation capacity
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors and the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies issued a joint statement warning that traditional public policy guardrails cannot govern rapidly advancing artificial intelligence. The two senior advisory bodies called on the European Union to establish sovereign capacity to evaluate complex AI models rather than delegating safety assessments to commercial technology firms. The statement, titled ‘The next phase of artificial intelligence ,  Governing for safety, security and human agency,’ sets out four core principles for European policymakers. The advisors delivered the four primary recommendations to the College of Commissioners. The joint statement was published on 16 Nov 2026.

The first recommendation is to keep existing rules strong, with safety, cybersecurity and human agency remaining mandatory prerequisites for AI development. The advisors warn against regulatory backsliding and say political hesitation risks weakening statutory obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and that lobbying to dilute compliance deadlines must be resisted. The second is to calibrate development and deployment to degrees of danger, so the pace at which foundation models and autonomous systems are released correlates with potential hazards. Where models pose severe cybersecurity, biosecurity or critical-infrastructure risks, deployment must be contingent on verified mitigation rather than post-incident response. The third is to build independent public evaluation capacity, with the advisors urging the EU to develop public testing facilities and warning the bloc cannot remain dependent on self-attestations or proprietary safety benchmarks supplied by commercial developers.

The fourth is to establish an ecosystem for continuous learning, in which regulatory frameworks and scientific risk assessments evolve dynamically alongside advancing model capabilities, since static compliance checklists are obsolete and authorities must create adaptive monitoring loops that ingest empirical evidence from operational deployments. The Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, established under the Scientific Advice Mechanism, comprises seven eminent researchers appointed in their personal capacity to deliver evidence-based policy counsel. The European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies operates as an independent advisory body examining where scientific discovery intersects with fundamental European rights. Officials within the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation confirmed that the move reflects mounting concern that commercial market pressures threaten to bypass fundamental safety reviews. The GCSA and EGE argued that relying exclusively on commercial developers to determine whether their proprietary models trigger GPAI systemic risk thresholds introduces an inherent conflict of interest that undermines European safety objectives.

The advisors asserted that safety and market competitiveness are complementary, and that reliable, audited and trustworthy systems form the only durable foundation for widespread societal adoption in medicine, public administration and critical engineering. In independent coverage by Wisevoter, titled Scientists Urge Europe to Enforce AI Rules, observers underscored that the European advisory apparatus is pivoting attention away from theoretical rule-drafting toward concrete technical verification capabilities. European academic organizations welcomed the advisors’ insistence on public evaluation infrastructure. Policy commentators at European Interest had previously pointed out that public scientific research risks marginalization if access to frontier models and evaluation tools remains gated behind commercial licensing agreements.

University consortia emphasized that independent evaluation capacity within member states would provide academic researchers with transparent benchmarks and reproducible verification protocols. For universities, research hospitals and academic research offices, the recommendations highlight procurement due diligence and audit trails, expansion of research ethics committee remits, academic participation in public evaluation testbeds, and safeguarding scientific reproducibility. Both bodies have previously advised the Commission on computational technologies, delivering opinions on artificial intelligence in crisis management and publishing detailed guidance on the successful and timely uptake of artificial intelligence in science in the EU. The joint statement arrives as the operational burden of the AI Act, finalized in 2024, has shifted toward secondary rulemaking and practical enforcement.

Critical milestones currently under negotiation include the general-purpose AI Code of Practice and implementation frameworks that clarify downstream compliance obligations. The European Commission has introduced legislative proposals including the Cloud and AI Development Act (COM(2026) 502 final). The advisors warn that without substantial budgetary investment in public technical staff, automated evaluation tooling and independent laboratory verification, regulatory bodies risk becoming rubber-stamping entities for proprietary commercial claims. Following publication of the joint statement on November 16, 2026, the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation and DG CONNECT are scheduled to review the advisors’ recommendations.

Attention will center on whether the European Commission incorporates explicit funding for independent evaluation infrastructure into upcoming Horizon Europe work programmes and the implementation roadmaps for the Cloud and AI Development Act. In parallel, the European AI Office is preparing the final administrative drafts of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, where stakeholder negotiations over independent auditor access remain under way. Under existing voluntary frameworks, major model providers conduct internal red-teaming exercises and issue selective model cards. The articles leave open whether the Commission will adopt the recommendations and how the negotiations over independent auditor access will conclude.

stories.Headline: Bureau of Industry and Security requires licenses to export advanced AI chips to certain data centers
stories.Summary:
The Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on November 16, 2026. This rule requires licenses to export, reexport, or transfer advanced artificial intelligence chips to certain data centers. It targets facilities providing significant computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5 destinations. The rule also applies to data centers whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those same locations. These restrictions apply to chips anywhere in the world.

Licenses are now required for advanced computing items under ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090 shipped to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. The rule covers data centers providing more than 12 million in aggregate total processing performance to restricted customers. It formally rescinds the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule and its associated authorizations. The rule takes effect upon publication in the Federal Register. It uses the term Super Intelligence instead of artificial intelligence following Executive Order 14434.

The Bureau of Industry and Security is responsible for implementing these new export controls. Officials stated the rule relies on existing power over chip shipments rather than regulating remote access directly. They explained that serving restricted customers after chips arrive counts as a new in-country transfer. BIS noted that due diligence is meant to prevent evasion through corporate spinoffs or restructurings. They will review all license applications on a case by case basis.

Cloud providers, chip suppliers, and data center operators are affected by these new compliance requirements. Some companies, including Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance, reportedly used chips in Japan, Malaysia, and Thailand. The rule affects any party holding the chips, even those not involved in the original shipment. Exporters must now verify the know your customer checks of foreign data centers. Those already supplying restricted power must obtain a license within 90 days.

The Bureau of Industry and Security previously concluded in 2009 and 2014 that cloud computing was not subject to regulations. Remote access allowed Chinese companies to rent computing power in the United States or third countries. This created a loophole because the physical chips never had to cross any international borders. The current rule addresses this by regulating the chips behind the capacity rather than the activity. It uses Sections 1753 and 1754 of the Export Control Reform Act.

The Bureau of Industry and Security will accept public comments for 60 days after the rule is published. Congress is pursuing the Remote Access Security Act, which passed the House on January 12, 2026. This bill awaits action in the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. The Secretary of Commerce may add more high risk destinations to the license list. The articles leave open whether the Senate will pass its own version, S. 3519.

stories.Headline: GitHub and Microsoft report 99 verified AI security findings across six open source projects
stories.Summary:
GitHub and Microsoft have disclosed early results from a pilot that uses artificial intelligence to identify and help fix security flaws in open source software, and across six widely used projects the system produced 99 verified private reports. The pilot combined Codename MDASH, Microsoft's multi-model scanning system, with an AI triage process from GitHub Security Lab and manual checks by Microsoft researchers. The goal was to cut the number of raw alerts reaching maintainers and instead send private reports with proof-of-concept material and suggested fixes. The system flagged 9,791 possible issues across the six projects, and after automated filtering and manual review maintainers received 99 private reports. More than half had already been fixed when the figures were published, with 55 of the 99 reported issues fixed and 14 already included in a software release.

The six projects in the pilot were AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick and Netty, and the work addresses a growing problem for open source projects whose maintainers are increasingly dealing with large numbers of AI-generated vulnerability submissions, including duplicates and issues that are not actually security flaws. Under the process described by the companies, Codename MDASH first scanned each code base using Microsoft's MAI Cyber model and proposed fixes, and a triage agent built by GitHub Security Lab then removed duplicate findings, tested their validity and narrowed the list to higher-impact issues. Researchers from Microsoft FORGE Lab manually checked the remaining reports, and only then were reports sent to maintainers through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting system, with each including a suggested fix while maintainers retained control over whether and when to patch the issue. The pilot was designed around two principles, to send only findings that matter and not to send unverified reports to maintainers, reflecting wider concern across the software industry that AI has sharply lowered the cost of finding potential flaws but not the cost of validating and fixing them. The first fixes were shipped roughly a week after the initial scans, and in one example highlighted by the companies Caddy maintainers fixed all 22 reports they received within a week or less.

On ImageMagick, which was described as being maintained by a two-person team, the pilot generated 22 reports, and one maintainer said the format of the reports reduced the time needed to assess and fix some issues, describing a security advisory as normally taking around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand and make a fix. A maintainer assessment cited by the companies came from FastMCP, saying the Codename MDASH scan provided unique insights into the security of the project above and beyond what AI scanners had provided in the past, and a further maintainer comment focused on the volume of low-quality reports, saying Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports. The pilot remains limited in scale and still depends heavily on human review, with seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers spending about two days per project checking findings by hand, a level of scrutiny that may be difficult to expand broadly without additional resources. That challenge is one of the project's main lessons, because while AI can generate large numbers of possible findings cheaply, open source security still relies on careful human validation and maintainers' own judgment when deciding how to patch code.

GitHub is now extending AI security scans to all alumni projects in its Secure Open Source Fund, with findings reviewed before they are reported privately, and the fund has supported 216 projects so far, with the participating repositories accounting for software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month. Each project in the fund receives USD $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors alongside security training, and more than 300 maintainers in the programme have fixed more than 4,000 vulnerabilities, while broader data also shows more than 850 secret leaks prevented or resolved and more than 1,500 vulnerable dependencies updated. The six projects in the MDASH pilot were all alumni of that fund, and GitHub said the support package for alumni will now also include AI security scans and access to Copilot Max. The broader significance lies in how flaws in open source software can affect commercial software supply chains far beyond the original projects, because when maintainers publish a security advisory and it is reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert downstream repositories that rely on the affected package. A spokesperson said maintainers do the fixing and that the job is to make sure they never do it alone.

Articles.Title: GitHub & Microsoft pilot AI bug scans in open source - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Illinois reports say data center power demand delays coal plant closures until 2033
stories.Summary:
Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering Illinois plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change, according to a pair of state reports released Monday. Under a law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. But big new data centers require so much electricity that it has become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand. The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year, because cleaner sources including wind and solar are not being built quickly enough.

In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate, and the goal of shutting four of them down by 2030 remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed, and eleven so-called peaker plants that burn oil or natural gas as backups were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen, and peakers in Waukegan will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation.

Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at the Respiratory Health Association in Chicago, said fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people. Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County, called the recommendation disappointing and said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. She said her community is tired of dirty energy. Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants, but state officials said that is not being advised, and the state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants.

Illinois is not running out of power yet, but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, that the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity. Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city. State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month, and hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, and the Integrated Resource Plan released by the Illinois Commerce Commission.

Articles.Title: AI data centers block pollution, climate efforts in Illinois - WBEZ

stories.headline_source: AI data centers block pollution, climate efforts in Illinois

stories.Headline: Malaysia plans full AI exposure in schools next year as PAGE urges a balanced approach
stories.Summary:
The Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia successfully conducted its 16th annual general meeting in September 2026 to continue its campaign for English language instruction. This educational lobby group previously advocated for the use of smartphones as teaching aids, though many teachers initially insisted that these devices remain at home. While some developed nations are now restricting technology, the Madani government has decided to implement full scale exposure to artificial intelligence within the Malaysian education system. This new curriculum is scheduled to begin next year for students entering Year One and Form One.

Several countries are currently spending significant funds to return to traditional learning methods to combat digital fatigue and protect cognitive focus. Sweden spent more than 2.1 billion krona, or 875 million ringgit, over two years to bring printed textbooks and teaching guides back into classrooms. Denmark committed 540 million Danish krone, which is 330 million ringgit, over ten years for physical books while making schools and after school clubs handphone free. Other nations including Finland, Italy, France, and Norway have restricted or banned phones, while Madrid, Spain, is capping primary student screen time to two hours per week.

Datin Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, the chairman of the Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia, expressed concerns regarding the eagerness to put screens in front of developing children. She argued that implementation must be guided by child safety, equity, and educational outcomes so that students do not surrender their ability to think independently. She noted that professors at Harvard University are increasingly banning laptops, as an analysis by The Harvard Crimson in September 2026 found such bans had more than doubled. She believes pupils still need physical books and handwriting practice to avoid being distracted by digital notifications.

The group suggests that Malaysia should learn from developed countries that have come full circle by finding a healthier balance between digital and traditional education. The author warns that excessive self promotion without adequate preparation could lead to failure, citing the recall of 8,878 Chery Omoda 5 cars and 600 other vehicles. The goal is for students to use technology to solve problems and make informed decisions rather than depending on it to think for them. The group will continue to serve as a channel between concerned parents, the Ministry of Education, and other stakeholders.

Articles.Title: Edunation: PAGE comes full circle as AI hits classrooms - The Edge Malaysia

stories.Headline: Knightcorp report warns AI and cloud gaps leave insurance cover open to dispute
stories.Summary:
Knightcorp has launched its Forerunner Report - Technology, which examines insurance issues linked to AI, cyber risk, cloud exposure, directors' liability and connected devices, according to an article published by IT Brief Australia on 16 November 2026. The research argues that insurance reviews are struggling to keep pace with how technology businesses now operate, particularly when companies rely on AI tools, cloud infrastructure and third-party software platforms. It presents insurance less as an annual procurement exercise and more as part of broader risk governance for finance leaders, boards and technology teams. One of the report's central findings is that policy wording may not clearly address AI-related claims, and Knightcorp said some professional indemnity and cyber policies are silent on AI, which could leave room for disputes over whether cover applies when businesses build AI into their own products or use AI embedded in third-party platforms.

The report says AI exclusions are appearing in some policy wordings, citing Lander & Rogers, which adds pressure on companies to check whether their existing insurance arrangements match their use of the technology. On cloud cover, Knightcorp said undeclared systems, or systems that do not fit a policy's wording, can become a point of dispute during claims, and it suggests businesses map third-party systems that handle client data and then test how each one is treated in policy applications and wording. The report applies the same logic to connected hardware, saying companies that make or supply smart devices should check whether new mandatory security standards apply to them, including rules banning universal default passwords on in-scope consumer devices manufactured after a specified threshold. It also highlights action by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission over misleading sustainability claims, noting that penalties in greenwashing cases involving Mercer Superannuation and Vanguard Investments fell on the companies involved, and it notes that organisations covered by the Privacy Act that use automated decision-making in certain ways will need to disclose that use in their privacy policies.

Trent Brown, Chief Executive Officer of Knightcorp, said the issue for companies is whether insurance arrangements still reflect the pace of change inside technology businesses, and he said the question is no longer simply whether a company is insured but whether its risk and insurance arrangements still reflect the business it has become. Brown said that uncertainty is most likely to surface in policy interpretation and claims handling, particularly once an incident has already occurred. Justin Geldart, Account Director at Knightcorp, said that where a policy is silent on AI the outcome is uncertain and coverage can be disputed, and he encouraged technology leaders to ask how their cover treats AI they build versus AI they buy because the answer can differ. Jessica Tanner, Technology Account Director at Knightcorp, said claims tend to be tested on what was declared and how the policy defines it, and that for a technology business the practical question is whether the wording and the application reflect the platforms the business actually relies on.

The report also refers to a Federal Court development in the Medibank matter, where Deloitte reports prepared after the cyber incident were found not to be protected by legal professional privilege, underlining the importance of how post-incident reviews are commissioned. It includes several tools intended to help organisations assess these questions, including a matrix of exposures, a broker checklist for AI risk, examples of where claims uncertainty can begin, and an 11-question insurance readiness checklist. It also features a client endorsement from Spriggy Co-Founder Alex Badran, who said that before working with Knightcorp it felt like the company was trying to piece together off-the-shelf solutions from different providers and that Knightcorp spent the time to understand its unique needs and built insurance solutions to fit its business.

Articles.Title: Knightcorp warns tech leaders over AI & cloud gaps - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: Knightcorp warns tech leaders over AI & cloud gaps

stories.Headline: Vection wins Italian business award in Melbourne for its Algho sign language AI system
stories.Summary:
Vection Technologies won an Innovation Award at the Italian Business Awards 2026 in Melbourne for its Algho Sign Language system, with UNOX presenting the award at the annual event hosted by the Italian Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Australia for Victoria and Tasmania. The company said the recognition highlights a product designed to let deaf people hold live conversations in sign language with an AI agent, supporting two-way conversations in International and Italian Sign Language. The system reads hand gestures, posture and facial expressions, then responds by signing in real time rather than using pre-recorded video. According to Vection, the sign-recognition tools, generation models and 3D agents used in the system were developed internally and integrated into its broader Algho conversational AI platform.

The sign language system is already operating in several Italian transport hubs, including Roma Termini and Milano Centrale railway stations and Cagliari airport. At Milan Bergamo Airport, Vection said its accessibility system, developed with Sorint.tek, serves as the main self-service terminal for passengers with disabilities, and it also serves wheelchair users and blind passengers. Based on unaudited airport data cited by Vection, 97% of passengers with disabilities can use the system independently, compared with 38% on a standard kiosk. The product was developed with ENS, Italy's national association for deaf people, and the National Research Council of Italy, and Vection also said it is developing real-time human interpreter support as an additional feature.

The award comes as the business expands in Australia following its acquisition of Digital Experience Labs, which Vection described as an applied AI, process automation and decisioning services business. Vection said Algho Sign Language is one application of its broader Algho AI platform, which allows organisations to build and deploy AI agents without coding and is used for customer engagement, internal knowledge management, business process automation and decision support. Earlier this year, Vection announced about AUD $4 million in new Algho AI contracts across 10 industry sectors in Italy, including rail transport, healthcare, water utilities, hospitality and education, and it said those contracts were close to the AUD $4.6 million in AI contracts it secured in the whole first half of FY26. In a separate agreement, the company announced a three-year framework deal with Swiss technology company URBANnext to commercialise Algho across European smart cities, public infrastructure and urban services, including a minimum annual purchase commitment of AUD $2.5 million and a minimum aggregate contract value of AUD $7.5 million over the initial term.

Vection linked the latest award to its work on practical uses for AI in public-facing services, and it has positioned Algho as a platform for use across multiple sectors as well as in accessibility settings. Luis Nejo, Chief Executive Officer APAC at Vection Technologies, said the company was proud to receive the recognition from the Italian business community in Australia and that Algho Sign Language shows what inclusive AI can do outside the lab, with deaf passengers in some of Italy's busiest stations and airports now able to ask for help in their own language in real time.

Articles.Title: Vection wins award for sign-language AI in Melbourne - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: MathWorks expands TÜV SÜD certification to cover AI tool guidance for functional safety workflows
stories.Summary:
MathWorks has expanded TÜV SÜD certification for MATLAB, Simulink, Stateflow and System Composer to include generic AI tool classification guidance under ISO 26262, the automotive functional safety standard governing electrical and electronic systems in vehicles, according to an announcement reported on 17 November 2026. The certification applies to selected AI-assisted engineering workflows in functional safety applications and covers products included with the company's IEC Certification Kit. It focuses on Model-Based Design workflows that use the Simulink Agentic Toolkit for model development, model review and test-case generation. MathWorks said it is the first tool vendor to provide this type of guidance for selected AI-assisted workflows in functional safety, based on specific use cases evaluated by TÜV SÜD.

The guidance is intended to show how AI-assisted workflows can be introduced into safety-critical development in a controlled, auditable way, with scope covering work on Simulink models, model reviews and the generation of test cases tied to engineering processes. MathWorks said its approach links agentic AI systems directly to Model-Based Design workflows rather than limiting their use to text prompts, and the Simulink Agentic Toolkit lets AI agents interpret model structure, create and modify designs, run simulations, generate tests and connect requirements to models. The toolkit combines Simulink-specific tools with skills developed by the company's engineers and domain specialists for tasks including model development, algorithm specification, plant modelling, testing, validation and requirements generation, while engineers remain responsible for validating outputs produced with AI assistance. The Polyspace Agentic Toolkit extends AI-assisted workflows into software analysis and verification, including code robustness analysis, coding-standard compliance and defect detection, and the underlying framework is built on Model Context Protocol, which supports AI agent platforms including GitHub Copilot, Codex, Gemini CLI and Claude Code.

Michael Carone, Principal Product Marketing Manager for the Simulink Platform at MathWorks, said engineering teams are looking for ways to benefit from agentic AI without sacrificing the rigour that system development demands. He said that by connecting AI agents to Simulink models, simulations and testing workflows, MathWorks is helping engineers apply agentic AI within established engineering processes while preserving the accountability required for complex engineered systems. The move comes as engineering teams assess how AI can be used in sectors where traceability, validation and review are mandatory, and safety-related industries such as automotive typically require documented processes showing how designs were produced, checked and approved. MathWorks, founded in 1984 and headquartered in Natick, Massachusetts, employs more than 6,500 people across 34 offices worldwide.

Articles.Title: MathWorks expands TÜV SÜD certification for AI workflows - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: MathWorks expands TÜV SÜD certification for AI workflows

stories.Headline: Plaud urges Australian employers to put privacy and consent at the centre of workplace AI use
stories.Summary:
Plaud, an AI device and software company, used comments from Megumi Yoshinaga, its Head of APAC and MEA Growth, to urge Australian employers to make privacy and consent central to workplace AI use as AI assistants become more common in meetings and office work, according to an IT Brief Australia article published on 17 November 2026. Yoshinaga said organisations should focus not only on what AI tools can do but also on what information they capture, where it is stored, who can access it and whether it can be deleted. The comments focus on AI note-taking and transcription tools, whose conversations can include customer details, personal data, intellectual property, commercial discussions and confidential plans, which such tools can reproduce quickly and at scale. A recurring concern is the use of personal AI accounts for work conversations, which Yoshinaga said can leave transcripts and company knowledge spread across personal accounts or cloud folders with uneven access controls.

Plaud argues that workplace AI discussions in Australia are entering a new phase in which trust matters as much as functionality, since early adoption focused on speed and convenience such as generating content, summarising meetings and automating tasks. Yoshinaga said that as different AI tools offer similar outputs, organisations are likely to look beyond product features, so privacy, security and user control will play a larger role in procurement and deployment decisions. On consent, she said employees and meeting participants should not be left guessing whether a conversation is being recorded or transcribed, and that employers should build consent into normal workflows so participants understand what is captured, why, who may access it and what happens afterwards. On ownership, she said organisations should be able to identify where information created by AI assistants resides and who has authority to remove it, arguing that transcripts become company records as soon as they are produced and may carry obligations around access, retention, security and deletion, a problem made more complex because the person who starts a recording is not necessarily the only person whose information is captured.

Yoshinaga said technology providers also have a responsibility to make privacy choices understandable, with settings not hidden behind technical complexity so users can make informed choices without specialist knowledge. Plaud said its approach includes a default policy under which user content is not used to train its own or third-party AI models unless a user has given explicit, informed consent in advance, and that user data is encrypted and stored on regional cloud infrastructure based on the user's location. For employers considering AI note-taking tools, Yoshinaga said they should examine what information is captured, where it is processed and stored, whether it is used to train models, how long it is retained and how much control users or organisations have over deletion, and she pointed to centrally managed workspaces as one way to gain clearer oversight of users, devices, subscriptions and collaboration. She said that when every product can summarise a meeting, a key question is whether you would trust it in the room.

Articles.Title: Plaud urges Australian employers to tighten AI privacy - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: Plaud urges Australian employers to tighten AI privacy

stories.Headline: EY survey finds tax teams keen on AI, but data lags
stories.Summary:
EY has published its 2026 Tax and Finance Operations Survey, which found that interest in AI agents in tax functions has risen sharply, according to IT Brief Australia. The survey gathered responses from 1,600 Chief Financial Officers and senior finance and tax leaders across 30 jurisdictions and 22 industries. The findings show a gap between expectations for AI and the ability of tax and finance teams to put those plans into practice. While 77% of respondents said they expect AI agents to benefit the tax function, up from 21% a year earlier, 71% said they remain at a completely nascent or exploratory stage of maturity.

Data issues emerged as the main obstacle, with 64% of tax and finance leaders identifying insufficient AI-ready data as the biggest barrier to advancing AI initiatives. Only 16% considered their tax function highly effective at accessing, organising, using and reusing data, and among respondents who said their function is not effective with data, 61% pointed to data silos and 52% cited poor data quality. A further 43% said the inability to execute a sustainable data, AI and technology strategy was the biggest challenge to delivering their function's purpose. The survey also found that 83% said building a workforce in which humans work alongside AI agents is important, while 81% said hiring professionals with AI-related skills is a priority, and 60% ranked strategic thinking and problem-solving among the five most critical skills for future tax professionals.

Marna Ricker, Global Vice Chair-Tax at EY, said many organizations have already invested in AI and the challenge is transforming their data, governance and talent capabilities to ensure they get return on their AI investments. She said ambition alone will not be enough as AI becomes embedded in business decision-making, and that tax leaders have an opportunity to use trusted data, knowledge, AI and human judgment to unlock capital. Stuart Lang, Global Tax and Finance Operate Leader at EY, said the future tax function won't separate compliance from insight, and that every filing and reconciliation generates trusted data and knowledge that can become a source of tax intelligence for the business. He said realizing that potential will require leaders to make deliberate choices about workforce and talent priorities, investing not only in technology but in people skills and culture.

Beyond AI adoption, the survey found that 79% of organisations are adapting operations in response to geopolitical developments, and nearly two-thirds, or 64%, are not fully prepared for real-time tax demands as tax administration becomes more digital and immediate. Among respondents already using co-sourcing, 86% said it gave them a greater ability to focus on higher-value activities, 78% reported improved tax risk management, and 77% said it helped them navigate legislative and regulatory change more successfully. With most respondents still in the early stages of AI-agent maturity, the survey points to a market in which ambition is running ahead of execution.

Articles.Title: EY survey finds tax teams keen on AI, but data lags - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Nearly 60% of legal leaders say AI adoption outpaces governance, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey published by Diligent Institute and Wilson Sonsini on 16 November 2026 found that nearly 60% of senior legal leaders believe AI adoption is moving faster than governance in their organisations, and it put average board readiness to oversee AI risk at 2.9 out of 5. The Q4 General Counsel Risk Index draws on responses from about 200 General Counsel, Chief Legal Officers and other senior legal executives. It found that 41% of respondents have yet to reach a basic AI governance framework, including 14% with no formal approach and 27% still developing policies and guidelines. About 70% of respondents represented organisations based in North America, while 51% came from private companies and 28% from publicly held companies.

Respondents ranked regulatory change as the leading risk facing their organisations, cited by 55%, with AI-related risk at 49% and cyber threats at 47%. Some 59% of legal leaders said their organisation faced a high level of risk, while workforce, culture and talent issues were cited by 34%, geopolitical conflict by 26% and supply-chain disruption by 24%. Around 67% of respondents said legal reviews vendors and assesses privacy, data, confidentiality and intellectual property issues tied to AI systems, but only 23% said their legal teams regularly brief the board or senior leadership on AI-related risks. The survey also tracked shifts from the previous quarter, with regulatory change rising from 48% to 55%, AI-related risk from 39% to 49% and cyber threats from 39% to 47%, while concern about geopolitical conflict fell from 52% to 26%.

Dottie Schindlinger, Executive Director of Diligent Institute, said nearly six in 10 legal leaders report that AI adoption is outpacing governance and that the gap is a risk in itself, because as AI spreads it becomes harder to keep clear visibility into how it is used, what data it touches and who is accountable. She said boards do not need every director to be an AI expert, but they do need enough fluency to challenge assumptions and ensure oversight keeps pace with adoption. Sachin Kohli, Partner at Wilson Sonsini, said that as risks like AI and cybersecurity evolve at breakneck speed, boards need a clear understanding of their potential legal, regulatory and disclosure implications and of how management is responding. He said legal leaders have a critical role in connecting these risks across the enterprise, working alongside risk, compliance and security to translate complex challenges into actionable insights and give boards visibility to anticipate emerging risks.

The research adds to a broader debate over whether companies are putting enough controls around fast-moving AI deployments, and for Australian businesses it comes as regulators including ASIC and APRA continue to press boards for stronger accountability and better visibility over operational risks. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: AI adoption outpaces governance, legal leaders warn - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: AI adoption outpaces governance, legal leaders warn

stories.Headline: Miro finds AI boosts individual productivity but not team collaboration
stories.Summary:
Miro released research on 17 November 2026 examining how artificial intelligence is affecting productivity and team performance in Australia and New Zealand, and the study found a clear gap between gains in individual productivity and broader organisational results. The survey covered more than 9,500 leaders and workers globally, including 1,031 respondents in Australia and New Zealand. It found that 83 per cent of workers said AI had improved their individual productivity at work, while 72 per cent said it had increased output speed. That uplift was far less clear in other areas, with only 59 per cent of respondents in Australia and New Zealand saying AI had improved output quality.

A majority of respondents said AI had not improved decision-making or collaboration between colleagues and teams, and one in four said it had not improved organisation-wide productivity. Another 23 per cent said AI had not delivered better business outcomes such as revenue growth, cost reduction or operational efficiency. The survey found that 69 per cent of respondents said most AI-assisted work happens in private sessions rather than shared spaces, and half of enterprises reported difficulty with information silos that limit access to shared context across systems. Another 37 per cent of leaders said visibility into how AI is being used was poor or non-existent, while 63 per cent reported compliance and security concerns in the absence of unified governance.

Pete Bradd, Chief Evangelist at Miro, said individuals are getting more capable while the connections that make a team smart are getting thinner, and he pointed to research linking team intelligence to social perceptiveness and equal turn taking more than to the intelligence of individual members. He said the data points to the wrong direction, citing that 44 per cent say AI has made their culture less collaborative and 31 per cent feel disconnected from colleagues because of increased AI use. Dave Ross, Product Evangelist Leader at Miro, said customers report gains in AI-driven productivity at the individual level but many find scaling these gains across the organisation a challenge. He said faster execution is a benefit, but decision-making and decision quality is the real bottleneck, and the research points to a growing need for a place where AI and people can collaborate on critical decisions instead of in fragmented individual single-player tools.

The survey also found that nearly half of respondents said context switching had increased over the past year, while 59 per cent said they faced a higher volume of AI-generated output to review. Just over half, or 53 per cent, said they were seeing more low-quality AI-driven output that requires extra human review and rework, and more than one in 10 said decision-making, creativity, collaboration and work-life balance had worsened because of increased AI use. On workplace culture and role design, 65 per cent of workers worried role boundaries would blur, 49 per cent feared related roles would merge, 48 per cent were concerned about a decline in collaboration culture, and 22 per cent said work felt lonely because of increased AI use. Miro said its survey found that two-thirds of enterprise decision-makers planned to implement what it described as an AI workhub within 12 months, and the wider dataset covered respondents in product development, IT, operations and other functions across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

stories.Headline: Google adds TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx to its eighth-generation AI chip line-up
stories.Summary:
Google expanded its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit line-up with two new systems, TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, bringing its TPU releases this year to four systems, according to an announcement reported on 18 November 2026. TPU 8tx is aimed at secure and confidential inference, while TPU 8i Max is designed for workloads that need large context windows and greater compute density within the same rack footprint. Google said the launch reflects broader demand from customers using AI for model training, inference and autonomous agents. It added that TPUs are now used by nearly 100 customers, including frontier laboratories, trading firms, retailers and universities.

TPU 8tx is built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and is paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, and Google said it is intended for regulated enterprises and government users that want to run models and agents alongside sensitive data. According to Google, TPU 8tx protects data and model weights while they are in use through hardware-level confidential computing, and it uses the same Boardfly network introduced for lower-latency reasoning workloads, delivering up to half the latency of TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. TPU 8i Max combines two low-latency TPU 8i chips into a single package, doubling compute, SRAM and high-bandwidth memory bandwidth compared with TPU 8i, according to the company. Google said the design fits twice the silicon into the existing rack footprint, allowing data centres to deploy more compute per square foot and per watt.

The launch expands Google's eighth-generation TPU family to four products: TPU 8t for large-scale training, TPU 8i for lower-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing and TPU 8i Max for high-context workloads. Google said this system-level approach allows it to respond more quickly to changing customer requirements than waiting for a full new chip generation, and that rather than redesigning silicon each time, it modifies the surrounding compute, networking, storage and packaging to create more specialised systems. Google said businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models' massive context windows as computing moves from human to agent scale, and that some highly regulated customers are asking for specialised encryption capabilities for unique workloads.

Alongside the hardware additions, Google outlined software efforts including native PyTorch code and Hugging Face models on TPUs through the open-source TorchTPU project, TPU back ends for open-source inference engines including vLLM and SGLang, and a TPU agent suite in preview. Google said its open-source XLA Serving Engine allows customers to train models in Python and serve them in a C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs and CPUs, while Agent Compute Engine suspends and resumes idle agent sessions to reduce infrastructure costs. Google said TPU Sync can reduce key-value transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90%, and that GKE dynamic slicing now lets users reconfigure TPU topologies on demand, cutting job start-up times by up to five times and improving fault recovery by up to 4.5 times. Google also said it has been using AI tools from Google DeepMind in its chip design process, including AlphaChip reinforcement learning systems and Gemini-based design tools, which it said have helped cut parts of chip layout work from weeks to hours.

stories.Headline: OpenSSF CTO Robinson explains Scorecard, SLSA and AI security limits
stories.Summary:
Christopher Robinson, the chief technology officer of the Open Source Security Foundation and chief security architect of the Linux Foundation, spoke on 16 November 2026 about software supply chain security at a time of rising incidents. He explained how tools such as Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework and Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts, known as SLSA, help harden software and secure infrastructure. The discussion also covered global cybersecurity regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act and the role of AI in software engineering. OpenSSF provides guidance, best practices, tooling and training to upstream open-source developers and maintainers.

Scorecard evaluates a project's security posture and signals to consumers whether it follows security best practices, while the Security Baseline, an evolution of Scorecard, lists 41 recommended security controls and practices. The baseline curates actions from regulations such as the EU CRA and frameworks such as the NIST Secure Software Development Framework, and Robinson noted that non-profit open-source maintainers are generally exempt from the CRA while commercial consumers must comply. SLSA addresses provenance, pedigree and integrity by securing development infrastructure, and it defines progressive maturity levels for hardening IDEs, developer workstations, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines and distribution systems. OpenSSF is also deploying an Open Source Software Cyber Reasoning System, a modular harness where developers plug in AI models and apply specific security skills and domain context.

Robinson cautioned that AI makes it easy to bypass foundational security controls when guardrails are not explicitly built in, and he described AI as a helpful assistant that accelerates workflows rather than a replacement for human engineering judgment. He said countries including the UK, India, Japan and Australia are watching the EU CRA's rollout, and he expects other regions to introduce CRA-aligned legislation while hoping for harmonized standards that avoid fragmented compliance burdens. He added that open-source software gives organizations the most reliable foundation for maintaining autonomy and avoiding vendor lock-in. He concluded that open-source projects need clear, explicit contribution guidelines that define their stance on AI tools.

stories.Headline: Secure Code Warrior finds budget AI models can produce safer code than premium versions
stories.Summary:
Secure Code Warrior released findings from its SCW AI Trust Index on November 18, 2026, regarding the security of AI-generated code. The research tested more than 30 AI models from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Alibaba, and Mistral to evaluate their safety. This study used AI systems to build over 15,000 applications and 41.3 million lines of code across 11 programming languages. The results showed a 15-fold gap between the best and worst performers, with vulnerabilities ranging from 0.24 to 3.66 per 1,000 lines of code.

The findings indicate that curated security rule sets can reduce measured risk by as much as 70 percent. While GPT-6-Astra-High led or tied for first in four frameworks, fifteen different models ranked first in at least one of the 11 frameworks. Budget models sometimes outperformed premium ones, such as GPT 6 Luna which cost USD $0.10 a run and had a risk score of 19.4. In contrast, Claude Opus 5.5 cost USD $8.17 a run and recorded a higher mean risk score of 43.6.

Pieter Danhieux, the Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Secure Code Warrior, stated that assumptions about newer or more expensive models are not always correct. He explained that models do not use secure coding by default, meaning the prompts and rules provided determine the safety of the output. Danhieux emphasized that security leaders need an evidence-based view of inherited risks because model behavior can shift with every new release. He argued that this highlights the critical need for strong governance regarding how AI coding models are utilized.

These results arrive as software teams rely more on large language models for their daily coding work. External survey data suggests that AI will likely account for 65 percent of committed code by 2027. This trend increases the pressure on security teams to understand the specific risks tied to different models and prompting strategies. The company noted that human-only commits typically introduce fewer vulnerabilities, citing Stanford University research that found roughly 0.08 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines.

stories.Headline: Superintendent Ben Mainka wants AI to enhance student thinking with guardrails in place
stories.Summary:
Ben Mainka, the superintendent of the Novi school district in Michigan, spoke with The Metro about how artificial intelligence should affect learning and thinking, especially for young people, in a conversation broadcast in November 2026. He said he wants AI to enhance student thinking and to assist teachers with administrative tasks, but only so long as guardrails are in place. The same program also featured Daniel Cook, an English professor at Saginaw Valley State University, who in a recent debate argued that college students should have a slower, less digital learning experience. The Metro described the segment as a conversation with Robyn Vincent, and it directed listeners to the full discussion through the media player on the page.

The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond those already mentioned, and they do not set out any specific policy, rule or change that follows from the professor's position. What the professor's argument requires is only described in general terms, as a slower and less digital learning experience for college students, without any detail on how that would work in practice. The superintendent's position is likewise general, favoring AI that enhances student thinking and helps teachers with administrative work while guardrails are in place. The articles do not say what those guardrails would be, who would set them, or when any of this might happen.

Responsibility for the discussion rests with the two educators who made the arguments, Mainka for the school district and Cook for the university, and the articles attribute the views to them directly. Mainka is quoted as wanting AI to enhance student thinking and to assist teachers with administrative tasks so long as guardrails are in place, and Cook is described as arguing in a recent debate that college students should have a slower, less digital learning experience. The articles do not record any further remarks from either of them beyond those positions. No other person is named as responsible for any decision or proposal in the coverage.

The context the articles provide is limited to the setting of the discussion, which was a segment on The Metro, a program on WDET 101.9 FM that airs weekdays from 10 a.m. to noon ET and is available on demand. The program framed the conversation around how AI powers smartphones, appears across social media and answers Google searches, and asked how the technology should affect learning and thinking, especially for young people. The articles do not say what happens next, whether any policy will follow, or when the debate or any related decision will continue. The piece was produced by Sam Corey, a producer for 101.9 WDET.
