stories.Headline: InfoQ opens registration for six five-week online cohort workshops starting in January 2027
stories.Summary:
InfoQ opened registration on November 17, 2026, for six online cohort workshops that start between January 9 and January 22, 2027, the article by Artenisa Chatziou states. The six cohorts cover AI Engineering, Software Architecture, and High-Performing Teams, and each program runs five weeks. The workshops bring senior engineers, architects, and engineering leaders together to work through technical and organizational decisions with experienced practitioners. Participants apply frameworks from QCon and InfoQ to decisions from their own work and compare approaches with practitioners from other organizations. Working across different organizational contexts helps expose trade-offs and assumptions that may not emerge from an internal discussion alone, the article says.

Each cohort combines four hours of live facilitated sessions per week, independent application work, and a program-specific capstone, and participation costs USD 1,470 per person. The AI Engineering Program covers RAG architectures, agent design, platforms, and evaluation, and three January cohorts are planned. Hien Luu, an AI/ML leader and author of MLOps with Ray, starts January 9, with Saturday sessions at 09:00 PST. Adi Polak, Director of Developer Experience Engineering at Confluent, starts January 21, with Thursday sessions at 08:00 PST. Lan Chu, a principal engineer at Rabobank and author of Post-training LLMs, starts January 22, with Friday sessions at 14:00 CET, and her QCon London 2026 presentation examined a production RAG system built on more than 10,000 documents and used by more than 300 people.

The InfoQ Architect Program covers distributed systems, decentralized decisions, platform engineering, and AI architecture, and its capstone involves co-authoring a technical article examining AI's role in software architecture or platform engineering. Selected articles may be published on InfoQ. Both architecture cohorts start January 22 and are facilitated by Luca Mezzalira, an independent software architect and author of Building Micro-Frontends. Friday sessions are offered at 09:30 GMT and 10:00 EST. The High-Performing Teams Program examines team structure, ownership, delivery flow, AI responsibilities, and engineering metrics as one operating model, and its January 12 cohort is facilitated by Olimpiu Pop, an InfoQ Podcast co-host with experience in solutions architecture, engineering management, and CTO roles, with sessions on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 16:00 to 18:00 CET.

The article says faster coding does not necessarily improve delivery when reviews, approvals, or infrastructure dependencies become the constraint, and that AI agents change how responsibilities are divided and which work requires human judgment. Participants in the teams program evaluate constraints in their own team environments, compare approaches with peers, and develop a proposed target operating model covering responsibilities, workflow, and measurement. The live online workshops focus on discussion and application rather than recorded lectures, and participants work with an experienced facilitator and a small cross-company peer group. Sessions are not recorded, allowing participants to discuss organizational constraints more openly. Certification requires attendance, active participation, and successful completion of the program capstone.

The article lists related events, including QCon San Francisco from November 16 to 20, 2026, with early bird registration ending November 10, and QCon AI New York on December 15 and 16, 2026, also with early bird ending November 10. It lists QCon London from April 13 to 16, 2027, across 15 engineering tracks, with early bird ending November 10, and QCon AI Boston on July 8 and 9, 2027, with registration open. It also lists a High-Performing Teams Certification cohort on November 17, 2026, an AI Engineering Certification cohort on January 9, 2027, for the Americas, another on January 21, 2027, for the Americas, an AI Engineering Certification cohort on January 22, 2027, for EMEA, and an Architect Certification cohort on January 22, 2027. The article names InfoQ, C4Media Inc., and the author Artenisa Chatziou, and states that InfoQ.com and all content are copyright © 2006-2026 C4Media Inc.

The article says the programs go beyond studying technical material, with participants returning to discuss what they tried and learned. It says participants in the architect program apply the material to architecture decisions they currently own, compare trade-offs with peers, and practice communicating their reasoning to stakeholders. It says participants in the AI Engineering Program work through technical approaches and failure modes, applying them to AI systems or proposals from their own work. It says production AI involves decisions beyond model selection, including how context is retrieved and maintained, how much autonomy agents should have, and how reliability, latency, and inference costs are managed. It says architecture choices are shaped by system requirements, team boundaries, platform ownership, and organizational constraints.

Full schedules, syllabi, and registration details are available on the InfoQ Online Certification Programs website, the article states. The article gives no further information on the six January cohorts, on the facilitators beyond their stated roles, or on the capstones beyond what it describes. It does not say how many participants each cohort will take or where the live sessions will be held beyond being online. It does not say what happens to the co-authored articles that are not selected for publication on InfoQ. It does not give the dates of the five-week programs beyond their start dates.

stories.Headline: Indian legal AI buyers now test accuracy, integration and adoption over demos, Legora's Heather Paterson says
stories.Summary:
Competition is intensifying in India's legal technology market, where law firms and corporate legal departments are increasingly looking beyond product presentations, ETLegalWorld reported on Nov 15, 2026. Buyers now assess whether artificial intelligence tools deliver measurable improvements in legal workflows, the article said. Most legal AI platforms can perform routine tasks such as drafting, document review and legal research. The differentiating factors are increasingly the accuracy of outputs, integration with existing systems, data governance and sustained adoption. The article was published by Kumar Aditya.

Heather Paterson, VP of Legora APJ, said providers would be judged by their ability to drive adoption rather than by being early entrants. She said approximately two-thirds of Legora's Asia-Pacific team comprised lawyers or consultants working with clients on change management, including through live matters as legal engineers and engagement managers. She pointed to one large Indian corporation that has recorded regular usage among 98% of its legal team. Legora has made five acquisitions this year, adding capabilities including regulatory horizon scanning and litigation fact intelligence. Its exclusive partnership with Manupatra brings Indian case law, statutes and commentary into the platform.

Paterson advised firms and in-house teams to look past the demo and ask what happens after the contract is signed. She said the winners won't be whoever got there first, but whoever drives real adoption. She argued lawyers do not want separate applications for research, review, translation and drafting, saying every extra login slows adoption. She said Legora was investing in an agentic operating system that could work across an entire legal matter. She added that a single platform could help manage costs by routing individual tasks to the models best suited to them.

Probir Roy Chowdhury, Partner at JSA, said law firms were evaluating AI tools through trial groups across practice areas, with lawyers giving feedback on where the tools add value. He said the more meaningful assessment comes when lawyers work against tight deadlines, such as reviewing a large volume of documents. He said the lawyer will still review and validate the output. He said a useful way of evaluating a tool is to treat it much like a junior associate. Saloni Agara Dwarakanath, AVP and Head of Legal, India, at Apex Group, said autonomous AI agents require organisations to rethink governance and accountability.

Dwarakanath identified three key areas: embedding governance into AI adoption, retaining organisational accountability for AI-driven decisions, and strengthening controls around data and third-party risks. She said organisations should establish AI governance frameworks involving Legal, IT, Information Security, Compliance and business teams, defining permitted use cases, risk thresholds, approval mechanisms and clear ownership. She said decisions with material legal, financial, regulatory or employee implications must retain human oversight, escalation mechanisms and the ability to intervene or override outcomes. She said vendor assessments should cover data ownership, confidentiality, intellectual property rights, model training, cybersecurity, data retention and audit rights. She said ownership of the consequences must remain human.

Sooraj Sharma, Co-founder and Partner at Clavius Legal, said firms should measure time saved against the effort required to verify and correct outputs. He said a draft that takes ten minutes to generate and three hours to verify has saved very little. He suggested firms test tools against completed matters, checking whether a tool identified every change-of-control clause in a data room and traced regulatory obligations to the rule currently in force. He flagged the risk of tool fatigue when lawyers navigate multiple platforms with overlapping capabilities and separate verification requirements. Priti Suri, Founder and Managing Partner at PSA, said Indian lawyers were experiencing fatigue with the growing number of similar-looking tools and the difficulty of integrating them into existing systems.

Suri said firms were evaluating platforms on three India-specific considerations: understanding of Indian statutes and regulators, handling of client data under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, and ability to connect with systems already used by organisations. She said what matters now is integration depth, configurability and cost. The article said the legal AI market is entering a more demanding phase. It said the assessment is no longer limited to how quickly a tool can generate a draft or review documents. It said the question is whether a tool can deliver reliable outputs, integrate with existing workflows and operate within clear governance and accountability frameworks.

stories.Headline: Google SRE managers Betsy Beyer and David Huska publish a rewritten SRE book for AI and cloud systems
stories.Summary:
Google announced a completely rewritten second edition of Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems on November 17, 2026, ten years after the original book was first published. The book was announced by Google's SRE programme manager Betsy Beyer and software engineer David Huska. The new edition updates thinking on site reliability engineering to encompass modern cloud architectures, platform engineering and AI workloads. It keeps the original emphasis on applying good software engineering techniques to operations work. The authors position the edition as a response to a production environment that has changed substantially since 2016, when the first edition appeared.

The authors argue that the central problem is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure but maintaining reliability as systems become more distributed, interdependent and continuously changing. The revised guidance describes user-centred, multi-tiered SLOs, dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement, where teams once relied on basic availability metrics and manually applied error-budget policies. The book replaces static dashboards, basic logs and manual alert triage with OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing and automated anomaly correlation. It describes a movement from custom scripts addressing isolated tasks towards declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms and self-healing systems. Google contrasts scheduled game days and synthetic load tests with continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification, and says manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment and optimisation for GPU and TPU clusters.

Beyer and Huska wrote that modern production environments operate under constant change, with more complex system boundaries, deep dependencies and failure modes more complex and damaging than ever before. They wrote that rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification. Google argues that the underlying culture has not changed, and the authors restate the importance of reliability-focused culture and expand the book's coverage of the human aspects of systems engineering. The book covers the reliability of large GPU and TPU clusters, network topologies, non-deterministic model outputs, latency behaviour and the pipelines used for training, fine-tuning and data processing.

The post welcomes generative AI support for incident triage and postmortem writing, natural-language queries over telemetry, and predictive models that identify resource bottlenecks before they cause an outage. The examples in the announcement mostly place AI in a supporting role, gathering and organising evidence for engineers rather than claiming that AI can replace operational judgement. InfoQ reported in October 2026 that Datadog had released Scout, a specialist model intended to investigate production problems inside its Bits AI SRE product, and other vendors exploring similar territory include Honeycomb's Canvas Agent, Splunk AI SRE and New Relic's SRE Agent. InfoQ also reported in February 2026 on Google Cloud SREs using the Gemini CLI during real outages, using AI to help engineers work through incidents rather than as an autonomous replacement for on-call staff. Google describes a move beyond dedicated SRE teams attached to particular applications towards hybrid models, platform-engineering integration and reliability champions embedded in product teams, because many organisations cannot staff a central SRE team for every service.

The original SRE book became influential because it gave a public account of how Google operated large-scale services, describing practices such as service level objectives, error budgets, toil reduction, incident management and postmortems. InfoQ's 2016 review noted that the book presented SRE as the application of software engineering to an operations function, with engineers expected to automate repetitive operational work rather than simply respond to it. The second edition does not present SRE as a fixed set of practices but describes how those practices have changed as organisations moved from early cloud migration and monolithic applications towards microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless systems and internal developer platforms. David Blank-Edelman made a related point in a presentation, You Are Asking the Wrong Questions (about Reliability and SRE), delivered at InfoQ Dev Summit Boston in 2025, arguing that reliability work should start from the customer's perspective rather than the component's perspective and describing SRE as fundamentally collaborative. He also challenged the conventional focus on a single root cause, favouring an examination of the contributing factors behind a failure.

The second edition is available in physical format through Google Books and in digital format from O'Reilly. For teams already practising SRE, its value is likely to lie less in introducing familiar concepts than in showing how those concepts have been adapted for platforms, distributed systems and AI-heavy infrastructure. For organisations earlier in their reliability journey, it remains a substantial reference on how to make operations a software-engineering problem rather than a collection of manual tasks. The articles do not say when the second edition was released beyond the November 17, 2026 announcement. The articles leave open how widely organisations will adopt the revised practices.

stories.Headline: Linux Foundation finds 58% of development teams release code faster than security staff can review it
stories.Summary:
A Linux Foundation report published on November 16, 2026 found that 58% of software development teams are releasing code faster than their security staff can review it, according to DevOps.com. The report, State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026, surveyed 308 cybersecurity practitioners working in businesses and open source projects. It found that 60% of respondents said AI coding tools add external software dependencies to their applications, while just 16% reported fewer dependencies. Development teams review only 53% of indirect dependencies, leaving much of their software infrastructure without adequate scrutiny.

Among experienced AI cybersecurity professionals, 93% expressed concern about software supply chain attacks, 90% about prompt injection attacks and 87% about the maintenance demands of frequent software updates. Some 76% of experienced practitioners believe AI makes it easier for attackers to combine multiple vulnerabilities into more sophisticated exploits. Only 30% of surveyed teams have assigned specialized personnel to handle AI-related cybersecurity threats, a figure that rises to 35% among businesses but falls to 16% for open source projects. About one-third of organizations have adopted official security policies addressing AI, while 35% rely on informal guidelines, and while 76% identify approved AI tools, only 57% require human review of AI-generated code and just 36% include provisions for automated security scanning.

Among teams with dedicated AI security personnel, 43% investigate and resolve most new security alerts immediately, compared with 23% among teams without dedicated AI security resources. Practitioners credited AI-assisted security tools with identifying approximately 30% of the vulnerabilities they discovered during the previous year, and 69% of practitioners using these tools reported meaningful improvements in cybersecurity. Those tools helped practitioners complete security-related development tasks 17% faster on average, but inaccurate vulnerability alerts added an estimated 30% to workloads. Some 82% of respondents agreed that excessive dependence on AI tools weakens developers' fundamental security skills.

The Linux Foundation recommends stronger controls over third-party software, formal AI security policies, continued developer training and greater use of automated security testing.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO following a GPU cloud scandal
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and director of Nvidia on Thursday, November 14, 2026. This sudden departure followed reporting that focused on the business of GPU clouds. The scandal involves the Nvidia Cloud Partners programme and its relationship with specific chip providers. Huang's resignation was effective immediately upon the announcement by the company. The reporting suggests that his leadership style and specific associations led to this outcome.

The changes include the CFO becoming interim CEO while the board names its first chair. The board is now searching for a permanent replacement among internal and external candidates. The scandal involves Alice Huang, a former managing director of Megaspeed in Singapore. Megaspeed is a GPU cloud and an Nvidia Cloud Partner that may have exported chips to China. These events relate to a private dinner in Taipei seen by Reuters in May 2025.

Nvidia stated that Jensen Huang resigned from his three primary leadership roles effective immediately. The company did not provide further details beyond the resignation and the interim leadership plan. The board is now responsible for finding a permanent chief executive to lead the firm. They are currently reviewing candidates from both inside and outside the organization. The CFO will manage operations until a permanent successor is officially named.

Federal investigators and US intelligence officials expressed concerns regarding Alice Huang and her business dealings. Officials worried that she might have been acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence services. Indian startups like Gnani are affected because they rely on GPU clouds for AI compute. These firms use clouds like Yotta, Neysa, and E2E Networks to access Nvidia chips. Reliance Jio and Tata Communications are the only Indian firms with the advanced GH200 chips.

The background involves a supply chain where TSMC in Taiwan makes most of the chips. Jensen Huang previously told staff not to consider the risk of Taiwan being cut off. He ran the company with a temper that made employees afraid to question his decisions. Indian AI firms prioritize the availability of 256 H100 chips over the cost of rental. This creates a market where access to compute is the most valuable product.

Nvidia will continue to supply chips to the three main companies leasing AI compute in India. The company will likely continue releasing software that affects how these clouds operate. The board must still decide which candidate will take over as the permanent CEO. It remains unclear how the US intelligence investigation will impact other Cloud Partners. The articles leave open whether more executives will face scrutiny over chip exports.

stories.Headline: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler
stories.Summary:
Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, and Simran Arora wrote about the Together Compiler on November 16, 2026. This new framework uses AI agents to rewrite and fuse GPU kernels during a model's forward pass. The team previously built megakernels that executed an entire forward pass within one single fused GPU kernel. They deleted those megakernels this year to move toward a more flexible optimization system. This shift allows the company to handle increasingly heterogeneous AI inference and new model architectures.

The Together Compiler beats hand-written megakernels by 28 percent on B200 hardware. It achieved 2,118 tokens per second compared to 1,649 tokens per second on Llama 3.2 1B. Using multi-kernels and agent loops on H100 hardware reached over 1100 TPS for Llama 1B. The team found that CUDA Graphs and PDL on Torch Inductor kernels recovered 98 percent of megakernel performance. This new approach is more scalable than the previous system which served only one customer.

The authors stated that AI inference is becoming more heterogeneous with new architectures released every week. They explained that achieving peak performance across different regimes requires optimization frameworks that can keep up. The researchers noted that Torch Compile's heuristics and benchmarking leave performance on the table. They argued that the space of possible optimizations is too large for guessing the right flags. Consequently, they believe the system should search for optimizations systematically instead of relying on local heuristics.

The authors found that Torch Inductor's greedy fusion algorithm misses opportunities to merge beneficial kernels. They noted that Inductor's benchmarking ignores caching behavior, making isolated benchmarks 39 to 58 percent slower. This affects models like Llama 1B, where Inductor delivers 669 TPS without the new optimizations. Mixture-of-experts architectures like GLM 5.3 are also affected by unrealistic benchmarking inputs. These discrepancies lead to faulty compiler decisions that slow down the overall inference process.

The company spent two years investigating what a next-generation system for inference optimization should look like. They previously developed specialized implementations including FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, and the original megakernels. They discovered that enabling the freezing flag improved throughput by 10 to 26 percent at large batch sizes. However, that same flag caused a 49 percent slowdown when the batch size was one. As of Q3 2026, Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags to control memory and scheduling.

The team will share their journey in three parts, starting with the failures of Torch Compile. Part two decomposes megakernel performance gains into simpler primitives to explain why they are not always ideal. Part three will cover the bitter lessons learned from crafting agent-driven optimization infrastructure. The articles leave open the specific details of the final production system's internal agent loops. They also do not detail the specific results for the 40 plus models chosen for production.

stories.Headline: India's data protection rules drive cybersecurity demand from May 2027, K7 white paper says
stories.Summary:
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules are expected to increase demand for cybersecurity professionals and managed security services, according to a white paper by K7 CyberSecurity reported by TechGig on November 16, 2026. The principal privacy, security and breach-notification obligations under the rules take effect from May 13, 2027, which is the deadline by which companies must strengthen their systems for data protection, risk monitoring and breach response. Businesses are likely to increase investments in access monitoring, data protection, incident response and security operations centres as that date approaches. The K7 white paper is titled "Turning DPDP Compliance into a Security-Led Capability" and highlights the need for organisations to establish stronger monitoring systems.

Rule 6 requires organisations to put in place safeguards covering encryption or masking, access controls, monitoring and review of access, continuity after a security compromise, specified data and log retention, and processor security provisions in contracts. Companies must also protect personal data across business applications, cloud services, devices, portals and third-party suppliers, and must keep evidence that their safeguards are actually working. The DPDP Act sets maximum penalties of ₹250 crore for failure to maintain reasonable security safeguards and ₹200 crore for failure to meet breach-intimation obligations, both subject to inquiry and the statutory process. After a personal data breach, affected individuals and the Data Protection Board must be informed without delay, and an updated detailed report must reach the Board within 72 hours of awareness unless an extension is permitted.

The report says human teams must retain control over legal classification, regulatory communication and disruptive containment decisions, while managed SOC services, including those using AI agents for bounded work, can connect security information across systems and keep records for audits and incident reporting. K7's briefing advises companies to move beyond relying only on security policies or dashboards and to demonstrate whether safeguards were actually effective. The report notes that an integrated security approach helps organisations identify weaknesses, investigate incidents and show compliance, since security controls, current state, incident investigations and retrievable evidence form one operating chain. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the May 13, 2027 start of the principal obligations.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as AI industry faces potential financial bubble burst
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, November 13, 2026, which has shaken confidence in the center of the artificial intelligence boom. This sudden leadership change occurred while the industry was already struggling with significant financial and political uncertainty. The company named CFO Colette Kress as the interim leader to manage the current vacuum. This event adds an explosive risk to a strained market that may be facing a dot-com style reckoning.

The situation requires a new approach to infrastructure spending, as providers project spending 7 trillion dollars through 2030 against expected revenues of only 3.6 trillion dollars. Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of 81 billion dollars in October, yet its IPO terms imply a valuation below 2 trillion dollars. OpenAI grew third quarter revenue by 50 percent to 10 billion dollars, though its adjusted operating losses reached 10.9 billion dollars. These numbers highlight a gap between the massive costs of expansion and the actual financial returns.

RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas stated that the departure of Huang could trigger a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble. Professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh noted that the turmoil matters if lenders lose confidence that Nvidia will back future projects. Investor Paul Kedrosky explained that the fact that the technology works is exactly what makes a financial bubble possible. MIT professor Ricardo Caballero argued that while AI will be transformative, this does not preclude the existence of a speculative bubble.

The broader context includes rising borrowing costs and a wave of election victories for candidates who are skeptical of artificial intelligence. Bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China are also mounting following the downfall of Huang. A retreat in investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a simple market correction into a much larger financial reckoning. This cycle could vaporize trillions in investor wealth even if the technology eventually succeeds in transforming the world.

Articles.Title: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.

stories.headline_source: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.

stories.Headline: Trump administration tightens AI chip loophole to block Chinese access via third countries
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration announced on Monday, November 16, 2026, that it is tightening a loophole regarding advanced artificial intelligence chips. This action targets Chinese technology firms that have bypassed United States restrictions by using third countries to access high end semiconductors. The announcement comes just days before President Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week. This move follows an international scandal involving Nvidia that led to the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang.

The new rule from the Commerce Department requires buyers of advanced semiconductors from specific nations to secure a license for any sale or transfer. This regulation specifically impacts buyers from Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand because they are viewed as having a higher than normal risk of evading sanctions. These measures are set to go into effect in 90 days to stop the use of shell companies and rented computing power. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will have wide discretion to orally inform companies about stricter export rules if he believes there is an unacceptable risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Howard Lutnick on Sunday for failing to properly oversee chip exports to China during a CNBC interview. Bessent stated that the Treasury, State, War, and USTR departments wanted to put a company called Megaspeed on the entity list for months. He noted that President Trump made it clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s to avoid giving the Chinese an advantage. The scandal involves allegations that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, spied for China while having an affair with Jensen Huang.

President Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with President Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. This first of its kind summit will focus on the reduction of nuclear weapons in addition to the issue of artificial intelligence chips. Democrats are expected to take control of Congress next year and will likely probe the administration's AI policies. Lawmakers have already asked the Commerce Department to preserve all records related to Nvidia as part of this ongoing investigation.

Articles.Title: U.S. to Clamp Down On AI Chip Loophole Ahead Of Trump Meeting With Xi

stories.Headline: Nebius reports record third quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571%
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. held its third-quarter earnings call, Tipranks reported on Sunday, November 15, 2026, and the call carried a strongly optimistic tone led by record revenue, improving profitability and intense demand for AI computing. Nebius reported record third-quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571% from a year earlier and 68% from the second quarter. Management said most of the growth came from capacity added during the past 12 months. Nebius AI Cloud generated $973.8 million in revenue, a 643% year-over-year increase, and the segment represented about 99% of group revenue. Group adjusted EBITDA reached $465.8 million, compared with a loss of $5.2 million a year earlier and $236.2 million in the second quarter.

Agreements completed in the quarter exceeded $25 million per megawatt, compared with $20 million to $25 million in the prior quarter. Nebius said it was signing multibillion-dollar AI cloud agreements in the fourth quarter, following its first contracts worth more than $1 billion announced three months earlier. Databricks, Datadog and Snowflake signed multiyear agreements with Nebius for the first time during the quarter, while Palantir also entered into a multiyear deal. More than 90% of third-quarter contract value included a prepayment, and the weighted average share of prepayments rose by about 20 percentage points from the second quarter. These payments covered more than 100% of the capital required to bring contracted capacity online, up from 50% to 60% previously.

The payback period for new capacity shortened to one year and seven months from one year and 10 months in the prior quarter. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash and equivalents, alongside a $775 million asset-backed financing facility and a $5.75 billion convertible notes offering. It also raised about $1 billion through its share program, while management cited more than $40 billion of similar committed revenue available for future asset-backed financing. The adjusted EBITDA margin rose to 47.5% from 40.6%, while the AI Cloud margin increased to 53.2% from 50%. Nebius builds its own compute infrastructure, racks and storage while developing its software platform in-house.

Management said AI-native companies still accounted for most of the more than $12 billion in contract value signed since the start of the third quarter. Token Factory accelerated in the third quarter and early fourth quarter, and management said it is on track for annual recurring revenue in the hundreds of millions. The company integrated the Eigen, Clarifai and Inferize acquisitions, and Inferize adds model-loading capabilities designed to reduce cold starts and improve GPU use for workloads with uneven demand. Most of the company’s next gigawatt of capacity is expected to come from owned sites, and Alabama, Missouri, two Finland projects and Pennsylvania were identified as important capacity locations. Token Factory has acted as a launch partner for models from Meta, Reflection, NVIDIA and other developers.

Several colocation sites, including New Jersey, are behind schedule, although management said none of the affected capacity had been canceled. Some deployments have moved into 2027, shifting part of expected 2026 revenue into the beginning of the following year. Vineland was delayed after DataOne decided to wind down temporary generation sooner than expected, and management said the site would still experience a gap and a delay of roughly two months. Nebius reduced its 2026 revenue outlook to $3.0 billion to $3.2 billion from $3.0 billion to $3.4 billion, attributing the change to the timing of third-party capacity. The company now expects 2026 capital expenditures of about $27 billion, above its previous range of $20 billion to $25 billion.

Nebius recognized about $325 million of nonrecurring revenue in the quarter from an asset-light rollout in which partners fund capacity and deploy Nebius’ architecture and AI cloud platform. Management said quarterly EBITDA margins can move when new sites incur rent, power and staffing costs before generating revenue, and fourth-quarter results will include some of these early costs. For 2026, Nebius expects an adjusted EBITDA margin of about 40%, more than $10 billion in customer prepayments, contracted power of 5 gigawatts by year-end and ARR to exceed $7 billion in February. Nebius expects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, with pretax breakeven targeted for the fourth quarter. It expects $40 billion to $45 billion of capital spending for more than one gigawatt of new capacity, with 75% to 85% funded through prepayments and asset-backed financing, while customer prepayments are expected to reach $17 billion to $20 billion.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl finds 64% of leaders report positive AI returns as readiness for external risks falls to 24%
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl released findings from its third annual Readiness Report on November 10, 2026, in New York, showing a widening divide between AI returns and readiness to manage risks. The report found that 64% of leaders report positive returns on AI investments, up 10 points from 2025. Average readiness across external risks fell seven points to 24%, with the steepest declines in readiness for cyber threats and competitive disruption. The report captures the attitudes and actions of 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries. The data shows organizations racing to deliver returns on significant AI investments while feeling ill-equipped to navigate the implications for the AI era.

Significantly fewer leaders describe themselves as in the experimentation phase compared to a year ago, down 13 points from 2025 to 49%. Nearly half, 48%, substantially changed their AI strategies this year, with implications across tech, people and governance. About a quarter, 24%, saw an AI investment fail, and 21% canceled a major AI initiative. Just 27% have formally updated roles and responsibilities around AI, and 29% have fully implemented change management for AI adoption. Those who have done both are 28 points more likely to be completely ready for their AI implementation and 8 points more likely to report positive ROI on their AI investments.

Martin Schroeter, Chairman and CEO of Kyndryl, said that as AI creates significant opportunity, organizations are now focusing on how to make early returns sustainable. He said this year's Readiness Report shows a new kind of readiness gap, with AI ambitions moving faster than the systems needed to support them. He said the bar for readiness keeps moving as AI becomes more integrated in enterprises. He said Kyndryl's data shows that focusing on people, technology and governance can help organizations win with AI and keep the ability to adapt as opportunities evolve. Kyndryl is described as a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services and trades on the NYSE under KD.

For the third year in a row, security concerns topped the list of external risks and contributed most to the overall decline in readiness. Just 26% of firms said they were completely ready for cyberattacks, a drop of 11 points from last year. Three in four leaders say AI helps their organizations identify threats faster, even as confidence in their ability to respond to cyberattacks has declined. The second-largest drop in readiness came from leaders' concerns about competitive disruptions outside of their industry, down 10 points from 2025 to 23%. Retailers are weighing how to benefit from AI shopping assistants without forfeiting direct customer relationships, software companies face questions about SaaS models as AI rebalances the build-versus-buy equation, and financial institutions are challenged by emerging lending models.

The research captures how leaders are considering digital sovereignty in a year marked by greater actions by governments, most visibly in the European Union. Leaders in the EU are slightly less likely to have taken sovereignty-related actions compared to those in the rest of the world. 68% say solutions offering full operational control, should they need it, are worth a premium of 10% or more, and 60% say greater control is worth slower deployment and adoption of advanced capabilities. For the third year in a row, leaders said upgrading their IT infrastructure was the number one action their organizations are taking to mitigate external risks, and 71% rate their infrastructure as mostly or fully modernized. Yet two-thirds of CIOs surveyed think their technology foundations need significant re-architecture before being fully ready for AI at scale.

The report is Kyndryl's third annual Readiness Report, and the 2026-27 Readiness Report is promoted on Kyndryl's site as exploring how organizations are navigating AI adoption, IT modernization and evolving business demands. Kyndryl's 2026 People Readiness Report is described as revealing a decline in workforce readiness as AI adoption surges, and what leading organizations are doing to prepare. The articles state that 66% of CIOs believe their infrastructure requires significant re-architecture before it can support AI at scale. The articles do not state what Kyndryl plans to do next with the findings, and they leave open which specific countries or industries drove the declines. More to follow.

stories.Headline: VA official Zack Schwartz announces homepage redesign to prepare for AI enhancements
stories.Summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs updated its homepage last week to provide a more simplified experience for users. Zack Schwartz, the principal deputy assistant secretary of the Office of Information and Technology, announced these changes at the VA Modernization Forum on November 13, 2026. The redesign followed a period of extensive veteran testing and the analysis of nearly 90,000 survey responses. This initial update serves as a foundation for further artificial intelligence enhancements planned for the coming months.

The new website features pre-filled forms, natural language searching, magic links, and a single sign-on capability. To improve security, the agency collaborated with global cybersecurity firms to implement a security wrapper similar to those used in commercial banking. The department also partnered with the identity verification service CLEAR last month to help thousands of veterans create accounts via in-person kiosks. Future updates scheduled for January and throughout next year will make the site more compatible with large language models.

Zack Schwartz stated that the office is moving away from science experiments to keep pace with evolving technology. He explained that the agency is studying how large language models navigate the site to build better skills for younger veterans. Schwartz noted that while the financial costs of artificial intelligence remain unknown, the agency is working with America.gov to improve services. He emphasized that success depends on building relationships and listening to criticism rather than simply deploying new technology.

The agency intends to serve as a representative example for other federal offices regarding the use of super intelligence. Schwartz plans to meet with incoming Federal Chief Information Officer Carter Farmer to discuss these advancements in the artificial intelligence space. By automating internal processes, the department hopes to reduce costs and allow staff to focus on critical veteran-facing activities. These incremental changes are designed to deliver consistent results for veterans regardless of which administration is in power.

Articles.Title: VA website gets a redesign with more AI-friendly updates coming, IT official says

stories.Headline: US restricts remote AI compute access for China and other embargoed nations
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration announced new export controls on Monday to stop companies in China and other restricted nations from remotely accessing AI infrastructure. These rules target the D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes Russia, Iran, North Korea, China, and 18 other nations. The Commerce Department now requires licenses to export, transfer, or reexport AI chips and servers to any global data center providing compute to these restricted entities. This action follows the resignation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang and reports that a customer named Megaspeed bought thousands of chips to bypass existing laws.

The new regulations apply to any network or data center with a total processing performance over 12 million, which equals roughly 750 Nvidia H200 or H100 chips. Licensing requirements are also now mandatory for advanced semiconductor transfers to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to higher risks of diversion. Existing operators must obtain licenses within 90 days, although the rules do not apply to commercial recommendation systems used for social media or e-commerce. Additionally, the administration rescinded the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule from the Biden era to remove unnecessary restrictions on allies and American firms.

The Commerce Department stated that these restrictions are a logical extension of current controls designed to undermine the ability of concerning countries to train advanced Super Intelligence models. Officials explained that such computing power could support intelligence or military activities that threaten foreign policy interests or the national security of the United States. The government believes these changes prevent the use of specific items at power levels capable of running advanced models. This move comes as Chinese AI firms reportedly rush to secure overseas computing capacity before further restrictions are implemented.

Articles.Title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

stories.headline_source: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely

stories.Headline: Varonis reveals TheMailer phishing kit that uses AI to personalize lures and evade filters
stories.Summary:
Varonis research revealed a new phishing kit called TheMailer on November 17, 2026. This commercial tool uses attacker supplied AI models to personalize lures and evade filters. It allows cybercriminals to scale their campaigns to tens of thousands of targets. The kit orchestrates most elements of an attack through its integrated AI functionality. It leverages large language models to a degree rarely seen in the criminal ecosystem.

Buyers pay between 3,000 and 6,000 dollars in cryptocurrency for a lifetime license. Operators must provide their own API keys, SMTP servers, proxies, and target email lists. They can choose models including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Grok, Gemini, and Mistral. The tool can generate lures from short prompts or real brand emails. It adjusts content for spam filters and removes common AI writing patterns.

Varonis senior security researcher Daniel Kelley wrote about the kit in a blog post. He stated that the tool can rewrite lures until they bypass spam filters. Kelley told Dark Reading that the kit is built to scale against targets. He noted that a single campaign reached nearly 25,000 emails. He described the tool as opportunistic phishing with the polish of something targeted.

The kit affects organizations that rely on content filters to block malicious emails. Varonis believes the tool has a large customer base despite unknown success rates. Defenders are warned that bad grammar is no longer a reliable sign of phishing. Users should be wary of urgency, unexpected requests, and account statement alerts. Organizations are urged to monitor for lookalike domains and check full redirect chains.

Phishing kits and phishing as a service platforms have gained popularity in recent years. Most AI tools previously focused on generating lures or coding realistic phishing websites. They were used for conducting reconnaissance and automating simple, repetitive tasks. TheMailer differs by automating the phishing process from end to end. It personalizes the email address, body, and subject line for each recipient.

Kelley expects more kits to follow because buyers will ask for these features. Varonis recommends enforcing email authentication practices like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. They suggest using least privilege access and data monitoring to limit potential damage. Training should reflect how emails look in a post AI world. The articles leave the actual success rates of the kit's tasks open.

Articles.Title: 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat - Dark Reading

stories.headline_source: 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat

stories.Headline: Ransomware groups use AI to raise global attacks as ransom payments fall
stories.Summary:
Ransomware groups used AI tools to increase their attacks globally during 2026, according to reports released in November of that year. These cybercriminals used large language models to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data more quickly. While global incidents rose, the number of attacks targeting companies in the United States remained fairly steady. Halcyon reported that ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches in the third quarter of 2026. This figure represents an increase of nearly 40 percent over the previous quarter.

The number of groups claiming success grew from 75 in the first quarter to 111 in the third quarter. In the retail sector, 62 percent of attacks succeeded in encrypting data, which is up from 48 percent in 2025. However, only 32 percent of retailers paid ransoms, compared to 58 percent who paid in 2025. The median ransom demand dropped to 700,000 dollars in 2026 from 2 million dollars in 2024. About one third of claimed successes came from groups that did not exist six months prior.

Cynthia Kaiser of Halcyon said AI removed language barriers for phishing and created a state of emergency in Japan. She stated that AI allows attackers to find sensitive data quickly and create better social engineering messaging. Chester Wisniewski of Sophos noted that the efficacy of ransomware in generating money for criminals has been declining. He observed that five or six new group names appeared in just the last few weeks. Duy-Phuc Pham of Trellix said AI allows small crews to do the work of large ones.

Retail firms saw a 71 percent recovery rate from backups, with most recovering their data within one week. Local government and school districts are also affected, and Wisniewski stated that none of them are paying ransoms. The Gentlemen became the most active group, surpassing Qilin in the number of victims they targeted. Manufacturing remains the top target because shared platforms can expose engineering data beyond one company. Europe has seen an increase in attacks while the share of US victims stayed the same or decreased.

AI enables attackers to scan, exploit, and move through networks with very little human effort. This technology allows gangs to broaden their campaigns across more industries and more regions globally. Law enforcement spent the year targeting shared services like criminal VPNs and laundering services that groups depend on. The growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat despite the decline in payments. The ability to target smaller populations was previously limited by historical language barriers.

Manufacturing will likely remain the top targeted sector in 2027 as international organizations account for a greater share. Kaiser expects continued growth in attacks, especially in countries outside of the United States. The articles leave open whether more attacks will actually result in more money for the criminals. It remains unclear if the pain felt by new countries will improve international cooperation against these threats. The Gentlemen are now considered the obvious next target for law enforcement agencies.

Articles.Title: Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, But Payments Decline - Dark Reading

stories.headline_source: Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, But Payments Decline

stories.Headline: Ronen Schwartz says purpose-built storage keeps AI accelerators fully utilized
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud published a blog post on November 16, 2026, titled “Beyond the compute bottleneck: Maximizing the ROI of AI accelerators with purpose-built storage.” Ronen Schwartz, VP of Product Management for Storage at Google Cloud, wrote the post. The post says the infrastructure mandate for enterprise AI has shifted from acquiring accelerators to keeping them fully utilized. It says storage accounts for only a small sliver of total AI spend, but the wrong storage can put committed compute capital at risk. It says insufficient storage throughput has become a primary impediment to AI success across the industry.

The post cites a Gartner prediction that enterprises will deploy over 150,000 agents in the next few years. It says Cloud Storage Rapid delivers up to 15 TB/s of throughput and 20 million queries per second with sub-millisecond latency from a single bucket. It says Rapid Cache delivers up to 2.5 TB/s of aggregate read throughput with no code changes and takes idle cold-start times from hours to minutes. It says Google Cloud Managed Lustre, built in partnership with DDN, provides up to 10 TB/s of throughput per instance. It says many models now process context windows that exceed 100,000 tokens.

Schwartz said organizations are eager to move AI initiatives forward, but preventing idle compute requires a purpose-built approach to data I/O. He said the most common architectural misstep is treating AI as a single, general-purpose workload. He said compute, networking and storage need to be deeply integrated to solve I/O challenges and keep accelerators busy. He said organizations should evaluate token economics rather than just legacy storage metrics. He said AI infrastructure needs enterprise-grade reliability, built-in security and automated cost discipline for optimized TCO.

The post says nine out of the world’s ten leading AI frontier model labs run on Google Cloud infrastructure. It says Google Cloud spent the last two years co-designing its storage architecture with these frontier labs and with Google’s own foundation model teams. It says Salesforce AI Research serves complex agentic inference workloads with up to 40% fewer GPUs. It says Thinking Machines Lab uses Cloud Storage Rapid Cache to stabilize read throughput peaks above 1.8 TB/s and achieve an 89% cache hit ratio. It says Shopify deployed 50+ unique Rapid Caches worldwide, achieving over 2 TB/s peak throughput and up to a 90% latency reduction from baseline.

The post says Atlassian adopted Managed Lustre on Google Kubernetes Engine to turn preemption interruptions into quick five-minute restores, delivering nearly 5x higher throughput and boosting GPU utilization by 70% compared to NVMe-based systems. It says Harmonic relies on Managed Lustre to train mathematical reasoning models, eliminating 50% of experiment interruptions, cutting startup times in half and increasing data retrieval speeds by 15x. It says Colossus is the planet-scale distributed file system powering Google Search, YouTube and Gemini. It says this shared infrastructure supports billions of users daily. It says Managed Lustre’s new Dynamic Tier consolidates hot and cold data into a single namespace, eliminating traditional caching performance cliffs.

The post says Managed Lustre Cloud Storage Mirror automatically synchronizes datasets in the background so they are ready before training begins. It says the post was posted in Storage & Data Transfer and tagged AI infrastructure. It lists related articles, including one introducing Z4M storage-optimized compute for AI/ML and parallel file systems by bob Napaa. It lists another related article on what’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October by Alex Barrett. It lists a related article introducing Google Cloud’s U4 compute for ultra-low latency trading by Disha Chopra and one on Cloud Storage end-to-end checksums by Denis Serenyi.

stories.Headline: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
stories.Summary:
TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research and Microsoft Security that learns from an AI coding agent's past sessions in a repository to cut waste in future sessions, and it does so without modifying the agent or its underlying model. The work was described in a Microsoft Research post dated November 16, 2026, and in a paper titled TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents. The researchers first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository's tasks in sequence. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, the plugin reduced costs by 18.4 to 30.9 percent across multiple AI coding agents, with costs falling in every repository tested while task success rates remained broadly stable.

The profiling found three kinds of waste that recurred. After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30 percent of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository, while only 7 percent matched an action in another repository's history. The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 of them were never called. The 17 percent of tasks that failed accounted for 32 percent of the spending. The researchers also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy, and each lowered costs in some repositories but not others, which the team said suggests effective cost control must adapt to the repository rather than apply the same strategy everywhere.

After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session's log and updates what it knows about the repository, then acts through three mechanisms using only interfaces the agent already provides. The plugin turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. The researchers framed their question simply: whether experience in a repository can help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently. The post does not say what happens next beyond the plugin being open source and available for use with existing agents.

Articles.Title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient

stories.Headline: Menlo Partners reports health AI spending reaches $3.7 billion as providers invest in clinical copilots
stories.Summary:
Health AI investments reached $3.7 billion, more than double the total from the past year, according to a new Menlo Partners report described in a Healthcare Dive article dated November 16, 2026. The report polled more than 550 U.S. healthcare and life sciences executives and found that healthcare remains the AI industry's biggest vertical. Provider organizations are now looking to deploy AI in new areas, with front-office operations and clinical copilots named as the most popular ones. The findings show that provider interest is moving beyond ambient scribing, which had been one of the most popular uses of AI in healthcare. Year-over-year growth was less than double for ambient scribing and for coding and billing, while clinical copilots that assist providers with patient care grew roughly five-fold to $550 million.

Patient engagement and front-office functions grew about five-fold as well, to $450 million, making those two the biggest AI growth areas for providers. Providers account for the bulk of healthcare AI spend at 77%, and the survey showed they seem willing to move away from incumbent health IT vendors in these areas. More than two-thirds of providers would rather keep coding, billing and chart review within their EHR, but only 16% said the same for patient navigation. OpenEvidence is the most popular choice for clinical copilots, and Utah's regulatory sandbox has allowed Doctronic to process prescription renewals for 191 medications. The report authors wrote that healthcare AI is expanding into more complex workflows, including clinical decision support, drug discovery and patient interactions, which were traditionally relegated to humans.

Even ARPA-H is investing $62.7 million to create 24/7 AI agents that can monitor heart failure patients between visits, with the intention of the AI becoming FDA-approved. In ambient scribing, AI startups are ceding ground to incumbent health IT companies, and in 2026 legacy vendors such as Microsoft's Dragon Copilot and Epic's Art took 68% of new ambient scribing dollars. Those companies now hold 46% market share, while AI startups lost 13% of market share, pushing some of them to expand outside ambient scribing. Abridge has recently struck a deal with Availity to create real-time prior authorization, the report said, while Heidi has partnered with R1 to integrate payer prior authorization policies into the clinical encounter. The article also notes that the agency said it would increase the number of MA plan audits and complete its backlog of reviews by investing in technology and growing its medical coding workforce.

Articles.Title: Health AI spend doubles as providers invest in clinical copilots, front-office AI

stories.Headline: Donald Trump posts AI clips on Truth Social during nationwide FAA ground stop
stories.Summary:
Donald Trump posted artificial intelligence clips on Truth Social during a nationwide FAA ground stop. The president shared these images starting Friday while flights were disrupted across the country. He focused on the Iran war, midterm losses, and White House renovations. One Sunday post showed Air Force troops praying beside Boeing C-17 Globemaster III aircraft. He also shared fake images of Defense Secretary Markwayne Mullin and his son.

The ground stop occurred on November 13 and cost the economy billions of dollars. Officials blamed faulty copper wiring and a router in Arkansas for the failure. The FAA had launched an 875 million dollar AI system called SMART on November 10. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says 50 billion dollars is needed to upgrade the network. Previous funding included 25 billion dollars from Joe Biden and 12.5 billion in 2025.

Trump said the White House is now flawless after he fixed 18 broken windows. He claimed the renovations took him ten minutes a day because he knows construction. He mentioned a helipad built in September for Chinese President Xi Jinping to use. Trump called a reporter pathetic for asking about the crumbling airline industry. He insisted the new ballroom fits like a glove and the stone was broken.

Robert W. Mann Jr. said a single router taking down a national network is implausible. House Democrats expressed safety concerns in an October 13 letter regarding the SMART system. They claimed the aviation workforce had little input and limited training for the AI. The administration blames the failure on equipment that is 50 years old. Trump wrote that new funding would create the best system in the world.

The FAA rolled out the SMART system three days before the nationwide grounding happened. This system centralizes data on staffing, flight paths, and weather to help specialists. The startup Air Space Intelligence designed the system for the federal government. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin denied the AI was related to the outage. The administration is now asking Congress for more money to fix the issues.

Trump continues to post about the Alaska Senate race between Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola. He wants the Justice Department to sue Alaska and block the vote certification. Peltola has a comfortable lead with 97 percent of the ballots already counted. The articles do not say if Congress will approve the requested FAA funding. They leave open whether the SMART system will be audited by House Democrats.

Articles.Title: Trump Keeps Posting Weird AI Slop Instead of Talking About FAA Outage

stories.headline_source: Trump Keeps Posting Weird AI Slop Instead of Talking About FAA Outage

stories.Headline: Unitree CEO warns that AI robotics breakthroughs will strain mass production capabilities
stories.Summary:
Unitree Robotics CEO Wang Xingxing discussed the potential for a technical breakthrough in general-purpose robot models on Tuesday morning. He shared these insights during his appearance at the APEC CEO Summit 2026 held in Shenzhen, Guangdong province. The leader noted that the increasing utility of large language models has created high expectations for robots to solve practical problems. He believes that while the technology is advancing, the ability to scale up production will present significant challenges.

The primary technical obstacle involves creating models that allow robots to function in homes without needing repeated retraining for every unique setting. This advancement would require robots to begin working immediately upon deployment rather than undergoing extensive site-specific adjustments. Such a shift would change how the industry approaches the deployment of general-purpose machines in domestic environments. The goal is to move beyond current limitations to achieve a more seamless integration of AI into physical robotics.

Wang Xingxing is responsible for leading the company and provided these perspectives on the current state of the industry. He explained that the success of AI in other fields has pushed the robotics sector toward similar breakthroughs. The CEO emphasized that the gap between technical possibility and mass production remains a critical point of concern. He suggested that the industry must overcome these specific hurdles before robots can be widely adopted for everyday household tasks.

Articles.Title: Nearing AI Robotics Breakthrough Would Strain Production, Unitree Founder Says - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Databricks launches AI Index to track enterprise model performance and spending patterns
stories.Summary:
Databricks launched the AI Index on November 16, 2026, to track enterprise model performance and spending. This public resource provides insights into how companies adopt and pay for various artificial intelligence models. The company created this tool because developers now face a massive variety of proprietary and open-weight options. New flagship models have launched roughly every 3.7 days since May 2026, making selection more difficult. Databricks aims to help customers inform their investments by sharing internal evaluation data and usage trends.

The Index uses anonymized data from over 10,000 companies using Unity Gateway, including Fortune 500 and Global 2000 firms. It tracks token and spend shares for providers like OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as weekly individual spending patterns. The resource includes coding-agent evaluations based on real workflows from Databricks engineers, such as reviewing pull requests. These benchmarks evaluate models across nine AI labs using harnesses like Codex and Claude Code to measure success rates. The system monitors specific models including DeepSeek V4.1, GLM 5.3, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

Databricks executives stated that customers repeatedly asked for comparisons of new models to help guide their own corporate investments. They explained that their internal Day 1 rollout process allows them to evaluate new releases within a few days. The company noted that model quality strongly influences market share, as seen when Claude Opus 5.5 launched. They argued that enterprises must evaluate model and harness combinations against their own workloads rather than relying on rankings. Databricks also suggested that intelligent model routing can help match specific tasks to the most appropriate models.

Enterprises are affected by these trends, with many shifting workloads between different model versions and providers to manage costs. The number of companies using two or more providers grew as single-provider reliance fell from 64 percent to 28 percent. Open-weight models gained ground, with their share of enterprise token traffic rising from 7.3 percent to 30.9 percent. Some users face extreme cost differences, such as GPT-6 Luna costing 32 times less per task than Claude Opus 5.5. Spending remains concentrated, with the 99th-percentile user spending 699.74 dollars compared to a median spend of 2.49 dollars.

The company based these findings on data from its 12,000 employees and the Unity Gateway governance tool. They previously published a coding-agent benchmark in July to establish a foundation for these continuous evaluations. Research shows that open-weight models like DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3 now achieve a 93.1 percent pass rate. Databricks found that Opus 5.5 delivered better quality at a 29 percent lower cost than its predecessor. They also observed that Claude Fable 5.1 has a high success rate but costs nearly five times more than Muse Wonder.

Databricks will provide weekly updates to the Index as new proprietary and open-weight model releases are evaluated. The company encourages enterprises to use Unity Gateway to access and switch models without facing provider lock-in. Developers can now use the Unity Gateway CLI to integrate approved models across various supported coding harnesses. The articles leave open how specific industries will adapt their budgets as median weekly spending continues to grow. It remains unclear which specific model-harness combinations will dominate the cost-quality frontier in the coming months.

stories.Headline: Amateur creators use AI to produce a viral historical short drama with 12 billion views in China
stories.Summary:
A group of six amateurs created a viral AI-generated short drama called Armed Into the Song Dynasty, which first premiered in August. The production team includes a former rideshare driver, a stay-at-home mother, an interior designer, a wholesale business owner, and a former pharmaceutical sales representative. This historical series has already reached ten seasons and consists of approximately 1,000 episodes that each last about three minutes. The show has gathered more than 12 billion views on Bilibili and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

The series is adapted from a web novel by Chagen’er that began publishing in April and follows five modern soldiers traveling back to the Northern Song dynasty. This production reflects a broader industry shift, as 490,000 micro-dramas were released in the first nine months of 2026, which is 13 times the total for 2025. An October report from the National Radio and Television Administration stated that AI-generated content now makes up over 90 percent of these dramas. The same report noted that the monthly active audience for short dramas has now exceeded 600 million viewers.

Zhang Hansheng, the 54-year-old head of the production team, told domestic media that the series cost roughly 1 million yuan, or 150,000 dollars, to produce. While Zhang declined to share the specific earnings of the team, rumors of high returns have encouraged other grassroots creators to learn AI tools. Some viewers expressed interest in making their own dramas, though others warned about scams involving AI-related courses. This success follows other historical AI dramas like Inkstone Edge Green Plum and Assuming a Noble Identity, which premiered last year.

The rise of these high-quality productions challenges the reputation of short dramas as mindless entertainment featuring formulaic characters and implausible plots. However, critics have requested more scrutiny regarding how artificial intelligence depicts the history of China. Last year, the National Radio and Television Administration began a campaign against AI videos that distort heroic, revolutionary, or historical themes. They specifically targeted content that alters classic television, film, or literary works to ensure historical accuracy is maintained.

Articles.Title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit - Sixth Tone

stories.headline_source: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit

stories.Headline: MIMIT Health reports $2M in annual savings from AI workflow overhaul
stories.Summary:
MIMIT Health, a Chicago-based multi-specialty physician group practice, reported $2 million in annual operational savings from an AI-powered workflow overhaul, Healthcare IT News reported on November 16, 2026. The group connected its electronic health record and administrative workflows so artificial intelligence agents could handle tasks such as insurance verification while staff coordinated care. Dr. Paramjit Chopra, a practicing interventional radiologist and founder and CEO of MIMIT Health, led the effort. The transformation began with disconnected systems and cumbersome processes that slowed patient intake and created unnecessary work for staff. MIMIT Health built what it calls an intelligent healthcare operating system, or iHOS, through CIMSS Innovative Solutions, a healthcare technology and consulting company Chopra also founded and leads.

The reported $2 million in annual savings includes $500,000 in lower system maintenance costs and a 15% reduction in inventory costs, accounting for about $150,000 per year. Revenue, profit and production at MIMIT Health each approximately doubled from 2025 to 2026. Providers now see 40% more patients without added hours, which kept labor costs from rising with volume. Staff save about three hours every day, and new patient onboarding that once meant chasing information across separate systems is now completed in minutes. MuleSoft connects the existing systems, including the AdvancedMD EHR, while Snowflake supports storage and analysis and Salesforce Data 360 unifies patient context with zero-copy access between Snowflake and Data 360.

Chopra said physicians want patients to receive the right care at the right time, which he called a sacred responsibility, but much must happen before a patient reaches the examination room. He said referrals, patient contact, information collection, insurance verification and appointment scheduling were not connected, so patients could not move through them without unnecessary friction. He noted that fragmentation carried an economic cost, because every repeated task consumed paid time and every incomplete handoff created more work. He said fixed calculations and required workflow rules remain in reliable software processes, while models help interpret information, summarize context and support decisions. He said the operating principle is to define what an agent may access, what it may do, when it must escalate and which decisions require human authorization.

Chopra said clinical judgment and accountability remain with the clinicians, and that people handle conversations, exceptions and decisions. He said the contact center captures the referral, the eligibility team documents coverage, care coordinators prepare the account and care episode, and schedulers work from assigned cases. He said AdvancedMD patient profiles sync to Salesforce, documents can be referenced from Box, and Slack connects the teams. He said Tableau gives real-time visibility into inventory and revenue, including accounts payable and receivable tied to insurance payments. He said the group wants to turn recovered capacity into patient care and give people more time to work at the level of their training.

The articles state that healthcare organizations are investing heavily in artificial intelligence, but turning that technology into measurable financial and operational results remains a challenge. Before the overhaul, patient information was scattered across disconnected systems, and chart notes, treatment approvals and patient communication each needed separate tools or manual work. Staff managed complex scheduling by hand, and providers spent their time on dictation summaries, chart notes and pre- and post-op follow-ups. Reviewing a single patient's notes before a procedure could take half a day, meaning uncertainty and waiting for the patient and administrative work competing with care for staff and providers. Salesforce Health Cloud offered MIMIT Health a foundation for organizing the clinical and operational work around the patient.

Chopra said he sees iHOS as an important enabler of the group's ability to scale, giving its people and agents a shared foundation for coordinating work around patients. He said shared information reduces searching, shared definitions reduce confusion, clear workflows make responsibility visible, agents help with defined tasks, and people bring judgment, relationships and accountability. He said the business result reflects that broader operating model, with patient intake as an important entry point. The articles leave open how MIMIT Health will measure the savings going forward and what further growth the practice expects. The articles do not state when the overhaul began or how long it took to complete.

Articles.Title: MIMIT Health credits AI-powered workflow overhaul with $2M in annual savings
