stories.Headline: Canada and the UK renew their AI security partnership with shared standards and joint evaluations
stories.Summary:
On 13 October 2026, Canada and the UK renewed their AI security partnership, which was first signed in 2024 as the AI Safety Partnership. The renewal aims to foster the safe and responsible development and deployment of AI. The agreement commits both countries to three priorities: interoperable standards, enhanced information-sharing and closer technical cooperation. The Canadian AI Safety Institute and the UK AI Security Institute will hold regular exchanges and coordinated evaluation activities. The Canadian Institute of Advanced Research contributed CAD $1 million to the UK AI Security Institute's Alignment Project.

The renewed partnership covers mutually recognised or shared AI security standards, improved information exchange including on frontier risk, and expanded technical arrangements. Neither country has passed a single comprehensive law governing AI across every sector. Canada's proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act was abandoned when Parliament was dissolved in 2025. The UK has deliberately chosen not to legislate. No legislation in either country sets out exactly how organisations must assess AI risks.

The article recommends that organisations implement a consistent and repeatable process to answer the same questions both regimes ask. These questions are whether the impact of the AI system has been assessed before deployment, whether decisions have been documented, whether there is meaningful human oversight and whether there will be ongoing monitoring. Such a process would let organisations respond to the partnership priorities, evidence compliance in both jurisdictions and prepare for any future legislation. The article was co-authored by Carole Piovesan, Managing Partner at INQ Law in Toronto. It was published by Stephenson Harwood on 16 November 2026.

Canada's legal environment is fragmented across jurisdictions and sectors, including privacy, human rights, consumer protection and competition law. The federal Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems sets out commitments on accountability, safety, fairness, transparency, human oversight and robustness. The Directive on Automated Decision-Making is binding on federal institutions and is supported by the Algorithmic Impact Assessment, which scores a system's risk and scales safeguards accordingly. In June 2026 the federal government tabled Bill C-36, which would enact the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act as Canada's new private-sector privacy law. A companion bill, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), would impose digital safety duties on social media platforms and chatbot services, with both regimes overseen by a new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada.

Health Canada has issued pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' Guideline E-23 on Model Risk Management, in force from 1 May 2027, expressly captures AI and machine learning models at federally regulated financial institutions. The Standards Council of Canada has convened work on AI standards and trust frameworks. In 2017 Canada became the first country to launch a national AI strategy, and its successor, AI for All, launched in June 2026, aims to lift business AI adoption from just over 12% to 60% by 2034. Canada now has a dedicated Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation, whose priorities flow from the Prime Minister's May 2025 mandate letter to Cabinet.

Budget 2026, tabled on 5 November 2026, includes access to 500 MW of sovereign AI compute, approximately CAD $1 billion over five years for a Government Transformation Fund, a new Digital Transformation Canada, CAD $176.3 million over five years for the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission and a plan to explore a Technology Stability Board. The UK has adopted a principles-based approach covering safety, security and robustness, transparency and explainability, fairness, accountability and governance, and contestability and redress, enforced by sector regulators. The Financial Conduct Authority's AI Update outlines how existing financial services rules apply to AI, and the Information Commission has issued guidance on AI and data protection and has been tasked with preparing a formal Code of Practice on AI and automated decision-making. The Competition Markets Authority's AI Strategic Update sets out six principles aimed at fostering competition and consumer protection. If an AI system uses personal data, a data protection impact assessment is one of the most useful tools available to assess risk.

Reforms under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 removed the general prohibition on solely automated decision-making that produces legal or similarly significant effects, replacing it with a requirement for a lawful basis such as legitimate interests, provided no special category data is involved. Organisations must still ensure transparency, provide individuals with the opportunity to make representations, allow access to human intervention and enable individuals to challenge decisions. The EU AI Act came into force on 1 August 2024, and its broad extraterritorial reach applies to organisations based in the UK and Canada that place AI systems or general-purpose AI models on the EU market. The EU's digital omnibus on AI has deferred the rules for high-risk AI systems from 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2027 for Annex III and 2 August 2028 for Annex I. Providers of high-risk AI systems must operate a robust risk management system, keep detailed technical documentation and records, design systems to allow effective human oversight, demonstrate compliance via a conformity assessment before the system is placed on the market and conduct post-market monitoring.

stories.Headline: AI tools reduce game prototype creation costs to as low as 10 yuan
stories.Summary:
An Anthropic engineer named Felix Rieseberg released a web game called Saltline last week. This game was created entirely using artificial intelligence through a short prompt. The AI model Fable 5.2 ran for eight hours to output the complete product. Rieseberg spent 550 US dollars to create all the models, sounds, and textures. The resulting game features realistic lighting and high-definition textures that meet AAA production standards.

The project Inspiration Defense requires HTML, CSS, native JavaScript, and low-poly Three.js for its 3D version. It uses a nine stage development process including an engineering baseline and a mainline state machine. The game features five story levels where players survive ten minutes to defeat a final boss. Development involved DeepSeek v4 pro and Kimi k3.1 pro to create four different demos. These AI tools reduced the creation cost to between 10 and 20 yuan.

The author of the article acted as the producer and designer for the project. He stated that AI is currently very good at replicating existing works and basic interactions. He noted that the most important part of a good game is being fun. The author observed that DeepSeek produced a rough and barely functional version of the game. He found that Kimi provided more refined graphics, hit animations, and better boss battle scenes.

Players of FPS games are affected by the rise of loot-shoot-exfiltrate games like Escape from Tarkov. Fans of Black Myth: Wukong played an AI web version that restored basic action mechanics. Players of Deep Space Pawnshop enjoy complex synthesis systems despite the simple pixel-style graphics. The author noted that ordinary people can now turn their ideas into playable prototypes. He questioned if professional game developers might collectively lose their jobs to AI.

The author compared AI web games to native games made with Unity, Godot, or Unreal Engine. He noted that web games are niche because they are small and require no installation. He tested AI games based on the CrossFire Transport Ship map to verify visual similarity. He used the roguelite horde survival genre, citing Brotato and Vampire Survivors as classic examples. The project used Test-Driven Development to ensure the code passed specific acceptance checklists.

The author intends to continue the project because the current demos are low quality. He wants to improve the games beyond the basic functional state provided by the AI. The articles leave open whether AI can create truly original games without reference objects. It remains unclear if AI can fully replace professional production cycles and teams. The author did not specify the final cost for a fully polished version.

stories.Headline: Al Kingsley writes a plain English guide to explain how AI works and where it may go
stories.Summary:
Al Kingsley wrote in School Management Plus on 16 November 2026 that school leaders and staff often pretend to understand artificial intelligence during meetings rather than admit they do not know the basics, because teaching is a profession built on knowledge and an information gap can feel like a failing. He said the problem is not the technology itself, since AI is not a scary human overlord yet, but that without knowing how it works and what its quirks are, leaders and staff cannot make informed decisions for colleagues and students. He argued that anyone who does ask what others may regard as simple questions will find their colleagues grateful, and he guaranteed it. He described his book, Unpicking AI ,  one token at a time, as deliberately and definitively not a book about AI in schools, with no education jargon at all.

The book is a simple, accessible guide to AI in general, written for anyone who wants to understand what it is before deciding how to use it, and it emphasises plain English. It first explains where AI came from, showing that the ideas started many, many years ago, which makes media headlines seem less futuristic and less overwhelming. It then explains how AI actually works, and once you realise it learns from vast amounts of data, you can see why it is so impressive and why it sometimes gets things oh-so confidently wrong. The book also looks at where AI might end up in the future, in easy language, because at this point nobody actually knows, even the tech bros.

Kingsley said that when we get our questions answered we all gain confidence, whatever the subject, and that with a new understanding of AI your questions will improve. Asking whether to ban it will become a question of what it can do, where to look out for problems and how to help students use it constructively in school. He returned to the meeting scenario, where someone who knows how AI works fearlessly asks to check that everyone knows what they are talking about before deciding. Kingsley is due to speak at the Schools and Academies Show in Birmingham this week at a talk entitled Choosing the Right Technology for Your Secondary School: The Questions Leaders Should Be Asking.

stories.Headline: AI workers face overtime and stagnant pay as elite salaries skew averages
stories.Summary:
AI industry professionals are facing high anxiety and overtime work, according to a report published on November 18, 2026. Many workers find that their daily reality is far less glamorous than the public narrative suggests. Ordinary practitioners are struggling with a gap between their expectations and the actual market reality. While some top experts earn huge sums, most employees face stagnant wages and intense pressure. This disconnect is driven by a small group of elite earners who inflate average salary figures.

High salaries of one million yuan are entry thresholds for some talent programs at major tech companies. Other roles in AI Infra and agent development start at hundreds of thousands of yuan per year. Yang Han, a master's graduate from a top 20 QS institution, now earns a medium salary. Chen Mo applied for nearly 200 positions during autumn recruitment but did not receive a single offer. Thomas secured four offers because he held 985 degrees and relevant big tech internship experience.

Yang Han stated that AI practitioners are less glamorous than the outside world imagines. She noted that capital is the invisible hand pressing a countdown clock over the industry. Wu Le joked that he is just a senior proofreader because AI completes most tasks. He admitted that companies prefer capable people who can get started immediately over new graduates. Mike observed that the internet industry now emphasizes a full alignment of qualifications like the financial industry.

New graduates are affected because big tech firms have suspended recruitment for many junior positions. Coding agents have erased the premium for handwritten code, allowing one developer to replace three people. Middle managers are collapsing due to repeated project interruptions and unreachable performance indicators. Many students with top degrees are getting zero offers during campus recruitment cycles. Workers like Wu Le feel pushed forward by the rhythm of AI rather than using it.

The industry evolved rapidly from chatbots to image and video generation, then to office agents. In 2025, six out of every ten yuan of global venture capital flowed into AI enterprises. AI startups took 81 percent of global VC investment in the first quarter of the current year. MIT analyzed over 300 enterprise AI projects and found 95 percent had no quantifiable profit impact. Companies use a horse racing mechanism where multiple teams compete for the same customers and orders.

Practitioners are relocating to stable positions, such as state owned enterprises or underlying AI infra work. Some workers are moving away from the front line to avoid frequent project interruptions. The articles leave open whether AI innovations like glasses and headsets will solve real problems. It remains unclear how AI will intervene in human lives one year from now. Investors continue to worry about the lack of realized returns despite staggering amounts of capital expenditure.

stories.Headline: OpenAI shuts down Sora and Atlas while Character.AI files for bankruptcy as thirteen AI products fail
stories.Summary:
At least thirteen well known AI applications in the United States failed recently. These projects ceased operations, underwent major adjustments, or faced development dilemmas. Tech giants and star startups were both affected by these outcomes. A TechCrunch report by Zhidx detailed these failures on November 17, 2026. The products faced shutdowns or market exits due to various industry pressures.

OpenAI shut down Sora on April 26 and the Atlas browser on August 9. OpenAI also deactivated the DALL-E GPT on August 30 and adjusted ChatGPT. Apple delayed the new Siri, which entered English beta on September 14. Microsoft pushed the Recall preview to Copilot+ PC users on April 25, 2025. Character.AI filed for bankruptcy on October 13, 2026, and Notion Mail closed September 22.

Notion stated that users now use AI Agents for email tasks instead. Bill Lennon announced on X that Ollie would cease services November 6. Disney offered 20 million dollars for a license to Character.AI intellectual property. Microsoft redesigned Recall after public doubts about privacy and data security issues. OpenAI diverted resources from Sora to other businesses in March 2026.

Users of the complex ChatGPT interface criticized the July 9 desktop update. Cybersecurity researcher Alexander Hagenah created a tool to extract Recall data on April 15. Character.AI faced lawsuits involving minors using chatbots, which increased its operating burden. Ollie users were lost to competing personal Agent applications like Muse and Instinct. Many large enterprises struggle to move Agentic AI projects into formal production.

Character.AI reached a one billion dollar valuation in 2022 and 20 million users. It lost eight to nine million dollars monthly due to computing and employees. Ollie raised 7.5 million dollars total between 2023 and 2025 before failing. HFS Research found only 26 percent of enterprise AI projects reached production. Many products failed because of high costs, security issues, or low retention.

Some companies will continue adjusting strategies while others exit the market entirely. Tech giants still face unstable product experiences and immature AI technology risks. The industry continues to expand with new startups emerging despite these high profile failures. Articles leave open whether other star AI products will face similar shutdowns soon. Future success depends on solving privacy risks and reducing high operating costs.

stories.Headline: Jinjiang Literature City faces backlash over AI detection accuracy and author compliance
stories.Summary:
Readers began posting AI detection results for Jinjiang Literature City novels on social platforms at the start of November 2026. These netizens used tools like Zhuque to check if authors used artificial intelligence for their stories. Some works showed AI suspicion rates over 80 percent, including those by top authors. The controversy grew as people questioned how the platform handles non-compliant creations. Yule Zibenlun tested 30 samples to verify the accuracy of these detection tools.

Jinjiang requires authors to sign an Original Creation Commitment Letter to ensure their work is manual. The platform allows AI for proofreading, creative elements, and rough outlines, but prohibits content that affects originality. If reported, Jinjiang uses at least three tools from Zhuque, Yuewen, DeepSeek, Zhipu, and Qianwen. Content is non-compliant if three or more tools show a suspicion rate exceeding 60 percent. Penalties include locking chapters, one-month yellow cards, or permanent bans from the leaderboard.

Jinjiang has not responded to this specific wave of controversy regarding its top authors. The platform's current rules aim to balance AI assistance with the need for original labor. Yule Zibenlun found that Zhuque is not very accurate and often misjudges text. Some AI-generated text was identified as manual, while some manual text was flagged as AI. The reporter described the tool as following a lenient graduation and strict admission principle.

Some readers refuse to pay for AI content and have demanded refunds for their subscriptions. They argue that manual creation is the primary value of the content they purchase. Authors who insist on original creation call for the platform to resist AI to protect their enthusiasm. Some creators worry they must prove their innocence to avoid being unfairly punished. Netizens noted that new authors are often punished while top authors avoid supervision.

Previous Weibo posts with 10,000 likes lamented the difficulty of distinguishing AI writing in modern romance. Some authors were denounced for leaving residual AI modification instructions directly in their main text. One author posted her writing software records showing 550,000 words to prove her originality. Other users found that a historical romance novel with 50,000 collections had high AI suspicion rates. Some works whose copyrights were sold were also caught in the AI checking wave.

The controversy continues as readers debate if AI tools affect the commercial value of stories. Some believe the reading experience matters more than whether a tool produced the text. Others argue that copyright holders should be informed if a work contains AI-generated content. It remains unclear if different degrees of AI use should follow different charging rules. The articles leave open whether the platform will strictly investigate AI or protect authors.

stories.Headline: Netflix tests AI lip re-rendering and finds gains not cost-effective
stories.Summary:
Netflix product staff re-rendered actors' lip animations in post-production so lip movements matched dubbed audio, and the company ran A/B tests on some films with directors and actors willing to try it, 36Kr reported on 18 November 2026. The tests showed user engagement rose significantly, but the AI caused visual flaws that needed manual correction, and the gain appeared only in drama and romance scenes with dense lines. The team judged continued large-scale investment in the capability not cost-effective, though the calculation may be reassessed as AI models advance. Mckenzie Lock, who led product, operations and creative work at Netflix, has gone through many such choices, the article said. The article shared a recent interview with Lock on how she promoted AI transformation inside the enterprise in recent years.

Netflix offers more than 17,000 titles in over 200 countries and regions, supports more than 30 languages and has over 300 million users, the article said. Lock's team set out to reform Netflix's creative and operational processes and held one non-negotiable goal: find links that are cumbersome, slow or defective and use AI on them, while ensuring content quality is not affected and production staff's work results are not compromised. Lock said most product decisions are essentially choices about how to deal with complexity, and that good design does not eliminate complexity but places it in the right position. A few years ago, when the internal AI reform started, the team did not first focus on what the latest models could do. Instead, Lock raised two open questions: what ultimate experience do we want to create for members, and in what aspects do current production processes really fail to meet members' needs?

Lock's team ran an imagination exercise, setting technical constraints aside, asking what users should be able to do, such as whether a viewer who pauses a series for three months and reopens it could first see a plot recap tailored to them. The team did not design the future process only in the conference room; it went to observe front-line work, distributed questionnaires to employees in different positions and organized experts and managers to discuss the results. They invited people with different views to state their reasons so potential differences could be seen before the project moved forward. Lock said employees' hesitation towards AI does not necessarily mean resistance to change and may be a reminder that important issues remain unresolved in the plan. During the survey phase the team created a two-column "Current Status vs. Future Comparison" table for each workflow, outlining on the left the current workflow including budget constraints, quality differences, linear correlation and time cost, and on the right how a person's work might change if AI were introduced.

Lock's team also created imagined press releases and social media posts about the upcoming process changes to "report" the transformation in advance and stimulate creative workers' expectations. Netflix writes important strategic choices in a binary format where both options are attractive, and in the AI transformation the team faced whether to learn first in low-risk scenarios or cover the most high-impact works first. Blockbuster hits like Stranger Things have a large audience and wide reach, so success could bring more significant benefits, but these works have higher quality requirements and the cost of problems is greater. The team chose to experiment first in relatively low-risk content and processes, learn from real production and then gradually expand according to technology maturity and confidence gained. On whether to invest in measurement first or scale up as soon as possible, Netflix chose the former, meaning time and resources go into early testing and expansion may not be that fast.

Lock stressed that AI investment should be aligned with the company's core metrics, not just with new metrics unique to AI, and that most AI investments should not be primarily targeted at reducing costs. Dubbing is core work for Netflix's creative team, but dubbing production is expensive and time-consuming and resources are often concentrated on the most popular titles, so the team wanted AI to help voice actors produce high-quality dubbing for more titles of different genres. After finding that re-rendering lip animations was not cost-effective, they changed direction and built an AI model to help dubbing staff identify moments needing special attention between lip movements and translated lines, improving alignment by adjusting translated lines and other methods. On the homepage, promotional materials such as stills, copywriting and trailers are personalized by the recommendation system, so a sufficiently diverse material library covering the entire content library is the core of the strategy. An algorithm Hollywood has long used assumes that the more marketing money spent, the more views gained, so directors and showrunners naturally think streaming platforms work the same way.

The team tested this hypothesis and concluded that stills and clips from many titles perform as well as specially customized concept art, so they automated production of clips and stills on a large scale and reserved customized concept art and trailers for the small number of popular titles that truly need them. Lock's team soon found that if the system is optimized only towards one easily quantifiable metric, the results may deviate from the user experience the team really wants. The algorithm is good at selecting images, and close-up photos of certain actors may attract users to click or watch, but if the system keeps selecting similar images the homepage may become monotonous and users may not clearly distinguish a suspense drama from a natural documentary. Worse, the system may select an actor who does not have many scenes but is attractive to audiences in specific regions as the main visual, giving users inaccurate expectations about the title. Later the team worked with creative experts to formulate more detailed specifications and adjusted the model and evaluation methods, focusing not only on viewing results but also on whether materials fit the content's temperament and help users understand the work.

Almost all of Netflix's systems run on tags, words describing content semantics that support recommendations of series on the user's homepage, and for many years the work depended on manual labor. Content analysts watch an entire title from start to finish, write long contextual documents and then manually add tags, tagging a single title can take more than twice the length of the title, and training an analyst who can work independently on tagging takes two months. The team wanted to replace this assembly line with AI-generated tags, but the taxonomy has been built over years and consists of thousands of concepts and values. Teams across the company have quietly built processes on certain tags with different weights, and most tags are extremely subjective editorial judgments, not factual judgments, and two people may not even agree on the same tag, let alone machines. If the entire old process were handed directly to AI, that would assume in advance that all these steps and tags must be retained, so the team first narrowed the scope of the problem, sorted out and streamlined the centrally mana

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Columbia professor Sandra Matz finds AI assistance reduces the uniqueness of people's choices
stories.Summary:
Professor Sandra Matz of Columbia University ran an experiment with the ice cream store Baskin Robbins, which is famous for its 31 flavors, offering a different one every day for a full month without repetition. When she handed the decision-making power of flavor selection to ChatGPT, the brand with a huge variety of flavors basically only had two choices in the eyes of AI, Walnut Cream and Mint Chocolate Chip. She asked the question repeatedly 100 times, and ChatGPT gave only these two options 96 times. Matz said in her TEDx speech that if this continues for a long time, Baskin Robbins may eventually only have these two flavors left, because if no one chooses the other 29 flavors anymore, merchants would have no reason to keep offering them. Matz believes that AI is inadvertently flattening the diversity of human choices.

Matz and her team analyzed more than 110,000 real social media choices and experimental data from 1,000 American users. They found that whether using a general LLM agent or a personally adjusted version, the uniqueness of the choices people make with AI assistance will decrease significantly. Although the personalized version slightly alleviates the convergence between people, it compresses the breadth of an individual's own choices at a deeper level. When you tell ChatGPT what flavor you like, AI will 100% recommend that explicitly stated favorite, without any deviation. A 2025 study analyzed 2,200 college application essays and found that in terms of collective diversity growth rate, human contributions are more than three times that of GPT.

Matz said that algorithms focus on exploitation, continuously reinforcing options that have already proven to be effective. She said this is beneficial to businesses and sometimes necessary for consumers, because there are far too many choices in modern life. She said that without AI to help filter, we can hardly cope with the complexity of modern life. She said that AI systems, especially recommendation models trained on massive user data, tend to optimize short-term satisfaction by making you click, making you stay, and preventing you from churning. She said that in the face of massive data, what the majority likes is an easily accessible signal.

New York Times reporter Kashmir Hill handed over all the decision-making things for a whole week to AI, including where to eat, what clothes to buy, and what shows to watch. After a week, she felt that she had fallen into a certain basic state, with life becoming predictable and choices impeccable, but there were no more surprises. She began to miss the occasional wrong turn, walking into a restaurant she would never have gone to, and accidentally finding it more delicious than the recommended ones. Italy briefly banned ChatGPT in 2023 due to data privacy issues, and researchers took this opportunity to conduct a natural experiment, analyzing the marketing content of restaurants on social media. During the ban, the lexical similarity of the content decreased by 15%, the syntactic similarity decreased by 12%, the semantic similarity decreased by 2%, while the user interaction rate rose by about 3.5%.

Studies tracking changes in writing complexity of academic papers, news reports and Reddit texts before and after the large-scale popularization of ChatGPT found that the variance decreased by between 21% and 50%. In the field of recommendation system research, this kind of phenomenon is called the rich get richer effect. Guided by algorithms, users may browse a wider range of categories, but their final purchase behavior is more concentrated on popular products, and overall sales diversity decreases instead. Byung-Chul Han wrote in The Disappearance of the Other that the spread of homogenization is not cancerous, but somnolent, and that it does not encounter resistance from the immune system. Byung-Chul Han described affirmative violence as a kind of harm composed of excessive similarity and excessive smoothness, without heterogeneous friction, no resistance brought by the Other, only continuous consent and appropriateness. The article says that the bias of recommendation systems towards exploitation is a long-standing structural problem, and the emergence of large language models only extends this mechanism from content recommendation to the level of decision-making agents.

Some people are actively asking AI to provide unexpected options, asking it to give some options that you are not often asked about but worth trying. Some people choose to deliberately not use AI in certain decisions, because its suggestions are so good that it has optimized away the possibility of taking a wrong turn. The article says that actively making mistakes has become one of the few ways for humans to defend their aesthetic power in the AI era. The article asks what evidence can be presented to prove that heterogeneity still exists in the human soul. The article says that if we do not want life to become a standard curve in the algorithm's statistical table, this question remains open.

stories.Headline: NAVER launches AI Tab to turn search answers into purchases and bookings
stories.Summary:
In June 2026, NAVER launched “AI Tab,” a new service that combines generative AI technology with the search assets NAVER has built up over many years. NAVER published the “NAVER AI Tab Service Brief” together with a research team led by Professor Kim Kyung-oe of Yonsei University. The brief is an in-depth look at how AI Tab is being used, based on real service data. AI Tab goes beyond simply providing search results and tailors its answers to each user’s question. It brings together rich information updated in real time across NAVER, from restaurant reservation availability to authentic product reviews.

AI Tab builds its answers from experience-based information accumulated across NAVER Cafe, Blog, and Jisik-iN. It brings together into a single answer the posts that NAVER users used to search for and compare on their own. It also cites its sources, so users can visit the original posts to explore more examples. When generating an answer, AI Tab draws on the NAVER service that best fits the question. If a user asks about a product, it calls on NAVER Shopping; if they ask about a place, it calls on NAVER Map/Place, and reflects those results in its answer.

According to NAVER’s internal survey, more than half of AI Tab users said that seeing an AI answer led them to actually make a purchase, book a reservation, or visit a place. Real service data showed the same trend, with click-through rates for NAVER Shopping and Map/Place within AI Tab each exceeding 40%. Professor Kim Kyung-oe of Yonsei University, who led the research, said he had been using AI Tab even before starting the research and felt that finding information had become much easier. He said AI Tab summarizes the key points first, so he could choose to look only at what he needed. He also said he finds AI Tab especially useful in everyday moments, like looking for places to visit or comparing products.

Kim said the biggest change is that search is becoming more like a conversation, with people asking questions in full sentences and following up based on the answers. He said analysis of AI Tab confirmed this shift, with users in their teens and twenties showing a relatively high share of multi-turn usage, exchanging several questions with the AI. He said users in other age groups showed different behaviors, such as checking the sources of the information AI provided or verifying it through additional searches. He said AI is not simply replacing traditional search but changing the very way users explore and use information. He said users treat AI answers as a starting point to explore and compare further, and then turn that into actual choices and actions.

Kim said AI Tab’s greatest strength is its ability to connect users’ information search to real action. He said people need qualitative information such as other people’s experiences, reviews, and ratings, but also concrete information such as price, location, business hours, and reservation availability. He said NAVER has years of accumulated content on Blog and Cafe, plus a wide range of services such as Shopping, Map, and Reservation. He said AI Tab can provide both the qualitative information users need to make judgments and the concrete information they need to act, and then connect that to actions like purchases and reservations. He said that with typical generative AI services the answer itself is often the final output, and users have to move to another service to buy or book something.

Kim said it will become increasingly difficult for services to stand out simply by providing accurate and useful search results or answers. He said competitiveness in the search market will depend not just on how well a service provides information, but on how effectively it helps users turn that information into real decisions and actions. He said he hopes AI Tab evolves beyond a service that simply answers questions accurately into one that helps users achieve their goals more easily and efficiently. He said it is important to understand users’ context and goals, organize the information they need, and naturally connect it to their actual choices and actions. NAVER said it will continue to develop AI Tab so it can better understand each user’s goals and help them take real action.

stories.Headline: BSI survey finds half of business leaders say AI cuts entry-level roles
stories.Summary:
Research commissioned by the British Standards Institution, the UK's national standards body, has found that businesses are increasingly using artificial intelligence to do work traditionally performed by junior employees. Half of the 1,287 business leaders surveyed, 49%, said AI has already reduced entry-level opportunities for starters, and the same proportion expect their organisation to cut entry-level roles because of AI. In a separate finding, 52% of respondents said AI is reducing junior headcount, up from 45% who said the same last year. The report, Human by Design: Thriving in the AI Workforce, was published as the Milburn review into the sharp rise in young people not in education, employment or training was released.

The report notes that 59% of business leaders see AI as crucial to their organisation's growth, but it warns that cutting jobs may build future problems by severing the talent pipeline through which inexperienced workers become experienced ones. It says removing entry-level work may deliver short-term efficiencies, yet organisations will still need employees who have skilled up and progressed internally, and that people develop judgement and expertise by doing the work themselves with the guidance of a human mentor. BSI also finds that people consulting chatbots rather than colleagues endangers the routes by which core expertise and skills develop, and it argues that AI's greatest long-term risk to the workforce may be eroding the career pathways, learning opportunities and sense of purpose through which people develop expertise, confidence and ambition. Rather than handing work to AI, BSI says organisations should assess the value employees bring and redesign jobs so that learning, judgement and progression are preserved.

Kate Field, global head of human and social sustainability at BSI, said the sentiment seems to be to adopt AI or die, but too little thought is being given to the long-term consequences of replacing human talent with AI. She said there are serious questions about what working alongside AI means for people's psychological safety and wellbeing at work, and about the repercussions of decisions that could corrode skills development or reduce opportunities for collaboration and creativity. BSI warns that automation could worsen youth unemployment, saying that while AI is far from the sole cause, there are fears it is poised to exacerbate an already significant challenge with consequences that will reverberate for generations. The standards body says policymakers face pressure to ensure education and training keep pace with a labour market being reshaped by AI, and that if this happens, new workers will be valuable to employers because they will be able to adapt as AI transforms requirements.

Articles.Title: Half of employers say AI is reducing entry-level opportunities - Computing UK

stories.Headline: Abhijit Bhaduri and Karen Blake urge employers to audit AI hiring tools for bias and keep human oversight
stories.Summary:
AI recruitment tools can process applications quickly, but systems trained on historical hiring data may repeat existing biases and reject candidates with unconventional experience, Computing UK reported on 17 November 2026. The article said the increasing use of artificial intelligence in recruitment has made candidates feel their own true voice is unacceptable. It said applications are tweaked to make them more machine-parsable and chatbots are deployed to craft "more professional" CVs. It said the result is that all applications start to look alike, each written in slick, bland corporatese. It said the majority will be rejected automatically, without a human being as much as glancing at them.

The article said employers should combine automation with human intervention, examine rejected applications, track outcomes across demographic groups and scrutinise training data before procuring hiring technology. It said keyword filters may misinterpret career gaps, caring responsibilities and informal business experience. It said employers should audit rejected candidates and measure progression through each recruitment stage. It said IT and HR leaders should examine training data, bias controls and human-oversight provisions before buying recruitment software. It said these steps should be taken at the procurement stage if possible.

Abhijit Bhaduri, a former Microsoft general manager for global learning and development and author of the forthcoming AIdentity, said "It's a very, very poor system." He said automated systems cannot judge what really makes people tick, nor can they predict how they will perform as part of a team. He said "I think it's absolutely stupid to outsource the best part about building a really unique combination of people and to do it through machines. It's a tragedy." He said HR AI systems can be efficient for sorting but can be used the wrong way, optimising what can be measured rather than what makes an individual valuable. He said organisations need to stop confusing efficiency with effective hiring.

Karen Blake, head of the Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion in Science and Health coalition and a member of the Women in Tech Taskforce at the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, said automated tools have introduced a distance between candidate and hirer. She said many talented people are being screened out, often without feedback and sometimes within hours of applying, while organisations become increasingly indecisive with roles left open for months. She said someone who spent three years caring for a parent with dementia has learned patience and judgement, and someone who helped run the family shop as a teenager probably understands margins and customers better than most graduates. She said biases built unwittingly into automated systems particularly disadvantage returners, women, neurodivergent candidates, older workers and those with unconventional career paths. She said "These systems process applications in huge numbers, so a single flaw gets repeated thousands of times and ends up deciding who is treated as a candidate at all."

The article said the recruitment playing field has never been level, and those who went to the right school or have been coached in professional-sounding corporate language have always had an advantage. It said the mass standardisation of speech patterns by LLMs has created a new norm that "feeds recruitment's oldest habit of hiring the safe bet," Blake asserted. It said the promise that AI will reduce headcount is already threatening the first rung of the career ladder in several professions. It said Bhaduri believes future jobs will arise at the intersections between existing disciplines, and that hunar, "the irreducible human signature formed by lived experience, judgment, taste, memory, victory, failure, culture, instinct and practice," cannot be replicated by AI. It said Bhaduri suggests choosing three candidates from an automated system but seven from a different system where somebody who doesn't fit the mould can come in.

The article said Blake advises focusing on being curious rather than looking impressive, and that your network matters far more than your followers. It said Bhaduri insists developing hunar means avoiding becoming over-reliant on chatbots, starting with the human first. It said overuse of chatbots risks reducing an individual's distinctiveness towards a common denominator and has a deleterious effect on memory and sense-building. It said Blake states "AI tools are often trained on your past hiring and can only find people who look like your past, and your past is rarely what your future needs." It said recruitment tools are often bought for reasons of speed and cost, but procurers should also scrutinise the training data and measures used to reduce bias.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI has broken recruitment. Here’s how employers can fix it - Computing UK

stories.Headline: Harvey Nash lets non-IT staff build AI tools under guardrails, CIO Ankur Anand says
stories.Summary:
Harvey Nash has spent several months running an approach it calls Citizen AI, in which employees outside the IT department build their own AI tools, agents and prototypes inside clear guardrails, according to Group CIO Ankur Anand, who described the work in a case study published by Computing UK on 17 November 2026. The company says the method joins a growing group of businesses taking the same route, and it treats the effort as much as a way to build a culture of innovation as a technology programme. Anand said the aim is to put AI into the hands of the people who best understand Harvey Nash's clients, processes and business problems, and to let them experiment within defined limits. The article gives one worked example, in which a content manager built a content agent that lets recruitment consultants find approved posts and assets, personalise them to their role and tone, and publish them to their social channels.

The approach changes how ideas become systems at the firm. Anand said that turning an idea into a technology solution once required specialist skills, funding and space on a development roadmap, and that AI now lowers that barrier so people can test whether an idea solves a real problem before the organisation commits significant resources. The goal is not to create hundreds of unofficial production systems but to support experimentation, after which Technology takes a proven concept and makes it enterprise-ready by addressing architecture, security, data protection, integration, testing, resilience, support and ownership. Harvey Nash uses Microsoft Copilot as its approved general-purpose enterprise AI environment, and its policy requires other AI applications used for company business to be approved by Group Technology, with specific protection for company, client, candidate, supplier and personal information. The company separates general AI use, agent creation and more advanced capabilities so that access reflects what someone is trying to achieve, and it distinguishes simple agents business users can build themselves from complex ones involving integrations that need technology team support.

Anand said guardrails are essential but should not make experimentation so difficult that innovation stops, and he set out expectations around an approved environment, controls on sensitive information and appropriate human judgement. He said the most important capability for an AI citizen is not necessarily coding but understanding a problem well enough to describe it, knowing its context and data, and judging whether the result is useful, and that people still need AI literacy to understand data sensitivity, test outputs and know when human accountability is essential. He said anyone who uses AI owns the work that comes out of it, so a person who sends an AI output in a client proposal, candidate email or board paper is accountable rather than the tool, and he said managers must make clear what data can and cannot go into an AI tool and give people time to learn. Every agent that moves beyond personal use needs a named owner who answers for what it does, what data it touches and whether it still does its job, with owners reviewing access as roles change and switching off agents that are no longer used or safe. Anand also flagged cost as an easily overlooked guardrail, saying agentic AI increasingly has consumption-based economics, so Harvey Nash monitors usage rather than treating AI as unlimited computing.

Anand described IT's role as changing, saying his team does not need to originate every innovation or build every prototype but should create an environment where innovation can emerge safely, identify the proof points that matter and turn the strongest ideas into secure, resilient enterprise capabilities. He said Citizen AI is about dramatically increasing the number of experiments an organisation can run, giving people at the coalface the freedom and guardrails to turn ideas into proven concepts, with Technology stepping in to scale an idea once it shows real value. The article does not say what results Harvey Nash has measured beyond the ability to count posts created through the content agent, which includes a gamification element to encourage usage. It also does not say what happens next beyond the stated plan of moving proven ideas into enterprise-ready systems.

stories.Headline: Liquid AI releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra decision models that accept text, images and audio
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI released two new decision models, d1.2 and d1.2-ultra, on November 17, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. A decision model does not write text, because it returns calibrated probabilities over a fixed set of answers instead. The d1.2 family now accepts text, images and audio, and it adds five new answer types. The d1.2-ultra model scores 75 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, which is the top score among decision models on that index.

The models run only on the hosted Liquid API, and no weights are available yet, though Liquid AI says it will open them at some point. Parameter sizes are not disclosed, and the models take up to 65,536 input tokens per question and 128 questions per call. The d1.2 model scores 69 on the same index, and Liquid AI reports a 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 benchmarks in its own test. The new answer types cover reading a value, finding every span, locating objects, estimating a number with a range, and picking every option that applies. Audio can be the subject of a question or the question itself, the API takes 16-bit PCM WAV at 10 tokens per second, and both models answer 95% to 97% of questions correctly on held-out ESC-50 and FLEURS recordings.

The index combines six evaluations, with AA-Paperclip carrying 30% of the weight, four others carrying 15% each and When2Call carrying 10%, and its Decision Score penalizes confident wrong answers. On the chart shared by Liquid AI, Drex Max v1.1, SubQ Snap 1.2 and GLiDE v1.2 follow at 73, and d1.2 at 69 is 2 points below the deprecated d1-ultra at 71. Liquid AI argues that no model scores higher than d1.2 for less money, and it says d1.2 is faster and costs less than half as much as d1.2-ultra. The earlier d1, d1.1 and d1-ultra models are now deprecated and do not support audio or the new tasks. The calibration figures come from Liquid AI's own test on held-out splits of public datasets, and no public benchmark exists yet.

Articles.Title: Liquid AI Releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra: Omnimodal Decision Models That Top the AA Decision Index

stories.Headline: NVIDIA releases NVKE and NVKR as open-source projects for managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released two open-source projects, the NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and the NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), for running managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure, and both were recently announced as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. NVKE serves as the control plane for a managed Kubernetes service, while NVKR builds the OS images, container images and packages that those clusters depend on. Both projects ship under the Apache 2.0 license and are currently in public preview. NVKE is written in Go, uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API, and has no runtime dependency on NVKR.

A local evaluation of NVKE needs 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of RAM and 100 GiB of disk with no GPU, while a full footprint calls for 3 CPU servers for the management cluster, 3 CPU servers per workload control plane and a pool of GPU worker nodes. The software runs on your own NVIDIA GPU bare-metal servers provisioned through NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo), and node images build for both amd64 and arm64. No throughput or provisioning-time benchmarks are published, and the quality signal is certification rather than speed, with conformance testing on Kubernetes 1.36. After install, the NVKE API serves plain HTTP on port 30080 with authentication off, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup procedure.

NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions that produces executables, container images, Helm charts and node images, and its Recipes define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. Hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references, and NVKR can also build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. A node must present an attested SPIFFE identity before it gets join credentials, and the README says SPIRE uses TPM for this, while per-cluster etcd encryption is available. An OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart exports logs, metrics and traces over OTLP, and three companion projects plug into workload clusters: AI Cluster Runtime for the GPU runtime, NodeWright for node packages and NVSentinel for break-fix automation.

The repo describes NVKE as a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters rather than a distribution, and it exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster. Customers get standard clusters and use kubectl, while the operator manages them through the NVKE API or the nvkectl CLI. Bootstrap begins when nvkectl bootstrap site starts a temporary single-node kind cluster on a bootstrap host, after which NVKE requests 3 servers from NICo, which boots them from the node image before the temporary cluster is deleted. Compared with Gardener from SAP and Kamaji from Clastix, NVKE uses a dedicated control plane per cluster with its own etcd and node pools, and the articles give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao sets out a framework for AI data retention
stories.Summary:
A November 13, 2026 post on X by Fireworks AI cofounder and CEO Lin Qiao set out a framework for understanding AI data retention, and MarkTechPost explained it on November 17, 2026 by describing two standard API designs that decide where control of the data lifecycle sits. In the first design, a customer uploads a file or dataset, runs jobs against it, and then deletes it, with the platform keeping the data stored and available until deletion is requested. In the second design, a customer sends data, the platform computes and returns a result, and no application state stays behind, which is the pattern called zero data retention. The article says data retention has become one of the most misunderstood terms in AI infrastructure, and that after a wave of AI security headlines many development teams now ask whether their AI provider keeps their data.

The article describes zero data retention as a per-endpoint commitment not to persist covered prompts and outputs after an eligible request, with eligibility depending on the endpoint, request flags and account settings rather than the vendor name. It says stored features such as batch, file and dataset features keep data until it is deleted or expires, and it advises preferring ephemeral endpoints because deletion is the customer's job after an upload. Among the examples it gives, OpenAI Batch requires uploading a JSONL input file and then creating the batch, Amazon Bedrock batch inference keeps input JSONL files in an S3 location the customer chooses, the Gemini Batch API runs jobs from an input file the customer provides, and Fireworks AI Batch requires creating a dataset and then submitting jobs against it. The article says OpenAI batch files last 30 days by default and Anthropic batch data 29 days, that OpenAI non-batch files persist until deleted, and that Fireworks AI managed training datasets have no time limit and are deleted by the customer, while Amazon Bedrock and Google batch jobs read and write the customer's own cloud storage.

On the ephemeral side, the article lists OpenAI Chat Completions, where store defaults to false, Amazon Bedrock Converse, where content is only used to generate the response, and Google Gemini text generation, which is stateless when store is false. It also lists Fireworks AI Chat Completions, direct or through Nexus, whose schema has no store field, and the Fireworks AI Training SDK including Serverless Training, where forward_backward sends tokenized batches per call, no dataset is uploaded, and training data is not stored at rest. The article says a synchronous response alone does not establish zero data retention, and it cites OpenAI's data controls as describing two layers, application state that a feature must keep, such as uploaded files, and abuse-monitoring logs held for safety review, noting that a platform can be at zero on one layer and not the other. According to the article, Qiao said Fireworks AI keeps nothing after a deletion request, and the article adds that the same split has shaped data processing systems for decades.

Articles.Title: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained

stories.headline_source: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained

stories.Headline: Perplexity adds Multiagent feature to allow up to 16 AI agents to cross-check complex tasks
stories.Summary:
Perplexity added a feature called Multiagent to its Computer research platform on November 17, 2026. This new system allows a lead agent to manage a team of up to 16 supporting agents to complete complex tasks. These agents work in parallel, share findings directly with one another, and cross-check each other's work. The lead agent plans the overall task, assigns specific parts to the team, and merges all findings into one final response for the user.

This update introduces the highest effort level available, sitting above the Ultra setting. It requires a Perplexity Max plan, which costs 167 dollars per month when billed annually, and is available only on the web. The default team utilizes three model families, specifically Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon. Users can name specific models in their queries, and the system allows agents to coordinate edits within shared files.

Perplexity stated that this tool is designed for large, interconnected work such as annual report reviews and year-end tax preparation. The company explained that the lead agent acts as the single point of contact for the user while coordinating the supporting agents. This builds upon effort controls launched on September 17, 2026, which previously offered Light, Standard, High, and Ultra settings. The company positions this diversity of models as a key difference from competitors like Kimi and Grok.

stories.Headline: UNESCO publishes a teaching guide to help educators teach critical thinking about AI-generated information
stories.Summary:
UNESCO published a teaching guide on 17 November 2026 to help educators prepare learners to question AI-generated information and understand how automated systems shape what people encounter online. The publication, titled AI Answers. You Decide. ,  Teaching Media and Information Literacy in AI-Mediated Information Environments, offers discussion questions, activities and examples for educators, teacher-training institutions and curriculum developers. It extends UNESCO's existing media and information literacy curriculum to address an information environment increasingly influenced by AI. The guide addresses the reliability and authenticity of AI-generated content alongside questions about the systems, interests and data behind it.

The guide's scope includes convincing synthetic text, images, audio and video, as well as the algorithms that influence which information people see. Five connected areas organize the material: AI in everyday life, AI and the media, AI, the human mind and knowledge, AI, power and human rights, and AI and the future. The knowledge strand focuses on critical thinking, informed trust and evaluating AI-generated information, while the media strand examines changes to journalism, content creation and access to information. Questions about power and human rights bring algorithmic bias, inequality and sustainability into the curriculum, and the future-focused material encourages learners to participate in shaping inclusive, human-centered approaches to AI.

The publication is a companion to UNESCO's Media and Information Literate Citizens: Think Critically, Click Wisely! curriculum, launched in 2021 and subsequently piloted and adapted in more than 40 countries. The new guide was developed with eight international experts and peer-reviewed by ten additional specialists. Mariya Gabriel, Assistant-Director General for Communication and Information at UNESCO, said artificial intelligence is transforming how people learn, communicate and access information, and that people must retain the ability to think critically, question what they see and make informed choices. Anne Leppäjärvi, who authored the guide, said AI does not change the foundations of media and information literacy but the environment in which they are applied, and that the goal is to equip learners with critical thinking skills rather than keep up with every technological change.

Educators can adapt the guide's conceptual explanations, discussion questions, practical activities and examples to their own educational settings. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that, and they give no further dates or plans for the guide's rollout.

Articles.Title: UNESCO releases AI media literacy teaching guide to strengthen critical thinking - EdTech Innovation Hub

stories.Headline: Mercor raises $750m Series D at $20bn valuation as annualised revenue passes $2bn
stories.Summary:
Mercor, a San Francisco company that pays doctors, lawyers, bankers and engineers to teach AI models how real work is done, announced in November 2026 a US$750m Series D at a US$20bn valuation, after its annualised revenue passed US$2bn in June 2026, up from US$1m two years earlier. The company was founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody, who is CEO, Adarsh Hiremath, who is Co-CEO, and Surya Midha, as an AI recruiting marketplace, and it found its market when AI labs needed experts rather than crowdworkers to write tasks, grade model responses and build verifiers for post-training. Its network counts more than five million domain experts, and it was paying out more than US$2m a day by March 2026, with contractors typically keeping 60% to 70% of gross billings. The Information reported US$614m in gross revenue for the first half of 2026, up 70% from the year before, and the company has more than 700 full-time employees as of November 2026.

Felicis led a US$350m Series C at a US$10bn valuation in October 2025, and investors in the Series D include Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, funds managed by affiliates of Apollo, G Squared, General Catalyst, Glade Brook Capital, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group, XTX Ventures and Zoom. Mercor says it works with all of the top five AI labs and six of the Magnificent Seven tech companies, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta named in reports, and it is pushing into enterprises. In July 2026 it agreed to acquire Deeptune, an a16z-backed start-up backed by a US$43m Series A that has recreated hundreds of enterprise apps, including Salesforce, as environments, and whose team is joining Mercor's New York office. Its APEX benchmarks measure AI on economically valuable work, and in October 2026 AI outperformed 12 licensed CPAs on APEX-Accounting; Mercor also post-trained a 397bn-parameter open model with SkyRL, built at UC Berkeley with Anyscale, lifting its APEX-Agents score by 70% in relative terms, and released datasets and traces on Hugging Face.

Foody said every job in the economy will need its own AI agents and every company will need a way to train and evaluate them on its own work, adding that Mercor spent the last two years building that infrastructure with the frontier labs and is now bringing it to enterprises. Hiremath said every company deploying AI needs to know whether it works and the answer is different for each one, because a model can score well on a public benchmark and still fail on the systems, policies and edge cases that define how a specific business runs, so Mercor builds custom benchmarks with each enterprise and uses them as the starting point for post-training. The company's setbacks have been real: a late March 2026 supply-chain breach led Meta to pause all its work with Mercor while it investigated the security breach, according to WIRED.

The next product is the training environment, a simulated workplace where an agent can practise a task and be scored, and Mercor said in a post on X that training AI to do real professional work requires covering the full distribution of apps, worlds and tasks across the economy, noting that Deeptune built the apps for the leading AI labs. Mercor's technology partners include Cognition, which co-launched the APEX-SWE software engineering benchmark with Mercor, Anyscale, Hugging Face, which hosts the datasets, model weights and evaluation traces released in September 2026, Modal, whose cloud infrastructure runs sandboxed agent trials, and Daytona, which provides sandboxed environments for agent training runs. The firm appears to have recovered from the breach and is pushing from frontier labs to enterprises.

Articles.Title: Mercor: How the AI Training Firm Hit a US$20bn Valuation - AI Magazine

stories.Headline: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Ads to 44 countries through exclusive reseller Aleph
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 12, 2026, that it is expanding the market presence of ChatGPT Ads across 44 different countries. The company selected Aleph to serve as the exclusive reseller to provide local invoicing and in-person support for brands and agencies. This new arrangement allows advertisers in these specific regions to contract and pay for services through a local entity. These businesses can now access local market expertise and training while utilizing the advertising platform.

The expansion covers 14 Latin American nations, including Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Puerto Rico, and Uruguay. In Europe and Central Asia, the 16 participating countries are Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan. The Middle East and Africa include 10 nations, specifically Egypt, Kenya, Kuwait, Morocco, Nigeria, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates. This change does not affect the ability of global advertisers to target any country where the ads are available.

OpenAI stated that over one hundred thousand marketers have already used the platform, which has seen significant progress over ten months. The company explained that this announcement simply provides additional local ways for businesses to purchase advertising space. They mentioned a continued focus on broadening access to AI and protecting user trust while developing new measurement solutions. The organization intends to create more optimization tools and new formats as they build the full potential of the system.

The company noted that ChatGPT Ads are not available in mainland China or Hong Kong because the models are not available there. However, businesses based in those two markets may still advertise to users in other available regions through authorized partners. Advertisers can still choose to buy ads directly through the Ads Manager or via global technology partners. OpenAI will continue to improve the platform based on feedback from the businesses and people using the service.

stories.Headline: Revolut deploys ChatGPT and Codex to cut coding time and automate financial crime screening
stories.Summary:
Revolut has adopted OpenAI's ChatGPT, API and Codex across its global operations, OpenAI reported on November 16, 2026, in a customer story titled "How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar." Revolut was built to challenge the way people interact with money, and that ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets and 800,000 businesses. Its consumer base has grown by 23% in the last 12 months, according to the article. One of Revolut's largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models, which examines information, applies Revolut's rules and completes the defined process automatically. The release of GPT-5.5 was a turning point, when the models became capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent.

Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, from task start to feature merge, according to AI Lead David Abitbol. One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents. Revolut used one day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context. More transactions are screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one. Revolut also developed a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Abitbol said Revolut has a systematic framework so anyone building with AI follows the same standards across development, A/B testing and business metric prediction, holding every engineer to the same quality standard. He said the biggest problem AI can tackle today is the scaling of humans versus the demand Revolut gets. Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri said the result translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system customers can trust. Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik said he realised he did not need a whole team of developers and could launch different agents and assign each a particular task. Pitik also said every developer is responsible for the code they produce and that they do not blindly trust AI.

Amiri said the most critical decision is always about accountability, and that if an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand it well enough to stand by it. He said you earn real confidence in AI by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go. Global Head of Business Marketing Kim Maniovich said partnering with OpenAI enables Revolut to build solutions in a way that is lean, cost-efficient and tailored to how the company works. Maniovich said the average Revolut employee has three different jobs, and that month on month the targets get more aggressive but also more attainable. Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov said Revolut can shift focus from things that are important but hard to do without AI to things that matter for customers.

According to one report cited in the article, over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025. For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement protections for customers. The volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank. In a phishing investigation, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. Amiri said that with stronger AI tools, those connections can be uncovered instantly and investigators can dig deeper into the questions that really matter.

Abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks such as blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience, turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use. Maniovich said she hopes Revolut can take the values it operates by every day, its unapologetic ambition and desire to never settle, and enable people to apply them to their own lives through the products it builds. The article says Revolut's next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money. The article does not say when any of these future products will launch.

Articles.Title: How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Sales with over 30 partner plugins
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Sales on November 17, 2026, according to a post on openai.com dated that day. The product is a new Sales experience built around a Sales plugin from OpenAI with dedicated skills for sellers. It also includes more than 30 new and enhanced partner plugins inside ChatGPT. OpenAI said the aim is to help every sales team understand customers better, spend less time on busywork and close more deals. The post said the tools let teams use information from the tools they already rely on to prepare for calls, tailor proposals and follow up faster.

The Sales plugin gives ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up. Partner plugins named in the post include Confluence, Guru and Seismic for learning sales processes and product updates, and ChatGPT Voice for rehearsing pitches and handling objections. Content tools named include ChatGPT Slides, Gamma, Figma and Canva, plus ChatGPT Sites for interactive demos or ROI calculators. Account tools named include Salesforce, HubSpot, Close CRM and monday CRM, and buyer-finding tools named include Apollo, Clay and Common Room, with Outreach and Salesloft for planning outreach. Call-note tools named include the Meetings plugin in ChatGPT, Gong, Otter.ai and Granola, Backstory is named for spotting deal risk, the Data plugin and Hex for analyzing sales data, and Docusign, Ironclad, PandaDoc and ServiceNow CPQ for quotes and agreements.

OpenAI said sellers can delegate work to their dot, an always-on agent in ChatGPT that can use the same plugins and customer context to prepare meeting briefs, track deal updates and bring relevant changes and proposed next steps for review. Sandeep Chellani, SVP and Head of Technology at The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, said the Salesforce Plugin for ChatGPT lets relationship builders uncover deeper insights about donor prospects and research partners and reduces the time and effort to gather and synthesize that information. Prof. Dr. Gunnar Gombert, Co-Founder and Managing Director of NeoBid, said the company uses HubSpot with ChatGPT for Sales to research real estate prospects, enrich CRM data, prioritize opportunities and prepare personalized outreach. Gombert estimated this reduces manual effort for these activities by around 65%, giving more time to help clients optimize energy procurement across their property portfolios. Sushanth Raman, CEO of Pallet, said ChatGPT for Sales and Rox are central to how the company operates and scales, and that Rox gives a clear view of the pipeline and surfaces deal risks early.

JR Harrell, EVP, Business Execution at Datasite, said Atlassian provides the connective tissue that allows OpenAI's frontier models to reason across the entire enterprise, and that grounding ChatGPT for Sales in the Teamwork Graph has democratized data. Jacob Tuwiner, Founder at Sculpted, said that in GTM the winners ship their best ideas before their competition, and that building in Clay for years meant clicking through menu after menu. Tuwiner said anyone can now use ChatGPT for Sales and Clay to ship a play in minutes that used to take an expert hours, days or weeks, and that Workflows shows every step instead of a giant table while Audiences takes the same play to a whole enterprise market. The post said availability of partner plugins and features varies by plan, region and workspace settings. It said ChatGPT Business and Enterprise admins can enable ChatGPT for Sales by opening the Admin Console, selecting their workspace and selecting Plugins, then making the Sales plugin and relevant partner plugins available for members to install or installing them by default.

The post said admins should review access to the required apps and the actions they can use, and that workspace members can complete any required account connections when prompted. It said OpenAI is continuing to build ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugin ecosystem around the work sales teams do every day. OpenAI said its goal is to bring more of that work into ChatGPT, with connected tools and customer context that carries from finding an opportunity to preparing for a conversation and following through. The post listed related OpenAI announcements, including dots on September 29, 2026, the Admin plugin for ChatGPT Work and Codex on August 25, 2026, and an expanded Oracle partnership on October 27, 2026. The post said people can install the Sales plugin to get started and learn more about ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugins.

The post did not give prices for ChatGPT for Sales or say which plans, regions or workspace settings include which partner plugins. It did not say when the more than 30 partner plugins became available or list all of them by name. It did not give a date for the next update to ChatGPT for Sales or say what that update will add. It did not say how many teams or sellers use the product. It did not give figures for time saved beyond NeoBid's estimate of around 65% less manual effort.
